You won't say 'Geschenk zu' alone — learn the full pattern: 'jemandem ein Geschenk + zu + Infinitiv' or simply 'jemandem ein Geschenk bringen/geben/kaufen' without 'zu' when using a finite verb. Useful verbs that follow: kaufen (to buy), bringen (to bring), machen (to make), bedanken (sich bedanken für das Geschenk — to thank for the gift).
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, meiner Schwester ein Geschenk zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I plan to buy my sister a gift.

meaning: a (short) story/tale 'about' or 'involving' someone/something (used to introduce what the story is about).
additional_notes: Literally 'story with'. Commonly used to say 'the story about/with X' or to introduce a story you will share. Can refer to a specific anecdote known to listeners (Die Geschichte mit dem Tuch) or to any tale you tell. Follows the noun phrase that names the person/thing involved (Geschichte mit der Maus).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine lustige Geschichte mit meinem Nachbarn.
native_language_example: I have a funny story about my neighbor.

meaning: "the story already" — used to say someone has heard/known a story before.
additional_notes: Geschichte means "story" or "tale"; schon means "already". Together they appear in sentences like "Hast du diese Geschichte schon gehört?" (= Have you already heard this story?). In German word order varies: schon often comes after the object or near the verb. Useful for asking if someone has heard something before or stating prior knowledge.
target_language_example: Hast du die Geschichte schon gehört?
native_language_example: Have you already heard the story?

meaning: "Geschichte" = story; "sehr" = very — together they appear as 'a story that is very ...' or 'I liked the story very much.'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase. It shows the noun Geschichte (story, tale, history) used with the adverb sehr (very). In the examples sehr can modify a verb phrase (Mir hat ... sehr gefallen = I liked ... very much) or an adjective describing Geschichte (sehr unwahrscheinlich = very unlikely / sehr ernst = very serious). Word order in German places sehr before the adjective or after the verb phrase it modifies. Use 'Mir hat deine Geschichte sehr gefallen' to say 'I really liked your story.'
target_language_example: Mir hat seine Geschichte sehr gefallen.
native_language_example: I really liked his story.

meaning: lit. 'story/history will' — part of sentences where 'wird' is the verb 'will/is going to' or passive auxiliary referring to 'Geschichte' (the story/the history).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase. 'Geschichte' means 'story' or 'history'. 'wird' is the 3rd-person singular of 'werden' and can form the future tense ('will') or the passive voice ('is/are ...-ed' or 'will be ...'). Look at context to decide: e.g. 'Die Geschichte wird euch gefallen.' uses future ('will please you'); 'Die Geschichte wird über uns richten.' uses future/passive sense ('will judge us'); 'wird veröffentlicht' would be passive ('will be published').
target_language_example: Die Geschichte wird morgen veröffentlicht.
native_language_example: The story will be published tomorrow.

meaning: literally 'business and' — part of compound phrases or coordination with 'und' (and); not a fixed phrase by itself.
additional_notes: This appears to be the word 'Geschäft' ('business; shop; deal') followed by the conjunction 'und' ('and'). On its own 'Geschäft und' is incomplete; you will usually see 'Geschäft' in different senses: a shop (store), a business/company, a deal/transaction, or the idiom 'Geschäft und Vergnügen' (business and pleasure). Context decides the meaning. When learning, treat 'Geschäft' as the key word and remember to add what follows 'und' to complete the phrase.
target_language_example: Er hat sein Geschäft und seine Familie unter einen Hut gebracht.
native_language_example: He balanced his business and his family.

meaning: "the law is" (a short phrase used to state something about a law or to emphasize that a rule must be followed)
additional_notes: Gesetz ist is simply the phrase 'Gesetz' (law) + the verb 'ist' (is). It's used to describe or judge a law (e.g., its status, fairness) or in the fixed expression 'Gesetz ist Gesetz' meaning 'the law is the law' (i.e., rules must be obeyed). Useful for talking about whether a law is in force, fair, or binding.
target_language_example: Dieses Gesetz ist seit letztem Jahr in Kraft.
native_language_example: This law has been in force since last year.

meaning: 'face and' — the word 'Gesicht' (face) followed by 'und' (and); used when listing 'face and ...' (e.g. face and hands, face and name).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — simply the noun 'Gesicht' (face) plus the coordinating conjunction 'und' (and). Appears in phrases where two items are listed (e.g. Gesicht und Hände = face and hands). Pay attention to word order and articles: in full phrases you will usually hear 'das Gesicht und die Hände' or 'ein Gesicht und einen Namen'.
target_language_example: Wasch dir das Gesicht und die Hände!
native_language_example: Wash your face and your hands!

meaning: to show one's face; to appear or make an appearance (often after being absent or avoiding someone)
additional_notes: Used when someone turns up somewhere after a period of absence or has the courage to appear. Can be neutral or slightly critical or surprised (e.g. "Er hat sich lange nicht blicken lassen — jetzt zeigt er plötzlich Gesicht"). Often used with verbs like 'zeigen' or 'sich zeigen'.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit wollte er nicht kommen, aber gestern hat er endlich Gesicht gezeigt.
native_language_example: After the argument he didn't want to come, but yesterday he finally showed his face.

meaning: 'health is...' — the start of proverbs or statements valuing health.
additional_notes: Used to introduce general statements about the importance or value of health (e.g. 'Gesundheit ist wichtig'). Often followed by adjectives, nouns or comparisons (wichtiger, alles, das größte Geschenk, mehr wert als ...). Common in everyday and formal speech; not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: Gesundheit ist wichtiger als Geld.
native_language_example: Health is more important than money.

meaning: part of the verb phrase 'Gitarre spielen' (to play the guitar); 'Gitarre zu' on its own is not a complete expression — it's the noun 'Gitarre' plus the infinitive marker 'zu' used in constructions like 'zu Gitarre spielen' (rare) or more commonly appears in sentences with 'Gitarre spielen' (to play the guitar).
additional_notes: Beginners should learn the common expression 'Gitarre spielen' (to play the guitar). German often forms infinitive phrases with 'zu' (e.g. 'lernen, Gitarre zu spielen' = 'to learn to play the guitar'). In natural speech you will usually see 'Gitarre spielen' or constructions like 'lernen, Gitarre zu spielen' or 'beginnen, Gitarre zu spielen'. 'Gitarre zu' by itself is not used as a fixed phrase.
target_language_example: Ich habe gelernt, Gitarre zu spielen.
native_language_example: I learned to play the guitar.

meaning: to bring good luck; to cause someone to have luck.
additional_notes: Used to wish or say that something will produce good luck for someone. Common in greetings and well-wishes (e.g., for the new year). Often appears with verbs like "wird" or wishes using "möge". Can be used with formal (Ihnen) or informal (dir) address.
target_language_example: Möge dieses Geschenk dir Glück bringen.
native_language_example: May this gift bring you luck.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say someone experienced good fortune or avoided bad outcomes. Often used in past or present tense: (Ich) habe Glück gehabt = I was lucky / I had luck. Can be used in statements like 'Du hast Glück' or with other verbs: 'Wir hatten Glück' = 'We were lucky.'
target_language_example: Du hast heute Glück gehabt, dass das Restaurant nicht voll war.
native_language_example: You were lucky today that the restaurant wasn't full.

meaning: ‘Happiness/fortune is…’ — a phrase used to define or describe what happiness or luck is.
additional_notes: Glück can mean both 'happiness' and 'good luck/fortune' depending on context. 'Glück ist' often begins a sentence that defines, describes or comments on the nature of happiness/fortune. The verb following may vary (e.g. nouns, clauses, or comparisons). Useful for expressing opinions or asking about what happiness means.
target_language_example: Glück ist, mit Menschen zusammen zu sein, die einen verstehen.
native_language_example: Happiness is being with people who understand you.

meaning: 'luck with' / 'to be lucky with' (having good or bad fortune regarding someone or something)
additional_notes: Used after the noun that you have luck with. Common structure: 'Glück mit + Dativ' (e.g. 'Glück mit dem Wetter', 'Glück mit ihm'). Can express having had good luck or lack of luck. In English often translated as 'to be lucky with' or 'to have (no) luck with'.
target_language_example: Wir hatten nie Glück mit Männern.
native_language_example: We never had any luck with men.

meaning: 'luck and' — used to link 'luck' with another noun or to introduce a positive outcome (often followed by another word or a verb).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of fixed phrases (e.g. 'Glück und Pech', 'Glück und Frieden') or before a verb to say someone experienced a fortunate event ('Er hatte Glück und ...'). In greetings (wishes) it pairs 'Glück' with another good thing. Not a complete phrase by itself—expect a second element after 'und'.
target_language_example: Ich hatte Glück und bekam die Stelle.
native_language_example: I was lucky and got the job.

meaning: Gold is (…).
additional_notes: Simple present construction: noun + 'ist' (third-person singular of 'sein') to state a fact about gold. You can replace 'Gold' with any noun to make similar factual statements (e.g., 'Wasser ist...', 'Eisen ist...'). Useful for comparisons and general facts.
target_language_example: Gold ist selten und begehrt.
native_language_example: Gold is rare and sought after.

meaning: An exclamation starting with 'Gott' (God) to express strong emotion about what follows (surprise, frustration, fear, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase with a single meaning; it's simply beginning an exclamation with 'Gott' or 'Oh Gott' followed by a clause about oneself (ich...). Common in spoken German to intensify feelings. Tone can be informal or neutral depending on context; be aware this invokes a religious word but is often used idiomatically like English 'Oh God' or 'God, I...'.
target_language_example: Oh Gott, ich habe den Zug verpasst!
native_language_example: Oh God, I missed the train!

meaning: Not a fixed idiom — the noun 'Gott' (God) followed by the accusative pronoun 'mich' (me). Depending on context and word order, the two words can appear together in exclamations, subordinate clauses, or elliptical colloquial speech (e.g., 'damit Gott mich segne', 'Weil Gott mich hasst'). On its own 'Gott mich' is uncommon in neutral modern prose and often requires surrounding words (verbs, conjunctions) to be grammatical.
additional_notes: This sequence is compositional rather than idiomatic. Standalone occurrences like 'Gott mich' are typically fragments, poetic, archaic, or colloquial; they usually form part of a larger clause (e.g., verb before/after). Watch case and word order: 'mich' is accusative and requires a transitive verb or construction that governs the accusative. Examples provided are useful to see how the pair appears in context.
target_language_example: Er betete, damit Gott mich segne.
native_language_example: He prayed so that God would bless me.

meaning: Thank God; fortunately.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to show relief or gratitude about something positive or avoided trouble. Common in spoken and written German. Can start a sentence or be inserted mid-sentence. Similar use to English 'thank goodness' or 'thank God'. Not literal religious speech in many contexts — often just an exclamation.
target_language_example: Gott sei Dank hat der Bus Verspätung — ich komme noch rechtzeitig.
native_language_example: Thank God the bus was late — I'll still arrive on time.

meaning: literally 'God and' — this is the start of a phrase or exclamation where 'Gott' (God) is joined with another noun or idea (e.g. 'Gott und Vaterland'); not a fixed idiom on its own.
additional_notes: By itself 'Gott und' is not a complete phrase; it appears as the beginning of compound expressions (Gott und Vaterland, Gott und Teufel) or as part of emphatic exclamations. Use it when listing or pairing 'God' with another concept. The exact meaning depends on the second word. It is compositional (you can understand it from the parts) and not informal.
target_language_example: Sie singen: Für Gott und Vaterland!
native_language_example: They sing: For God and fatherland!

meaning: 'God knows' — used to say something is unknown or to emphasize truth of a statement.
additional_notes: Literally 'God knows'. Commonly used like English 'God knows' or 'who knows' to express uncertainty (Gott weiß, warum = God knows why) or to add emphasis/credibility to a confession or statement (Gott weiß, ich war oft genug untreu = God knows I have been unfaithful enough). Can be followed by a clause introduced by was/warum/that-clause. Not necessarily religious — often idiomatic.
target_language_example: Gott weiß, wie das noch enden wird.
native_language_example: God knows how this will end.

meaning: degrees Celsius (unit for temperature)
additional_notes: Used after a number to state a temperature (e.g., 'fünf Grad Celsius' = 5 °C). Commonly abbreviated as '°C' in writing. In spoken German you can also say just 'Grad' when the scale is clear (e.g., 'fünf Grad'), but 'Grad Celsius' is explicit.
target_language_example: Heute sind es zehn Grad Celsius.
native_language_example: Today it is ten degrees Celsius.

meaning: 'the grass is' (simple subject + verb; used to state the color/condition of grass)
additional_notes: A simple present tense phrase: 'Gras' (grass) as subject and 'ist' (is). Often followed by an adjective (e.g. grün, gelb) to describe the grass. Can be used generically ('Gras ist grün' — grass is green) or about specific grass ('Das Gras ist gelb' — the grass is yellow). Helpful for forming basic descriptive sentences in German.
target_language_example: Das Gras ist heute sehr nass.
native_language_example: The grass is very wet today.

meaning: the Great Houses; (important/famous noble houses or powerful families)
additional_notes: Refers to prominent, powerful families or noble houses (often in a historical, fantasy or political context). Capitalization and plural: 'die Großen Häuser' is the nominative plural with adjective strong/declension depending on article. In everyday modern German you might also see 'große Häuser' for 'big houses' (literal size) — here 'Großen' with a capital G and context implies status, not physical size.
target_language_example: Die Großen Häuser haben einen Boten geschickt.
native_language_example: The Great Houses have sent a messenger.

meaning: 'grandmother and' — the word Großmutter (grandmother) followed by the conjunction und (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the noun Großmutter ('grandmother') plus the conjunction und ('and'). In your examples it appears either in a list (Großmutter und Großvater = grandmother and grandfather) or as part of a longer noun phrase (z. B. ‚die Wohnung meiner Großmutter und ihre Pillen‘ = my grandmother's apartment and her pills). Pay attention to possession: ‚meiner Großmutter und ihre Pillen‘ can be ambiguous; more precise German would match case/possessive forms (‚die Wohnung meiner Großmutter und ihre Pillen‘ is understandable colloquially).
target_language_example: Großmutter und Großvater kommen morgen zu Besuch.
native_language_example: Grandmother and grandfather are coming to visit tomorrow.

meaning: reason to (do something); cause for (an emotion or action).
additional_notes: Used with the noun 'Grund' plus a reflexive infinitive clause with 'sich' to indicate someone has (or lacks) reason to feel or act a certain way. Common patterns: 'einen Grund haben, sich zu ...' or 'es gibt keinen Grund, sich zu ...'. Typically followed by reflexive verbs expressing emotions or reactions (sich sorgen, sich fürchten, sich freuen, sich schämen, sich scheiden zu lassen in passive contexts).
target_language_example: Es gibt keinen Grund, sich Sorgen zu machen — also kein Grund, sich zu ängstigen.
native_language_example: There is no reason to worry — so no reason to be afraid.

meaning: reason to / reason for (doing something or believing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or a clause introduced by an infinitive phrase (often followed by an infinitive verb: z. B. 'Grund zu lügen', 'Grund zu bleiben') or with 'zu' + verbless noun phrases ('Grund zu Zweifel'). Often appears in negative: 'keinen Grund zu ...' = 'no reason to ...'. Can also be used with verbs like 'glauben' ('Grund zu glauben').
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Grund zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I have no reason to stay.

meaning: 'Good wishes for' (used in set phrases like 'Alles Gute zum ...' = 'Best wishes for ...').
additional_notes: Usually appears in fixed expressions: 'Alles Gute zum Geburtstag' (Happy birthday), 'Alles Gute zum Jubiläum' (Best wishes on the anniversary). 'Gute' here is part of the phrase 'Alles Gute' (all the best) and 'zum' = 'zu dem' (for the). Use with an occasion (Geburtstag, Jubiläum, Geburtstag, Abschluss, etc.).
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: All the best for your birthday!

meaning: 'hair is' — used to describe someone’s hair (length, color, condition, etc.).
additional_notes: A simple subject-predicate phrase: 'Haar' (hair) + verb 'ist' (is). Common in descriptions: possession is usually marked by possessive pronoun (mein/dein/sein/ihr). Use singular 'Haar' for hair in general (collective). For talking about individual hairs you would use 'ein Haar'.
target_language_example: Ihr Haar ist sehr glänzend.
native_language_example: Her hair is very shiny.

meaning: literally 'hair and' — used to list hair plus another feature (e.g., hair and eye color); sometimes appears when joining 'hair' with another noun in a description.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — it's just the noun Haar ('hair') followed by the conjunction und ('and'). Common in descriptions of people: 'Haar und (Augenfarbe)', e.g. 'blondes Haar und blaue Augen'. Note sentence 5 uses 'ihr Haar und einen Knopf...' where 'Haar und' simply joins two objects of a verb ('öffnete ihr Haar und einen Knopf...'). Pay attention to adjective endings agreeing with Haar (neuter: 'das Haar' → 'blondes Haar', 'langes Haar').
target_language_example: Sie hat langes, braunes Haar und grüne Augen.
native_language_example: She has long brown hair and green eyes.

meaning: get off at (a stop/station).
additional_notes: Used with public transport: 'an der Haltestelle aussteigen' = to get off at a particular stop. In sentences it's usually 'an der nächsten/achte(n) Haltestelle aussteigen' or imperative 'Steigen Sie an der ... aus.' The particle 'aus' is part of the separable verb 'aussteigen' and moves to the end in main clauses.
target_language_example: Steigen Sie an der Haltestelle aus und gehen Sie links.
native_language_example: Get off at the stop and turn left.

meaning: hand on my (usually followed by a body part, e.g. 'Schulter' = shoulder)
additional_notes: This is a fragment: normally part of the phrase 'legte seine Hand auf meine Schulter' (placed his hand on my shoulder). Use with a noun in the accusative (meine + feminine noun like Schulter). Common in descriptions of touch or comforting gestures.
target_language_example: Er legte seine Hand auf meine Schulter.
native_language_example: He placed his hand on my shoulder.

meaning: 'hand out' or 'hand off' in the sense 'take your hand out (of something)' — a short imperative telling someone to remove their hand from something.
additional_notes: Used in spoken German as a concise command (often with accusative object following: e.g. 'Hand aus meiner Tasche!'). Common in informal contexts. In full sentences you might also hear 'Zieh deine Hand aus ...' or 'Hände weg von ...' for similar meanings. The phrase is compositional and literal: 'Hand' = hand, 'aus' = out.
target_language_example: Hand aus der Jackentasche!
native_language_example: Hand out of the jacket pocket!

meaning: hand in hand; together; closely connected or physically holding hands.
additional_notes: Used both literally (people holding hands) and figuratively to say two things are closely linked or should work together. Common fixed expression. Word order stays as shown.
target_language_example: Die Eltern gingen Hand in Hand durch den Park.
native_language_example: The parents walked hand in hand through the park.

meaning: literally 'hand into the' — used as part of a phrase indicating putting a hand into something (needs an object in the dative: den + masculine/neuter noun in dative).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase on its own; it's the beginning of a verb phrase like 'die Hand in den Mantel stecken' (to put the hand into the coat). After 'in' the noun that follows determines the article and case. 'den' here is the accusative masculine singular or dative plural/neuter depending on context, but in the common construction 'in den Mantel' it's accusative (movement into). Beginner learners should pay attention to whether the verb implies movement (accusative) or location (dative) and to the correct article for the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Er steckt die Hand in den Mantel.
native_language_example: He puts his hand into the coat.

meaning: to (hold) one's hand in front of something (e.g. mouth or eyes); used in phrases like 'die Hand vor den Mund/den Augen halten' — to cover or shield with the hand.
additional_notes: Usually appears in fixed phrases: 'die Hand vor den Mund halten' (cover your mouth) and 'die Hand vor die Augen halten' (shield your eyes or can't see because it's so dark/foggy). In reflexive form: 'sich die Hand vor den Mund halten'. Common in instructions (e.g. when coughing) and descriptions (can't see because of fog). Literal meaning is clear from components.
target_language_example: Halte dir die Hand vor den Mund, wenn du hustest.
native_language_example: Hold your hand in front of your mouth when you cough.

meaning: to dry oneself with a towel (literally: towel off).
additional_notes: This is a separable verb construction: 'abtrocknen' (to dry off) combined with 'Handtuch' as the instrument. In sentences the verb appears as 'trocknete ... ab' or imperative 'trockne ... ab'. Common when talking about drying hands, face, body after bathing or swimming. Word order: object ('mit einem Handtuch') can come before or after the verb.
target_language_example: Trockne dich nach dem Schwimmen mit einem Handtuch ab.
native_language_example: Dry yourself off with a towel after swimming.

meaning: the capital of (feminine/genitive or partitive construction).
additional_notes: Used to say the capital city of a country, region or state. 'Hauptstadt' = capital city. 'der' is the feminine/genitive/definite article that agrees with the following noun (e.g. der Ukraine, der Lombardei). When naming a country in nominative (Deutschland) you often say 'die Hauptstadt von Deutschland' instead. You can also use 'Hauptstadt von' + Dative for many cases (e.g. 'die Hauptstadt von Deutschland').
target_language_example: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt der Bundesrepublik Deutschland.
native_language_example: Berlin is the capital of the Federal Republic of Germany.

meaning: used to form a relative clause meaning 'the house in which/that.../where', referring to a specific house
additional_notes: Combines Haus with the preposition in to introduce a relative clause (in dem / in dem + relative pronoun) describing location. In spoken German you can also use 'wo' colloquially: 'das Haus, wo...'. Use appropriate case and gender: 'in dem' contracts to 'im' in simple statements ('im Haus'), but in relative clauses you often keep 'in dem' or 'in dem' → 'in dem' with the relative pronoun (or use 'in dem' = 'in which').
target_language_example: Das ist das Haus, in dem meine Tante wohnt.
native_language_example: That's the house in which my aunt lives.

meaning: literally 'house on/at' — used with a location to say a house is on/at/in a place
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; here 'Haus' (house) plus the preposition 'auf' (on/at) appears in examples with different cases and contexts. 'auf' can mean 'on' (a hill, block) or 'at/in' (island, region) depending on the noun and context. Word order and articles change: 'auf Salina' (on Salina/island), 'auf dem Hügel' (on the hill), 'auf Kyūshū' (on Kyūshū), 'auf dem Land' (in the countryside), 'auf dem Block' (on the block/street). Use correct case after 'auf' (usually dative for locations: 'auf dem ...').
target_language_example: Sie haben ein kleines Haus auf der Insel.
native_language_example: They have a small house on the island.

meaning: literally 'house out' but used in constructions like 'von ... aus' where 'Haus' is the place; indicates starting point or viewpoint when used in phrases such as 'von meinem Haus aus' (from my house). It can also appear in other structures where 'aus' belongs to a different phrase (e.g. 'ein Haus aus dem Mittelalter' = a house from the Middle Ages).
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone idiom—usually occurs as part of 'von ... aus' (e.g. 'von meinem Haus aus'). Means 'from (the house)' or 'from the house's location' when indicating where something starts or what can be seen/reached from that house. Be careful: in 'ein Haus aus dem Mittelalter' the 'aus' is part of a different construction (meaning 'from' in the temporal/material sense), so the sense differs.
target_language_example: Die Schule ist von meinem Haus aus zu Fuß zu erreichen.
native_language_example: The school can be reached on foot from my house.

meaning: 'the house of' (genitive construction: 'the house of [someone]')
additional_notes: This is the noun 'Haus' (house) followed by the genitive article 'des' (masculine/neuter singular). It marks possession: 'Haus des Mannes' = 'the man's house' or 'the house of the man'. In modern spoken German people often use the dative with 'von' (das Haus von dem Mann) instead of the genitive. Adjust the following noun to the correct genitive form (e.g. des Mannes, des Lehrers).
target_language_example: Das ist das Haus des Lehrers.
native_language_example: That is the teacher's house.

meaning: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the words 'Haus ist ein' — literally 'house is a'. Used when a sentence starts with or contains 'Haus ist ein ...' followed by a noun or noun phrase.
additional_notes: You will not use 'Haus ist ein' by itself as an idiom. It's the combination of the noun Haus (house) + the verb ist (is) + the indefinite article ein (a/an). In German word order, these three words frequently appear together when describing what a particular house is (e.g. 'Das Haus ist ein Geisterhaus' — 'The house is a haunted house') or in locational sentences with different structure (note: for location, German more commonly uses 'Vor dem Haus ist ein Garten' or 'Hinter dem Haus ist ein Garten' where 'ist ein' follows a prepositional phrase). Pay attention to articles and cases: after prepositions like 'vor' or 'hinter' you often use a definite/dative form (e.g. 'Vor dem Haus ...').
target_language_example: Das Haus ist ein Museum.
native_language_example: The house is a museum.

meaning: literally 'house is in' — not a standard fixed German phrase; likely a fragment meaning 'the house is in/located in...' when followed by a place
additional_notes: This looks like an incomplete clause rather than a standalone phrase. In German you'd normally say 'Das Haus ist in Berlin.' (The house is in Berlin.) Use with a location or context after 'in'. For a complete sentence include an article/subject (Das Haus) and a location (in + place).
target_language_example: Das Haus ist in der Stadt.
native_language_example: The house is in the city.

meaning: literally 'house is not' — used to negate statements about a house (e.g. not big, not far, not clean).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase in German; it's the noun 'Haus' + the verb 'ist' + the negation 'nicht'. Use 'nicht' to negate adjectives, adverbs, or prepositional phrases that describe the house (e.g. nicht groß, nicht weit, nicht isoliert). Word order: 'Haus ist nicht' is followed by the complement you negate (often 'besonders groß', 'sehr groß', 'so dreckig wie deins', 'weit von hier', 'isoliert'). For possession, include a determiner: 'Dieses Haus ist nicht…', 'Unser Haus ist nicht…'.
target_language_example: Unser Haus ist nicht sehr alt.
native_language_example: Our house is not very old.

meaning: a house with (something); used to describe a house that includes or has a particular feature.
additional_notes: Combine 'Haus' (house) with 'mit' (with) + a noun or noun phrase to specify a feature or characteristic (e.g., 'mit Garage', 'mit Schwimmbecken', 'mit dem roten Dach'). Word order: 'Haus mit [feature]'. Use appropriate articles/case after 'mit' (dative: 'mit dem roten Dach', 'mit einer Garage'). Can be used in identification or description.
target_language_example: Wir haben ein Haus mit großem Garten gefunden.
native_language_example: We found a house with a large garden.

meaning: has left the house (completed action).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: Haus = house, verlassen = to leave, hat = auxiliary for present perfect (Perfekt). Used to report that someone has already left the house. Often appears in subordinate clauses with dass (that) or in questions asking whether someone noticed or heard about it. Replace 'Haus' with other locations (z. B. 'die Wohnung verlassen hat').
target_language_example: Hast du bemerkt, dass er das Haus verlassen hat?
native_language_example: Did you notice that he has left the house?

meaning: the house was
additional_notes: A combination of the noun Haus (house) and the past-tense form war (was). Commonly appears in sentences describing the state, location, or existence of a house in the past. Depending on word order and context, war can be the main verb linking to an adjective or location (e.g. "Das Haus war aufgeräumt." = "The house was tidy."), or it can indicate existence/location with an introductory word (e.g. "Hinter dem Haus war ein großer Garten." = "Behind the house there was a big garden."). Word order matters in German: subject–verb–complement vs. existential constructions.
target_language_example: Das Haus war gestern sehr laut.
native_language_example: The house was very noisy yesterday.

meaning: 'the house' + passive/going-to marker (house is being / will be ...).
additional_notes: This shows the noun 'das Haus' used with the verb 'wird' (3rd person singular of 'werden') to form passive or progressive meanings: 'wird gebaut' = 'is being built' (present passive) and 'wird zerstört werden' = 'will be destroyed' (future passive). Also used in fixed expressions like rules ('In diesem Haus wird nicht gerannt' = 'You don't run in this house'). Pay attention to word order and participles: past participle usually goes to the end (wird + Partizip II), and for future passive add another 'werden' (wird ... werden).
target_language_example: Das Haus wird morgen gestrichen.
native_language_example: The house will be painted tomorrow.

meaning: to do (one's) homework
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when referring to school homework. Often used with possessive (meine/deine/seine) or without when context is clear. Literally 'to make house-tasks'. Can be used as an imperative or in questions/statements.
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt meine Hausaufgaben machen.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework now.

meaning: should have stayed at home (expresses regret about not staying home).
additional_notes: This is the perfect/modal construction using 'sollen' to express a past obligation or regret (English 'should have'). Word order: 'hätte(n) ... zu Hause bleiben sollen' or 'hätte(n) zu Hause bleiben sollen' with auxiliary 'hätte(n)'. 'zu Hause' means 'at home' (note two-word form: 'zu Hause', capitalized 'Hause'). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gestern zu Hause bleiben sollen.
native_language_example: I should have stayed at home yesterday.

meaning: sent (someone) home; sent (someone) to their house
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a past or perfect construction (e.g., 'nach Hause geschickt', 'er hat mich nach Hause geschickt'). Common verb phrase: 'nach Hause schicken' = to send someone home. 'Hause' here is an older/dative form of 'Haus' used in fixed expressions; in modern colloquial German 'nach Hause' is very common. Use when someone is made to go home or dismissed.
target_language_example: Der Lehrer hat die Schüler nach Hause geschickt.
native_language_example: The teacher sent the students home.

meaning: at home; to/at the house (archaic or poetic word order of 'zu Hause')
additional_notes: 'Hause' is an older form of 'Haus' used in fixed expressions. The normal modern phrase is 'zu Hause' (with 'zu' before 'Hause' or as the set phrase 'zu Hause'). 'Hause zu' — with 'zu' after — is archaic, poetic, or found in certain fixed or inverted constructions; it's rarely used in everyday speech. Use 'zu Hause' for 'at home' and 'nach Hause' for 'to home.'
target_language_example: Ich bleibe heute Hause zu.
native_language_example: I'll stay at home today.

meaning: to drive (or go) home
additional_notes: This phrase is a non-standard or archaic variant of the usual modern German expression 'nach Hause fahren' (to drive home) or 'nach Hause gehen' (to go home). Native speakers use 'nach Hause fahren/gehen' or the verbs 'heimfahren/heimgehen'. 'Hause zu fahren' may appear in older texts, poetic contexts, or unusual word orders; learners should prefer 'nach Hause fahren'. It can appear in infinitival constructions with 'zu' (e.g., in indirect speech) but is uncommon.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er wolle heute Abend nach Hause zu fahren. (non-standard/archaic word order)
native_language_example: He said he wanted to drive home this evening.

meaning: 'skin is' — describes a quality or state of skin
additional_notes: Used to state a property (color, texture, hardness, smell) of someone's or something's skin. 'Haut' = skin (noun, feminine). Followed by an adjective or adjective phrase. Common in everyday descriptions and comparisons.
target_language_example: Seine Haut ist sehr trocken nach dem Schwimmen.
native_language_example: His skin is very dry after swimming.

meaning: 'home is' — used to say what 'home' (Heimat) means or how it is described.
additional_notes: Heimat means 'home' or 'homeland' with emotional, cultural connotations (not just a house). 'Heimat ist ...' is a sentence starter to give a description, location, or feeling about one's home (e.g., 'Heimat ist fern' = 'home is far away'). Useful for expressing belonging, origin, or characteristics of one's home.
target_language_example: Für mich Heimat ist der Markt am Samstag.
native_language_example: For me, home is the market on Saturday.

meaning: 'Sir, I...' — a formal or respectful way to address a man before saying something about yourself or making a request.
additional_notes: Used in formal, polite, or literary contexts. 'Herr' = 'Mr.' or 'sir'; when followed by 'ich' it typically begins a sentence where the speaker addresses a man and then speaks about themselves (requests, explanations, introductions). Can appear as 'mein Herr' (my sir) or with adjectives like 'verehrter Herr' (esteemed sir) or 'gnädiger Herr' (gracious sir). Not common in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Verehrter Herr, ich möchte Ihnen kurz mein Anliegen schildern.
native_language_example: Esteemed sir, I would like to briefly explain my concern to you.

meaning: A formal address: 'Gentlemen, I...' used to begin a statement to a male group or in formal settings.
additional_notes: Meine Herren is a polite/formal way to address a group of men or an audience (can be used rhetorically even if not all are men). It often introduces an important comment, request, or a speaker taking the floor. In modern everyday speech it's less common and can sound old-fashioned or formal; in mixed-gender audiences you might instead hear 'Meine Damen und Herren'.
target_language_example: Meine Herren, ich eröffne die Sitzung.
native_language_example: Gentlemen, I hereby open the meeting.

meaning: 'heart and' — used in fixed expressions that combine 'Herz' (heart) with another word to form idioms (e.g. 'Herz und Verstand', 'Herz und Nieren').
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase; 'Herz und' appears as the first part of common German idioms where 'Herz' is paired with another noun to express ideas like emotion vs. reason (Herz und Verstand), a thorough test (Herz und Nieren), or to indicate both feelings and something else. Translate depending on the full expression. Useful to recognize as the start of idiomatic compounds.
target_language_example: Herz und Verstand müssen zusammenarbeiten.
native_language_example: Heart and mind must work together.

meaning: 'heart' used with an infinitive construction (e.g. jemanden/etwas 'Herz zu erobern' = 'to win someone's heart') — here 'Herz' is the noun and 'zu' is the particle used before an infinitive.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. In the examples, 'Herz' appears in expressions like 'sein Herz zu stehlen', 'ihr Herz zu erobern' or 'ein Herz zu machen'. The structure is noun + 'zu' + infinitive (often part of a larger verb phrase). The meaning depends on the verb: 'Herz erobern' = win someone's heart; 'Herz stehlen' = steal someone's heart (poetic); 'Herz pflegen' = care for the heart (literal or figurative). For beginners: learn the verbs that commonly pair with 'Herz' and remember 'zu' marks the infinitive in subordinate or infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Er will ihr Herz zu erobern versuchen.
native_language_example: He wants to try to win her heart.

meaning: 'heart of' (genitive plural/phrase used in expressions like 'in the hearts of...')
additional_notes: Literally means 'hearts of'. Often appears in phrases like 'im Herzen der Stadt' (in the heart of the city) or 'in den Herzen der Menschen' (in the hearts of the people). Depending on context the noun after 'der' determines case/gender/number (e.g. 'im Herzen der Stadt' uses singular feminine). 'Herzen' can be singular in dative ('im Herzen' = in the heart) or plural/genitive in constructions like 'die Herzen der Kinder' (the hearts of the children).
target_language_example: Die Erinnerung lebt in den Herzen der Menschen weiter.
native_language_example: The memory lives on in the hearts of the people.

meaning: 'need help' (second person singular: 'you need help').
additional_notes: A shortened phrase built from 'Hilfe brauchen'. Common in questions or offers: 'ob du Hilfe brauchst' (if you need help) or imperatives like 'Wenn du meine Hilfe brauchst, ...'. Used with 'du' (informal singular). For formal or plural use, change pronoun and verb: 'brauchen Sie' or 'braucht ihr'.
target_language_example: Wenn du Hilfe brauchst, frag mich ruhig.
native_language_example: If you need help, feel free to ask me.

meaning: 'help for' or 'assistance to/for' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say who or what receives help. Follows the noun/pronoun that identifies the recipient (Hilfe für + accusative object). Common in both formal and informal contexts. You can also say 'Hilfe leisten' (to provide help) or 'Hilfe holen' (to fetch/get help).
target_language_example: Wir organisieren Hilfe für neue Nachbarn.
native_language_example: We are organizing help for new neighbors.

meaning: asked for help (past participle form of 'um Hilfe bitten').
additional_notes: This is the past participle used in perfect tenses (e.g., 'hat um Hilfe gebeten' = 'has asked for help') or in passive/compound forms. The full verb phrase is 'um Hilfe bitten' (to ask for help). Common construction: [Person] hat/wann hast du ... um Hilfe gebeten? It requires the preposition 'um' plus the accusative object 'Hilfe'.
target_language_example: Wir haben gestern um Hilfe gebeten.
native_language_example: We asked for help yesterday.

meaning: 'help' + conditional 'could' — used in sentences like 'Without your help I could not (do it)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it combines 'Hilfe' (help) with the conditional/possibility verb form 'könnte' (could). You'll often see it in structures like 'Ohne deine/Ihre Hilfe könnte ich ... nicht.' to express that something would not be possible without someone's help. Use 'deine' for informal you and 'Ihre' for formal you.
target_language_example: Ohne deine Hilfe könnte ich das Projekt nicht beenden.
native_language_example: Without your help I could not finish the project.

meaning: literally 'sky to' — not a standalone fixed expression; appears as part of larger constructions like 'am Himmel zu sehen' (to be seen in the sky) or 'den Himmel zu sehen' (to see the sky).
additional_notes: Do not treat 'Himmel zu' as an independent idiom. 'Himmel' means 'sky' or 'heaven'; 'zu' is a particle that will be part of verb constructions (e.g. 'zu sehen' = 'to see'). Typical full phrases: 'am Himmel zu sehen' (visible in the sky), 'den Himmel zu sehen' (to see the sky). Use complete phrases rather than the fragment 'Himmel zu' alone.
target_language_example: Es waren viele Sterne am Himmel zu sehen.
native_language_example: There were many stars to be seen in the sky.

meaning: used to state what one's hobby is (literally: 'my hobby is that...')
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences like 'Mein Hobby ist das Fischen.' It's a slightly formal/neutral way to introduce an activity as a hobby by using the nominalized verb with the definite article 'das' (das + Verb‑infinitive used as a noun). In everyday speech Germans often say 'Mein Hobby ist Fischen' (without 'das') or 'Ich sammle Insekten als Hobby.' The structure: 'Mein Hobby ist das + [nominalized verb]' or 'Mein Hobby ist das Sammeln von ...'.
target_language_example: Mein Hobby ist das Lesen von Romanen.
native_language_example: My hobby is reading novels.

meaning: Hochzeit ist — 'the wedding is...' used to state when or how a wedding/event is (taking place) or to describe its importance.
additional_notes: This phrase combines Hochzeit (wedding) with the verb sein (is). Beginners will most often see it used to give the time/date/location of a wedding (e.g. 'Die Hochzeit ist in zwei Wochen.' = 'The wedding is in two weeks.'). It can also be used to comment on the wedding as an event (e.g. 'Diese Hochzeit ist hier das Ereignis des Jahrhunderts.'). The verb sein must agree with the subject (Die Hochzeit ist ...). To say where it takes place use 'in' or 'auf' or 'bei' depending on context: 'Die Hochzeit ist in der Kirche / auf dem Land / bei meinen Eltern.'
target_language_example: Die Hochzeit ist am 12. Juni um 15 Uhr in der Kirche.
native_language_example: The wedding is on June 12 at 3 PM in the church.

meaning: to give hope; to make someone feel hopeful
additional_notes: Used when something or someone causes another person or group to feel more optimistic about an outcome. Common in contexts such as medicine, research, relationships, news, or future prospects (e.g., a study gives hope for a cure). Can be used impersonally (Das Ergebnis gibt Hoffnung) or with an indirect object (Die Nachricht gibt den Patienten Hoffnung). Often appears in perfect/simple tenses (hat Hoffnung gegeben/geben).
target_language_example: Die neuen Studien scheinen Hoffnung zu geben.
native_language_example: The new studies seem to give hope.

meaning: to give hope; to raise someone's expectations
additional_notes: Used when someone or something causes another person to feel hopeful or optimistic about an outcome. Can be used positively (encouraging) or negatively (raising false expectations). Common construction: 'jemandem Hoffnung machen' (to give someone hope).
target_language_example: Die Ärztin wollte uns nicht zu viel Hoffnung machen.
native_language_example: The doctor didn't want to give us too much hope.

meaning: "hope and" — the start of a phrase pairing 'Hoffnung' (hope) with another noun or concept.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'Hoffnung und' simply begins combinations like 'Hoffnung und Vertrauen' (hope and trust) or 'Hoffnung und Geduld' (hope and patience). Used to link hope with a second quality or idea. Make sure to complete the phrase with a second noun or concept when you use it.
target_language_example: Mit Hoffnung und Geduld wird alles besser.
native_language_example: With hope and patience everything will get better.

meaning: 'hope to' or 'hope of' (used when followed by a verb in infinitive construction introduced by zu, or as part of a larger phrase expressing hope)
additional_notes: 'Hoffnung zu' by itself is uncommon as a standalone phrase; it typically appears inside constructions like 'die Hoffnung zu + Infinitiv' (e.g. 'die Hoffnung zu gewinnen') or in fixed contexts ('Hoffnung zu haben'). For expressing 'hope for something' with a noun, German often uses 'Hoffnung auf + Akk.' or 'die Hoffnung, ... zu + Infinitiv' for verb phrases. Use articles and context to form grammatical sentences (e.g. 'Ich habe die Hoffnung, ... zu ...').
target_language_example: Ich habe die Hoffnung zu überleben, obwohl die Lage ernst ist.
native_language_example: I have the hope of surviving, although the situation is serious.

target_language_multi_word_term: in die Hose gemacht / (sich) in die Hose gemacht
meaning: to have (almost) wet oneself; to be (almost) very scared or embarrassed.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning literally 'made into the trousers' — used to say someone wet themselves (often from fear or embarrassment). Common in past forms: 'hat in die Hose gemacht' (wet themselves) or 'hätte sich in die Hose gemacht' / 'hatte sich fast in die Hose gemacht' (almost wet themselves / was very scared). Can be used literally (actual urination) or figuratively (extreme fear/shock). The reflexive form 'sich in die Hose machen' is typical.
target_language_example: Als der Hund laut bellte, hätte sie sich fast in die Hose gemacht.
native_language_example: When the dog barked loudly, she almost wet herself.

meaning: 'in the hotel' or 'in which (hotel)'.
additional_notes: This phrase uses a relative or locative structure with the preposition 'in' + dative (dem) to say something is located inside a hotel or to introduce a relative clause: 'das Hotel, in dem...' = 'the hotel in which...' In everyday speech you may also hear the contracted form 'im Hotel' when not using a relative clause (e.g. 'Ich bin im Hotel'). Use 'in dem' (or contracted 'im') for location; in relative clauses keep 'in dem' or use the appropriate relative pronoun form 'in dem'/'in dem' depending on gender and number.
target_language_example: Das ist das Hotel, in dem wir bleiben werden.
native_language_example: That is the hotel in which we will stay.

meaning: 'the hotel was' (simple past description)
additional_notes: Combination of noun 'Hotel' + past-tense verb 'war' (1st/3rd person singular of 'sein' in Präteritum). Used to describe past states or qualities of the hotel (e.g., its function, condition, price, view). In English translate as 'the hotel was...'. Grammar point: 'war' is past; for present use 'ist'.
target_language_example: Das Hotel war neu und modern.
native_language_example: The hotel was new and modern.

meaning: literally 'dog at/on' — part of phrases showing location or what is being touched/attached (e.g. 'am Baum' = at the tree, 'am Halsband' = at the collar).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the noun 'Hund' followed by the contraction 'am' (an + dem) which means 'at the' or 'on the' depending on context. Common uses: describing where the dog is (e.g. am Baum, am Strand) or what part of the dog is touched/held (e.g. am Halsband = at the collar). Choose the noun after 'am' appropriately (am Baum, am Halsband, am Strand).
target_language_example: Sie hielt den Hund am Halsband fest.
native_language_example: She held the dog by the collar.

meaning: to feed (the) dog; to give food to a dog.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: Hund (dog) + füttern (to feed). Used when talking about giving meals to a dog or arranging who will feed the dog. You can change the subject or object (z. B. meinen Hund füttern, den Hund füttern). Questions often use wie oft/ wievielmal am Tag to ask frequency.
target_language_example: Ich muss zuerst den Hund füttern.
native_language_example: I need to feed the dog first.

meaning: 'dog is' (subject 'dog' + verb 'is') — simple present description.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common short structure: Hund (dog) + ist (is). Used to describe or ask about a dog's state, size, age, color, etc. In full sentences you'd usually include a possessive or determiner (dein, sein, unser, welcher) before Hund. Word order: Subject + verb (ist) + complement.
target_language_example: Der Hund ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: The dog is very friendly.

meaning: 'dogs and' — the word 'Hunde' (dogs) followed by the conjunction 'und' (and).
additional_notes: This is simply the plural noun 'Hunde' (dogs) plus the conjunction 'und' (and). It appears before another noun or phrase (e.g., 'Hunde und Katzen' = 'dogs and cats'). Nothing special grammatically — 'Hunde' is the plural of 'Hund'. Watch out: the phrase can be part of neutral statements, comparisons, or (unfortunately) offensive or discriminatory sentences in context. The meaning depends on what comes after 'und'.
target_language_example: Ich sehe oft Hunde und Katzen im Park.
native_language_example: I often see dogs and cats in the park.

meaning: the phrase 'Hunger und' is simply 'hunger and' — used to link 'Hunger' (hunger) with another noun or idea.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom — it's just the word 'Hunger' (hunger) followed by the conjunction 'und' (and). You'll see it in lists or paired expressions (e.g. 'Hunger und Durst' = 'hunger and thirst', or in contrasts/emphasis like 'nur Hunger und Krieg' = 'only hunger and war'). Use 'und' to connect nouns, adjectives, or clauses. Pay attention to articles and negation: 'Ich hatte keinen Hunger und keine Lust' negates both parts.
target_language_example: Nach der langen Reise hatten wir Hunger und Durst.
native_language_example: After the long trip we were hungry and thirsty.

meaning: 'Hut ab' is an expression meaning 'hats off' — used to show respect or admiration for someone or something.
additional_notes: Often said to praise someone's achievement or courage (English: 'hats off'). Can be used on its own ('Hut ab!') or within a sentence. Note: literal use 'den/ihren Hut abnehmen' means 'take off your hat' (a polite request to remove a hat indoors). Context determines whether it's idiomatic (praise) or literal (physically removing a hat).
target_language_example: Hut ab, das war eine großartige Leistung!
native_language_example: Hats off, that was a great performance!

meaning: 'hat and' — the conjunction 'and' connecting the noun 'Hut' (hat) with another item.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'Hut' (hat) followed by the conjunction 'und' (and). Appears when listing items (e.g., 'a hat and a coat') or in instructions where 'Hut' is one of several elements. Pay attention to noun gender and plural/possessive forms (der Hut, den Hut, meinen Hut). Word order and case will change depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Sie nahm ihren Hut und ging nach draußen.
native_language_example: She took her hat and went outside.

meaning: 'hat to' as a sequence of words that appears in various constructions; by itself not a fixed idiom. It can occur in literal phrases (e.g. jemanden bitten, den Hut zu holen), in admonitions (mit dem Hut zu spielen) or as part of idioms like 'auf der Hut sein' (be on guard) when word order places 'Hut' before 'zu'. Meaning depends on the surrounding verb and context.
additional_notes: 'Hut zu' on its own is not an established standalone phrase in German. Learners will most often encounter 'Hut' (the noun 'hat') combined with verbs and particles (holen, nehmen, spielen) or the fixed idiom 'auf der Hut sein'. Word order can produce the sequence 'Hut zu' (e.g. 'seinen Hut zu holen', 'mit deinem Hut zu spielen', 'auf der Hut zu sein' in some subordinate clauses). Pay attention to the verb that follows to determine the correct translation.
target_language_example: Bitte höre auf, mit deinem Hut zu spielen!
native_language_example: Please stop playing with your hat!

meaning: literally 'half is' — used to talk about one half of something (quantity, portion, group) and state something about it.
additional_notes: Hälfte means 'half' (a noun: die Hälfte). In sentences it often appears with a verb like ist/ist schon weg/ist für dich to describe the state, size, ownership or portion of that half. Common structures: 'Deine Hälfte ist ...' (your half is ...), 'Die andere Hälfte ist ...' (the other half is ...). Used for both physical portions (cake, money) and abstract groups (people).
target_language_example: Die eine Hälfte ist für mich, die andere Hälfte ist für dich.
native_language_example: One half is for me, the other half is for you.

meaning: 'hands on' (used in commands: put/place your hands on ...)
additional_notes: Common in commands or instructions (often by police, in emergencies, or during physical guidance). Usually followed by a location: 'Hände auf den Rücken' (hands on your back) or 'Hände auf den Boden' (hands on the floor). Can be plural imperative (addressing one or more people). Not a fixed idiom—meaning comes from the words.
target_language_example: Hände auf den Rücken und langsam drehen!
native_language_example: Hands on your back and turn slowly!

meaning: literally 'hands on the...' — used to describe placing someone's hands on a body part (e.g. shoulders, hips).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the verb construction 'die Hände auf ... legen' (to place/put one's hands on...). The full structure often includes a person receiving the action (dative) and the body part (accusative with definite article): jemandem die Hände auf die Schultern legen. Common in descriptions of physical contact or posture.
target_language_example: Sie legte ihm die Hände auf die Schultern.
native_language_example: She placed her hands on his shoulders.

meaning: Hands up (raise your hands).
additional_notes: Common command used by police, in robberies, or to order people to raise their hands. Can be literal (raise your hands) or an imperative command ("Hands up!"). Formal commands use "Nehmen Sie die Hände hoch" or "Heben Sie die Hände hoch." Informal/familiar form to one person would be "Hebe die Hände hoch" or plural "Hebt die Hände hoch."
target_language_example: Bitte, Hände hoch und bleiben Sie stehen!
native_language_example: Please, hands up and stay where you are!

meaning: used with verbs like waschen or abwischen to indicate 'hands with' (what you use on your hands), e.g. 'wash your hands with (something)'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase: Hände appears as the direct object (die Hände/dir die Hände) and mit introduces the instrument/substance used (mit Seife, mit warmem Wasser, mit einem Taschentuch). Pronouns and reflexive forms are common (mir die Hände, dir die Hände, uns die Hände). Word order: verb — (reflexive pronoun) — die Hände — mit + instrument.
target_language_example: Wasche dir die Hände mit Seife!
native_language_example: Wash your hands with soap!

meaning: to shake hands (greet or agree by clasping hands)
additional_notes: Common German verb phrase for the physical action of shaking hands when meeting someone or making an agreement. Used with a definite article or possessive: 'die Hände schütteln' or 'uns die Hände schütteln'. In past tense: 'hat die Hände geschüttelt'. Can be literal (greeting) or figurative (to make a deal).
target_language_example: Wir sollten uns zur Begrüßung die Hände schütteln.
native_language_example: We should shake hands to greet each other.

meaning: Hands off! / Don't touch (that).
additional_notes: A short, firm command telling someone not to touch or approach something or someone. Commonly used to warn or threaten; can be followed by 'von' + object (Hände weg von ...). Suitable in urgent or angry situations.
target_language_example: Hände weg von meinem Rucksack!
native_language_example: Hands off my backpack!

meaning: used with a verb to refer to 'the hands' as the body part (e.g. 'to wash one's hands').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but part of constructions with a reflexive verb: sich die Hände zu waschen / trocknen / verbinden etc. In English you would say 'to wash one's hands', 'to dry one's hands'. German uses the definite article (die) and the reflexive pronoun (sich) + verb. In some examples 'die Hände zu Hilfe nehmen' means 'to use (one's) hands to help' (i.e. to use hands as assistance).
target_language_example: Sie muss sich die Hände zu waschen, bevor sie isst.
native_language_example: She must wash her hands before she eats.

meaning: 'houses and' (the noun Häuser followed by the conjunction und = 'and')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's simply the plural noun Häuser (houses) followed by the conjunction und (and). You'll see it when someone lists things (e.g., 'houses and a boat'). Word order and endings follow normal German grammar: Häuser is the plural of Haus. Use und to connect items in a list.
target_language_example: Sie hat drei Häuser und ein Auto.
native_language_example: She has three houses and a car.

meaning: ups and downs; the good and bad moments of life or relationships.
additional_notes: Common idiom used to describe fluctuating fortunes, emotions, or events. Often used with life (das Leben), a relationship (eine Beziehung) or someone's experiences. You can add possessive pronouns (seine/ihre) to refer to a specific person or thing.
target_language_example: Unsere Freundschaft hatte Höhen und Tiefen, aber wir blieben Freunde.
native_language_example: Our friendship had ups and downs, but we stayed friends.

meaning: 'what the hell' / 'where the hell' / adds strong surprise, anger or emphasis to a question
additional_notes: An exclamation used to make questions stronger and more emotional. Often inserted after a question word (was, wer, wo, wie) or before a verb. It's informal and somewhat coarse — avoid in polite or formal situations. The literal image refers to 'hell', but you don't translate it literally in English: use 'what the hell', 'who the hell', 'where the hell', etc.
target_language_example: Was zur Hölle ist hier passiert?
native_language_example: What the hell happened here?

meaning: 'the idea is' or 'it is an idea that...'; used to state or evaluate an idea.
additional_notes: Combination of Idee (idea) and the verb ist (is). Used to say what an idea is or to comment on whether something is a good idea. Common in sentences like 'Seine Idee ist dieselbe wie meine.' (His idea is the same as mine.) and 'Weiß nicht, ob das eine gute Idee ist.' (I don't know if that's a good idea.). Word order and context determine whether you describe the idea or judge it.
target_language_example: Meine Idee ist, dass wir früher anfangen.
native_language_example: My idea is that we should start earlier.

meaning: 'idea with' / 'idea involving' — used to talk about an idea that includes or involves something or someone; also appears in questions with 'eine Idee (mit wem/was...)' meaning 'any idea who/what...?'
additional_notes: Often used in two ways: 1) In questions like "Hast du eine Idee mit wem...?" it functions like English "Any idea who...?" 2) As part of a phrase describing an idea that includes something ("die Idee mit dem Heim" = "the idea of/with the home"). Word order: when asking about people, German normally uses 'mit wem' (not 'wem mit'). 'Idee' is feminine: 'eine Idee'.
target_language_example: Hast du eine Idee mit wem wir ins Museum gehen könnten?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea who we could go to the museum with?

meaning: to (give/send/owe) you money — 'Ihnen' is the formal or plural 'to you', 'Geld' = money.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: a verb (schulden, leihen, schicken, etc.) plus 'Ihnen Geld' means someone owes, lends, sends, or gives money to 'you' (formal or plural). 'Ihnen' is the dative form used for formal singular 'you' (Sie) or plural 'you' (ihr/Sie). Word order can change depending on the sentence (e.g., 'schickt ihm Geld', 'ich schicke Ihnen Geld').
target_language_example: Wenn du willst, leihe ich Ihnen Geld.
native_language_example: If you want, I'll lend you money.

meaning: to/with you at
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal 'you') followed by the preposition 'an' used in different contexts. In scenes 1–2 'zu Ihnen an den Tisch' means 'to/at your table' or 'to join you at the table' (an + den Tisch = at the table). In examples 3–7 'an' is used with gefallen (Was gefällt Ihnen an X?) and means 'about' or 'in' — i.e. 'What do you like about X?' 'Ihnen' is formal you (dative). Keep word order in mind: German uses dative pronouns for the indirect object (Ihnen) and 'an' combines with a noun phrase (an + den/diesem/etc.).
target_language_example: Darf ich mich zu Ihnen an den Tisch setzen?
native_language_example: May I sit down at your table?

meaning: to you too
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something applies or is done for the person addressed (formal 'Sie' → dative 'Ihnen'). 'Auch' means 'also/too' and follows the dative pronoun. In different contexts it can mean 'also', 'too', or 'as well' (e.g., giving something, assigning blame, saying something additionally). Formal register because 'Ihnen' is the polite dative form.
target_language_example: Ich habe Ihnen auch etwas mitgebracht.
native_language_example: I brought something for you too.

meaning: to you this
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal or dative plural/informal polite form of 'you' (dative). 'diesen' is a demonstrative pronoun/adjective (masculine accusative) meaning 'this' and agrees with a masculine direct object. Together they indicate that something masculine/singular is being given, shown, recommended, assigned, etc., to you (formal). In English you usually say 'this to you' or more naturally 'this for you' or 'I'll give/bring/recommend this to you.' Word order in German often places the indirect object (Ihnen) before the direct object (diesen).
target_language_example: Ich schenke Ihnen diesen Mantel.
native_language_example: I give this coat to you.

meaning: I already told you (formal) that you should/should not ...
additional_notes: This phrase is formal because of the dative/formal pronoun 'Ihnen' (you, formal). 'Doch' adds emphasis or reminds the listener (like 'after all' or 'as I told you'). 'daß/daß' (modern spelling 'dass') introduces a subordinate clause with 'Sie' as the subject; the verb of the subordinate clause goes to the end. Often used to repeat or remind someone of prior advice or instructions; can express frustration. The subordinate clause may contain a modal verb (sollen) indicating obligation or prohibition ('sollen' + nicht = should not).
target_language_example: Ich habe Ihnen doch gesagt, daß Sie heute früher nach Hause gehen sollen!
native_language_example: I already told you that you should go home earlier today!

meaning: a polite way to refer to 'you' (formal) with 'actually'/'in fact'—used to soften, qualify, or emphasize a statement or question.
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal dative/accusative 'you' (capitalized). eigentlich (literally 'actually') is often used to soften a comment, show hesitation, add contrast, or add emphasis. Together they appear in phrases like 'Das sollte ich Ihnen eigentlich nicht sagen' (I probably shouldn't tell you) or in questions 'Ist Ihnen eigentlich klar...?' (Are you actually/aware...?). In exclamations ('Was fällt Ihnen eigentlich ein!') it can add surprise or indignation. Tone and context decide whether it's polite, tentative, or sharp.
target_language_example: Ist Ihnen eigentlich bewusst, dass das Formular heute fertig sein muss?
native_language_example: Are you actually aware that the form has to be finished today?

meaning: to you a/an
additional_notes: A common formal/polite pattern: Ihnen means "to you" or "for you" (formal singular or plural), and ein introduces a singular noun. It often appears with verbs like zeigen, schicken, empfehlen, kaufen, or verraten, where someone does something for or to the person addressed.
target_language_example: Ich kann Ihnen ein Taxi rufen.
native_language_example: I can call you a taxi.

meaning: to you for
additional_notes: Commonly appears in polite expressions of thanks or when stating what someone is owed. 'Ihnen' is the dative polite/formal 'you' (formal Sie → Ihnen). 'für' introduces the reason or thing (accusative). Often part of phrases like 'Ich danke Ihnen für ...' (I thank you for ...) or 'Ich schulde Ihnen für ...' (I owe you for ...). In casual speech with friends/family, 'Ihnen' would be replaced by 'dir'.
target_language_example: Ich danke Ihnen für Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: I thank you for your help.

meaning: given to you (formal or plural)
additional_notes: A past participle phrase using the dative pronoun Ihnen (formal singular or plural 'to you'). Commonly appears in perfect tense constructions (hat ... gegeben / habe ... gegeben) or relative clauses. For informal singular use dir gegeben; for informal plural use euch gegeben. Can refer to tangible items (books, money), advice, medicine, etc. Context determines who 'Ihnen' refers to (formal you or plural you).
target_language_example: Was haben Sie mit den Büchern gemacht, die ich Ihnen gegeben habe?
native_language_example: What did you do with the books that I gave you?

meaning: polite offering or willingness to do something for you (formal 'you').
additional_notes: Used in polite/formal sentences with the dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal you). 'Gern' (or 'gerne') expresses that the speaker is happy/willing to do the action — English equivalents: 'happy to', 'glad to', 'would be pleased to', 'I'd be happy to'. Common in offers, thanks, and requests. Word order: 'Ihnen gern' often appears after verbs like helfen, geben, danken, würde ... fragen.
target_language_example: Ich kann Ihnen gern morgen die Unterlagen schicken.
native_language_example: I can gladly/I'll be happy to send you the documents tomorrow.

meaning: a polite way to say 'to you' with 'gladly/would like to' — used to politely offer, thank, believe, or do something for someone (formal you).
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal dative form of 'you' (Sie). 'Gerne' (or 'gerne' after modal verbs) softens the sentence and expresses willingness, politeness, or desire (English: 'gladly', 'would like to', 'I'd be happy to'). Common in formal contexts (customers, superiors). Word order can vary: 'Ich möchte Ihnen gerne…', 'Ich würde Ihnen gerne…'.
target_language_example: Ich würde Ihnen gerne helfen.
native_language_example: I would like to help you.

meaning: physically/mentally well (to be well for 'you' formal).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in the common question 'Geht es Ihnen gut?' meaning 'Are you okay?/How are you?' 'Ihnen' is the formal dative 'you' (Sie → Ihnen). Use with people you address formally (strangers, elders, superiors). For informal singular use 'dir' (Geht es dir gut?) and for plural informal use 'euch'. Often used both as a question and in statements like 'Schön, dass es Ihnen gut geht.'
target_language_example: Geht es Ihnen gut nach dem Unfall?
native_language_example: Are you OK after the accident?

meaning: good for you; suits you (formal 'you').
additional_notes: Used with the dative formal pronoun 'Ihnen' to say something is beneficial for someone (e.g. 'tut Ihnen gut' = 'will do you good') or that something looks/suits someone (e.g. 'steht Ihnen gut' = 'it suits you'). Formal register (Sie). English equivalents: 'good for you', 'will do you good', 'suits you'.
target_language_example: Viel Schlaf tut Ihnen gut.
native_language_example: A lot of sleep will do you good.

meaning: to you now
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal dative pronoun 'to/for you' (formal singular or plural). Jetzt means 'now' or 'at this moment'. Together they frequently appear in polite or formal statements: Ich werde Ihnen jetzt ... (I will now ... to/for you). Word order can vary: jetzt can come before or after Ihnen depending on emphasis. Use Ihnen with formal contexts (Sie).
target_language_example: Ich kann Ihnen jetzt eine Lösung anbieten.
native_language_example: I can offer you a solution now.

meaning: 'no' or 'not any' for a masculine/neuter singular object when speaking formally (dative/accusative context); used to say you do not give/offer something to 'you' (formal).
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal dative/accusative form of 'you' (Sie). Kein negates a noun and agrees in gender/case with that noun. In examples 1–2 it appears in phrases like 'Ihnen kein besseres Schiff' = 'no better ship for you' (formal). In examples 3–4 the structure is slightly different: 'Ich glaube Ihnen kein Wort' uses Ihnen as dative (to you) and kein to negate 'Wort' ('not a single word' / 'don't believe you'). Useful when politely addressing someone formally (Sie).
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, dass ich Ihnen kein anderes Angebot machen kann.
native_language_example: I'm sorry that I can't make you any other offer.

meaning: not to you
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Ihnen is the formal/plural dative form of Sie ('to you' or 'for you'), and nicht negates the verb or clause. In sentences like Ich muss Ihnen nicht sagen ..., the full meaning depends on the verb: 'I don't have to tell you ...'.
target_language_example: Ich kann Ihnen nicht helfen.
native_language_example: I can't help you.

meaning: to you (formal) never / will never tell you / I'll never ... to you (formal)
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal dative pronoun 'to you' (Sie → Ihnen). 'nie' means 'never'. Together they often appear in sentences like 'ich verrate Ihnen nie...' (I will never tell you...) or 'Das vergesse ich Ihnen nie' (I'll never forget that for you). The order can vary depending on sentence structure; 'Ihnen nie' emphasizes that the action will not be done to/for the formal you.
target_language_example: Ich werde Ihnen nie die Wahrheit verschweigen.
native_language_example: I will never hide the truth from you.

meaning: to talk with you / to speak to you (formal).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the verb phrase 'mit Ihnen reden' (reden mit + dative). 'Ihnen' is the formal dative pronoun 'you' (Sie → Ihnen). Use in formal or polite contexts (boss, stranger, elder). Word order: 'mit Ihnen reden' or 'mit Ihnen reden müssen/wollen'. The standalone sequence 'Ihnen reden' without 'mit' is not correct; always include 'mit' (mit Ihnen reden).
target_language_example: Ich muss kurz mit Ihnen reden.
native_language_example: I need to speak with you briefly.

meaning: speak to you
additional_notes: Formal/respectful form using the dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal 'you'). Appears in phrases like 'mit Ihnen sprechen' (to speak with/to you). In English both 'speak to you' and 'talk to you' are natural. Use in polite requests: 'Könnte ich bitte einen Moment mit Ihnen sprechen?' Note word order: in German you say 'mit Ihnen sprechen' (not 'Ihnen sprechen' alone in most contexts).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you for a moment?

meaning: to you, really
additional_notes: Ihnen is the formal or polite dative pronoun 'to you'. 'wirklich' means 'really' or 'truly'. Together they're commonly used as a polite emphasis: "I really (want/try) to [do something] for/to you" or "We really don't... you". Word order can vary (e.g. "wir wollen Ihnen wirklich nicht weh tun" or "ich versuche wirklich, Ihnen zu helfen"). Formal register (Sie/Ihnen) is used when speaking politely or to strangers.
target_language_example: Ich möchte Ihnen wirklich danken für Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: I really want to thank you for your help.

meaning: to talk with you (formal).
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrase using the formal pronoun 'Ihnen' (capitalized). 'mit ... zu reden' is an infinitive construction often used after adjectives (nett, schön) or verbs (wünschen, verbieten). For informal speech use 'mit dir zu reden'.
target_language_example: Es war schön, mit Ihnen zu reden.
native_language_example: It was nice to talk with you.

meaning: to speak with you (formal)
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrasing using the dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal 'you') plus infinitive 'sprechen' in constructions like 'mit Ihnen zu sprechen' (to speak with you). Common in polite expressions: 'Es war mir eine Freude, mit Ihnen zu sprechen' (It was a pleasure to speak with you). Use 'dir zu sprechen' for informal singular, and 'mit Ihnen' is optional but typical: 'mit Ihnen zu sprechen' = 'to speak with you.'
target_language_example: Ich freue mich darauf, mit Ihnen zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I look forward to speaking with you.

meaning: you ... that/it
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Here, `Ihr` is the subject pronoun meaning `you` when talking to more than one person, and `das` means `that` or `it`. In questions and other inverted word order, the verb often comes first, so `Ihr` and `das` can appear next to each other: `Warum tut Ihr das?` = `Why are you doing that?` Also, capitalized `Ihr` for plural `you` is old-fashioned or stylistic; in modern standard German, `ihr` is more usual.
target_language_example: Habt Ihr das schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen that already?

meaning: you (pl.) the
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's the combination of the polite/informal plural subject pronoun Ihr (you, plural or archaic/formal in some contexts) followed by the definite article die. In modern German 'Ihr' with a capital I can be formal 'you' (archaic) or the familiar plural 'you' (common). In the example sentences the structure is part of larger clauses: e.g. 'Habt Ihr die Minen aufgegeben…?' = 'Have you (plural) given up the mines…?' or 'Hier habt Ihr die Chance…' = 'Here you have the chance…'. Note: 'Ihr' is a pronoun and must agree with the verb (second person plural). The word 'die' is just the feminine/plural definite article or relative pronoun depending on context.
target_language_example: Habt ihr die Tür geschlossen?
native_language_example: Have you (pl.) closed the door?

meaning: in your life (formal, dative).
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrase using the formal pronoun 'Ihr' (capitalized) in the dative case (Ihrem = to/for/in your). Used to talk about someone's life (events, people, experiences). If addressing friends/family or informal situations, use 'deinem Leben' (singular informal) or 'eurem Leben' (plural informal).
target_language_example: Was ist das Wichtigste in Ihrem Leben?
native_language_example: What is the most important thing in your life?

meaning: 'in your position' / 'if I were you' (used to give advice or a recommendation)
additional_notes: Usually appears in the phrase 'an Ihrer Stelle' (formal) or 'an deiner Stelle' (informal). It's a polite way to say 'if I were you' before giving advice or a suggestion. Use 'Ihrer' for the formal 'Sie' and 'deiner' for the informal 'du'. Common structure: 'An Ihrer Stelle würde ich ...'.
target_language_example: An Ihrer Stelle würde ich das Angebot annehmen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would accept the offer.

meaning: I'd/We'd/They'd say 'If I were you...' — used to give advice (literally: 'in your place, would...').
additional_notes: Common polite formula for giving advice. Often appears as 'An Ihrer Stelle würde ich...' (formal you) or 'An deiner Stelle würde ich...' (informal). The verb clause follows (e.g. 'würde ich ...'). Use the conditional to suggest what you would do in the other person's situation.
target_language_example: An Ihrer Stelle würde ich den Vertrag noch einmal prüfen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would check the contract again.

meaning: information for / information intended for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say who the information is meant for (polite/formal Sie, plural ihr, singular du, or pronoun sie). Also appears in the structure 'etwas für jemand(en) halten' meaning 'to consider something to be (adjective)' — e.g. 'etwas für glaubwürdig halten' = 'to consider something credible.' Word order and capitalization: Informationen is plural noun (capitalized).
target_language_example: Ich habe Informationen für dich.
native_language_example: I have information for you.

meaning: to be interested (in something/someone)
additional_notes: Use with an object introduced by an accusative noun or commonly with the preposition an + dative: Interesse an etwas haben (to be interested in something). Often used to state or ask whether someone has interest in an offer or topic. Can be formal or neutral; to be more informal, use interessiert sein or interessiert sein an + Dativ.
target_language_example: Hast du Interesse haben an dem Kurs?
native_language_example: Are you interested in the course?

meaning: 'the internet is' — a simple subject + verb phrase used to describe the internet.
additional_notes: Use this phrase to start a statement about the internet (e.g., its nature, quality, or problems). 'Internet' is neuter in German (das Internet). You can follow 'Internet ist' with nouns, adjectives, or adjective phrases. Informal modifiers like 'so was von' (so very) often appear in spoken German: e.g. 'Mein Internet ist ...' to talk about your connection.
target_language_example: Das Internet ist manchmal nervig.
native_language_example: The internet is sometimes annoying.

meaning: "the jacket is" (subject + verb) — used to describe the jacket's state or possession
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun 'Jacke' (jacket) and the verb 'ist' (is). You will see it in sentences describing size, condition, location, or ownership (e.g. 'Die Jacke ist dir zu klein' = 'The jacket is too small for you'). Use appropriate dative pronouns (mir/dir/Ihnen) to indicate who is affected. For asking about ownership, use 'Wessen Jacke ist das?' ('Whose jacket is that?').
target_language_example: Die Jacke ist mir zu warm.
native_language_example: The jacket is too warm for me.

meaning: 'in this/that year' + 'on' (used to indicate that an event/date falls on a particular day in a given year) or as part of time expressions with prepositions (e.g. 'das ganze Jahr auf' in 'sich auf etwas freuen') depending on context.
