target_language_example: Ich mache jeden Morgen einen Spaziergang im Park.
native_language_example: I take a walk in the park every morning.

meaning: 'in the morning' followed by a time or place (literally 'morning in the')
additional_notes: Used to say something happened or someone was somewhere during the morning. Usually combined with a month, day, place, or part of the day: e.g. 'Morgen im April' (a morning in April), 'heute Morgen im Büro' (this morning in the office), or 'den ganzen Morgen im Bett' (the whole morning in bed). Note word order: 'heute Morgen' is common; 'Morgen im' appears when 'morning' is followed by 'in' + a noun (month, building, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir haben ihn gestern Morgen im Park getroffen.
native_language_example: We met him yesterday morning in the park.

meaning: 'in the morning was' — a simple past description referring to something that was true in the morning.
additional_notes: Combines 'Morgen' (morning) with the past-tense verb 'war' (was). Used to describe the state, condition, or behavior of something/someone earlier that morning. Often appears as 'am Morgen war' or 'heute Morgen war' (this morning was). Word order may include time adverb first: 'Am Morgen war es kalt.'
target_language_example: Heute Morgen war das Café noch geschlossen.
native_language_example: This morning the café was still closed.

meaning: "Tomorrow I am" (literal) or part of a sentence meaning "This morning I ..." depending on context; here examples use "Heute Morgen bin ich" = "This morning I ..."
additional_notes: Alone, "Morgen bin ich" usually means "Tomorrow I am..." (talking about the next day). In the provided example sentences the phrase appears as "Heute Morgen bin ich" meaning "This morning I..." followed by a past-tense verb (e.g. "aufgestanden" = got up, "über den Weg gelaufen" = ran into). Pay attention to time words: "Heute Morgen" = this morning (past), "Morgen" = tomorrow (future). Verb placement: in perfect/past constructions with "bin" + past participle for verbs of motion (e.g. ankommen, laufen).
target_language_example: Morgen bin ich den ganzen Tag im Büro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I will be in the office all day.

meaning: 'mouth' used in fixed expressions with 'und' (part of phrases like 'von der Hand in den Mund' or imperative 'Halt den Mund und...')
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; 'Mund' (mouth) appears in several common multi-word expressions with 'und'. Examples: 'von der Hand in den Mund' (living hand-to-mouth = having barely enough money), and imperatives like 'Halt den Mund und ...' (shut your mouth and ... / be quiet and ...). In commands involving the mouth (e.g. at the dentist) you may see 'öffnen Sie bitte den Mund und ...' (please open your mouth and ...). 'Mund' is a basic noun; remember the accusative article 'den' in phrases like 'den Mund halten' (shut up).
target_language_example: Halt den Mund und hör einfach zu!
native_language_example: Shut up and just listen!

meaning: music by / the music of (used to indicate who created or performed the music)
additional_notes: Followed by a person, group, or source. Equivalent to 'music by [someone]' in English. Can refer to composer, performer, or origin (e.g. 'Musik von Mozart', 'Musik von Joy Division', or 'Musik von einem Grammophon'). Word order: 'die Musik von X' or simply 'Musik von X'.
target_language_example: Hörst du gern die Musik von Beethoven?
native_language_example: Do you like Beethoven's music?

meaning: ‘Courage is…’ — used to make statements about courage (Mut) as a quality.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the phrase 'Mut ist' starts sentences that evaluate or describe courage. 'Mut' = courage/bravery; 'ist' = is. Common in sentences like 'Mut ist die beste Verteidigung' (Courage is the best defense). Useful for short statements or proverbs about bravery.
target_language_example: Mut ist oft wichtiger als Erfahrung.
native_language_example: Courage is often more important than experience.

meaning: to encourage; to give someone confidence or courage.
additional_notes: Used when you want to support or reassure someone so they feel braver or more confident. Common with indirect object in dative: jemandem Mut machen (e.g., Ich mache dir Mut). Can be used for people or groups and in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir Mut machen — du schaffst das!
native_language_example: I want to encourage you — you can do it!

meaning: call (one's) mother (on the phone).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase 'jemanden anrufen' (to call someone) with the object 'Mutter' (mother). In German the separable verb 'anrufen' often splits: e.g. 'rief sie ihre Mutter an' (she called her mother). Use appropriate pronouns and word order: past tense 'rief ... an', present 'ruft ... an', imperative 'Ruf / Rufen Sie ... an'.
target_language_example: Sie ruft heute Abend ihre Mutter an.
native_language_example: She will call her mother tonight.

meaning: '(and) your/their mother too' or a short retort meaning 'same to you' when referencing someone's mother
additional_notes: In the examples, 'Mutter auch' is used in two ways: literally to say that someone’s mother is also named Mary (sentence 1: 'dessen Mutter auch Mary heißt' — here 'auch' modifies 'Mutter'), and as a short spoken retort (sentences 2–3) meaning 'your mother too' or 'same to you' — often informal and sometimes teasing or rude. When used as a retort it usually stands alone or follows 'und' ('Und Mutter auch' / 'Und deine Mutter auch'). Tone and context determine whether it's playful or insulting.
target_language_example: A: Du hast gewonnen. B: Und deine Mutter auch!
native_language_example: A: You won. B: And your mother too!

meaning: with/for (one's) mother while doing something; 'help/assist mother with' (used before a verb in -en form, e.g. beim Kochen = with cooking).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'Mutter' (mother) with the preposition + article contraction 'beim' (bei + dem) and is followed by a noun formed from a verb (a gerund-like noun, e.g. 'Kochen', 'Abwasch'). It expresses doing or helping with an activity together with or for one's mother. Use dative for the person: 'meiner Mutter beim ... helfen' or 'der Mutter beim ... helfen'.
target_language_example: Ich helfe meiner Mutter beim Putzen.
native_language_example: I help my mother with the cleaning.

meaning: refers to whether one's mother lets or has someone take the trash outside (i.e. 'Does your mother let [you/someone] take the trash out?').
additional_notes: This multi-word string is a fragment rather than a complete sentence; in natural German it appears within sentences using the verb lassen (e.g. 'Lässt deine Mutter dich den Müll nach draußen bringen/tragen?'). 'Nach' combines with 'draußen' (nach draußen) to indicate 'out'. The phrase can be used with different pronouns (dich, euch, Sie) and with bringen/tragen depending on context. Informal register typically uses 'dich/euch'; formal uses 'Sie'.
target_language_example: Lässt dich deine Mutter den Müll nach draußen bringen?
native_language_example: Does your mother let you take the trash outside?

meaning: the mother of (the ...).
additional_notes: A genitive construction meaning 'the mother of [someone]'. Often followed by a noun in the genitive (e.g. 'des Jungen' = 'of the boy'). In everyday spoken German the genitive is sometimes replaced by 'die Mutter von ...' (e.g. 'die Mutter von dem Jungen'). Use 'des' for masculine or neuter singular genitive (strong article).
target_language_example: Die Mutter des Mannes wartet draußen.
native_language_example: The mother of the man is waiting outside.

meaning: 'mother goes' or 'mother is doing' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's the noun 'Mutter' (mother) plus the verb 'gehen' (to go) or the 3rd-person singular of 'gehen' used in different contexts. 1) 'Mutter geht' can mean 'mother goes' (she goes somewhere) — often followed by a destination or purpose: e.g. 'Mutter geht auf den Markt.' 2) In contexts with 'wie es ... geht' (wie es ihrer Mutter geht), 'geht' is part of the idiom 'wie es jemandem geht' meaning 'how someone is doing/feeling' (not physical movement). Pay attention to word order and pronouns/case: 'Meiner Mutter geht es gut' = 'My mother is well.'
target_language_example: Meiner Mutter geht es gut; sie geht jeden Tag spazieren.
native_language_example: My mother is well; she goes for a walk every day.

meaning: said mother / what (one's) mother said; depends on context — can refer to what the mother said or the act of saying something to the mother
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short sequence combining Mutter (mother) and gesagt (said). Meaning depends on word order, tense and grammatical case. Examples: as part of a clause reporting speech ("was deine Mutter gesagt hat" = "what your mother said") or as part of a question about telling something to the mother ("Hast du das deiner Mutter gesagt?" = "Did you tell your mother?"). Pay attention to pronouns (deiner/ihre/seiner) and word order (verb placement in German clauses).
target_language_example: Du hast gehört, was deine Mutter gesagt hat.
native_language_example: You heard what your mother said.

meaning: 'my/your/the mother has [done something to/for] me' — a clause showing actions by someone's mother that affect the speaker (or the person addressed).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a fragment: 'Mutter hat mich' begins a sentence where 'Mutter' is the subject and 'mich' is the accusative object. The full meaning depends on the verb and context that follow (e.g. bezahlt, angerufen, säubern lassen, nicht gesehen). Word order: in perfect tense use 'hat' + past participle (Meine Mutter hat mich angerufen = My mother called me). Can refer to the speaker ('me') or to 'you' if 'deine Mutter hat mich...' (your mother...).
target_language_example: Meine Mutter hat mich gestern überrascht.
native_language_example: My mother surprised me yesterday.

meaning: to help (one's) mother.
additional_notes: Common phrase using the dative: 'der Mutter' or possessive pronouns (deiner/eurer/ihrer/Ihrer) indicate whose mother. Verb 'helfen' requires the dative case for the person receiving help. Can be used in commands, obligations, or statements about assisting one's mother with tasks.
target_language_example: Du musst deiner Mutter helfen.
native_language_example: You have to help your mother.

meaning: a pattern meaning 'my/your/his/her mother is a ...' used to describe someone's mother
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the subject 'Mutter' with the verb 'ist' and the indefinite article 'eine' to introduce a noun or adjective phrase describing the mother. Change the possessive (meine/deine/seine/ihre) and adjective/noun as needed. Word order and gender matter: 'eine' is used because Mutter is feminine. If the complement is an adjective describing the mother without a noun, you can say 'meine Mutter ist (sehr) nett' (no article).
target_language_example: Meine Mutter ist eine tolle Lehrerin.
native_language_example: My mother is a great teacher.

meaning: to see (one's) mother; to visit or meet one's mother.
additional_notes: Simple verb phrase: sehen (to see) + Mutter (mother). Used to say someone wants to meet, visit, or have a meeting with their mother. Context determines whether it's a brief visit, a planned meeting, or an emotional reunion. Often appears with possessive pronouns (meine Mutter, deine Mutter, seine Mutter) or names to clarify whose mother is meant.
target_language_example: Gloria will unbedingt ihre Mutter sehen.
native_language_example: Gloria really wants to see her mother.

meaning: to be a mother
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'to be a mother' (biological or role). In sentences it can be used in identification (That must be my mother), hypothetical/desire contexts (I would be a mother now), or asking if someone will take on the role (Do you want to be our mother?). Verb 'sein' is conjugated as needed.
target_language_example: Sie möchte später Mutter sein.
native_language_example: She wants to be a mother later.

meaning: ‘mother and I’ — refers to the speaker together with their mother.
additional_notes: Used to talk about actions, states or opinions involving the speaker plus their mother. Word order can vary ("Mutter und ich" or "Meine Mutter und ich" or "Deine Mutter und ich") depending on context and possessive. In German, subject pronouns like "ich" remain second in coordinated subjects ("Mutter und ich sind..."), but in casual speech people sometimes drop the possessive pronoun ("Mutter und ich" instead of "meine Mutter und ich").
target_language_example: Mutter und ich gehen morgen zum Arzt.
native_language_example: Mother and I are going to the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: mother of (someone); used to indicate someone's mother or to send regards via someone.
additional_notes: A simple genitive/possessive construction: 'Mutter von X' = 'the mother of X'. Common in spoken and written German. Can also be used in phrases like 'Grüß deine Mutter von uns' (send our greetings to your mother) or in titles/roles ('als Mutter von Pendragon' = 'as the mother of Pendragon'). Word order: you can also say 'Xs Mutter' (Pendragons Mutter) for possessive form. Polite/formal: 'Grüßen Sie Ihre Mutter von mir' uses formal 'Sie' and 'Ihre'.
target_language_example: Grüß die Mutter von Anna von mir.
native_language_example: Give Anna's mother my regards.

meaning: 'the girl who/that' (relative clause marker referring to a girl)
additional_notes: Mädchen is neuter in German (das Mädchen) even though it means a female person. Use das as the relative pronoun for neuter singular nouns: 'das ...' = 'who/that ...' in English. In spoken German you may also hear 'die' used colloquially, but standard grammar uses 'das' with Mädchen. The clause that follows describes or identifies the girl.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen, das neben der Schule wohnt, ist sehr nett.
native_language_example: The girl who lives next to the school is very nice.

meaning: 'the girl with (whom)'. Used to introduce a relative clause with the preposition 'mit' (with).
additional_notes: This is the structure for forming relative clauses when the relative pronoun is object of the preposition 'mit'. In spoken/written German you normally say 'mit dem/mit der/mit denen' depending on gender and number: 'mit dem' for masculine/neuter dative singular, 'mit der' for feminine dative singular, and 'mit denen' for plural. For people you often translate as 'with whom' or simply 'who/that ... with' in English (e.g. 'the girl with whom Tom was'). In informal English you can usually say 'the girl Tom was with.'
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen, mit dem ich gestern gesprochen habe.
native_language_example: That's the girl I spoke with yesterday.

meaning: 'to look like a girl' or 'to appear as a girl'.
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase sehen ... aus (aussehen) with a comparison: 'wie ein Mädchen' = 'like a girl'. German word order places aus after the verb (er sieht ... aus). It can describe appearance (sentences 1,2,4,5,6). Note sentence 3 uses 'mit den anderen Mädchen auskommen' (to get along with the other girls) — here 'Mädchen' is part of a different verb phrase (auskommen) and not 'aussehen'. Pay attention to context: aussehen = appearance; auskommen = getting along.
target_language_example: Sie sieht heute aus wie ein Mädchen aus dem Urlaubskatalog.
native_language_example: She looks today like a girl from the holiday catalogue.

meaning: "you are a girl" — phrase order where Mädchen precedes bist; typically part of a larger sentence or used for emphasis/poetic/questioning
additional_notes: Combines Mädchen (girl) and bist (2nd-person singular of "sein"). Standard neutral order is "du bist ein Mädchen" or "du bist Mädchen". The sequence "Mädchen bist" occurs in inverted word order (e.g., for emphasis, in questions, or in coordinated/contrastive structures: "Das bin ich, und das Mädchen bist du"). Note: Mädchen is grammatically neuter (das Mädchen) but refers to a female; verbs agree with the person (du bist).
target_language_example: Das bin ich, und das Mädchen bist du.
native_language_example: That's me, and the girl is you.

meaning: literally 'girls have' — the verb 'haben' used with the plural noun 'Mädchen' (girls) to form statements like 'the girls have (done/been...)'.
additional_notes: Mädchen is a neuter noun in German (das Mädchen) but its plural is Mädchen (same form). When talking about more than one girl, use plural verb forms (haben). The exact meaning depends on the rest of the sentence (e.g., 'haben gewonnen' = 'have won', 'haben getanzt' = 'have danced', 'haben gesehen' = 'saw/ have seen'). Word order and tense follow normal German grammar.
target_language_example: Die Mädchen haben gestern im Park gespielt.
native_language_example: The girls played in the park yesterday.

meaning: 'the girl has' (auxiliary + subject).
additional_notes: Mädchen = 'girl' (neuter noun in German: das Mädchen). 'hat' is the 3rd-person singular present of 'haben' and is used as an auxiliary for the perfect tense (e.g., 'hat gefangen' = 'has caught') or as a main verb meaning 'has' (possession). In spoken/written German you will often see 'hat' combined with a past participle (perfect tense) or used with objects/clauses (e.g., 'Welches Mädchen hat dir das gegeben?'). Pronoun agreement: although a girl is female, the noun is grammatically neuter, but verbs use 3rd-person singular forms.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen hat gestern ein Buch gelesen.
native_language_example: The girl has read a book yesterday.

meaning: "the girl here" or "the girl (who is) here".
additional_notes: A simple noun phrase combining Mädchen (girl) with hier (here). Used to refer to a specific girl present in the location or context. In German word order you can place hier after the noun for emphasis on location. Mädchen is neuter (das Mädchen) even though it refers to a female person; adjectives and articles agree with neuter gender. Context determines whether it means 'this girl here' or 'the girl who was/is here'.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen hier heißt Anna.
native_language_example: The girl here is called Anna.

meaning: 'the girl in' (followed by a place or clothing).
additional_notes: A short phrase used to identify or describe a specific girl by saying where she is or what she is wearing. 'Mädchen' = girl (neuter noun), 'im' is the contraction of 'in dem' and means 'in the' for masculine/neuter singular nouns. You will usually see it followed by a noun (place, item of clothing, etc.), e.g. 'im Zirkus' (in the circus), 'im rosa Kleid' (in the pink dress).
target_language_example: Wer ist das Mädchen im roten Mantel?
native_language_example: Who is the girl in the red coat?

meaning: 'girl in' — used to refer to a girl described by the clothing, location, age group, or situation that follows 'in'.
additional_notes: Mädchen is 'girl' (neuter noun). 'in' is a preposition meaning 'in' or 'wearing' depending on context. After 'in' the following noun may take the dative or accusative depending on movement vs. location; often you will see dative with static descriptions (e.g. 'in dem rosa Kleid' → 'in the pink dress'). Commonly used to point out which girl by describing what she wears or where she is (e.g. 'das Mädchen in Weiß' = 'the girl in white'). Also used in phrases like 'ein Mädchen in Sosukes Alter' = 'a girl in Sosuke's age' (meaning 'a girl around Sosuke's age').
target_language_example: Wer ist das Mädchen in dem roten Mantel?
native_language_example: Who is the girl in the red coat?

meaning: “girls in my…” — start of a phrase meaning the girls who are in (my) [class, family, group].
additional_notes: This is a fragment used before a noun (usually Klasse, Schule, Familie, Gruppe). Word order: "die Mädchen in meiner Klasse" = the girls in my class. When referring to possession, the following noun (Klasse, Schule etc.) determines the correct article and case. Common in comparisons or descriptions (Kein(e) der Mädchen in meiner Klasse ...).
target_language_example: Die Mädchen in meiner Klasse sind sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: The girls in my class are very friendly.

meaning: 'the girl is' (or 'the girl has' in some perfect/passive contexts) — simple subject + verb 'sein' used in sentences about a girl.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the noun Mädchen (girl) plus the verb ist (is). Use it to describe a girl (state, condition, location) or as part of passive/perfect constructions when combined with past participles (e.g. 'ist entführt worden' = 'has been kidnapped'). Remember Mädchen is grammatically neuter (das Mädchen) but refers to a female person. Word order and helping verbs can change meaning: 'Das Mädchen ist entführt worden' = 'The girl has been kidnapped.' 'Aus dem Mädchen ist eine Frau geworden' uses 'ist geworden' (has become).
target_language_example: Das Mädchen ist gestern gerettet worden.
native_language_example: The girl was rescued yesterday.

meaning: "the girl is" (used to describe or identify a girl)
additional_notes: Mädchen = 'girl' (neuter noun in German: das Mädchen). 'ist' = 'is' (3rd person singular of sein). Used to state location, profession, appearance, identity, condition, etc. Word order can change: you can say 'Das Mädchen ist ...' or use 'Dieses Mädchen ist ...'. Note that 'Mädchen' is grammatically neuter, but refers to a female person.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen ist meine Schwester.
native_language_example: The girl is my sister.

meaning: a girl with (used to describe a girl plus a feature, object, or who is accompanied by someone)
additional_notes: Mädchen = girl (neuter noun: das Mädchen). 'mit' = with. Together 'Mädchen mit ...' introduces a description or accompaniment (e.g. physical trait, object, or person). The noun phrase that follows uses the dative case after 'mit' (dem/der/den + adjective endings as needed). Common in spoken and written German to identify or describe someone.
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen mit den langen Haaren.
native_language_example: That's the girl with the long hair.

meaning: 'the girl looks' or 'the girl appears' (used to describe someone's appearance or how they seem)
additional_notes: Often used with 'aus wie' or 'wie' + noun/pronoun to say someone resembles or appears like someone/something: 'Das Mädchen sieht aus wie seine Mutter' = The girl looks like his/ her mother. Word order can change: 'Das Mädchen sieht (wie seine Mutter) aus' or 'Das Mädchen sieht aus wie...'. In present tense 'sieht' is the 3rd person singular of 'sehen' used in the fixed expression 'sich (irgendwie) aussehen' constructions meaning 'to look/appear'.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen sieht heute glücklich aus.
native_language_example: The girl looks happy today.

meaning: literally 'girl of' — used to describe a girl associated with a place, person, or group (e.g. 'the girl next door', 'the girls from ...').
additional_notes: Mädchen means 'girl'. When followed by von + noun, it indicates origin, association, or belonging (e.g. von nebenan = 'from next door'; von der Villa Borghese = 'from the Villa Borghese'). In English you often translate this as 'the girl next door', 'the girls from...', or 'the girl of/for...'. Word order and articles can change: 'das Mädchen von nebenan' or 'die Mädchen von der Villa Borghese'.
target_language_example: Sie ist das Mädchen von nebenan, das jeder kennt.
native_language_example: She is the girl next door whom everyone knows.

meaning: 'the girl was' — past-tense description referring to a female child/person
additional_notes: Mädchen = girl (can mean a child or young woman). 'war' is the simple past (Präteritum) of 'sein' (to be). Together they start a past-tense statement about a girl: her state, feelings, age in the past, or characteristics. Common in descriptions (Das Mädchen war nervös.), age phrases (als sie ein kleines Mädchen war = when she was a little girl), and with reflexive constructions (war sich ... bewusst = was aware). Word order may continue with adjectives, prepositional phrases, infinitive constructions, or clauses.
target_language_example: Das Mädchen war gestern sehr müde.
native_language_example: The girl was very tired yesterday.

meaning: 'girl' used in combination with the particle 'zu' (to/too) often appearing before an infinitive or as part of constructions where 'zu' links the noun with a verb or adjective phrase (e.g., 'Mädchen zu sehen' — 'to see a girl').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence where the noun Mädchen is followed by the particle zu. 'Mädchen' is a neuter noun (das Mädchen) with plural identical (die Mädchen). 'Zu' can be the infinitival marker (followed by an infinitive), a preposition in some dialects/contexts, or part of comparative constructions ('zu jung' = 'too young'). The meaning depends entirely on the construction: e.g. 'Mädchen zu sehen' = 'to see a girl'; 'Mädchen zu treffen' = 'to meet girls'; 'wie ein kleines Mädchen zu heulen' = 'to cry like a little girl'.
target_language_example: Es tut mir im Herz weh, dieses arme Mädchen zu sehen.
native_language_example: It hurts my heart to see this poor girl.

meaning: ‘men and…’ — the phrase 'Männer und' is the beginning of a noun phrase meaning 'men and (other group, usually women)'.
additional_notes: Used to list men together with another group (most commonly 'Frauen' = women). In German word order the two nouns are joined by 'und' (and). Often completed by 'Frauen' but can pair 'Männer' with other nouns. Useful in plural statements about people (counts, generalizations, actions).
target_language_example: Männer und Frauen arbeiten oft zusammen.
native_language_example: Men and women often work together.

meaning: literally 'murderer is' — used as part of sentences stating or identifying who the murderer is.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the words 'der Mörder ist' (or variations like 'ein Mörder ist') commonly appear when identifying or talking about a murderer. 'Mörder' = murderer (noun). 'ist' = is (3rd person singular of 'sein'). Word order may change in questions or subordinate clauses (e.g. 'wer der Mörder ist' = 'who the murderer is').
target_language_example: Ich weiß, wer der Mörder ist.
native_language_example: I know who the murderer is.

meaning: 'my (female) neighbor is...' used to describe who or what the neighbor is (nationality, profession, appearance, character).
additional_notes: Nachbarin = female neighbor (noun, feminine). The pattern 'Meine Nachbarin ist …' is a simple subject–verb–complement sentence: use an adjective, a noun with an article or a nationality (capitalized in German), or a profession (often capitalized when used as a noun like 'Ärztin'). For nationality and professions, you can say 'Meine Nachbarin ist Französin / Ärztin.' For adjectives use the appropriate form: 'Meine Nachbarin ist nett.'
target_language_example: Meine Nachbarin ist Lehrerin und sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: My (female) neighbor is a teacher and very friendly.

meaning: for the whole afternoon / all afternoon
additional_notes: Used after a noun phrase with a time expression (den ganzen Nachmittag / den Nachmittag) + über to indicate an action lasted through that period. Common structure: [subject] + [verb] + [den ganzen/den] Nachmittag über + [rest]. Equivalent to 'den ganzen Nachmittag' but emphasizes duration. Informal register is neutral; widely used in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Wir haben den ganzen Nachmittag über im Park gelesen.
native_language_example: We read in the park all afternoon.

meaning: a message/news (that) has (done something) — 'hat' is the auxiliary verb used with 'Nachricht' in perfect tenses
additional_notes: This combination shows the noun 'Nachricht' (news, message) used with the auxiliary 'hat' to form the perfect tense (e.g., 'hat sich verbreitet', 'hat uns getroffen', 'hat mich erreicht'). 'Nachricht' can mean 'news' (information about events) or 'message' (a communication). The helper 'hat' agrees with the subject of the clause and is followed by a past participle. In many examples the sentence would be: 'Die Nachricht hat ... [past participle]'.
target_language_example: Die Nachricht hat mich sehr überrascht.
native_language_example: The news surprised me a lot.

meaning: to send a message (a note, text, or short communication).
additional_notes: Common verb phrase used for sending a message by text, email, card, or with an item (e.g., sending flowers with a message). Can be followed by a recipient (jemandem eine Nachricht schicken) or by what it costs/means. Uses dative for the person: jemandem eine Nachricht schicken.
target_language_example: Ich sollte dir heute eine Nachricht schicken.
native_language_example: I should send you a message today.

meaning: to receive messages (e.g. texts, emails, notifications).
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask whether someone has received one or more messages. 'Nachrichten' here means messages (not necessarily news). 'bekommen' = to get/receive. Use appropriate pronoun and verb form: Haben Sie ...? / Hast du ...? / Habt ihr ...?
target_language_example: Hast du meine Nachrichten bekommen?
native_language_example: Did you get my messages?

meaning: 'during the night on' or 'spent the night on/in (somewhere)'.
additional_notes: Used to say where someone spent a night. Often appears in constructions like 'die Nacht auf dem Sofa verbringen/zugebracht haben' or 'in jener Nacht auf dem Fußboden schlafen'. Word order can vary (e.g. 'die Nacht auf dem Sofa verbringen' or 'in jener Nacht auf dem Sofa'). 'auf' governs the following noun phrase with the appropriate article and case (usually Dative: auf dem Sofa, auf dem Fußboden; but if motion is implied, Accusative).
target_language_example: Sie verbrachte die Nacht auf dem Sofa.
native_language_example: She spent the night on the sofa.

meaning: to spend the night at (someone's place).
additional_notes: Used with a person in dative (bei + name/pronoun) to say that someone stayed/slept at that person's home for one night or during a specific night. Common patterns: 'eine Nacht bei jemandem übernachten', 'die Nacht bei ihm/dir verbringen', or 'in jener Nacht bei Tom sein'. Time words (eine Nacht, die Nacht, jene Nacht) often appear before 'bei'.
target_language_example: Ich habe letzte Woche eine Nacht bei Anna übernachtet.
native_language_example: I spent one night at Anna's last week.

meaning: to drive through the whole night / to keep driving all night
additional_notes: Used to say someone drove continuously during the night without stopping to sleep. Often appears as a question (Bist du ...?) or statement (Ich bin ...). 'Durchgefahren' is the past participle of 'durchfahren' in the sense of continuing to drive; context shows continuous action overnight.
target_language_example: Wir sind die ganze Nacht durchgefahren, um rechtzeitig anzukommen.
native_language_example: We drove through the whole night to arrive on time.

meaning: used to say 'one/a (something) last night' or 'during the night (a...)' — combines Nacht (night) with an indefinite object (einen...).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but shows the pattern 'Nacht' (often with a time word like letzte/gestern/letzte Nacht/past night) + accusative object (einen ...). It appears in sentences like 'letzte Nacht einen Traum haben' (to have a dream last night) or 'letzte Nacht einen Brief schreiben' (to write a letter last night). Remember to use the correct article case: 'einen' is masculine accusative. If the noun is feminine use 'eine' (letzte Nacht eine Nachricht), neuter 'ein' (letzte Nacht ein Geräusch).
target_language_example: Letzte Nacht einen langen Film gesehen habe ich nicht.
native_language_example: I didn't watch a long movie last night.

meaning: used in time expressions to mean 'night after night' (repeatedly each night) or in contexts like 'last night' when combined with a modifier; depends on construction.
additional_notes: Nacht für appears in German in two main patterns: 1) 'Nacht für Nacht' (or 'Tag für Tag') = 'night after night' — a repetitive, habitual action. 2) with a time word like 'letzte Nacht' or 'gestern Nacht' you would not normally split with 'für'; example 3 in the input uses 'letzte Nacht ... für diese Prüfung' where 'für' belongs to the verb phrase (lernen für = study for). So pay attention to which words 'für' connects to: in 'Nacht für Nacht' ('night for night') it's idiomatic and compositional meaning 'repeatedly every night'. In sentences like 'letzte Nacht für diese Prüfung lernen' the 'für' belongs to 'lernen für (etwas)' = 'study for (an exam)'.
target_language_example: Er arbeitete Nacht für Nacht, bis das Projekt fertig war.
native_language_example: He worked night after night until the project was finished.

meaning: literally 'night here' — used to talk about spending or being at a place during the night.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; a combination of Nacht (night) + hier (here). Common uses: saying you'll stay at a place all night (Ich bleibe die Nacht hier), suggesting someone spend the night here (Du kannst die Nacht hier verbringen), or describing when something happened (mitten in der Nacht hier). Word order in full sentences usually places 'die Nacht' before the verb or after modal verbs.
target_language_example: Wir müssen nicht nach Hause gehen — wir können die Nacht hier bleiben.
native_language_example: We don't have to go home — we can stay here for the night.

target_language_multi_word_term: in den Schlaf weinen / sich in den Schlaf weinen (Nacht in den ...)
meaning: to cry oneself to sleep (lit.: to cry into sleep)
additional_notes: Common reflexive construction: 'sich in den Schlaf weinen' or with time phrases: 'jede Nacht in den Schlaf' = 'every night, (someone) cries themself to sleep'. Used to describe falling asleep as a result of crying. Word order varies: time expression (e.g. 'jede Nacht') can come before or after the verb. 'in den Schlaf' is a fixed accusative phrase meaning 'into sleep.'
target_language_example: Sie weint sich jede Nacht in den Schlaf.
native_language_example: She cries herself to sleep every night.

meaning: 'at night' or 'during the night' when used with a verb in perfect or present tenses (literally: 'night is').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the noun 'Nacht' with the verb 'ist' used in time expressions like 'In der Nacht ist ...' (During the night, ...). English usually uses 'at night', 'during the night' or 'last night' depending on context. With 'letzte' (last) you say 'Letzte Nacht ist ...' or 'In der Nacht' for a more general 'during the night'. Often followed by a past action: 'ist passiert', 'ist gestohlen worden', etc.
target_language_example: In der Nacht ist mein Telefon weggekommen.
native_language_example: During the night my phone disappeared.

meaning: all night; throughout the night.
additional_notes: Used after a time expression (often with 'die ganze') to say something lasts for the entire night. Commonly appears as 'die ganze Nacht lang' or simply 'die ganze Nacht'. Word order: 'die ganze Nacht lang' or 'die ganze Nacht' + verb. Emphasizes duration; interchangeable with 'die ganze Nacht' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Wir haben die ganze Nacht lang getanzt.
native_language_example: We danced all night long.

meaning: 'not (during) night' or 'didn't (at) night' — the noun Nacht ('night') combined with the negation 'nicht' to indicate that something did not occur during a particular night or that something will/would not happen/continue during the night.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a compositional combination. In German the exact word order and case often change: common variants include 'in der Nacht nicht', 'letzte Nacht nicht', 'diese Nacht nicht', 'nächste Nacht nicht' or 'jener/jenen Nacht nicht' depending on context. 'Nicht' negates the verb or clause; placement of 'nicht' relative to time phrases can shift emphasis. Use appropriate articles or time words when needed (z. B. 'in der Nacht nicht' for general nights, 'letzte Nacht nicht' for a specific past night).
target_language_example: Hast du dich in der Nacht nicht mit Jin-tae getroffen?
native_language_example: Didn't you meet Jin-tae during the night?

meaning: "(during) night saw" — the nouns 'Nacht' (night) and the past-tense verb 'sah' (saw); together they appear when talking about what someone saw during the night.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the word 'Nacht' (or a time expression like 'letzte Nacht', 'in jener Nacht', 'während der Nacht') followed by the past tense of 'sehen' (sah). Use it to say what someone saw at night. Word order in German often places the time expression at the beginning: 'Letzte Nacht sah ich...' = 'Last night I saw...'.
target_language_example: Letzte Nacht sah ich helle Lichter am Himmel.
native_language_example: Last night I saw bright lights in the sky.

meaning: The combination of 'Nacht' (night) with the preposition 'von' used after a time expression (e.g. 'letzte Nacht', 'jede Nacht') to mark the object of verbs like 'träumen' — i.e. 'to dream about/of (someone or something)'.
additional_notes: 'Nacht von' is not a fixed standalone phrase; it appears as part of constructions like 'letzte Nacht von ...' or 'jede Nacht von ...' where 'von' introduces the person/thing dreamed about. Use appropriate pronoun cases after 'von' (e.g. 'von dir', 'von euch', 'von Ihnen'). The literal translation is possible ('night of/about'), but English normally renders it as 'last night I dreamed about...' or 'I dream about ... every night.'
target_language_example: Ich habe letzte Nacht von Ihnen geträumt.
native_language_example: Last night I dreamed about you (formal).

meaning: literally 'night becomes' — not a fixed phrase on its own; part of expressions meaning 'it becomes night' or 'night is coming'.
additional_notes: Not an independent idiom; typically appears within sentences (e.g., with 'es wird Nacht' or followed by an adjective/clause). By itself it is uncommon; you need context or an impersonal 'es' (Es wird Nacht) or another verb/phrase after 'wird'.
target_language_example: Wenn Nacht wird, schließen wir die Fenster.
native_language_example: When night comes, we'll close the windows.

meaning: over the night / during the night (throughout the night).
additional_notes: Used after a time word (here 'Nacht') with 'über' to mean 'throughout' or 'during the whole night'. Often appears as 'die ganze Nacht über' (the whole night). It can describe something kept open/left on, someone staying somewhere, or actions/events that lasted the night (e.g. talking, being together). Word order: time phrase typically comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Wir haben die ganze Nacht über Karten gespielt.
native_language_example: We played cards throughout the night.

meaning: 'name for' — used to say that a particular name is suitable/appropriate for a person or thing.
additional_notes: Followed by the person or thing that would bear the name (dative/accusative context depends on sentence). Commonly used to give an opinion about whether a name fits someone/something (e.g., a baby, pet, character). Can be used with verbs like sein/werden/geben (ist/ wäre/geben).
target_language_example: Luna ist ein guter Name für die Katze.
native_language_example: Luna is a good name for the cat.

meaning: the name was
additional_notes: Used to report what someone's or something's name used to be or to introduce the name of someone/something in past reference. Common in sentences like "Der Name war ..." or "Sein Name war ...". Not a fixed idiom — simply two words: "Name" (noun) + "war" (past of "sein"). Word order and articles may vary (e.g. "Der Name war Anna.").
target_language_example: Der Name war Anna, aber jetzt verwendet sie einen Künstlernamen.
native_language_example: The name was Anna, but now she uses a stage name.

meaning: ‘name was’ — passive construction indicating something happened to someone's name (was mentioned, removed, spelled, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the start of a passive sentence with the noun 'Name' and the auxiliary 'wurde' (simple past passive of 'werden'). It is followed by a past participle (e.g. erwähnt, gestrichen, falsch geschrieben, entfernt). Use to report actions done to a name. For present passive use 'wird' (e.g. 'Dein Name wird erwähnt').
target_language_example: Dein Name wurde gestern von der Liste gestrichen.
native_language_example: Your name was removed from the list yesterday.

meaning: in the name of (the)...
additional_notes: Used to indicate acting with the authority, on behalf, or invoking the power of someone or something named after the phrase (usually followed by a genitive noun: 'des Vaters'). Common in formal, religious, or ceremonial phrases (e.g. prayers, blessings, commands). Word order: 'im Namen des ...' = 'in the name of the ...'.
target_language_example: Im Namen des Volkes verurteile ich dich.
native_language_example: In the name of the people, I condemn you.

meaning: 'name for' — used when talking about a name chosen or needed for someone or something.
additional_notes: Usually appears with a noun (e.g. 'euer Kind', 'unsere Gruppe') or pronoun and often with verbs like 'auswählen', 'ausgesucht haben', 'einigen (uns auf)', or 'haben'. Common in contexts of naming babies, groups, projects, or withdrawing a name from consideration. Word order: 'einen Namen für X'.
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einen Namen für unser Haustier?
native_language_example: Have you already chosen a name for our pet?

meaning: a (given) name for the… / 'name for the' (used when asking about or choosing a name for a baby/child).
additional_notes: This phrase is used when talking about picking a name for a baby or child. In full sentences you'll usually add the noun (e.g. 'Kind' or 'Baby') after 'das' or use 'für das Kind/Baby' directly. Common verbs with this phrase are 'auswählen/ausgesucht haben' (to choose/to have chosen) and 'müssen' (must). Word order: 'einen Namen für das Kind ausgesucht' or question: 'Hast du schon einen Namen für das Baby ausgesucht?'.
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einen Namen für das Baby ausgesucht?
native_language_example: Have you already chosen a name for the baby?

meaning: called (my) name; shouted someone's name.
additional_notes: Used to report hearing someone call a person's name. Often appears in past tense reports (e.g., "ich hörte, wie jemand meinen Namen rief"). The literal words are 'name' + 'called' (rufen = to call/shout). You can change the possessor (meinen, deinen, ihren) or tense (ruft, rief, hat gerufen).
target_language_example: Ich hörte, wie jemand laut meinen Namen rief.
native_language_example: I heard someone loudly call my name.

meaning: the names of (something or someone)
additional_notes: Used to indicate possession or association: the names that belong to or are related to a group, list, category, etc. Often appears in constructions like 'den Namen von ...' (accusative) when talking about removing, writing down, learning, or mentioning names. Word order can vary: 'die Namen von Tieren' = 'the names of animals'.
target_language_example: Schreib die Namen von drei Personen auf.
native_language_example: Write down the names of three people.

meaning: to make a fool of (someone); to treat someone as a fool
additional_notes: Literally looks like 'to hold fools'. Used when someone behaves as if another person is foolish or when someone deceives/insults another by treating them like a fool. More common forms include 'jemanden zum Narren halten' (to make a fool of someone). You usually need an object: 'jemanden'.
target_language_example: Er wollte mich doch nicht zum Narren halten.
native_language_example: He didn't really want to make a fool of me.

meaning: trying something new; testing or experimenting with something new (often used as part of the phrase 'etwas Neues ausprobi(e)ren').
additional_notes: 'Neues aus' by itself is not a complete verb phrase; it appears within constructions like 'etwas Neues ausprobiere(n)' or in sentences such as 'Ich probiere gerne einmal etwas Neues aus.' Capitalize 'Neues' when used as a noun. Common in spoken and written German for expressing willingness to try new things.
target_language_example: Ich probiere gerne einmal etwas Neues aus.
native_language_example: I like to try something new once in a while.

meaning: 'the number is' or 'this/that number is' (used to describe a telephone number, an item number, or a situation/thing informally).
additional_notes: Literal: 'Nummer' = number, 'ist' = is. Commonly used about phone numbers (Die Nummer ist besetzt = the number is busy/engaged) or to describe an item/issue (Diese Nummer ist zu groß = this number/size is too big). Context determines whether it refers to a phone number, a size/number, or informally to 'this thing/situation.'
target_language_example: Die Nummer ist falsch; versuch es noch einmal.
native_language_example: The number is wrong; try it again.

meaning: not (have/know) the number; don't have someone's phone number or don't recognize a phone number.
additional_notes: Used with 'haben' or 'kennen' to say you don't have or don't know a phone number. Often appears in full phrases like 'Ich habe deine Nummer nicht' (I don't have your number) or 'Ich kenne diese Nummer nicht' (I don't recognize/know this number). Word order may vary: 'die Nummer nicht' follows the verb/object in negative sentences.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe deine Nummer nicht.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have your number.

meaning: to be useful / to be of use
additional_notes: Formal phrase meaning that something will help or be beneficial. Often used with dative pronouns (mir, dir, Ihnen) or prepositional phrases (für + noun). Equivalent to 'useful' or 'helpful' in English; more formal than 'nützlich sein' but interchangeable in many contexts.
target_language_example: Dieses Buch könnte dir von Nutzen sein.
native_language_example: This book could be useful to you.

meaning: near my house; in the vicinity of my house
additional_notes: Literal phrase using the noun Nähe (nearness, vicinity) + possessive. Commonly used with prepositions: in der Nähe meines Hauses (more natural) or simply 'Nähe meines Hauses' in headings or clipped speech. Indicates location close to the speaker's home.
target_language_example: Der Supermarkt ist in der Nähe meines Hauses.
native_language_example: The supermarket is near my house.

meaning: to be nearby; to be in the vicinity
additional_notes: This exact phrasing 'Nähe sein' is uncommon in standard German; speakers usually say 'in der Nähe sein' or 'nah sein'. 'Nähe sein' may appear in poetic or abbreviated contexts or as part of larger constructions, but by itself it sounds elliptical. It can refer to physical proximity or, more rarely, to emotional closeness when used figuratively.
target_language_example: Er wollte Nähe sein, aber seine Worte klangen distanziert.
native_language_example: He wanted to be close, but his words sounded distant.

target_language_multi_word_term: zu Ohren gekommen / ist mir zu Ohren gekommen
meaning: to hear about something; to learn by hearsay
additional_notes: Used impersonally with dative (mir, dir, ihm, etc.). It means someone heard or learned something from others (not necessarily firsthand). Often introduces reported information: Mir ist zu Ohren gekommen, dass ... = I heard that ...
target_language_example: Mir ist zu Ohren gekommen, dass du eine neue Stelle hast.
native_language_example: I heard that you have a new job.

meaning: 'grandma and' (the start of a phrase referring to grandmother plus another person, usually 'Opa' = grandpa).
additional_notes: Oma und is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of a coordination (A und B). In the example sentences it pairs with 'Opa' (grandpa) or another relative. 'Oma' is informal/familiar for 'grandmother'. When speaking, Germans often shorten and say 'bei Oma und Opa' (at grandma and grandpa's).
target_language_example: Wir besuchen morgen Oma und Opa.
native_language_example: We are visiting grandma and grandpa tomorrow.

meaning: my uncle gave me / my uncle has given me
additional_notes: Used to say that 'my uncle' gave or bought something for the speaker. 'Hat ... geschenkt' or 'hat ... gekauft' are examples of the present perfect (Perfekt) used in spoken/written German to describe a past action. Word order: subject (Mein Onkel) + auxiliary (hat) + indirect object (mir) + direct object (das Geschenk) + past participle (geschenkt/gekauft). 'Mir' is the dative pronoun meaning 'to me'.
target_language_example: Mein Onkel hat mir ein Buch zum Geburtstag geschenkt.
native_language_example: My uncle gave me a book for my birthday.

meaning: 'my/your/his/etc. uncle has' — the verb haben (to have) with 'Onkel' (uncle).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common subject + verb pattern: 'Onkel' (uncle) as the subject and 'hat' (he/she/it has) as the 3rd person singular of 'haben'. Use it to state possessions, relationships, characteristics, abilities, or responsibilities of someone's uncle. Replace the possessive (mein/dein/sein/ihr) to match the owner: 'Mein Onkel hat...', 'Sein Onkel hat...'.
target_language_example: Unser Onkel hat ein Haus am See.
native_language_example: Our uncle has a house by the lake.

meaning: ‘uncle in [place]’ — used to say you are at or visiting your uncle in a specific town or city.
additional_notes: This is the noun 'Onkel' (uncle) followed by the preposition 'in' plus a place (city, town). It appears in sentences like 'bei meinem Onkel in Charleville' or 'meinen Onkel in New York besuchen'. Use 'bei' or no additional preposition depending on context: 'bei meinem Onkel in X' (staying at his place) or 'meinen Onkel in X besuchen' (visit him in that place). Word order and case change: 'bei meinem Onkel in ...' uses dative (meinem), 'meinen Onkel in ... besuchen' uses accusative (meinen).
target_language_example: Ich übernachte dieses Wochenende bei meinem Onkel in München.
native_language_example: I'm staying this weekend with my uncle in Munich.

meaning: '(my/your/etc.) uncle is/has' — used to say something about an uncle, often followed by a past participle like 'gestorben' (died).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun 'Onkel' (uncle) plus the verb 'ist' (is/has, as auxiliary for some intransitive past participles like 'gestorben'). In the example sentences 'ist' is the auxiliary used with the past participle 'gestorben' to form the perfect or simple past meaning 'died'. Replace 'Onkel' with the appropriate possessive (mein, dein, ihr, etc.) to indicate whose uncle. Word order and tense follow normal German rules.
target_language_example: Mein Onkel ist letztes Jahr gestorben.
native_language_example: My uncle died last year.

meaning: 'uncle and' — the start of a coordinated noun phrase (e.g. 'uncle and aunt')
additional_notes: Onkel und is not a fixed phrase by itself; it appears when listing relatives or people (Onkel und Tante = uncle and aunt). In German, the second noun must match case, gender, and number (e.g. 'ihren Onkel und ihre Tante' in accusative). Sometimes fragments like 'Onkel und sonst noch wen' are colloquial and mean 'uncle and who else'.
target_language_example: Sie besuchte ihren Onkel und ihre Tante.
native_language_example: She visited her uncle and her aunt.

meaning: literally 'uncle of' — used to say someone is the uncle of a person or 'an uncle of mine' (one of my uncles).
additional_notes: Use 'der Onkel von + name' to say 'the uncle of [name]'. To talk about one of your uncles in general, say 'ein Onkel von mir' = 'an uncle of mine'. More natural alternative: 'der Onkel von' can be replaced by the genitive 'Onkel + (des/der) ...' in formal contexts (e.g. 'der Onkel Cahits' for 'Cahit's uncle'), but 'von' is common in spoken and beginner German. Gender and articles follow 'Onkel' (der Onkel).
target_language_example: Ein Onkel von mir lebt in Berlin.
native_language_example: An uncle of mine lives in Berlin.

meaning: literally 'uncle lives' — used to say where your uncle lives (subject + verb).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun 'Onkel' (uncle) plus the verb 'wohnt' (lives). You will usually use it in a full sentence with a place: e.g. 'Mein Onkel wohnt in Berlin.' For different subjects change the verb (er wohnt, mein Onkel wohnt). Use possessive (mein/dein) or a name to make it clear whose uncle you mean.
target_language_example: Mein Onkel wohnt in Hamburg.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Hamburg.

meaning: 'the victim is' or 'the sacrifice is' (literal: 'victim/sacrifice is')
additional_notes: Opfer can mean 'victim' (person harmed) or 'sacrifice' (something given up). Context decides which meaning. 'Opfer ist ...' is simply the start of a clause identifying who or what the victim/sacrifice is (e.g. 'Das Opfer ist die Vermieterin' = 'The victim is the landlady'). Not an idiom; grammatical subject + verb. Watch gender and case: 'das Opfer' is neuter.
target_language_example: Das Opfer ist ein Nachbar.
native_language_example: The victim is a neighbor.

meaning: to put (something) in order / to tidy up (something).
additional_notes: This is a verb phrase built from Ordnung (order) plus the infinitive marker zu; it appears in constructions like 'Ordnung zu bringen' or 'Ordnung zu machen' meaning 'to bring into order' or 'to tidy up'. You will usually see a full verb with 'Ordnung zu' (e.g. 'bringen', 'machen', 'halten'). Commonly used when talking about organizing, cleaning, or restoring order. Not a standalone verb: needs the main verb after 'zu'.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, heute im Keller Ordnung zu bringen.
native_language_example: I plan to put the cellar in order today.

meaning: to put (something) in order; to fix, repair, or resolve (a problem, damage, situation)
additional_notes: Common construction: jemanden/etwas in Ordnung bringen = to fix, deal with, or set right someone/something. Can also imply disciplining or taking care of a situation depending on context. Neutral formality; used in everyday and formal contexts. Frequently appears with objects like Probleme, Schaden, Dinge, Situationen.
target_language_example: Er war immer da, um meine Probleme in Ordnung zu bringen.
native_language_example: He was always there to put my problems in order (to fix my problems).

meaning: place of / location of (used as part of a noun phrase: 'place of [something]')
additional_notes: A common noun phrase pattern: Ort + der/die/des + noun = 'place of the...'. Use to specify where something happens or exists (Ort der Stille = place of silence; Ort der Handlung = place of action). Gender and case of the following noun determine the article (der/die/des). Often used in written/descriptive German.
target_language_example: Das ist ein Ort der Ruhe.
native_language_example: That is a place of calm.

meaning: this place / this location (here).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the specific place being referred to (combines Ort = place + hier = here). Common in spoken and written German to point out or stress a location; word order can be `dieser Ort hier` or simply `Ort hier` in context. Literal translation is natural in English.
target_language_example: Dieser Ort hier ist perfekt zum Picknicken.
native_language_example: This place here is perfect for a picnic.

meaning: literally 'place to' — fragment used when 'Ort' (place) appears with infinitive 'zu' or in phrases like 'an einem Ort zu ...' or 'Ort zu betreten' depending on sentence; not a fixed phrase on its own.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone idiom. 'Ort' means 'place' and 'zu' can be part of different grammatical constructions (infinitive with zu: 'zu betreten' = 'to enter'; prepositional phrases: 'an einem solchen Ort' = 'in/at such a place'; or nominal phrases with 'zu' as particle). Beginners should treat 'Ort' and 'zu' separately: learn 'der Ort' = 'place' and the common combinations: 'einen Ort schaffen' (to create a place), 'einen Ort betreten'/'zu betreten' (to enter), 'an einem Ort' (at a place), 'an einem solchen Ort' (in/at such a place), and 'Worte, um ... zu' = 'words to ...'.
target_language_example: Er wollte einen Ort zu besuchen, an dem er Ruhe fand.
native_language_example: He wanted to visit a place where he found peace.

meaning: rises in the east / (the) east (as the direction where the sun) rises
additional_notes: Used with verbs like 'aufgehen' (to rise) to say the sun rises in the east. In German the full phrase is often 'im Osten auf' (im = in the). Here 'Osten auf' is the core content — beginners should learn the common fixed expression 'Die Sonne geht im Osten auf.'
target_language_example: Die Sonne geht im Osten auf.
native_language_example: The sun rises in the east.

meaning: 'seen the park' or 'saw the park' (past participle phrase)
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a sequence: 'Park' (noun) + 'gesehen' (past participle of sehen). It typically appears with a helping verb (haben) or as part of a clause, and requires correct article/case (e.g. 'den Park' in accusative when direct object). Examples can place it together across auxiliary and other words (e.g., 'Ich habe den Park gesehen').
target_language_example: Hast du den Park gesehen? — Ja, ich habe den Park gesehen.
native_language_example: Have you seen the park? — Yes, I have seen the park.

meaning: 'met' or 'ran into (someone) in the park.'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the verb 'treffen' (to meet/meet up/run into) used with the location 'im Park' (in the park). Depending on context, treffen can mean 'meet' (planned) or 'run into' (by chance). Word order in German: location usually follows the verb or appears after the object. Common past forms: ich habe ... getroffen (Perfekt) or ich traf ... (Präteritum).
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich meine alte Nachbarin im Park getroffen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my old neighbor in the park.

meaning: literally 'park is' — the verb phrase 'is' used with 'Park' to state location, condition, or comparison.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom; 'Park' (park) is a noun and 'ist' is the 3rd-person singular of 'sein' (to be). Beginners will see this combination when saying where the park is (location), describing it (quality, accessibility), or making comparisons. Word order and articles matter (Der Park ist..., Dieser Park ist..., Gegenüber dem Park...).
target_language_example: Der Park ist heute sehr voll.
native_language_example: The park is very crowded today.

meaning: park bench
additional_notes: A Parkbank is a bench found in parks or other public outdoor areas. Used to describe sitting, resting, talking, reading, or feeding birds. Common collocations: 'auf der Parkbank sitzen' (to sit on the park bench), 'auf einer Parkbank' (on a bench).
target_language_example: Wir trafen uns auf der Parkbank und unterhielten uns.
native_language_example: We met on the park bench and talked.

meaning: to look for a parking space / to search for a place to park
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when trying to find a place to park a car. Often used with verbs like müssen (had to), lange (for a long time), or when describing a general action (wenn ... würde). Can be separated by other words in a sentence (e.g., nach einem Parkplatz suchen).
target_language_example: Ich musste gestern lange nach einem Parkplatz suchen.
native_language_example: I had to look for a parking space for a long time yesterday.

meaning: a construction combining the noun 'Party' with the particle 'zu' used in infinitival or complement clauses (e.g. to enjoy/attend/tell about a party) — not a fixed idiom but appears in sentences like ‚die Party zu genießen‘ or ‚von der Party zu erzählen‘.
additional_notes: Party is a feminine noun (die Party) borrowed from English. 'zu' here is the infinitive marker or part of a prepositional phrase (e.g. von der Party zu erzählen). The exact form and case depend on the verb and preposition: ‚die Party zu genießen‘ (Akkusativ + zu + infinitive), ‚von der Party zu erzählen‘ (von + Dativ + zu + infinitive), ‚sich auf der Party zu amüsieren‘ (auf + Dativ + zu + infinitive). Pronunciation: [ˈpar.ti]. This entry focuses on the multi-word sequence 'Party zu' as it commonly appears before an infinitive or as part of verbal complements.
target_language_example: Alle außer Tom schienen die Party zu genießen.
native_language_example: Everyone except Tom seemed to enjoy the party.

meaning: to be unlucky; to have bad luck
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say someone experienced misfortune or an unfortunate outcome. Often used in everyday speech: "Du hast Pech" (you're unlucky) or as a sympathetic remark: "Das ist Pech." Not literal — 'Pech' originally means 'pitch' but here means 'bad luck.'
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern wirklich Pech gehabt; zuerst hat der Bus Verspätung, und dann habe ich meinen Geldbeutel verloren — Pech haben eben.
native_language_example: I was really unlucky yesterday; first the bus was late, and then I lost my wallet — just bad luck.

meaning: "The horse is" — the subject 'Pferd' (horse) + the verb 'ist' (is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun Pferd (horse) followed by the 3rd-person singular form of sein (to be). Use it to say something about a horse (e.g., its age, color, condition). In normal speech you would more often see just 'Das Pferd ist ...' or 'Mein Pferd ist ...' rather than 'Pferd ist' alone. 'Ist’s' in sentence 1 is a contraction of 'ist es' (is it) or poetic elision; beginners should learn 'ist' as 'is'.
target_language_example: Das Pferd ist braun.
native_language_example: The horse is brown.

meaning: 'Pizza is' — a phrase used to describe pizza (state, quality, opinion).
additional_notes: This is simply the subject 'Pizza' + verb 'ist' (3rd person singular of 'sein'). Beginners will see it in sentences like 'Pizza ist kalt' or 'Pizza ist mein Lieblingsessen.' Use it to state facts, qualities, or opinions about pizza. Replace 'Pizza' with other nouns to form similar statements (e.g. 'Das Buch ist neu').
target_language_example: Pizza ist heute Abend lecker.
native_language_example: Pizza is tasty tonight.

meaning: literally 'plan has' — used to say a plan possesses or includes something (e.g. advantages).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the verb haben (to have) used with the noun Plan. In sentences like "Unser Plan hat viele Vorteile" it means "Our plan has many advantages." The structure is: [Possessor] + Plan + hat + [object]. In the negative example "Wenn man keinen Plan hat, ..." the phrase means "when one doesn't have a plan." Use haben with appropriate person/number (ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben).
target_language_example: Unser Plan hat genug Zeit für Pausen.
native_language_example: Our plan has enough time for breaks.

meaning: to need space (room); to require physical or personal space
additional_notes: Used when someone or something requires more physical room (e.g., in a crowded area, furniture, luggage) or when a person needs emotional/personal space. Can be used literally or figuratively. Commonly appears with objects (Ich brauche Platz im Koffer.) or personal feelings (Ich brauche etwas Platz von dir.).
target_language_example: Ich brauche heute Abend Platz brauchen, um nachzudenken.
native_language_example: I need some space tonight to think.

meaning: to have room/space (for something) or to have time/availability (for someone/something)
additional_notes: Commonly used for physical space (e.g., in a car, bag, room) and for availability in one’s schedule. Often appears with für (Platz für etwas) or with temporal expressions. Can be used in questions ("Hast du Platz?" / "Hast du Platz für ...?") and in statements ("Ich habe Platz für ..." / "Wir haben noch Platz").
target_language_example: Hast du heute Nachmittag Platz haben, um auf einen Kaffee zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you have time/room this afternoon to go for a coffee?

meaning: a place/space in (often used figuratively: a place in someone's heart or in a location).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show location or figurative placement. Common in phrases like "Platz in meinem Herzen" (a place in my heart). Can be literal (a seat/place in a room) or figurative (emotional significance). Followed by dative (e.g., "in meinem Herzen", "in der Welt").
target_language_example: Du hast immer einen Platz in meinem Herzen.
native_language_example: You will always have a place in my heart.

meaning: to make room; to make space (for someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or order someone to move so there is space. Can be polite (Würden Sie mir bitte Platz machen?) or commanding (Platz machen!). Often followed by 'für' + noun to indicate what the space is for. Common in spoken and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas Platz machen für meinen Koffer?
native_language_example: Can you make a little room for my suitcase?

meaning: to sit down; to take a seat.
additional_notes: Polite, standard expression used to invite someone to sit. Common in formal and informal contexts (use Sie for formal). Literally 'take place/seat' — used when offering or instructing people to sit, e.g. before a meeting, performance, or meal.
target_language_example: Bitte Platz nehmen, die Vorstellung beginnt gleich.
native_language_example: Please take a seat, the performance is about to begin.

meaning: 'place/seat' + coordinating 'and' — the word 'Platz' (place/seat/position) followed by 'und' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's simply the noun Platz used in different senses (seat, spot, rank) and sometimes followed by the conjunction und in a sentence. Pay attention to context: Platz can mean a physical seat (Setz dich auf deinen Platz), a location (einen Platz suchen), or a rank/position (den vierten Platz). The example combination 'Platz und' appears when Platz is directly followed by another clause or action linked with 'und' (and).
target_language_example: Setz dich auf deinen Platz und warte hier.
native_language_example: Sit in your seat and wait here.

meaning: often part of phrases meaning 'room/space to (do something)' or 'place to (do something)'; usually follows a noun like 'Platz' and a verb or infinitive.
additional_notes: Alone 'Platz' means 'space' or 'place'. 'Platz zu' on its own is incomplete; you will usually see it in constructions like 'Platz zu haben' (to have room to do something), 'Platz zu geben' (to give someone space), or 'Platz zum Sitzen' (a place/space to sit). Note the preposition that follows can be 'zu' + infinitive or 'zum' (zu + dem) before a noun. Word order and articles matter: 'Platz zum Sitzen' = 'place to sit', 'Platz zu sitzen' is incorrect.
target_language_example: Hast du noch Platz zum Sitzen?
native_language_example: Do you still have room to sit?

meaning: a poker (game / poker night) taking place this weekend
additional_notes: Intended to mean 'poker this weekend'. Note: correct German spelling is 'Wochenende' (with 'en'); the provided term 'Wochende' is a misspelling. Usage would be understood in casual speech but use the correct spelling in writing. To ask about it you could say: 'Gibt es Poker dieses Wochenende?' or 'Spielen wir Poker dieses Wochenende?'.
target_language_example: Poker dieses Wochende findet bei mir statt.
native_language_example: Poker this weekend is happening at my place.

meaning: 'the police (are) here' or 'is the police here?'.
additional_notes: A short phrase combining Polizei (police) and hier (here). Context determines whether it's a statement ('The police are here') or a question ('Is the police here?'). Word order and intonation matter: 'Die Polizei ist hier.' = statement; 'Ist die Polizei hier?' = question. In colloquial speech people may just say 'Polizei hier?' to ask if police are present. Used when noticing or asking about police presence.
target_language_example: Polizei hier? Was ist passiert?
native_language_example: Police here? What happened?

meaning: 'the police already' or 'have the police ... yet' (depends on sentence)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of 'Polizei' (the police) with the adverb 'schon' (already/yet). 'Schon' often appears in questions or negatives to ask whether something has happened yet (e.g. 'Hat die Polizei schon ...?') or to emphasize that even the police would not do something (e.g. 'Die Polizei schon gar nicht' = 'certainly not the police'). Pay attention to word order: in questions 'schon' can come after the subject or elsewhere depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Hat die Polizei schon den Bericht erhalten?
native_language_example: Have the police already received the report?

meaning: 'to turn oneself in to the police' (to surrender to police custody)
additional_notes: Used when a person voluntarily gives themselves up to the police, often because they are wanted or have committed a crime. Reflexive construction: sich der Polizei stellen. Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Ich werde mich morgen der Polizei stellen.
native_language_example: I will turn myself in to the police tomorrow.

meaning: 'the police will' — future construction indicating what the police are expected to do
additional_notes: Polizei is feminine singular in German but often treated as a collective noun; combined with the auxiliary verb 'wird' (3rd person singular of 'werden') it forms the simple future: 'the police will ...'. Use 'die Polizei wird' + infinitive to say what the police will do. Context can be warning, prediction, or plan. For plural actions directed at people, German still uses 'wird' (not 'werden') because 'Polizei' is grammatically singular.
target_language_example: Die Polizei wird morgen kommen, um Fragen zu stellen.
native_language_example: The police will come tomorrow to ask questions.

meaning: ‘is a police officer’ — states that someone’s occupation is a police officer (noun in masculine form: Polizist).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase; it's the noun Polizist (police officer, masculine) combined with the verb ist (is). In natural German you'd usually include a subject: e.g. 'Er ist Polizist' or 'Tom ist Polizist.' Word order changes in questions: 'Ist Tom Polizist?' The noun has gender and plural forms (die Polizistin = female, die Polizisten = plural). Context may require an article or pronoun: 'Der Polizist ist...' or 'Ein Polizist ist...'.
target_language_example: Ein Polizist ist voller Geheimnisse, wie ein Priester.
native_language_example: A police officer is full of mysteries, like a priest.

meaning: 'the post/ post office is' — used to say where the post office is or that mail/post has arrived.
additional_notes: Post usually means 'post' or 'post office' in German. In these examples 'Die Post ist ...' describes location (where the post office is) or announces arrival ('The mail is here!'). For asking the location, use 'Könntest du/ ihr mir sagen, wo die Post ist?' Note: 'Post' can also mean 'mail' (the letters/parcels) depending on context.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wissen Sie, wo die Post ist?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know where the post office is?

meaning: to receive/get a prize (an award or gift).
additional_notes: Commonly used when someone is given a prize, award, or small gift. 'Preis' here means prize/award (not 'price'). Conjugate bekommen as usual (z.B. du hast bekommen, er hat bekommen). Can be used for singular/plural recipients.
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Preis bekommen.
native_language_example: She received a prize.

meaning: ‘prices will (do something)’ — used with a verb to talk about future changes in prices.
additional_notes: Wird oft mit Verben wie fallen (fall), steigen (rise) oder weiter steigen (continue to rise). 'werden' here is the auxiliary for the future tense or a prediction: 'Die Preise werden steigen' = 'The prices will rise' or 'Prices are going to rise.' Common in news and conversations about the economy or shopping.
target_language_example: Die Preise werden wahrscheinlich nächstes Jahr fallen.
native_language_example: The prices will probably fall next year.

meaning: has a problem / there is a problem (with someone or something).
additional_notes: Combination of the noun 'Problem' and the verb 'haben' (to have). Used to state that a person or thing 'has' a problem or that a problem exists. Word order and articles may change (e.g. 'ein Problem hat', 'das Problem hat'). Common in statements and questions about difficulties or issues.
target_language_example: Jedes Problem hat eine Lösung.
native_language_example: Every problem has a solution.

meaning: indicates something is 'too (adjective) ... to ...' (too X to do Y).
additional_notes: Used to say that the problem (or situation) is so (difficult/hard/etc.) that the action cannot be done. Common structures: "Das Problem ist zu schwierig für mich zu lösen." or the more formal/colloquial alternative with "als dass": "Das Problem ist zu schwierig, als dass ich es lösen könnte." The adjective (z. B. schwierig, schwer) agrees in meaning; the second part can use an infinitive with "zu" or a subordinate clause with "als dass" + Konjunktiv II/Präteritum form.
target_language_example: Dieses Problem ist zu kompliziert, als dass ich es alleine lösen könnte.
native_language_example: This problem is too complicated for me to solve alone.

meaning: lit. 'problem can' — used as part of sentences meaning 'the problem can (be)...' or 'a problem can (be)...' (indicates possibility or ability regarding a problem).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination of noun + modal verb (Problem + kann). 'kann' is the 3rd person singular of 'können' (can/to be able to). You'll usually see it in passive or modal constructions: 'Das Problem kann gelöst werden' (The problem can be solved) or with 'nicht' to negate possibility. Word order follows normal German sentence rules (verb second in main clauses, modal + infinitive at end).
target_language_example: Das Problem kann mit ein bisschen Arbeit gelöst werden.
native_language_example: The problem can be solved with a bit of work.

meaning: a problem with; used to say something or someone causes trouble or difficulty
additional_notes: Used to describe an issue involving a thing or a person. With a noun, it often means 'there is something wrong with X' (e.g. 'the problem with eggs...'). With a person, it can mean 'someone has a problem with someone' (they dislike or have conflict) or 'discuss a problem with someone' (talk about it together) depending on verb and context. Commonly followed by a noun or name and can pair with verbs like haben (have), diskutieren (discuss), or sein (is).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Problem mit dem Computer.
native_language_example: I have a problem with the computer.

meaning: to be (a) problem; to cause or constitute a problem
additional_notes: Commonly used to say that something will or could be a problem. Combine with articles/adjectives (ein Problem, ein großes Problem) or possessive (mein Problem). Often appears with modal verbs (könnte, wird) and clauses describing the issue.
target_language_example: Das könnte ein großes Problem sein, wenn wir zu spät anfangen.
native_language_example: That could be a big problem if we start too late.

meaning: used with an infinitive to mean 'to [do something] about the problem' or 'to solve the problem'.
additional_notes: In German the noun 'Problem' can combine with 'zu' + infinitive (often with verbs like lösen, vermeiden, beheben) to express the action related to the problem: e.g. 'das Problem zu lösen' = 'to solve the problem'. Often appears after verbs/adjectives that require an infinitive clause (versuchen, unmöglich, möglich, es ist ...). Word order and commas may vary: with a full clause you can use 'dass' or an infinitive construction.
target_language_example: Wir müssen das Problem zu lösen versuchen.
native_language_example: We must try to solve the problem.

meaning: problems in / problems at (a place, group, or area)
additional_notes: Used to say that problems exist within a specific location, group, area, or context. Followed by a noun in the dative case when indicating location (e.g., in der Schule, in unserer Region). Can describe personal, organizational, or regional difficulties. Not a fixed idiom—it's the noun 'Probleme' + preposition 'in'.
target_language_example: Sie hat Probleme in der Klasse.
native_language_example: She has problems in the class.

meaning: Indicates constructions where 'Probleme' is followed by an infinitive clause introduced by 'zu' (e.g. 'problems doing something' or 'problems to ...' in clauses), often appearing as part of 'Probleme, ... zu + Infinitiv' meaning 'problems (to) doing/understanding/etc.'
additional_notes: 'Probleme zu' is not a standalone fixed phrase but occurs within infinitive constructions: the pattern is typically 'Probleme, ... zu + Infinitiv' (comma optional in colloquial speech). More commonly German also expresses 'problems with X' using 'Probleme mit + Dativ'. Be careful with word order: the infinitive clause with 'zu' usually appears after a comma or a relative element (e.g. 'Ich habe Probleme, das Programm zu installieren.' — note this example uses 'Probleme, das ... zu ...' rather than immediate adjacency; contexts where the noun 'Probleme' is directly followed by 'zu' can occur in constructions like 'Probleme zu lösen' as a noun phrase meaning 'problems to solve').
target_language_example: Wir haben viele Probleme zu lösen.
native_language_example: We have many problems to solve.

meaning: to use a program (software).
additional_notes: Benutzen means 'to use' and is commonly used with objects like 'Programm'. Polite/formal and informal pronouns change the verb form: du kannst, Sie können, ihr könnt. Useful for instructions or recommendations about software or tools.
target_language_example: Du kannst dieses Programm benutzen, um deine Videos zu schneiden.
native_language_example: You can use this program to edit your videos.

meaning: 'to (the) audience' used with verbs like zuhören or sprechen (i.e. directed toward the audience).
additional_notes: This phrase combines Publikum (the audience) with the particle zu, commonly appearing after a verb that separates the prefix (e.g. zuhören, zu sprechen as part of 'vor Publikum zu sprechen'). Often you will see: 'für das Publikum' (for the audience) or verbs with 'zu' as part of an infinitive construction ('vor Publikum zu sprechen' = to speak in front of an audience) or as part of 'zuhören' (Hört das Publikum zu? = Is the audience listening?). Context determines whether 'zu' is part of a separable verb (zuhören) or part of an infinitive phrase.
target_language_example: Vor Publikum zu sprechen ist aufregend.
native_language_example: To speak in front of an audience is exciting.

meaning: used to introduce the main point or a specific fact; 'the point is' / 'the fact is'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the phrase 'Der Punkt ist ...' to emphasize the main issue or a particular detail.
