target_language_example: Der Unterricht beginnt um neun Uhr.
native_language_example: The lessons begin at nine o'clock.

meaning: 'there is class' / 'the lesson is' (used to talk about classes/lessons and their state)
additional_notes: Unterricht means 'class' or 'lesson'. With 'ist' it often describes the state of the lesson (e.g. finished, happening, not allowed). Common constructions: 'Der Unterricht ist beendet' / 'Der Unterricht ist zu Ende' = the lesson is over. 'Heute ist Unterricht' or 'es ist Unterricht' = there are classes today. Often used with adjectives or prepositional phrases.
target_language_example: Ich habe völlig vergessen, dass heute Unterricht ist!
native_language_example: I completely forgot that there are classes today!

meaning: to go on vacation / to take a holiday (with infinitive 'zu' used in some constructions).
additional_notes: Urlaub means 'vacation/holiday'. In German you say 'in den Urlaub fahren' (to go on vacation) or 'Urlaub machen' (to take a vacation). The chunk 'Urlaub zu' appears when combining with another verb in infinitive constructions (e.g. 'vorhaben, in den Urlaub zu fahren' or 'sich vorstellen, allein in den Urlaub zu fahren'). Beginners should learn set phrases: 'in den Urlaub fahren' and 'Urlaub machen'.
target_language_example: Wir haben beschlossen, nächsten Monat in den Urlaub zu fahren.
native_language_example: We decided to go on vacation next month.

meaning: A direct address to 'Father' followed by 'I'—used to begin a personal statement to one's father (literal or religious).
additional_notes: This phrase is simply the start of a sentence addressing 'Vater' (father). It appears in both family contexts (speaking to one's dad) and religious contexts (addressing God as Father). After the comma comes the speaker's statement about themselves (e.g., asking, confessing, declaring). For beginners: treat it as 'Father, I ...' or 'Dad, I ...' depending on formality and context.
target_language_example: Vater, ich habe gute Nachrichten.
native_language_example: Father, I have good news.

meaning: depends on verb: with anrufen = 'call (one's) father'; with angeben = 'show off about one's father'; with anlügen = 'lie to one's father'; with anschauen = 'look at the father'.
additional_notes: This entry shows 'Vater' (father) combined with separable verbs that place the particle 'an' apart from the verb stem (e.g., anrufen → rufe ... an). The meaning changes depending on the main verb: 'anrufen' = to call (phone), 'anzugeben' is not correct here but 'angeben' = to boast (used as 'mit jemandem angeben' = to show off about someone), 'anlügen' = to lie to someone, 'anschauen/ansehen' = to look at. In German the separable prefix appears at the end of the clause in finite forms: Ich rufe meinen Vater an. Imperative: Ruf deinen Vater an! Pay attention to case: 'meinen Vater' (accusative) after these transitive verbs.
target_language_example: Ich rufe meinen Vater an, weil ich eine Frage habe.
native_language_example: I'm calling my father because I have a question.

meaning: "father of" (possessive: indicates someone is the father of something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to show possession/relationship: 'Vater des Kindes' = 'father of the child'. Often appears in fixed expressions (e.g. proverb 'Der Wunsch ist Vater des Gedankens' where it means 'is the origin/source of'). Word order: 'Vater des' uses the genitive case; 'des' agrees with a masculine/neuter noun in singular. In everyday spoken German, people often use the dative construction 'der Vater von ...' instead.
target_language_example: Der Vater des Jungen wartet vor der Schule.
native_language_example: The father of the boy is waiting in front of the school.

meaning: literally 'father said' — refers to what (your/the) father said.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's the past participle construction using 'sagen' with the subject 'Vater' (father). Context determines possessive (mein/mein Vater, dein Vater, ihr Vater) or whether 'Vater' is used as a name/title. Beginners will see it in reported speech or when referring back to something the father said. Word order and auxiliary verb (hat/haben) change depending on sentence.
target_language_example: Was hat Vater gesagt?
native_language_example: What did father say?

meaning: seen (my/your/etc.) father — the past participle phrase used to say someone saw a father.
additional_notes: Combine a possessive (mein, dein, seinen, unseren, etc.) + Vater + gesehen to say that someone saw that person's father. Used in questions (Hast du meinen Vater gesehen?) and statements (Ich habe deinen Vater gesehen.). 'Gesehen' is the past participle of sehen; full perfect tense normally includes a form of 'haben' (Ich habe Vater gesehen). In casual speech the auxiliary may be omitted in short answers, but learners should use the full form.
target_language_example: Hast du meinen Vater gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen my father?

meaning: ‘(my/your) father has me…’ — the beginning of sentences where someone’s father is the subject and 'mich' is the direct object (me).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common sentence start: 'Vater hat mich ...' or with a possessive: 'Mein/Dein Vater hat mich ...'. It introduces an action the father did regarding 'me' (e.g., asked, let, hit). The rest of the sentence will use a past tense construction (Perfekt or Präteritum with a past participle or infinitive structure). Pay attention to word order: in Perfekt you often see 'hat mich + past participle' (e.g. 'hat mich darum gebeten'), or causative constructions like 'hat mich ... lassen' (e.g. 'hat mich das Auto waschen lassen').
target_language_example: Mein Vater hat mich zur Schule gebracht.
native_language_example: My father brought me to school.

meaning: literally 'father had' — the past tense phrase '(your/my/etc.) father had'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun 'Vater' (father) plus the past-tense auxiliary/main verb 'hatte' (had). It appears in sentences to talk about something the father possessed, experienced, or felt in the past (e.g., fear, hopes, possessions). Word order and possession depend on context: e.g. 'dein Vater hatte' = 'your father had', 'mein Vater hatte' = 'my father had'.
target_language_example: Mein Vater hatte früher ein altes Auto.
native_language_example: My father had an old car in the past.

meaning: literally 'father always' — not a fixed phrase; appears when 'Vater' (father) is used with the adverb 'immer' (always).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom. 'Vater' is a noun meaning 'father'. 'Immer' is an adverb meaning 'always' or 'ever'. Together they appear in sentences like 'Das sagen Mutter und Vater immer' (Mother and father always say that) or in comparative constructions 'du wirst deinem Vater immer ähnlicher' (you are becoming more and more like your father). Pay attention to case and word order: verbs and pronouns change depending on tense and person (e.g. 'deinem Vater' uses dative with 'ähnlich').
target_language_example: Er hilft seinem Vater immer, wenn er Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He always helps his father when he has time.

meaning: 'father is coming' or 'father comes' (he is arriving/returning)
additional_notes: Simple present or near-future idea in German: Kontext decides if it's a statement about a usual routine (He usually comes), a specific arrival now (He is coming/arriving), or a future return (He will come/return). In German headlines or family speech the article (der) is often dropped: 'Vater kommt' instead of 'Der Vater kommt' or 'Mein Vater kommt'.
target_language_example: Vater kommt heute früher nach Hause.
native_language_example: Father is coming home earlier today.

meaning: 'father must' or 'my/your/the father must' — expresses that the (speaker's or another) father is required to do something, is likely to have done/been something, or must find out.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun Vater plus the modal verb muss (must). Meaning depends on context: (1) obligation/necessity (Dein Vater muss das sofort erfahren! = Your father must find out immediately; Mein Vater muss die Arbeit machen. = My father has to do the work), (2) deduction/assumption about the past or state when used with perfect or adjectives (Der Vater muss dick gewesen sein. = The father must have been fat / was probably fat; Dein Vater muss wohl sehr enttäuscht gewesen sein. = Your father was probably very disappointed). Word order and pronoun (mein/dein/der) determine whose father and nuance.
target_language_example: Sein Vater muss morgen zum Arzt gehen.
native_language_example: His father must go to the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to be a father
additional_notes: Used both literally (to be a male parent) and in phrases expressing becoming a father (werde bald Vater sein = will be a father soon). Can be used with possessive pronouns (mein Vater sein = to be my father) or as a role/quality (ein guter Vater sein = to be a good father). Word order: sein follows the noun in infinitive or predicate position.
target_language_example: Nächsten Monat werde ich Vater sein.
native_language_example: Next month I will be a father.

meaning: ‘father and I’ — used to talk about yourself together with your father.
additional_notes: Simple coordination of two subjects. Word order can change (e.g., 'mein Vater und ich' is common); in spoken German people sometimes say 'mein Vater und ich' or 'dein Vater und ich' depending on context. Used like in English to describe actions, feelings, events involving both people. If using possessive, include it (mein/dein).
target_language_example: Mein Vater und ich gehen morgen angeln.
native_language_example: My father and I are going fishing tomorrow.

meaning: 'father of' (indicates someone is the father of a person or people).
additional_notes: Used to show parentage. Can be followed by a proper name, a pronoun/group (e.g. 'denen' for 'them'), or a noun phrase (e.g. 'drei Kindern' with 'Vater von' sometimes shortened to 'Vater' + dative). In casual speech Germans may also say 'Er ist Sams Vater' (possessive) instead of 'der Vater von Sam'.
target_language_example: Er ist der Vater von Maria.
native_language_example: He is Maria's father.

meaning: '(my/your/the) father was a ...' — a simple past (was) phrase to describe someone's father.
additional_notes: Use with a noun or adjective to state who someone's father was (profession, trait, or character). Word order: subject (Vater) + past verb (war) + indefinite article (ein) + noun/adjective. Replace 'Vater' with a possessive if needed (Mein Vater war ein... / Ihr Vater war ein...). Can be followed by nouns (ein Schneider), adjectival phrases (ein großer Mann) or nouns with qualifiers (ein begabter Musiker).
target_language_example: Mein Vater war ein Lehrer.
native_language_example: My father was a teacher.

meaning: "father wants" (the father desires or requests something)
additional_notes: This is the subject (Vater) plus the verb wollen in the present (wants). It introduces what the father wishes, asks, or expects. In full sentences you'll often see a subordinate clause with dass/daß or an infinitive phrase explaining what he wants (e.g. "dass du Fußball spielst" = that you play football). Word order and formality can change: "Dein Vater will dich" (direct object) vs. "Ihr Vater will, daß Sie ..." (formal you).
target_language_example: Vater will, dass ich pünktlich nach Hause komme.
native_language_example: Father wants me to come home on time.

meaning: an appointment or date with (someone).
additional_notes: Verabredung means a meeting, appointment, or (romantic) date. 'Verabredung mit' is followed by a person (dative case: mit + dem/der/ihm/ihr). Can be formal (appointment) or informal/romantic (a date) depending on context. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Abend eine Verabredung mit Maria.
native_language_example: I have an appointment/date with Maria this evening.

meaning: 'The connection is' (used to describe quality or state of a connection: good, bad, unstable, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used about internet, phone or audio/video calls, or physical links. Followed by an adjective (gut, schlecht, gestört, langsam, normal). Can describe speed, clarity, stability. In spoken situations used to explain problems during calls.
target_language_example: Die Verbindung ist langsam, kannst du das Video anhalten?
native_language_example: The connection is slow, can you pause the video?

meaning: a suspicion that... / I suspect that...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief or suspicion about something, often followed by a subordinate clause with 'dass' + verb at the end. Common in everyday and formal contexts to express doubt or concern. You can say 'Ich habe den Verdacht, dass...' (I have the suspicion that...) or more simply 'Ich vermute, dass...' for 'I suppose/think that...'.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Verdacht, dass er die Wahrheit nicht sagt.
native_language_example: I suspect that he is not telling the truth.

meaning: in comparison to / compared with
additional_notes: Used to compare one thing with another. Often appears in phrases like 'im Vergleich zu' (in comparison to) or 'zum Vergleich mit' (for comparison with). Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. 'im Vergleich zu früher', 'im Vergleich zu anderen Ländern').
target_language_example: Im Vergleich zu letztem Jahr sind die Preise gesunken.
native_language_example: Compared with last year, prices have gone down.

meaning: 'promises and' — the word Versprechen (promises) followed by 'and', used when listing or addressing promises together with another idea (often implied continuation).
additional_notes: This phrase isn't a fixed idiom; it's simply the noun Versprechen ('promises') followed by the conjunction und ('and'). In the example sentences the structure appears in contexts like 'your promises and mine' or in imperative sentences urging someone to keep their promises and (also) be reliable — the second part after 'and' may be explicit (e.g. 'be reliable') or implied. Versprechen is a neuter plural noun in these uses. Formal and informal forms of the imperative differ (du, Sie, ihr).
target_language_example: Achte auf dein Versprechen und halte es.
native_language_example: Pay attention to your promise and keep it.

meaning: literally 'contract is' — used to state the status or nature of a contract (e.g. 'the contract is valid/invalid/fulfilled').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; 'Vertrag ist' appears as the start of a sentence stating a contract's condition. Common completions: 'Der Vertrag ist gültig/ungültig/erfüllt/gekündigt.' The standalone sentence 'Vertrag ist Vertrag.' is a colloquial way to say 'a contract is a contract' (i.e. rules must be followed).
target_language_example: Der Vertrag ist gekündigt, weil die Frist abgelaufen ist.
native_language_example: The contract is terminated because the deadline expired.

meaning: (part of an infinitive clause) 'to [do something with] the contract' — used when a verb (like unterschreiben, lesen) follows; 'the contract' plus the infinitive marker 'zu'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: 'Vertrag' (contract) + 'zu' used before an infinitive verb in German (e.g. 'den Vertrag zu unterschreiben' = 'to sign the contract'). In sentences you will usually see the article and case (den Vertrag) and then 'zu' immediately before the infinitive verb or in a split infinitive construction. For beginners: learn that 'zu' often appears with infinitives (similar to English 'to' + verb) and that the object (den Vertrag) comes before 'zu'.
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, den Vertrag zu unterschreiben.
native_language_example: I forgot to sign the contract.

meaning: a quarter of (something)
additional_notes: Used to express a fraction (¼) of a noun introduced by the genitive article 'des' (of the). Common in quantities: ein Viertel des Kuchens = one quarter of the cake. Can also appear with other numerals (drei Viertel des = three quarters of). Word order: numeral + noun + des + noun (genitive).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Viertel des Apfels gegessen.
native_language_example: I ate a quarter of the apple.

meaning: an idea/imagination of it; a sense of it
additional_notes: Used to say someone does or does not have an idea, impression, or sense of something. Often appears in negative sentences with 'keine Vorstellung davon haben' = 'to have no idea how ...' 'davon' refers back to the thing previously mentioned. Can be followed by clauses introduced with 'wie' (how) or by nouns.
target_language_example: Du hast keine Vorstellung davon, wie schwierig das Projekt ist.
native_language_example: You have no idea how difficult the project is.

meaning: to aim a weapon at; to point a weapon toward (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun in the dative or accusative that follows 'auf' to indicate the target (e.g. 'auf den Polizeibeamten', 'auf Maria'). Can describe physically pointing/aiming or firing at the target (context decides: 'auf jemanden richten' = aim at; 'auf jemanden feuern' = shoot at). Common verbs with this phrase: 'richten (eine Waffe auf ...)', 'feuern (mit einer Waffe auf ...)'.
target_language_example: Er richtete die Waffe auf die Tür, bevor er eintrat.
native_language_example: He aimed the weapon at the door before entering.

meaning: 'Wagen' (car) + preposition 'auf' — not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on context (e.g. location 'on', direction 'onto', part of verb construction 'warten auf' = to wait for, or 'auf jemandem angemeldet sein' = registered to someone).
additional_notes:
This is not a single idiomatic phrase. 'Wagen' = car. 'auf' is a versatile preposition whose meaning and case (Dative or Accusative) change with context. Common uses shown by examples:
- Location/direction: 'auf die Auffahrt' (onto the driveway) — movement uses accusative, static location uses dative.
- Registration/ownership: 'auf jemanden angemeldet sein' = registered in someone's name.
- As part of a separable verb phrase: 'im Wagen auf uns warten' (warten auf = to wait for).
For beginners: learn 'Wagen' = car and be aware that 'auf' combines with verbs (warten auf) or indicates position/direction or registration depending on context.
target_language_example: Tom wartet im Wagen auf uns.
native_language_example: Tom is waiting for us in the car.

meaning: 'car/vehicle here' or 'the wagon/car here' — used to refer to a car or cart that is located here or nearby.
additional_notes: Wagen means 'car', 'vehicle', or 'cart' depending on context (formal/old-fashioned can be 'carriage'). 'Hier' means 'here' or 'nearby'. Together they point to a vehicle that is at or should be brought to the current location. Common in requests (Bring den Wagen hier...), questions about availability (Haben Sie einen Wagen hier?) or to ask why a vehicle is in a place (Was macht der Wagen hier?). Word order in normal German would usually vary (e.g. 'den Wagen hierher', 'einen Wagen hier', 'meinen Wagen hier abstellen').
target_language_example: Stell den Wagen hier bitte ab.
native_language_example: Please park the car here.

meaning: to drive/put/bring a car or cart into (somewhere); 'Wagen' = car/vehicle/cart, 'in' = into/inside
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun Wagen (vehicle) and the preposition in (into). Common uses: describe a vehicle being driven into a place (Fahr den Wagen in die Garage), moved/placed inside (Stellen Sie den Wagen in die Garage), or set into motion (setzte den Wagen in Bewegung). Word order and verb choice change the meaning: with verbs like fahren, stellen, bringen, nehmen, or setzen, 'in' takes the accusative to indicate movement into an enclosed space. 'Wagen' can also mean a cart or carriage (e.g., pulled by horses).
target_language_example: Fahr den Wagen in die Garage, bitte.
native_language_example: Drive the car into the garage, please.

meaning: 'the car is' — simple subject + verb phrase used to describe a car.
additional_notes: Wagen means 'car' (slightly formal or regional; more common: Auto). 'ist' is the 3rd-person singular of 'sein' = 'is'. Together they start sentences that describe the car's condition, age, speed, price, or location. Word order can change in questions (e.g. 'In welchem Wagen ist die Toilette?'). Useful for basic descriptions: Mein Wagen ist ... / Sein Wagen ist ...
target_language_example: Unser Wagen ist größer als euer Wagen.
native_language_example: Our car is bigger than your car.

meaning: 'wagen mit' — literal combination of 'Wagen' (cart/vehicle) + the preposition 'mit' (with); often appears as part of phrases meaning 'the cart/vehicle with ...' or in informal/exclamatory commands 'Ab in den Wagen mit dir!' (Get in the cart/vehicle!).
additional_notes: Usually not a fixed idiom by itself; 'Wagen mit' is just the noun 'Wagen' followed by the preposition 'mit' to add more information (e.g. 'Wagen mit vier Pferden' = 'vehicle with four horses'). In spoken/colloquial German you may also see 'Ab in den Wagen mit dir!' as an imperative telling someone to get into the vehicle. Context determines whether 'mit' introduces an instrument, accompaniment, or a defining attribute.
target_language_example: Ab in den Wagen mit dir!
native_language_example: Get in the (car/vehicle), now!

meaning: literally 'car and' — part of two actions connected by 'und' (and); here used in sentences that join 'get in the car' with another action like 'drive off' or 'push'.
additional_notes: 'Wagen' means 'car' (or 'wagon' in older contexts). The phrase 'Wagen und' itself isn't an idiom; it's simply the noun followed by the coordinating conjunction 'und' to connect two verbs or actions in a sentence (e.g. 'stieg in den Wagen und fuhr weg' = 'got in the car and drove off'). Useful to recognize structure: [verb + in den Wagen] und [second verb].
target_language_example: Sie stieg in den Wagen und startete den Motor.
native_language_example: She got into the car and started the engine.

meaning: 'no choice but (to...)' — expresses that there is no alternative except doing something.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the set phrase 'keine (andere) Wahl als ...' followed by an infinitive clause introduced by 'zu' (e.g. 'zu gehen') or an infinitive without 'zu' in colloquial speech. Use it to say you have no alternative. Common variants: 'keine Wahl', 'keine andere Wahl als'.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine andere Wahl als zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I have no other choice but to stay.

meaning: that (someone) told the truth / has told the truth
additional_notes: This phrase is the past infinitive clause used after verbs like glauben, wissen, sicher sein, akzeptieren, or in questions: 'dass [person] die Wahrheit gesagt hat' = 'that [person] told the truth.' Often appears with question words or verbs expressing doubt, acceptance, or consequence. Word order: 'dass' + subject + 'die Wahrheit gesagt hat' (perfect tense).
target_language_example: Ich bin mir sicher, dass sie die Wahrheit gesagt hat.
native_language_example: I'm sure that she told the truth.

meaning: negation of 'the truth' (used with verbs to say someone does not know, cannot know, must not know, or does not believe the truth).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun 'die Wahrheit' (the truth) combined with 'nicht' (not). In German word order, 'nicht' usually negates the verb or a phrase and its position can change meaning. Examples: "die Wahrheit nicht kennen" = to not know the truth; "die Wahrheit nicht glauben" = to not believe the truth; "die Wahrheit nicht wissen" = cannot/should not know the truth. Pay attention to verb placement and modal verbs (können, dürfen) which affect where 'nicht' appears.
target_language_example: Sie darf die Wahrheit nicht sagen.
native_language_example: She must not tell the truth.

meaning: tells the truth
additional_notes: Phrase composed of Wahrheit (truth) + sagt (says). Typically appears within clauses (e.g., 'dass ... die Wahrheit sagt') or in commands/requests asking someone to ensure another person tells the truth. Adjust verb form for person and politeness (sagen, sagt, sagen Sie, sag).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass Tom die Wahrheit sagt.
native_language_example: I hope that Tom tells the truth.

meaning: to know the truth
additional_notes: Used to talk about being aware of the real facts or reality. Often appears after verbs or adjectives that require an infinitive (e.g., 'gut sein, zu ...', 'alt genug, um ... zu'). Can be used in neutral or moral contexts (is it good to know the truth?) and with people as subject (someone seems to know the truth).
target_language_example: Ich möchte jetzt die Wahrheit zu kennen.
native_language_example: I want to know the truth now.

meaning: to tell the truth; honestly speaking
additional_notes: Often used in phrases like "um die Wahrheit zu sagen" (to tell the truth / honestly). It introduces a frank statement or opinion. Literal components: Wahrheit = truth, zu sagen = to say. Common in both formal and informal speech.
target_language_example: Um die Wahrheit zu sagen, fand ich den Film langweilig.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I found the movie boring.

meaning: 'Water, please.' (requesting water politely)
additional_notes: Very common phrase used when ordering or asking for water in restaurants, cafés, or from someone. Can be used with a gesture; you can add 'ein Glas' (a glass) or 'eine Flasche' (a bottle) before it. Polite and neutral; 'bitte' makes it courteous.
target_language_example: Ein Glas Wasser bitte.
native_language_example: A glass of water, please.

meaning: the ...'s water / the water of ... (genitive: 'the water of')
additional_notes: Wasser des is the start of a genitive phrase: 'Wasser des X' = 'the water of the X' (e.g. 'Wasser des Lebens' = 'the water of life'). In German the noun after 'des' is in the genitive (masculine/neuter singular). Beginners will more often see fixed phrases like 'das Wasser des Lebens' (the water of life). Word order: article (das) + Wasser + des + noun.
target_language_example: Das Wasser des Brunnens ist sauber.
native_language_example: The water of the well is clean.

meaning: water for / water to (used to indicate who or what something is intended for)
additional_notes: Wasser für combines the noun 'Wasser' (water) with the preposition 'für' (for). It appears when talking about supplying or having water intended for a person, place, purpose, or comparison (e.g., 'water for agriculture', 'water for me'). In German word order, the thing being provided often follows 'für'. Use the appropriate article/pronoun as needed (z. B. 'Wasser für das Dorf', 'Wasser für mich').
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte Wasser für die Pflanzen holen?
native_language_example: Can you please get water for the plants?

target_language_multi_word_term: ins Wasser fallen / ins Wasser gefallen
meaning: to fail or be canceled; literally 'to fall into the water'.
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone physically falls into water) and idiomatically to mean plans or events were ruined, canceled, or failed. In idiomatic use it's often passive/impersonal: 'etwas fällt ins Wasser' = 'something falls through' or 'gets cancelled'. Common past participle: 'ins Wasser gefallen'.
target_language_example: Unser Ausflug ist wegen des Sturms ins Wasser gefallen.
native_language_example: Our trip was canceled because of the storm.

meaning: to have water / to get some water (context-dependent)
additional_notes: Can mean either possession ('to have water available') or a polite request when used with 'haben' in questions—e.g. 'ein Glas Wasser haben?' meaning 'may I have a glass of water?'. Common in everyday spoken German. Use context to tell whether it's about having supply or asking to receive some.
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte ein Glas Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have a glass of water?

meaning: 'water in' — the noun 'Wasser' (water) followed by the preposition 'in' (in/inside) introducing a location or container.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: Wasser (neuter noun) + in (preposition) + a noun in the dative case when indicating 'water inside/in' something (e.g., im Glas = in dem Glas). 'im' is the contraction of 'in dem'. The following noun determines the meaning (Überfluss, Glas, Teich, Topf, Schrank). Pay attention to articles and case: use 'im' for masculine/neuter singular dative (in dem).
target_language_example: Es ist noch Wasser im Kühlschrank.
native_language_example: There is still water in the fridge.

meaning: to match or measure up to someone (usually used in negative: 'cannot measure up to')
additional_notes: An idiom meaning to be as good as someone or to equal someone's abilities or status. Often used in negative sentences: 'jemandem das Wasser nicht reichen können' = 'cannot measure up to someone'. Literal image: offering someone a glass of water, but actual meaning is about comparison. Common in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich kann dir in Mathe nicht das Wasser reichen.
native_language_example: I can't measure up to you in math.

meaning: part of verb phrases involving 'Wasser' (water) plus an infinitive marker 'zu' — usually appears when 'Wasser' is the object and there's an infinitive clause following 'zu' (e.g. 'etwas Wasser zu wollen' = 'to want some water').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. In the examples, 'Wasser' is the noun 'water' and 'zu' is the infinitive marker used with another verb (wollen, stoßen, bringen) to form an infinitive clause: 'etwas Wasser zu wollen' (to want some water), 'ins Wasser zu stoßen' (to push into the water), 'ein Glas Wasser zu bringen' (to bring a glass of water). For beginners: focus on recognizing 'Wasser' = water and that 'zu' before a verb marks an infinitive (similar to 'to' + verb in English).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte Wasser zu trinken geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me water to drink?

meaning: literally 'way/path of'; used as the beginning of possessive/genitive phrases (the way of the ...).
additional_notes: Weg des is the noun 'Weg' (way, path) followed by the genitive article 'des' (masculine/neuter). It introduces a genitive phrase meaning 'the way/path of [someone or something]'. In everyday spoken German, the genitive is less common and may be replaced by 'von' + dative (e.g. 'der Weg von ...'). Use 'Weg des' in formal or written contexts or fixed expressions (e.g. 'auf dem Weg des Friedens' or 'der Weg des Lebens'). Remember that 'des' requires the genitive case and the following noun will be in genitive form.
target_language_example: Der Weg des Lernens ist lang, aber lohnend.
native_language_example: The path of learning is long but rewarding.

meaning: a way/path into (something); figuratively: a means to enter or reach (can be literal or metaphorical)
additional_notes: Used with a noun to indicate a physical entrance (den Wald, den Raum) or a figurative access (ihr Herz). Word order and case depend on the noun: usually followed by an accusative phrase (in + accusative) for direction/movement. Can appear in different forms (einen Weg in etwas bahnen, keinen Weg in etwas finden, Weg in den/die/das ...).
target_language_example: Er suchte einen Weg in das alte Haus.
native_language_example: He looked for a way into the old house.

meaning: the way/route to (a place); the journey toward (a destination).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a physical route or the act of going to a place. Often appears in phrases like 'auf den Weg nach ... sein/machen/nehmen' (to be on one's way/to set off/to take another route). Can be literal (route) or more general (a product 'finding its way to' a region). 'nach' is used with geographic place names without definite articles (countries, cities, fictional places).
target_language_example: Wir sind jetzt auf dem Weg nach Berlin.
native_language_example: We are now on our way to Berlin.

meaning: a way/path from (indicating origin or route starting point)
additional_notes: Used to talk about a route or the origin of travel. Often appears in phrases like 'der Weg von ... nach ...' (the way from ... to ...). In contexts like 'kam den ganzen Weg von ...' it emphasizes coming all the way from a place. 'Weg' is masculine (der Weg); preposition 'von' means 'from'.
target_language_example: Sie sind den ganzen Weg von Berlin gekommen.
native_language_example: They came all the way from Berlin.

meaning: to go a way / to follow a path; to choose a course of action (figurative).
additional_notes: This phrase appears as an infinitive construction often after verbs like 'haben', 'sein', 'beginnen', or nouns that take an infinitive with 'zu' (e.g. 'der Weg, ... zu gehen'). Literally 'to go a way' or 'to go on the way'. In everyday German it's commonly used both literally (to walk/go along a path) and figuratively (to take a certain approach or follow a plan). Word order in full sentences will vary (e.g. 'den Weg zu gehen' with articles).
target_language_example: Wir müssen diesen Weg zu gehen, wenn wir das Problem lösen wollen.
native_language_example: We have to take this path if we want to solve the problem.

meaning: 'not Christmas' used to negate liking or deserving Christmas; commonly appears with verbs (e.g., nicht mögen, nicht leiden, nicht verdienen).
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the word Weihnachten (Christmas) combined with the negation nicht. It appears after the object in German word order: verb ... Weihnachten nicht (e.g., Ich kann Weihnachten nicht leiden = I can't stand Christmas). Use nicht to negate verbs or adjectives relating to Christmas. Capitalize Weihnachten (a noun).
target_language_example: Ich kann Weihnachten nicht ausstehen.
native_language_example: I can't stand Christmas.

meaning: 'Christmas and' — the word Weihnachten (Christmas) followed by 'und' (and).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom by itself — it's simply the noun Weihnachten plus the conjunction und. It appears when listing holidays, events, or comparing/similing metaphors (e.g. 'as if it were Christmas and I am Santa'). Watch word order: Weihnachten is a noun (neuter), so it behaves like any other noun in sentences. Useful when saying things like 'at Christmas and Easter' (an Weihnachten und Ostern) or 'Christmas and birthdays'.
target_language_example: An Weihnachten und Ostern ist die Kirche voll.
native_language_example: At Christmas and Easter the church is full.

meaning: for a while not / haven't ... for a while (negative time expression)
additional_notes: Used to say that something did not happen or someone was not seen for a period of time. Often appears with verbs in perfect or simple past (e.g. 'habe ... nicht gesehen') or in phrases like 'eine Weile nicht' or 'noch eine Weile nicht' to mean 'not for some time' or 'not yet for some time.' 'Weile' = 'a while'; 'nicht' negates the action/time.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn schon eine Weile nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: I haven't seen him for a while.

meaning: the phrase 'Wein in' is not a fixed expression; it's the noun 'Wein' (wine) followed by the preposition 'in' used to indicate where wine is (inside something) or that wine is poured into something.
additional_notes: This is a composition of the noun 'Wein' (wine) and the preposition 'in' (in/into). Usage depends on case and verb: 'Wein in der Flasche' (location — wine in the bottle) uses dative; 'wein in das Glas' or contracted 'ins Glas' (movement into) uses accusative when indicating pouring. 'Mehr Wein in sein Glas schenken' and 'goss etwas Wein in ein Glas' show pouring (movement into = accusative). 'Wein in Schlückchen' is less common; here it means 'wine in small sips' (advocative/phrase-like).
target_language_example: Sie goss Wein in das Glas und reichte es ihm.
native_language_example: She poured wine into the glass and handed it to him.

meaning: the White Death (a personified name — likely a character, force, or title).
additional_notes: Used as a proper name or title (capitalized). Not a common everyday German phrase; appears in fiction or poetic contexts to refer to a personified figure (e.g., death, assassin, spirit) called 'the White Death'. Treat it like a name: use definite article 'der Weiße Tod'.
target_language_example: Der Weiße Tod hat das Dorf besucht.
native_language_example: The White Death visited the village.

meaning: to give birth (to bring a child into the world).
additional_notes: Literary or formal phrase used to express that someone gives birth — synonyms: ‚ein Kind zur Welt bringen‘ or ‚gebären‘. The specific two-word form ‚Welt bringen‘ typically appears as part of the phrase ‚(ein Kind) in die Welt bringen/ zur Welt bringen‘; standing alone without context is uncommon. More colloquial: ‚ein Kind bekommen/ zur Welt bringen/ gebären‘.
target_language_example: Sie hat gestern ihr erstes Kind in die Welt gebracht.
native_language_example: She gave birth to her first child yesterday.

meaning: the world of (used to talk about a field, community, or realm related to something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun in the genitive to describe a domain, sphere, or community (e.g. Welt der Musik = the world of music). Common in greetings or descriptions: 'Willkommen in der Welt der ...' or 'in der Welt der ...'. The noun following 'der' will change with gender/number (genitive).
target_language_example: Willkommen in der Welt der Bücher!
native_language_example: Welcome to the world of books!

meaning: to exist in the world; to have (more/fewer) people/things like someone/something in the world
additional_notes: Used in constructions like 'Es müsste mehr Menschen wie X auf der Welt geben' — literally 'There should be more people like X in the world.' Common in opinions or wishes about how the world would be better if there were more (or fewer) people of a certain kind. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Menschen wie dich müsste es viel mehr auf der Welt geben'). 'Welt geben' by itself is not a fixed idiom; the verb 'geben' combines with 'auf der Welt' to express existence/quantity in the world.
target_language_example: Es müsste mehr Lehrkräfte wie Maria auf der Welt geben.
native_language_example: There should be more teachers like Maria in the world.

meaning: to give birth (to someone).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrasal verb 'zur Welt bringen' (literally 'to bring into the world'). Used to say someone gave birth to a child. Formal or neutral tone; commonly used in news, announcements, and everyday speech. Often used with objects: 'ein Kind/ Zwillinge/ ein gesundes Kind zur Welt bringen.'
target_language_example: Sie hat gestern ein gesundes Mädchen zur Welt gebracht.
native_language_example: She gave birth to a healthy girl yesterday.

meaning: 'not (the) world' / negation with 'Welt' — usually 'world' with a negation or in negative constructions
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun Welt (world) combined with the negation nicht. In German word order, nicht can negate the whole clause or a specific element; placement matters. Examples above show different uses: negating existence (Es gibt in dieser Welt nicht = 'does not exist in this world'), refusing something that involves someone's world (Ich will deine Welt nicht = 'I don't want your world'), or negating ability/impact (Sie werden die Welt nicht prägen = 'They will not shape the world'). Translate according to context: sometimes 'not in this world', 'does not exist', 'will not', or simply 'do not'.
target_language_example: So etwas gibt es in dieser Welt nicht.
native_language_example: Something like that does not exist in this world.

meaning: to see the world; to travel and visit different countries/places.
additional_notes: Common expression meaning to travel, gain experience, or visit other places. Often used with verbs like wollen/möchten/wünschen. Can be literal (visit other countries) or more general (experience different cultures).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nach dem Studium die Welt sehen.
native_language_example: I want to see the world after graduation.

meaning: 'are (of) the world' — the verb 'sind' (are) used with 'Welt' (world) in plural/collective expressions.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's two words that appear together when forming sentences about 'the world' with the verb 'sein' (to be). Depending on context, 'Welt' (world) may be part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'Alle Sprachen der Welt sind...') where 'sind' agrees with the true subject (here 'Alle Sprachen'). Pay attention to subject-verb agreement: 'Welt' alone is singular ('Die Welt ist...'), but in expressions like 'Die Augen der Welt sind...' the subject ('Die Augen') is plural, so you use 'sind'.
target_language_example: Die Probleme der Welt sind oft sehr komplex.
native_language_example: The problems of the world are often very complex.

meaning: the weather in (a place).
additional_notes: Used to talk about weather conditions at a specific location. Combine with a place name: Wetter in + [Ort]. Common in questions and statements about past, present or general weather. Grammar note: 'in' is a preposition requiring the following noun (place) in the correct case (usually dative for countries with articles, e.g. 'in der Schweiz').
target_language_example: Wie ist das Wetter in Berlin heute?
native_language_example: How is the weather in Berlin today?

meaning: used to talk about how the weather will become or change ("the weather is becoming/will be...").
additional_notes: „Wird" is the 3rd-person singular of werden and here expresses change or future: e.g. ‚Das Wetter wird besser.‘ = the weather is getting better / will be better. Often followed by an adjective (besser, kälter) or a subordinate clause (wie das Wetter wird). Common in questions about forecasts: ‚Weißt du, wie das Wetter wird?‘
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, das Wetter wird am Wochenende sonnig.
native_language_example: I hope the weather will be sunny on the weekend.

meaning: 'the most important thing is' or 'what matters most is'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase 'Das Wichtigste ist, ...' followed by a clause explaining the main point or priority. Use to introduce the key fact, priority, or main idea. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Das Wichtigste ist, dass du gesund bleibst.
native_language_example: The most important thing is that you stay healthy.

meaning: literally 'wind has' — used as the start of sentences with the verb 'haben' to describe actions or changes caused by the wind (e.g. has stopped, has blown down, has calmed).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the combination of the noun 'der Wind' with a perfect-tense verb using 'hat' (e.g. 'hat aufgehört', 'hat sich gelegt'). Common verbs: aufhören (to stop), umfahren (to knock down), sich beruhigen/sich legen (to calm down), sich drehen (to change direction), jemanden im Stich lassen (to let someone down). Pay attention to reflexive verbs (sich beruhigen, sich gelegt) which require the reflexive pronoun and often 'hat' as auxiliary.
target_language_example: Der Wind hat heute Morgen nachgelassen.
native_language_example: The wind has died down this morning.

meaning: literally 'wind and' — used as part of fixed expressions like 'bei Wind und Wetter' or in poetic lists meaning 'wind and (other forces)'.
additional_notes: By itself 'Wind und' is not a standalone phrase; it appears in combinations or lists (e.g. 'bei Wind und Wetter' = in all kinds of weather) or in poetic contexts ('der Wind und die Bäume'). Often used to link 'wind' with another element. Useful to recognize in set phrases and poetic sentences.
target_language_example: Bei Wind und Wetter gehen wir spazieren.
native_language_example: We go for a walk in all kinds of weather.

meaning: 'reality is' (used to state what reality is like or to assert that something is real).
additional_notes: Wirklichkeit = 'reality'. Combined with the verb 'ist' (is) it begins statements describing reality or asserting that something exists in reality. Common in general statements (e.g. 'Reality is frightening') or in contrasts (what is real vs. what is imagined). Grammar: 'Wirklichkeit' is a singular feminine noun; follow with adjectives, clauses, or subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass' or relative pronouns.
target_language_example: Die Wirklichkeit ist oft komplizierter, als man denkt.
native_language_example: Reality is often more complicated than you think.

meaning: to become reality; to come true
additional_notes: Used when an idea, plan, wish or vision is realized. Often appears with subjects like 'ein Traum', 'ein Plan', 'eine Idee' (e.g. 'Der Traum wird Wirklichkeit' or using the infinitive 'Wirklichkeit werden' in subordinate or infinitive constructions). Common in both written and spoken German. 'Wirklichkeit' = reality; 'werden' = to become. The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Nach Jahren harter Arbeit konnte sein Traum Wirklichkeit werden.
native_language_example: After years of hard work, his dream was able to become reality.

meaning: "is a joke" — combination of the noun 'Witz' (joke) and the verb 'ist' (is). Used to state or question that something is a joke.
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like 'das ist ein Witz' (that is a joke) or 'Bitte sag mir, dass das ein Witz ist' (please tell me that's a joke). Can be used in informal and formal contexts (use 'sag' vs 'sagen Sie'). Not an idiom; literal, compositional meaning.
target_language_example: Bitte sag mir, dass das ein Witz ist!
native_language_example: Please tell me that's a joke!

meaning: to be a joke / to be meant jokingly (often used to express disbelief that something is serious).
additional_notes: Commonly used in phrases like "Das soll doch ein Witz sein?" to show surprise, disbelief or hope that something is not serious. Tone can be incredulous, offended, or pleading. Often appears with modal verbs (sollen, sollten) and adverbs (doch, wohl, nur). Not a fixed idiom with a single translation—context decides whether it means "that's a joke" or "you must be joking."
target_language_example: Bitte sag mir, das soll doch ein Witz sein?
native_language_example: Please tell me that's supposed to be a joke?

meaning: literally 'week a(n)'; here shows frequency or occurrence per week (e.g. 'every week a...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase — it's the words 'Woche' and 'einen' appearing together in sentences to express 'one (something) per week' or refer to 'last week a(n)'. Common patterns: 'jede Woche einen ...' = 'every week a ...' (regular frequency). 'letzte Woche einen ...' = 'last week a ...' (refers to a single event in the past). Order and articles change with gender/case of the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ich schreibe jede Woche einen Brief.
native_language_example: I write a letter every week.

meaning: 'week in' — used to say someone spent or spends a week in a place (e.g. im Krankenhaus = in the hospital).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it's the noun Woche (week) followed by a prepositional phrase with im (in + dem). Common patterns: "eine Woche im Krankenhaus" (a week in the hospital), "letzte Woche im..." (last week in...). Note sentence 6 uses "pro Woche im Supermarkt einkaufen" which is slightly awkward in German — more natural is "pro Woche im Supermarkt" or "pro Woche im Supermarkt einkaufen gehen". Use im when the location is masculine or neuter and you mean 'in the [place]'.
target_language_example: Ich war eine Woche im Hotel.
native_language_example: I was in the hotel for a week.

meaning: 'in the week' / part of the phrase used when saying how often one goes into a place during a week (appears in constructions like "in die Kirche in der Woche" or in separated word order such as "jede Woche in die Kirche" meaning "every week to the church").
additional_notes: The sequence "Woche in die" itself is not a fixed phrase; it typically appears as part of larger expressions like "jede Woche in die Kirche" or "einmal in der Woche in die Bibliothek gehen." Word order in German can separate "Woche" and "in die" depending on sentence structure (e.g. "Gehen Sie jede Woche in die Kirche?"). Use "jede/zweimal/einmal in der Woche" for frequency and "in die + [place]" for motion into a place.
target_language_example: Gehen Sie jede Woche in die Kirche?
native_language_example: Do you go to church every week?

target_language_multi_word_term: in der Woche / jede Woche / einmal in der Woche
meaning: expressions meaning 'per week' or 'every week' / 'once a week'.
additional_notes: German uses several ways to say recurring weekly actions: 'jede Woche' = every week; 'einmal in der Woche' or 'einmal pro Woche' = once a week; 'mindestens einmal in der Woche' = at least once a week. 'Anfang letzter Woche' / 'am Anfang der letzten Woche' are time phrases meaning 'at the beginning of last week'. Word order and articles change with context (e.g. 'in der Woche' often needs a determiner and case). These are not idiomatic—they are literal and common.
target_language_example: Er wäscht einmal in der Woche sein Auto.
native_language_example: He washes his car once a week.

meaning: a week later / one week later
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened seven days after a referenced time or event. Often appears as 'eine Woche später' (one week later) or 'Woche später' after a noun (e.g. 'Das Gleiche ist eine Woche später...'). Can be used in past or narrative contexts.
target_language_example: Eine Woche später bekam ich gute Nachrichten.
native_language_example: One week later I got good news.

meaning: past-time expression using 'Woche' (week) with the verb 'war' (was) — 'the week was...' or 'last week was...'.
additional_notes: Combines the noun Woche (week) with the past-tense of sein (war). Common uses: describe how a particular week felt (Die Woche war stressig), state events in the past referring to a week (Letzte Woche war er krank), or indicate time elapsed (Nach einer Woche war ich satt). In many cases you may see time words before 'Woche' (Letzte Woche = last week, Vor einer Woche = one week ago).
target_language_example: Letzte Woche war das Wetter schön.
native_language_example: Last week the weather was nice.

meaning: literally 'week will' — not a fixed phrase; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g. 'die Woche wird ...' = 'the week will ...').
additional_notes: This is not an independent idiom. 'Woche' = 'week' and 'wird' = third-person singular of 'werden' ('will' / 'becomes'). Beginners will see 'Woche wird' as two words that belong in sentences like 'Die Woche wird stressig.' (The week will be stressful.) or 'Nächste Woche wird das Wetter besser.' (Next week the weather will be better.). Word order can change: 'Nächste Woche wird es kalt.'
target_language_example: Nächste Woche wird das Treffen verschoben.
native_language_example: Next week the meeting will be postponed.

meaning: 'week to' or 'week until' — used as part of a time expression meaning 'until (the) week (of/ending) ...' or in phrases like 'die Woche zu etwas' (closing the week with ...) depending on context.
additional_notes: Alone, 'Woche zu' is incomplete and depends on surrounding words. Common uses: 1) In calendar/time phrases: e.g. 'in der Woche zu Ostern' (in the week of/around Easter) or 'zur Woche zu' in dialect/colloquial speech meaning 'toward the end of the week'. 2) In constructions like 'die Woche zu etwas machen/abschließen' it can mean 'to close/finish the week with ...' Beginners will most often see full expressions such as 'in der Woche zu' or 'am Ende der Woche'.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns in der Woche zu Ostern.
native_language_example: We will meet in the week of Easter.

meaning: 'weeks at' or 'weeks with' (used to say that someone stays at or spends a certain number of weeks at someone's place or with someone).
additional_notes: Combines a time expression (e.g., zwei Wochen = two weeks) with the preposition bei + person/place to indicate staying at someone's home or being with someone for that duration. Word order: number of weeks usually comes before 'bei' (e.g., 'für zwei Wochen bei mir'). Can be used with verbs like aufnehmen, bleiben, wohnen, or in time expressions like 'vor zwei Wochen bei ihm' (two weeks ago at/with him).
target_language_example: Ich bleibe drei Wochen bei meiner Tante.
native_language_example: I'll stay with my aunt for three weeks.

meaning: 'weeks in' — used to say someone spent or will spend a number of weeks in a place (e.g. im Bett, im Krankenhaus).
additional_notes: Usually appears with a time expression (z. B. drei Wochen, einige Wochen, nächsten Wochen) plus a location introduced by im (in + dem). Common contexts: hospital (im Krankenhaus), bed (im Bett). Can indicate past (war ... im), present (ist seit ... im), or future/obligation (müsse die nächsten Wochen im ... bleiben). Word order: time phrase + im + place.
target_language_example: Sie bleibt zwei Wochen im Hotel.
native_language_example: She is staying in the hotel for two weeks.

meaning: what (someone) did over the weekend; literally 'made weekend'.
additional_notes: Common in questions about past activities: 'Was hast du letztes Wochenende gemacht?' = 'What did you do last weekend?' The structure is: time expression (z. B. 'letztes Wochenende' or 'am Wochenende') + 'machen' in past (hast ... gemacht / haben ... gemacht). Use informal 'du' or formal 'Sie' depending on who you address.
target_language_example: Was hast du letztes Wochenende gemacht?
native_language_example: What did you do last weekend?

meaning: indicates going/being somewhere for the weekend (to [place] for the weekend).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (fahren, ziehen, kommen, etc.) or stative verbs to say someone goes to or stays at a place over the weekend. The structure is: (verb) ... (übers/über das) Wochenende + nach + [city/place]. "übers Wochenende" and "über das Wochenende" are common variants. If talking about next weekend, add "nächstes Wochenende".
target_language_example: Ich fahre übers Wochenende nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I'm going to Berlin for the weekend.

meaning: to go fishing again on the weekend; to resume fishing on weekends
additional_notes: Literal phrase composed of Wochenende (weekend), wieder (again) and angeln (to fish). Commonly used in informal speech to indicate that someone will fish again during the weekend. In full sentences, word order often changes (e.g., 'Am Wochenende wieder angeln' can appear as part of a clause).
target_language_example: Ich plane, am Wochenende wieder angeln zu gehen.
native_language_example: I plan to go fishing again on the weekend.

meaning: 'an apartment' used with 'eine' (indefinite article) in questions or statements referring to an apartment
additional_notes: This phrase shows the noun Wohnung (apartment) with the indefinite article eine. Common in questions about features (e.g., 'Gibt es zu der Wohnung eine Garage?' — 'Does the apartment have a garage?') or in statements ('dass diese Wohnung eine Falle war' — 'that this apartment was a trap'). Pay attention to word order: in questions the article follows the noun when using structures like 'Gibt es ... eine ...?'. The gender of Wohnung is feminine (die Wohnung), so the correct indefinite article is 'eine'.
target_language_example: Hat die Wohnung eine Terrasse?
native_language_example: Does the apartment have a terrace?

meaning: 'apartment' (the word Wohnung) combined with the particle 'zu' in different constructions — not a single fixed phrase; meaning depends on context (e.g. 'to find an apartment', 'to search the apartment', 'apartment for sale').
additional_notes: This is not one set phrase. 'Wohnung' = apartment/flat. 'zu' can be part of infinitive constructions (eine Wohnung zu finden = to find an apartment), part of a verbal phrase (Ihre Wohnung zu durchsuchen = to search your apartment), or a separate label (Wohnung zu verkaufen! = apartment for sale). Pay attention to word order and verbs: 'helfen, eine Wohnung zu finden' (help to find an apartment); 'in meiner Wohnung zu suchen' (to search in my apartment).
target_language_example: Wir versuchen, eine günstige Wohnung zu finden.
native_language_example: We are trying to find an affordable apartment.

meaning: 'the clouds are' — simple present statement about clouds
additional_notes: Wolken (clouds) + sind (are). This is a basic subject–verb phrase in German used to describe the clouds (appearance, quality, opinion). You can replace the adjective or clause after 'sind' to say how the clouds are (e.g. grau, dicht, schön) or add a relative clause (e.g. 'das, was...'). Useful for making simple observations about the sky.
target_language_example: Die Wolken sind heute sehr dunkel.
native_language_example: The clouds are very dark today.

meaning: to keep one's word; to keep a promise
additional_notes: Used when someone follows through on a promise or commitment. Commonly appears with a possessive (mein Wort, Ihr Wort, ihr Wort). Can be used as an infinitive, past (hielt), or in questions (Werden Sie Ihr Wort halten?).
target_language_example: Ich werde mein Wort halten.
native_language_example: I will keep my word.

meaning: one more word; another word
additional_notes: Literally 'word more.' Not a common fixed phrase in German by itself — you'd more often hear forms like 'noch ein Wort' or 'ein Wort mehr'. 'Wort mehr' can appear in larger constructions (e.g. 'ein Wort mehr' = 'one more word') or in poetic/literary contexts. Use 'noch ein Wort' in everyday speech to mean 'one more word' or 'one more thing to say.'
target_language_example: Gib mir ein Wort mehr, damit der Satz stimmt.
native_language_example: Give me one more word so the sentence is correct.

meaning: to have a (short) word/talk with someone; to speak briefly with someone.
additional_notes: Often used in the phrase "ein Wort mit jemandem (zu) reden/reden wollen" or "ein Wort mit jemandem haben". It implies a short, usually private or direct conversation — can be neutral, a quick question, or a minor complaint. Commonly followed by the person (dative): "ein Wort mit dir/ihm/ihr". Verb forms: "ein Wort mit jdm. haben", "ein Wort mit jdm. reden".
target_language_example: Ich muss noch ein Wort mit dir haben.
native_language_example: I need to have a word with you.

meaning: 'a word to' or 'a comment about' (used to introduce a brief remark or comment about something)
additional_notes: Often used in phrases like "ein Wort zu + Dativ" (e.g. "ein Wort zu diesem Thema") meaning 'a few words about this topic'. Common in spoken and written German to signal you're adding a short comment or explanation. It is not usually used alone; it appears as part of structures such as "ein Wort zu...", "noch ein Wort zu...", or "ein letztes Wort zu...".
target_language_example: Darf ich ein Wort zu diesem Punkt sagen?
native_language_example: May I say a word about this point?

meaning: literally 'words into' — used to say to put/insert words into something or to change/add words in text; often appears with a noun or phrase following 'in'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the noun 'Worte' (words) plus the preposition 'in'. Common uses: 1) instructing someone to write or copy words into a book/form (e.g. 'Worte in dein Notizbuch schreiben'); 2) inserting words into someone's mouth ('jemandem Worte in den Mund legen'); 3) changing words in a document ('Worte in dem Bericht ändern'). Match the case of the following noun (usually accusative or dative depending on the verb and preposition).
target_language_example: Bitte schreibe diese Worte in das Formular.
native_language_example: Please write these words into the form.

meaning: to say a few words; to give a short speech or remark
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to speak briefly at an event (e.g., a celebration, meeting, funeral). Often appears as 'ein paar Worte sagen' or 'ein paar Worte zu etwas sagen' (to say a few words about something). Polite/formal contexts use 'Wollen Sie ein paar Worte sagen?'.
target_language_example: Möchtest du zur Feier des Tages ein paar Worte sagen?
native_language_example: Would you like to say a few words for the celebration?

meaning: to say a few words (about); to speak (briefly) — used with verbs like 'sagen' or phrases meaning 'lose no more words'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; 'Worte zu' appears with verbs such as 'sagen' (ein paar Worte zu sagen = to say a few words about) or in set expressions like 'ohne weitere Worte zu verlieren' (without further ado/loss of words). Use it when indicating brief speech or remark about a topic.
target_language_example: Erlauben Sie mir, ein paar Worte zum Thema zu sagen.
native_language_example: Allow me to say a few words on the topic.

meaning: used in the fixed expression "Kein Wunder, dass du..." = "No wonder that you..." (expresses that something is not surprising).
additional_notes: The full phrase is usually "Kein Wunder, dass du..." or "Kein Wunder, dass..." It comments that a result or feeling is understandable given the circumstances. Can be used neutrally or sarcastically. Followed by a clause with "dass" + subject + verb (e.g. "dass du Angst hattest"). Informal tone depends on context; the phrase itself is common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Kein Wunder, dass du gestern so müde warst.
native_language_example: No wonder that you were so tired yesterday.

meaning: (Usually used as part of 'Kein Wunder, dass ...') — 'No wonder that ...' or 'It's no surprise that ...'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as the fixed expression 'Kein Wunder, dass ...' to comment that something is unsurprising given the circumstances. Use before a clause introduced by 'dass' (that). Tone is neutral; can be used in everyday speech and writing. You can also say 'Kein Wunder, denn ...' or 'Es ist kein Wunder, dass ...' for slight variation.
target_language_example: Kein Wunder, dass er so müde war — er hat die ganze Nacht gearbeitet.
native_language_example: No wonder he was so tired — he worked all night.

meaning: 'anger is' — the start of a sentence stating something about anger.
additional_notes: This is simply the noun Wut (anger) plus the verb ist (is). Used to make general statements or opinions about anger (e.g., 'Anger is ...'). Useful for forming simple descriptive sentences. Word order: noun + ist + complement.
target_language_example: Wut ist manchmal hilfreich, wenn sie dich vor Gefahren schützt.
native_language_example: Anger is sometimes helpful when it protects you from danger.

meaning: "is a magician/wizard" — predicate phrase indicating that someone or something is a magician or wizard.
additional_notes: This is a short predicate sequence: Zauberer = magician/wizard, ist = is. It's typically part of a larger sentence (word order and articles may vary): e.g., "Er ist Zauberer." Can be used literally or figuratively (e.g., "dunkler Zauberer"). The exact two-word sequence "Zauberer ist" may occur when continuing a sentence or in certain word orders (e.g., "Der Zauberer ist wieder da.").
target_language_example: Der Zauberer ist wieder da.
native_language_example: The magician is back.

meaning: to shut/close the gate or fence (literally 'fence closed'); used when closing a gate or securing an enclosure.
additional_notes: This is a colloquial short phrase: Zaun means 'fence' and zu means 'closed/to'. Often you might hear people say simply 'Den Zaun zumachen' or 'Mach den Zaun zu' to tell someone to close or latch a gate. Use with imperative: 'Mach den Zaun zu!' = 'Close the gate/fence!'.
target_language_example: Mach bitte den Zaun zu, damit die Hunde nicht weglaufen.
native_language_example: Please close the gate so the dogs don't run away.

meaning: time to (do something) with someone; used in phrases like "mehr Zeit mit jemandem verbringen/reden/spielen".
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but shows the pattern 'Zeit (haben/wünschen) + , + mit + [person] + [Infinitiv/zu + verb phrase]' (often without 'zu' in colloquial speech). It expresses having (or wanting) time to spend doing an activity together (talking, playing) or time to compete with someone. In English: 'time to ... with (you/him/her)'. The comma in the examples separates the clause but isn't required grammatically.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Abend Zeit, mit dir zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I have time tonight to talk with you.

meaning: Fragment literally 'time as with me'; not a standard idiomatic phrase — interpreted as part of comparisons or nonstandard word order. In natural German you'd usually say 'Zeit mit mir' or 'Zeit mit mir verbringen' to mean 'time with me' or 'spend time with me'.
additional_notes: This sequence ('Zeit als mit mir') is not a grammatical fixed expression by itself. It could appear inside comparative constructions (e.g., 'lieber Zeit als mit mir' — still awkward; better: 'lieber Zeit mit dir als mit mir') or result from incorrect word order. Prefer 'Zeit mit mir' or 'Zeit mit mir verbringen'.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er hätte lieber Zeit als mit mir — ein unbeholfener Satz; korrekt wäre: 'lieber Zeit mit dir als mit mir'.
native_language_example: He said he'd rather have time than be with me — an awkward sentence; correct would be: 'rather spend time with you than with me'.

meaning: 'time until' or 'time left until' (a deadline or an event).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the remaining time up to a specific point or deadline. Often followed by a date, time, or event (e.g., 'Zeit bis zum Ende', 'Zeit bis 20 Uhr'). Can appear in phrases like 'Wie viel Zeit bis ...?' (How much time until...?) or 'Die Zeit bis dahin' (the time until then).
target_language_example: Wie viel Zeit bis zum Abflug bleibt uns?
native_language_example: How much time until the departure do we have?

meaning: to need time (to do something, to get used to something, or for a process to take place)
additional_notes: Used when a person or thing requires time — for example to heal, to learn, to decide, or to adjust. Often appears with an infinitive or a noun: 'Ich brauche Zeit' or 'Das braucht Zeit'. Can be used in personal and impersonal contexts; tone is neutral and common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um mich an den neuen Job zu gewöhnen.
native_language_example: I need time to get used to the new job.

meaning: to give (someone) time; to allow more time or a delay.
additional_notes: Used when asking or saying that someone should be allowed extra time for a task, decision, or to adjust. Common in requests (Können Sie mir Zeit geben?) and general sayings (Man muss der Zeit Zeit geben = you must give time to time / be patient). Often followed by a person (mir, uns) and/or a time expression (bis zum Ende der Woche, ein wenig).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir noch zwei Tage Zeit geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me two more days?

meaning: to have time; to be available
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about having free time or availability. Common in requests (Könnte ich eine Minute deiner Zeit haben?) and polite offers (wenn Sie Zeit haben). Can be followed by an infinitive clause, an indirect question, or 'für' + noun (Zeit dafür haben). Tone can be formal or informal depending on pronoun (Sie/du/ihr).
target_language_example: Könnte ich eine Minute deiner Zeit haben?
native_language_example: Could I have a minute of your time?

meaning: had time (to do something) — past tense indicating someone possessed time or free time.
additional_notes: Common past-tense phrase using Zeit (time) with hatte (past of haben). Often followed by an infinitive clause introduced by um ... zu, oder by a purpose or result clause. Use with a personal subject: "Sie hatte Zeit", "Er hatte Zeit". Word order can vary in subordinate clauses (e.g., "..., dass er Zeit hatte").
target_language_example: Da sie Zeit hatte, ging sie spazieren.
native_language_example: Since she had time, she went for a walk.

meaning: 'time in' (used to say someone spends or spends time in a place or doing something)
additional_notes: A common phrase pattern: Zeit (time) + im (in the + masculine/neuter dative). It appears in sentences that describe spending time in a location or on an activity. You will usually see it followed by a noun in the dative (e.g., Internet, Krankenhaus, Gefängnis). For English, translate with 'time on/in/at' depending on context: 'time on the Internet', 'time in the hospital/prison'.
target_language_example: Sie hat letzte Woche viel Zeit im Garten verbracht.
native_language_example: She spent a lot of time in the garden last week.

meaning: time (spent) in [a place or situation]
additional_notes: Used to talk about the amount or quality of time someone spent in a place or situation. Often followed by a location or activity (e.g., in Therapie, in Algerien, in den Staaten). Context determines whether it's asking about duration (How much time?) or quality (Did you have a good time?).
target_language_example: Wir hatten eine tolle Zeit in Berlin.
native_language_example: We had a great time in Berlin.

meaning: 'time is' — the start of statements about time or a way to say 'the time has come' or to describe how time passed.
additional_notes: Literally 'time is'. Commonly used as the beginning of phrases: e.g. 'Die Zeit ist gekommen' = 'the time has come' (it's time). Also used with adjectives or verbs to describe time passing: 'Die Zeit ist schnell vergangen' = 'time passed quickly.' Usually followed by an adjective, past participle, or a clause.
target_language_example: Die Zeit ist gekommen, jetzt müssen wir handeln.
native_language_example: The time has come; now we must act.

meaning: to take one's time; to allow time (for something); not to hurry
additional_notes: Used when telling someone to not rush or when saying you will do something slowly/with care. Often appears in forms like 'Lass dir Zeit' (informal singular), 'Lassen Sie sich Zeit' (formal), or 'Wir lassen uns Zeit' (we'll take our time). Can be used reflexively (dir/uns) or impersonally.
target_language_example: Wir sollten uns Zeit lassen, um alles gründlich zu prüfen.
native_language_example: We should take our time to check everything thoroughly.

meaning: 'no more time' / 'no time left'.
additional_notes: Used after phrases like 'keine' to say there's no time remaining for something. Common structure: 'keine Zeit mehr (zum + verb-infinitive)' = 'no time left to ...'. Can be used urgently (e.g. in emergencies) or casually (e.g. ran out of time to study).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr, den Bericht zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I have no time left to write the report.

meaning: to save time; to do something more quickly or efficiently
additional_notes: Common verb phrase. Used when choosing a faster method or skipping steps to reduce the amount of time spent. Often appears with verbs like 'wollen', 'können', or in suggestions: 'um Zeit zu sparen' = 'in order to save time'. Can be used both transitively and intransitively with helpers.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, Zeit zu sparen, indem ich früh aufstehe.
native_language_example: I'm trying to save time by getting up early.

meaning: to spend time (doing something or with someone).
additional_notes: Use with an activity (Zeit mit Freunden verbringen) or a verb expressed with 'Zeit damit verbringen, ...' + infinitive (e.g., Zeit damit verbringen, etwas zu tun). Conjugate 'verbringen' normally: ich verbringe Zeit, er verbringt Zeit. Common in everyday speech and neutral in register.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mehr Zeit verbringen, um meine Hobbys zu pflegen.
native_language_example: I want to spend more time to pursue my hobbies.

meaning: 'to lose time' / 'to waste time' — to delay or spend time unproductively when speed is important.
additional_notes: Commonly used when there's urgency and you should act quickly. Often appears in imperatives or statements like "Wir dürfen keine Zeit verlieren" (We mustn't waste any time). Can mean both losing progress/time and wasting time through delays.
target_language_example: Beeil dich — wir dürfen keine Zeit verlieren.
native_language_example: Hurry up — we mustn't waste any time.

meaning: to waste time
additional_notes: Used when someone spends time unproductively or on something unnecessary. Can be used reflexively with pronouns (ich verschwende Zeit / ich habe Zeit verschwendet) or in imperative/advice (Verschwende deine Zeit nicht). Often followed by an activity: Zeit mit etwas verschwenden (to waste time on something).
target_language_example: Ich möchte meine Zeit nicht verschwenden.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste my time.

meaning: time before (something); time spent in front of (something) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) temporal: 'die Zeit vor X' = the period before X (e.g. 'die Zeit vor dem Internet'). 2) locative/activity: 'Zeit vor + Dative (dem Fernseher, dem Computer)' = to spend time in front of something (watching/using). Context tells you which meaning applies. Often followed by a noun in the dative.
target_language_example: Früher war das Leben einfacher — die Zeit vor dem Handy fehlt mir manchmal.
native_language_example: Life used to be simpler — I sometimes miss the time before the phone.

meaning: used in expressions to say 'time is becoming [something]' — most commonly 'time is running short' (die Zeit wird knapp) or 'time will show' (die Zeit wird zeigen).
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'Zeit wird' is the beginning of different expressions. Two common continuations: 'die Zeit wird knapp' = 'time is running out/short' (urgent), and 'die Zeit wird zeigen' = 'time will tell' (uncertain future). Choose the rest of the clause to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Die Zeit wird knapp — wir müssen jetzt los.
native_language_example: Time is running out — we have to go now.

meaning: time to (do something); it's time to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to say that now is the right moment to do that action. Often appears in structures like "Es ist Zeit, (etwas zu tun)" or shorter spoken forms like "Zeit zu gehen". In full sentence you usually need "es ist" or another subject, but colloquially you can omit it: "Zeit zu gehen." Use the infinitive with "zu" (zu + verb).
target_language_example: Es ist Zeit zu gehen.
native_language_example: It's time to go.

meaning: back in time; to go/return back in time
additional_notes: Used in contexts of clocks being slow (behind the correct time) or time travel/returning to an earlier time. Often appears as part of verbs/phrases: 'hinter der Zeit zurückbleiben' (to run slow), 'in der Zeit zurückreisen' (to travel back in time), or the imperative 'kehrt ... zurück' (return to your time). Word order in German can vary: 'in der Zeit zurück' or 'zurück in der Zeit'.
target_language_example: Er möchte in die Vergangenheit reisen und in der Zeit zurück gehen.
native_language_example: He wants to travel to the past and go back in time.

meaning: time together (spending time with someone)
additional_notes: Used to talk about spending time with one or more people. Often combined with verbs like verbringen (to spend) or verbringen with time expressions (viel, einige, mehr). Can refer to casual social time, dating, family time, or friends. Word order in full sentences is usually „Zeit zusammen verbringen“ or „Zeit zusammen verbringen“ with pronouns/subjects: e.g. ‚wir verbringen Zeit zusammen.‘
target_language_example: Wir sollten dieses Wochenende mehr Zeit zusammen verbringen.
native_language_example: We should spend more time together this weekend.

meaning: 'over a period of time' or 'during (the whole) time' — used after measures of time (meiste Zeit, die ganze Zeit) to mean 'throughout' or 'about' depending on context.
additional_notes: Usually appears after time expressions like 'die ganze Zeit', 'meiste Zeit'. It emphasizes duration (throughout that time). In sentence 2 it follows 'die ganze Zeit' + 'über' and can sound like 'all the time' or 'constantly' (often with a slight emphasis). It is separable in word order: the time phrase comes first, then 'über'. Not a standalone preposition; it combines with the time phrase. Can be translated as 'during', 'throughout', 'all the time', or 'about' (in contexts where someone talks about a topic continuously).
target_language_example: Sie hat die ganze Zeit über von dem Urlaub gesprochen.
native_language_example: She talked about the vacation the whole time.

meaning: '(the) moment/time (is)' — used to talk about whether a particular time or moment is appropriate or the right one.
additional_notes: Often appears in phrases like ‚der richtige Zeitpunkt ist…/jetzt ist der richtige Zeitpunkt‘ or ‚der beste Zeitpunkt ist…‘. Used to refer to a specific point in time (Zeitpunkt) and judge its suitability. Common in questions (Ist jetzt der richtige Zeitpunkt?) and statements (Der Zeitpunkt ist günstig.).
target_language_example: Meinst du, der richtige Zeitpunkt ist jetzt?
native_language_example: Do you think the right time is now?

meaning: "center of" (followed by a noun in genitive).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is the central point of something else. It is a fixed combination of the noun 'Zentrum' (center) plus the genitive article 'des' (masculine/neuter singular). In sentences you will normally see 'Zentrum des + [noun in genitive]'. Common in literal (e.g., 'Zentrum des Sturms') and figurative uses (e.g., 'Zentrum des Universums', 'Zentrum der Aufmerksamkeit' — note: feminine nouns use 'der' not 'des').
target_language_example: Das ist das Zentrum des Ortes.
native_language_example: That is the center of the place.

meaning: "the stuff is" — used to state something about some unspecified stuff or things (often informal).
additional_notes: "Zeug" is a general, informal word meaning "stuff", "things", or "gear"; context decides what it refers to (medicine, belongings, equipment, etc.). "Zeug ist ..." appears when commenting on the quality, condition, location, or status of that stuff. Common in spoken German; the rest of the sentence or prior context specifies what "Zeug" means.
target_language_example: Trink es langsam, das Zeug ist stark.
native_language_example: Drink it slowly, the stuff is strong.

meaning: 'to' as part of the phrase 'to reach/achieve a goal' (i.e. 'to reach the goal')
additional_notes: Ziel zu appears when talking about achieving a goal, usually with a verb like erreichen: 'ihr Ziel zu erreichen' = 'to reach her goal'. In German the structure is often: (etwas) tun, um + [object] + zu + infinitive. Here ‚Ziel zu erreichen‘ is the infinitive clause expressing purpose. You normally say simply 'ihr Ziel erreichen' in main clauses, but after 'um' use 'zu + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Er arbeitet hart, um sein Ziel zu erreichen.
native_language_example: He is working hard to reach his goal.

meaning: to enter a room; to lock oneself in a room (depending on verb construction).
