Common constructions: "alles um dich herum" / "alles um mich herum" / "alles um sich herum" / "sich um ... drehen" (to revolve around). "Um" here indicates spatial or figurative 'around'.
target_language_example: Alles um mich herum hat sich verändert.
native_language_example: Everything around me has changed.

meaning: everything below / anything under (a certain amount, level, or category)
additional_notes: Used to refer to all items, amounts or cases that are below a given threshold. Common in contexts like prices, ages, limits, or categories: e.g. "alles unter 10 Euro" = everything priced under €10. Often followed by a number, noun or phrase that sets the limit. Word order may change in full sentences (e.g. "alles, was unter... ist").
target_language_example: Wir verkaufen alles unter 20 Euro im Sonderangebot.
native_language_example: We are selling everything under 20 euros in the special offer.

meaning: 'everything will be alright' or 'everything will be fine'.
additional_notes: A reassuring phrase used to comfort someone or express optimism about the future. Common in spoken German; can be used alone or with a name/condition. Tone can be soothing, hopeful, or sometimes dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — alles wird gut.
native_language_example: Don't worry — everything will be alright.

meaning: to know everything / to have complete knowledge
additional_notes: Used literally or hyperbolically. Often appears in negative or general statements (e.g. 'Nobody can know everything') or as an imperative/desire to have full information ('We must know everything'). Common in everyday speech; not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: Niemand kann alles wissen.
native_language_example: Nobody can know everything.

meaning: 'everything for' / 'all part of' depending on context.
additional_notes: This phrase combines alles (everything/all) with zum (contraction of zu + dem). Meaning changes with context: 1) in sales/advertising (Alles zum halben Preis) it means 'everything at/for (a price)'; 2) when talking about belonging or being included (Das gehört alles zum Plan / Gehört alles zum Job) it means 'all that is part of' or 'all that belongs to'; 3) in idiomatic uses (Alles zum Guten wenden) it is part of a fixed expression meaning 'everything will turn out for the best.' Word order and context determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Das gehört alles zum Paket.
native_language_example: All of that is included in the package.

meaning: everything back / return everything
additional_notes: Used to say returning things or giving money back. Context decides exact meaning: can mean 'give/pay everything back' (Ich zahle dir alles zurück), 'hold back/restrain everything' (Die halten alles zurück — here 'zurückhalten' contracted), or instructing to leave or put everything back (Lassen Sie alles zurück; alles zurück ins Regal). Often appears as part of verbs like 'zurückgeben', 'zurücklegen', 'zurückstellen' or the separable verb 'zurückhalten'.
target_language_example: Bitte leg die Bücher alles zurück ins Regal.
native_language_example: Please put all the books back on the shelf.

meaning: than English (used for comparisons).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective or verb to compare something with English. Typically appears as 'besser als Englisch' (better than English) or 'einfacher als Englisch' (easier than English). In sentence 4 the word order is awkward; correct would be 'Er spricht Japanisch ebenso wie Englisch' or 'Er spricht sowohl Japanisch als auch Englisch.'
target_language_example: Ich finde Spanisch leichter zu lernen als Englisch.
native_language_example: I find Spanish easier to learn than English.

meaning: as (you) — used when addressing a group politely (formal plural) or when comparing something to 'you'.
additional_notes: Als Ihr is a combination of the conjunction 'als' (meaning 'as' or 'than') and the personal pronoun 'ihr' (you, plural, informal). In standard German, when directly addressing someone formally you would use 'Sie' not 'Ihr'. 'Als ihr' (lowercase i) can appear in sentences like comparisons ('als ihr') meaning 'than you (pl.)' or in temporal clauses if 'ihr' is the subject. Capitalized 'Ihr' is the polite formal possessive/dative pronoun (rare in modern usage); typically don't use 'als Ihr' to address someone formally. Pay attention to capitalization: 'Ihr' (capital I) can be formal 'you' in letters; 'ihr' (lowercase) is informal plural 'you' or 'her/their' depending on context.
target_language_example: Er kam früher als ihr.
native_language_example: He arrived earlier than you (plural).

meaning: 'than boys' (used in comparisons)
additional_notes: Used after an adjective, adverb, verb phrase or quantity to compare girls (or another subject) with boys. In sentences like "mehr Mädchen als Jungen" it means "more girls than boys." Word order can vary ("als Jungen an unserer Schule" or "an unserer Schule mehr Mädchen als Jungen"). "als" is the comparative connector; remember German comparisons often omit 'are' (sein) when using 'mehr ... als ...'.
target_language_example: In der Klasse sind mehr Mädchen als Jungen.
native_language_example: There are more girls than boys in the class.

meaning: 'as a person' or 'in one's capacity as a human being'
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone in their role or nature as a human being (feelings, responsibilities, identity). Can contrast human perspective with other roles (e.g. professional, divine) or highlight human limitations/qualities. Often placed before a clause or noun phrase.
target_language_example: Als Mensch will ich ehrlich behandelt werden.
native_language_example: As a person, I want to be treated honestly.

meaning: 'as a girl' or 'than girls' (depending on sentence structure).
additional_notes: This phrase can be used two ways: 1) with a verb like 'betrachten' to mean 'as a girl' (in the role/identity of a girl). 2) in comparisons with 'als' to mean 'than girls' (e.g. 'Jungen sind größer als Mädchen' = 'Boys are taller than girls'). Context and sentence word order determine which meaning applies. 'als' + noun is common in comparisons and identity statements.
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet als Mädchen immer fleißig.
native_language_example: She always works diligently as a girl.

meaning: as a student / when (I/you/etc.) was a (school) student.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a time or role in the past: 'when I was a student' or 'in the role of a student'. 'Schüler' usually means a school pupil (typically primary/secondary). If referring to a university student, use 'Student'. Can be used with different subjects (als Schüler habe ich..., als Schüler schrieb er...).
target_language_example: Als Schüler habe ich jeden Tag Vokabeln gelernt.
native_language_example: When I was a student I learned vocabulary every day.

meaning: than tea (used in comparisons: prefer A to tea).
additional_notes: Used as part of a comparison with lieber (prefer) or ähnlich comparative structures: X ist (mir) lieber als Tee / Ich trinke X lieber als Tee. 'als' introduces the thing being compared (the standard). The phrase alone ('als Tee') is not a full sentence — it needs a comparison (e.g. lieber, besser als, wichtiger als).
target_language_example: Ich trinke Wasser lieber als Tee.
native_language_example: I prefer to drink water rather than tea.

meaning: than water (used in comparisons: '… than water')
additional_notes: This is the comparative particle 'als' followed by the noun 'Wasser'. Use with comparative adjectives or verbs to compare something to water (e.g., 'billiger als Wasser' = 'cheaper than water'). Word order: adjective/adverb + als + Wasser. Not an idiom—just a literal comparison.
target_language_example: Luft ist leichter als Wasser.
native_language_example: Air is lighter than water.

meaning: 'as an old' (used before a feminine noun) — indicates someone/something is acting or being described in the role or appearance of an old (woman).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the preposition 'als' (as) with the adjective 'alte' (old) in the feminine or plural form before a noun (e.g. alte Frau/damen/Knochen). Use depends on the noun that follows. It can describe disguise ('verkleidete sich als alte Frau'), a hypothetical description ('als alte Frau sterben'), a comparison with age ('als alte Knochen' — colloquial), or a dismissive phrase (can be insulting in contexts). Adjective endings change with gender/case/number, so 'alte' may become 'alter/alten/ältere' in other contexts.
target_language_example: Er trat als alte Frau auf der Bühne auf.
native_language_example: He appeared on stage as an old woman.

meaning: introduces a subordinate clause after a comparison, often translated as "than" or "that" (used with verbs to compare actions or outcomes).
additional_notes: Used in comparative structures where the second part is a clause (often expressing a result, preference, or contrast). Common after expressions like "lieber" (prefer) or in moral/conditional comparisons. Formal/literary in some contexts; in speech Germans often use simpler constructions (e.g. "als" + infinitive or omit "dass"). Word order follows subordinate-clause rules (verb goes to the end).
target_language_example: Ich trinke lieber Wasser, als dass ich Limonade trinke.
native_language_example: I prefer to drink water rather than (that) I drink lemonade.

meaning: as/than your (feminine singular possessive) — used in comparisons or time clauses depending on context.
additional_notes: ‘Als’ can mean 'when' (past time) or 'than' (comparison). Here 'deine' is the feminine singular possessive pronoun 'your' (referring to a feminine noun like Mutter/Frau/Diebin). In comparisons use 'als' = 'than' (e.g. 'besser als deine Mutter' = 'better than your mother'). In past-time clauses use 'als' = 'when' with a following noun phrase ('Als deine Mutter und ich jung waren' = 'When your mother and I were young'). Word order and meaning depend on the sentence.
target_language_example: Als deine Schwester hier war, haben wir zusammen gekocht.
native_language_example: When your sister was here, we cooked together.

meaning: used in comparisons meaning 'than three' (part of expressions like 'more than three' or 'less than three').
additional_notes: Appears after comparative words: 'mehr als drei' = more than three, 'länger als drei Monate' = longer than three months, 'weniger als drei' = less than three. German uses 'als' (not 'wie') after comparatives. Word order: comparative + als + number/noun.
target_language_example: Ich habe mehr als drei Bücher gelesen.
native_language_example: I have read more than three books.

meaning: when you were a (child/young) — used to talk about someone's past age or stage.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions about someone's past (e.g., childhood). In German, the noun after 'ein' changes: 'als du ein Kind warst' (when you were a child) or 'als du ein kleiner Junge warst' (when you were a little boy). The phrase often requires a noun and a form of 'sein' (warst). For polite/formal or plural 'you', use 'als Sie ein...' or 'als ihr ein...'.
target_language_example: Als du ein Kind warst, hast du gerne im Wald gespielt?
native_language_example: When you were a child, did you like playing in the woods?

meaning: 'when he/it ... out' — introduces a past-time clause describing something that happened as someone came out of/left a place.
additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate temporal clause in the past (often with simple past or imperfect) meaning 'when' or 'as' something happened while someone exited, stepped out of, or emerged from somewhere. The verb for movement follows 'aus' (e.g., aus dem Zug stieg, aus der Höhle trat, aus dem Haus lief). 'Als' is typically used for single events in the past (not repeated actions).
target_language_example: Als er aus dem Auto stieg, sah er den Hund an der Straße.
native_language_example: When he got out of the car, he saw the dog on the street.

meaning: when he saw the policeman / as he saw the police officer.
additional_notes: Uses 'als' to introduce a single past event ('when' in English). The clause 'als er den Polizisten' is an incomplete clause that needs a main clause (e.g. 'lief er davon'). Word order: in the subordinate clause the verb goes to the end only when the clause continues; here 'als er den Polizisten sah' is the full subordinate clause. You can also place the time clause after the main clause: 'Er lief davon, als er den Polizisten sah.'
target_language_example: Als er den Polizisten sah, versteckte er sich hinter dem Auto.
native_language_example: When he saw the policeman, he hid behind the car.

meaning: when he (did something) to/with her; 'als' = when (past single event), 'er' = he, 'sie' = her/she (accusative).
additional_notes: Common structure in past-time clauses: 'als' introduces a single past event. Word order: verb of main clause follows the clause with 'als' (e.g. Die Party war ..., als er sie verließ). 'Sie' here is most often accusative (her) but can be nominative (she) depending on context—use pronoun case from the verb. This phrase is not idiomatic; it's a simple combination of words.
target_language_example: Als er sie sah, lächelte sie.
native_language_example: When he saw her, she smiled.

meaning: first; first of all; as the first thing
additional_notes: Used to indicate the first person/thing in sequence or the first action someone does. Can appear at sentence start (meaning 'first of all') or after a verb/object to mean 'came in first' or 'did first'. Formal and common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Als erstes habe ich meine E-Mails gelesen.
native_language_example: First, I read my emails.

meaning: 'as false' / 'to be proven false' (used to say something turns out to be untrue)
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like 'sich herausstellen' or 'sich erweisen' to say that a statement, rumor, or piece of information proved to be false. In English you can translate whole phrase combinations as 'turned out to be false' or 'was shown to be false.' The short phrase 'als falsch' on its own usually appears in passive or reflexive constructions (z. B. 'als falsch herausstellen/erweisen' or 'als falsch markiert').
target_language_example: Die Behauptung stellte sich als falsch heraus.
native_language_example: The claim turned out to be false.

meaning: as a great/very big (something); used to introduce how something is regarded or described.
additional_notes: Als + adjective (here große) is used to say 'as [adjective]' or 'regarded as [adjective]'. It often appears with nouns (als große Lüge = as a big lie; als große Ehre = as a great honor). Agreement: adjective form (große) matches the gender/case of the noun. In some contexts 'große' can mean 'great' (important) or 'big' (physically large) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Er wurde als große Hilfe angesehen.
native_language_example: He was regarded as a great help.

meaning: 'as if we/they/he/she had' — part of a conditional/simile structure meaning 'as if' followed by a subjunctive verb (Konjunktiv II).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or imagined situation (English 'as if' or 'as though'). The verb after 'als' appears in Konjunktiv II (here 'hätten' for plural subjects). Subject pronoun and verb agree: e.g. 'als hätte ich', 'als hättest du', 'als hätten wir/sie'. Common in spoken and written German to express doubt, surprise, or comparison.
target_language_example: Er redet, als hätten wir nie Probleme gehabt.
native_language_example: He talks as if we had never had problems.

meaning: 'as if you had' (subjunctive phrase used to introduce a hypothetical or unreal comparison).
additional_notes: Combines "als" (as/like) with the subjunctive form of "haben" (hättest) for second person singular (du). Often appears in longer clauses like "als hättest du ..." or after verbs expressing perception (wirkt, sieht aus), or in conditional/hypothetical statements: it compares reality to an imagined situation. You will also see other persons: "als hätte er" (he), "als hätten wir" (we).
target_language_example: Du redest, als hättest du alles schon entschieden.
native_language_example: You talk as if you had already decided everything.

meaning: 'when I was a child' (used to talk about past childhood).
additional_notes: Used to introduce memories or descriptions of what happened during one's childhood. Often appears with verbs in the past (Präteritum or Perfekt) or with past-subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) when expressing wishes or unreal situations. Word order: 'Als ich Kind war' or 'Als ich ein Kind war' (both common).
target_language_example: Als ich Kind war, habe ich jeden Sommer bei meinen Großeltern gespielt.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played at my grandparents' every summer.

meaning: 'when I heard the news' (introduces a past event or reaction).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past-time clause describing what happened or how someone felt at the moment they heard some news. 'Als' here signals a single past event (not ongoing or repeated). The verb in the clause often follows at the end (e.g., 'als ich die Nachricht hörte'). Common in storytelling or reporting past reactions.
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, war ich sprachlos.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was speechless.

meaning: when I was a child / as a child.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past time frame referring to childhood. Followed by a verb in a past tense (e.g., simple past or perfect) or an imperfect action. Common in stories or memories. 'Als' (not 'wenn') is used for single past time references. Word order: verb comes after the subject (e.g., 'Als ich ein Kind war...').
target_language_example: Als ich ein Kind war, spielte ich jeden Sommer im Garten.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played in the garden every summer.

meaning: when I was in / when I was at (a place or situation).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past time clause about something that happened while the speaker was in a certain place or situation. 'Als' here is a subordinating conjunction meaning 'when' (for single past events). It is followed by a clause with the past tense; 'im' is a contraction of 'in dem' and combines with a noun (e.g. Koma, Garten, Gefängnis, Wald, Ausland, Krankenhaus). Word order: verb goes to the end of the subordinate clause (e.g. 'als ich im Krankenhaus war').
target_language_example: Als ich im Zug war, habe ich ein interessantes Gespräch geführt.
native_language_example: When I was on the train, I had an interesting conversation.

meaning: the beginning of a time clause: 'when I ... (after I ...)' — used to introduce what happened while or after you looked/searched for something or arrived somewhere
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it usually starts a subordinate clause: 'als ich nach X suchte/fragte/ankam' ('when I looked for X/asked about X/arrived'). 'Als' refers to a single past event (not repeated), and 'ich' is the subject. Common continuations include verbs like suchen, fragen, kommen, schauen, sehen. For repeated/past-habit actions use 'als ich ... oft' or use 'wenn' for general/repeated situations.
target_language_example: Als ich nach dem Bahnhof fragte, zeigte mir ein Mann den Weg.
native_language_example: When I asked for the train station, a man showed me the way.

meaning: when I (was) going/returned home / when I got home
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a time clause using 'als' (for a single past event) followed by a first-person subject and 'nach Hause' (to/at home). You need a verb or clause ending after it (e.g. 'kam', 'ging', 'war'). In spoken German you might hear 'nach Hause' or 'nach Hause kam' omitted or shortened; in writing include the verb: 'als ich nach Hause kam'. Use 'als' for one past event, not 'wenn' (which is for repeated events or general conditions).
target_language_example: Als ich nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I got home, nobody was there.

meaning: when I said / when I said that...
additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker said in the past. Often followed by a subordinate clause with dass or a direct quotation. 'Als' here is a temporal conjunction meaning 'when' (past). Not to be confused with 'als' in comparisons (e.g. größer als). Common in storytelling or reporting what happened after/when the speaker said something.
target_language_example: Als ich sagte, dass ich nicht bleiben kann, verabschiedeten sie sich freundlich.
native_language_example: When I said that I couldn't stay, they said goodbye politely.

meaning: when I was that age / when I was as old as (you)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a memory or past situation by comparing the speaker's past age to the listener's (or another person's) current age. Often completed with 'wie du', 'wie ihr' or 'wie er/sie' (as in 'als ich so alt war wie du'). Common in storytelling or reminiscing. The phrase places the reference in the past (past tense).
target_language_example: Als ich so alt war wie du, bin ich jeden Sommer bei meiner Tante geblieben.
native_language_example: When I was as old as you, I stayed with my aunt every summer.

meaning: more than ever / than before
additional_notes: Used after comparative constructions (often with adjectives or verbs) to say something is at its highest/strongest level compared to any earlier time. Equivalent to English 'more than ever' or 'than ever before.' Common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich schottischer als je zuvor.
native_language_example: I feel more Scottish than ever before.

meaning: better/faster/etc. than anyone else that I know
additional_notes: Phrase compares someone's ability or action to all other people the speaker knows. The final word after 'ich' is usually omitted in examples but implied (kennt/kenne). Commonly completed as 'als jeder andere, den ich kenne.' Can be used with adjectives or adverbs (besser, schneller, stärker, etc.).
target_language_example: Du spielst Klavier besser als jeder andere, den ich kenne.
native_language_example: You play the piano better than anyone else I know.

meaning: as the last thing; lastly; in the end
additional_notes: Used to indicate the final item in a sequence or the last action someone does. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence: e.g. listing steps ("als letztes mache ich...") or giving a final comment ("Als letztes möchte ich sagen..."). Similar to "zuletzt" or "abschließend."
target_language_example: Als letztes prüfe ich noch einmal alle Türen.
native_language_example: Lastly, I check all the doors one more time.

meaning: as/than with me (used in comparisons when mentioning someone who is/was with the speaker)
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom on its own; it appears in comparative contexts like 'als (du) mit mir' or 'als er/sie mit mir ...' meaning 'than with me' or 'as with me'. Word order can vary depending on the sentence. Often you'll see 'als ich mit ihm war' (than when I was with him) or 'als er mit mir sprach' (when/than he spoke with me). Pay attention to case and verb position in the full sentence.
target_language_example: Das war einfacher als mit mir gerechnet.
native_language_example: That was easier than expected with me.

meaning: as ... as possible (used after adjectives or adverbs, often in the fixed phrase 'so ... als möglich')
additional_notes: Usually appears in comparisons like 'so schnell als möglich' or 'so bald als möglich' to mean 'as ... as possible' or 'as soon as possible'. More common word order is 'so ... wie möglich' in many contexts (e.g. 'so schnell wie möglich'), but 'als möglich' is heard in some fixed expressions and regional uses; learners should prefer 'wie möglich' for general use. Place it after an adjective/adverb: 'so + adjective/adverb + als möglich'.
target_language_example: Bitte kommen Sie so bald als möglich.
native_language_example: Please come as soon as possible.

meaning: more than just a/an (used to say something is more significant than a simple label).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone/something is more than the simple description that follows. Often appears as 'mehr als nur ein' (more than just a) or 'mehr als nur eine' depending on gender. Common in comparisons and evaluations.
target_language_example: Er ist mehr als nur ein Freund für mich.
native_language_example: He is more than just a friend to me.

meaning: 'next' or 'what happens/is done next; after that.'
additional_notes: Used to refer to the next action, event, or step in sequence. Common in questions and statements about plans or narrative/events. Can be placed after verbs or at clause position: 'was als nächstes (zu tun ist/geschah)'.
target_language_example: Was machen wir als nächstes?
native_language_example: What do we do next?

meaning: as if
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or unreal comparison — something that is not true or is doubtful. Often followed by a verb in a subjunctive (Konjunktiv) in formal German, but in spoken/colloquial German the indicative is frequently used (e.g., "als ob nichts geschehen wäre" or "als ob nichts geschehen ist"). Common in negative or ironic remarks (e.g., "Als ob mir das passieren würde!").
target_language_example: Er tat so, als ob er alles wüsste.
native_language_example: He acted as if he knew everything.

meaning: than beautiful (used in comparisons: 'rather/ more ... than beautiful').
additional_notes: Appears after words like 'eher' or 'mehr' to compare qualities (e.g. 'eher süß als schön' = 'more cute than beautiful'). Common pattern: [eher/mehr] + adjective + als + schön. Used to say someone/thing has one trait more than 'beautiful'.
target_language_example: Er ist eher freundlich als schön.
native_language_example: He is more friendly than beautiful.

meaning: as if (he/she/it were)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical, unreal, or imagined situation in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv I/II) — often translated 'as if' or 'as though'. Common in reported speech and when saying someone behaves in a certain way (tut so, als sei ... / tut so, als wäre ...). In everyday spoken German you may also hear 'als wäre' instead.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als sei er reich.
native_language_example: He acts as if he were rich.

meaning: 'as if (they/we/etc. were)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or unreal comparison (subjunctive mood). 'Seien' is the Konjunktiv I plural form of 'sein' used after 'als' to mean 'as if' or 'as though'. It often appears in written or formal contexts; in spoken German Konjunktiv II (wären) or indicative (wären/als ob) can also be used. The subject after 'als seien' determines the implied verb form in English ('were' or 'was').
target_language_example: Er redete mit ihr, als seien sie Freunde.
native_language_example: He spoke to her as if they were friends.

meaning: when she heard the news / when she received the message
additional_notes: This phrase introduces a past-time clause describing what happened at the moment she heard the news. 'Als' is used for a single past event (not repeated); 'die Nachricht' can mean 'the news' or 'the message' depending on context. In full sentences you'll usually continue with a past-tense main clause (e.g., 'brach sie zusammen').
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, weinte sie leise.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she cried quietly.

meaning: when she (it) — 'als' = when (single past moment); 'sie' = she; 'es' = it (object).
additional_notes: This is a short sequence of words that appears in sentences where 'als' introduces a single past/sudden moment (or a comparison). 'es' usually refers to some event or thing mentioned earlier (it). In examples: 1) reaction when she found out (past moment), 2) comparison structure ('hotter than they are' — here word order differs but shows comparative use), 3) when she heard it ring. Word order can change depending on tense and clause. 'als' (not 'wenn') is used for single past events or comparisons.
target_language_example: Als sie es sah, lächelte sie.
native_language_example: When she saw it, she smiled.

meaning: 'as' or 'when' + 'our' (depends on context); a combination of the conjunction/particle als and the possessive unser
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the word als (which can mean 'as' for roles/comparisons or 'when' for past events) followed by the possessive unser ('our'). Meaning depends on the sentence: 1) als unser Kommandant = 'as our commander' (role/comparison). 2) als unser Vater ... gearbeitet hat = 'when our father ... worked' (time, past). Pay attention to word order and tense: als is used for single past events/time clauses; for comparisons 'als' compares unequal things.
target_language_example: Als unser Lehrer hat er viel Geduld gezeigt.
native_language_example: As our teacher he showed a lot of patience.

meaning: ‘as if you were’ — introduces a hypothetical or imagined situation about 'you'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to describe something that seems true but isn't necessarily. 'Als wärst' is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) form for 'du' of 'sein' in colloquial speech; the full form is 'als wärest'. It often translates as 'as if' or 'as though' in English and can soften statements, express doubt, imagination, or criticism.
target_language_example: Du tust nicht so, als wärst du verletzt.
native_language_example: Don't act as if you were hurt.

meaning: as if (they/we) would; introduces a hypothetical or imagined situation (often followed by a clause with a subjunctive).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) to describe something that seems or appears to be the case but isn't necessarily true. Often translated as "as if" or "as though." In spoken German the verb form (würden + infinitive) or würde + subject + verb may be contracted or omitted depending on context.
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als würden wir uns schon lange kennen.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if we had known each other for a long time.

meaning: as if (someone) knew / as though (someone) knew
additional_notes: Used in hypothetical or comparative statements to describe someone's behavior or speech that suggests they have knowledge (or pretend to) — often follows verbs like tun (to do), reden (to talk), aussehen (to look). In German the verb in the subordinate clause is in the subjunctive II (wüsste). Can be translated 'as if he/she knew' or 'as though he/she knew'.
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als wüsste er das Geheimnis.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if he knew the secret.

meaning: used after a comparison with 'mehr' or 'weniger' to mean 'than two' (e.g. 'more than two' / 'less than two').
additional_notes: In German comparative constructions you often see 'mehr als zwei' (more than two) or 'weniger als zwei' (less than two). 'als' here is not the same as 'als' meaning 'when' or 'as' — it's the word used after comparatives (mehr/ weniger/ größer/ kleiner) to introduce the comparison. Common patterns: 'mehr als zwei Tage', 'weniger als zwei Stunden'.
target_language_example: Wir haben weniger als zwei Stunden, um das zu erledigen.
native_language_example: We have less than two hours to finish that.

meaning: a combination of 'also' (so/therefore) + the separable verb prefix 'an-' used with verbs that separate; 'also' here often means 'so' or 'thus' and 'an' begins a separable verb (e.g. anfangen → fängst du an).
additional_notes: In the examples 'also' can mean 'so/therefore' or serve as a discourse marker ('so' in English). 'An' is not a standalone word here but the separable prefix that attaches to verbs like anfangen (to begin), anrufen (to call), anfangen zu + infinitive, or aussehen/anfühlen (to feel/look like) when the verb is split in main clauses. Word order: in German main clauses the prefix moves to the end (Du rufst also an = You therefore call (someone)). Translate depending on the full verb: 'rufst ... an' = 'call', 'fing ... an' = 'began', 'suchen ... an' in the example is unusual (likely 'fängst du an' intended), 'fühlt ... an' = 'feels (like)'.
target_language_example: Du fängst also an, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: So you are starting to learn German.

meaning: A casual spoken filler used to wrap up or move on in conversation; equivalent to English 'so then', 'anyway', or 'well then'.
additional_notes: Common in colloquial German as a discourse marker. Signals a conclusion, a change of topic, or that the speaker is ready to leave or proceed. Tone and context determine the best English equivalent. Not formal—mainly conversational or informal settings.
target_language_example: Also bis, ich muss jetzt los.
native_language_example: Well then, I have to go now.

meaning: 'please' or 'come on' (used to express request, mild surprise or to ask for calm/attention).
additional_notes: Depends on tone and context. Can be a polite request ('please'), an urging 'come on' or 'now really' showing surprise or disbelief, or a way to ask for quiet/attention ('so, please...'). Common in spoken German. Not strongly formal or very informal; tone matters.
target_language_example: Also bitte, sag mir die Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Please, tell me the truth.

meaning: so, then; (used to draw a conclusion) 'so it's a/you/this...'
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a conclusion or inference from what was just said or observed. Depending on context, 'also' can mean 'so/thus' and 'ein' is the indefinite article 'a/an' or part of a noun phrase. Together they often translate as 'so it's a...' or 'so you're a...'. Tone is neutral and appropriate in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Also ein Geheimagent — das erklärt vieles.
native_language_example: So a secret agent — that explains a lot.

meaning: 'so/then go' or 'well, let's go' — used to draw a conclusion or to start/confirm going somewhere or leaving
additional_notes: Also is a common discourse particle meaning 'so', 'well' or 'then'. Combined with gehen it can introduce a conclusion ("so/then I go"), a suggestion/decision ("so, let's go"), or a question asking for permission to leave. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be decisive, confirmatory, or polite. Not idiomatic slang.
target_language_example: Also gehen wir jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: So then we go home now.

meaning: 'so () he/she/it/ I went' — 'so/therefore (subject) went' (past tense of gehen with so/also = therefore/so).
additional_notes: Combination of 'also' (therefore/so) + past tense 'ging' (went). Used to show a result or consequence: 'so/therefore [subject] went...'. Subject can be ich/er/sie/wir etc.; English often uses 'so' or 'therefore' before the clause. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich hatte Hunger, also ging ich in die Küche.
native_language_example: I was hungry, so I went into the kitchen.

meaning: so/therefore can (used to draw a conclusion about ability or possibility)
additional_notes: Combine 'also' (so/therefore) with a modal verb like 'kann' to state a conclusion about what someone can or cannot do. Common in spoken and written German to infer possibilities or permissions from prior information. Word order: 'also' usually starts the clause or comes before the verb ('Also kann ich...').
target_language_example: Also kann ich morgen früher gehen.
native_language_example: So I can leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: 'so/therefore only' or more naturally 'only' used to draw a conclusion or emphasise restriction after considering something
additional_notes: Often used to comment or draw a conclusion from prior information (like 'so then' or 'so, ... only'). In many contexts it emphasises that something is limited/exclusive (only) or expresses a reaction/conclusion (so, then). Word order: 'also' here functions as a discourse particle ('so/therefore') and 'nur' means 'only'. Together they often translate as 'so... only' or simply 'only' depending on context. Tone can be neutral or mildly questioning/surprised.
target_language_example: Du hast also nur das Brot gekauft?
native_language_example: So you only bought the bread?

meaning: 'so... that' used to show degree: 'so old that' (often in comparisons like 'so ... that ...')
additional_notes: This is the construction 'so [adjective], dass ...' (so + adjective + that). Here 'alt, dass' appears with 'alt' (old): 'so old that...'. It expresses cause or result: the adjective's degree leads to the following consequence. In English 'so... that...' or 'so old that...'. Common in spoken and written German. Word order: main clause with 'so alt', then 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (verb goes to the end).
target_language_example: Das Haus ist so alt, dass man die Balken ersetzen muss.
native_language_example: The house is so old that you have to replace the beams.

meaning: 'how old is your...'
additional_notes: Used to ask someone's age of a person or the age of an object. Combine with a noun: e.g. 'Wie alt ist dein Auto?' For informal situations use 'dein' (your, singular informal). For formal or plural 'your' use 'Ihr' or 'euer' respectively: 'Wie alt ist Ihr Auto?' (formal) or 'Wie alt ist euer Auto?' (plural you). The full question is usually 'Wie alt ist dein + noun?'.
target_language_example: Wie alt ist dein Hund?
native_language_example: How old is your dog?

meaning: 'how old is this' (asking the age of an object or thing)
additional_notes: Common question pattern using 'wie alt' + verb + demonstrative ('dieser' = this). Change 'dieser' gender/case to match the noun: dieser (m.), diese (f.), dieses (n.), diese (pl.). Used for objects, people, animals, buildings, etc.
target_language_example: Wie alt ist dieser Baum?
native_language_example: How old is this tree?

meaning: to have been a certain age (in the past) — the predicate 'alt' (old/years old) combined with the past plural/singular formal/imperative form of 'sein' (waren/war) in past contexts.
additional_notes: 'alt waren' is used to talk about how old someone or a group was at a past time. Common in comparative clauses (Als ... so alt waren wie ...) and in direct questions (Wie alt waren ...?). Use appropriate agreement: 'ich war' (singular), 'du warst', 'er/sie/es war', 'wir/Sie/sie waren'. The multi-word expression 'alt waren' appears when the subject is plural or when using the formal 'Sie'.
target_language_example: Als Tom und ich so alt waren wie Sie, war alles ganz anders.
native_language_example: When Tom and I were as old as you (formal), everything was completely different.

meaning: were (you) old
additional_notes: Used in questions or statements about someone's age in the past. "alt" = old/years old; "warst" is the 2nd person singular past tense of "sein" (to be). Often appears in phrases like "Wie alt warst du?" (How old were you?). In English we usually say "how old were you" or "you were X years old." Word order in German places the verb (warst) after the subject in statements and often after the question word in questions.
target_language_example: Wie alt warst du, als du umzogen bist?
native_language_example: How old were you when you moved?

meaning: How old were you when you... (asks someone's age at the time of an event).
additional_notes: Use this phrase to ask about the age someone was at a specific past event. It is the familiar/informal second-person form (du). Structure: "Wie alt warst du, als du + past-tense clause?" The clause that follows can use Präteritum or Perfekt depending on the verb (common: "als du geboren wurdest", "als du angefangen hast").
target_language_example: Wie alt warst du, als du das erste Mal geflogen bist?
native_language_example: How old were you when you flew for the first time?

meaning: to grow old; to get older
additional_notes: Used to talk about aging (literally 'become old'). Commonly appears with wishes or conditions (e.g. 'in Würde alt werden' = 'to grow old with dignity') and in personal contexts ('Mit dir möchte ich alt werden' = 'I want to grow old with you').
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit meinen Freunden alt werden.
native_language_example: I want to grow old with my friends.

meaning: 'as old as' (used to compare ages or ages of objects)
additional_notes: Used in comparisons, often with 'so ... wie' or directly between two nouns/pronouns: e.g. 'Er ist alt wie sein Bruder' (He is as old as his brother). In everyday German you'd more commonly say 'so alt wie' (so ... as) or use 'genauso alt wie'. When stating someone's age you normally say 'Er ist 30 Jahre alt' rather than 'alt 30'.
target_language_example: Sie ist genauso alt wie ich.
native_language_example: She is exactly as old as I am.

meaning: 'the old man is' — a simple subject + adjective + verb phrase used to describe an older man.
additional_notes: Used to state a quality, condition or opinion about an older man. Word order: 'Der alte Mann' = the old man (subject); 'ist' = is; then an adjective, adjective phrase or predicate (e.g. 'blind', 'verrückt', 'die Freundlichkeit in Person'). Useful for making basic descriptive sentences. Adjust gender/number if needed (die alte Frau ist, die alten Männer sind).
target_language_example: Der alte Mann ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: The old man is very friendly.

meaning: old man
additional_notes: Literally 'old man'. Used both descriptively to mean an elderly man (e.g. in stories) and colloquially as a form of address—like 'mate', 'man', or 'pal'—often informal and sometimes familiar or slightly brusque depending on tone and context. When used as a direct address it appears after a comma: '..., alter Mann?'.
target_language_example: Alter Mann, pass doch auf!
native_language_example: Man, watch out!

meaning: 1) literal: an old house; 2) idiomatic (informal, colloquial): an affectionate greeting like "old friend" or "pal" ("Na, altes Haus!").
additional_notes: Can be used literally to describe a building that is old. Informally, "Na, altes Haus!" is a friendly, somewhat old-fashioned greeting addressing someone you know (similar to "hey, old chap" or "hey there, buddy"). Context determines meaning—use the idiomatic sense only in speech among friends.
target_language_example: Na, altes Haus! Lange nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: Hey, old buddy! Long time no see.

meaning: at the beginning; in the beginning; at first
additional_notes: Used to refer to the start of a time period, process, story, project, etc. Can mean 'at first' (initially) or 'at the beginning (of something)'. Often followed by a verb or a phrase indicating what happened then. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Am Anfang war das Projekt sehr klein.
native_language_example: At the beginning the project was very small.

meaning: slang: 'screwed', 'done for', or 'don't care' depending on context; literally 'at the ass'.
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used in many ways: as an exclamation (Am Arsch! = No way!/Screw that!), to say someone is in trouble or ruined (Wir sind am Arsch = We're screwed/finished), to express indifference when combined with 'vorbei' (Das geht dir am Arsch vorbei = You don't give a damn), or to threaten (Die kriegen dich am Arsch = They'll get you). Tone is coarse — avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Wenn das so bleibt, sind wir bald am Arsch.
native_language_example: If this stays like that, we'll be screwed soon.

meaning: to be devastated; extremely upset or crushed.
additional_notes: Used to describe very strong emotional distress or heartbreak (e.g., after bad news, a breakup, failure). It's idiomatic: literally 'to be destroyed on the ground' but means emotionally devastated. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Nach der Absage war sie am Boden zerstört sein — sie konnte kaum sprechen.
native_language_example: After the rejection she was devastated — she could hardly speak.

meaning: at the end
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- spatial: 'at the end' (e.g. at the end of a hall).
- temporal/conclusive: 'in the end' meaning 'finally' or 'ultimately'.
- idiomatic/emotional: 'am Ende sein' = 'to be exhausted/defeated/at one's wit's end'. Context determines the best translation.
Can appear with a following noun (am Ende der Straße) or alone (Ich bin am Ende).
target_language_example: Am Ende der Straße steht ein kleines Café.
native_language_example: At the end of the street there's a small café.

meaning: on the horizon; at the horizon (visible line where sky and earth/sea meet).
additional_notes: Used to describe something seen or located at the visible boundary between sky and land/sea. Common in literal (sun, ship) and figurative uses (on the horizon = coming soon). Often appears with verbs like sehen, erscheinen, versinken.
target_language_example: Ein Boot ist am Horizont zu sehen.
native_language_example: A boat can be seen on the horizon.

meaning: alive
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is alive or to be kept alive. Commonly appears in phrases like "am Leben sein" (to be alive), "am Leben bleiben" (to stay alive), "am Leben halten/erhalten" (to keep alive). Often follows verbs (sein, bleiben, lassen, erhalten).
target_language_example: Ist deine Großmutter noch am Leben?
native_language_example: Is your grandmother still alive?

meaning: to stay alive; to remain alive.
additional_notes: Used to talk about surviving or continuing to live (literal physical survival). Common in urgent or dramatic contexts (warnings, commands, questions about who survives). Structure: 'am Leben bleiben' often follows modal verbs (wollen, müssen, dürfen) or questions.
target_language_example: Du musst am Leben bleiben, egal was passiert.
native_language_example: You must stay alive, no matter what happens.

am Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder

target_language_multi_word_term: am Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder
meaning: arrived on Monday and (then) left again the next day.
additional_notes: This phrase describes someone arriving on Monday and departing the following day. 'am Montag' = on Monday; 'am nächsten Tag' = the next day; 'wieder' emphasizes 'again' or 'returned to a previous state' (here: left again). Common in past-tense narration (Perfekt or Präteritum) about short visits or stays.
target_language_example: Er ist am Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder gegangen.
native_language_example: He arrived on Monday and left again the next day.

meaning: in the end; at the end; finally (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common phrase with two main uses: (1) temporal/summary meaning 'in the end, finally' (e.g. Am Schluss fand er die Wahrheit heraus = In the end he found out the truth). (2) positional meaning 'at the end' or 'at the rear' (e.g. am Schluss des Zuges = at the end of the train). Context decides which sense is meant. Often interchangeable with 'am Ende' for the temporal sense. Informal in some spoken uses but neutral overall.
target_language_example: Am Schluss waren alle Aufgaben erledigt.
native_language_example: In the end, all tasks were finished.

meaning: a day
additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about frequency (per day) or time of day (during daytime). Use 'dreimal am Tag' = 'three times a day'. When meaning 'during the day' it contrasts with 'nachts' (at night).
target_language_example: Ich trinke zwei Liter Wasser am Tag.
native_language_example: I drink two liters of water a day.

meaning: at the destination / at the goal; nearly or already having reached the goal.
additional_notes: Used both literally (reaching a physical destination) and figuratively (reaching an objective or completing a task). Common modifiers: 'fast am Ziel' (almost there), 'noch nicht am Ziel' (not there yet), 'schon am Ziel' (already there). Can appear with verbs like 'sein' (to be) and 'ankommen' (to arrive).
target_language_example: Wir sind gleich am Ziel.
native_language_example: We'll be at the destination/goal soon.

meaning: on the other (side/end) or at the other (place/location).
additional_notes: Used to point to something or someone located at the opposite side or at a different place (often followed by a noun with a location: Ende, Ende der Welt, Ende des Tisches). Can mean 'on the other end' or 'at the other side' depending on context. 'am' = an + dem (at the).
target_language_example: Sie wartet am anderen Ende des Bahnsteigs.
native_language_example: She is waiting at the other end of the platform.

meaning: all over (the whole of something, usually body parts).
additional_notes: Used with a noun in dative (e.g., 'am ganzen Körper', 'am ganzen Leib') to say something covers the entire area. Common in descriptions of marks, pain, bleeding, etc. Often followed by body-related nouns. Literal word order: 'an dem ganzen' contracted to 'am ganzen'.
target_language_example: Er hatte am ganzen Arm Narben.
native_language_example: He had scars all over his arm.

meaning: 'on board' (on or into a vehicle, ship, plane) or figuratively 'on board' (involved, present)
additional_notes: Used literally to say someone or something is on or gets onto a ship, plane, train, bus, etc. Also used figuratively to mean someone is part of or involved in a group or plan (e.g., "Are you on board?" → "Bist du dabei?"/"Bist du einverstanden?"). Common in commands (Alle an Bord!) and descriptions (jemand kam an Bord).
target_language_example: Die Passagiere gingen an Bord des Flugzeugs.
native_language_example: The passengers boarded the plane.

meaning: lacking money / in need of money; (also) about/for money when used in 'an ... interessiert'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with fehlen (es fehlt jemandem an Geld = someone lacks money). With a negative or reversed word order it means 'to not lack money' (ihr fehlt es nicht an Geld). In a different construction (X ist an Geld interessiert) it means 'interested in money' (focused on money). Use the dative with people: es fehlt ihm an Geld. Informal: "Hast du irgendwas an Geld?" = "Do you have any money?"
target_language_example: Mir fehlt es im Moment an Geld.
native_language_example: I'm short of money at the moment.

meaning: to/for your (formal, feminine/plural noun) — used with 'an' + accusative to mean 'think of/knock on/talk to your ...'.
additional_notes: An Ihre is the combination of the preposition 'an' (which takes the accusative or dative) and the formal possessive pronoun 'Ihre' (your, capitalized for formal Sie). Use accusative after verbs like 'denken an' (think of), 'klopfen an' (knock on), or with phrases like 'gehen an' (go to/for). 'Ihre' agrees with the noun in gender/number: here examples show feminine or plural nouns (Ihre Karriere, Ihre Kinder, Ihre Kollegen, Ihre Familie, Ihre Tür, Ihre Predigt, Ihre Mutter). In spoken German the formal 'Ihre' is used when addressing someone with 'Sie'.
target_language_example: Denken Sie an Ihre Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Think about your health.

meaning: a combination of the preposition 'an' (to/about/at) + 'all' meaning 'all' or 'all of it/them' — used to refer to everything or everyone in a group when speaking about thinking, believing, remembering, or acting toward them.
additional_notes: In German, 'an' is a preposition that takes different meanings depending on context (think of, believe in, remember, act on). 'all' (often 'all die', 'all das', 'all seinen' etc.) quantifies 'everything' or 'all of the' followed by a noun or pronoun in the appropriate case. The phrase 'an all' itself is not a fixed idiom; you will usually see 'an' + 'all' plus a noun phrase (e.g. 'an all die Zeit', 'an all das', 'an all seinen Problemen'). Word order and case depend on the verb and the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ich denke oft an all die schönen Momente.
native_language_example: I often think about all the beautiful moments.

meaning: to/for everyone; 'to all' (addressing or referring to a group)
additional_notes: Used when addressing, greeting, toasting, or referring to all members of a group. Can appear at the start of a message (e.g. 'An alle, ...' = 'To everyone, ...') or within a sentence after verbs that take 'an' + accusative (e.g. 'erinnern an alle' = 'remember all of them'). Common in greetings (Frohe Weihnachten an alle), toasts (Prost an alle), announcements, and warnings.
target_language_example: An alle: Bitte Rückmeldung bis Freitag.
native_language_example: To everyone: Please reply by Friday.

meaning: to blame someone for everything / to blame someone for all of it
additional_notes: Used with a person as indirect object (jemandem an allem die Schuld geben). Means to hold someone responsible for (almost) every problem or mistake. Common structure: [Person] gibt [jemandem] an allem die Schuld. Often used critically — the blamer thinks the other is responsible for all problems.
target_language_example: Sie gibt mir an allem die Schuld, obwohl es nicht meine Schuld war.
native_language_example: She blames me for everything, even though it wasn't my fault.

meaning: about/everything; literally 'to/on everything' — used with verbs like denken/erinnern to mean 'think of everything' or 'remember everything'.
additional_notes: Usually follows verbs with the preposition 'an' (denken an, sich erinnern an). 'An alles denken' = to think of everything / to make sure nothing is forgotten. 'Sich an alles erinnern' = to remember everything. Context and verb determine exact English phrasing.
target_language_example: Sie hat an alles gedacht, bevor wir losfuhren.
native_language_example: She thought of everything before we left.

meaning: at/on the corner (of a street or building).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location at the corner where two streets meet or the corner of a building. Common in directions (e.g., 'turn at the corner') and descriptions ('the house on the corner'). 'Ecke' is feminine, so 'an der' is the dative form of the preposition + article.
target_language_example: Das Café ist an der Ecke neben der Bank.
native_language_example: The café is on the corner next to the bank.

meaning: at/on the hand; holding someone's hand (physically).
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to the hand or to holding someone's hand. Common in questions about injury (e.g. hurt on the hand), about what someone is wearing on their hand (e.g. ring), or who someone is holding by the hand. Context tells whether it means 'on the hand' (location) or 'by the hand' (holding).
target_language_example: Er ging mit dem Kind an der Hand über die Straße.
native_language_example: He walked across the street holding the child's hand.

meaning: at/from the nose; used literally for nose bleeding and in the idiom 'an der Nase herumführen' meaning 'to lead someone by the nose' (to deceive or manipulate someone).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) literal: part of body expressions like 'an der Nase bluten' (to have a nosebleed). 2) idiomatic: in the fixed phrase 'jdn an der Nase herumführen' meaning to trick, deceive, or manipulate someone (often by misleading them). Context tells which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Er hat mich die ganze Zeit an der Nase herumgeführt.
native_language_example: He led me by the nose the whole time (i.e., he deceived me).

meaning: it's time; it's about time (to do something).
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'es' or in phrases to say that the right moment has come to do something. Often followed by an infinitive with 'zu' (e.g. 'an der Zeit sein, zu ...') or appears in clauses like 'es ist an der Zeit, ...'. Polite/formal neutral register.
target_language_example: Es ist an der Zeit, mit dem Projekt zu beginnen.
native_language_example: It's time to start the project.

meaning: to (get) to work; to start working or return to work.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to tell someone to begin or resume working. Often appears with verbs like 'machen' (mach dich an die Arbeit = get to work), 'gehen' or 'müssen' (Ich muss an die Arbeit = I have to go back to work). Can mean starting a specific task or returning to one's job.
target_language_example: Mach jetzt bitte an die Arbeit — wir haben viel zu tun.
native_language_example: Please get to work now — we have a lot to do.

meaning: to (go) out into the fresh (air); used with Luft to mean 'get some fresh air'.
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own; it's normally followed by Luft (an die frische Luft) meaning 'to get fresh air' or 'go outside for fresh air'. Common in suggestions or needs: Ich muss an die frische Luft (I need to get some fresh air). Use with gehen (gehen an die frische Luft) or bleiben/kommen depending on context.
target_language_example: Wir sollten kurz an die frische Luft gehen.
native_language_example: We should go outside for some fresh air for a moment.

meaning: to this
additional_notes: Literal meaning depends on context. Commonly used with verbs like schicken (send) or kommen (get/obtain) to mean 'to this/these' (direction or target) or with erinnern/glauben to mean 'about/remember/ believe in these'. Word order: 'an' is a preposition that takes the accusative here (diese = accusative feminine/plural depending on noun). Choose the correct English equivalent based on the verb: e.g. 'an diese Adresse' = 'to this address', 'an diese Märchen glauben' = 'to believe in these fairy tales', 'sich an diese Dinge erinnern' = 'to remember these things', 'an diese Bücher gekommen sein' = 'to come by/get these books'.
target_language_example: An diese Adresse kannst du das Paket schicken.
native_language_example: You can send the package to this address.

meaning: to/at your (plural, informal) — used with verbs that take the preposition 'an' (e.g. think of, knock on, follow).
additional_notes: Eure is the informal plural possessive 'your' (addressing more than one person). 'An' is a preposition that can mean 'on', 'at', 'to', or 'about' depending on the verb and context. Together 'an eure' appears before a noun (e.g. 'An eure Plätze', 'an eure Pflicht') or with verbs like 'denken an' (think of), 'klopfen an' (knock on), 'halten an' (stick to/follow). Word order and case depend on the noun that follows (usually accusative after 'an' for movement/attention).
target_language_example: Denkt an eure Aufgaben, damit alles fertig wird.
native_language_example: Think of/remember your tasks so everything gets finished.

meaning: to her
additional_notes: Used with verbs and nouns to indicate direction toward or relation with a female person or a feminine noun (ihr = her). Can mean physical contact (e.g., press something to her), intention to obtain something from her (come by/obtain from her), or a figurative relation (toward her life/end). Context determines whether to translate as 'to her', 'at her', 'toward her', or 'from her' (in phrases like 'gelangen an ihr' = 'to get at/obtain from her').
target_language_example: Er schenkte das Buch an ihr.
native_language_example: He gave the book to her.

meaning: to/on/at her (depending on context) — 'an' + feminine/plural possessive 'ihre', used with verbs that require the preposition 'an' (e.g. erinnern an, denken an, sich machen an).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the preposition 'an' followed by the feminine or plural possessive 'ihre' (her/their). Meaning depends on the verb and case: many verbs use 'an' + accusative (e.g. 'an etwas erinnern' = to remind of), while 'sich an etwas machen' means to start doing something ('an ihre Arbeit machen' = start her work). Pay attention to word order: possessive agrees with the noun that follows (ihre Adresse, ihre Gesundheit, ihre Vitamine, ihre Großmutter, ihre Arbeit).
target_language_example: Er erinnert sie an ihre Schlüssel.
native_language_example: He reminds her of her keys.

meaning: 'to' or 'in' + 'every' (used with accusative objects); means 'to every' / 'on every' / 'at every' depending on context.
additional_notes: Combination of the preposition 'an' (which can mean 'to', 'on', 'at', depending on verb and context) and the accusative 'jeden' ('every' for masculine singular or generic 'every' before a noun). The exact English translation depends on the verb: e.g. 'an ... anbringen' = 'attach to/on every', 'sich an jemanden erinnern' = 'remember every', 'an etwas glauben' = 'believe in every'. Follows accusative case when used with 'an' indicating direction or specific objects. Common in phrases like 'an jeden einzelnen' (to every single one).
target_language_example: Er glaubt an jeden Mythos, den er hört.
native_language_example: He believes in every myth he hears.

meaning: to (someone) who I... (used to introduce a person you know or knew whom something/someone reminds you of).
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a sentence like 'Das erinnert mich an jemanden, den ich ... kannte/treffen habe'. It literally links a memory ('reminds me of someone') to a relative clause describing that person (e.g. 'den ich kannte' = 'whom I knew', 'den ich in New York getroffen habe' = 'whom I met in New York'). Use appropriate past/present perfect verb forms after 'den ich'.
target_language_example: Dieses Foto erinnert mich an jemanden, den ich auf der Arbeit kannte.
native_language_example: This photo reminds me of someone whom I knew at work.

meaning: on (rainy) — used to say 'on rainy (days)'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'an' with an adjective in the dative plural ('regnerischen') and is followed by a time word like 'Tagen' (days). It means 'on rainy days' and is used to talk about things that happen during those days. You will often see it with time expressions (an regnerischen Tagen, an heißen Sommertagen).
target_language_example: An regnerischen Tagen trinke ich gerne heißen Tee.
native_language_example: On rainy days I like to drink hot tea.

meaning: to be on (powered, operating)
additional_notes: Commonly used for electronic devices, lights, machines, or systems to indicate they are powered or operating. Opposite: "aus sein" (to be off). Not typically used for people being present at a location; use other constructions (e.g. "zu Hause sein"). Can sometimes appear in contexts like events or services, but then other verbs are often preferred (e.g. "Der Kurs findet statt").
target_language_example: Die Lampe ist an sein.
native_language_example: The lamp is to be on.

meaning: to which (used with feminine/plural nouns or in questions asking about destination/recipient/objects of thought)
additional_notes: Used in questions with the preposition 'an' + the interrogative 'welche' (which/which ones). 'An' can mean 'to', 'at', 'bordering', or 'about' depending on the verb (e.g. grenzen an — to border, denken an — to think of/about, gehen an/zu — to go to a university). 'Welche' agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to (use welcher/welches for masculine/neuter). Word order: 'An welche + noun + verb...'.
target_language_example: An welche Stadt denkst du gerade?
native_language_example: Which city are you thinking of right now?

meaning: 'I assume you' / 'I suppose you' (formal) — used with 'nehmen' as 'Ich nehme an, Sie ...' to express assumption; also note 'anweisen' and 'ansehen' produce different meanings with 'Sie'.
additional_notes: Most often appears as the phrase 'Ich nehme an, Sie ...' meaning 'I assume/suppose you ...' (formal usted). It's followed by a clause expressing a guess (present or past). Be careful: similar word order with 'Sie' appears in other verbs: 'Ich wies Tom an, Sie zu entlassen' ('wies an' = instructed to dismiss her/them) and 'Sehen Sie mich an' (imperative 'look at me'). So don't confuse 'nehmen an' (to assume) with separable verbs like 'ansehen' (to look at) or 'anweisen' (to instruct). Formal 'Sie' is the polite you; capitalized 'Sie' indicates polite form.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, Sie haben die Unterlagen bekommen.
native_language_example: I assume you have received the documents.

meaning: 'please' used after the verb particle/an expression 'an' plus 'bitte' to form a polite or urgent request; often occurs when 'an' is part of a separable verb (e.g. an*hören*, an*flehen* used in examples) or in constructions where 'an' appears next to 'bitte' for emphasis.
additional_notes: This entry treats the sequence 'an, bitte' as the particle 'an' appearing in examples together with 'bitte' immediately following for emphasis or urgency. 'An' itself is not a standalone polite word; it is usually the separable prefix of a verb (e.g. 'anhören', 'anflehen' in colloquial reductions). The examples show natural uses where 'an' appears in the verb form and 'bitte' follows to make a plea more urgent or polite. Register: can be formal or informal depending on verb form and pronoun (Sie vs. du). Word order: 'bitte' commonly follows the verb or clause; punctuation and intonation add urgency.
target_language_example: Hören Sie mich an, bitte!
native_language_example: Please listen to me!

meaning: 'that' or 'which' (neutral demonstrative 'das') used to refer back to a whole idea or clause; often means 'that'/'which'/'it' in conversational German.
additional_notes: This is the neutral demonstrative pronoun 'das' used to refer to a previously mentioned action, fact, or whole clause (not a specific noun). In many cases it translates as 'that' or 'it' in English. Common in spoken and written German to summarize or comment on something: e.g. 'Ich nehme an, das...' = 'I assume that...' Also appears after verbs like 'leisten', 'lassen', 'riegen' etc. (e.g. 'das ist alles' = 'that's all'). Not a fixed phrase with 'an'—here the comma separates previous word and 'das' starts the clause.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, das stimmt nicht.
native_language_example: I assume that is not true.

meaning: used with verbs like 'flehen' or 'raten' to mean 'to urge/advise someone not to do that'.
additional_notes: This construction appears with verbs that take 'an|flehen' or 'raten' + a pronoun (dich/Ihnen/dir/euch) and an infinitive clause introduced by 'das nicht zu' (often followed by an infinitive at sentence end). It expresses a strong request or advice not to perform a specific action. In spoken/written German you'd often see the full phrase as part of 'jemanden anflehen, das nicht zu tun' or 'jemandem raten, das nicht zu tun.'
target_language_example: Ich bitte dich an, das nicht zu tun.
native_language_example: I plead with you not to do that.

meaning: This is the sequence of two words: the verb or particle 'an' (part of separable verbs) followed by the demonstrative pronoun 'das' — often appears when a sentence has a separable verb or preposition 'anfangen/anschauen' etc. followed by 'das' as 'that/the'.
additional_notes: The input shows 'an' as the separable prefix of verbs like anfangen (to begin) or as a particle used with verbs of direction, and 'das' as the neuter demonstrative pronoun or definite article meaning 'that' or 'the'. In written German you often see the prefix 'an' separated and placed before the object or clause: e.g. 'fängt an, das...' = 'begins to (do) that...'. Beginner learners should know: when a verb is separable, the prefix moves to the end of the clause in main clauses (Ich fange an, das ...), but in subordinate clauses it stays attached (dass er anfängt, das ...).
target_language_example: Er fängt an, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: He begins to solve the problem.

meaning: 'to begin' or 'to start' (e.g. 'anfangen, ein- + infinitive' — to start doing something).
additional_notes: This shows the construction with verbs like anfangen/fing an + ein + infinitive or more simply anfangen + zu + infinitive. In the examples, 'anfangen' (fing an = started) is followed by 'ein' plus a verb in infinitive (colloquial/old-fashioned) or by a noun phrase introduced by 'ein' meaning 'a' (e.g. 'ein Buch'). Here the key is 'anfangen' (to begin). The sequence 'fing an, ein ... zu + infinitive' can be a reduced or colloquial form; modern standard uses 'anfing, ein Buch zu lesen' or 'fing an, ein Buch zu lesen' is fine. Note: 'ein' is also the indefinite article 'a/an' in German — distinguish by context.
target_language_example: Sie fing an, ein Lied zu singen.
native_language_example: She began to sing a song.

meaning: Two separate items: 'an' (a preposition/partikel used in many constructions) and 'sie' (she/they or formal you); here 'sie' = 'her' as accusative pronoun in examples.
additional_notes: This entry groups two common small words that appear together in the example sentences but are separate words. 'an' appears in several uses: as part of separable verbs (e.g., anfangen, anbieten — the prefix 'an' separates: 'fing an', 'bot ... an'), as a preposition (needs a following noun or phrase), and as a particle in commands or hypotheticals (e.g., 'Nehmen wir an...' = 'let's assume'). 'sie' can be nominative 'she' or 'they' or accusative 'her/them'; in the provided examples it is accusative 'sie' = 'her' (object: 'betet sie an' worships her; 'bot ... sie ... zu fahren' offered to drive her; 'nahm ... und fing an, sie zu mischen' — 'sie' = 'them' (cards) here is plural accusative). Pay attention to context and capitalization: 'Sie' (capital S) can also mean formal 'you'. Word order: with separable verbs the prefix 'an' goes to the end in finite forms (er fängt an → 'fing an' in past).
target_language_example: Er bot ihr an, sie nach Hause zu fahren.
native_language_example: He offered her to drive her home.

meaning: Two separate items: 'an' (a particle used with verbs like anfangen/ansprechen/anziehen or in separable verbs) and 'wir' (we).
additional_notes: This input shows 'an' used in different ways: as the separable prefix of verbs (e.g. anfangen → fang ... an; anrufen → ruf ... an; anschreien → schreien ... an; anrühren → rühren ... an) and as part of the fixed phrase 'ich nehme an' (I assume) where 'an' belongs to the verb nehmen (idiomatic). 'Wir' is the personal pronoun 'we'. Pay attention to word order with separable verbs: the prefix 'an' goes to the end in main clauses (Fang gleich an.). In compound sentences 'wir' follows normal subject position. Useful for beginners: learn common separable verbs with 'an' (anfangen, anrufen, anschreien, anrühren) and the phrase 'ich nehme an' = 'I assume'.
target_language_example: Fang gleich an, wir müssen los.
native_language_example: Start right away, we have to go.

meaning: used to compare sensations or similarities: 'feels/acts like' or 'is like'.
additional_notes: Common in similes after verbs like fühlen (sich anfühlen), ziehen (anziehen) or others: verb + an wie + noun/clause. It links a sensory or relational verb with a comparison (English 'like' or 'as'). Word-for-word: an (at/on) + wie (how/like), but together they function as a comparison marker. Use with proper word order: e.g. 'fühlt sich an wie...' or 'ziehen an wie...'.
target_language_example: Das Tuch fühlt sich an wie Seide.
native_language_example: The cloth feels like silk.

meaning: to begin to read, to start reading.
additional_notes: Often appears as 'anfangen zu lesen' or with the separable verb 'anfangen' + 'zu' + infinitive (e.g. 'fing an zu lesen' = 'began to read'). In spoken German you may also hear 'anfing zu lesen' or simply 'fing an zu lesen' in past tense. Use with a subject (e.g. 'Er fing an zu lesen').
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich hin und fing an zu lesen.
native_language_example: She sat down and began to read.

meaning: used in the phrase 'alles andere als' to mean 'far from', 'anything but', or 'by no means'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'alles andere als' + adjective/noun. It emphasizes that something is the opposite of the described quality (e.g. 'far from calm', 'anything but innocent'). Often used to express strong contrast or surprise. Not literal: don't translate word-for-word as 'other than'.
target_language_example: Das Ergebnis war alles andere als zufriedenstellend.
native_language_example: The result was anything but satisfactory.

meaning: 'others not' — used to contrast people/things that do have/do something with those that do not
additional_notes: Commonly follows a clause describing some ability, quality, or action: first mention says who/what does/has something, then 'andere nicht' contrasts those who don't. Often short for 'andere (tun/haben/etc.) nicht' — the verb is omitted and understood from context.
target_language_example: Manche verstehen den Witz, andere nicht.
native_language_example: Some understand the joke, others don't.

meaning: 'others are' — used to contrast different people or things (some are X, others are Y).
additional_notes: Commonly used to contrast groups or items. 'andere' can stand alone without a noun when context is clear (e.g. 'einige sind..., andere sind...'). Word order: subject + verb (sind) follows the contrasted topic. Can refer to people or things. In informal speech you may also hear 'die anderen sind...'.
target_language_example: Einige Schüler lernten viel, andere sind faul.
native_language_example: Some students studied a lot, others are lazy.

meaning: the other side of the river
additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite bank or side of a river from the speaker's current location. In German you usually say "auf der anderen Seite des Flusses" (with the article and preposition "auf" or "an"). Without the article it appears as a noun phrase; beginners will commonly hear the full phrase: "auf der anderen Seite des Flusses."
target_language_example: Wir wohnen auf der anderen Seite des Flusses.
native_language_example: We live on the other side of the river.

meaning: in other words; to put it differently.
additional_notes: Used to restate or clarify what was just said. Often appears in the phrase "mit anderen Worten" (literally: "with other words") but can also be used without "mit" in some contexts. Useful for giving a simpler explanation or rephrasing.
target_language_example: Mit anderen Worten: Du musst pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: In other words: you must be on time.

meaning: the other side (of something) / on the other side
additional_notes: Usually appears in phrases like 'auf der anderen Seite' (on the other side / on the other hand). 'anderen' is the weakly declined form of 'ander-' used with the feminine/neuter/masculine depending on article and case; 'Seite' = side. Common uses: physical location (the other side of a street/river) or figurative contrast (on the other hand). Remember to include the correct article and case: e.g. 'auf der anderen Seite' (dative, feminine) or 'die andere Seite' (nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Seite des Flusses ist ein Park.
native_language_example: On the other side of the river there is a park.

meaning: the other side of the river
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location across the river from the speaker or a reference point. In full German you'd normally say "auf der anderen Seite des Flusses" (with the preposition "auf"). "anderen Seite des Flusses" on its own is the noun phrase part. Can be used for houses, towns, people, etc.
target_language_example: Das Café ist auf der anderen Seite des Flusses.
native_language_example: The café is on the other side of the river.

meaning: the other side of the street
additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition (auf der anderen Straßenseite = on the other side of the street). Refers to the opposite side from the speaker or a reference point. 'anderen' is dative feminine here (die Straßenseite → der Straßenseite).
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Straßenseite ist ein Supermarkt.
native_language_example: There is a supermarket on the other side of the street.

meaning: 'the others are' — used to describe other people/things and say what they are or where they are.
additional_notes: A combination of 'die anderen' (the others) + verb 'sind' (are). Used to contrast one or more items/people with the rest. Can refer to characteristics, professions, locations, or comparisons. Word order: 'Die anderen sind ...' is the normal neutral form. If gender/number changes, 'die' may change (e.g. 'die anderen' for plural).
target_language_example: Einer ist krank, die anderen sind gesund.
native_language_example: One is sick; the others are healthy.

meaning: of a different kind/type; another kind of
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe that something is a different variety or type than expected. Often follows the noun it modifies (e.g., 'ein Problem anderer Art' = a problem of a different kind). Formal to neutral register; common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Das ist ein Problem anderer Art.
native_language_example: That is a problem of a different kind.

meaning: the other side (of a river/lake); the opposite bank
additional_notes: Used when talking about the opposite shore or bank of a body of water. Can be literal (crossing to the other bank) or metaphorical (reaching a different situation/state). 'Ufer' is neuter: das Ufer; 'anderes' agrees in gender/case (anderes Ufer = nominative/accusative singular).
target_language_example: Wir müssen ans andere Ufer schwimmen.
native_language_example: We have to swim to the other bank.

meaning: anything/something other than; different from
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that something is different from or besides something else. Often appears in questions or negatives (e.g. 'noch was anderes als' = 'anything else besides'). Can be followed by verbs, nouns, or clauses. Word order and small words (wie, was) may vary in colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Gibt es noch etwas anderes als Kaffee?
native_language_example: Is there anything else besides coffee?

meaning: have no choice/option but to (do something).
additional_notes: Used in the fixed expression '(mir/uns/etc.) bleibt(n) nichts anderes übrig, als zu + infinitive' to say someone has no alternative except to do X. Common in past and present. Often shortened in speech to 'mir bleibt nichts anderes übrig, als...' or 'es blieb mir nichts anderes übrig, als...'. The pronoun (mir/uns/dir) matches the person affected.
target_language_example: Da es keinen Bus gab, blieb mir nichts anderes übrig, als zu laufen.
native_language_example: Because there was no bus, I had no choice but to walk.

meaning: started learning French; 'angefangen' = (have) started, used with an activity.
additional_notes: The structure shows 'anfangen' (to start) followed by an activity introduced with a comma and the object (here 'Französisch' = French). More common constructions: 'anfangen, ... zu + infinitive' (Hast du angefangen, Französisch zu lernen?) or 'mit + Dativ anfangen' (Ich habe mit dreizehn angefangen). Questions often use 'wann' (when) or 'warum' (why). Use 'anfangen' in perfect tense with 'haben' (ich habe angefangen).
target_language_example: Wir haben letztes Jahr angefangen, Französisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: We started learning French last year.

meaning: called and (then)... — links two actions where someone phoned and another action happened or was done.
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written German to describe a phone call followed by another action. 'Angerufen' is the past participle of 'anrufen' (to call). The 'und' connects the call to what happened next (e.g., hung up, talked to someone, said goodbye, told someone). The second verb often appears in the past tense or as a reflexive (sich verabschiedet).
