additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to evening time. Often follows a verb or time expression: e.g. 'Ich arbeite bis abends' = I work until the evening / I work late into the evening. Can be more general (until nighttime) rather than a precise clock time.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben bis abends im Café.
native_language_example: We'll stay in the café until the evening.

meaning: 'up to' or 'until' (followed by a noun indicating an endpoint or limit)
additional_notes: Used to indicate reaching a physical endpoint (e.g. Ende der Straße) or a time limit (e.g. Ende der Zeit, Ende ihrer Tage). Commonly appears as 'bis ans Ende (der ...)' or 'bis ans Ziel'. It combines 'bis' (until/up to) + 'an' (at/to) and is followed by the noun in the accusative. Use 'bis zum' or 'bis zur' when the noun takes a different preposition form.
target_language_example: Gehen Sie bis ans Ende der Straße und dann links.
native_language_example: Go up to the end of the street and then turn left.

meaning: See you soon; talk to you soon.
additional_notes: A casual farewell used when you expect to meet or speak again soon. Common in everyday conversations, messages, and emails. Can stand alone or be followed by a name or place (e.g., "Bis bald in Paris"). Politeness level: neutral/informal — appropriate with friends, colleagues, and acquaintances.
target_language_example: Bleib gesund und bis bald!
native_language_example: Stay healthy and see you soon!

meaning: 'until then' or 'by then' (refers to a point in time mentioned or understood)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future or previously mentioned point in time. Can mean 'until that time' (ongoing period up to then) or 'by that time' (something happening before or at that point). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir haben noch drei Tage; bis dahin muss das erledigt sein.
native_language_example: We have three days left; it must be done by then.

meaning: See you then; goodbye for now (used when parting, often implying you'll meet or speak again).
additional_notes: A casual farewell used in spoken German. Works alone or with a name (e.g. "Bis dann, Anna"). Slightly informal but common in neutral contexts. Use when you expect to meet or talk again at a later time. Can be shortened to just "bis dann" or combined with mild interjections like "na gut, bis dann."
target_language_example: Bis dann, wir sehen uns morgen!
native_language_example: See you then, we'll meet tomorrow!

meaning: until yesterday; up to and including yesterday
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something was true, required, or valid up to yesterday. Can be used literally (time frame) or hyperbolically/urgently (e.g. 'I needed it by yesterday' meaning 'I needed it immediately'). Often appears in deadlines and comments about past status. 'Bis gestern noch' emphasizes that something was true until yesterday but no longer is.
target_language_example: Ich brauchte den Bericht bis gestern.
native_language_example: I needed the report by yesterday.

meaning: See you in a short while / see you soon (very near future).
additional_notes: Used when you expect to meet the person again soon — usually within minutes or the same day. Less formal than 'auf Wiedersehen' but can be used with titles (e.g., 'Herr Wenger'). Common in everyday spoken German. Not suitable for long-term goodbyes.
target_language_example: Ich mache kurz Besorgungen. Bis gleich!
native_language_example: I'm running a quick errand. See you in a bit!

meaning: 'until today' / 'to this day' (expresses that something still holds now or has been true up to now)
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, fact or state continues up to the present moment. Can be used with positive or negative statements and with verbs in present or perfect contexts. Often interchangeable with "bis jetzt" or "noch heute" in some contexts, but "bis heute" emphasizes continuity up to today or that something remains true to this day.
target_language_example: Bis heute habe ich den Mut nicht gefunden, ihm zu danken.
native_language_example: To this day I haven't had the courage to thank him.

meaning: up to here; as far as this point (can be literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used both physically (reaching/swimming up to a point) and figuratively (being fed up or being deeply involved). In colloquial/strong expressions like sentence 1, it expresses 'I'm fed up up to here' — i.e. I've had enough. Often combined with gestures (pointing to chest/neck) or words like 'hinauf', 'hinaus' or 'da drin' to clarify meaning.
target_language_example: Ich bin mit der Arbeit bis hier — ich brauche eine Pause.
native_language_example: I'm up to here with the work — I need a break.

meaning: so far; up to now; until now.
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to talk about what has happened or been true up to the present moment. Can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence. Often interchangeable with 'bisher' or 'bislang' in many contexts.
target_language_example: Bis jetzt habe ich alle Aufgaben erledigt.
native_language_example: So far I have completed all the tasks.

meaning: until tomorrow / see you tomorrow (goodbye)
additional_notes: Commonly used both as a time expression meaning 'up to tomorrow' (deadline) and as a farewell meaning 'see you tomorrow'. Context tells you which meaning is intended. Pronunciation: [bɪs ˈmɔʁɡn].
target_language_example: Bis morgen, dann klären wir den Rest.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow, then we'll sort out the rest.

meaning: 'see you later' (see you in a short while; later today)
additional_notes: A casual farewell used when you'll meet or speak with the person again soon (later the same day or in a short time). Less formal than 'auf Wiedersehen', similar to 'bis später' or 'bis dann'. Common in spoken German and with friends, colleagues, or acquaintances.
target_language_example: Alles klar, bis nachher!
native_language_example: All right, see you later!

meaning: 'until next week' or as a goodbye: 'see you next week.'
additional_notes: Can be used as a time expression meaning 'until next week' (deadline or time period). Commonly used as a farewell equivalent to 'see you next week.' Context tells whether it's a deadline (e.g. tasks due) or a parting phrase. If specifying a day, add the day (e.g. 'bis nächste Woche Mittwoch').
target_language_example: Bis nächste Woche, wir sprechen dann weiter.
native_language_example: See you next week, we'll talk then.

meaning: until late into (e.g. the night).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (most commonly 'Nacht') to say someone stayed up or did something late. Usually followed by a noun in accusative (die Nacht). Common in statements about working, studying, reading, etc. Can be combined with verbs like bleiben, arbeiten, lernen, sitzen, aufbleiben.
target_language_example: Ich habe bis spät in die Nacht gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked until late into the night.

meaning: 'see you later' / 'until later' — a casual way to say you'll meet or speak again later
additional_notes: Common informal farewell used when you expect to see or contact the person later the same day or soon. Can be used with names or vocatives (e.g., 'Bis später, Dad'). Tone ranges from friendly to neutral. Not strictly formal; use 'auf Wiedersehen' or 'bis bald' in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt los — bis später!
native_language_example: I have to go now — see you later!

meaning: 'until when' / 'how long (until)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask until what time or date something lasts or when someone will leave. Common in questions about opening hours, visits, stays, deadlines. Often followed by a time expression or an infinitive clause (e.g., 'bis wann bleiben Sie?').
target_language_example: Bis wann bleibst du dieses Mal in Berlin?
native_language_example: Until when are you staying in Berlin this time?

meaning: 'up to' / 'as far as' / 'until' depending on context
additional_notes: Common multiword preposition/phrase with several related uses: (1) indicating a limit or maximum amount/number — 'up to' (e.g., bis zu drei Bücher); (2) indicating spatial extent — 'as far as' (Geh bis zu dem Baum); (3) indicating time up to a point or deadline — 'until'/'up to' (Ich hatte Zeit bis zu Lois Flug). Context determines the best English translation. When followed by a noun it takes the accusative (bis zu + dem → bis zum).
target_language_example: Die Veranstaltung dauert bis zu zwei Stunden.
native_language_example: The event lasts up to two hours.

meaning: until the end; to the very end; through to completion.
additional_notes: Used to indicate continuing something up to its conclusion (time, action, commitment). Can be literal (until the end of a period or event) or figurative (supporting someone 'to the end', completing a treatment). Often followed by a time phrase (e.g. bis zum Ende der Woche) or stands alone (bis zum Ende).
target_language_example: Ich bleibe bei dir bis zum Ende.
native_language_example: I'll stay with you until the end.

meaning: completely; head over heels (usually with emotions, especially love or happiness).
additional_notes: An idiomatic phrase meaning extremely or to be deeply affected by something (often love or a big smile). Commonly used with verbs like verliebt sein (to be in love) or grinsen (to grin). Literally: 'up to over both ears.'
target_language_example: Sie war bis über beide Ohren in ihn verliebt.
native_language_example: She was head over heels in love with him.

meaning: until the (something) / until that (something) happens.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause showing when something will happen or should be done. Followed by a verb clause (subordinate clause) with verb at the end in written German, but in everyday spoken German you may hear normal word order after 'bis' in informal speech. Can be used with specific events (bis das Licht grün wird) or more abstract ideas (bis das richtige Leben anfängt).
target_language_example: Warte, bis das Wetter besser ist.
native_language_example: Wait until the weather is better.

meaning: 'until the' or 'until they/the (feminine or plural) ... arrive/do something'.
additional_notes: Combines the subordinating conjunction bis (until) with the definite article/pronoun die. Used to introduce a clause indicating the time or condition when something will happen—often followed by a verb. 'die' can refer to plural people/things or feminine singular (context decides). In conversational German the clause may omit words (colloquial ellipsis). Word order in the bis-clause is verb-final: e.g. 'bis die da sind' (until they are there).
target_language_example: Warte hier, bis die Polizei da ist.
native_language_example: Wait here until the police are there.

meaning: 'until I (do/know/say) it' — indicates something continues up to the moment when I do/say/know something.
additional_notes: Commonly used in subordinate time clauses with 'bis' to mark the endpoint of an action. The exact meaning of 'es' depends on context (e.g. permission, an object, information). Often followed by a verb in perfect or present/subjunctive depending on mood (e.g. 'bis ich es dir erlaube', 'bis ich es gefunden habe', 'bis ich es Ihnen sage').
target_language_example: Warte hier, bis ich es überprüft habe.
native_language_example: Wait here until I have checked it.

meaning: until I’m back / until I return
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to wait, keep watch, or pause an action until the speaker comes back. Common in spoken and written German. Often completed as "bis ich wieder da bin" (with "bin"). Can be polite or informal depending on context and pronoun (Sie/du).
target_language_example: Behalten Sie alles im Auge, bis ich wieder da bin!
native_language_example: Keep an eye on everything until I get back!

meaning: until my / until (something) of mine (happens).
additional_notes: ‘bis’ means ‘until’. With a possessive noun phrase like ‘mein Vater’ it expresses a time point up to which an action continues (e.g. 'stay until my father comes home'). The verb in the subordinate clause normally appears at the end (word order for subordinate clauses). Can be used with different persons/possessions: bis meine Mutter, bis mein Geld, etc. One example sentence contains strong vulgar language; avoid using that in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Ich warte hier, bis mein Bruder zurückkommt.
native_language_example: I'll wait here until my brother comes back.

meaning: bit/bitten oneself — literal past of 'sich beißen': to bite (one's) — used for actions like biting one's lip or clenching one's teeth (to hold back words, pain, or emotion).
additional_notes: This is the simple past form (3rd person singular) of 'sich beißen' used reflexively: 'er/sie biss sich ...'. Common expressions: 'sich auf die Lippe beißen' (to bite one's lip) and 'sich die Zähne zusammenbeißen' (to grit one's teeth). These actions often show someone is trying to restrain speech, hide emotion, or endure discomfort. Use present tense 'beißen sich' (they), or perfect 'hat sich gebissen' rarely for this meaning; more common is present/perfect of the reflexive phrase (e.g. 'er hat sich auf die Lippe gebissen').
target_language_example: Sie biss sich auf die Lippe, bevor sie antwortete.
native_language_example: She bit her lip before she answered.

meaning: a little better; somewhat improved
additional_notes: Common phrase to describe a small improvement in health, mood, appearance, or situation. Often used with verbs like aussehen, fühlen, gehen (Wie geht's?). 'ein bisschen besser' is the full phrase; 'bisschen besser' without 'ein' is also heard in casual speech. Use to ask or report slight recovery or improvement.
target_language_example: Mir geht es heute ein bisschen besser.
native_language_example: I'm feeling a little better today.

meaning: a little too / slightly too (followed by adjective or adverb).
additional_notes: Used to soften criticism or state that something or someone exceeds a desired degree by a small amount. Appears before adjectives/adverbs (e.g., zu groß, zu früh, zu spät). 'ein bisschen zu' is interchangeable with 'ein wenig zu'. Word order: 'ist ein bisschen zu + adjective/adverb' or with verbs: 'kommt ein bisschen zu spät.'
target_language_example: Das Hemd ist ein bisschen zu groß.
native_language_example: The shirt is a little too big.

meaning: 'you are' + 'too' (used with adjectives/adverbs to say someone is too [early/late/etc.])
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular present of 'sein' (du bist) followed by 'zu' meaning 'too' or 'too much' before an adjective or adverb. Common in sentences like 'Du bist zu früh gekommen' (You came too early) or 'Du bist zu spät' (You are too late). 'Zu' must agree with the adjective/adverb that follows; the full phrase often includes a past participle (gekommen) for events: 'bist zu früh gekommen'.
target_language_example: Du bist zu müde, um weiterzuarbeiten.
native_language_example: You are too tired to keep working.

meaning: Present-tense forms of the verb sein (to be): 'bist' = 2nd person singular informal (du) 'are'; 'ist' = 3rd person singular (er/sie/es) 'is' and used impersonally (es ist) or in some contexts with Sie (formal) when grammatical subject is 3rd person.
additional_notes: 'bist' and 'ist' often appear together in complex sentences where a subordinate clause contains 'bist' and the main clause contains 'ist' (e.g., 'Dass du hier bist, ist ...'). Common in constructions expressing states, identities, or impersonal observations. 'bist' requires the informal 'du' subject. 'ist' agrees with er/sie/es or with the main clause's subject (including impersonal 'es').
target_language_example: Dass du hier bist, ist sicher auch vertraulich.
native_language_example: That you are here is probably also confidential.

meaning: 'you are probably' or 'you must be' (expressing a confident guess about someone)
additional_notes: Used to make a polite or confident guess about the listener's state, feelings, actions, or identity. 'Bestimmt' softens the statement into a prediction or assumption. Common in everyday speech. Word order: subject (du) + bist + bestimmt + complement. Tone can be friendly, sympathetic, or speculative depending on context.
target_language_example: Du bist bestimmt müde nach der langen Reise.
native_language_example: You are probably tired after the long trip.

meaning: it's your turn (you're up).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are next to act, speak, or perform a task (e.g. make coffee, take a turn in a game). Often appears with a name: 'Du bist dran, [Name]'. Can be followed by 'mit' + noun/verb phrase to specify the task (e.g. 'bist dran mit Kaffee' = you're the one to make/get the coffee). Informal, common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Anna, du bist dran mit dem Abwasch.
native_language_example: Anna, it's your turn to do the dishes.

meaning: 'are you and' — literal sequence of 'bist du' (are you) followed by 'und' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiomatic phrase in German; it's simply the words 'bist du' immediately followed by 'und'. It appears when a speaker begins a question and then adds another clause or continues the sentence (e.g. in pauses or ellipses). On its own it is incomplete and usually requires additional words to form a grammatical sentence.
target_language_example: Bist du und...?
native_language_example: Are you and...?

meaning: 'are you too' (used to ask if someone is excessively something or willing/ready to do something)
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Bist du zu + adjective/infinitive/ready' or 'Bist du zu + [adjective]?' Often asks if someone is 'too' something (e.g., too busy, too tired, too old). With an infinitive it can appear in questions about willingness or readiness, but word order in standard German usually places the infinitive at the end (e.g., 'Bist du bereit zu kämpfen?'). Some example patterns: 'Bist du zu beschäftigt, um ...?' (too busy to ...), 'Bist du zu müde?' (too tired), 'Bist du bereit zu kämpfen?' (are you ready to fight?).
target_language_example: Bist du zu müde, um noch zu arbeiten?
native_language_example: Are you too tired to work any more?

meaning: You're really a ... (adds emphasis before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a characteristic of the person addressed. Can be positive or negative depending on the noun that follows: e.g. 'ein Esel' (insult) or 'ein guter Lehrer' (compliment). Informal and common in spoken German. Word order: 'Du bist echt ein + noun'.
target_language_example: Du bist echt ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: You're really a good friend.

meaning: you are a very
additional_notes: Combination of 'du bist' (you are) + 'ein sehr' (a very) used before a noun phrase with an adjective. In natural German you would usually say 'du bist sehr ...' for adjectives without an article (e.g. 'du bist sehr geduldig') or 'du bist ein sehr ...' when the noun requires the indefinite article (often when the adjective is part of a noun phrase: 'du bist ein sehr guter Mensch'). In the example sentences 'bist ein sehr' appears because the speaker uses the indefinite article before a noun modified by an adjective.
target_language_example: Du bist ein sehr netter Freund.
native_language_example: You are a very nice friend.

meaning: you are exactly / you are precisely (used to emphasize correctness, position, or quality)
additional_notes: This is the verb 'sein' (du bist) plus 'genau' used to emphasize precision. Depending on sentence, it can mean 'you are exactly the one', 'you are exactly right', 'you are right behind me' (with position), or 'you are exactly as good as...'. 'Genau' can modify a noun phrase, an adverbial phrase, or an adjective. In spoken German you may also hear 'du bist genau derjenige' or shorter 'du bist genau richtig'.
target_language_example: Du bist genau der Freund, den ich brauche.
native_language_example: You are exactly the friend I need.

meaning: you are just as (adjective/adverb) / you are equally
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Du bist genauso [adj] wie [jemand/etwas]' = 'You are just as [adj] as [someone/something]'. Used to compare equality (often with emphasis or criticism). 'genauso' can modify adjectives, adverbs, or noun phrases (with an article). Word order: 'bist' (2nd person singular of 'sein') + 'genauso' + adjective/adverb. Tone can be neutral or negative depending on context; many example sentences show insults.
target_language_example: Du bist genauso freundlich wie deine Schwester.
native_language_example: You are just as friendly as your sister.

meaning: are now
additional_notes: Combination of the 2nd-person singular form of sein (bist) + jetzt (now). Used to say that someone is in a new state or situation at the present moment. Common in statements and questions (e.g. surprise about a new status). Informal contraction into "du bist jetzt" is typical in speech.
target_language_example: Du bist jetzt verantwortlich für das Projekt.
native_language_example: You are now responsible for the project.

meaning: you are my (used before a feminine singular noun or endearing role).
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb 'bist' (2nd person singular of 'sein' = 'you are') plus the possessive pronoun 'meine' (my) used before feminine singular nouns (die Freundin, die Tochter, die Königin) or feminine abstract nouns (die Freiheit). In German word order you normally say 'Du bist meine ...'. The gender of the possessed noun matters: use 'mein' (masculine/neuter), 'meine' (feminine/plural). 'Bist meine' is not a fixed idiom — it's just a common phrase pattern for expressing possession or endearment.
target_language_example: Du bist meine beste Freundin.
native_language_example: You are my best friend (female).

meaning: ‘you are not the’ — used to say someone is not the only/first/etc. person in a situation.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in sentences like “Du bist nicht der Einzige/Erste…”. It reassures or points out that others share the same experience or made the same mistake. Word order can change with endings (der/die/das, der Einzige, der Erste). Informal or formal register depends on context; 'du' is informal.
target_language_example: Du bist nicht der Einzige, der sich verlaufen hat.
native_language_example: You are not the only one who got lost.

meaning: you're only a
additional_notes: Used to downplay someone's role, status or identity — often dismissive. Followed by a noun (e.g. beruf, role, insult). The literal order is 'are only a'. Tone can be neutral (factual) or rude/insulting depending on context and the noun used.
target_language_example: Du bist nur ein Praktikant, wir brauchen keine Entscheidung von dir.
native_language_example: You're just an intern; we don't need a decision from you.

meaning: 'you are to blame' or 'it's your fault'.
additional_notes: Used to accuse someone directly — informal/direct. Often appears with 'an' or 'daran' and a clause introduced by 'dass' or a noun phrase (e.g. 'du bist schuld daran', 'du bist schuld am Tod...'). Tone can be strong or emotional; in neutral contexts use milder phrases like 'du trägst die Verantwortung' or 'du bist verantwortlich'.
target_language_example: Du bist schuld daran, dass wir zu spät kamen.
native_language_example: You are to blame for us being late.

meaning: you're such a (someone) — used to insult or emphasize a negative trait
additional_notes: Common in spoken German to criticize or insult someone by calling them 'such a ...'. Followed by a noun (often negative: Idiot, Lügner). Tone is usually angry or scolding. Word order: 'Du bist so ein + Noun' (informal you). For feminine/neutral nouns or with articles, adjust: 'Du bist so eine ...' or 'Du bist so ein ...' depending on gender.
target_language_example: Du bist so ein Egoist!
native_language_example: You're such a selfish person!

meaning: you're dead
additional_notes: Literally 'you are dead'. Used both literally (someone is dead) and idiomatically/threateningly to mean 'you're finished' or 'I'm going to get you'. Tone can be aggressive; common in insults or threats. Informal and often rude when used to threaten someone. Context determines whether literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Pass auf, oder du bist tot!
native_language_example: Watch out, or you're dead!

meaning: please (wait) until I (come back); 'please wait until I return'.
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used to ask someone to wait for you. 'Bitte' makes the request polite. 'Bis ich' is followed by a verb (usually 'zurückkomme' or 'wiederkomme') in the present tense to indicate 'until I come back/return'. Can be used with different pronouns and verb forms (Warte, Warten Sie, Wartet) depending on formality and number.
target_language_example: Warte bitte, bis ich zurückkomme.
native_language_example: Please wait until I come back.

meaning: please let (someone) know / please inform (someone).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to inform you or others about something (often about decisions, changes, needs, or problems). Common with verbs like sagen, geben, or melden: (mir/uns/ihm) bitte Bescheid sagen/gem geben. Polite and very common in everyday and formal contexts. Use appropriate pronoun (mir, uns, ihm, ihr) to indicate who should be informed.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte Bescheid, wenn du fertig bist.
native_language_example: Please let me know when you are finished.

meaning: please (do) your… / please (show) your… (polite request followed by a possessive noun)
additional_notes: Used in polite requests or instructions in formal 'Sie' address. 'Bitte' means 'please' and 'Ihre' is the formal possessive 'your' (capitalized for formal Sie). It must be followed by a noun (Einladung, Hände, Adresse, Stimme, etc.). Word order: 'Bitte' can come before the verb or after the verb in imperatives and polite questions (e.g., 'Darf ich bitte Ihre Einladung sehen?' or 'Legen Sie bitte Ihre Hände...').
target_language_example: Bitte Ihre Tasche hier abstellen.
native_language_example: Please put your bag down here.

meaning: a polite request structure meaning 'please [show/bring/provide] your ...' used when addressing one person formally (Sie).
additional_notes: Composed of 'bitte' (please) and the formal accusative/polite possessive 'Ihren' (your, formal Sie). Used with formal imperative or polite questions: 'Bitte Ihren Ausweis' = 'please (show) your ID.' The noun after 'Ihren' will be in accusative case. Use when speaking formally to someone you would address as 'Sie'.
target_language_example: Dürfte ich bitte Ihren Ausweis sehen?
native_language_example: May I please see your ID?

meaning: please everyone / could everyone (please)
additional_notes: Used to address or request action from a group of people. 'Bitte' is polite; word order can vary (e.g. 'Kommt bitte alle her'). Can be followed by an imperative or instruction. In plural informal speech 'ihr' may appear (e.g. 'Würdet ihr bitte alle...').
target_language_example: Bitte alle kurz stillstehen.
native_language_example: Please everyone stand still for a moment.

meaning: the particle 'bitte' (please) used with separable verbs whose prefix is 'an-' to form polite requests/imperatives (e.g. 'Bitte anhalten' → 'Halten Sie bitte an!' = 'Please stop!').
additional_notes: In German many verbs have separable prefixes (here 'an-'). In commands or requests the prefix separates and goes to the end: verb + ... + an. 'Bitte' is placed to make the sentence polite. Examples: 'Halten Sie bitte an!' (Please stop!), 'Ruf mich bitte an.' (Please call me.). Word order and formal/informal address affect the verb form (Sie/du).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich morgen bitte anrufen?
native_language_example: Can you please call me tomorrow?

meaning: please (also); 'please' + 'also'—used to ask for something in addition or to include the speaker/request in a request.
additional_notes: Combine 'bitte' (please) with 'auch' (also/too). Common in requests to ask for an extra thing ('Do this for me too') or to include the speaker ('Can I also...'). Word order can vary: 'Kann ich bitte auch...?', 'Mach mir bitte auch...'. Tone is polite; context determines whether it's a simple addition or a mild complaint ('Please be objective, too').
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte auch das Salz geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me the salt too?

meaning: 'please' + verbs with auf (particle) — used with separable-verb constructions that include auf (e.g. aufpassen, auf etwas warten, auf etwas zeigen, auf etwas hinzufügen).
additional_notes: In German, many verbs are separable and place the particle (here: auf) at the end of the sentence in main clauses. 'Bitte' is a politeness word placed before the verb or particle to make a request (e.g. 'Bitte aufpassen' = 'Please watch (out/over) ...'). In full sentences you will normally see the object or prepositional phrase where needed: 'Bitte auf mich warten' is more natural as 'Warte bitte auf mich!'. The particle 'auf' itself has no meaning alone here — its meaning depends on the verb (aufpassen = look after, auf etwas warten = wait for, auf etwas zeigen = show on, hinzufügen auf/zu often uses 'zu' or 'auf WhatsApp' as platform).
target_language_example: Warte bitte auf mich!
native_language_example: Please wait for me!

meaning: 'please help yourself' (inviting someone to take/serve food or use something)
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used when offering food, drinks, or items; usually appears as 'Bitte bedienen Sie sich' (formal) or 'Bitte bedien dich' (informal). Can be followed by a location or item (bei den Keksen, beim Obst). Tone is welcoming and permissive.
target_language_example: Bitte bedienen Sie sich am Buffet.
native_language_example: Please help yourself at the buffet.

meaning: 'please' + 'with' → used to politely ask someone to stay with, help with, or contact someone about something
additional_notes: Combines the politeness marker bitte with the preposition bei. Common uses: asking someone to stay with a person or animal (bleib bitte bei ...), to ask for help with a task or object (hilf mir bitte bei ... / helfen Sie mir bitte bei ...), or to ask someone to get in touch at/with someone (meld dich bitte bei mir). Word order: bitte can appear before or after the verb or pronoun (e.g., Du bleibst bitte bei Ponyo / Bleib bitte bei Ponyo). Formality: use "bitte" with du or Sie as shown.
target_language_example: Hilf mir bitte bei dem Projekt, ich brauche deine Ideen.
native_language_example: Please help me with the project, I need your ideas.

meaning: a polite request meaning 'please until' or 'please by' (used to ask for something to be done or delivered up to a certain time or date)
additional_notes: Combine bitte (please) with bis (until/by) to set a polite deadline or time limit. Common in phrases like 'Bitte bis morgen' (please [do it] by tomorrow) or 'Bitte bis 15 Uhr' (please until/by 3 PM). You usually omit the verb when context makes it clear (e.g., in emails or notes).
target_language_example: Bitte bis Freitag zurückschicken.
native_language_example: Please send it back by Friday.

meaning: 'please bring' or 'please take' (a polite request to bring or take someone/something)
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (often a waiter, driver, or helper) to bring an object, food, or a person to a location or to take someone somewhere. With formal 'Sie' in examples; can be used with du (bitte bring) in informal contexts. Word order: 'Bitte bringen Sie ...' + direct object or destination (e.g. 'mich zu dieser Adresse').
target_language_example: Bitte bringen Sie mir ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: Please bring me a glass of water.

meaning: please help (with that/this); please do it as part of that
additional_notes: Dabei follows a verb or helper (helfen) and refers to assisting with the action or task just mentioned ("with it/that"). Bitte is a polite request marker. Word order: bitte can appear before or after the verb; dabei stays near the verb or at the end. Common in requests like "Hilf mir bitte dabei" or "Kannst du mir bitte dabei helfen?"
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte dabei helfen, den Schrank aufzubauen?
native_language_example: Can you please help me with assembling the cabinet?

meaning: “please the/that” — polite request followed by a direct object (English: “please [give/bring/etc.] the/that …”).
additional_notes: In German, bitte (please) often comes before the object or verb. 'Bitte das …' appears when asking someone politely to give, bring, or do something with a specific item mentioned next (e.g. 'bitte das Menü' = 'please [bring] the menu'). The verb may be omitted in casual requests (especially when addressing service staff), but context implies actions like geben, bringen, or reichen.
target_language_example: Kellner, geben Sie uns bitte das Wasser.
native_language_example: Waiter, please give us the water.

meaning: a polite request to ask someone to give or lend you something of theirs (please your...)
additional_notes: Combine bitte (please) with a possessive pronoun (dein = your) and a noun: 'bitte dein + [object]' is a casual way to ask someone to give or lend you that item. Word order: in full sentences you'd normally say the verb first: 'Gibst du mir bitte dein Telefon?' or 'Leih mir bitte dein Buch.' 'Bitte' makes the request polite. Use 'Ihr' or 'Ihr(e)' for formal/plural: 'Geben Sie mir bitte Ihr Telefon.'
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte dein Fahrrad leihen?
native_language_example: Can you please lend me your bike?

meaning: “please your…” — a polite request asking someone to give, lend, or tell something that belongs to them (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to make polite requests. 'Bitte' = please; 'deinen' is the masculine/neuter accusative or masculine genitive/other forms depending on the noun that follows. In these examples it's accusative (e.g. deinen Namen, deinen Schlüssel, deinen Wagen, deinen Stift). The phrase must be completed by a noun. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Leih mir bitte deinen Stift' or 'Bitte leih mir deinen Stift').
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte deinen Rucksack geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me your backpack?

meaning: please the
additional_notes: Combination of 'bitte' (please) and the definite article 'den' (accusative masculine singular). Used when politely asking someone to give, do, or confirm something that is a masculine accusative direct object (e.g., den Teller, den Zucker, den Kessel, den Erhalt). Word order varies; 'bitte' can come before or after the verb. You will often replace 'den' with another article (die/das/den/den + noun) depending on the gender and case of the noun. Not a fixed idiom—it's just 'please' + 'the'.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte den Schlüssel.
native_language_example: Please give me the key.

meaning: please think / please remember / please consider (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to remember something (denken an + Akk.) or to consider/reflect on something (denken über + Akk. / nachdenken). Can also be used to ask someone not to think something (denken nicht). Context and preposition change the exact meaning: "an" = remember/think of; "über...nach" = think about/consider; without preposition often appears in commands like "bitte denken Sie jetzt nicht an...".
target_language_example: Bitte denken Sie an den Müll und schließen Sie die Tür.
native_language_example: Please think of the trash and close the door.

meaning: 'please this' — polite request to indicate a specific thing (this one).
additional_notes: Combine 'bitte' (please) with a demonstrative like 'dieses' (this [neuter/accusative]) to politely ask someone to do something with or give you a specific item. Word order can vary: 'Bitte dieses Formular ausfüllen.' (spoken/short) or more formally 'Füllen Sie bitte dieses Formular aus.' Use gender/case agreement: dieses (neuter accusative), diesen (masculine), diese (feminine/plural) as needed.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte dieses Buch.
native_language_example: Please give me this book.

meaning: please (give) a glass (of ...).
additional_notes: A polite phrase used when requesting a glass of a drink (e.g., water, milk). Often followed by the drink: 'bitte ein Glas Wasser' or 'bitte ein Glas Milch'. Can be used with different verbs (geben, bekommen, haben, bringen). Use 'bitte' to be polite.
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein Glas Wasser bekommen?
native_language_example: May I please get a glass of water?

meaning: please (give me) a/an — polite request when ordering or asking for one item
additional_notes: Commonly used in everyday situations like ordering food or drinks: you say 'Bitte eine ...' followed by the item (and sometimes size or type). 'Bitte' is polite; the noun after 'eine' must match gender/case (eine = feminine nominative/accusative or indefinite for numbers when used colloquially). In spoken German you may also hear simply 'Eine bitte' or just 'Bitte' with the item named. Adjust article if the item is masculine (einen) or neuter (ein).
target_language_example: Bitte eine Cola.
native_language_example: Please (give me) a cola.

meaning: please (for) a/an — used when asking someone politely to wait or to get something (a moment, a doctor, etc.).
additional_notes: Common in polite requests. Often followed by a noun like 'Augenblick', 'Moment' or a person/item like 'Arzt'. Can appear with different verb forms (imperative: 'Warte bitte einen Moment', formal polite: 'Warten Sie bitte einen Moment', or indirect: 'Können Sie bitte einen Arzt rufen?'). 'Bitte' marks politeness; 'einen' is the accusative masculine/neuter indefinite article matching the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte einen Moment warten?
native_language_example: Could you please wait a moment?

meaning: please remind (me/others) ...
additional_notes: A polite request to ask someone to remind you or another person of something. Often followed by a reflexive pronoun (dich/mich) and 'an' + noun/phrase or a clause introduced by 'daran' or a direct object with an infinitive clause (e.g., mich, morgen das Papier einzureichen). When addressing someone formally use 'Bitte erinnern Sie ...'.
target_language_example: Bitte erinnere mich morgen an den Termin.
native_language_example: Please remind me about the appointment tomorrow.

meaning: 'please (do) something' or 'please (give/say) something' — a polite request to do or provide an unspecified thing or action.
additional_notes: Combines bitte (please) with etwas (something). Use with verbs to politely ask someone to do or give something vague or unspecified: e.g. to ask for 'something to drink', to ask someone to 'say something', 'sing something', or more urgently 'do something'. Word order follows normal German verb rules (e.g. Bitte etwas sagen → Sag bitte etwas.). Can be formal (Sie) or informal (du/ihr) depending on pronoun and verb form.
target_language_example: Sag bitte etwas, wir hören dir zu.
native_language_example: Please say something, we're listening to you.

meaning: please here / please (do something) here
additional_notes: Common polite request directing someone to a specific spot or place in speech or writing. Often used with verbs like warten (wait), unterschreiben/unterzeichnen (sign), or beim Zeigen (e.g., 'bitte hier entlang' = 'this way, please'). 'Bitte' makes the phrase polite. Word order may vary (e.g., 'Bitte warten Sie hier.').
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte hier, bis ich zurückkomme.
native_language_example: Please wait here until I come back.

meaning: 'please come' (plural or informal plural 'you' — asking multiple people or using 'ihr').
additional_notes: Used to politely ask a group (or someone addressed with 'ihr') to come, come over, return, or visit. 'Kommt' is the present tense of 'kommen' for 'ihr'. If speaking formally to one person use 'bitte kommen Sie'. Context often adds direction or time (z. B. 'an Bord', 'her', 'heut Nachmittag', 'besuchen').
target_language_example: Bitte kommt morgen zu mir!
native_language_example: Please come to my place tomorrow!

meaning: Please read (polite request).
additional_notes: A polite imperative phrase using 'bitte' + infinitive 'lesen' or the polite form 'lesen Sie'. Commonly used to ask someone to read something aloud or to read it themselves. In formal contexts use 'Bitte lesen Sie...' (Sie = polite you). For informal (du) use 'Bitte lies...'. Can be used with objects (den Text, das Buch, es) or with an action (vorlesen = read aloud).
target_language_example: Bitte lesen Sie den Text laut vor.
native_language_example: Please read the text aloud.

meaning: please do/make (polite request; often followed by an object or noun phrase).
additional_notes: Common in polite requests when addressing someone formally (Sie). Usually followed by what you want done (e.g., 'die Rechnung machen' = make the bill). In many contexts native speakers prefer 'Bitte stellen Sie mir die Rechnung' or simply 'Die Rechnung, bitte.' 'Bitte machen' on its own is incomplete; include the object or action.
target_language_example: Bitte machen Sie mir die Rechnung.
native_language_example: Please make the bill for me.

meaning: 'please' + 'my' used together to politely ask someone to do something involving something that belongs to the speaker (e.g. 'please [do something with] my ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the politeness word bitte and the possessive meinen (masculine accusative singular or generic masculine). Word order varies: bitte can appear before or after the verb. 'meinen' must match the gender/case of the noun (meinen Stift = accusative masculine). In formal situations use 'bitte' as shown; in very formal commands use 'Bitte geben Sie mir ...' or 'Könnten Sie bitte ...' for politeness.
target_language_example: Geben Sie mir bitte meinen Pass.
native_language_example: Please give me my passport.

meaning: please (do something) with / please come along / please connect me to
additional_notes: „bitte mit" combines the polite particle „bitte" with the preposition/particle „mit". Depending on context it can mean: asking someone to come along (Komm bitte mit mir), asking to speak/connect to someone (Verbinden Sie mich bitte mit X / Könnte ich bitte mit Tom sprechen), asking someone to do something using something together (Würden Sie bitte mit dieser Kamera ein Foto... = use this camera), or to ask to be spared from something in fixed phrases (Verschone mich bitte mit ... = spare me (the) ...). Word order: “bitte” can come before or after verbs or objects (Komm bitte mit / Sprich bitte mit ihm).
target_language_example: Komm bitte mit mir zum Konzert.
native_language_example: Please come with me to the concert.

meaning: please name / please tell (me).
additional_notes: Polite request using the formal Sie form (often appears as 'Bitte nennen Sie ...'). Used to ask someone to give a name, a detail, or specific information. If speaking informally to friends, use 'nenn(e) mir bitte' or 'nenne mich ...' with du. The structure can be followed by a person, a time, a reason, etc.
target_language_example: Bitte nennen Sie mir Ihren Namen.
native_language_example: Please tell me your name.

meaning: please (add) another / please still / please more
additional_notes: A polite short phrase used when asking for more of something or asking for something to be added/continued. Context decides exact translation: e.g. at a café it can mean 'one more, please' (bitte noch ein Bier), with instructions it can mean 'please continue' or 'please still'. It often appears before or after the item: 'Bitte noch ein Stück' or simply 'Bitte noch!'.
target_language_example: Bitte noch ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: One more glass of water, please.

meaning: please (give) a little more / a bit more (of something).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask for an additional small amount of something (time, drink, etc.). Common in requests: 'bitte noch etwas Bedenkzeit' (a bit more time to think) or 'bitte noch etwas Wein' (a little more wine). Word order can change (e.g. 'Könnte ich bitte noch etwas Wasser haben?').
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte noch etwas Zeit.
native_language_example: Please give me a little more time.

meaning: Please come in / Please let me in (polite request to enter).
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase combining 'bitte' (please) with the short form 'rein' (colloquial for 'herein' = 'inside'). Used to invite someone into a room/house (Komm bitte rein!, Kommen Sie bitte rein!) or to ask to be let in (Lasst mich bitte rein.). 'Rein' is informal; for formal/written use prefer 'herein' or 'herein/bitte treten'. Word order can vary: 'Bitte rein!' 'Komm bitte rein!' 'Kommen Sie bitte rein!'.
target_language_example: Kommen Sie doch bitte rein, die Besprechung hat gerade begonnen.
native_language_example: Please come in, the meeting has just started.

meaning: please call (ask someone to telephone someone); polite request to phone or call back
additional_notes: Often followed by an object or particle: 'bitte rufen Sie mich an' (please call me) or 'bitte rufen Sie zurück' (please call back). Formal polite form uses 'Sie' or 'bitte rufen Sie ... an'; with friends use 'bitte ruf ... an' or just 'ruf ... an bitte'. Common in phone messages, notes, and requests.
target_language_example: Bitte rufen Sie mich heute Nachmittag an.
native_language_example: Please call me this afternoon.

meaning: please send / please send someone
additional_notes: Polite request phrasing using formal Sie (Bitte schicken Sie ...). Can be used for sending objects (documents, fax, message) or people/services (doctor, ambulance). For informal du use 'bitte schick' or plural ihr 'bitte schickt'. Often followed by direct object or indirect object plus method (per Fax, mir, in mein Zimmer).
target_language_example: Bitte schicken Sie mir die Unterlagen per E‑Mail.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents by email.

meaning: please sit (down)
additional_notes: A polite request telling someone to sit. Usually followed by a reflexive pronoun (dich) or a location (e.g. hier). Common in spoken German; full form is 'bitte setz dich' or formal 'bitten Sie, setzen Sie sich'. Can be softened with 'doch' or limited in time ('einen Augenblick').
target_language_example: Bitte setz dich kurz auf den Stuhl.
native_language_example: Please sit down on the chair for a moment.

meaning: please speak / please say (used to request someone to speak or repeat something).
additional_notes: A polite request using 'bitte' + verb 'sprechen'. Usually appears with a pronoun and formal/informal verb form: 'Bitte sprechen Sie ...' (formal) or 'Bitte sprich ...' (informal). Can ask someone to speak clearly, to use a language, to repeat after you ('mir nachsprechen'), or to talk to someone. Word order often continues with details: 'Bitte sprechen Sie deutlich', 'Bitte sprechen Sie Französisch'.
target_language_example: Bitte sprechen Sie deutlicher, ich kann Sie kaum verstehen.
native_language_example: Please speak more clearly, I can hardly understand you.

meaning: please (do it) later; asking someone to do something at a later time.
additional_notes: A polite request combining bitte (please) with später (later). Used in calls or face-to-face to ask someone to call back, come back, or perform an action later. Tone can be formal or informal depending on pronoun (Sie, du). You may hear variations: 'Rufen Sie bitte später an.' or 'Können Sie bitte später zurückrufen?'.
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte später nochmal zurückrufen?
native_language_example: Could you please call back later?

meaning: 'please' + imperative of stellen (to put/place/turn off/connect/introduce) — a polite request to place, put, switch off, connect, or present someone, depending on context.
additional_notes: Bitten with stellen appears in commands: 'Bitte stellen Sie den Motor ab.' (please switch off), 'Bitte stellen Sie die Eier in den Kühlschrank.' (please put/place). The exact meaning comes from the verb stellen + context: abstellen (switch off), durchstellen (connect someone on the phone), sich aufstellen (line up), sich vorstellen (introduce oneself). In formal speech use 'Bitte stellen Sie...' with Sie for polite requests. For informal du use 'Stell bitte...'.
target_language_example: Bitte stellen Sie mich mit dem Support-Team in Verbindung.
native_language_example: Please put me in touch with the support team.

meaning: please step/enter (used with verbs like 'ein', 'vor', 'zurück'); a polite request to move in a certain way.
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone phrase — 'bitte treten' is usually followed by a directional particle or preposition (e.g. 'ein' = enter, 'vor' = step forward, 'zurück' = step back) or a pronoun ('Sie'). Formal polite register when addressing one or more people (Sie). Common in doors, meetings, queues, or official settings.
target_language_example: Bitte treten Sie ein und nehmen Sie Platz.
native_language_example: Please come in and take a seat.

meaning: polite request to ask for, request, or to ask someone to do something (literally 'please [do something] at/about').
additional_notes: Bitte um combines bitte (please) with a verb that takes 'um' + time or object depending on context. With verbs like 'bitten (jemanden) um etwas' it means 'to ask for something' (request). In imperative/use with verbs like 'wecken', 'rufen', 'kümmern', 'um' introduces the thing or time (e.g. 'um sechs Uhr' = 'at six o'clock'). Here 'bitte' makes the sentence polite: 'please (do X)'. Word order: 'Kümmert euch bitte um sie.' = 'Please take care of her.'
target_language_example: Kümmere dich bitte um den Hund.
native_language_example: Please take care of the dog.

meaning: 'please' used with separable verbs whose prefix is 'um' to soften an imperative or request (e.g., when asking someone politely to turn around).
additional_notes: 'Bitte' commonly appears between the imperative verb and the separable prefix 'um' (imperative verb + bitte + um). It softens the command and can be used with informal singular (du), informal plural (ihr), and formal (Sie). Word order examples: 'Dreh bitte um!' (du), 'Dreht euch bitte um!' (ihr), 'Drehen Sie sich bitte um!' (Sie).
target_language_example: Dreh bitte um!
native_language_example: Please turn around!

meaning: please leave (something/somewhere); a polite or firm request to go away
additional_notes: Commonly used with formal Sie (e.g. "Bitte verlassen Sie ...") to ask someone to leave a place, vehicle, or property. Can be polite or firm depending on tone and context; often followed by what to leave (das Gelände, mein Haus, meinen Wagen). Not a fixed idiom — regular verb + politeness word.
target_language_example: Bitte verlassen Sie sofort das Gebäude!
native_language_example: Please leave the building immediately!

meaning: 'please wait' (a polite request to pause or stay where you are).
additional_notes: Common phrase used in announcements, on signs, or when asking someone to wait a moment. Can be followed by formal 'Sie' (Bitte warten Sie) for polite/formal contexts, or used alone/informal situations as 'Bitte warten.' Often used in customer service, public transport, and phone prompts.
target_language_example: Bitte warten Sie kurz, ich überprüfe das für Sie.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment, I'll check that for you.

meaning: 'please to the' — a short polite phrase used before instructions like 'please go to' or 'please head to'.
additional_notes: This is not normally used alone; it appears before a place, person, or action (e.g. 'bitte zur Anmeldung' = 'please to the reception/registration'). Common in signs, announcements, or when giving directions. Use with definite noun phrases (often followed by a noun in dative or accusative depending on the verb omitted).
target_language_example: Bitte zur Kasse!
native_language_example: Please to the checkout! (i.e. Please go to the checkout.)

meaning: please give me a
additional_notes: Common phrase used when ordering or requesting one item in informal spoken German (e.g., in a bar or restaurant). Often followed by a noun like 'Bier' or 'Glas Wasser'. Literal translation is 'please a', so English requires adding 'give me' or 'I'd like'. Tone is polite but casual. You can add size/type if needed: e.g. 'Bitte ein kleines Bier.'
target_language_example: Bedienung! Bitte ein Kaffee.
native_language_example: Waiter! I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: you're welcome; please go ahead / here you are (polite), depending on context.
additional_notes: Very common polite phrase. Used as a response to thanks = "you're welcome". Also used to grant permission or invite someone to do something ("please, go ahead") and when handing something to someone ("here you are"). Tone and intonation determine meaning (exclamation for 'you're welcome', neutral for 'here you are', question/offer intonation for 'please go ahead'). Formal but friendly; suitable in most situations.
target_language_example: Wenn Sie etwas lesen wollen, bitte schön.
native_language_example: If you want to read something, go ahead.

meaning: to be asked/requested to do something (expresses that someone is supposed to ask or that someone is to be asked)
additional_notes: This is not an idiomatic fixed phrase but a sequence of the verb bitten (to ask/request) and the modal sollen (to be supposed to). It commonly appears in reported speech or instructions where someone is expected to ask another person or where one is told that they should ask. Word order and endings change with tense and subject (e.g. Man soll ihn bitten / Er hat gebeten sollen in dependent constructions). For learners, prefer clear constructions like 'jemanden bitten, etwas zu tun' or use 'sollen' and 'bitten' separately to avoid confusion.
target_language_example: Man soll ihn bitten sollen, das Formular auszufüllen.
native_language_example: One is supposed to ask him to fill out the form.

meaning: 'to ask for' or 'to request' (something).
additional_notes: Use 'bitten um' with an object in the accusative (e.g. um Hilfe, um Rat). Commonly used for polite requests: jemand um etwas bitten = to ask someone for something. Conjugate 'bitten' normally (ich bitte, du bittest, er bittet). In perfect tense the word order can separate 'bitten' and 'um' (e.g., 'Ich habe ihn um Hilfe gebeten').
target_language_example: Ich bitte dich um Hilfe.
native_language_example: I ask you for help.

meaning: to be drunk (colloquial).
additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning 'to be intoxicated' from alcohol. Common in spoken German. Not used for being 'sad' (English 'blue') — in German 'traurig sein' means sad. You can say 'ein bisschen blau sein' (a little drunk) or 'total blau sein' (completely drunk).
target_language_example: Er war gestern Abend ziemlich blau sein.
native_language_example: He was pretty drunk last night.

meaning: a black eye (bruise around the eye from a hit).
additional_notes: Used to describe a bruised, swollen eye caused by a blow. Literally 'blue eye' but corresponds to English 'black eye'. Can be used literally; sometimes used figuratively to mean a setback or embarrassment, but primarily physical injury.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit hat er ein blaues Auge.
native_language_example: After the fight he has a black eye.

meaning: 'stay where (you are)'.
additional_notes: Used as an imperative telling someone to remain in their current location. Often followed by a pronoun (du, ihr) or name. Common in commands like 'Bleib, wo du bist!' and can be followed by extra instructions (e.g. 'und keine Bewegung' = 'and don't move'). Informal register (spoken commands).
target_language_example: Bleib, wo du bist, und ich komme gleich zurück.
native_language_example: Stay where you are, and I'll be right back.

meaning: stay on / remain at (a place, position, level, or course).
additional_notes: Imperative form of bleiben + auf (preposition used with a following noun or implied object). Used to tell someone to stay in a specific place or maintain a position/level/direction. Common in commands: 'Bleib auf deinem Posten!' (stay at your post), 'Bleib auf Kurs' (stay on course). The exact English preposition may vary (on, in, at) depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Bleib auf deinem Stuhl, bis ich zurück bin.
native_language_example: Stay on your chair until I come back.

meaning: 'stay with' (imperative + preposition + dative: telling someone to remain together with a person or keep thoughts/attention on something)
additional_notes: Used as an imperative: 'Bleib' (stay) + 'mit' (with) + dative object (mir, uns, ihm, ihr, den Gedanken). Common for telling someone to stay physically with a person or to keep attention on something. Word order: 'Bleib mit mir hier.' or 'Bleib mit den Gedanken bei der Arbeit.'
target_language_example: Bleib mit mir hier, bis ich zurückkomme.
native_language_example: Stay with me here until I come back.

meaning: to stick with; to remain with; to keep (to) (something or someone)
additional_notes: Used with a person, group or an idea/position. With people it means to stay with or remain alongside someone (e.g. 'bei den Nonnen' = stay with the nuns). With abstract things (e.g. 'bei unserer Haltung') it means to keep or stick to a position or decision. Common structure: bleiben + bei + dative.
target_language_example: Ich bleibe bei meiner Entscheidung. — Wir bleiben bei unserer Haltung. — Sie bleiben bei den Frauen.
native_language_example: I stick with my decision. — We stick to our position. — They stay with the women.

meaning: to stay here; remain in this place (used in statements or commands).
additional_notes: Common phrase combining bleiben (to stay/remain) with hier (here). Used to tell someone to stay in the current location or to state that you/they will stay. Word order varies with sentence type: in statements the verb follows the subject (Wir bleiben hier), while in commands the verb may come first or use a polite form (Bleiben Sie hier!). Contractions or emphasis can alter placement in colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Ja, wir bleiben hier.
native_language_example: Yes, we are staying here.

meaning: to leave something as it is; to stop doing something; to give up (doing something).
additional_notes: This separable verb pair (bleiben lassen) is used mainly in two senses: 1) 'leave/let something be' (e.g., leave it alone, leave the light on/off) and 2) 'stop/quit doing something' (similar to 'aufhören' or 'etwas aufgeben'). In finite clauses the parts can be separated (e.g., 'Das lassen wir besser bleiben.'), while infinitive constructions keep the order 'bleiben lassen' (e.g., 'Ich werde das bleiben lassen.'). Common in advice, refusal, or expressions of giving up: 'Lass das bleiben!' = 'Don't do that / cut it out.'
target_language_example: Das sollten wir besser bleiben lassen.
native_language_example: We should better leave that alone / stop doing that.

meaning: stay and (then)... — used to link 'stay' with a following action
additional_notes: Combines the verb bleiben ('to stay') with 'und' ('and') to connect staying somewhere with another action. Common in simple sentences: 'Ich bleibe und mache X' = 'I stay and do X'. Word order after 'bleiben und' follows normal German rules (infinitives or finite verbs as appropriate). Not idiomatic — it's literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben und warten auf den Bus.
native_language_example: We stay and wait for the bus.

meaning: you stay here / you remain here (spoken to one person, singular informal)
additional_notes: Present tense of bleiben (to stay) + hier (here). Used to tell or order someone to stay in this place. Informal singular (du) form; tone can be neutral request or a command depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Du bleibst hier, bis ich zurück bin.
native_language_example: You stay here until I come back.

meaning: 'stays' or 'remains' (does something like 'stay in a state' or 'keep doing/being')
additional_notes: Used with different complements: 'auf euren Posten bleiben' = stay at your posts (remain where you are/do your duty); 'auf ewig bleiben' = remain forever; 'auf der Hut bleiben' = stay on guard/be watchful; 'auf Abstand bleiben' = keep your distance. The verb bleiben (to stay/remain) combines with prepositional phrases or adverbs; word order may separate parts (bleibt ... auf).
target_language_example: Bitte bleibt auf dem Laufenden, wenn sich etwas ändert.
native_language_example: Please stay informed if anything changes.

meaning: 'is left for you' / 'remains for you' — used to say what someone has as an option, time, responsibility, etc.
additional_notes: Common construction: 'Es bleibt dir ...' or '... bleibt dir ...' Often followed by 'nichts anderes übrig' (you have no other choice), 'nicht viel Zeit' (you don't have much time), or 'überlassen' (up to you). The dative pronoun 'dir' marks the person affected. Can express necessity, lack of options, remaining time, or that something is up to someone.
target_language_example: Es bleibt dir noch eine Stunde, um die Prüfung zu machen.
native_language_example: You have one hour left to take the exam.

meaning: 'remains a' or 'continues to be a' (followed by a noun)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something continues to be (or is still) a certain kind/type. Common in sentences like 'er ist und bleibt ein ...' (he is and remains a ...). Often expresses permanence, unchanged status, or that something keeps its character (can be neutral, positive, or negative). Follows the noun phrase it describes (e.g. 'ein Märchen', 'ein Geheimnis').
target_language_example: Er ist und bleibt ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: He is and remains a good friend.

meaning: 'stay in' or 'remain in' (imperative/plural or statement with 'er/sie/es bleibt in ...')
additional_notes: Used with a location, state, or group to tell people to stay/keep within something (e.g., cover, formation, small groups, sight). Can be an imperative addressing multiple people (Bleibt in ...!) or a statement about someone/something remaining in a state/place (Er bleibt in Gefangenschaft). Followed by a noun phrase with the appropriate article/case.
target_language_example: Bleibt in Sichtweite, bis Hilfe kommt.
native_language_example: Stay within sight until help arrives.

meaning: stayed (at home) all day (closed/stayed in)
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone stayed at home all day instead of going out or to work. ‚zu Hause bleiben‘ = to stay at home. The phrase often appears with ‚anstatt/statt (zu)‘ to indicate an alternative action not taken. Word order: 'blieb' (past of bleiben) + time phrase + 'zu' (short for 'zu Hause' when context clear) or simply 'zu Hause'.
target_language_example: Sie blieb den ganzen Tag zu Hause, anstatt einkaufen zu gehen.
native_language_example: She stayed at home all day instead of going shopping.

meaning: literally 'stayed three' or 'remained three'; not a fixed standalone phrase but the past-tense verb 'blieb' (from bleiben) followed by the number 'drei'. Often occurs within a larger sentence meaning 'there were/only three left' or 'it stayed at three'.
additional_notes: This is not grammatically complete on its own in many contexts. More natural variants include 'Es blieben drei' (there remained three) or 'Es blieb bei drei' (it stayed at three). Word order and verb agreement matter: with a plural subject you'd normally use 'blieben' rather than 'blieb'. You may encounter 'blieb drei' in colloquial or clipped speech or when a singular neuter subject is implied; check surrounding words for correct agreement.
target_language_example: Nach dem Sturm blieb drei unserer Häuser ohne Strom.
native_language_example: After the storm, three of our houses were left without power.

meaning: there was no other option / I had no choice
additional_notes: Used to say that someone had to do something because no alternative was possible. Often followed by 'als' + infinitive or clause (e.g. 'als zuzustimmen', 'als ihn zu entlassen'). Common in past tense (blieb...).
target_language_example: Mir blieb nichts anderes übrig, als zu gehen.
native_language_example: I had no choice but to leave.

meaning: remained (his) / stayed (his) — used to say someone stayed in a certain state for a long time (often 'sein Leben lang' = 'his whole life').
additional_notes: Usually appears in constructions like 'er blieb sein Leben lang ...' or 'er blieb sein ganzes Leben lang ...' meaning 'he remained ... for his whole life.' 'Blieb' is the past (preterite) of 'bleiben' (to remain/stay). 'Sein' here is the possessive 'his' and belongs to phrases like 'sein Leben lang' (his whole life). Translate the whole phrase, not word-by-word.
target_language_example: Er blieb sein Leben lang glücklich.
native_language_example: He remained happy his whole life.

meaning: 'just/only here' or 'merely here' (often expressing limitation, complaint, or helplessness)
additional_notes: bloß = just/only/merely (can add emphasis, frustration, or minimize an action). When combined with hier (here) it often conveys 'I'm just here' or 'you're only here'—sometimes implying boredom, resignation, or that something is pointless. Can be used in questions to express worry or exasperation (e.g. Warum sind wir bloß hier?). Tone and context determine whether it's soft (simply 'only') or emotional ('why on earth are we here?').
target_language_example: Ich sitze bloß hier und warte auf dich.
native_language_example: I'm just sitting here waiting for you.

meaning: 'just/from only' or 'only from' depending on context; often used to mean 'just' or 'merely' before a source or in exclamations
additional_notes: bloß is a common particle meaning 'just', 'only', or used for emphasis (often in questions or exclamations: e.g. "Was willst du bloß...?" = "What on earth do you want?"). When combined with von it can mean 'from' with the sense of 'only coming from' or indicate source ("das kam bloß von mir" = "that only came from me"). Word order and context determine whether bloß modifies the verb/phrase (emphasis) or restricts origin (only from). Informal but common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Das Problem kam bloß von einem Missverständnis.
native_language_example: The problem came only from a misunderstanding.

meaning: 'he brought' or 'he caused' (simple past of bringen with subject 'he').
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase: brought (to a place), brought home, or caused/committed (with verbs like 'umbringen' in separable forms or reflexive contexts). Use with objects or people: e.g. jemanden bringen (to take/bring someone) or etwas bringen (to bring something). Word order: in statements the past tense verb appears in second position in full sentence fragments like these.
target_language_example: Letzte Woche brachte er mir ein Paket.
native_language_example: Last week he brought me a package.

meaning: 'need help' (I need help).
additional_notes: Common expression to ask for assistance. Usually used with a subject pronoun (Ich brauche Hilfe). Can be followed by 'bei' + noun (bei den Hausaufgaben) or 'mit' + noun (mit meiner Arbeit) to specify what help is needed. Can be urgent when said alone with emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Hilfe bei meiner Matheaufgabe.
native_language_example: I need help with my math problem.

meaning: I need your (formal).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'brauchen' (to need) in the first person singular (ich brauche) with the formal possessive pronoun 'Ihre' (your, capitalized for formal Sie). Use before a noun: 'Ihre Hilfe' (your help), 'Ihre Unterschrift' (your signature), 'Ihre Meinung' (your opinion). For informal situations with friends/family use 'deine' instead of 'Ihre'. Word order: 'Ich brauche Ihre + noun.'
target_language_example: Ich brauche Ihre Hilfe, bitte.
native_language_example: I need your help, please.

meaning: I need time (to do something / for myself).
additional_notes: Used to say you require more time — either alone (für mich), to do/learn something (um ... zu), or generally. Common in personal, emotional, or practical contexts. Can be shortened to just "Ich brauche Zeit." to mean "I need time" without details.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um mich zu entscheiden.
native_language_example: I need time to decide.

meaning: I need your ... (informal singular; followed by a noun).
additional_notes: ‘brauche’ is the first-person singular of ‘brauchen’ (to need). ‘deinen’ is the accusative masculine or accusative weak-declension form of ‘dein’ (your) used before masculine nouns (e.g. Rat, Pass, Beistand). This phrase is informal and addresses one person you know (du). After ‘brauche deinen’ you must add the noun: e.g. ‚brauche deinen Rat‘ = ‚I need your advice.‘
target_language_example: Ich brauche deinen Schlüssel, kannst du ihn mir geben?
native_language_example: I need your key, can you give it to me?

meaning: need you
additional_notes: Literally 'need you'. Used to say someone is needed or not needed. Context and sentence negation determine meaning (e.g. 'ich brauche dich' = 'I need you'; 'ich brauche dich nicht' = 'I don't need you'). Can express emotional, practical, or romantic need depending on context. Word order can change with pronouns ('ich brauche dich', 'brauche ich dich?').
target_language_example: Ich brauche dich heute Abend.
native_language_example: I need you this evening.

meaning: 'I need a' (feminine or feminine-gendered noun) / general 'I need a...'
additional_notes: Used to state that you need or require something. 'Brauche' is the first-person singular of 'brauchen' (to need). 'Eine' is the indefinite article for feminine nouns (or for any noun when gender not considered by learner—many beginners use 'eine' before nouns). If the noun is masculine use 'einen' (Ich brauche einen Stift), and for neuter use 'ein' (Ich brauche ein Buch). Can be followed by a noun or noun phrase. Polite requests often use 'Ich brauche bitte...' or better phrased as a question: 'Könnte ich bitte ... haben?'
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Jacke, es ist kalt.
native_language_example: I need a jacket, it's cold.

meaning: I need something / I need a little (of) something.
additional_notes: Common way to say you need something. 'Brauche' is from 'brauchen' (to need). 'Etwas' can mean 'something' or 'some' (a small amount) depending on context: 'etwas Hilfe' = some help, 'etwas Milch' = some milk. For full sentences include the object (accusative). Polite requests often use 'Ich brauche bitte ...' or the modal 'Ich hätte gern ...' for softer phrasing.
target_language_example: Ich brauche etwas Zeit, um das zu erledigen.
native_language_example: I need some time to finish this.

meaning: I need someone (to do something / to be there).
additional_notes: Common phrase to express a personal need for another person (help, support, trust, protection, comfort, etc.). Often followed by a relative clause introduced by der/dem (who/whom) describing what that person should do or be. 'brauche' = first person singular of brauchen. Use ‚jemanden‘ (accusative) for an unspecified person.
target_language_example: Ich brauche jemanden, der mir beim Umzug hilft.
native_language_example: I need someone who will help me move.

meaning: 'need that' or 'need it' (accusative demonstrative).
additional_notes: Phrase combines the verb brauchen (to need) with the accusative demonstrative pronoun/determiner das (that/it/the). Used when referring to a specific object or previously mentioned thing. Word order may vary in full sentences (e.g. Wir brauchen das Auto). Register: neutral; can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on pronouns and context.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen das Geld.
native_language_example: We need that money.

meaning: need a
additional_notes: A common construction using the verb brauchen (to need) + an indefinite article and noun. Use brauchen + accusative: 'eine' is the feminine/neuter accusative indefinite article for feminine nouns (eine) or used before words starting with vowel sound when English would say 'an'. In English you say 'need a/an' + noun. For other genders/articles use brauchen + einen (masculine) or brauchen + ein (neuter).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen eine Jacke für den Ausflug.
native_language_example: We need a jacket for the trip.

meaning: 'you don't need to (yourself)' — used with verbs to tell someone they don't have to do something (informal singular).
additional_notes: This is the informal singular second-person form of brauchen + reflexive pronoun dich. It's often used with 'nicht' and an infinitive (zu + verb or reflexive verb) to say someone doesn't need to do something, e.g. 'Du brauchst dich nicht zu rechtfertigen' = 'You don't need to justify yourself.' Use 'brauchen' in this negative construction with an infinitive instead of 'müssen' when meaning 'need to.' For formal/plural: 'brauchen sich' (ihr) or 'brauchen Sie sich' (formal).
target_language_example: Du brauchst dich nicht zu sorgen.
native_language_example: You don't need to worry.

meaning: how long do you need to (in order to)...
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask how much time someone requires to do something. Structure: 'Wie lange brauchst du, um + zu + infinitive (or + object + zu + infinitive)'. Common in casual and neutral contexts. You can replace 'du' with other pronouns (braucht ihr, braucht er/sie/es, brauche ich).
target_language_example: Wie lange brauchst du, um das Formular auszufüllen?
native_language_example: How long do you need to fill out the form?

meaning: you need a (feminine or indefinite noun).
additional_notes: Second-person singular informal (du) form of 'brauchen' + indefinite article 'eine'. Used to tell someone they need something. The noun that follows is usually feminine (eine) or any noun with the feminine article; can imply necessity or recommendation. For other persons/forms, change the verb and article as needed (ich brauche eine, wir brauchen eine, du brauchst ein/einen depending on noun gender).
target_language_example: Du brauchst eine Pause.
native_language_example: You need a break.

meaning: needs him / needs it (referring to a male person or a masculine/neutral noun in accusative).
additional_notes: braucht is the 3rd-person singular of brauchen (to need). ihn is the accusative pronoun 'him'. Depending on context, 'ihn' can refer to a male person or to a masculine/animate noun previously mentioned. In plural subjects use braucht (ihr braucht ihn = you all need him) or brauchen (wir/ sie brauchen ihn). Word order can change in questions or subordinate clauses (e.g., "Braucht ihr ihn?" / "..., weil sie ihn braucht").
target_language_example: Die Stadt braucht ihn, um das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: The city needs him to solve the problem.

meaning: how long (one) needs until / how much time is needed until
additional_notes: This is the phrase braucht man bis + time expression or event. It asks or states the amount of time required before something happens or is ready. Common in questions: "Wie lange braucht man bis... ?" (How long does one need until...?). Can be used with first/second/third person: 'brauche ich bis', 'brauchst du bis', 'braucht man bis'.
target_language_example: Wie lange braucht man bis zur nächsten Haltestelle?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get to the next stop?

meaning: bring yourself after / get yourself to (a place/time) — imperative or instruction to move or prepare oneself
additional_notes: This phrase combines bringen (to bring) with a reflexive pronoun dich and a following adverb/preposition (e.g. ‚bringe dich nach Hause/Bringe dich nach vorne‘) or is part of longer constructions like ‚Bringe dich nach vorn/Bringe dich nach Hause‘. By itself ‚bringe dich nach‘ is incomplete; it needs a destination or complement (nach + place or direction). Often used to tell someone to go or move themselves somewhere or to get ready to be in a certain position. Tone can be neutral or firm depending on context.
target_language_example: Bringe dich nach Hause, es wird spät.
native_language_example: Get yourself home, it's getting late.

meaning: literally 'bring you'; a verb + accusative pronoun sequence used in various contexts to mean 'take/bring you (somewhere)', 'cause you to feel/do something' (with zu/infinitive or zu + noun), or, in the transitive perfective construction 'jemand bringt dich um', 'kill you'.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on surrounding words and word order. Common patterns: 'wir bringen dich zum/ins/...' = we will take/bring you to a place; 'bringen dich zurück nach ...' = bring you back to a place; 'bringen dich zum Lachen/Weinen/etc.' = make you laugh/cry (bringen + zu + noun/infinitive = cause); 'bringen dich um' = kill you (very strong/violent). In sentences the finite verb is conjugated and 'dich' is the accusative object. The exact sequence 'bringen dich' appears when another verb or auxiliary causes inversion or in subordinate/infinitive constructions (e.g., 'werden dich bringen', 'können dich bringen'). Register: neutral for transport/causation, highly colloquial/violent for threats. Watch for pronoun cases and prepositions (zum/ins/nach).
target_language_example: Was für Filme bringen dich zum Lachen?
native_language_example: What kind of movies make you laugh?

meaning: bring him / take him (somewhere or do something to him).
additional_notes: ’bringen’ is the verb 'to bring' or 'to take' (depending on direction/context). With the pronoun 'ihn' (him), the phrase means 'bring him' or 'take him' to a place or into an action. Context determines the destination or action (e.g. 'ins Krankenhaus bringen' = take him to the hospital; 'bringen ihn weg' = take him away; 'bringen ihn um' = kill him — note this is a very different, violent meaning). Word order in a full sentence is usually 'bringen ihn' in subordinate or main clauses with object pronouns; in many present-tense main clauses native speakers may say 'sie bringen ihn' or 'wir bringen ihn'.
target_language_example: Wir bringen ihn morgen zum Arzt.
native_language_example: We'll take him to the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to be able to bring (something/someone) into a certain state or to be able to achieve or accomplish something
additional_notes: Combines the verb bringen (to bring, cause, achieve, make happen) with können (can/to be able to). Used to indicate whether someone has the capability to make something happen, get something working, cause a reaction, or succeed. Exact nuance depends on context (e.g., make run, make laugh, bring to completion). Normal German word order and tense rules apply, so forms like ‚bringen können‘ (infinitive combination), ‚bringen konnten‘ (past infinitive) or finite forms with können (ich kann ... bringen) appear in sentences.
target_language_example: Es ist fraglich, ob wir die Maschine zum Laufen bringen können.
native_language_example: It is questionable whether we can get the machine running.

meaning: they bring / they take (someone or something)
additional_notes: Phrase is the verb bringen (to bring/take) followed by the third-person plural pronoun sie (they). Capitalization matters: 'sie' = they, 'Sie' = formal you. Word order may change for yes/no questions: 'Bringen sie ...?' Context and objects determine exact translation (bring vs. take).
