meaning: the last time (I/you/he/she/they) [did] a (masculine) ...
additional_notes: This is a fragment used before a masculine noun (einen + masculine noun in accusative) to say when something happened previously. Often followed by an action or event: e.g. „das letzte Mal einen Film gesehen habe“ (the last time I watched a film). Depending on the sentence subject and verb, word order and case may change. You will commonly hear full phrases like „das letzte Mal, als ich einen ...“ (the last time I ... a ...).
target_language_example: Das letzte Mal einen Film habe ich vor zwei Jahren gesehen.
native_language_example: The last time I watched a film was two years ago.

meaning: to have the final say; to be the last one to speak in a discussion
additional_notes: Used when someone insists on ending a conversation or argument with their opinion. Often implies stubbornness or wanting control in a discussion. Commonly used in criticism: 'Du musst immer das letzte Wort haben.'
target_language_example: Bei Streit will sie meistens das letzte Wort haben.
native_language_example: In an argument she usually wants to have the final say.

meaning: intended to mean 'the last time (you) [did/had] a ...' (combines 'das letzte Mal' with an accusative masculine noun introduced by 'einen'), though the written form 'das letztemal einen' is nonstandard
additional_notes: Correct standard German is 'das letzte Mal' (three words when followed by an accusative object: e.g. 'das letzte Mal einen ...'). The form 'das letztemal' (one word, wrong spelling) is incorrect. Use appropriate verb and pronoun forms for formality: 'Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal einen Anzug getragen?' (formal) or 'Wann hast du das letzte Mal einen Anzug getragen?' (informal). Word order: temporal phrase 'das letzte Mal' usually appears after the verb or before the direct object as in the examples. The masculine accusative noun after 'einen' must match what you mean (einen Anzug, einen Knopf, einen Ölwechsel, etc.).
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letztemal einen Anzug getragen?
native_language_example: When did you last wear a suit?

meaning: colloquial/nonstandard spelling of 'das letzte Mal jemandem' — 'the last time (to someone)'; used to ask when you most recently did something directed at someone (e.g. helped, complimented, forgave).
additional_notes: The form 'das letztemal' written together is nonstandard; standard spelling is 'das letzte Mal'. The phrase combines 'das letzte Mal' (the last time) with a dative recipient (jemandem). Common in spoken, informal German; formal writing should use the standard spacing and capitalization. Word order: 'das letzte Mal' + dative (jemandem) + verb. Example sentences often ask about specific actions (geholfen, ein Kompliment gemacht, verziehen/ vergeben, gesagt, etc.).
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letztemal jemandem ein Kompliment gemacht?
native_language_example: When did you last give someone a compliment?

meaning: colloquial/erroneous form intended to mean "the last time in" or to ask "when (were) you last in (somewhere)"
additional_notes: This form is nonstandard: correct spelling and spacing is "das letzte Mal in" (note capitalization and separation: Mal). Typical question: "Wann warst du das letzte Mal in ...?" or plural "Wann wart ihr das letzte Mal in ...?" The examples below preserve the exact (nonstandard) form requested but are not recommended in formal writing or careful speech.
target_language_example: Wann warst du das letztemal in Boston?
native_language_example: When were you last in Boston?

meaning: 'that/which on' — combination of the relative pronoun 'das' and the preposition 'auf' introducing a relative clause describing something located on or upon something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that appear together when a neutral-gender or demonstrative/relative pronoun (das) is used with the preposition 'auf' to form a relative clause: e.g. 'das Haus, das auf dem Hügel steht' = 'the house that stands on the hill.' Pay attention to case after the preposition 'auf' (usually dative with location: 'auf dem Hügel').
target_language_example: Das Buch, das auf dem Tisch liegt, gehört mir.
native_language_example: The book that is lying on the table belongs to me.

meaning: a relative pronoun phrase meaning 'that' (referring to a neuter or generic noun) followed by the masculine accusative article 'einen' + noun (i.e. 'that [has/was/wore] a ...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase — it's the relative pronoun 'das' (that/which) introducing a subordinate clause, immediately followed by 'einen' (masculine accusative indefinite article) and a noun. English equivalents: 'that has a...', 'that wore a...', 'that caused a...'. Word order: in the relative clause the verb goes to the end. Useful when describing something previously mentioned (das = that/which).
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen, das einen Hund hat.
native_language_example: This is the girl that has a dog.

meaning: a relative clause meaning 'that/which I had/kept with me' or 'that I have with me' (refers to something the speaker carries or has at home).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the relative pronoun das (referring to a neuter noun) with ich bei (short for 'ich bei mir' or 'bei mir gehabt/gescreossen/hatte'). It introduces a relative clause describing possession or location: 'that I had/that I have with me' or 'that I have at my place'. Verb tense (habe/hatte/geschossen habe) determines present vs. past. Common in spoken and written German. 'bei mir' (with/at me) is often omitted in the example input but understood.
target_language_example: Das ist das Buch, das ich bei mir habe.
native_language_example: That's the book that I have with me.

meaning: 'that/which' + 'in' (relative clause: which is/that is in...).
additional_notes: This is the relative pronoun 'das' (neuter singular or general relative pronoun) followed by the preposition 'in' starting a relative clause: it introduces extra information about a noun and locates it (in a place, building, country, or container). Word order: the verb of the relative clause goes to the end (e.g. 'das in Galiläa liegt', 'das in Japan hergestellt wurde'). Can refer to people, things, or places depending on the gender/number of the noun it replaces; 'das' is used for neuter nouns or as a generic 'which/that'.
target_language_example: Das Haus, das in der Straße steht, ist alt.
native_language_example: The house that is on the street is old.

meaning: 'that/which ... with' — introduces a relative clause meaning 'that/which is with.../who is with...'.
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses: 'das' is the neuter relative pronoun (can mean 'that' or 'which') and 'mit' is the preposition 'with'. Together they start a clause describing someone/something that is 'with' someone else (e.g. 'das Mädchen, das mit John spricht' = 'the girl who is speaking with John'). Word order after 'mit' follows normal German (preposition + object/person, then verb at the end of subordinate clauses where applicable). Formal/polite address uses 'Ihnen' after 'mit' for 'with you' (formal).
target_language_example: Das Buch, das mit dem Geschenk kommt, ist für dich.
native_language_example: The book that comes with the gift is for you.

meaning: 'that' or 'which' + reflexive verb (used when the verb is reflexive in the relative clause).
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun 'das' (that/which) with the reflexive pronoun 'sich' to introduce a relative clause where the verb is reflexive. English often uses 'that/which' + a reflexive construction (e.g. 'that/which ... itself' or simply 'that ...'). Word order: 'das sich' appears at the start of the relative clause, followed by the verb later in the clause.
target_language_example: Das ist das Buch, das sich schnell verkauft hat.
native_language_example: That's the book that sold itself quickly.

meaning: 'that we' (relative pronoun + pronoun) — introduces a clause describing something related to 'we'.
additional_notes: Used to connect a noun to a relative clause where 'wir' is the subject of the clause. In English it corresponds to 'that we' or 'which we'. The relative pronoun 'das' refers back to a neuter noun or a general idea; word order in the relative clause is standard German (verb at the end).
target_language_example: Das Buch, das wir gelesen haben, war spannend.
native_language_example: The book that we read was exciting.

meaning: "that English" (used to introduce a clause about English)
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'dass' (that) followed by the noun 'Englisch' (English). It introduces a subordinate clause giving a fact, opinion, or reported speech about the English language. Word order: in German subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass' the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g. 'dass Englisch schwierig ist'). Useful in statements and questions with verbs like 'denken', 'sagen', 'zeigen', 'lernen'.
target_language_example: Ich weiß, dass Englisch wichtig ist.
native_language_example: I know that English is important.

meaning: 'that God' — introduces a clause stating something about God (used after verbs of thinking, believing, saying, hoping, praying, etc.).
additional_notes: dass is the subordinating conjunction 'that' and sends the verb to the end of the clause in German. 'dass Gott ...' is followed by a verb at the end (e.g. 'dass Gott mich segne', 'dass Gott mir vergibt'). Common after verbs of belief, knowledge, asking, hoping, or praying. Capitalization: Gott (God) is a noun and is always capitalized. Use 'dass' (double s) for the conjunction; spoken German sometimes reduces it but writing requires 'dass'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass Gott uns hilft.
native_language_example: I hope that God helps us.

meaning: that your
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction dass (that) with the possessive pronoun Ihre (your). Ihre is the formal singular or plural OR the capitalized polite form (Sie) possessive; it agrees in capitalization with formal address. Used in sentences to introduce a clause about something belonging to or concerning the listener(s). Word order: dass begins a subordinate clause, so the verb typically goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass Ihre Reise gut verläuft.
native_language_example: I hope that your trip goes well.

meaning: ‘that you came’ (polite/formal) — used to thank or acknowledge someone's arrival.
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a subordinate clause introduced by dass and commonly appears with a thanking verb: Danke, dass Sie gekommen sind. Sie is the formal 'you' (capitalized). The full clause usually ends with the perfect tense kommen → gekommen sind. Use this when addressing someone formally (Sie). Informal equivalent: 'dass du gekommen bist.'
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass Sie gekommen sind.
native_language_example: Thank you very much that you came. / Thank you very much for coming.

meaning: 'that you with' — introduces a subordinate clause about something the listener (formal Sie) did, is doing, or is connected to (often followed by a person, company, vehicle, or activity).
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'dass' (that) + the formal pronoun 'Sie' (you) + the preposition 'mit' (with). 'Mit' will usually be completed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. mit Air Pandora, mit uns, mit Tom, mit Fieber) and expresses accompaniment, association, or the entity involved. Use the formal 'Sie' in polite or formal situations. Word order in the subordinate clause sends the verb to the end: e.g. 'dass Sie mitfahren' → 'that you travel with'.
target_language_example: Danke, dass Sie mit uns gekommen sind.
native_language_example: Thank you for coming with us.

meaning: 'that time is money' — a phrase stating time has monetary value (i.e., don't waste time).
additional_notes: This is the clause form using 'dass' + the proverb 'Zeit ist Geld'. Native speakers would usually say 'Zeit ist Geld' by itself. 'dass Zeit Geld ist' appears inside a sentence after verbs like 'sagen', 'denken', 'erinnern' (e.g. 'Er sagte, dass Zeit Geld ist'). Use when reporting someone's words or thoughts.
target_language_example: Sie erinnerte mich daran, dass Zeit Geld ist.
native_language_example: She reminded me that time is money.

meaning: 'that all' (introduces a clause saying everyone/everything of a group ...)
additional_notes: Common combination: 'dass' (that) + 'alle' (all/everyone). Used to report beliefs, thoughts, or statements about an entire group. Follows verbs like glauben, denken, sagen. Word order: 'dass' begins the subordinate clause, verb goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass alle Schüler pünktlich kommen.
native_language_example: I believe that all students arrive on time.

meaning: that others / that other people (do something)
additional_notes: Combines the subordinating conjunction 'dass' (that) with 'andere' (others). Used to introduce a subordinate clause about what other people do, want, or feel. Word order: verb goes to the end of the clause when 'dass' introduces it (e.g. 'dass andere an dein Geld kommen'). 'Andere' can mean 'other people' or 'someone else' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass andere mich respektieren.
native_language_example: I hope that others respect me.

meaning: that that is a / that this is a (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: A common sequence used to introduce a subordinate clause with 'dass' (that) followed by a demonstrative 'das' (this/that) and an indefinite article 'ein' before a noun. It marks that the speaker is stating what something is (often expressing surprise, judgment, or information). Word order: 'dass' starts the subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass das ein Missverständnis ist.
native_language_example: I hope that that is a misunderstanding.

meaning: 'that this/that here' — introduces a clause pointing to something close or currently discussed
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause (with 'dass') that refers to something near the speaker, something in the current situation, or what was just mentioned ('das hier' = 'this' or 'this here'). Common in spoken and written German. Word order: 'dass' + subject + 'das hier' + verb(s) (verb goes to the end of the clause).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass das hier hilft.
native_language_example: I believe that this will help.

meaning: that that is/that it is/that it turned out that way (introduces a clause describing how something is).
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written German to introduce a subordinate clause that explains how something is or turned out. 'dass' = 'that'; 'das' can mean 'that' or 'it' (referring to a situation or thing); 'so' = 'so/that way'. Together they often translate as 'that it is like that' or 'that it turned out that way.' Word order: the verb of the subordinate clause goes to the end (e.g., 'dass das so gekommen ist').
target_language_example: Ich hätte nicht gedacht, dass das so schwierig ist.
native_language_example: I wouldn't have thought that it would be so difficult.

meaning: 'that' + 'this/these' — a conjunction plus a demonstrative used to introduce a subordinate clause referring to a specific person/thing(s).
additional_notes: dass = 'that' (introduces reported content or a subordinate clause). diese = demonstrative 'this' or 'these' (depends on gender/number of the noun that follows). Together they commonly appear when reporting thoughts, beliefs, or pointing to a specific object/person (e.g. 'that this/these ...'). Word order: in the subordinate clause introduced by 'dass', the verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass diese Entscheidung falsch ist.
native_language_example: I believe that this decision is wrong.

meaning: that you (your) — introduces a subordinate clause referring to something the person possesses or should do.
additional_notes: Common connector: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (that...), 'du' is the informal singular 'you', and 'deine' is the feminine/ plural/possessive form 'your' agreeing with the following noun (e.g. deine Manieren, deine Grenzen). Word order changes in subordinate clauses: the verb goes to the end (e.g. ...dass du deine Manieren vergisst). Useful in spoken and written German for giving advice, wishes, or statements about someone.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du deine Hausaufgaben machst.
native_language_example: I hope that you do your homework.

meaning: a sequence introducing a subordinate clause meaning 'that you ... for/forever/for someone' depending on context; here 'dass' = 'that', 'du' = 'you', 'für' = 'for/forever'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common combination: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause, 'du' is the subject 'you', and 'für' can mean 'for' (benefit, purpose) or 'for/forever' as part of expressions like 'für immer' (forever). The exact translation of 'für' depends on the words that follow ('für mich' = for me, 'für sie' = for her/them, 'für immer' = forever). Word order: in German subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass', the verb typically goes to the end.
target_language_example: Dass du für mich da bist, bedeutet mir sehr viel.
native_language_example: That you are there for me means a lot to me.

meaning: "that you (are) happy."
additional_notes: Part of a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass' (that) plus the subject 'du' (you) and adjective 'glücklich' (happy). Commonly follows verbs of wanting, thinking, or feeling (e.g., 'ich bin glücklich, dass...', 'wir wollen, dass...'). In German subordinate clauses the verb moves to the end (e.g., 'dass du glücklich bist').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du glücklich bist.
native_language_example: I hope that you are happy.

meaning: 'that you today' used to introduce a clause about what someone does or is today ("that you ... today").
additional_notes: Common structure: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause; 'du' is the subject 'you'; 'heute' means 'today' and usually comes near the verb or at the end of the clause. In English this becomes 'that you ... today'. Word order in German subordinate clauses sends the verb to the end: e.g. 'dass du heute ...' or 'dass du ... heute ... wirst'.
target_language_example: Ich habe gehört, dass du heute frei hast.
native_language_example: I heard that you have the day off today.

meaning: 'that you now' — introduces a clause about what someone is doing or should do right now.
additional_notes: Commonly follows verbs like denken, wissen, wollen, möchten, sein + froh, etc. Used to report or command something concerning the person 'du' at the present moment. In English often translated as 'that you are/come/leave now' or simply 'that you now'. Word order: 'dass' starts a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end (e.g. 'dass du jetzt gehst' or 'dass du jetzt hier bist').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du jetzt mit dem Projekt anfängst.
native_language_example: I hope that you start the project now.

meaning: that you and (someone) ... — introduces a clause saying what two people do or are.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with 'dass' (that) followed by 'du und + name' (you and someone else). The verb at the end must agree with a plural subject (ihr or third-person plural) and is placed at the end of the clause. In spoken or informal German you may hear word order variations or contractions, but standard written German keeps the verb at the end. Watch for correct verb agreement: 'seid/arbeitet/geheiratet habt' not singular forms.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du und Marie morgen kommen könnt.
native_language_example: I hope that you and Marie can come tomorrow.

meaning: 'that you again' — used to introduce a clause meaning 'that you [do/are] again' (e.g. that you are back, that you recover, that you do something again).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in sentences where the speaker expresses relief, desire, or a condition about someone doing or being something again (e.g. being back, recovering, living somewhere again). 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause; word order places the verb at the end of the clause. Context determines the exact English translation: 'that you are back', 'that you come back', 'that you recover', etc.
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, dass du wieder hier bist.
native_language_example: I'm happy that you're here again.

meaning: "that you to" — part of a clause introducing what someone wants, says, knows, hopes, etc., often followed by a verb or destination.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a sequence: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (that...), 'du' is the subject (you), and 'zu' often begins a verbal phrase with a following infinitive or indicates direction (e.g. 'zu mir kommen' = 'come to me'). In many examples 'zu' is followed by a verb with kommen/gehen or a prepositional phrase. Word order in German subordinate clauses places the conjugated verb at the end.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du zu meiner Party kommst.
native_language_example: I hope that you come to my party.

meaning: "that someone" or "that one (person)" — introduces a clause saying that a particular (unspecified) person does something or is something.
additional_notes: dass is the subordinating conjunction 'that' used to introduce content clauses. Einer is an indefinite pronoun meaning 'one' or 'someone' (masculine/neutral). Together they appear when the speaker refers to a single person (often unspecified) in the subordinate clause: Es schmerzt mich, dass einer von uns zum Dämon wurde = 'It pains me that one of us became a demon.' Word order: the verb of the subordinate clause goes to the end. If the subject is more specific, Germans often use jemand (someone) or jemandem (dative) depending on case.
target_language_example: Ich befürchte, dass einer die Wahrheit weiß.
native_language_example: I fear that someone knows the truth.

meaning: 'that he (will have) success' — part of a clause expressing that someone will be successful.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the start of a subordinate clause using 'dass' (that) + subject 'er' (he) + noun 'Erfolg' (success). In the examples the full idea is 'dass er Erfolg haben wird' (that he will be successful). Use 'dass' to introduce reported content or beliefs; the verb in the subordinate clause typically goes to the end (e.g., 'haben wird').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass er Erfolg haben wird.
native_language_example: I hope that he will be successful.

meaning: 'that he' + preposition 'at/on/in' (beginning of a clause where 'an' starts a prepositional phrase).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause ('that'), 'er' is the subject ('he'), and 'an' is a preposition that begins a phrase (e.g. 'an dem Verbrechen', 'an diesem Tag', 'an jenem Tage', 'an einem warmen Ort', 'an jedem Tag'). Pay attention to noun cases after the preposition (often dative: 'an dem' → 'am'). Word order: in subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass', the conjugated verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Ich weiß, dass er an dem Projekt arbeitet.
native_language_example: I know that he is working on the project.

meaning: that he (the...) — 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause; 'er' = he; 'den' is a masculine/neuter accusative/article for a specific noun that follows.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: 'dass' starts a subordinate clause (that...), 'er' is the subject (he), and 'den' is the accusative article pointing to a masculine noun mentioned or understood (e.g. den Hund, den Preis, den Anruf). Word order in German subordinate clauses places the verb at the end (e.g. ‚dass er den ... gesehen hat / bekommen hat / hereinlassen soll').
target_language_example: Ich habe gehört, dass er den Brief bekommen hat.
native_language_example: I heard that he received the letter.

meaning: 'that he (would) like to' or 'that he likes to'.
additional_notes: Common part of reported speech: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (that). 'Er' = he. 'Gerne' expresses liking or willingness to do something (enjoys, likes to). Tense and mood (e.g. würde, unterrichte, spreche) change the meaning: present = he likes to..., Konjunktiv/conditional (würde) = he would like to.... Used when reporting what someone said.
target_language_example: Sie erzählte mir, dass er gerne in Deutschland arbeitet.
native_language_example: She told me that he likes to work in Germany.

meaning: a clause starter meaning 'that he in...' used to introduce what someone (he) is/was/will be doing or experiencing in a place or time.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common combination: 'dass' (that) + subject 'er' (he) + the preposition/article contraction 'im' (in dem = in the). It begins a subordinate clause giving information about 'him' and is followed by a noun (e.g. Gefängnis, Restaurant, Juni). Word order in German subordinate clauses places the verb at the end: e.g. 'dass er im Gefängnis sitzen könnte' = 'that he could be sitting in prison.'
target_language_example: Sie glaubt, dass er im nächsten Monat zurückkommt.
native_language_example: She believes that he will return next month.

meaning: "that he (is) too..." or "that he (verb) too..." — introduces a subordinate clause about someone doing something to an excessive degree or a reason involving him.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a 'dass'-clause (subordinate clause) giving a reason, explanation, or a limiting comment about a male person (er). 'zu' is followed by an adjective (zu beschäftigt = too busy) or an infinitive in constructions like 'zu viel trinkt' (drinks too much). Word order: the finite verb goes to the end of the clause (…dass er zu viel trinkt). Can also appear in phrases like 'nur dass er zu…' (only that he…).
target_language_example: Es ist traurig, dass er zu wenig schläft.
native_language_example: It's sad that he sleeps too little.

meaning: 'that it is/that there is ... at/on/...'
additional_notes: This is a common German sequence where 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (that...). 'es' is a dummy pronoun or neutral subject. 'an' is a preposition that requires an object or phrase to complete the meaning (e.g. 'an mir', 'an dir', 'an so einem Ort'). The exact translation depends on the preposition phrase that follows 'an' (e.g. 'an mir' = 'on me' or 'suited to me', 'an dir' = 'your turn/responsibility' in some contexts, 'an so einem Ort' = 'in such a place'). Word order: in subordinate clauses the verb goes to the end (dass ... ist/steht/gibt).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass es an der Zeit ist, zu gehen.
native_language_example: I think that it is time to leave.

meaning: that it/the thing (is) — used to refer to a specific thing or idea previously mentioned
additional_notes: Common in sentences with 'dass' (that) introducing a subordinate clause. 'es' is a neutral pronoun (it/that), 'das' often points to a specific thing or idea (that one). Together they emphasize or identify the thing being talked about (e.g. 'that this is the thing'). Word order and meaning depend on the rest of the sentence; sometimes 'das' is a demonstrative pronoun ('that'), sometimes it repeats 'es' for emphasis. Useful after verbs of thinking, knowing, believing, saying, or evaluating (denken, wissen, glauben, sagen, reden).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass es das ist, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: I hope that this is what you need.

meaning: that there is a/one (something).
additional_notes: Part of a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass' (that). 'Es' is a dummy subject and 'einen' is the accusative masculine indefinite article/pronoun — the phrase appears when saying 'that there is a (masculine) ...' In German you usually complete it with a noun or clause (e.g. 'dass es einen Fehler gibt' = 'that there is a mistake'). Word order: verb (e.g. 'gibt') goes to the end of the 'dass' clause.
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass es einen Fehler gibt.
native_language_example: He said that there is a mistake.

meaning: "that (it) you" — introduces a subordinate clause referring to something affecting 'you' (plural/informal).
additional_notes: Contains the subordinating conjunction 'dass' (that) + neutral pronoun 'es' (it/that) + dative/accusative plural informal pronoun 'euch' (you, plural informal). Used to report beliefs, feelings, or facts about something related to the group 'you'. Word order: 'dass' sends the verb to the end of the clause (e.g. 'dass es euch gefällt'). 'Euch' is informal plural (you all).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass es euch gefällt.
native_language_example: I hope that you (all) like it.

meaning: that it is/that it is for (used to introduce a subordinate clause that includes a purpose/recipient/affected person or opinion).
additional_notes: This sequence appears at the start of a subordinate clause: 'dass' (that) + a clause containing 'es' (it) and 'für' (for). 'Für' indicates beneficiary, target, or perspective (for you, for her, for women). The exact translation depends on the verb and context: e.g. 'in Ordnung ist' → 'that it is okay for you'; 'sehr schwer ist' → 'that it is very hard for her'. Keep word order: subordinating 'dass' sends the conjugated verb to the end.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass es für ihn wichtig ist.
native_language_example: I think that it is important for him.

meaning: that it will be tomorrow / that tomorrow (something will happen).
additional_notes: Common clause starter used after verbs of thinking, believing, saying, or guessing (e.g., glaube, denke, wette). 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause; word order changes (verb goes to the end). 'es' is a neutral subject placeholder (it) and 'morgen' means tomorrow. Use with future or present tense to talk about expected events on the next day.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass es morgen sonnig wird.
native_language_example: I believe that it will be sunny tomorrow.

meaning: that it is/was/— + 'too' or 'too many/much' (introduces a clause saying something is excessive or occurs too late).
additional_notes: Combines the subordinating conjunction 'dass' (that) with the dummy subject 'es' (it) and 'zu' (too). Used to report or think that something is excessive, happens too late, or that there is 'too' much of something. The verb (ist/war/sei/gibt) comes at the end of the clause in German. Context determines whether 'zu' means 'too' (adjective/adverb: too late, too small) or 'too many/much' (with nouns: zu viele = too many, zu viel = too much).
target_language_example: Ich weiß, dass es zu teuer ist.
native_language_example: I know that it is too expensive.

meaning: 'that I called' (part of a sentence: dass ich angerufen habe = that I called / have called).
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own — in German you normally say "dass ich angerufen habe" (perfect tense) to report that you called someone. It appears in subordinate clauses introduced by "dass" (that). Word order: in a "dass" clause the conjugated auxiliary (haben) goes to the end: "dass ich angerufen habe." Common in reported messages: "Sag Tom bitte, dass ich angerufen habe."
target_language_example: Sag Anna, dass ich angerufen habe.
native_language_example: Tell Anna that I called.

meaning: "that I (am/was) there" or "that I will be there" — introduces a clause saying that the speaker is present or will be present.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass' (that). Verb tense and context determine whether it means 'am there', 'was there', or 'will be there' (e.g., 'dass ich da bin', 'dass ich da war', 'dass ich da sein würde'). Used to report or express feelings about the speaker's presence.
target_language_example: Sie waren überrascht, dass ich da war.
native_language_example: They were surprised that I was there.

meaning: that I a… (start of a clause: 'that I' + feminine/indefinite noun or numeral)
additional_notes: A common sequence introducing a subordinate clause with 'dass' (that) followed by 'ich' (I) and an indefinite article 'eine' or the numeral 'eine' (one). Used before a feminine singular noun (eine Frau, eine Woche) or when 'eine' means 'one' (eine Woche = one week). The clause continues after these three words. Word order: verb often goes to the end in German subordinate clauses (e.g., 'dass ich eine Woche lang im Bett bleiben solle').
target_language_example: Er hat gehört, dass ich eine kleine Wohnung suche.
native_language_example: He heard that I am looking for a small apartment.

meaning: 'that I a...' — beginning of a subordinate clause with 'dass' (that) + subject 'ich' (I) + an indefinite masculine accusative or nominative object 'einen' (a/an).
additional_notes: This sequence appears at the start of a 'dass'-clause (that-clause) and is followed by a noun phrase and the rest of the clause (e.g. Fehler, Schlüssel, Dreh). 'Einen' is the masculine accusative (or sometimes nominative in some dialects) form of 'ein'. You will often see it before masculine nouns: einen Fehler (a mistake), einen Schlüssel (a key), einen Dreh (a turn/quirk). 'Dass' introduces reported content or explanations: 'I told him that I made a mistake' = Ich habe ihm erzählt, dass ich einen Fehler gemacht habe.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihr gesagt, dass ich einen Fehler gemacht habe.
native_language_example: I told her that I made a mistake.

meaning: that I am (right now) ...
additional_notes: Common phrase used to report what you are doing at this moment. 'gerade' means 'just' or 'right now' and indicates an action in progress. Often used in reported speech after verbs like 'sagen' (tell) or 'mitteilen' (inform). The rest of the sentence completes the action: e.g. 'dass ich gerade dusche' = 'that I am showering right now.'
target_language_example: Sag ihm, dass ich gerade arbeite.
native_language_example: Tell him that I am working right now.

meaning: "that I always" (introduces a clause about something the speaker consistently does or experiences).
additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that require a 'dass' (that) clause. It connects to a statement about the speaker's habitual action, state, or promise. Word order: 'dass' starts the subordinate clause, verb goes to the end (e.g., 'dass ich immer beschäftigt war'). Common in statements, promises, explanations.
target_language_example: Ich verspreche, dass ich immer ehrlich zu dir bin.
native_language_example: I promise that I will always be honest with you.

meaning: 'that I [my]...' — introduces a clause about something the speaker possesses or did (often followed by a noun like 'Brieftasche', 'Schlüssel', 'Mutter' in examples).
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'dass' ('that') + subject 'ich' ('I') + possessive pronoun 'meine' ('my' for feminine or plural nouns). 'Meine' agrees with the noun that follows (meine Tasche, meine Schlüssel — note: 'Schlüssel' is plural so 'meine' can appear). In spoken or written German you often see 'dass ich meine' followed directly by the noun or by past participles (e.g. 'dass ich meine ... verloren habe').
target_language_example: Ich dachte, dass ich meine Tasche im Bus liegen gelassen habe.
native_language_example: I thought that I had left my bag on the bus.

meaning: a clause starter meaning 'that I my...' used to introduce a subordinate clause where 'ich' is the subject and 'meinen' begins an object or noun phrase (accusative masculine/possessive).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence of words that commonly appears when a speaker introduces a subordinate clause about themselves and uses the masculine accusative form meinen (either as a possessive determiner 'my' before a masculine noun: meinen Sohn/Bruder/Rang, or as the accusative of the possessive pronoun 'mine' in some contexts). English translations depend on the rest of the clause: e.g. 'that I want to keep my rank', 'that I don't like you', 'that I killed my brother'. Word order in German subordinate clauses places the verb at the end.
target_language_example: Glaubst du wirklich, dass ich meinen Bruder getötet habe?
native_language_example: Do you really think that I killed my brother?

meaning: that I only / that I just
additional_notes: Used to report what someone wants to convey about themselves — often to downplay, limit, or qualify an action or trait. 'nur' means 'only/just' and narrows the statement after 'dass ich'. Common in spoken and written German. Word order: 'dass' + subject + 'nur' + verb or complement (position of 'nur' can vary for emphasis).
target_language_example: Sag ihr, dass ich nur geholfen habe.
native_language_example: Tell her that I only helped.

meaning: "that I (am) so" or "that I (do) so" — part of a subordinate clause introducing what 'I' am or do in a certain way.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the start of many subordinate clauses with 'dass' (that) + subject 'ich' (I) + adverb or adjective 'so' (so/like this). English translations depend on the rest of the clause: e.g. 'that I am like that', 'that I behave like this', 'that I said so'. In German word order, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end of the clause: 'dass ich so bin', 'dass ich so denke', 'dass ich so gesagt habe'. Use 'dass' to introduce reported content or reason.
target_language_example: Er glaubt, dass ich so bin.
native_language_example: He believes that I am like that.

meaning: 'that I (to...)' — a clause starter used before a verb or verb phrase, e.g. to report what someone says/thinks/does
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself but the beginning of a subordinate clause: 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause and pushes the conjugated verb to the end of the clause. After 'dass ich zu' you usually expect an infinitive with 'zu' (e.g. 'dass ich zu kommen versuche' — though more natural would be other constructions) or 'zu' as a preposition followed by a noun/infinitive phrase. Common patterns: 'dass ich zu ... komme/komme' (verb at the end), 'dass ich zu + infinitive' (with 'zu' before an infinitive), or 'dass ich zu + noun' (prepositional). Because it's a fragment, pay attention to word order: the finite verb for 'ich' appears at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass ich zu dem Treffen kommen sollte.
native_language_example: He said that I should come to the meeting.

meaning: that you (plural) all / that all of you ...
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass' to address a group (informal 'ihr'). 'Ihr' is the familiar plural 'you' (you all). 'Alle' emphasizes every person in the group. Common in requests, expectations, statements about the group's behavior or qualities. Word order: verb of main clause + dass + subject (ihr alle) + rest of clause. In polite/formal situations use 'dass Sie alle'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass ihr alle pünktlich seid.
native_language_example: I hope that all of you are punctual.

meaning: that nobody / that no one
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with 'dass' (that) + 'keiner' (nobody). 'Keiner' can refer to people in general or specific groups; gender/number is neutral here. In formal contexts you may see 'keiner von ihnen' or 'keiner von euch/ihr' for clarity. Word order: verb goes to the end of the clause (…dass keiner es tut).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass keiner das verloren hat.
native_language_example: I hope that nobody lost that.

meaning: "that one/you/people ... that" — introduces a clause meaning 'that (people) ... (it)'.
additional_notes: Common way to report or ask about what people in general, someone unspecified, or 'one' does or can do. 'Dass' introduces a subordinate clause; 'man' is the impersonal pronoun (one/people/you); 'das' usually refers back to something mentioned. In English this often becomes 'that you/one/people ... it' or simply 'that ...'. Word order: verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g. 'dass man das nicht darf').
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass man das jetzt noch ändern kann?
native_language_example: Do you think that one can still change that now?

meaning: 'that our' (introduces a clause stating something about 'our' + noun).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'dass' (that) with the possessive pronoun 'unsere' (our, feminine/plural or before plural nouns). Used to introduce subordinate clauses. Word order after 'dass' places the verb at the end of the clause in German (e.g., 'dass unsere Schüler in Gefahr sind' — 'that our students are in danger'). 'Unsere' agrees in gender/number/case with the noun it modifies (unsere Welt, unsere Kinder, unsere Mannschaft).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass unsere Freunde bald kommen.
native_language_example: I hope that our friends will come soon.

meaning: 'that we (do) that' / 'that we (do) it' — introduces a clause about something we do or that applies to us.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger sentence with 'dass' (that) introducing a subordinate clause. 'wir' = we. 'das' usually refers back to an action or situation (it/that). Depending on context, it can mean 'that we (do) it', 'that we (have) that', or 'that that (thing) relates to us'. Word order: in a subordinate clause the verb goes to the end (e.g., 'dass wir das Geld stehlen').
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass wir das schaffen können.
native_language_example: I believe that we can manage/that we can do it.

meaning: 'how long does it take until' or 'how long until...' (asks about the time until something happens)
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used to ask how much time passes before a future event occurs. Often appears in questions with 'Wie lange' at the start: 'Wie lange dauert es, bis ...?'. The clause after 'bis' contains the event (often with a verb). You can replace the event with a noun phrase or clause: 'bis Tom hier ist', 'bis die Ampel grün wird'.
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es, bis der Bus kommt?
native_language_example: How long does it take until the bus arrives?

meaning: doesn't take (long); won't last long.
additional_notes: Common short phrase used to reassure someone that something will be quick. Often appears as 'dauert nicht lang' or 'dauert nicht lange' and frequently used in spoken, informal contexts. Can be used with or without 'es' (Es dauert nicht lange.). Addressees like 'Kind' or 'Schatz' show casual tone.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das dauert nicht lange.
native_language_example: Don't worry, that won't take long.

meaning: won't take much longer / doesn't last much longer
additional_notes: Used to say that something will end soon or that only a short time remains until something happens. Often appears in fixed phrases like 'Das dauert nicht mehr lange' or 'Es dauert nicht mehr lange bis ...'. Can be followed by a clause or left standalone as reassurance.
target_language_example: Es dauert nicht mehr lange bis die S-Bahn kommt.
native_language_example: The S-Bahn won't take much longer to arrive.

meaning: assume that; presume (that).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like gehen (gehen davon aus) or an individual (ging davon aus) to mean 'to assume' or 'be under the impression that'. Usually followed by 'dass' + clause. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich gehe davon aus, dass das Meeting um 10 Uhr beginnt.
native_language_example: I assume that the meeting starts at 10 o'clock.

meaning: to assume or expect (something); to proceed on the assumption that
additional_notes: Common phrase used to express a reasonable expectation or assumption about a situation. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'dass' (e.g. 'Ich gehe davon aus, dass...') or used with pronouns and contexts (e.g. 'Man kann davon ausgehen, dass...'). Neutral register and very common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Man kann davon ausgehen, dass das Treffen um zehn Uhr beginnt.
native_language_example: One can assume that the meeting starts at ten o'clock.

meaning: 'far from (that)' / 'not at all (that)'
additional_notes: Used to say that something is far from being true or true of a situation. Often appears as 'weit davon entfernt' (far from it). Can be followed by an infinitive clause (z. B. 'weit davon entfernt, X zu sein') or stand alone as a short response ('Weit davon entfernt.').
target_language_example: Er ist weit davon entfernt, fertig zu sein.
native_language_example: He is far from being finished.

meaning: to tell someone about something / to talk about it
additional_notes: Uses the preposition 'von' with pronoun 'davon' (about that/about it). Often followed by a person introduced with a dative (e.g., 'jemandem davon erzählen') or a question with direct object omitted because 'davon' refers to something already known. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wirst du Tom davon erzählen?
native_language_example: Will you tell Tom about it?

meaning: to have/receive some of it; to gain or get from that (often: 'of it' or 'from that')
additional_notes: Common phrase where 'davon' refers back to something mentioned (something countable or uncountable). Used to ask for or state how many/which/what share someone gets (e.g. pieces, items, benefit). In questions it often means 'Can I have some of that?' or 'May I have one of those?'. In abstract uses it can mean 'what would I gain from that?'. Word order: 'davon' usually follows the verb or appears earlier in the clause depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Kann ich noch zwei davon haben?
native_language_example: Can I have two more of those?

meaning: 'to think of it' / 'to make of it' (asks for or states an opinion about something)
additional_notes: Used with a reference (davon = of that/about that). Common in questions and requests for opinion: Was hältst du davon? / Was sollen wir davon halten? Can be formal or informal. The verb halten is conjugated and typically appears with a question word (was, wie, etc.) or modal verbs. Often used in phrases like "Was soll man davon halten?" or "Sagen Sie mir ehrlich, was Sie davon halten."
target_language_example: Ich weiß auch nicht, was wir davon halten sollen.
native_language_example: I don't know either what we should make of that.

meaning: to hear about it / to hear of it
additional_notes: Used when talking about hearing information or news about something or someone. Commonly appears in questions and statements like 'Ich habe davon gehört' or 'Hast du davon gehört?'. Can refer to hearing by word of mouth or learning that something exists. Often used with verbs like 'haben' (haben ... gehört) or in infinitive constructions (davon hören).
target_language_example: Ich will davon hören, wenn du Neuigkeiten hast.
native_language_example: I want to hear about it when you have news.

meaning: to talk about that / to mention that
additional_notes: Used to say someone is discussing or referring to something previously mentioned or understood from context. 'Davon' = 'of/about that'; 'sprechen' = 'to speak'. Common constructions: 'Wir haben davon gesprochen' (we talked about that) or 'Kannst du davon sprechen?' (can you talk about that?).
target_language_example: Wir sollten morgen davon sprechen.
native_language_example: We should talk about that tomorrow.

meaning: to dream about/of something (either during sleep or as a wish/longing).
additional_notes: Literally 'to dream of/about it' (davon = of/about it). Often used with 'davon träumen, ...' plus an infinitive clause or noun phrase: e.g. 'Ich träume davon, ...' Use for both literal dreaming while asleep and figurative dreaming (hopes, wishes).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht aufhören, davon zu träumen.
native_language_example: I can't stop dreaming about it.

meaning: 'to know about it' or 'to be aware of it'
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone has knowledge or awareness of something. Commonly appears with personal pronouns and in questions or negations (e.g. ‚Ich weiß davon.‘, ‚Er wusste nichts davon.‘). The construction combines the adverb ‚davon‘ (of/about that) with the verb ‚wissen‘ and is often used with subordinate clauses introduced by ‚dass‘ or with infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Ich möchte wissen, ob du davon wissen kannst.
native_language_example: I want to know whether you could know about that.

meaning: 'of/about it/them was' — part of phrases like 'none of that was' or 'one of them was' (davon + sein in past forms).
additional_notes: Davon = 'of it/them' or 'about it/them' (from da + von). Combined with a form of sein (war, waren) it links to something mentioned before: e.g. 'keine davon war' = 'none of them was'. Context determines whether davon refers to things or abstract ideas. Common in sentences talking about parts of a group or previously mentioned topics.
target_language_example: Ich habe drei Vorschläge gelesen, aber keiner davon war gut.
native_language_example: I read three proposals, but none of them was good.

meaning: to make/bring someone to do something; to cause someone to (do) something.
additional_notes: Used with a person as object and an infinitive clause (zu + infinitive) indicating the action you want them to do. Common construction: jemanden dazu bringen, + zu + Infinitiv. Implies causing, persuading, forcing, or convincing someone to act. Tone can be neutral, persuasive, or coercive depending on context.
target_language_example: Wie kann ich ihn dazu bringen, mir zu helfen?
native_language_example: How can I get him to help me?

meaning: to belong to something; to be part of something; to be included
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something is included as a member, component, or part of a group, list, category, or set of responsibilities. Common constructions: 'dazu gehören X' (X is included), 'Zu den Aufgaben gehören...' or 'Dazu gehört, dass...' (It includes that...). Can be followed by nouns or clauses. Tone: neutral; usable in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Zu den Kosten dazu gehören Miete und Strom.
native_language_example: The costs include rent and electricity.

meaning: to happen / to come to that (situation); to join (someone) or join in an activity in some contexts
additional_notes: Common idiom with two main uses: 1) to indicate that a situation or event occurs or may occur (often impersonal with 'es': 'es kommt dazu', 'es kann dazu kommen', 'es würde dazu kommen'); 2) to ask or offer to join someone physically or join an activity (e.g. 'Darf ich dazu kommen?'). Word order and context determine meaning. Frequently appears in perfect or conditional constructions and with modal verbs.
target_language_example: Ich hatte gehofft, es würde nicht dazu kommen.
native_language_example: I had hoped it wouldn't come to that.

meaning: to say (something) about it / to comment on that
additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention someone's opinion or comment about a specific topic or situation. Kann mit Personen (Was würde dein Vater dazu sagen?) or as a general request for input (Willst du noch etwas dazu sagen?). 'Dazu' refers back to something already mentioned; 'sagen' = to say. Common in questions.
target_language_example: Bevor wir entscheiden: Möchtest du noch etwas dazu sagen?
native_language_example: Before we decide: Do you want to say anything about it?

meaning: 'that' + polite/formal or plural 'you' (introdues a subordinate clause referring to you).
additional_notes: daß (modern spelling: dass) is a conjunction meaning 'that' used to introduce subordinate/content clauses. Sie (capitalized) is the formal singular or plural 'you'. Together they introduce what 'you' do, feel, must, etc. Note: spelling reform changed 'daß' to 'dass' in 1996, but older texts and some examples may still use 'daß'.
target_language_example: Es ist nett, daß Sie mir helfen!
native_language_example: It is nice that you (formal) are helping me!

meaning: "that you (did/said/are/etc.) that" — introduces a subordinate clause reporting or asking about what someone did, saw, is, thinks, etc.
additional_notes: This uses the older spelling "daß" (with ß). Modern German orthography uses "dass du das" (double s). It is composed of the conjunction "dass/daß" (that) + the pronoun "du" (you) + the pronoun "das" (that/it). The final "das" can refer to an action, statement, object, or identity depending on context; translate accordingly. Common in reported statements and questions (e.g., "I know that you saw that," "Is it true that you were the one?").
target_language_example: Ich weiß, daß du das gesehen hast.
native_language_example: I know that you saw that.

meaning: that she/they/you (formal) herself/themselves/yourself (reflexive) — fragment introducing a subordinate clause with a reflexive pronoun; modern spelling: 'dass sie sich'.
additional_notes: 'daß' is the older spelling of 'dass' (both understood, use 'dass' in new orthography). 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they' (context decides); when capitalized 'Sie' it means formal 'you'. 'sich' is the reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs. This fragment appears before the verb at the end of a 'dass'-clause: e.g. 'Ich weiß, daß sie sich umgezogen hat.' Word order: conjugated verb moves to clause end in subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Ich weiß, daß sie sich umgezogen hat.
native_language_example: I know that she has changed (her clothes).

meaning: formal 'that you (yourself)' — used in subordinate clauses addressing someone formally (Sie) with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: daß (modern spelling: dass) introduces a subordinate clause meaning 'that'. Sie is the formal 'you'. sich is the reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (e.g. sich kümmern, sich entschuldigen). Common in formal requests or statements. Word order: verb goes to the end of the clause (haben, entschuldigen, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich möchte, daß Sie sich kurz vorstellen.
native_language_example: I would like you (formal) to introduce yourself briefly.

meaning: that that really happened / that this really happened
additional_notes: This phrasing uses pre-1996 German orthography: 'daß' is now spelled 'dass' in modern German. The first 'das' can be a demonstrative pronoun referring to an event or situation. Common in questions or statements expressing doubt, surprise, or the need for evidence (e.g., asking whether something actually occurred). In contemporary writing use 'dass das wirklich passiert' instead.
target_language_example: Haben Sie Beweise, daß das wirklich passiert ist?
native_language_example: Do you have evidence that that really happened?

meaning: 'that you today' — used to introduce a clause about what 'you' do or are doing today (modern spelling: "dass du heute").
additional_notes: This is the conjunction 'daß' (now spelled 'dass') + pronoun 'du' + time adverb 'heute'. It commonly introduces subordinate clauses meaning 'that you (will/do/did) today...' or expresses wishes, statements, or questions about the person's actions or state today. Word order: verb moves to the end of the clause (e.g. 'daß du heute gekommen bist'). Formal written German uses 'dass'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, daß du heute Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I hope that you have time today.

meaning: 'that he it' — part of a subordinate clause meaning 'that he (it/that) ...', used to introduce reported content or an object pronoun referring to something mentioned earlier.
additional_notes: Spelling note: modern German uses 'dass' instead of older 'daß'. 'dass' = 'that' (conjunction). 'er' = 'he'. 'es' = neuter pronoun 'it' or 'that' referring to a previously mentioned thing or proposition. Word order in German subordinate clauses places the conjugated verb at the end, so 'dass er es getan hat' = 'that he did it'. The phrase 'dass er es' is compositional and commonly appears in reported speech, questions, requests, or wishes (e.g., with wollen, hoffen, meinen).
target_language_example: Du glaubst doch nicht, daß er es getan hat?
native_language_example: You don't really think that he did it, do you?

meaning: "that I (should) you/for you" — introduces a subordinate clause stating that the speaker does something for the person (dative 'dir' = to/for you); modern spelling: 'dass ich dir'.
additional_notes: 'daß' (modern 'dass') is the subordinating conjunction 'that'. 'ich' = I. 'dir' is dative 'you' (to/for you). Common with verbs expressing desire, expectation, requests, or orders (wollen, möchten, erwarten, wollen, verzeihen, sagen, erzählen, etc.). Word order: main clause, dass + subject + indirect object + ... + verb at end (infinite or conjugated dependent form). In English often: "that I help you," "that I tell you," "that I forgive you."
target_language_example: Erwartest du noch von mir, daß ich dir helfe?
native_language_example: Do you still expect me to help you?

meaning: "that it was me" — used to report a thought or belief that the speaker was the person responsible (older orthography: daß instead of modern dass).
additional_notes: This entry uses the pre-reform spelling "daß" as requested; modern German spelling is "dass ich es war". Typical in reported/thought contexts (introduced by verbs like denken, glauben): e.g. "Dachten Sie wirklich, daß ich es war...?" Often followed by a relative clause identifying the action or victim: "daß ich es war, der/die ... hat/hatte". Neutral register; can be used in both formal and informal contexts depending on pronouns and verb forms. Word order: subordinate clause introduced by daß/dass, predicate "ich es war". Emphasis is on the speaker being the one who performed the action.
target_language_example: Dachten Sie wirklich, daß ich es war, der Ihnen die Reifen aufgeschlitzt hat?
native_language_example: Did you really think that it was me who slashed your tires?

meaning: 'that you (plural) yourselves' — introduces a clause addressing a group (informal), with a reflexive pronoun.
additional_notes: Daß (modern spelling: daß → dass) is the conjunction 'that'. Ihr is the 2nd-person plural 'you' (informal). Euch is the reflexive/object form used with reflexive verbs (sich etwas nehmen, sich etwas anhören, sich entschuldigen, sich ein neues Telefon kaufen — in German some verbs use reflexive forms for actions affecting the person). Together they appear in subordinate clauses: 'that you (all) ... yourselves'. Common in thanks, requests, suggestions, or instructions. Use 'dass ihr euch' in informal situations (when speaking to multiple people).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, daß ihr euch morgen Zeit nehmt.
native_language_example: I hope that you (all) make time tomorrow.

meaning: that she/they/you (formal) a — beginning of a subordinate clause (older spelling of 'dass') introducing a clause where 'sie' is the subject and 'eine' is an indefinite article or numeral
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence of words. 'daß' is the pre-reform spelling of 'dass' (use 'dass' in modern writing). 'sie' can mean 'she', 'they', or formal 'you' depending on context. 'eine' is the feminine or nominative/accusative indefinite article or the numeral 'one'. The sequence simply begins a subordinate clause: 'that she ... a ...'. Ensure modern texts use 'dass sie eine'.
target_language_example: Er sagte, daß sie eine Chance bekommen würde.
native_language_example: He said that she would get a chance.

meaning: your girl / your daughter (context-dependent)
additional_notes: Can mean 'your daughter' (literal child) or informally 'your girl' meaning a girlfriend or a female person associated with you. Context (tone, situation) decides which. 'Mädchen' is grammatically neuter in German (das Mädchen) even when referring to a female person. 'Dein' agrees with that neuter noun here. Use 'deine' only with plural or different genders (e.g. deine Freundin = your (female) friend).
target_language_example: Ist sie wirklich dein Mädchen, oder nur eine Bekannte?
native_language_example: Is she really your girl, or just an acquaintance?

meaning: your day (how your day went / your special day).
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask or talk about someone's day (Wie war dein Tag? = How was your day?). Can also mean 'your day' as in 'today is your day' (i.e. things go well for you) or the opposite ('Heute ist nicht dein Tag' = today is not your day / things aren't going well). Informal familiar form using 'dein' (singular informal you).
target_language_example: Wie war dein Tag heute?
native_language_example: How was your day today?

meaning: your older (male) — short for "dein älterer Bruder" (your older brother) or generally 'your older one' when referring to a male person.
additional_notes: "Älterer" is the comparative adjective 'older' used as a noun (substantivized adjective). With "dein" it commonly refers to an older male family member (often 'Bruder') mentioned or understood from context. If you mean an older female, use "deine Ältere" (less common) or explicitly "deine ältere Schwester". Word order: adjective follows the possessive (dein älterer Bruder). In sentences you will often see the full phrase "dein älterer Bruder," but in casual speech people may shorten it to "dein Älterer."
target_language_example: Ist dein älterer heute zu Hause?
native_language_example: Is your older brother at home today?

meaning: your people; your group, team, or followers (people connected to you)
additional_notes: Used to refer to people who belong to, work for, support, or are associated with the person you're speaking to. Context tells whether it means friends, coworkers, followers, soldiers, family, etc. Can be informal; tone depends on context (neutral, friendly, or accusatory).
target_language_example: Hast du deine Leute informiert?
native_language_example: Did you inform your people?

meaning: your school (informal: speaking to one person)
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: 'deine' is the informal singular 'your' (du). Used when speaking to friends, family, or children. 'Schule' means school (building or institution). Word order: normally 'deine Schule' can be followed by location, distance, size questions (e.g. 'Wo ist deine Schule?', 'Ist deine Schule weit entfernt?'). If addressing more than one person or formally, use 'eure Schule' (you plural) or 'Ihre Schule' (formal).
target_language_example: Wo ist deine Schule? Kommt man mit dem Bus dorthin?
native_language_example: Where is your school? Can you get there by bus?

meaning: 'your rights' (legal or moral rights belonging to you)
additional_notes: Plural phrase used to talk about a person's entitlements or legal protections (e.g., consumer rights, workers' rights, human rights). 'Deine' is the informal singular possessive (du). For formal or plural address use 'Ihre Rechte' (formal you) or 'eure Rechte' (informal plural you).
target_language_example: Du solltest deine Rechte kennen, bevor du unterschreibst.
native_language_example: You should know your rights before you sign.

meaning: in your head / in your mind
additional_notes: Literal: 'in your head' (dative). Used for thoughts, imagination, internal hearing, feelings or mental images. Common in phrases like 'nur in deinem Kopf' (only in your head) or 'hörst du es in deinem Kopf' (you hear it in your head). Informal/neutral everyday expression.
target_language_example: Das Problem existiert nur in deinem Kopf.
native_language_example: The problem exists only in your head.

meaning: after your shift / of your shift (possessive: your shift).
additional_notes: deiner is the dative/genitive feminine or dative masculine/neuter singular form of 'du' (your). In this phrase it is dative singular feminine because 'Schicht' (shift) is feminine and verbs like 'nach' take the dative. Commonly used to talk about actions happening after someone's work shift (e.g., 'after your shift, shall I pick you up?'). Replace 'deiner' with other possessives for different persons (meiner, seiner, ihrer, unserer, eurer, Ihrer).
target_language_example: Kommst du nach deiner Schicht noch auf einen Kaffee?
native_language_example: Are you coming for a coffee after your shift?

meaning: in your position; if I were you
additional_notes: Used in conditional advice/ recommendations. Usually appears in the phrase 'An deiner Stelle…' (literally 'at your place'). Followed by a conditional verb (würde…, ginge…, würde ich …). Common for giving suggestions or warning someone.
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich das Angebot annehmen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would accept the offer.

meaning: If I were you, I would ... (giving advice or a suggestion).
additional_notes: A polite, hypothetical way to give advice. It uses the dative phrase 'deiner Stelle' ('in your place') plus the conditional 'würde ich'. Follow with an infinitive or complete clause: e.g. 'deiner Stelle würde ich das tun' or 'deiner Stelle würde ich gehen'. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Deiner Stelle würde ich den Termin absagen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would cancel the appointment.

meaning: 'in the evening' or 'on the evening' (dative form of 'der Abend')
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific evening (point in time). 'An dem Abend' is the full phrase meaning 'on that evening' or 'on the evening' and often contracts in speech/writing to 'am Abend' when not specifying a particular day. Here 'dem Abend' is the dative case (after the preposition 'an').
target_language_example: An dem Abend haben wir lange gesprochen.
native_language_example: On that evening we talked for a long time.

meaning: after dinner / after the evening meal (dative form used after 'nach').
additional_notes: Abendbrot is a common German word for the evening meal (often a light meal). 'Nach dem Abendbrot' means 'after dinner' and uses the dative article 'dem' because 'nach' requires the dative. Use it to talk about activities that happen after the evening meal.
target_language_example: Nach dem Abendbrot sehen wir zusammen einen Film.
native_language_example: After dinner we watch a movie together.

meaning: to be finished with dinner / to have finished preparing or eating dinner
additional_notes: Common German phrase using 'mit ... fertig sein' (to be finished with ...). Can refer to finishing preparing the meal or finishing eating it — context tells which. Often used in questions (Bist du mit dem Abendessen fertig?) and with time expressions (vor dem Abendessen = before dinner). Verb forms: 'bin fertig', 'bist fertig', 'sind fertig', 'ist fertig geworden' (became finished).
target_language_example: Wir sind jetzt mit dem Abendessen fertig.
native_language_example: We are finished with dinner now.

meaning: from abroad; from a foreign country
additional_notes: Used with verbs of coming or returning (zurückkommen, zurückkehren, kommen) or to indicate origin of something (e.g. a call). 'Aus' + dative 'dem Ausland' (= 'from the abroad'). Common in everyday German to say someone or something came from another country.
target_language_example: Er ist gestern aus dem Ausland zurückgekehrt.
native_language_example: He returned from abroad yesterday.

meaning: the bathroom (dative case of 'das Bad').
additional_notes: This is 'das Bad' in the dative case (used after certain prepositions or verbs that require the dative, e.g. 'aus dem Bad' = 'out of the bathroom', or after indirect objects). In everyday speech 'Bad' often means bathroom; context shows location or movement from the bathroom. Word order: 'aus dem Bad' = 'from/out of the bathroom'.
target_language_example: Er kommt gerade aus dem Bad.
native_language_example: He is just coming out of the bathroom.

meaning: literally 'the bus or' — typically part of a larger phrase contrasting the bus with something else (e.g. 'dem Bus oder dem Zug' = 'the bus or the train').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression; it's the dative form of 'der Bus' (dem Bus) followed by the coordinating conjunction 'oder' (or). You'll normally see it inside a longer sentence offering a choice or contrast. Remember German articles and nouns must match case: 'dem Bus' is dative (used after certain prepositions or verbs, or when indicating the indirect object).
target_language_example: Wir fahren dem Bus oder dem Zug zum Flughafen? — Wir nehmen den Zug.
native_language_example: Do we go by the bus or the train to the airport? — We'll take the train.

meaning: by bus to (the) — indicates traveling to a place by bus (with 'zur' = to the, feminine or dative contraction of 'zu der').
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say you go somewhere by bus. 'mit' takes the dative, so 'dem Bus' is dative masculine ('der Bus' → 'dem Bus'). 'zur' is a contraction of 'zu der' and precedes a feminine noun (e.g. 'zur Arbeit' = to work). For other destinations/genders/forms: 'zum' = 'zu dem' (masculine/neuter), 'zu' + place name (no article) or 'in die' for into + accusative, etc.
target_language_example: Ich fahre jeden Morgen mit dem Bus zur Schule.
native_language_example: I go to school by bus every morning.

meaning: 'before falling asleep' or 'before sleep' (dative form used with 'vor').
additional_notes: This phrase appears after the preposition 'vor' as in 'vor dem Einschlafen' to mean 'before going to sleep' or 'before you fall asleep'. Common with activities: lesen, pinkeln gehen, Medizin nehmen, etc. 'Einschlafen' is a verb (to fall asleep); here it's used as a noun (gerund/nominalized verb) and takes the dative 'dem'.
target_language_example: Ich trinke immer Tee vor dem Einschlafen.
native_language_example: I always drink tea before falling asleep.

meaning: on the ice (on icy surface)
additional_notes: Dem Eis is the dative form of ‚das Eis‘ used with prepositions like ‚auf‘ to indicate location (on the ice). Common in contexts about slipping or being on an ice surface (frozen water or icy ground). Use word order: ‚auf dem Eis ausrutschen‘ = to slip on the ice.
target_language_example: Sie stand auf dem Eis und verlor das Gleichgewicht.
native_language_example: She was standing on the ice and lost her balance.

meaning: A fragment consisting of the dative noun phrase 'dem Essen' ('to/for the food' or 'during the meal') immediately followed by the article 'die' that begins a feminine or plural noun; not a standalone fixed phrase and usually part of a larger sentence.
additional_notes: 'dem Essen' is dative singular of 'das Essen' and can mean 'to/for the food' or 'during/at the meal' depending on context. 'die' is the feminine/plural nominative or accusative definite article and typically introduces the next noun. The sequence 'dem Essen die' on its own is ungrammatical as a complete sentence; it almost always continues with another noun or clause. Possible correct continuations include contexts like giving something to the food (figurative) or indicating contrast/presentation in a larger structure, but more idiomatic alternatives often use 'beim Essen' (during the meal) or reorder the sentence.
target_language_example: Wir gaben dem Essen die letzte Würze, bevor wir es servierten.
native_language_example: We gave the food the final seasoning before we served it.

meaning: 'out the window' + purpose 'in order to / to...'.
additional_notes: This appears in the structure 'aus dem Fenster, um ... zu + infinitive' (leaned out of the window in order to ...). 'dem Fenster' itself is dative after 'aus' (aus dem Fenster = out of the window). The 'um ... zu' part expresses purpose ('in order to' / 'to'). Together they show someone doing something from the window for a specific reason. Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's a combination of location (aus dem Fenster) and purpose (um ... zu).
target_language_example: Sie lehnte sich aus dem Fenster, um das Feuerwerk zu sehen.
native_language_example: She leaned out the window to see the fireworks.

meaning: with the finger; using a finger (to point, touch, trace, etc.)
additional_notes: A dative phrase used after verbs describing actions done 'with' the finger (e.g. zeigen mit dem Finger, fahren mit dem Finger). Common in concrete actions: pointing (auf etwas zeigen), touching, tracing text, or keeping a finger on a trigger (am Abzug). Use the definite article because German often says 'mit dem Finger' rather than just 'mit Finger'.
target_language_example: Sie zeigte mit dem Finger auf den Vogel.
native_language_example: She pointed at the bird with her finger.

meaning: 'at/on the cemetery' (dative form of 'der Friedhof')
additional_notes: Used when indicating location (on/at) the cemetery. 'Friedhof' = cemetery; the article changes to 'dem' because motionless location after preposition 'auf' often takes dative. In English you usually say 'at the cemetery' or 'in the cemetery'.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um drei Uhr auf dem Friedhof.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the cemetery at three o'clock.

meaning: 'in the field (of)' or 'in the area (of)'.
additional_notes: Used with subjects/areas of knowledge or expertise. Common structure: 'auf dem Gebiet (der) + [field]' or 'auf dem Gebiet + [verb phrase]'. Often follows 'auf' and takes dative 'dem'. Indicates specialization or topic.
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet auf dem Gebiet der Informatik.
native_language_example: She works in the field of computer science.

meaning: to look exactly like (someone); to be the spitting image of someone.
additional_notes: Used in the fixed expression 'jemandem wie aus dem Gesicht geschnitten sein' or 'wie aus dem Gesicht geschnitten' to say one person strongly resembles another (often a parent/child). It's idiomatic — you wouldn't literally cut a face. Common with dative: 'er ist seiner Mutter wie aus dem Gesicht geschnitten.'
target_language_example: Er ist seinem Großvater wie aus dem Gesicht geschnitten.
native_language_example: He looks exactly like his grandfather.

meaning: with the rifle / the rifle (dative: 'with the rifle')
additional_notes: Dem Gewehr is the dative form of 'das Gewehr' (the rifle). It appears after prepositions or verbs that require the dative, and often translates as 'with the rifle' or 'to/for the rifle' depending on context. Common verbs with it include 'schießen mit' (to shoot with) and 'umgehen mit' (to handle). Use 'das Gewehr' in nominative, 'des Gewehrs' or 'des Gewehres' in genitive, 'dem Gewehr' in dative, and 'das Gewehr' in accusative.
target_language_example: Er trägt dem Gewehr vorsichtig über die Schulter.
native_language_example: He carries the rifle carefully over his shoulder.

meaning: in the belief (that); under the impression (that).
additional_notes: Used with a clause or phrase to say someone holds a certain belief or impression. Often appears in expressions like "jemanden in dem Glauben lassen" (to let someone remain under the impression) or "mit dem Glauben kämpfen" (to struggle with belief). The phrase requires a following 'dass' clause or an implied idea.
target_language_example: Sie ließ ihn in dem Glauben, dass alles in Ordnung sei.
native_language_example: She let him remain under the impression that everything was fine.

meaning: on the grass (dative of 'das Gras').
additional_notes: Used after prepositions that require the dative (here 'auf' with location: 'on/at'). 'Gras' is neuter (das Gras); in the dative singular it becomes 'dem Gras'. Commonly used to describe someone or something lying or sitting on the grass.
target_language_example: Wir liegen auf dem Gras und lesen.
native_language_example: We are lying on the grass and reading.

meaning: with the hammer (using a hammer).
additional_notes: Literal dative phrase: dem Hammer is the dative form of der Hammer. Used to indicate the instrument or tool with which an action is done (mit + dative). Common in literal contexts (hitting, nailing, etc.). Not idiomatic here.
target_language_example: Er befestigte das Schild mit dem Hammer.
native_language_example: He fixed the sign with the hammer.

meaning: to have left the house / gone out of the house
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb 'sein' (e.g. Ich bin ... gegangen). It means you left your home/building to go outside or somewhere else. Common in questions about time (Wann bist du aus dem Haus gegangen?) and negatives (nicht aus dem Haus gegangen). Use appropriate subject and auxiliary: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind, ihr seid, Sie sind.
target_language_example: Gestern bin ich um 8 Uhr aus dem Haus gegangen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I left the house at 8 o'clock.

meaning: 'to go out of the house' (but grammatically incorrect; standard: aus dem Haus gehen or das Haus verlassen)
additional_notes: The phrase as given (dem Haus gehen) mixes a dative article with the infinitive and is not a correct standalone expression in German. The correct forms are: "aus dem Haus gehen" (to go out of the house) or "das Haus verlassen" (to leave the house). Use "aus dem Haus gehen" when emphasizing the motion out of the building; use "das Haus verlassen" for simply leaving. Example sentences given use the standard "aus dem Haus gehen."
target_language_example: Ich wollte gerade aus dem Haus gehen, da begann es zu regnen.
native_language_example: I was just about to go out of the house when it started to rain.

meaning: to/at the horizon (dative case of 'der Horizont')
additional_notes: This is the dative form of 'der Horizont' (the horizon). It's used after prepositions or verbs that require the dative (e.g. 'am Horizont' = 'on the horizon', 'gegen den Horizont' would be accusative). Common in phrases like 'am Horizont' (on the horizon) or 'vor dem Horizont' (in front of the horizon). Note: native English speakers usually use 'horizon' without an article; German often uses the article and case.
target_language_example: Die Sonne verschwindet dem Horizont nahe.
native_language_example: The sun is close to the horizon.

meaning: from/out of the classroom (dative form of 'das Klassenzimmer').
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion like 'aus' + dative to indicate movement out of the classroom. 'Klassenzimmer' is neuter (das Klassenzimmer); after the preposition 'aus' it takes the dative 'dem'. Common in commands and descriptions (e.g., someone being sent out).
target_language_example: Bitte geh jetzt aus dem Klassenzimmer.
native_language_example: Please go out of the classroom now.

meaning: in the dress; wearing the dress (indicates being inside/inside of a garment).
additional_notes: Dem Kleid is the dative form of 'das Kleid' (the dress). It's used after prepositions or verbs that require the dative (e.g., 'in' when meaning 'wearing' or 'being in' a garment). Common in compliments: 'in dem Kleid siehst du ... aus' = 'you look ... in that dress.' In spoken German, 'in dem' often contracts to 'im' (im Kleid), though both are correct; using 'dem' can emphasize the specific dress.
target_language_example: Du siehst fantastisch in dem Kleid aus.
native_language_example: You look fantastic in the dress.

meaning: to/for the human
additional_notes: Dative singular of der Mensch. Used when something is directed at, belongs to, or concerns people in general or a specific person (depending on context). Can mean 'to/for the human' (general, collective sense) or 'to/for the person' (specific). Often appears in proverbs or general statements about humanity (e.g. 'Der Mensch ist dem Menschen ein Wolf' = 'man is a wolf to man').
