target_language_example: Sie nahm das Buch aus der Hand und gab es mir.
native_language_example: She took the book out of her hand and gave it to me.

meaning: 'hate' (a strong feeling of dislike or hostility).
additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Used to talk about intense negative feelings toward people, ideas, or things. Commonly contrasted with 'die Liebe' (love). In German, nouns are capitalized. Often used with prepositions: 'Hass auf + accusative' (hate toward), 'Hass gegen/gegenüber' (hate against/toward).
target_language_example: Die Liebe ist stärker als der Hass.
native_language_example: Love is stronger than hate.

meaning: of the heart; beloved / dear (used in expressions like »König der Herzen« — 'king of hearts').
additional_notes: Literally 'of the hearts' (genitive plural). Often used in fixed expressions or titles to mean 'beloved' or 'cherished by many' (e.g. »König der Herzen«). Also appears in literal contexts about the anatomical heart (e.g. »die Vertreter der Herzen« = 'representatives of the hearts'), but that is rare. Grammar note: der Herzen is the genitive plural of 'das Herz'.
target_language_example: Er wurde zum König der Herzen erklärt.
native_language_example: He was declared the king of hearts.

meaning: the (pair of) pants / trousers (dative or genitive form of 'die Hose').
additional_notes: Hose (die Hose) means 'pants' or 'trousers' in German. 'Der Hose' appears as a grammatical form: genitive singular ('of the pants') or dative singular after certain verbs/prepositions ('to/at the pants', usually 'an der Hose' etc.). In everyday speech you'll more often see forms like 'die Hose', 'der Hose' in contexts like 'an der Hose' (at the pants) or 'einen Riss in der Hose' (with 'in' + dative = in the pants). In informal or slang contexts, references to 'in der Hose' can also imply something about a person's body or possession (e.g., joking about having a 'big hammer in the pants').
target_language_example: Du hast einen Riss in der Hose.
native_language_example: You have a rip in your pants.

meaning: the half / half of (genitive or dative form of 'die Hälfte')
additional_notes: Used to refer to 'half' of something (a portion or time). Appears in contexts like 'after half' (after half of a film), 'in half the time' (mit 'in der Hälfte der Zeit' or 'in der Hälfte der Zeit' is possible), or 'from half (of it)'. It is the dative/genitive form of 'die Hälfte' and often follows prepositions (nach der Hälfte = after half of...). The exact translation depends on context (time, quantity, portion).
target_language_example: Wir sind nach der Hälfte der Strecke angekommen.
native_language_example: We arrived after half of the route.

meaning: the job; the (paid) work, task or position
additional_notes: Commonly used in spoken and informal German to refer to a job, task, assignment, or paid position. Can mean a specific task (Der Job ist erledigt = the task is done) or a job/position (Wieso wird der Job so gut bezahlt?). Often interchangeable with 'die Arbeit' or 'die Stelle' depending on context. Informal and loanword from English.
target_language_example: Der Job ist erledigt.
native_language_example: The job is done.

meaning: of the boys
additional_notes: genitive plural of die Jungen (“the boys”). It is used to show possession or connection, as in die Schlafsäle der Jungen (“the boys' dormitories”), and also in phrases like einer der Jungen (“one of the boys”).
target_language_example: Die Fahrräder der Jungen stehen vor der Schule.
native_language_example: The boys' bicycles are in front of the school.

meaning: in the canteen / in the cafeteria (dative singular of 'die Kantine').
additional_notes: Used to indicate location (where something happens) with verbs that require the dative. 'Kantine' = workplace/school cafeteria or casual cafeteria. Common collocations: 'in der Kantine essen', 'sich in der Kantine treffen', 'in der Kantine sitzen'.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um zwölf in der Kantine.
native_language_example: We'll meet at twelve in the canteen.

meaning: of (one's) childhood / from childhood
additional_notes: ‘der Kindheit’ is the genitive singular form of ‘die Kindheit’ (childhood). It’s used to show possession or origin (e.g. 'a friend from childhood' or 'in childhood'). In everyday speech you may also see 'aus der Kindheit' or 'seit der Kindheit' to mean 'from/ since childhood.'
target_language_example: Sie ist eine Freundin aus der Kindheit.
native_language_example: She is a friend from childhood.

meaning: on/from the clothing; of the clothing (dative/strong declension form of 'die Kleidung').
additional_notes: ‚Kleidung‘ = clothes; ‚der Kleidung‘ is the dative singular (used after prepositions like an, auf with dative, or to show location/contact) or the genitive singular in some fixed phrases. In examples it means 'on the clothing' (e.g. blood/sperm found on someone's clothes) or 'from the clothing' (removing sand from clothes). Word order: article + noun; beginners should learn basic cases to know when to use 'der Kleidung' vs. 'die Kleidung' or 'der Kleidung' as genitive.
target_language_example: Er wischte das Wasser von der Kleidung.
native_language_example: He wiped the water off the clothing.

meaning: 'the war is over' (literal components: 'der Krieg' = the war; 'zu Ende' = over/finished).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences as part of the clause 'wenn/als/wo der Krieg zu Ende ist' or 'in dem Jahr, in dem der Krieg zu Ende war' meaning 'when the war is over/was over' or 'in which the war ended'. Common connector words: 'wenn' (when/if), 'als' (when, for past single events), 'in dem Jahr, in dem' (the year in which). 'zu Ende' is placed after the noun it modifies ('der Krieg').
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, ob er zurückkommt, wenn der Krieg zu Ende ist.
native_language_example: I don't know if he'll come back when the war is over.

meaning: the man in (used to describe a man by what he's wearing or where he is, e.g. 'the man in black')
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by a noun or adjective that describes the man (e.g. 'der Mann in Schwarz' = 'the man in black' or 'der Mann in Ihrem Hotelzimmer' = 'the man in your hotel room'). It's a simple descriptive construction similar to English 'the man in ...'. Word order: 'der Mann' (subject) + 'in' + the following noun phrase. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Der Mann in der roten Jacke wartet draußen.
native_language_example: The man in the red jacket is waiting outside.

meaning: ‘in/on/with the machine’ or ‘on the (air)craft’ depending on context (dative of die Maschine).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of die Maschine. 'Machine' can mean a machine/device, but in older or colloquial contexts (e.g. travel/war stories) 'die Maschine' can mean an aircraft or ship. The exact English preposition (in/on/with) depends on the verb and context: 'mit der Maschine' = 'with the machine' or 'by machine'; 'in der Maschine' = 'inside the machine' or 'on/aboard the aircraft' if 'Maschine' means plane. Pay attention to the article: der is dative feminine.
target_language_example: Er arbeitet mit der Maschine in der Fabrik.
native_language_example: He works with the machine in the factory.

meaning: literally 'the person is that' — not a standard fixed phrase; likely incomplete fragment meaning 'that's the person' or 'that's what makes someone (human)'.
additional_notes: This sequence of words is not a common standalone expression in German. Context matters: it could be an incomplete sentence or poetic line. Possible interpretations: 1) As a fragment like "Der Mensch ist das", followed by something else (e.g. "Der Mensch ist das, was er isst") — 'Man is what he eats'. 2) In conversational correction it could be part of "Der Mensch ist das" meaning 'that is the person' but standard German would be "Das ist der Mensch" or "Der ist das?". For beginner learners, use complete, common alternatives instead of this fragment.
target_language_example: Der Mensch ist das nicht alleine — er braucht Gemeinschaft.
native_language_example: Humans are not alone in that — they need community.

der Mensch ist das einzige Tier

target_language_multi_word_term: der Mensch ist das einzige Tier
meaning: humans are the only animals (that ...); used to state a unique human ability or trait.
additional_notes: Usually followed by a relative clause introduced by 'das' + verb (e.g. 'das sprechen kann') naming the ability or trait that distinguishes humans from other animals. Can be used in general statements about human uniqueness. Formality: neutral/standard.
target_language_example: Der Mensch ist das einzige Tier, das denken kann.
native_language_example: Humans are the only animals that can think.

meaning: the crowd / in the crowd (when used with 'in').
additional_notes: Literally 'the people-crowd'. Often used with verbs like verschwinden (disappear) or jemanden aus den Augen verlieren (lose sight of someone). In German the article and case change with prepositions: 'in der Menschenmenge' (dative), 'in die Menschenmenge' (accusative, movement into). Used for a large group of people in a public place.
target_language_example: Der Dieb verschwand in der Menschenmenge.
native_language_example: The thief disappeared into the crowd.

meaning: of the middle of / in the middle of (followed by a noun in genitive)
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a genitive construction: 'der Mitte der' = 'the middle of the ...'. It commonly appears in expressions like 'in der Mitte der Stadt' (in the middle of the city) but note that standard German usually uses the dative 'in der Mitte von' or simply 'mitten in' instead of the genitive. Use 'der Mitte der' when the following noun is in genitive or in fixed formal/written expressions.
target_language_example: In der Mitte der Stadt steht ein Brunnen.
native_language_example: In the middle of the city there is a fountain.

meaning: of the men
additional_notes: Genitive plural of "die Männer." It is used to show possession or connection (for example, "die Stimmung der Männer" = "the men's mood") and also after quantity/group words like "die meisten," "einige," "einer," "die Anzahl," or "die Mehrheit" to mean "of the men."
target_language_example: Die Namen der Männer stehen auf der Liste.
native_language_example: The names of the men are on the list.

meaning: the news; the message (dative or genitive form of 'die Nachricht').
additional_notes: ‘die Nachricht’ means 'news' or 'message'. 'der Nachricht' appears in different grammatical roles: as dative (e.g. 'bei der Nachricht' = 'at/on hearing the news') or genitive (less common) depending on the sentence. Common verbs/phrases: 'begeistert sein von der Nachricht' (to be excited about the news), 'bestürzt sein von der Nachricht' (to be shocked by the news), 'den Erhalt der Nachricht bestätigen' (to confirm receipt of the message). Use articles and case correctly: nominative is 'die Nachricht', accusative 'die Nachricht', dative 'der Nachricht'.
target_language_example: Ich bin von der Nachricht überrascht.
native_language_example: I am surprised by the news.

meaning: of the victims / belonging to the victims (genitive plural of 'die Opfer')
additional_notes: This is the genitive plural form of 'die Opfer' (the victims). It shows possession or relation (e.g. 'die Familien der Opfer' = the families of the victims). In other contexts 'der Opfer' can appear after certain prepositions or verbs that require the genitive. For beginners, you'll more often use 'von den Opfern' (using dative with 'von') in spoken German, but 'der Opfer' is common in written and formal German.
target_language_example: Die Fotos der Opfer wurden veröffentlicht.
native_language_example: The photos of the victims were published.

meaning: during the break / at break time
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase using the genitive article 'der' with 'Pause' (die Pause). Commonly used to say when something happens (Während der Pause, in der Pause, in der Pause störe ich...). Can appear after time expressions or with prepositions (während, in). For beginners: translate as 'during the break' or simply 'at break'.
target_language_example: Während der Pause esse ich ein Brötchen.
native_language_example: During the break I eat a sandwich.

meaning: the computer / the calculator (depends on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'computer' (PC) in everyday speech or 'calculator' for a device that calculates. Context tells which: talk about hardware, programs or being 'neu' usually means computer; 'rechnen' or small handheld suggests calculator. Masculine noun (der). Plural: die Rechner.
target_language_example: Der Rechner ist langsam, ich muss ihn neu starten.
native_language_example: The computer is slow, I have to restart it.

meaning: rice (the food).
additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning the grain/food 'rice'. Used like other German nouns with definite article 'der' in nominative singular. Common phrases: 'Reis ist fertig' (the rice is done/ready), 'Reis ist noch warm' (the rice is still warm). In cooking contexts you may see verbs like 'aufnehmen' (absorb) for liquid (e.g. 'der Reis nimmt die Flüssigkeit auf').
target_language_example: Der Reis ist fertig; wir können servieren.
native_language_example: The rice is ready; we can serve.

meaning: on the back / on the reverse side
additional_notes: Used to indicate the back side of an object (paper, card, photo, package). In German the noun is 'die Rückseite' (feminine); 'der Rückseite' appears in dative after prepositions like 'auf' (auf der Rückseite = on the back). Common with verbs like 'stehen', 'geschrieben', 'sein' and actions like 'unterschreiben'.
target_language_example: Die Adresse steht auf der Rückseite.
native_language_example: The address is on the back.

meaning: the treasure; also a term of endearment like "darling" or "sweetheart".
additional_notes: Most commonly means a valuable hidden object (treasure). Also used affectionately for a person (like "darling"). Gendered article 'der' is masculine. Context tells which meaning: talk about hiding/finding → literal treasure; addressing someone → affectionate. Plural: die Schätze.
target_language_example: Der Schatz ist endlich gefunden worden.
native_language_example: The treasure has finally been found.

meaning: colloquial/vulgar word for 'shit' — used to refer to nonsense, rubbish, a problem, or to express anger/frustration
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Often used in compounds or phrases (e.g. 'So ein Scheiß!' = 'What a load of crap!'; 'der ganze Scheiß' = 'the whole mess'). Depending on context it can mean 'rubbish/nonsense', 'a difficult situation', or function as an expletive. Avoid in formal or polite settings.
target_language_example: Der Scheiß ist schon wieder passiert – mein Zug hat Verspätung.
native_language_example: That shit happened again — my train is delayed.

meaning: the tail; slang: the penis (vulgar)
additional_notes: Literally means 'the tail' (animals, objects). However, in colloquial/vulgar German it is commonly used to refer to the male genitals; avoid using that sense in polite conversation. Can also appear in compound words (e.g., Schwanzflosse = tailfin). Gender is masculine: der Schwanz.
target_language_example: Der Hund wedelt mit der Schwanz.
native_language_example: The dog is wagging its tail.

meaning: fun; enjoyment; something enjoyable (noun).
additional_notes: Common masculine noun used to talk about fun or enjoyment. Can refer to an activity that is fun (Der Spaß beginnt) or a general sense of fun (der ganze Spaß). Often used in idiomatic phrases: "Der Spaß ist vorbei" (the fun is over) or "Der Spaß kann losgehen" (the fun can start). Can be used sarcastically to mean trouble or a negative outcome when paired with phrases like "hat ein Ende."
target_language_example: Der Spaß beginnt jetzt!
native_language_example: The fun starts now!

meaning: the place/spot; also 'the job/position' depending on context.
additional_notes: Very common phrase: can mean a physical spot (location) or an employment position. Context and surrounding words (prepositions, case, verbs) determine meaning. Examples: spatial uses with prepositions (an der Stelle, zu der Stelle, von der Stelle), and occupational uses (wegen der Stelle, ich bin wegen der Stelle hier). Capitalization and articles vary with case (der is dative/genitive feminine or genitive/ dative masculine/neuter depending on construction).
target_language_example: Sobald er davon hörte, eilte er zu der Stelle.
native_language_example: As soon as he heard about it, he hurried to the spot.

meaning: 'of the stars' (genitive plural of 'die Sterne')
additional_notes: A genitive phrase used to indicate possession or relation to 'the stars'. Common in poetic or descriptive contexts (e.g., 'Zahl der Sterne' = 'number of the stars', 'Hände der Sterne' = 'hands of the stars'). The literal translation is usually 'of the stars' or 'the stars' (in English possession).
target_language_example: Die Geschichten der Sterne faszinieren Kinder und Erwachsene.
native_language_example: The stories of the stars fascinate children and adults.

meaning: 'the voice' in the dative or genitive form; often appears in set phrases meaning 'to/for the voice' or 'of the voice' depending on context.
additional_notes: der Stimme is the definite-article + noun 'Stimme' in either the dative singular (die Stimme → der Stimme) or the genitive singular (showing possession). Common uses in examples: 'der Stimme deines Herzens' = 'the voice of your heart' (genitive after Folge), 'an der Stimme erkannt' uses dative with preposition 'an' (recognized by the voice), and 'sich enthalten der Stimme' is a formal/legal expression meaning 'to abstain from voting' (genitive with enthalten). Pay attention to the surrounding verbs/prepositions to tell whether it's dative or genitive.
target_language_example: Ich folge der Stimme meines Gewissens.
native_language_example: I follow the voice of my conscience.

meaning: was on the street / there was on the street (literally: 'the street was').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a fragment combining 'der Straße' (dative or genitive context) with the verb 'war' (past of 'sein'). In the examples it's used to say who or what was (or wasn't) on the street, or to describe conditions on the street (e.g., traffic). Word order in full sentences often is 'Auf der Straße war ...' = 'On the street there was ...' or 'Der Verkehr auf der Straße war ...' = 'The traffic on the street was ...'.
target_language_example: Auf der Straße war nur ein Hund.
native_language_example: There was only one dog on the street.

meaning: the students (genitive plural or part of a noun phrase: 'of the students' / 'the students' as plural after a quantifier).
additional_notes: Der Studenten is the genitive plural form of 'die Studenten' or appears after quantifiers/prepositions (e.g. 'die Hälfte der Studenten' = 'half of the students', 'einige der Studenten' = 'some of the students'). In many contexts it simply marks the group being referred to. Pronunciation and agreement: 'Studenten' is the plural; the article/form 'der' here is not the feminine singular article but the genitive/plural connector.
target_language_example: Die Noten der Studenten sind besser als letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: The students' grades are better than last year.

meaning: in/from the (hand)bag, pouch, or pocket (dative case of 'die Tasche').
additional_notes: ‘Tasche’ means bag, pocket, purse. 'der Tasche' is the dative singular form (used after prepositions like in, aus, aus der — e.g. 'in der Tasche' = in the bag; 'aus der Tasche' = out of the bag). Common with verbs like nehmen, holen, stehlen (pickpocketing). Context shows possession (meine Tasche) or someone else's.
target_language_example: Sie suchte ihr Handy in der Tasche.
native_language_example: She looked for her phone in her bag.

meaning: the cup (dative or genitive form of die Tasse).
additional_notes: This is the feminine noun 'die Tasse' in a case form. 'Der Tasse' can be dative (e.g. after prepositions like 'neben': 'links neben der Tasse') or genitive in contexts like 'der Rand der Tasse' (the rim of the cup). Note that 'der' here is the feminine article for these cases, not the masculine nominative article.
target_language_example: Das Buch ist links neben der Tasse.
native_language_example: The book is to the left of the cup.

meaning: of/in technology; the technology (genitive or following certain prepositions).
additional_notes: ‘Technik’ means technology, technique, or engineering. 'der Technik' is the feminine dative/genitive form (for feminine 'die Technik') used after prepositions (e.g. 'in der Technik' = in technology) or to show possession/relationship (genitive: 'das Zeitalter der Technik' = the age of technology). Context determines case and exact translation.
target_language_example: Wir sind von den Fortschritten der Technik beeindruckt.
native_language_example: We are impressed by the advances of technology.

meaning: the plate (dish).
additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning a plate used for food. Commonly used for ceramic, porcelain or plastic dishes. Definite article 'der' indicates nominative singular; other forms: den Teller (acc.), des Tellers (gen.), die Teller (pl.). Often appears in everyday contexts (washing, setting the table, dropping a plate).
target_language_example: Der Teller fiel krachend auf den Boden.
native_language_example: The plate crashed to the floor.

meaning: of/from/on the stairs (dative form of 'die Treppe').
additional_notes: ‘der Treppe’ is the dative singular form of 'die Treppe' and appears after dative prepositions or to indicate location (on/at the stairs) or movement from (e.g. 'von der Treppe' = from the stairs). Context determines whether it means 'on the stairs', 'at the stairs', or 'from the stairs'.
target_language_example: Wir warten auf der Treppe.
native_language_example: We are waiting on the stairs.

meaning: on the veranda / on the porch.
additional_notes: Der Veranda is the dative form of 'die Veranda' (feminine). It indicates location: sitting, standing, waiting, kissing, etc., 'on the veranda' (outside, attached to the house). Use im/auf depending on region; examples here use 'auf der Veranda' (common).
target_language_example: Wir sitzen heute Abend auf der Veranda und trinken Tee.
native_language_example: Tonight we're sitting on the veranda and drinking tea.

meaning: in/at the queue; in/at the line (of people waiting).
additional_notes: Warteschlange (feminine) means a line of people waiting. 'in der Warteschlange' is the dative phrase used to say someone is in/standing in the queue. Commonly used for waiting at shops, bus stops, customer service, etc. You can also say 'in der Schlange' (shorter).
target_language_example: Ich stand lange in der Warteschlange für Tickets.
native_language_example: I stood in the queue for a long time for tickets.

meaning: 'the wave' (dative or genitive/part of a phrase depending on context).
additional_notes: Welle means 'wave' (literal: water wave) but is often used figuratively for a movement, surge, or powerful group/force (e.g., a wave of people, a political/social movement, or an attacking force). 'der Welle' appears in contexts like dative (mit der Welle), genitive (wegen der Welle) or as part of a phrase (mit/gegen die Welle). Pay attention to the article and case to know the exact grammatical role. Not idiomatic by itself; meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Wegen der Welle müssen wir unsere Pläne ändern.
native_language_example: Because of the wave, we have to change our plans.

meaning: literally 'there is/are in the world' — used to state existence or presence of something in the world.
additional_notes: This phrase is part of the common German construction 'es gibt ... auf der Welt' (there is/are ... in the world). 'Der Welt' is the dative object of the preposition 'auf' ('on/in the world'). Use it to talk about how many or what kind of things or people exist worldwide. Word order can vary (e.g., 'Auf der Welt gibt es...' or 'Es gibt auf der Welt...').
target_language_example: Auf der Welt gibt es mehr als 7 Milliarden Menschen.
native_language_example: There are more than 7 billion people in the world.

meaning: the value; the worth; the price/importance of something.
additional_notes: Used for monetary value (price, amount) and abstract value (importance, worth, significance). Context determines translation: e.g. financial → 'value/price', personal/abstract → 'worth/importance'. Definite article 'der' indicates masculine noun; plural is 'die Werte'.
target_language_example: Der Wert dieser Münze ist hoch.
native_language_example: The value of this coin is high.

meaning: the (female) magazine/newspaper in dative or genitive form (singular).
additional_notes: Zeitschrift is a feminine noun meaning 'magazine' or 'journal'. 'der Zeitschrift' can be the dative singular (e.g. mit der Zeitschrift = with the magazine / finished with the magazine) or the genitive singular (e.g. der Zeitschrift = of the magazine). In the example sentences it is used mainly in the dative after prepositions like 'mit' and in time phrases like 'in der Zeitschrift' (in the magazine).
target_language_example: Hast du den Artikel in der Zeitschrift gelesen?
native_language_example: Did you read the article in the magazine?

meaning: the sugar (noun, masculine).
additional_notes: Refers to the substance sugar (granulated sugar). Uses the definite article 'der' in nominative singular. 'Zucker' is usually an uncountable noun in German when referring to the substance (no plural). The article 'der' shown here is nominative; cases change the article (e.g., den Zucker (accusative)).
target_language_example: Der Zucker ist im Beutel.
native_language_example: The sugar is in the bag.

meaning: 'the one who' (introduces a relative clause with a time/place/person; literal: 'the ... at/on/which')
additional_notes: Formed from the definite article 'der' plus the preposition+article 'am' (an + dem). Common in spoken/written German when referring to a specific person or thing described by what follows, e.g. 'der am ...' = 'the one who ...' or 'the one at/on ...'. Often appears in constructions like 'der am ... arbeitet' or 'der am Tisch sitzt'. The exact translation depends on context (who/which/that + relative clause).
target_language_example: Er ist der am meisten bekannte Sänger der Stadt.
native_language_example: He is the most well-known singer in the city.

meaning: of the other / the other's (feminine or plural genitive) or 'the other' (as a determiner for plural/feminine).
additional_notes: Context determines meaning: can be genitive ('of the other' / 'of the other ones') after a noun (e.g. 'Müttern der anderen Kinder' = 'mothers of the other children') or part of a noun phrase where 'andere' agrees in gender/case/number ('in der anderen Gruppe' = 'in the other group'). Word order and articles change with case. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich nehme das Buch der anderen Person.
native_language_example: I'll take the book of the other person.

meaning: 'the other side' or 'on the other side' (literally).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite side of something (physical side, another perspective, or another party). Context determines whether it means a concrete location (e.g. across the street) or an abstract idea (e.g. the other party in a discussion). Often appears in phrases like "auf der anderen Seite" (on the other hand / on the other side) when contrasting ideas.
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Seite des Flusses ist ein Park.
native_language_example: On the other side of the river is a park.

meaning: of the others
additional_notes: Used to refer to other people/things previously mentioned or understood from context. Often appears in fixed expressions like "eine nach der anderen" (one after another) or in comparisons "an das Niveau der anderen" (to the level of the others). The phrase is a genitive or dative/accusative plural depending on the construction; beginners can usually treat it as meaning "the others'."
target_language_example: Er passt sich an das Verhalten der anderen an.
native_language_example: He adapts to the behavior of the others.

meaning: the third (masculine or neuter noun); used to indicate order (3rd).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun or when referring to an ordinal position in general (e.g., month, floor, act, day). Agreement changes: die dritte (feminine), das dritte (neuter), die dritten (plural). Can also appear without a noun when context supplies it ("Der dritte?" = "The third one?").
target_language_example: Der dritte Stock ist oben.
native_language_example: The third floor is upstairs.

meaning: the first
additional_notes: Used to refer to the first person or thing in an order or sequence. In these examples it appears before masculine singular nouns in the nominative form. The form of erste changes with gender, case, and number: for example die erste, das erste, den ersten.
target_language_example: Der erste Bus kommt um sechs.
native_language_example: The first bus comes at six.

meaning: the following (masculine singular); used to introduce something that comes next.
additional_notes: Often appears before a noun or list item: 'der folgende Punkt' (the following point). Matches gender/number: feminine 'die folgende', neuter 'das folgende', plural 'die folgenden'. Common in written and spoken German to announce what comes next.
target_language_example: Der folgende Absatz erklärt die Regeln.
native_language_example: The following paragraph explains the rules.

meaning: the coming / the next (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase before a masculine noun to mean 'upcoming' or 'next' (e.g., der kommende Monat = the coming month). It agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun (kommen → kommende). Can also appear in other forms: die kommende (feminine), das kommende (neuter), die kommenden (plural).
target_language_example: Der kommende Montag ist ein Feiertag.
native_language_example: The coming Monday is a holiday.

meaning: the long (masculine nominative singular) — used before masculine nouns to mean 'the long ...'.
additional_notes: This is the definite article + adjective form for masculine nouns in the nominative case. The adjective 'lange' takes the weak ending '-e' after the definite article 'der'. Forms change with gender, case and number (die lange, das lange, den langen, etc.). Make sure adjective endings match the noun's gender and case. Example sentence 4 contains a grammar error: it should be 'In der langen Nacht...' because 'Nacht' is feminine and requires 'der' + 'langen'.
target_language_example: Der lange Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
native_language_example: The long river flows through the city.

meaning: the last
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun in the nominative, as in der letzte Zug. It usually means the final one in a series or the one furthest at the end. In some contexts, especially set expressions like der letzte Schrei, letzte can mean "latest" or "most fashionable." The form changes with gender, number, and case: die letzte, das letzte, den letzten, etc.
target_language_example: Der letzte Bus kommt um Mitternacht.
native_language_example: The last bus comes at midnight.

meaning: of/to the left (feminine dative or plural dative); 'on the left' in contexts like 'an der linken Seite' (at the left side).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of 'die linke' (feminine) or of a weak adjective following a definite article: used after prepositions that require the dative (e.g. an der, auf der, neben der) or with certain verbs. Common in phrases like 'an der linken Seite' (at the left side) or 'mit der linken Hand' (with the left hand). For beginners: focus on the meaning 'left' and the fixed phrases rather than the grammar endings at first.
target_language_example: Sie stand an der linken Seite des Autos.
native_language_example: She stood at the left side of the car.

meaning: the next
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to mean "the next" in time or sequence (e.g. next bus, next stop) or sometimes "the nearest" in space (depending on context). Adjusts for gender/number/case in German (nächste, nächster, nächstes). 'der nächste' specifically is masculine nominative singular form but beginners can learn it as the basic phrase used in questions like "Wann kommt der nächste Bus?"
target_language_example: Wissen Sie, wann der nächste Zug fährt?
native_language_example: Do you know when the next train leaves?

meaning: the damned / the bloody (insulting/emphatic: 'the damn...')
additional_notes: Used as an emphatic or insulting adjective before a noun. Adds anger, frustration, or strong emphasis (like 'damn' or 'bloody' in English). Can be rude—avoid in formal situations. Gender/declension follow the noun (here masculine nominative 'der verdammte'). Often used alone for emphasis: 'Der verdammte!'
target_language_example: Wo ist der verdammte Schlüssel?
native_language_example: Where is the damn key?

meaning: the past / the former (masculine singular)
additional_notes: Der vergangene is the masculine nominative singular form of 'vergangen' used as an adjective or nominalized adjective meaning 'past' or 'former' (e.g., the past day, the former president). You will often see it before a masculine noun (der vergangene Monat) or as a noun with a capital letter when nominalized (der Vergangene = 'the past one' or 'the person from the past'). Agreement changes with gender, case and number (die vergangene Woche, das vergangene Jahr, die vergangenen Jahre).
target_language_example: Der vergangene Monat war sehr kalt.
native_language_example: The past month was very cold.

meaning: 'the second' (masculine form) — used to indicate order: second one, second (item/person/thing).
additional_notes: This is the masculine nominative form. German ordinal adjectives agree in gender, case, and number: e.g. die zweite (feminine), das zweite (neuter), die zweiten (plural). Can be used for position (second place), sequence (second item), or to count occurrences (the second time/person). Often followed by a noun, but can stand alone when the noun is clear from context.
target_language_example: Der zweite Schüler hat die Aufgabe richtig gelöst.
native_language_example: The second student solved the exercise correctly.

meaning: of the apples (genitive plural of 'die Äpfel').
additional_notes: This is the genitive plural form used in phrases like 'die Hälfte der Äpfel' (the half of the apples). It literally means 'of the apples' and shows possession or part-whole relationships. Note German verb agreement with fractions/quantities can vary (singular or plural verbs are possible: 'Die Hälfte der Äpfel ist/war verfault' or 'sind/verfault' depending on emphasis and register). Use 'der Äpfel' after words that require a genitive plural (e.g., Hälfte, Ende, viele, einige in certain constructions).
target_language_example: Die Hälfte der Äpfel ist schlecht, wir müssen sie wegwerfen.
native_language_example: Half of the apples are bad, we have to throw them away.

meaning: to speak to the public / to address the public
additional_notes: This phrase is an infinitive construction with zu and is typically part of a larger verb phrase (e.g., 'versuchen, der Öffentlichkeit zu sprechen' is ungrammatical — correct: 'versuchen, vor der Öffentlichkeit zu sprechen'). More common variants include 'vor der Öffentlichkeit sprechen', 'in der Öffentlichkeit sprechen' or 'sich an die Öffentlichkeit wenden'. When used with 'zu' it usually appears after verbs that take an infinitive clause (e.g. 'beschließen, der Öffentlichkeit zu sprechen'), but note that 'vor der Öffentlichkeit zu sprechen' is the fully natural form.
target_language_example: Es ist wichtig, der Öffentlichkeit zu sprechen, wenn es um Transparenz geht.
native_language_example: It is important to speak to the public when it comes to transparency.

meaning: someone who knows/speaks French
additional_notes: This is a shortened spoken form often used after verbs like 'suchen' or in relative clauses: 'jemanden, der Französisch (spricht/kann)' = 'someone who speaks/can French'. Grammatically 'Französisch' is a noun (language) here; the article 'der' begins a relative clause ('der' = who). Use 'Französisch sprechen/können/lernen'.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen jemanden, der Französisch spricht.
native_language_example: We need someone who speaks French.

meaning: he needs / that one needs (colloquial reference to a person)
additional_notes: Der is a masculine pronoun used colloquially to refer to a male person (often with a slightly dismissive or familiar tone). 'braucht' is the 3rd-person singular of 'brauchen' (to need). Together they mean 'he needs' or 'that guy needs'. Context often implies what he needs (help, punishment, a lesson, etc.). Watch tone: using 'der' like this can sound informal or slightly rude.
target_language_example: Der braucht wirklich Hilfe, nicht nur Ratschläge.
native_language_example: That guy really needs help, not just advice.

meaning: 'the one who (of which)'; refers to a specific person (or thing) who is affected by, knows about, has read about, or is convinced by something mentioned before.
additional_notes: Combination of the relative pronoun 'der' (the one/who) and the adverbial pronoun 'davon' (of it/about that/from that). Used to point back to something already mentioned: e.g. 'der davon profitiert' = 'the one who benefits from that'. Agreement: 'der' changes with gender/case/number (die davon, das davon, die davon for plural).
target_language_example: Sie suchten jemanden, der davon Ahnung hat.
native_language_example: They're looking for someone who knows about that.

meaning: 'who/that (which) this' — part of a relative clause pointing to a masculine singular antecedent and introducing 'this' (neuter) as the object.
additional_notes: Combination of the relative pronoun der (masculine nominative singular) with the demonstrative dieses (neuter/genitive/accusative depending on context). Appears in relative clauses like 'der dieses Buch verfasst hat' = 'who wrote this book'. The gender and case refer to the nouns they replace: 'der' refers to a masculine noun (the subject of the relative clause). 'Dieses' refers to a neuter demonstrative (this + noun). Word order: relative pronoun + (optional) demonstrative + noun/verb. Common in formal and written German.
target_language_example: Die Frau, der dieses Geschenk gefällt, ist meine Nachbarin.
native_language_example: The woman who likes this gift is my neighbor.

meaning: "of the three" (used to specify one person/thing among three)
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a superlative or comparative to indicate 'the X of the three' (e.g. der Größte der drei = the tallest of the three). Grammatically, 'der' agrees with the gender and case of the noun being referred to; in examples it is a masculine nominative form referring back to a male person. For other genders/cases you would see forms like 'die drei' or 'das der drei' depending on context. Often used to compare members of a group of three.
target_language_example: Anna ist die Schnellste der drei.
native_language_example: Anna is the fastest of the three.

meaning: 'who' or 'that' (referring to a masculine singular person) + 'you' (plural, informal) — used as a relative clause subject/object: "who/that you (pl.)..."
additional_notes: This is the masculine singular relative pronoun der combined with the dative/accusative plural pronoun euch (you all). It appears in relative clauses referring to a person (der = 'who/that' for a man) and euch is the object (you plural). Word order: the relative clause follows the noun it describes. English equivalents depend on role in the clause: "who helped you," "that knows you," "who you found." Useful in spoken and written German. "der" changes with gender/case (die/ das/ dem/ den etc.).
target_language_example: Ich kenne einen Mann, der euch helfen kann.
native_language_example: I know a man who can help you (plural).

meaning: 'he/it goes' or 'that one goes' (present tense of 'gehen' with the demonstrative 'der')
additional_notes: A combination of the demonstrative/article 'der' plus the verb 'geht' (3rd person singular of gehen). Depending on context, 'der' can mean 'he', 'that one', or 'the one' (referring to a person or thing). Common in everyday speech: 'Der geht auf mich!' = 'That one is on me!' (meaning the cost is on me). Context determines whether it's physical movement ('he/it goes somewhere') or idiomatic uses (e.g., 'geht auf mich' = 'I'll pay').
target_language_example: Der geht heute Abend nicht mit uns.
native_language_example: He/That one is not going with us tonight.

meaning: 'who just' / 'who is currently' (masculine relative pronoun + adverb)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing someone (masculine singular) who has just done something or is doing something right now. 'Gerade' can mean 'just' (a moment ago / recently) or 'just now / currently' depending on context. The form changes with gender/case (die gerade, das gerade, den gerade etc.).
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, der gerade angekommen ist.
native_language_example: That's the man who just arrived.

meaning: the one who was here yesterday / who did something yesterday (relative clause reference).
additional_notes: Combination of the relative pronoun (der/die/das) with the time adverb 'gestern' is used to point to a specific person or thing mentioned or implied and to add the time 'yesterday'. It appears in relative clauses: 'der gestern...' = 'who/that yesterday...'. Gender/number of 'der' changes with the noun it refers to (der/die/das/die). Word order inside the relative clause follows normal German rules (verb often at the end for perfect/pluperfect).
target_language_example: Such den Mann, der gestern im Park war.
native_language_example: Look for the man who was in the park yesterday.

meaning: he/that one went / he/that one died (colloquial, depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'he/that one went' (Präteritum of gehen). In conversational German 'der' can refer to a person or thing previously mentioned. Meaning depends on context: often simply 'he/that one left/went', but in colloquial or violent contexts (e.g. 'ging drauf') it can mean 'he/it was killed / went down'. Word order is subject + past tense verb (ging).
target_language_example: Der ging gestern einfach ohne Abschied.
native_language_example: He just left yesterday without saying goodbye.

meaning: 'he/that one had' or 'that one + had' (past-tense of haben used with der)
additional_notes: Der is a demonstrative pronoun here (not the definite article). 'Der hatte' is used to refer to a previously mentioned or obvious male person/thing: 'he/that one had...'. In spoken German, especially in stories or informal speech, 'der' can mean 'that guy' or 'that one'. Context decides whether it means 'he' (a specific male) or 'that one' (thing/person).
target_language_example: Der hatte gestern lange gearbeitet.
native_language_example: He had worked a long time yesterday.

meaning: who (to her)
additional_notes: Relative clause construction: 'der' is a relative pronoun (masculine singular nominative or dative/acc. depending on antecedent and case) referring back to a masculine noun (e.g. 'Junge', 'der Hübsche'). 'ihr' is the dative or possessive pronoun meaning 'to her' or 'her' and indicates the person affected in the relative clause. Together they introduce a relative clause describing someone who does something to or for 'her' (e.g. 'who flirts with her', 'who helped her'). English often uses 'who (to her)' or simply 'who' with an indirect object ('who flirts with her').
target_language_example: Der Mann, der ihr das Buch gab, ist mein Bruder.
native_language_example: The man who gave her the book is my brother.

meaning: 'the' + 'in the' (combination of the definite article and the preposition with an article form); often the start of a relative or descriptive phrase: 'the ... in the ...' or 'who/which in the ...' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that frequently appear together: der (masculine or nominative/relative article) + im (contraction of in + dem = 'in the'). It depends on the sentence structure — 'der im' often begins a relative clause or noun phrase (e.g. der Mann, der im Park ist = the man who is in the park) or can be part of a longer noun phrase (das Haus der im Tal liegt is incorrect; correct: das Haus, das im Tal liegt). Watch word order and agreement: 'der' must match the noun it refers to (gender/case).
target_language_example: Der Mann, der im Park sitzt, liest ein Buch.
native_language_example: The man who is sitting in the park is reading a book.

meaning: a relative clause starter meaning 'who/that always' (refers to a person or thing that always does/has something).
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun 'der' (who/that) with the adverb 'immer' (always). Used to introduce a clause describing someone/something that always behaves or appears a certain way. Word order: 'der immer ...' + verb later in clause. Can refer to people or things; in spoken German you may also hear 'der ist immer so' or 'ist der immer so?'.
target_language_example: Der Mann, der immer lächelt, ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: The man who always smiles is very friendly.

meaning: A relative pronoun (der/die/das/den/etc.) + the preposition "in" used to introduce a relative clause that indicates someone or something is located in or active in a place (lives, works, studies, teaches, etc.).
additional_notes: "Der in" itself is not a fixed idiom but a segment appearing at the start of a relative clause. The relative pronoun must agree in gender, number and case with the antecedent (der/die/das/den/dem/deren etc.). "In" is the preposition meaning "in" (a city, country, building, institution). Common verbs that follow include leben, wohnen, arbeiten, studieren, lehren, besuchen. Word order in German places the verb at the end of the relative clause.
target_language_example: Mein Onkel, der in Paris lebt, hat uns besucht.
native_language_example: My uncle, who lives in Paris, visited us.

meaning: he comes / he is coming (or 'he'll come' depending on context).
additional_notes: Der is an informal pronoun used in spoken German to mean 'he' (referring to a person already known in context). In standard written German you'd expect 'er kommt'. 'Der kommt' often sounds colloquial and can imply a specific person (sometimes with a slightly dismissive or familiar tone). Tense/meaning depends on context: present ('he is coming' or 'he comes') or near future ('he will come'/'he'll come').
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, der kommt bestimmt gleich.
native_language_example: Don't worry, he'll come any minute.

meaning: 'the man' (singular masculine definite noun)
additional_notes: Basic noun: 'Mann' means an adult male person. Definite article 'der' is used for masculine nouns in the nominative singular. Pronunciation: /deːɐ̯ man/. Plural is 'die Männer' (the men). For 'a man' use 'ein Mann'. Use appropriate case endings and articles for other grammatical roles (e.g., accusative: 'den Mann', dative: 'dem Mann', genitive: 'des Mannes').
target_language_example: Der Mann liest eine Zeitung.
native_language_example: The man is reading a newspaper.

meaning: he/that one must / needs to (be) — expresses obligation or necessity about a person or thing mentioned
additional_notes: In spoken German, 'der' can point to a specific person or thing already mentioned and is followed by 'muss' to show necessity. Context decides whether 'der' means 'he' (a person) or 'that one/it' (a thing). Often used colloquially for emphasis: 'Der muss weg' = 'That one has to go'.
target_language_example: Der muss zum Arzt, er hat starke Schmerzen.
native_language_example: He has to go to the doctor; he has severe pain.

meaning: 'who/that never' (masculine relative pronoun + 'never')
additional_notes: Used when referring back to a masculine noun (der Mann, der Jirō, etc.). 'Der' is a relative pronoun here meaning 'who' or 'that'; 'nie' means 'never'. Combine to say someone who never does something. For feminine use 'die nie', for neuter 'das nie', and for plural 'die nie'.
target_language_example: Der Nachbar, der nie lacht, war heute fröhlich.
native_language_example: The neighbor who never laughs was cheerful today.

meaning: ‘the one who/that still…’ or ‘who/that yet…’ — used to refer to a person or thing that continues to have a property or to remain in a state.
additional_notes: ‘der’ is a relative or demonstrative pronoun (masculine singular) and ‘noch’ means ‘still/yet/else’. Together they often appear in relative clauses (der noch ... = the one who still...) or in spoken references when trying to recall a name (der noch gleich?). Usable with other genders/forms: die noch, das noch, die (plural) noch. In questions like „Wieso ist der noch hier?“ it means ‘why is he still here?’.
target_language_example: Ist das der Mann, der noch im Café sitzt?
native_language_example: Is that the man who is still sitting in the café?

meaning: literally 'who/that says' — a relative clause connector meaning 'who says' or 'who says that'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone says in a relative clause. 'der' is the masculine nominative relative pronoun (can change to die/das/den/etc. depending on gender/case). Common in spoken German to repeat the pronoun for emphasis (e.g. 'Wer ... der sagt es'). In commands or warnings it can appear after indefinite words (e.g. 'niemandem, der sagt...').
target_language_example: Ich kenne einen Lehrer, der sagt, Deutsch ist spannend.
native_language_example: I know a teacher who says German is exciting.

meaning: who/that his
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the relative pronoun 'der' (who/that) followed by the possessive pronoun 'sein' (his/its). It appears in relative clauses and links to a noun mentioned earlier. 'Der' agrees with the gender and number of the antecedent (masculine singular here); 'sein' agrees with the thing possessed, not with the relative pronoun. In English you usually translate the whole relative clause (e.g. 'who his...','that his...') as 'who/that [verb] his...'.
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, der sein Fahrrad repariert.
native_language_example: That's the man who is repairing his bicycle.

meaning: relative clause starter: 'who/that (has) his/its ...' — introduces a clause referring back to a masculine or neutral noun and possession ('his'/'its').
additional_notes: Combines the relative pronoun 'der' (who/that) with the possessive pronoun 'seinen' (his/its in accusative masculine or dative depending on verb). Forms will change with gender/case (die ihre, das sein, etc.). In the examples, 'der seinen ... gebracht hat' = 'who has brought his ...', 'der seinen Arsch an die Bullen verkauft' = 'who sold his ass to the cops', 'der seinen Spaß zu haben scheint' = 'who seems to be having his fun', and 'der seinen Kindern ... beibringen kann' = 'who can teach his children ...'. Useful for making relative clauses that mention possession.
target_language_example: Sie suchten einen Mann, der seinen Job kündigen würde.
native_language_example: They were looking for a man who would quit his job.

meaning: 'the one/from (who/which)'.
additional_notes: A combination of the relative/demonstrative article 'der' plus the preposition 'von'. Used to refer to a specific person or thing that is associated with or comes from someone/something (e.g., 'the one from Havana', 'the one from earlier', or as a relative clause 'the letter that was sent from...'). Context determines whether it's demonstrative ('the one from...') or part of a relative clause ('that/which/from'). Word order and punctuation in the sentence clarify the role.
target_language_example: Das ist der von gestern.
native_language_example: That's the one from yesterday.

meaning: 'who/that ... before/in front of' — combines the relative pronoun 'der' with the preposition 'vor' to introduce a relative clause describing position or time (in front of / before).
additional_notes: Used when a relative clause refers to something or someone located 'in front of' (physical position) or 'before' (time). The gender/case of 'der' must match the noun it replaces (masculine nominative singular here). Other forms: die/ das + vor (feminine/neuter or different cases) change accordingly (e.g. die vor, denen vor is uncommon — normally you use appropriate relative pronoun + 'vor'). Typical pattern: [main clause], der/die/das + vor + [phrase] + [verb].
target_language_example: Der Hund, der vor dem Haus liegt, schläft.
native_language_example: The dog that is lying in front of the house is sleeping.

meaning: ‘the (only) one who knows’ — used to indicate that a specific person (often the only one) has certain knowledge.
additional_notes: This is a relative-clause construction: determiner/noun (e.g. der Einzige / der einzige) + relative pronoun + verb. Masculine singular uses 'der' (die for feminine, die for plural with wissen). Common patterns: 'der Einzige, der weiß ...', 'der einzige, der ... weiß/kennt'. Emphasizes exclusivity of knowledge.
target_language_example: Bin ich der einzige, der weiß, wie das geht?
native_language_example: Am I the only one who knows how this works?

meaning: 'he wants to' or (colloquial) 'that guy wants to/keeps trying to...'
additional_notes: Informal spoken usage where 'der' refers to a man/guy (often with negative or critical tone). 'will' is 3rd-person singular of wollen. Common in sentences like 'Der will uns nicht in Ruhe lassen' = 'That guy keeps trying / won't leave us alone.' Not a polite or neutral way to refer to someone; can sound dismissive or accusatory.
target_language_example: Der will uns ausnutzen — pass auf!
native_language_example: That guy wants to take advantage of us — watch out!

meaning: 'he would' (colloquial spoken use of 'der' for 'er' + conditional 'würde')
additional_notes: In many dialects and casual spoken German, 'der' replaces the subject pronoun 'er' (he). Combined with 'würde' it expresses the conditional (would). So 'der würde' = 'he would'. Common in everyday speech; use 'er würde' in formal writing. Word order and follow-up clause behave like other conditional sentences.
target_language_example: Der würde dir sofort helfen, wenn du ihn fragst.
native_language_example: He would help you immediately if you asked him.

meaning: the one/that which goes to; 'that (which) to the' — used to introduce a relative clause where something is going to or directed toward a place or goal.
additional_notes: This is the combination of the relative pronoun der (masculine nominative singular or used as relative pronoun) plus the preposition zu in its contracted form zum (zu + dem). It appears at the start of a relative clause: 'der zum ... fährt' = 'that/which goes to the ...'. Word order follows German relative clauses: verb goes to the end. The gender/case of der must match the noun it refers to. You will also see 'die zum' (feminine/plural) or 'das zum' depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Das ist der Bus, der zum Bahnhof fährt.
native_language_example: That's the bus that goes to the train station.

meaning: in the same place / at the same spot
additional_notes: Used to say that something is located or happens in the identical position as something else or as before. Commonly appears with verbs of location or movement (stehen, parken, losfahren) and with time expressions (wieder). 'derselben' is the dative feminine/genitive form used with 'Stelle' here; you will also hear 'an der selben Stelle' or 'an derselben Stelle' (contracted).
target_language_example: Das Fahrrad steht immer an derselben Stelle.
native_language_example: The bike is always in the same place.

meaning: in the evening / during the evening (Genitive time expression).
additional_notes: Used to indicate time in the evening; often appears in phrases like 'im Laufe des Abends' (during the evening) or in routines ('des Abends' = 'in the evenings' / 'at evening time'). It's a genitive form of 'der Abend' used in set time expressions. Suitable for both single-evening references and habitual actions (context decides).
target_language_example: Des Abends lese ich oft ein Buch.
native_language_example: In the evenings I often read a book.

meaning: of the train station / (near) the station (genitive form referring to the station)
additional_notes: ‘des Bahnhofs’ is the genitive singular of 'der Bahnhof' (masculine). In common phrases like 'in der Nähe des Bahnhofs' it means 'near the station'. You will often see it in locations and descriptions of proximity. It can also be part of possessive expressions ('das Dach des Bahnhofs' = the station's roof).
target_language_example: Das Café liegt in der Nähe des Bahnhofs.
native_language_example: The café is located near the train station.

meaning: in the morning / in the mornings (habitual/time of day).
additional_notes: An older or slightly more formal genitive time expression meaning 'in the morning' or 'in the mornings' when talking about routine or time of day. Common alternatives are 'morgens' or 'am Morgen'. Used to describe habitual actions or when something regularly happens in the morning.
target_language_example: Ich trinke des Morgens zuerst Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink coffee first thing in the morning.

meaning: 'of the strong' — genitive form used to describe something caused by or belonging to a strong (something), e.g. 'because of the strong (rain/snow)'.
additional_notes: This is the masculine/neuter singular genitive of the adjective strong (stark) with the definite article (der/das → des). Commonly appears in weather-related phrases like 'des starken Regens' or 'des starken Schneefalls' to indicate cause or reason ('because of the heavy/strong rain'). In everyday speech, people often use 'wegen' + genitive (formal) or 'wegen' + dative (colloquial: 'wegen dem starken Regen').
target_language_example: Wegen des starken Winds blieben die Fähren im Hafen.
native_language_example: Because of the strong wind, the ferries stayed in the harbor.

meaning: quite often; frequently; from time to time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly but not always — more than occasionally. It is somewhat formal-neutral and common in spoken and written German. Can be placed after the verb or object (as in the examples). Similar to 'oft' or 'häufig', but slightly more emphatic than 'ab und zu'.
target_language_example: Ich gehe des Öfteren am Wochenende joggen.
native_language_example: I go jogging quite often on the weekends.

meaning: 'therefore I am' / 'that's why I am' (used to link a reason with 'I am/was ...')
additional_notes: Deshalb = therefore/that's why. 'deshalb bin' is not a fixed phrase by itself but part of a sentence where the speaker gives a reason and then states something about themselves using 'bin' (1st person singular of 'sein'). You will usually see it followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or a past participle (e.g. 'deshalb bin ich müde', 'deshalb bin ich Lehrer', 'deshalb bin ich gegangen'). Word order: 'deshalb' usually comes at the start or after the verb, then the verb 'bin' appears next to the subject 'ich' (often 'deshalb bin ich ...').
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern lange gearbeitet, deshalb bin ich müde.
native_language_example: I worked late yesterday, so that's why I am tired.

meaning: "therefore I am" or "that's why I'm" (gives a reason for a state or condition).
additional_notes: Deshalb means "therefore/that's why." When followed by the verb bin (first-person singular of sein), the phrase links a cause to a personal state or action. It's used in spoken and written German to explain why the speaker feels or is in a certain situation. You can replace bin with other verbs/persons (deshalb bin ich, deshalb bist du, deshalb sind wir, etc.).
target_language_example: Deshalb bin ich heute zu spät.
native_language_example: That's why I'm late today.

meaning: 'therefore is' / 'that's why (something) is' — links a reason to a result.
additional_notes: Deshalb = therefore/that's why; ist = is. Used to connect a cause (given earlier or implied) to a result or state. Common in spoken and written German. Word order: 'deshalb' usually comes at the start or after the verb; here it directly precedes the verb 'ist'.
target_language_example: Er hat viel geübt, deshalb ist das Konzert so gut.
native_language_example: He practiced a lot, therefore the concert is so good.

meaning: “his/its father” (genitive reference to the previously mentioned person or thing).
additional_notes: Dessen is the masculine/neuter singular genitive demonstrative pronoun meaning “of him/of it” or “whose” when referring back to a masculine or neuter noun. Use 'dessen Vater' to say 'the father of that person/thing' or 'his father' in formal/neutral contexts. For feminine antecedents use 'deren' (e.g. 'deren Mutter'). Common in written and spoken German to connect clauses.
target_language_example: Der Mann ist Lehrer, dessen Vater früher auch Lehrer war.
native_language_example: The man is a teacher, whose father used to be a teacher too.

meaning: the sooner/more ... the better; expresses that an increase (or earlier action) makes something better.
additional_notes: Used after a 'je' clause (Je ... desto/umso ...) to compare two linked ideas: the first part states a condition (Je früher/je mehr...), the second uses 'desto besser' to say the result is better. Common set phrase: 'Je ... desto/umso ...'. Can be used with time (earlier) or quantity/degree (more/faster).
target_language_example: Je früher du ankommst, desto besser.
native_language_example: The earlier you arrive, the better.

meaning: the more (the more ...); used in comparative correlative constructions (the more ... , the more ...).
additional_notes: Always appears in the paired structure 'Je ... , desto ...' (or 'Je ... desto ...') to express increasing degree or effect: 'Je + comparative/clause A, desto + comparative/clause B'. 'desto mehr' specifically means 'the more' in the second clause. Word order follows normal German clause rules (verb-second in main clauses).
target_language_example: Je länger du wartest, desto mehr wird es kompliziert.
native_language_example: The longer you wait, the more it becomes complicated.

meaning: 'that's why I am' / 'because of that, I am' (used to give a reason for being somewhere or in a state).
additional_notes: Deswegen = 'therefore' / 'because of that'. When followed by a form of 'sein' (bin = I am), it explains why the speaker is in a place or condition. Can be used in full sentences like 'Deswegen bin ich hier.' or negated: 'Deswegen bin ich nicht hier.' Word order: the reason (deswegen) often starts the sentence and is followed by the verb (bin) and the subject (ich).
target_language_example: Deswegen bin ich heute früh im Büro.
native_language_example: That's why I am at the office early today.

meaning: 'because of that' + auxiliary 'has' (used to form perfect tense) — roughly: 'that's why (someone) has/has done ...' or 'that's why (someone) ...' when followed by a past participle or reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Deswegen = 'for that reason' / 'because of that'. Hat is the 3rd-person singular present of haben, used as auxiliary in the Perfekt (present perfect). Together they often introduce a reason for a past action: 'Deswegen hat er X getan' = 'That's why he did X.' In spoken/written German you'll often see other auxiliaries (ist, haben) depending on the verb (e.g. 'deswegen ist er gegangen'). Word order: 'Deswegen' (front position) + verb (hat) + subject + past participle or reflexive form at the end.
target_language_example: Deswegen hat sie das Geschenk zurückgegeben.
native_language_example: That's why she returned the gift.

meaning: 'because of that' + 'is' — introduces a result or consequence ("that's why ... is/does").
additional_notes: Combines 'deswegen' (for that reason / therefore) with the verb 'ist' (is). Use to state a consequence or explain why something/someone is in a certain state or does something. Can be followed by nouns, adjectives, clauses. In spoken German you might also hear 'deshalb ist' or 'darum ist' with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Deswegen ist das Konzert abgesagt.
native_language_example: That's why the concert is canceled.

meaning: 'not because of that' or 'not for that reason' (used to negate a reason or request)
additional_notes: Combines 'deswegen' (for that reason/therefore) with 'nicht' to deny that something is caused by or justified by what was just mentioned. Common in short replies (e.g., 'Nein, deswegen nicht.') and in commands/advice (e.g., 'Sei deswegen nicht eifersüchtig.' = 'Don't be jealous because of that.'). Word order can change in longer sentences, but the phrase keeps the same meaning.
target_language_example: Du hast nur einmal mit ihr gesprochen — sei deswegen nicht eifersüchtig.
native_language_example: You only talked to her once — don't be jealous because of that.

meaning: ‘that’s why we/they are’ — explains the reason for someone’s presence or situation.
additional_notes: Deswegen = 'because of that' / 'therefore'. Combined with a conjugated verb (here 'sind' = 'are') it links a reason to who is present or affected. Common in spoken and written German. Can be used with different subjects: 'deswegen bin ich', 'deswegen sind wir', 'deswegen ist er'. Often followed by an exclamation, statement or question intonation depending on context.
target_language_example: Deswegen sind wir heute hier: um zu helfen.
native_language_example: That's why we're here today: to help.

meaning: 'you' (accusative) + 'that/it' — two common pronouns used together in sentences
additional_notes: This shows the accusative pronoun dich (you) and the demonstrative/neutral pronoun das (that/it). They often appear together in sentences where one refers to the person acted upon and the other to a thing or proposition. Use 'dich' when speaking to one person informally (du). Word order follows German syntax and can vary depending on emphasis; both pronouns are typically unstressed in normal speech.
target_language_example: Was veranlasst dich, das zu glauben?
native_language_example: What leads you to believe that?

meaning: 'you' (accusative) and 'me' (dative) used together in requests: 'I ask you to (do something) for me / toward me.'
additional_notes: This pattern appears in sentences with verbs like bitten (to ask/request) plus an infinitive or clause: 'Ich bitte dich, mir ...' = 'I ask you to ... me' or more naturally 'I'm asking you to ... for me' / 'please ... me'. 'dich' is the direct object (accusative) addressing the person you ask; 'mir' is the indirect object (dative) receiving the action or benefit. Common in polite requests and emotional appeals.
target_language_example: Ich bitte dich, mir heute Abend zuzuhören.
native_language_example: I'm asking you to listen to me tonight.

meaning: a phrase used to address 'you' (informal singular) followed by a conditional 'if I...'; often part of questions or statements meaning 'you, if I...' or more naturally 'you, if I [do something]?' / 'I'll [do something] and (call) you if I...'.
additional_notes: Dich is the informal singular 'you' (accusative). 'Wenn ich' means 'if/when I'. Together they appear in phrases either asking permission (Stört es dich, wenn ich...?) — 'Does it bother you if I...?' — or in promises/offers (Ich ruf dich, wenn ich... ) — 'I'll call you when I.../if I...'. Useful for polite requests, offers, or stating a conditional action. Pronunciation note: in spoken German the comma isn't spoken; word order may change in questions (e.g. 'Stört es dich, wenn ich rauche?').
target_language_example: Stört es dich, wenn ich das Fenster öffne?
native_language_example: Does it bother you if I open the window?

meaning: 'you' (accusative) + discourse particle 'also'—used to draw a conclusion, express surprise, or react to new information about 'you'. Comparable English renderings: "so you...", "ah, so you...", "then you...", "I see, you...".
additional_notes: 'Dich' is the accusative form of 'du' (you). 'Also' is a common German discourse particle signaling inference, surprise, confirmation, or realization. Word order places 'dich' (accusative object) before 'also' when the speaker wants to emphasize the reaction to the object. Tone and meaning depend on intonation and context (curious, surprised, confirming, reproachful, etc.). Examples include both neutral and emotive uses.
target_language_example: Dann hast du dich also doch noch entschlossen zu kommen.
native_language_example: So you decided after all to come.

meaning: 'call you' (on the phone).
additional_notes: A common German verb phrase using the separable verb anrufen (rufen = to call; an- prefix). In main clauses in present/future the verb can split: ich rufe dich an / ich werde dich anrufen. Use 'dich' for the informal singular 'you'. For formal use, say 'Sie anrufen'. Word order and punctuation affect splitting (e.g., subordinate clauses or infinitive constructions keep the full verb together).
target_language_example: Ich werde dich anrufen, sobald ich zuhause bin.
native_language_example: I will call you as soon as I'm home.

meaning: on/for you
additional_notes: This item is not a single fixed phrase but the pronoun 'dich' (you - accusative singular informal) plus the separable/prepositional particle 'auf' used with different verbs. Meaning depends on the verb and word order: - with 'freuen sich auf' = 'look forward to (something)' (e.g. 'freust du dich auf die Schule?') - with 'verlassen sich auf' = 'rely on (someone)' - with 'machen sich auf (etw.) gefasst' = 'prepare/get ready for (something)' - with 'setzen sich auf' = 'sit down on' (literal: place yourself onto) - with 'stellen sich auf (eine Seite)' = 'take (someone's) side' (figurative: position yourself on). Pay attention to separable verbs: 'auf' may move to the end of the clause in main clauses (ich mache mich auf = I get ready). 'dich' is accusative (used for 'du').
target_language_example: Freust du dich auf den Urlaub?
native_language_example: Are you looking forward to the vacation?

meaning: you (accusative) soon / see you soon (depending on context).
additional_notes: dich is the familiar singular accusative form of 'du' (you). bald means 'soon'. Together they appear in different structures: as part of verbs like 'sehen' (Ich sehe dich bald = I'll see you soon) or in reflexive verbs ('dich an etwas gewöhnen' = get used to something soon). Word order can change with auxiliary verbs: 'Du wirst dich bald ...' = 'You will soon ...'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, ich sehe dich bald wieder.
native_language_example: I hope I see you again soon.

meaning: you hurry / if you hurry (informal singular 'du')
additional_notes: Form is second-person singular reflexive of 'beeilen' (sich beeilen = to hurry). Commonly used in conditional sentences with 'wenn' to mean 'if you hurry' or as an instruction: 'Beeil dich!' (Hurry up!). Used in everyday speech. Pronunciation: [dɪç bəˈaɪ̯lst].
target_language_example: Wenn du dich beeilst, schaffst du es noch rechtzeitig.
native_language_example: If you hurry, you'll make it in time.

meaning: 'you' (accusative) + 'while/during' or 'with' (depends on verb + noun) — often part of verbs that require 'sich + bei + noun' or 'dich beim + Verb-ing' constructions
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common combination: 'dich' is the accusative reflexive/personal pronoun 'you' and 'beim' is a contraction of 'bei dem' meaning 'while/during' or 'at the (time of)'. Together they appear when the verb is reflexive or acts on 'dich' and is followed by an activity expressed by a noun derived from a verb (e.g. 'beim Fahren' = 'while driving') or a gerund-like noun. Meaning depends on the verb and noun that follow: 'dich beim Fahren' = 'you while driving', 'dich beim Lernen' = 'you while learning'. Another use: in idiomatic phrases like 'Ich nehme dich beim Wort' ('I take you at your word') where 'beim' = 'bei dem Wort' ('at the word').
target_language_example: Pass auf dich beim Fahrradfahren auf.
native_language_example: Watch out for yourself while cycling.

meaning: 'you' + 'definitely/probably' (object pronoun + adverb meaning 'surely' or 'probably')
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone (du), with dich as the accusative 'you' and bestimmt adding certainty or likelihood ('surely', 'probably', 'definitely'). Common in spoken German to soften statements or to express expectation. Word order: bestimmt usually comes after the pronoun or after the verb phrase (e.g. 'du erinnerst dich bestimmt noch').
target_language_example: Du kennst ihn dich bestimmt schon.
native_language_example: You probably already know him.

meaning: you (accusative) with that / about that (depending on context).
additional_notes: Combination of the accusative pronoun 'dich' (you) and the prepositional pronoun 'damit' (with that/about that). Used as the object in a sentence. English translation depends on the verb and context: 'are you okay with that?', 'leave you with that', 'tease you with that', 'finish you off with that', etc. Word order and meaning change with different verbs and tones.
target_language_example: Fühlst du dich damit wohl?
native_language_example: Do you feel comfortable with that?

meaning: you (accusative) from that/about it — used as a pronoun phrase in verbs expressing separation, prevention, persuasion, influence, etc.
additional_notes: A combination of the accusative pronoun 'dich' and the adverb/pronoun 'davon' ('of/from that' or 'about that'). Common in constructions like 'sich davon trennen' (to separate oneself from it), 'davon überzeugen' (to convince of it), 'davon abhalten'/'davon abbringen' (to prevent/stop from doing it), and 'sich davon fernhalten' (to keep oneself away from it). Word order can vary depending on sentence structure (e.g. 'Was hält dich davon ab?' or 'Halte dich davon fern!').
target_language_example: Was hat dich davon abgehalten, gestern zu kommen?
native_language_example: What prevented you from coming yesterday?

meaning: (part of constructions meaning) think of you / think about you
additional_notes: The phrase 'dich denken' by itself is not a standard standalone verb phrase in German. 'denken' typically combines with a preposition and the pronoun: 'an dich denken' = 'think of you' (have you in mind), 'über dich denken' = 'think about you' (have an opinion about you). In certain grammatical contexts (e.g., when the pronoun is moved for emphasis or in subordinate clauses) you may see 'dich denken' as part of a larger construction (e.g., 'was die anderen über dich denken'). For beginners: use 'an dich denken' for thinking of someone and 'über dich denken' for thinking about someone (opinions).
target_language_example: Du kümmerst dich zu viel darum, was die anderen über dich denken.
native_language_example: You worry too much about what others think of you.

meaning: This sequence is not a fixed phrase; it's the words 'dich' (you, accusative) + 'die ganze' (the whole/entire) and would appear inside a larger sentence (e.g. "dich die ganze Zeit" = "you the whole time").
additional_notes: Not a standalone multiword expression. 'dich' is the accusative singular informal 'you'. 'die ganze' is the feminine/functional form of 'the whole' and must agree with the noun that follows: die ganze Zeit (the whole time), die ganze Woche (the whole week). In natural German you will almost always see these together followed by a noun. Word order and case matter: 'dich' is used when that noun phrase is the object referring to 'you' (e.g. "Ich habe dich die ganze Zeit gesucht" — I looked for you the whole time).
target_language_example: Ich habe dich die ganze Zeit gesucht.
native_language_example: I looked for you the whole time.

meaning: 'you' (accusative) + 'there' — used to refer to someone being at or left at a specific place (informal singular you).
additional_notes: Combines the accusative pronoun 'dich' (informal singular 'you') with the adverb 'dort' ('there'). Common in phrases like 'dich dort treffen' (meet you there), 'dich dort lassen' (leave you there), or 'ich habe dich dort gelassen' (I left you there). Used in spoken and written German; 'dich' is informal — use 'Sie'/'Ihnen' for formal address.
target_language_example: Ich werde dich dort um 18 Uhr treffen.
native_language_example: I'll meet you there at 6 PM.

meaning: 'on it' / part of the phrase 'verlass dich drauf' meaning 'count on it' or 'you can rely on it'.
additional_notes: By itself 'dich drauf' is not a complete phrase; it appears in commands like 'leg dich drauf' (lie down on it) and idiomatic expressions like 'verlass dich drauf' (you can rely on it / count on that). 'Verlass dich drauf' is informal to neutral and used to promise certainty. 'Leg dich drauf' is literal: 'lay yourself on it' or 'put (something) on it' depending on context.
target_language_example: Verlass dich drauf, ich helfe dir morgen.
native_language_example: Count on it; I'll help you tomorrow.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase but the combination of the accusative pronoun 'dich' (you) with the separable particle 'ein' that appears with various verbs. The full meaning depends on the verb: e.g. 'lade dich ein' (invite you), 'krieg dich ein' (pull yourself together, colloquial), 'entscheide dich ein' is nonstandard — standard is 'entscheid dich (für)'. In sentences the separable prefix 'ein' often appears at the end in main clauses (Ich lade dich ein.).
additional_notes: 'dich ein' cannot be translated literally by itself; it must be read together with the verb. It's common in separable verbs (einladen, einschließen, einkriegen) and in some colloquial or nonstandard expressions. Word order: in main clauses the prefix 'ein' separates and goes to the end; in infinitive or subordinate clauses it stays attached (dich einzuladen).
target_language_example: Ich lade dich ein.
native_language_example: I'll invite you.

meaning: have/decide for yourself (part of the reflexive verb 'sich entscheiden' used in perfect tense or questions).
additional_notes: Core verb is entscheiden (to decide). In German the reflexive form is sich entscheiden (für + object) = to decide (for). 'dich entschieden' is the accusative reflexive form (du → dich) that appears in questions or perfect-tense constructions: e.g. 'Hast du dich entschieden?' Often followed by 'für' + noun or phrase, or by a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass' or an infinitive construction.
target_language_example: Also, hast du dich entschieden?
native_language_example: So, have you decided?

meaning: to learn/find out about you (someone); to get to know you more
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to learn information about another person. Often appears with verbs like erfahren (to learn/find out) plus an object (dich = you). Context can be neutral (get to know someone) or intrusive (wanting to know everything about someone). Common in phrases: „mehr über dich erfahren“ (learn more about you) or „alles über dich erfahren“ (find out everything about you).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mehr über dich erfahren.
native_language_example: I would like to learn more about you.
