target_language_example: Fahre nicht so schnell!
native_language_example: Don't drive so fast!

meaning: to run/operate at a regular interval (every ...); used with vehicles/time expressions — 'leave/come every ...'.
additional_notes: Common structure: [vehicle] + fahren + alle + [time period or plural noun]. With time: 'alle fünfzehn Minuten' = 'every fifteen minutes'. With plural nouns it can mean 'all of them' or 'everyone': context decides. Can be used with buses, trains, skis (in some dialects) — watch word order: time phrase usually follows (Die Busse fahren alle fünfzehn Minuten).
target_language_example: Die Straßenbahnen fahren alle zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: The trams run every ten minutes.

meaning: to be able to drive / to be able to go (by vehicle); 'can drive' or 'be able to go'.
additional_notes: A modal verb construction: können (to be able to/can) combined with fahren (to drive/to go by vehicle). Used to express ability, permission, or possibility to travel or drive. Tense and mood change with conjugation of können (e.g., werden fahren können = will be able to drive; hätte fahren können = would have been able to drive). Context determines whether it means 'drive' specifically or more generally 'go/leave by vehicle.'
target_language_example: Nächste Woche werde ich fahren können.
native_language_example: Next week I will be able to drive/go.

meaning: to let (someone) drive / to have (someone) drive (someone or something); to allow or arrange for someone to be driven
additional_notes: A causative/allowing phrase: lassen + infinitive. Here fahrenlassen means permitting or arranging for a person to drive (or to be driven by someone). Often used with a direct object for the person being driven (e.g. Tom fahren lassen = let Tom drive / have Tom drive) or with a reflexive and agent (sich fahren lassen) to mean 'have oneself driven' (e.g. by a chauffeur). Word order changes with tense and pronouns. Common in conversational German.
target_language_example: Ich lasse mich heute Abend vom Taxi fahren lassen.
native_language_example: I'm going to have a taxi drive me tonight.

meaning: 'to go/travel by (a vehicle or means)' or 'to go/drive with (someone)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used with a mode of transport (mit dem Bus, mit dem Rad, mit einem Boot) to indicate the means of travel. Can also be used with a person (mit Ihnen, mit ihm) meaning 'to go/drive with someone' or 'to go together with someone'. Word order: the conjugated verb fahren appears before mit + object in main clauses (Wir fahren mit dem Bus). Case: mit takes the dative (mit dem Bus, mit der Straßenbahn).
target_language_example: Manche fahren mit dem Rad in die Schule, andere nehmen den Bus.
native_language_example: Some (people) go to school by bike, others take the bus.

meaning: to drop (something); to let something fall.
additional_notes: A separable verb: in present tense the verb splits (ich lasse das Buch fallen → I drop the book). Commonly used for accidentally dropping objects or telling someone to drop/let go of something (e.g., a weapon). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., to abandon a topic), but primary meaning is physical dropping.
target_language_example: Tom hat sein Handy fallen lassen.
native_language_example: Tom dropped his phone.

meaning: if she / in case she
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conditional clause about a female person or 'she'. 'Falls' = 'in case' or 'if' (possible condition). The verb usually follows the subject (falls sie + verb...). Formality: neutral; can be used in spoken and written German. If referring to polite 'you' (Sie) capitalization changes meaning: 'falls Sie' = if you (formal).
target_language_example: Falls sie heute kommt, bringen wir Kuchen mit.
native_language_example: If she comes today, we'll bring cake.

meaning: is wrong / is incorrect.
additional_notes: A phrase combining the adjective 'falsch' (wrong, incorrect, false) with the verb 'ist' (is). Used to state that something is morally, factually, or logically incorrect. In sentences it usually follows a noun, clause, or demonstrative (das, dies) and can appear in reported clauses introduced by 'dass'.
target_language_example: Du weißt, dass das falsch ist.
native_language_example: You know that that is wrong.

meaning: wrong to (do something); incorrect to (do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say that an action or belief would be wrong or incorrect (Es ist falsch zu + Infinitiv). Common pattern: Es ist/Es wäre/Ich halte es für falsch zu + [Verb]. Note: 'falsch' alone also means 'wrong' or 'incorrect' and can be used predicatively (e.g. 'Das ist falsch.' or 'etwas scheint falsch zu sein').
target_language_example: Es ist falsch zu lügen, auch wenn es die Situation einfacher macht.
native_language_example: It is wrong to lie, even if it makes the situation easier.

meaning: to be wrong (to have an incorrect opinion, judgment, or assumption).
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, statement or assumption is not correct. Commonly appears with subjects like 'ich', 'du', 'er/sie/es', or nouns (e.g. 'Du liegst falsch' = 'You are wrong'). Can be used in various tenses: 'lag falsch' (was wrong), 'hat falsch gelegen' (has been wrong), though 'hat falsch gelegen' is less common in everyday speech than simple past or present. Tone can be neutral to mildly confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: Er könnte falsch liegen, aber ich würde das noch einmal prüfen.
native_language_example: He could be wrong, but I would check that again.

meaning: to spell/write incorrectly; to make a mistake when writing
additional_notes: Used when a word, name or text is written with mistakes (spelling, wrong letters) or more generally when something is written incorrectly. Can refer to handwriting or typing errors. Commonly used with objects (etwas falsch schreiben) or with a person's name (den Namen falsch schreiben) and in constructions like ‚jemanden falsch schreiben‘ or ‚etwas falsch schreiben‘.
target_language_example: Du wirst meinen Namen falsch schreiben, wenn du nicht auf die Buchstaben achtest.
native_language_example: You will write my name incorrectly if you don't pay attention to the letters.

meaning: to have boarded the wrong train
additional_notes: Used to say someone got on the wrong train (past tense idea). Literally: 'got into/boarded the wrong train'. Common in everyday situations about travel and commuting. Can be adapted for other vehicles (falschen Bus eingestiegen).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich verfahren und bin im falschen Zug eingestiegen.
native_language_example: I got lost and boarded the wrong train.

meaning: 'found the' (past tense of finden + feminine/plural/accusative article 'die')
additional_notes: Used to describe someone discovering or locating something in the past. 'Fand' is the simple past (preterite) of 'finden' (to find). 'Die' is the definite article for feminine singular or all plurals in the accusative case; context shows what 'die' refers to (e.g. die Ergebnisse, die Kamera, die Entwürfe). In spoken German, past perfect (hat gefunden) is also common: 'hat die gefunden.'
target_language_example: Sie fand die Schlüssel unter dem Sofa.
native_language_example: She found the keys under the sofa.

meaning: 'they begin/start' or imperative/formal 'catch!' depending on context
additional_notes: Two uses: (1) As part of the verb phrase "fangen an" + zu + Infinitiv = "to begin/start (to...)" — e.g. "Fangen sie an zu wachsen?" means "Do they start to grow?" Note capitalization: in sentences it's often "fangen sie" (they) but in questions/commands pronoun may be capitalized as "Sie" (formal you). (2) As the verb "fangen" (to catch) with pronoun "sie" = "they catch" or formal imperative "Fangen Sie!" = "Catch!/Start catching!" Context (word order, capitalisation, punctuation) tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Fangen sie jetzt an zu arbeiten?
native_language_example: Do they start working now?

meaning: 'don't touch me' (imperative, informal, direct)
additional_notes: A strong, direct command using the verb anfassen (to touch). Commonly used to push someone away or refuse physical contact. Informal and can be confrontational — often followed by insults in the example sentences. Use with people you don't know or in urgent situations; for polite refusal use "Bitte fass mich nicht an" or "Berühren Sie mich bitte nicht."
target_language_example: Fass mich nicht an! Das ist meine Tasche.
native_language_example: Don't touch me! That's my bag.

meaning: I can't believe it / I can't stand it (expression of strong surprise, disbelief, or disgust).
additional_notes: Common in the fixed phrase 'Ich fasse es nicht!' used to express disbelief, shock, or disgust about something. Often followed by an explanation introduced with 'dass...' or by interjections (e.g. 'einfach widerlich'). Not literal — 'fassen' normally means 'to grasp' or 'to touch', but here it means 'to comprehend/accept'.
target_language_example: Ich fasse es nicht, dass er ohne Entschuldigung gegangen ist!
native_language_example: I can't believe that he left without apologizing!

meaning: almost all (used before a plural noun or noun phrase)
additional_notes: Common phrase: 'in fast allen ...' = 'in almost all ...' or 'in nearly every ...'. 'fast' means 'almost' and 'allen' is the dative/plural form of 'alle' used after certain prepositions (here 'in'). Word order and case depend on the preposition and noun: e.g. 'in fast allen Bereichen' (in almost all areas).
target_language_example: In fast allen meinen Kursen habe ich gute Noten.
native_language_example: In almost all of my courses I have good grades.

meaning: almost everything; nearly all.
additional_notes: Used to say that nearly everything in a group applies. 'Fast' = almost; often placed before nouns or adjectives. Common in everyday speech. Can modify verbs like 'verstehen' (understand almost everything) or nouns like 'alles' (everything).
target_language_example: Ich habe fast alles verstanden!
native_language_example: I understood almost everything!

meaning: almost there; nearly arrived
additional_notes: Common short phrase used to say someone or something is very close to the destination or completion. Can be used as a full sentence (Fast da.) or within a sentence (Ich bin fast da.). Informal to neutral; often used in spoken language.
target_language_example: Ich bin in fünf Minuten fast da.
native_language_example: I'll be almost there in five minutes.

meaning: almost (the/that) — used to say something nearly happened or was nearly true
additional_notes: In these examples 'fast' means 'almost'. 'die' is the definite article used with feminine/plural nouns (e.g. die ganze Nacht, die Teller) or part of a noun phrase (die Rippen). Together they appear in common constructions: 'fast die ganze...' (almost the whole...), and 'fast die + verb in perfect/conditional' where an object (e.g. die Finger) follows. Use 'fast' before the noun or verb phrase to indicate something nearly occurred. Word order and article agree with the noun.
target_language_example: Ich habe fast die Prüfung bestanden.
native_language_example: I almost passed the exam.

meaning: almost a / nearly a
additional_notes: Used to say something came close to being or happening — often followed by a noun (ein + noun) or a time expression. Can describe events that nearly occurred (e.g., accidents, losses) or approximate quantities/durations. 'Fast' means 'almost' and does not change the article; word order may vary (e.g., 'Er hätte fast ein Auge verloren' or 'Fast ein halbes Jahr...').
target_language_example: Sie hatte fast ein Missverständnis verursacht.
native_language_example: She almost caused a misunderstanding.

meaning: almost (had) a/an — expresses that something nearly happened (often followed by a noun like 'Herzschlag', 'Fehler', 'Teller' or an event).
additional_notes: Used with verbs in perfect or conditional (e.g., 'habe fast', 'hätte fast') + a noun to say you nearly experienced or caused something. English equivalents: 'I almost had a heart attack', 'I almost dropped a plate', 'He almost caused an international incident.' Word order and gender/case of the noun still apply (einen for masculine accusative).
target_language_example: Ich hätte fast einen Unfall verursacht.
native_language_example: I almost caused an accident.

meaning: almost no / hardly any
additional_notes: Used before a noun (without article) to say that there is very little or almost none of something. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g., Wasser, Benzin, Französisch, Einkommen). The verb and context determine tense and number. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir haben fast kein Brot mehr.
native_language_example: We have almost no bread left.

meaning: 'almost nothing about' — indicates very little knowledge or information about someone/something.
additional_notes: Use with verbs of knowing/learning (wissen, kennen, erzählen, etc.). Word order: 'fast nichts' usually comes before 'über' + object. Can be followed by nouns, pronouns, or noun phrases (über das Problem, über Sie). Tone is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich weiß fast nichts über deine Pläne.
native_language_example: I know almost nothing about your plans.

meaning: almost never
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely. 'Fast' softens 'nie' (never), so it's less absolute than 'nie'. Can be placed before the verb or element it modifies (here before 'nie'). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich esse fast nie Süßigkeiten.
native_language_example: I almost never eat sweets.

meaning: 'almost (lost) — used with phrases about life/being killed' (as in 'almost lost one's life' / 'almost died')
additional_notes: Always appears with verbs about life or danger (ums Leben kommen/bringen). 'fast' = almost. 'ums' is a contraction of 'um das' in the fixed expression 'ums Leben' (literally 'around the life'). Use to say you nearly died or someone nearly caused your death.
target_language_example: Ich wäre gestern fast ums Leben gekommen.
native_language_example: I almost died yesterday.

meaning: almost (by/from) — used with passive or motion verbs to mean 'almost [was] ... by/ off'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with passive voice (von + vehicle/person) to say someone almost got hit ('fast von einem Auto überfahren worden') or with verbs of motion/position (von der Leiter fallen) to mean 'almost off'. 'Fast' = almost; 'von' indicates the agent (by) in passive or the source/location (off/from) in motion. Word order and verb form matter: often in constructions with wäre/wurde/sein + past participle (wäre fast von... überfahren worden / fiel fast von...).
target_language_example: Er wäre fast von dem Fahrradfahrer umgefahren worden.
native_language_example: He was almost run over by the cyclist.

meaning: almost hit by a car / nearly hit by a car
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where a person (or animal) narrowly avoided being struck by a car. 'Fast' means 'almost' and is placed before the verb or phrase it modifies; here the full phrase often appears as part of a sentence like 'Ich wurde fast von einem Auto überfahren.'
target_language_example: Ich wurde gestern fast von einem Auto überfahren.
native_language_example: I was almost hit by a car yesterday.

meaning: to feel out of place; inappropriate (not fitting in).
additional_notes: Used both to describe a person's feeling of not belonging (Ich fühle mich fehl am Platz) and to describe something that is inappropriate or ill-timed (Seine Kritik war fehl am Platz). Often follows verbs like fühlen, sein, or werden. Literal components: 'fehl' (missing/wrong), 'am Platz' (at the place).
target_language_example: Im Meeting fühlte ich mich fehl am Platz, weil alle schon Fachbegriffe kannten.
native_language_example: At the meeting I felt out of place because everyone already knew the technical terms.

meaning: ‘is missing a’ or ‘there is a missing (feminine/indefinite) thing’.
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (or when referring to an unspecified item) to say that something is missing or absent. Literally: fehlt = 'is missing', eine = 'a' (feminine/indefinite). Word order: subject or context + fehlt + eine + noun. Can also be used with other articles/genders by changing 'eine' (e.g. 'fehlt ein' for masculine/neuter).
target_language_example: Im Paket fehlt eine Gabel.
native_language_example: A fork is missing from the package.

meaning: is missing / there is a lack (of).
additional_notes: Used with dative pronouns/nouns to say someone lacks something. Common structure: [Person] + fehlt es + an + [noun]. The dative subject (dir, Ihnen, ihr) indicates who lacks it. Can also be used with 'doch' for emphasis (e.g. 'Dir fehlt es doch genauso!').
target_language_example: Dir fehlt es an Übung; du musst mehr trainieren.
native_language_example: You lack practice; you need to train more.

meaning: was finished / had finished
additional_notes: Past form of 'fertig sein' (to be finished). Used with a subject to say someone or something was done with an action. Often appears with 'mit' (mit ... fertig sein) to indicate completion of a task or followed by time clauses (z. B. bevor) to indicate timing.
target_language_example: Der Bus war bereits abgefahren, als meine Frau mit dem Anziehen fertig war.
native_language_example: The bus had already left when my wife had finished getting dressed.

meaning: "firmly" or "tightly" when followed by a verb or action (often part of a phrase like 'festhalten', 'festhalten und ...' or 'fest und + verb')
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something with strength, firmness, or intensity (e.g., holding, hugging, hitting). Often appears as the adverb 'fest' + coordinating conjunction 'und' before another verb or action in a sentence (e.g., 'fest und weinen' = holding tightly and crying). Common with physical actions (halten, umarmen, schlagen) and emotional expressions. Not a fixed idiom by itself—meaning comes from 'fest' (firm/tight) plus the following verb.
target_language_example: Sie hielt das Baby fest und sang ihm ein Lied.
native_language_example: She held the baby tightly and sang it a song.

meaning: firmly shut; tightly (closed) / firmly (hold) — describes closing or holding something tightly
additional_notes: Used with verbs like zu·machen (to close) or halten (to hold). 'fest zu' emphasizes that something is closed/held tightly or securely. Word order: 'fest zu' often appears before infinitive (e.g. 'fest zu machen') or after the verb in spoken commands ('Macht die Tür fest zu!'). Can also appear with pronouns/objects ('dich fest zu halten' = to hold you tight).
target_language_example: Mach die Tür bitte fest zu.
native_language_example: Please close the door tightly.

meaning: A very rude insult meaning 'fuck you.'
additional_notes: Strong vulgar language — extremely offensive. Used to express anger or dismiss someone. Do not use in polite conversation. Grammar: imperative form of 'ficken' (to fuck) with the accusative pronoun 'dich' (you). Variants include adding 'doch' for emphasis. Common in heated arguments or insults.
target_language_example: Nein, hör auf — fick dich!
native_language_example: No, stop it — fuck you!

meaning: 'fell onto' / 'fell on' (past tense of 'auffallen'/'auf etwas fallen' depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) of two related verbs: 'auf etwas fallen' (to fall onto/onto something — physical falling) and 'auf etwas/auf jemandem fallen' used in contexts like 'auf fünf Grad minus fallen' (to drop to — e.g., temperature). Use context to know whether it means 'fell onto' (physical) or 'fell to'/'dropped to' (numbers/levels).
target_language_example: Der Ball fiel auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: The ball fell onto the table.

meaning: past tense of verbs using 'fallen' or the impersonal 'fallen auf' — 'fell' (for falling) or 'fell on/was decided on' (in 'fiel ... auf').
additional_notes: This fragment combines the simple past form 'fiel' (from fallen: to fall) with the feminine/article 'die' starting a noun phrase (e.g., 'die Treppe' — the stairs). In examples it appears in two uses: (1) literal falling: 'Er fiel die Treppe hinunter.' = 'He fell down the stairs.' (German often omits a preposition between 'fiel' and a directional noun phrase like 'die Treppe hinunter'); (2) the impersonal phrase 'auf ... fallen' in past tense: 'Die Wahl fiel auf Tom.' → 'The choice fell on Tom' / 'Tom was chosen.' Note word order and case: with 'fiel die Treppe hinunter' the noun after 'die' is accusative (die Treppe → die Treppe as direction), while in 'fiel die Wahl auf Tom' 'die Wahl' is the subject.
target_language_example: Sie fiel die Treppe hinunter und verletzte sich am Bein.
native_language_example: She fell down the stairs and injured her leg.

meaning: 'I think' or 'I find' (polite/formal: addressing 'Sie') — used to give an opinion or suggestion to someone formally.
additional_notes: Common phrase structure: 'Ich finde, Sie ...' + clause. Used to state a personal opinion or recommendation politely (formal you = Sie). Followed by statements, advice (sollten ...), or judgments. Tone can be mild or critical depending on content. For informal situations with friends, use 'ich finde, du ...'.
target_language_example: Ich finde, Sie sollten sich heute ausruhen.
native_language_example: I think you should rest today.

meaning: I think that / I find that
additional_notes: A common spoken structure: 'Ich finde, (dass) ...' expresses a personal opinion. In casual writing/speech the conjunction 'dass' is often shortened to 'das' (though prescriptively 'dass' is correct). Use before a clause to state what you think. Can be followed by statements, judgments, suggestions.
target_language_example: Ich finde, das sollten wir morgen besprechen.
native_language_example: I think that we should discuss this tomorrow.

meaning: 'I think you...'; expresses the speaker's opinion/advice to 'you'.
additional_notes: This construction combines the verb 'finden' in the 1st person ('Ich finde') with a recommendation or opinion addressed to 'du' (using a modal verb like 'solltest' + infinitive). It's a common, polite way to give advice: 'Ich finde, du solltest ...' = 'I think you should ...'. Can be used with other modal verbs (könntest, musst, solltest) or directly with an imperative.
target_language_example: Ich finde, du solltest diesen Kurs nehmen.
native_language_example: I think you should take this course.

meaning: 'I think he...' or 'I find that he...'
additional_notes: Common spoken structure: 'Ich finde, ...' + clause gives your opinion. Followed by a full clause describing the person (er) or action. Equivalent to 'I think' or 'I feel' in everyday German; slightly subjective. Use with other pronouns: 'Ich finde, sie ...', 'Ich finde, das ...'.
target_language_example: Ich finde, er spricht sehr gut Deutsch.
native_language_example: I think he speaks German very well.

meaning: 'I think' or 'I find that' — a way to give your opinion.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal opinion or judgment. Commonly appears as 'Ich finde, ...' followed by a clause (often 'es' + verb). Neutral, everyday language. You can also say 'Ich finde, dass ...' (both are correct; 'dass' is optional).
target_language_example: Ich finde, es ist besser, vorher anzurufen.
native_language_example: I think it's better to call beforehand.

meaning: 'I think (that) she...' — gives your opinion about a female person.
additional_notes: This is the common German structure Ich finde, + clause. It introduces a personal judgment or impression. In English you can translate it as "I think/feel/believe (that) she..." The comma after finde is optional in German when followed by a clause (Ich finde, sie ...). Use with adjectives, comparisons, or descriptions (schönes Lächeln, ist besser, sieht großartig aus).
target_language_example: Ich finde, sie ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: I think she is very friendly.

meaning: 'I think (that) we...'.
additional_notes: This is the common spoken structure Ich finde, wir + verb..., used to give your opinion or suggestion about what 'we' should do. It is slightly conversational; you can also say Ich finde, dass wir... (more formal) or Ich denke, wir.... The comma after finde is natural in writing when introducing the clause.
target_language_example: Ich finde, wir sollten früher losfahren.
native_language_example: I think we should leave earlier.

meaning: imperative or statement with 'finden' + masculine/neuter accusative 'den' meaning 'find the' (you find the...).
additional_notes: ‘Finde’ is the 2nd person singular imperative of finden (or 1st/3rd person present: ich finde/er findet). Combined with the masculine/neuter definite article 'den' it means 'find the...'. Use it to tell someone to locate something (imperative) or as part of a sentence ('I find the...'). Word order: 'finde den' is followed by the noun: ‚Finde den Schalter.‘ Also appears in contexts like noticing or having an opinion: 'Ich finde den Schnee zu sauber' = 'I find the snow too clean' (I think it's too clean).
target_language_example: Finde den Schlüssel unter dem Sofa.
native_language_example: Find the key under the sofa.

meaning: 'find' or 'finds the' (imperative plural/formal or present tense + masculine/neuter accusative 'the')
additional_notes: This is the verb finden (to find) in the 2nd person plural imperative (Findet den! = You [plural] find the...) or 3rd person singular present (er/sie findet den = he/she finds the). In sentences shown it's usually an imperative command meaning 'Find the...'. 'Den' is the masculine/neuter accusative definite article (the) and changes with the noun that follows (den Feind, den Pokal, den Halbling). For English learners: translate as 'Find the ...'.
target_language_example: Findet den Schlüssel unter dem Tisch!
native_language_example: Find the key under the table!

meaning: 'he finds' or 'he thinks' (third-person singular present of finden)
additional_notes: Literal verb 'finden' means 'to find' (discover, locate) and also 'to find' in the sense of opinion — 'to find something [adjective]' = 'to consider/think something is...'. Word order here is subject after the verb (verb-second inversion) used in questions or for emphasis. In questions you may see inversion: "Findet er... ?" In statements normal order is "er findet..." but "findet er" appears after sentence elements or in replies/colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Findet er das Buch interessant?
native_language_example: Does he find the book interesting?

meaning: 'finds her/it' or 'does she find' depending on word order (present tense of finden + pronoun sie).
additional_notes: This is the 3rd person singular present form of finden (er/sie/es findet). 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'them'/'it' (feminine or formal/plural context) depending on context. Word order matters: 'Findet sie!' (imperative to a group: 'Find her/Find them') is different from 'Findet sie?' (question: 'Does she find...?'). In sentences like 'Man findet sie.' it means 'one finds it/her'. Use context to choose the correct English pronoun.
target_language_example: Er findet sie nicht mehr.
native_language_example: He doesn't find her anymore.

meaning: it all began / it all started
additional_notes: Past-tense phrase (simple past) using anfangen (to begin). Often appears as 'Es fing alles an...' to introduce when or where something started or how a story began. Can be followed by a time, place, event, or clause introduced by 'als' or 'mit'. Formal alternatives: 'Alles begann...' or perfect tense 'Es hat alles angefangen.'
target_language_example: Es fing alles an, als ich den Job bekam.
native_language_example: It all began when I got the job.

meaning: '(it) began' or '(it) started' (past tense of 'anfangen')
additional_notes: Literal structure: 'fing' is the simple past of 'anfangen' (to begin), and 'es' is the dummy subject 'it'. Common in narrative to say that something (weather, an event) started. Often appears with 'an' after the verb: 'fing es an' = 'it started'.
target_language_example: Gerade, als ich das Haus verließ, fing es an zu regnen.
native_language_example: Just as I left the house, it started to rain.

meaning: caught the (masculine or neuter singular direct object) — past tense of 'fangen' (to catch).
additional_notes: Used in simple past (Präteritum) to say someone caught something. 'Den' is the accusative masculine/neuter definite article for a specific noun (e.g., den Ball, den Dieb). In spoken German, the present perfect (hat ... gefangen) is often used instead, but the simple past is common in written or narrative contexts.
target_language_example: Er fing den Ball im Flug.
native_language_example: He caught the ball in midair.

meaning: caught a big (one) — past tense phrase meaning someone caught a large (fish or similar).
additional_notes: ‘fing’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of ‘fangen’ (to catch). ‘einen großen’ is the accusative masculine form used before a masculine noun like ‘Fisch’ (a big fish). The full sentence usually names the object (e.g. ‚fing einen großen Fisch‘). Use ‚fing‘ for past narration (written or formal spoken).
target_language_example: Sie fing einen großen Fisch am See.
native_language_example: She caught a big fish at the lake.

meaning: completely exhausted; wiped out (physically or mentally).
additional_notes: Common fixed expression used to say someone is very tired or drained after activity or stress. Can describe physical tiredness or emotional exhaustion. Not formal; often used in everyday speech. Literally 'fixed and ready' but meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Nach der Wanderung war ich total fix und fertig.
native_language_example: After the hike I was totally exhausted.

meaning: 'I beg you' (literally: 'I beg you').
additional_notes: Used to make a very strong, emotional request. Usually appears in the phrase 'ich flehe dich an' or 'ich flehe dich an, ...' and is more intense than 'bitte'. Often used in spoken or written appeals; can sound dramatic or urgent.
target_language_example: Ich flehe dich an, hilf mir bitte.
native_language_example: I beg you, please help me.

meaning: 'do you fly' / polite imperative 'fly' (formal you)
additional_notes: Uses the verb fliegen (to fly) with the formal pronoun Sie. In questions it asks when or whether the (formal) you will fly somewhere (e.g., 'When will you fly back?'). As an imperative, 'Fliegen Sie ...!' is a formal command or request (less common than the imperative forms of other verbs, but possible in formal contexts or announcements). The word order and punctuation determine whether it's a question or an imperative.
target_language_example: Wann fliegen Sie nach Berlin?
native_language_example: When will you fly to Berlin?

meaning: flying saucer (UFO)
additional_notes: Used to refer to an unidentified flying object (UFO) shaped like a disc; can be literal or humorous/pop-culture. Singular: die fliegende Untertasse. Plural: die fliegenden Untertassen.
target_language_example: Gestern sahen wir eine fliegende Untertasse am Himmel.
native_language_example: Yesterday we saw a flying saucer in the sky.

meaning: 'he flies' or 'he is kicked out' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'he flies' (from fliegen). Idiomatic uses: in contexts about being removed from a place/job/group, 'fliegt er (raus)' means 'he gets kicked out' or 'he's out' (often with raus). With planes or transport, it means he is flying/has a flight (e.g. 'fliegt er nach Miami' = 'he's flying to Miami'). Context determines whether it's literal (movement by air) or figurative (being expelled).
target_language_example: Wenn er so weitermacht, fliegt er bald raus.
native_language_example: If he continues like that, he'll be kicked out soon.

meaning: the following sentences
additional_notes: Used when referring to sentences that come next (e.g., in exercises or instructions). 'folgenden' is the accusative plural form of 'folgend' (following). Formal commands often use Sie/imperative or plural ihr/ihr-form; word order: verb + object (die folgenden Sätze) is common in instructions. If you need nominative, use 'folgende Sätze'.
target_language_example: Korrigieren Sie die folgenden Sätze.
native_language_example: Correct the following sentences.

meaning: 'I wonder how...' / 'I ask myself how...'
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or speculation about something. Usually appears as 'Ich frage mich, wie...' followed by a subordinate clause with verb-final word order. Can be followed by questions of time, quantity, manner, etc. Polite and neutral; common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, wie sie das Problem gelöst hat.
native_language_example: I wonder how she solved the problem.

meaning: to ask where (something/someone is or where someone lives/goes).
additional_notes: Use this phrase to politely inquire about location or destination. Common in questions introduced by 'Darf ich fragen,' (May I ask) for polite requests. Followed by a clause with 'wo' + verb (often position of person/thing or destination). Verb placement follows normal German word order for embedded questions: 'wo' comes first in the clause and the finite verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Darf ich fragen, wo du arbeitest?
native_language_example: May I ask where you work?

meaning: to be able to ask (someone); can ask
additional_notes: Combines the verb fragen (to ask) with the modal verb können (can/be able to). Used to say someone had the ability or opportunity to ask, often in conditional or past-periphrastic constructions (e.g. 'hättest fragen können' = 'you could have asked'). Word order and auxiliary forms change with tense/mood (e.g. 'Du hättest fragen können', 'Ich kann fragen').
target_language_example: Du hättest mich fragen können.
native_language_example: You could have asked me.

meaning: ask me
additional_notes: A common word order in German when the subject (people/they) and verb come before the object pronoun: e.g. 'Die Leute fragen mich' = 'People ask me'. Often followed by a question word or clause (warum, was, etc.) or 'danach' (about it). Use 'mich' for 'me' (accusative).
target_language_example: Warum fragen mich alle das?
native_language_example: Why is everyone asking me that?

meaning: I asked him whether/if...
additional_notes: This is a common reporting phrase used to introduce an indirect yes/no question. 'fragte' is the past tense (Präteritum) of 'fragen' and 'ob' means 'whether/if'. In German word order for indirect questions the verb usually goes to the end (e.g. 'ob er beschäftigt sei' or in spoken/simple past 'ob er beschäftigt war'). You can replace 'ihn' with other pronouns or names (e.g. 'fragte sie, ob...').
target_language_example: Ich fragte ihn, ob er morgen Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I asked him whether he has time tomorrow.

meaning: asked her (past tense).
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of fragen + the pronoun sie (her). Used to report questions someone asked a woman or 'they' (context). Often followed by a subordinate clause introduced by ob, wo, warum, was, etc. In spoken German, Perfekt (hat sie gefragt) is also common.
target_language_example: Gestern fragte sie ihn, ob er Zeit habe.
native_language_example: Yesterday she asked him if he had time.

meaning: to give (an animal) something to eat; to feed (an animal).
additional_notes: Used with animals: 'fressen' is the verb for animals eating (humans use 'essen'). Common construction: 'jemandem (dem Hund) zu fressen geben' or 'etwas zu fressen geben' = 'to feed (someone, usually an animal)'. Often appears in questions about whether an animal has been fed.
target_language_example: Hast du dem Hund zu fressen gegeben, bevor du zur Arbeit gegangen bist?
native_language_example: Did you give the dog something to eat before you went to work?

meaning: I'm looking forward to it
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of Ich freue mich. Commonly used in speech and informal writing. Followed by a verb with zu + infinitive or a phrase introduced by auf/über depending on context (e.g. Ich freu mich auf morgen = I'm looking forward to tomorrow; Ich freu mich, dich zu sehen = I'm happy to see you). Use with people you know; for formal situations use Ich freue mich.
target_language_example: Ich freu mich schon darauf, dich zu treffen.
native_language_example: I'm really looking forward to meeting you.

meaning: 'I was happy' / 'I was pleased' (past tense of freuen sich).
additional_notes: Part of the reflexive verb 'sich freuen' (to be happy/glad). 'Freute mich' is the simple past (Imperfekt) first/third person singular form used in narration or formal writing. Common constructions: 'sich über + Akk.' (happy about something), 'sich über + unexpected event', and 'sich für + person' (happy for someone). Also appears before an infinitive with 'zu' (e.g. 'freute mich, sie zu sehen'). In spoken everyday German, the present perfect ('habe mich gefreut') is often used instead.
target_language_example: Ich freute mich sehr über die gute Nachricht.
native_language_example: I was very happy about the good news.

meaning: happy/glad about that; pleased to hear or know that.
additional_notes: The phrase combines froh (glad) with das (that/it). It's used to express being glad about something just mentioned or heard. In English you'd say "I'm glad to hear that" or "he would be glad about that." Common with verbs like hören (to hear) or getan zu haben (to have done that). Word order in German: froh sein, das ... or froh, das ... zu + infinitive.
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, das zu hören.
native_language_example: I'm glad to hear that.

meaning: 'glad' or 'happy that' (used to say you are pleased about something).
additional_notes: Common expression followed by a subordinate clause introduced with 'daß' (traditional spelling; modern orthography uses 'dass'). The clause places the conjugated verb at the end. Use to express that someone is pleased or relieved about what follows. Can be used with formal 'Sie', informal 'du', or plural 'ihr'.
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, daß Sie angerufen haben.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you called.

meaning: Merry Christmas (a seasonal greeting).
additional_notes: Used to wish people a happy Christmas. Common in spoken and written German around Christmas time. Capitalization: Weihnachten is a noun and always capitalized; 'frohe' is usually lowercase unless at start of sentence. You can add a name or 'allen/an alle' to address everyone.
target_language_example: Frohe Weihnachten, Maria!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas, Maria!

meaning: Happy New Year (a wish for the new year).
additional_notes: Common greeting used around New Year's Day. Can be said aloud, in writing (cards, messages), or added after other wishes. Often used with 'Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen/euch allen ein ...' for 'I wish you...' Capitalization: as a fixed phrase nouns are capitalized in German ('Neues Jahr'), but in casual use you will often see 'Frohes neues Jahr!'.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir ein frohes neues Jahr!
native_language_example: I wish you a happy New Year!

meaning: Merry Christmas (a cheerful holiday greeting).
additional_notes: Used as a seasonal greeting around Christmas. 'Fröhliche' is the adjective 'merry' or 'joyful' and 'Weihnachten' is 'Christmas' (plural in German). Common in cards, spoken greetings, and messages. You can add a name after a comma (e.g., "Fröhliche Weihnachten, Anna!").
target_language_example: Fröhliche Weihnachten, Maria!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas, Maria!

meaning: got up early in order to / got up early to (do something).
additional_notes: Combines ‚früh aufstehen‘ (to get up early) with ‚um ... zu + infinitive‘ (in order to ...). Use when saying you woke up early for a specific purpose. Word order: ‚Ich stand früh auf, um + zu + Infinitiv.‘
target_language_example: Ich stand früh auf, um den Bus zu erwischen.
native_language_example: I got up early to catch the bus.

meaning: early here / early (in this place or at this time).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is earlier than expected at a place or time. 'früh' means early; 'hier' means here (this place or now). Common in questions or statements about arrival time: Warum bist du/ sind Sie so früh hier? — Why are you so early here? Can refer to early in the morning if context shows 'morgen früh' (tomorrow morning).
target_language_example: Warum bist du heute so früh hier?
native_language_example: Why are you so early here today?

meaning: early into / early to (used before a time noun or event, e.g. 'früh ins Bett' = early to bed).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase — it's 'früh' (early) followed by a prepositional contraction such as 'ins' (in + das) or part of a phrase like 'früh ins Bett gehen'. Commonly used to say you go to bed early or arrive early into something. Word order: 'früh ins [Noun]' or 'früh in die/den ...' depending on gender/case of the noun.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute früh ins Bett.
native_language_example: I'm going to bed early today.

meaning: early after / shortly after (a time or event)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens soon after a specified time or event. Often appears with a time expression (e.g., 'früh nach 6 Uhr' = shortly after 6 o'clock) or after a noun denoting an event. More common in spoken or informal contexts; you may also hear 'kurz nach' or simply 'nach' with a time. Word order: 'früh' precedes 'nach'.
target_language_example: Wir fahren früh nach dem Meeting los.
native_language_example: We leave shortly after the meeting.

meaning: earlier (in the morning); get up earlier.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of rising (aufgehen for sun, aufstehen for people) to indicate an earlier time in the morning. In sentences about the sun, früher auf (gehen) = 'rise earlier'. With people, used with aufstehen: früher aufstehen = 'wake/get up earlier'. Can be followed by time expressions or comparison words (als, als ich).
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen früher aufstehen.
native_language_example: I have to get up earlier tomorrow.

meaning: used to talk about past habitual actions (I used to ...).
additional_notes: Früher means 'earlier' or 'in the past'. In these examples it's followed by a conjugated form of 'sein' (bin) plus a past participle in conversational colloquial German (regional/informal). Standard German more commonly uses 'früher bin ich ...' with verbs of motion plus 'gegangen'/'geschwommen' or the simple imperfect: 'früher bin ich ... gegangen' or 'früher ging ich ...'. For beginners: translate as 'I used to.../In the past I...'.
target_language_example: Früher bin ich jeden Morgen mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule gefahren.
native_language_example: I used to ride my bike to school every morning.

meaning: used to indicate that something was once (in the past) a particular thing; 'used to be a/an ...'.
additional_notes: Früher means 'earlier' or 'formerly'. When followed by 'ein' + noun it expresses that in the past there existed or someone had that thing. Common with places, possessions, jobs, or habits. Word order: 'früher' usually comes before the verb or the noun phrase (e.g. 'Hier war früher ein ...' or 'Ich hatte früher ein ...').
target_language_example: Früher ein Kino, jetzt ein Supermarkt.
native_language_example: Used to be a cinema, now a supermarket.

meaning: used to say 'there used to be' or 'earlier there was/were' (talking about the past).
additional_notes: Früher = 'earlier' or 'in the past'. Gab is the past tense of geben (to give) but in the fixed expression 'es gab' it means 'there was/were'. 'Früher gab (es)...' is used to contrast past and present: 'There used to be...'. Often followed by 'es' (Früher gab es ...) or a direct noun phrase (Früher gab viele Läden).
target_language_example: Früher gab es hier einen Park, aber jetzt ist ein Haus gebaut worden.
native_language_example: There used to be a park here, but now a house has been built.

meaning: used to (think/feel/do) the same way in the past; 'earlier/the past just as (much)'.
additional_notes: Combines früher (earlier/in the past) + genauso (just the same/likewise). Use to say that in the past you had the same opinion, feeling or behavior as someone else. Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g. gedacht, gefühlt, gemacht). Can be placed before or after the verb depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Früher genauso dachte ich oft so wie du.
native_language_example: I used to think the same way.

meaning: used to talk about something you used to have or do (I/you/he/etc. used to have).
additional_notes: Früher means 'earlier' or 'in the past'. Combined with a form of haben (here habe = 'I have') it introduces statements about past habits or states: e.g. 'Früher habe ich...' = 'Earlier/in the past I used to...'. You will usually see different conjugations: ich habe → früher habe ich, wir hatten → früher hatten wir, etc. Often followed by the rest of the sentence describing the past situation.
target_language_example: Früher habe ich in einem kleinen Dorf gewohnt.
native_language_example: I used to live in a small village.

meaning: used with 'haben' to say 'in the past (we/they/you) used to have/did' — indicates habitual or past actions/conditions.
additional_notes: Früher = 'earlier' or 'formerly'. Combined with a conjugated form of haben + past participle it forms the spoken/perfect way to talk about past habits or states (e.g., "Früher haben wir ... getrunken/gelebt/gebracht"). In the example sentences 'haben' is the auxiliary for the perfect tense describing past habitual actions or situations. You can also say just 'früher' + simple past (e.g., "Früher lebten wir in Nagoya").
target_language_example: Früher haben wir jeden Sommer bei den Großeltern gewohnt.
native_language_example: We used to live with our grandparents every summer.

meaning: ‘used to’ (indicates something that happened or was true in the past).
additional_notes: Früher + verb (often with hat as auxiliary for perfect) expresses that an action or state was customary or true in earlier times but not necessarily now. It can be followed by a past participle (Perfekt) or by a verb in Präteritum in other constructions. Context may be personal (früher hat er…) or general (früher hat man… = people used to…).
target_language_example: Früher hat mein Vater jeden Sonntag gekocht.
native_language_example: My father used to cook every Sunday.

meaning: earlier here / used to be here before (at an earlier time).
additional_notes: Combines 'früher' (earlier, formerly) + 'hier' (here). Used to say someone lived or was at this place at an earlier time, or to indicate an earlier arrival. Can appear in statements, questions, and conditional/subjunctive contexts (e.g., expressing regret or counterfactuals).
target_language_example: Meine Eltern haben früher hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: My parents used to live here.

meaning: sooner or later; at some point in the future.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is inevitable or will happen eventually. Can imply certainty (it will happen) or likelihood. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Irgendwann müssen wir das Problem lösen — früher oder später.
native_language_example: At some point we have to solve the problem — sooner or later.

meaning: earlier; formerly (with 'zu' often starting an infinitive phrase: 'earlier to/than' or 'used to').
additional_notes: Früher means 'earlier' or 'in the past'. Paired with zu + infinitive (früher zu + Inf.) it can express doing something earlier or being accustomed to do something in the past (depending on context). Often you will see 'früher' alone (früher habe ich...) or 'früher zu' within phrases like 'früher zu Hause' (earlier at home) or before verbs: 'früher zu arbeiten' (to work earlier). Context determines exact translation.
target_language_example: Früher zu arbeiten war für mich normal.
native_language_example: Working earlier used to be normal for me.

meaning: drove to / went (by car) to the (masculine or neuter) place.
additional_notes: Simple past of fahren + zu + definite article (zum = zu + dem). Used to say someone went somewhere by vehicle (often car). The destination is usually a masculine or neuter noun with the dative article 'dem' (e.g., Flughafen → zum Flughafen). For feminine nouns you'd hear 'zur' (zu + der).
target_language_example: Er fuhr zum Supermarkt, um Brot zu kaufen.
native_language_example: He drove to the supermarket to buy bread.

meaning: 'does it work' / 'it works' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used both as a question (Funktioniert es?) to ask if something operates or succeeds, and as a statement when inverted in full sentences (Es funktioniert ...) or with context (Hier funktioniert es — it works here). Often appears with question words: Wie funktioniert es? (How does it work?), Warum funktioniert es? (Why does it work?).
target_language_example: Funktioniert es, wenn ich das Kabel anschließe?
native_language_example: Does it work if I plug in the cable?

meaning: drives (a/one) — third person singular of 'einfahren' or 'fahren' with article; here: 'drives a/one (vehicle)'.
additional_notes: In the example sentences 'fährt ein' is the present tense, third person singular form of 'fahren' plus the indefinite article 'ein' before a noun (ein Auto, ein Taxi). It means 'he/she/it drives a…' or 'drives one…'. Note: 'einfahren' as a separable verb can also mean 'to drive in', 'to break in' (e.g. new engine), but that meaning is not shown in these examples. Use 'fährt' + article/noun to say someone is driving a specific vehicle.
target_language_example: Sie fährt ein rotes Fahrrad.
native_language_example: She drives a red bicycle.

meaning: usually goes/commutes by (vehicle) — he/she usually travels by...
additional_notes: Used with a person (er/sie) and a mode of transport in dative (mit dem Fahrrad, mit dem Bus). 'fährt' is from fahren (to drive/ride/go by vehicle). 'gewöhnlich' = usually. Replace 'dem' with the appropriate article when the vehicle noun is masculine or neuter; for feminine nouns use 'mit der' (e.g. mit der Straßenbahn).
target_language_example: Er fährt gewöhnlich mit dem Zug zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: He usually goes to work by train.

meaning: drives/operates every (one) or goes every (time) — depends on context; literal: 'drives every'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's the verb fährt (from fahren) plus the quantifier jeden (masculine accusative of 'every' or 'each'). The meaning depends on the noun or implied object that follows. Examples: 'fährt jeden Tag' = 'goes/drives every day'; 'fährt jeden zum Bahnhof' = 'drives everyone to the station'. Pay attention to case and gender of the noun after 'jeden' (jeden is masculine accusative). For feminine use 'jede', neuter 'jedes', plural 'jede'.
target_language_example: Er fährt jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: He rides his bike to work every day.

meaning: does not go / does not run / is not operating (he/it/vehicle/transport)
additional_notes: Literal verb 'fahren' = to drive/ride/go (by vehicle or transport) or to operate (a machine). 'fährt nicht' is the 3rd person singular present negative form (or 2nd person formal 'Sie fahren nicht' would differ). Commonly used for vehicles, lifts, trains, machines, or colloquially about a person (e.g. 'Er fährt nicht' = he won't drive or he's not functioning). Context determines whether it's about transport, a device, or a person.
target_language_example: Der Lift fährt nicht.
native_language_example: The lift isn't working / The elevator isn't operating.

meaning: '(it) goes to' or '(it) travels to' (used for vehicles going to a place).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb fahren (to drive/go by vehicle) in third person singular and the contraction zum = zu + dem (to the). Commonly used on signs, timetables and when asking which bus/train goes to a destination: 'Welcher Bus fährt zum Bahnhof?'
target_language_example: Der Bus fährt zum Museum.
native_language_example: The bus goes to the museum.

meaning: depends on context: 1) 'falls/comes under' (a category or responsibility); 2) part of the separable verb 'in Ohnmacht fallen' = 'to faint'.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase — 'fällt' is the present tense of 'fallen' (to fall) and 'in' can start a prepositional phrase or be part of a separable verb. In sentence 1 it means 'falls into' a category/responsibility (idiomatically 'comes under' or 'is within (someone's area)'). In sentences 2–3 it is the verb phrase 'in Ohnmacht fallen' (to faint). Word order changes with tense and sentence type because some verbs in German are separable.
target_language_example: Das Problem fällt in meinen Zuständigkeitsbereich.
native_language_example: The problem falls within my area of responsibility.

meaning: does not fall / does not apply / is not considered (depending on context)
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'falls not' (from fallen = to fall). In everyday use, 'fällt nicht' often appears as part of longer phrases: e.g. 'Das fällt nicht unter die Regel' (that does not fall under the rule = does not apply), 'Das fällt nicht in meinen Verantwortungsbereich' (that is not my responsibility). It can also be used literally about something not dropping: 'Der Apfel fällt nicht' (the apple does not fall). Pay attention to the rest of the sentence to get the correct sense.
target_language_example: Das fällt nicht unter die Garantie.
native_language_example: That does not fall under the warranty / That is not covered by the warranty.

meaning: 'make yourself at home' (literally: 'feel yourself as at [your]')
additional_notes: A common informal invitation to guests meaning 'feel comfortable, behave as if you were at home'. Usually completed as 'fühl dich wie zu Hause' (with 'Zuhause' or 'zu Hause'). Used in casual spoken German. Often followed by addressing the person by name or nickname.
target_language_example: Komm rein, setz dich und fühl dich wie zu Hause.
native_language_example: Come in, sit down, and make yourself at home.

meaning: I feel today… (used to say how you feel today).
additional_notes: A common first-person expression: 'Ich fühle mich heute ...' + adjective or adverbial phrase to describe your current physical or emotional state. Often followed by adjectives (schlecht, glücklich, motiviert) or comparative phrases (viel schlechter). In spoken German you may also hear 'Ich fühle mich heute so ...' for emphasis. Use 'fühle' because the subject is 'ich' and reflexive pronoun 'mich' is required.
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich heute etwas müde, aber besser als gestern.
native_language_example: I feel a bit tired today, but better than yesterday.

meaning: I feel (here)... — used to say how you feel in this place or situation.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by adjectives or prepositional phrases (e.g. in Sicherheit, unwohl). 'Hier' emphasizes the current location/situation. Full phrase usually appears as 'Ich fühle mich hier ...' but you can change the pronoun (e.g. 'du fühlst dich hier') or tense. Useful for expressing comfort, safety, or discomfort.
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich hier sehr wohl.
native_language_example: I feel very comfortable here.

meaning: feel (a certain way) in/about (a place, situation, or someone's presence).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb (sich fühlen) plus a prepositional phrase with 'in' to describe how someone feels within a particular setting, situation, clothing, or another person's presence. Common adjectives: wohl (comfortable), unwohl (uncomfortable), lächerlich (ridiculous), wohler (more comfortable). Word order: Ich fühle mich in + [Dative phrase] + [Adjective].
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich in seiner Nähe unsicher.
native_language_example: I feel insecure in his presence.

meaning: I don't feel (well / ...); I am not feeling
additional_notes: Common part of the reflexive verb 'sich fühlen' (to feel). 'Fühle mich nicht' needs an adjective or complement to be complete (e.g. 'gut' = well, 'schuldig' = guilty). Often used to say you're unwell or to deny a feeling. Word order changes with pronoun/person: Ich fühle mich nicht, Du fühlst dich nicht, Er fühlt sich nicht.
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich nicht gut, ich gehe jetzt ins Bett.
native_language_example: I don't feel well, I'm going to bed now.

meaning: 'one feels' or 'people feel' (impersonal/general way to ask or say how someone feels)
additional_notes: Used impersonally to talk about feelings or sensations in general (like English 'one feels' or 'you feel' in a general sense). Often appears in questions with 'Wie fühlt man sich ...?' = 'How does one feel ...?' or statements like 'Fühlt man sich ...' followed by a description. 'Sich' (reflexive) is usually present in full sentences (fühlt man sich), but examples sometimes omit it in reduced phrases.
target_language_example: Wie fühlt man sich nach einer langen Reise?
native_language_example: How does one feel after a long trip?

meaning: "feels good" (describing how something feels physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'an' at the end: 'fühlt sich gut an.' Can describe physical sensations (e.g., a chair, massage) or emotional states (e.g., a decision, moment). Uses reflexive pronoun 'sich' and conjugates with the subject: 'es fühlt sich gut an', 'das fühlt sich gut an'. Informal spoken forms may drop the subject: 'Fühlt sich gut an.'
target_language_example: Das neue Sofa fühlt sich gut an.
native_language_example: The new sofa feels good.

meaning: I felt
additional_notes: Past tense first-person singular of 'fühlen' used in narrative or statements about past feelings or states. Commonly appears with 'mich' (fühlte ich mich) for reflexive uses (e.g. felt safe, felt better). Word order can vary in questions or subordinate clauses (ich fühlte, fühlte ich...).
target_language_example: Nach dem Spaziergang fühlte ich mich entspannt.
native_language_example: After the walk I felt relaxed.

meaning: I felt very (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Past tense first-person reflexive phrase from fühlen: 'ich fühlte mich' = 'I felt'. 'Sehr' intensifies the adjective that follows (e.g. erleichtert, unwohl, selbstsicher). Used to describe a strong feeling or state in the past. Structure: ich fühlte mich sehr + adjective.
target_language_example: Ich fühlte mich sehr glücklich nach dem Gespräch.
native_language_example: I felt very happy after the conversation.

meaning: formal 'brings you' or 'brings you here' — used to ask why someone is at a place or where they are going
additional_notes: Polite/formal form (Sie). Common in questions like 'Was führt Sie hierher?' meaning 'What brings you here?' or 'Was führt Sie nach ...?' — 'Why are you going/coming to ...?' Not casual; with friends use 'führt dich' or simpler 'Was machst du hier?'. 'Führen' here means 'to lead/bring' in a figurative sense.
target_language_example: Was führt Sie nach Berlin?
native_language_example: What brings you to Berlin?

meaning: 'leads you' or 'brings you' (literally), often used in questions to ask why someone came or what brought them somewhere
additional_notes: From the verb führen (to lead) + du (you). Common in questions: "Was führt dich (hier/zu mir)?" = "What brings you (here/to me)?" Can be used about physical guidance (a road leads you somewhere) or about reason/motivation (what brought you here). Word order: führt is verb for er/sie/es; dich is the object (you).
target_language_example: Was führt dich heute in die Stadt?
native_language_example: What brings you to town today?

meaning: behaved (in a certain way); acted.
additional_notes: Past tense of 'sich führen' (reflexive): describes how someone behaved or acted, often followed by 'wie' + a noun or adjective (e.g. 'wie ein Kind' = 'like a child'). Common in spoken and written German to criticize or describe behavior. Use with different pronouns: 'ich führe mich', 'du führst dich', 'er/sie führt sich'.
target_language_example: Sie führte sich bei der Party wie eine Königin auf.
native_language_example: She behaved like a queen at the party.

meaning: used to give an approximate number: 'about five (or so)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'fünf oder sechs', 'fünf oder zehn' etc., to indicate an estimate or small range. Often followed by another number (the alternative) or a unit (Minuten, Jahre). Tone is informal to neutral — fine for spoken and written German. You can replace 'fünf' with other numbers to form similar approximations.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben fünf oder sechs Tage.
native_language_example: We'll stay for about five or six days.

meaning: for books; used to indicate money, time or interest spent on books.
additional_notes: Commonly follows verbs like ausgeben (to spend), haben (to have), or Leidenschaft haben (to have a passion). Can refer to spending money (Ich gebe Geld für Bücher aus), spending time, or expressing interest/passion (Leidenschaft für Bücher). Word order: für + accusative (Bücher).
target_language_example: Ich spare jeden Monat 20 Euro für Bücher.
native_language_example: I save 20 euros every month for books.

meaning: for movies / for films (used to indicate purpose, suitability, preference, or target audience related to films)
additional_notes: Commonly follows a noun, verb, or adjective to show that something is intended for, about, or suitable for films. Context decides exact translation: e.g. 'ein Platz für Filme' = a place for movies; 'ideal für Filme' = ideal for films; 'etwas für Filme sammeln' = collect something for films. 'Filme' is the plural of 'Film.'
target_language_example: Das Sofa ist bequem und perfekt für Filme.
native_language_example: The couch is comfortable and perfect for movies.

meaning: for women; intended for or relating to women
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate that something is aimed at, applies to, or affects women. Can be literal (describing goods, services, rules) or figurative (describing suitability, impact, or relationships). Often follows verbs or nouns (e.g., 'geeignet für Frauen', 'nur für Frauen', 'Gift für Frauen').
target_language_example: Dieses Angebot ist nur für Frauen.
native_language_example: This offer is only for women.

meaning: for people / intended for people
additional_notes: Used to say something is meant for, suitable for, or concerns people. Can be general ('for people' in general) or specific when followed by a relative clause or description (e.g. 'für Menschen, die...'). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Das Programm ist für Menschen mit wenig Zeit gedacht.
native_language_example: The program is intended for people with little time.

meaning: for men; intended for or affecting men
additional_notes: Literal preposition phrase: 'für' = for, 'Männer' = men (plural). Used to indicate target group, who is affected, or suitability ('for men' as opposed to women/children). Can appear in contexts like warnings (Es ist tödlich für Männer), descriptions (Nur für Männer), or comparisons (für Männer wie uns). Capitalize 'Männer' as a noun in German.
target_language_example: Dieses Fitnessprogramm ist nur für Männer.
native_language_example: This fitness program is only for men.

meaning: for politics / about politics (used with interessieren: 'interested in politics')
additional_notes: Usually appears after the verb interessieren (sich interessieren für = to be interested in). 'für Politik' by itself is the prepositional object meaning 'in/for politics'. Use with reflexive pronoun: Ich interessiere mich für Politik. Can be used in questions and negatives: 'Interessieren Sie sich für Politik?' 'Ich interessiere mich nicht für Politik.'
target_language_example: Wir sprechen oft über Bücher, aber nicht für Politik.
native_language_example: We often talk about books, but not about politics.

meaning: ‘for you is’ — used to state how something relates to or affects 'you' (formal 'Sie').
additional_notes: A neutral/formal phrase using the polite pronoun Sie. It often appears in sentences that describe what is good, bad, possible, or true for the person addressed (e.g., what is easy, advisable, or unpleasant for them). Word order can change in a sentence (e.g., 'Das ist für Sie nicht gut' or 'Für Sie ist das nicht gut'). Use 'du' instead of 'Sie' in informal situations.
target_language_example: Für Sie ist es besser, zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: It is better for you to stay at home.

meaning: used in questions to ask what kind of people/guys/things those are
additional_notes: Commonly appears in fixed question phrases like "Was sind das für Typen?"—asking for the kind, character, or identity of people seen or mentioned. Tone can be neutral or slightly colloquial; context determines whether it sounds suspicious, curious, or disapproving. "Typen" here means "guys/people" (not technical types).
target_language_example: Was sind das für Typen, die da stehen?
native_language_example: What kind of people are those standing there?

meaning: literally 'for better' — used in constructions meaning 'consider (something) better' or 'deem something preferable'.
additional_notes: Appears in phrases like 'sich für besser halten' (to consider oneself superior) and in 'etwas für besser halten' (to judge something preferable or advisable). Often used with verbs like halten (to hold/consider). In past tense use: 'hielt es für besser, ...' = 'deemed it better to...'. Not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Ich halte es für besser, heute zu schlafen und morgen weiterzuarbeiten.
native_language_example: I consider it better to sleep today and continue working tomorrow.

meaning: in case (that); if (something happens).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a possible situation or contingency. Common in both spoken and written German. Can be followed by a full clause (subjunctive or indicative). Often used to give advice, instructions, or precautions.
target_language_example: Für den Fall, dass es regnet, nimm einen Schirm mit.
native_language_example: In case it rains, take an umbrella with you.

meaning: a short chunk meaning 'for you' used before a location phrase with 'in' (e.g. 'for you in the post', 'for you in the prison'); not a fixed idiom—it's the preposition 'für' + pronoun 'dich' followed by a location introduced by 'in'.
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase; it's the combination of 'für dich' ('for you') followed by 'in' plus a noun phrase (often with an article: 'in die Reinigung', 'in den Knast', 'in der Post', 'in meinem Hotel'). Word order and case change depending on the noun and article. Use it when saying that something is being done or placed for someone at a particular location.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Paket für dich in die Post gelegt.
native_language_example: I put the package for you in the post (at the post office).

meaning: for the future; with regard to what will happen later
additional_notes: Used to talk about future plans, expectations, warnings, or preparations. Common in everyday speech. Can refer to personal plans (e.g. 'Pläne für die Zukunft') or general future consequences (e.g. 'ein schlechtes Vorzeichen für die Zukunft').
target_language_example: Ich spare jeden Monat etwas Geld für die Zukunft.
native_language_example: I save some money every month for the future.

meaning: for three (people, items, units, etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate quantity or capacity (e.g., a table for three, tickets for three). It needs a noun or context to show what 'three' refers to: for three people = für drei Personen. In spoken German the noun is sometimes omitted when context is clear.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen einen Tisch für drei.
native_language_example: We need a table for three.

meaning: for a car / for one car
additional_notes: Used to indicate purpose, price, size, comparison, or allocation relating to a car. Context determines whether it means 'for a car' (general) or 'for one car' (single vehicle). 'Für' requires the accusative case; 'ein Auto' is indefinite singular neuter. Can appear in phrases like 'Platz für ein Auto' (space for a car) or 'zu teuer für ein Auto' (too expensive for a car).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen Platz für ein Auto in der Garage.
native_language_example: We need space for a car in the garage.

meaning: for a nice/beautiful (one) — used before a feminine or neuter noun in nominative/accusative when describing something as 'nice' or 'beautiful'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence of words: 'für' (for) + indefinite article 'ein' + adjective 'schönes' (with appropriate adjective ending). The adjective ending -es suggests the following noun is neuter in accusative or nominative (e.g., 'für ein schönes Geschenk' — for a nice gift). If the noun is feminine, the article would be 'eine' ('für eine schöne...'). Pay attention to gender and case to choose the correct article and adjective ending.
target_language_example: Ich habe für ein schönes Geschenk gespart.
native_language_example: I saved up for a nice gift.

meaning: for five (used with time, quantity, people, price etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate duration (für fünf Tage = for five days), quantity (für fünf Personen = for five people), price or portion (ein/e ... für fünf), or short time (für fünf Minuten). Context tells what 'five' refers to (minutes, days, people, servings). Followed by a noun or implied noun. In everyday speech the unit is often explicit; if omitted, meaning must be inferred from context.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben für fünf Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: We're staying in Berlin for five days.

meaning: "forever" or "for always" (an unlimited time).
additional_notes: Used to say that something lasts without end or for a very long time. Common in both literal and emotional contexts (e.g., relationships, places, situations). Can appear in statements, wishes, and descriptions.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, wir bleiben für immer Freunde.
native_language_example: I hope we stay friends forever.

meaning: forever young; always young.
additional_notes: Used to express the desire or idea of remaining young forever. Common in spoken and written German; can be literal (age/appearance) or figurative (feeling youthful). Often follows verbs like bleiben (to stay) or wollen/möchten (to want).
target_language_example: Willst du für immer jung bleiben?
native_language_example: Do you want to stay young forever?

meaning: for oneself; by itself; on its own
additional_notes: Has two main uses: 1) reflexive/possessive: 'for oneself' meaning privately or alone (e.g. 'behält es für sich' = keeps it to himself); 2) impersonal/resultive: 'speaking for itself' or 'stands on its own' meaning something is obvious or self-evident. Context decides nuance. Common in expressions like 'für sich alleine' (alone) or 'für sich sprechen' (to speak for itself).
target_language_example: Die Entscheidung muss jeder für sich treffen.
native_language_example: Each person has to make the decision for themselves.

meaning: considered dead / thought to be dead
additional_notes: Used with a person or pronoun to say someone is believed or declared dead. Often appears with verbs like halten (to think/consider) or erklären (to declare). Structure: [person] + für tot + halten/erklären. Tense of the verb shows when the belief occurred.
target_language_example: Als der Unfall passierte, hielten sie ihn für tot.
native_language_example: When the accident happened, they thought he was dead.

meaning: for many; for a lot of (people or things).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something applies to a large number or to many people/things. Often followed by a noun (e.g. 'für viele Menschen') or used in general statements ('für viele ist das wichtig'). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Für viele ist das eine wichtige Entscheidung.
native_language_example: For many, that is an important decision.

meaning: for charitable (purposes) / for charity
additional_notes: Usually appears before words like 'Zwecke' (purposes) or 'Organisationen' (organizations). Common in phrases about donating money, goods, or time. 'Wohltätig' = charitable; 'für wohltätige Zwecke' = to benefit charity. Formal register is neutral and suitable in written and spoken language.
target_language_example: Sie sammelten Geld für wohltätige Zwecke.
native_language_example: They collected money for charitable causes.

meaning: I'm afraid (that)... / I fear (that)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news, worries or an apologetic statement. Word order in German commonly places the verb first in the clause after the comma: "Ich fürchte, ich ..." = "I'm afraid I ...". Formality: neutral. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich fürchte, ich kann heute nicht zum Treffen kommen.
native_language_example: I'm afraid I can't come to the meeting today.

meaning: gave everything / did everything / confessed everything (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) 'gab alles' as part of 'alles geben' meaning to do one's utmost or try very hard (e.g. 'Er gab alles, um den Preis zu gewinnen' = he did everything/he gave it his all to win). (2) 'gab alles zu' (with particle 'zu') means to confess or admit everything (e.g. 'Er gab alles zu' = he admitted/confessed everything). Pay attention to word order and particles: with 'zu' it's confessing; without 'zu' it's usually 'to give everything' or 'to do one's best.'
target_language_example: Sie gab alles beim Rennen und gewann den dritten Platz.
native_language_example: She gave it her all in the race and won third place.

meaning: gave/returned it (simple past of geben + neutral 'das' = 'it')
additional_notes: Gab is the simple past (Präteritum) form of geben (to give). 'Das' is a neutral demonstrative or object meaning 'it' or 'that'. Together 'gab das' often appears in sentences like 'er gab das Buch zurück' (he returned the book) or 'sie gab das Leben hin' (she gave up her life) depending on the verb phrase and context. In many cases a separable prefix (e.g. zurückgeben → gab ... zurück) appears: 'gab das ... zurück' = 'returned it'.
target_language_example: Er gab das Handy seiner Schwester zurück.
native_language_example: He returned the phone to his sister.

meaning: 'gave you' (simple past of geben + dative pronoun 'you').
additional_notes: Used to describe someone giving something to 'you' in the past. 'gab' is the Präteritum (simple past) of 'geben' (to give). Word order: subject + gab + dative object (dir) + direct object (optional). In spoken German, the Perfekt ('hat dir gegeben') is also common. Pronunciation tip: 'gab' rhymes with English 'job'.
target_language_example: Er gab dir gestern ein Buch.
native_language_example: He gave you a book yesterday.

meaning: admitted / confessed (they admitted that ...)
additional_notes: This is the past tense (Präteritum) of 'zugeben' used with 'dass' or with an infinitive construction. Use it to say someone admitted or confessed something. In spoken German, the Perfekt form 'haben zugegeben' is more common, but 'gaben zu' appears in written or narrative past. Followed by a clause introduced by 'dass' or by 'zu' + infinitive.
target_language_example: Sie gaben zu, dass sie gelogen hatten.
native_language_example: They admitted that they had lied.

meaning: all ears; fully listening or very attentive
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone is paying close attention or is eager to listen. Common in spoken German. Usually used predicatively (ich bin ganz Ohr) or addressed to someone (bin ganz Ohr!).
target_language_example: Erzähl mir davon, ich bin ganz Ohr.
native_language_example: Tell me about it, I'm all ears.

meaning: completely alone; all by oneself.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is entirely alone (no one else present or to help). 'ganz' intensifies 'allein'. Common in both physical and emotional contexts. Word order: often follows the verb (was ganz allein).
target_language_example: Nach dem Umzug stand er ganz allein in der neuen Wohnung.
native_language_example: After the move he stood completely alone in the new apartment.

meaning: completely alone; all alone.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is entirely by themselves (physically or emotionally). 'Ganz' strengthens 'alleine'. Can describe being alone in a place or lacking company/support. Tone is neutral; can be surprised (Bist du ganz alleine?) or descriptive (Er sitzt ganz alleine.).
target_language_example: Sie stand ganz alleine im Park.
native_language_example: She stood all alone in the park.

meaning: completely different; very different
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is (now) very different from before or from something else. Can describe appearance, character, situation, place, etc. Often follows the noun (Deine Frisur ist ganz anders) or begins a sentence about change (Heute ist alles ganz anders).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug ist unser Alltag ganz anders.
native_language_example: Since the move, our daily life is completely different.

meaning: completely; totally (with a sense of fully/entirely).
additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase. Meaning depends on context and the verb or phrase it modifies: e.g. 'ganz aus Japan' = 'all the way from Japan' (completely from there), 'ganz aus dem Netz zurückziehen' = 'withdraw completely from the internet', 'ganz aus dem Häuschen' = 'completely excited/over the moon'. Not idiomatic by itself—its sense comes from the combination with the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Sie wollte sich ganz aus dem Projekt zurückziehen.
native_language_example: She wanted to withdraw completely from the project.

meaning: completely with / entirely up to (someone); fully with (someone) — depends on context.
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) 'ganz bei dir/ihnen/uns' means 'I fully agree with you' or 'I'm completely with you' (support/attention). 2) In expressions like 'liegt ganz bei dir' or 'liegt ganz bei Ihnen' it means 'it's entirely up to you' (the decision/responsibility rests with that person). Also appears in idiomatic question 'Bist du noch ganz bei Trost?' meaning 'Are you still in your right mind?' Tone is neutral; polite when using 'Ihnen'.
target_language_example: Die Entscheidung liegt ganz bei dir — du kannst wählen.
native_language_example: The decision is entirely up to you — you can choose.

meaning: completely according to; just like (someone/something); entirely in the style of
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done exactly in the way of someone or something, or fully matches a description. Often followed by a person (e.g., ganz nach Papa) or a noun phrase (ganz nach Plan). Can be used to describe behavior, decisions, results, or style. Common patterns: 'ganz nach + person' (just like someone) and 'ganz nach + noun' (exactly according to).
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist ganz nach ihrem Geschmack.
native_language_example: The gift is exactly to her taste.

meaning: quite
