additional_notes: A colloquial intensifier used to strengthen an adjective or verb phrase. Can mean 'quite/pretty' (moderate to strong degree) or 'really' depending on context. Tone can range from neutral to emphatic; with past participles it can imply notable change or a strong state (e.g., 'ganz schön verändert', 'ganz schön besoffen').
target_language_example: Du bist ganz schön spät heute.
native_language_example: You're pretty late today.

meaning: completely / absolutely
additional_notes: Used to emphasize totality or completeness. Often placed before adjectives, participles, verbs or at sentence end for strong affirmation or negation (e.g. 'ganz und gar nichts' = 'absolutely nothing'). Slightly more emphatic and formal than just 'ganz' or 'sehr'.
target_language_example: Das Problem ist ganz und gar gelöst.
native_language_example: The problem is completely solved.

meaning: the whole office / the entire office
additional_notes: Used to refer to all people or the entire physical office. 'Ganze' agrees with noun gender/number: 'das ganze Büro' (neuter singular). In spoken German the article is often included: 'das ganze Büro' or 'im ganzen Büro' (throughout the office).
target_language_example: Das ganze Büro feiert heute.
native_language_example: The whole office is celebrating today.

meaning: the whole house / the entire house
additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire building or everyone inside it. In standard German the correct form is "das ganze Haus" (with the article). Adjective "ganz" is inflected: masculine/neuter nominative takes "ganzes" in some contexts (but commonly "das ganze Haus"). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., 'the whole place').
target_language_example: Das ganze Haus ist heute leer.
native_language_example: The whole house is empty today.

meaning: an entire hour; a whole hour.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize duration (that something lasted a full hour). Often appears with 'eine/der ganzen Stunde' or with 'lang' (eine ganze Stunde lang). Common in past and present contexts: e.g. waiting, standing, talking. 'Ganze' agrees in gender/case with 'Stunde' (feminine).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine ganze Stunde auf dich gewartet.
native_language_example: I waited for you for a whole hour.

meaning: the whole truth; the complete truth.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or state the full, complete truth (not just part of it). Common in legal, serious, or everyday contexts when emphasizing that nothing should be hidden. Often appears in phrases like "die ganze Wahrheit sagen" (to tell the whole truth).
target_language_example: Sag mir bitte die ganze Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Please tell me the whole truth.

meaning: the whole weekend; all weekend
additional_notes: Used to indicate the entire duration of the weekend (from Friday evening to Sunday night or however the speaker defines it). In standard German, you will often see the neuter article/determiner: das ganze Wochenende. Can be used with verbs like verbringen (to spend) or wollen (to want) + adjective/infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Ich habe das ganze Wochenende mit Freunden gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked with friends the whole weekend.

meaning: the whole summer / all summer
additional_notes: Used with a definite article or in phrases like 'den ganzen Sommer (über)' to say something lasts for the entire summer. 'Über' can be added ('den ganzen Sommer über') for emphasis but meaning stays the same. Declines with case (e.g. 'den ganzen Sommer' = accusative). Often used with time expressions or verbs of staying/working/being together.
target_language_example: Ich war den ganzen Sommer in London.
native_language_example: I was in London the whole summer.

meaning: 'all day' or 'throughout the day' (used with verbs and phrases to indicate something happens or is thought about for the whole day)
additional_notes: Often appears as part of a verb phrase: 'den ganzen Tag an jemanden/etwas denken' = to think about someone/something all day; 'den ganzen Tag an etwas leiden' = to suffer from something all day; 'den ganzen Tag an (dem) ... gefesselt sein' = to be stuck/occupied at something all day. In German the accusative 'den ganzen Tag' marks the time span. Word order may vary (e.g., 'Ich denke den ganzen Tag an dich' or 'Den ganzen Tag denke ich an dich').
target_language_example: Ich denke den ganzen Tag an meine Familie.
native_language_example: I think about my family all day.

meaning: all day (long) — used with verbs to say something happens or is done for the whole day
additional_notes: This is part of a phrase: ganzen Tag (or den ganzen Tag) + verb. In German you usually say "den ganzen Tag" (with the accusative article) or omit the article in casual speech: "ganzen Tag". Add the verb after or before depending on sentence structure: e.g. "Ich arbeite den ganzen Tag" or colloquially "Wir waren ganzen Tag unterwegs." It emphasizes duration (the entire day).
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Tag auf dich gewartet.
native_language_example: I waited for you all day.

meaning: all day (long) with / spending the whole day with (someone or doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or state lasted the whole day. Often appears as 'den ganzen Tag mit + noun/verb-ing' (with someone / doing something) or 'den ganzen Tag' + verb phrase. 'ganzen Tag' takes accusative 'den' when time duration is expressed. Can be followed by people (mit Maria) or activities (mit Fotografieren / mit uns).
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Tag mit ihr telefoniert.
native_language_example: I talked on the phone with her all day.

meaning: 'not ... at all' (complete negation before a noun or adjective).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a total negation. Appears before nouns with articles (gar kein Zimmer), before adjectives in some colloquial expressions (gar kein schönes Wetter) or in fixed phrases (rein gar kein). Stronger than just 'kein' or 'nicht'; often used in spoken German. Word order: 'gar' directly precedes 'kein'.
target_language_example: Wir haben heute gar kein Brot im Haus.
native_language_example: We have absolutely no bread in the house today.

meaning: not at all
additional_notes: used to strengthen "nicht". It often adds emphasis: Das kann ich gar nicht = "I really can't do that" / "I can't do that at all." On its own, "Gar nicht!" means "not at all!" or "absolutely not!" In phrases like "gar nicht mal schlecht," it means "not bad at all."
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das gar nicht.
native_language_example: I don't understand that at all.

meaning: absolutely nothing
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the negation — stronger than just "nichts". Common in speech. Can appear before or after the verb phrase (e.g. "Ich weiß gar nichts" or "Wir können gar nichts tun").
target_language_example: Er hat mir gar nichts gesagt.
native_language_example: He told me absolutely nothing.

meaning: 'not at all' / 'nothing of' / 'not aware of' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used to say someone gets no benefit, knows nothing about something, or is not involved. With possession/benefit it means 'to get nothing from (someone/something)'. With knowledge it means 'to know nothing about'. 'Gar' strengthens 'nichts' (completely nothing). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich wusste gar nichts von dem Treffen.
native_language_example: I knew nothing at all about the meeting.

meaning: paid attention to what time (something/someone did something).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions using 'darauf geachtet' (to have paid attention) followed by 'um wieviel Uhr' (at what time). Use when asking if someone noticed or watched the exact time an event happened (e.g., when someone left or departed). Common in spoken and written German; word order: 'Haben Sie/Hast du darauf geachtet, um wieviel Uhr ...?'
target_language_example: Haben Sie darauf geachtet, um wieviel Uhr der Bus gekommen ist?
native_language_example: Did you notice what time the bus arrived?

meaning: paid attention to where I put/left my keys
additional_notes: This phrase is built from "darauf geachtet, wo..." meaning 'paid attention to where...'. It's used when asking if someone noticed the location of your keys. Common verbs with this structure: "hingetan/hingelegt/gelassen" (put/left). Formality: neutral, everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hast du darauf geachtet, wo ich meine Schlüssel hingelegt habe?
native_language_example: Did you pay attention to where I put my keys?

meaning: 'worked and' (past participle 'gearbeitet' plus conjunction 'und') — used to join two actions or results in the past.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence: gearbeitet is the past participle of arbeiten (to work) used in perfect tense (hat gearbeitet), and und simply links a second clause or result. You will see it in sentences like 'hat gearbeitet und ...' to say someone worked and then did or experienced something else. Word order and auxiliary verb (hat) follow German perfect tense rules.
target_language_example: Sie hat den ganzen Tag gearbeitet und ist jetzt müde.
native_language_example: She worked all day and is tired now.

meaning: short for 'gebe dir' — 'I give you' / 'I'll give you'.
additional_notes: Informal, spoken contraction of 'gebe dir' (first person singular of geben + dative pronoun). Common in casual conversation. Use in contexts like giving something (number, item), offering something (a drink), or introducing someone. In written or formal German use 'gebe dir' or the full sentence 'Ich gebe dir ...'.
target_language_example: Ich geb dir meine Telefonnummer.
native_language_example: I'll give you my phone number.

meaning: I give it
additional_notes: Usually part of a sentence like ich gebe es dir/ihm/ihr, where es means 'it' and the other pronoun shows who receives it. With a word like weiter, it can mean 'pass it on' (ich gebe es weiter). In formal reported speech, gebe es can also appear in a different construction from es gibt, meaning 'there are' (for example: da gebe es Probleme).
target_language_example: Ich gebe es dir später.
native_language_example: I'll give it to you later.

meaning: give (to) you (plural informal) — first person singular present of 'geben' with dative 'euch'.
additional_notes: Used when the speaker is giving something to a group of people addressed informally (ihr). 'Gebe' is the verb form for 'ich' (I). 'Euch' is the dative pronoun for 'you' (plural). Context can be literal (handing something over) or figurative (promising, refusing, or offering). Word order in German often places the verb second; in short replies you may hear just 'Ich gebe euch ...' or shorter 'Gebe euch ...' in colloquial speech.
target_language_example: Ich gebe euch morgen die Bücher.
native_language_example: I'll give you (all) the books tomorrow.

meaning: 'there will be' (future tense of 'geben' — to exist/occur/happen).
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses with a future meaning: indicates that something will exist or happen. Common structure: dass ... es (etwas) geben wird / dass (jemand) (etwas) geben wird. Often appears after 'dass' (that). In English translations use 'there will be' or 'will give' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass es Probleme geben wird.
native_language_example: I don't believe there will be any problems.

meaning: asked (someone) to do that / requested that (someone) do it.
additional_notes: Past participle 'gebeten' of 'bitten' (to ask/request). In the examples it appears with a direct object or with a person + infinitive clause introduced by a comma (e.g. 'jemand gebeten, das zu tun' = asked someone to do that). Common structure: '[Person] hat [jemanden] gebeten, [etwas] zu tun.'
target_language_example: Sie hat ihn gebeten, das Fenster zu schließen.
native_language_example: She asked him to close the window.

meaning: 'to have asked/ requested' — the perfect infinitive form of bitten used in perfect constructions (e.g. wir haben sie gebeten = we asked/requested her).
additional_notes: Appears in perfect tense constructions and in subordinate clauses (especially relative clauses with worum/wobei/worin). Common in both formal and informal registers. Literal components are transparent (bitten = to ask/request; haben = auxiliary 'have'). Often used with a direct object and an infinitive clause or with worum + clause (worum wir sie gebeten haben = what we asked her to do).
target_language_example: Maria hat alles getan, worum wir sie gebeten haben.
native_language_example: Maria did everything we had asked/requested her to do.

meaning: to be born
additional_notes: Passive expression used to talk about someone's birth (the person is the subject). Often used with a date, place, or in passive constructions: Er wurde 1990 geboren. Alternative forms: geboren sein (to be born [in a place/date]). In conversational German the perfect is common: Ich bin 1995 in München geboren (using sein + past participle).
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen als Teil eines Beispiels ‚geboren werden‘ nicht wörtlich erleben.
native_language_example: I will not literally experience ‚being born‘ tomorrow; this is used here only as an example.

meaning: to be made/caused to do something (past participle construction)
additional_notes: This is part of the verb phrase 'jemanden dazu bringen, etwas zu tun' (to make/bring someone to do something). 'gebracht' is the past participle used with haben (e.g. 'hat mich dazu gebracht, ...') and 'es zu' refers to 'to do it' or 'to eat it' in the examples. Use with a person as object: 'Er hat mich dazu gebracht, es zu tun.' = 'He made me do it.'
target_language_example: Meine Freunde haben mich dazu gebracht, es zu probieren.
native_language_example: My friends made me try it.

meaning: you have brought / you brought (Perfekt, 2nd person singular — 'du hast ... gebracht').
additional_notes: Part of the German present perfect (Perfekt) formed with the past participle 'gebracht' of 'bringen' and the auxiliary 'haben' in the 2nd person singular ('du hast ... gebracht'). Can be used for literal bringing (objects or people) and figurative uses (e.g. 'Schande gebracht haben' — to have brought shame). In main clauses the auxiliary 'hast' appears in second position and the past participle 'gebracht' moves to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich möchte nur wissen, warum du mich hierher gebracht hast.
native_language_example: I just want to know why you brought me here / why you have brought me here.

meaning: a broken heart; emotional pain from love or loss.
additional_notes: Used to describe deep sadness or emotional suffering, usually from a romantic breakup or unrequited love. Grammatically it's a noun phrase: gebrochenes (past-participle used as adjective) + Herz (neuter). Can be used literally (rarely) for physical heart injury, but in everyday language it means emotional hurt.
target_language_example: Nach der Trennung hatte er ein gebrochenes Herz.
native_language_example: After the breakup he had a broken heart.

meaning: 'die' as a demonstrative/relative pronoun referring to people or things mentioned (those/the ones); used after 'gedacht' in phrases like 'daran gedacht, die...' meaning 'remembered to... the.../those...'.
additional_notes: This appears in sentences with 'daran gedacht, die...' or 'an ... gedacht, die ...'. 'gedacht' is past participle of 'denken' (to think/remember). 'daran gedacht, die Fenster/Tore/Brote ...' = 'remembered to (do something) the windows/gates/bread...'. In sentence 6 it means 'thought of people like you, the (simple) ordinary people' — here 'die' is a relative/demonstrative pronoun meaning 'those people'. Common beginner pattern: 'Hast du daran gedacht, die Fenster zu schließen?' = 'Did you remember to close the windows?'
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, die Lampen auszuschalten?
native_language_example: Did you remember to turn off the lights?

meaning: had thought / thought (in the past, often in comparisons like 'than I had thought')
additional_notes: Commonly used in the structure 'als ich gedacht hatte' or 'wie ich (mir) gedacht hatte' to compare expectations with reality (e.g. 'lower than I had thought'). 'mir' can be added for emphasis: 'wie ich mir gedacht hatte'. It's past perfect (pluperfect) of 'denken' and often appears in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Das Konzert war besser, als ich gedacht hatte.
native_language_example: The concert was better than I had thought.

meaning: 'to have thought of (doing something)' — used with daran/etwas to mean 'to think of (doing)'.
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the construction 'an etwas gedacht zu haben' or with 'daran gedacht zu ...' meaning 'to have thought about doing something' or 'to think of doing something'. Common with verbs like 'haben' in perfect or modal contexts: 'daran gedacht zu kündigen' = 'to think about quitting'. In sentences it frequently uses a past infinitive form (gedacht zu + haben) or appears after 'daran/etwas'.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal daran gedacht zu kündigen?
native_language_example: Have you ever thought about quitting?

meaning: to be patient (with/to).
additional_notes: Used with the adjective 'geduldig' and the infinitive construction 'zu sein' or with 'mit' + dative to indicate being patient with someone/something. Common in advice or descriptions of behavior: 'geduldig zu sein' = 'to be patient'. In sentences above it's the infinitive phrase (e.g. 'geduldig zu sein').
target_language_example: Versuche, geduldig zu sein, wenn die Kinder Fragen stellen.
native_language_example: Try to be patient when the children ask questions.

meaning: 'liked' (perfect tense of gefallen; literally 'has pleased').
additional_notes: From the verb gefallen (to please; to be liked). Used with a dative experiencer (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen): e.g. 'es hat mir gefallen' = 'I liked it.' 'gefallen hat' appears in perfect-tense statements and relative clauses: 'das Restaurant, das dir gefallen hat' = 'the restaurant you liked.'
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass es ihm sehr gut gefallen hat.
native_language_example: He says that he liked it very much.

meaning: to be found / to be discovered (passive: someone/something is found)
additional_notes: Passive construction of finden (to find). Used when the subject is the thing or person that is found or discovered, or when a solution is to be found. Can express desire ('I want to be found') or necessity ('a solution must be found'). Word order: gefunden = past participle, werden = auxiliary for passive. Common in both literal (lost items, people) and figurative (solutions, answers).
target_language_example: Sie möchte nicht gefunden werden.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to be found.

meaning: are dangerous
additional_notes: Combination of the adjective gefährlich (dangerous) and the verb sind (are). Used to state that someone or something is dangerous. The verb form changes with the subject (ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind). In this multi-word term the verb is plural; it appears in subordinate clauses after dass/daß or in sentences referring to plural subjects.
target_language_example: Ich weiß, daß Tom und Maria gefährlich sind.
native_language_example: I know that Tom and Maria are dangerous.

meaning: I like the color (it pleases me).
additional_notes: Uses the verb gefallen (to please). Grammatically the color is the subject (Die Farbe gefällt mir). Native English speakers usually translate as 'I like the color...'. The phrase here is in the informal dative construction 'Mir gefällt die Farbe X.' Use 'gefällt' for singular colors; for plural things use 'gefallen'.
target_language_example: Mir gefällt die Farbe Rot sehr.
native_language_example: I really like the color red.

meaning: he likes it / it pleases him
additional_notes: From the verb gefallen (to please; to like something). German uses gefallen with the thing as subject and the person as dative (ihm = to him). Common patterns: 'Das gefällt ihm' (He likes that), 'Es gefällt ihm, ...' + infinitive clause, and questions 'Gefällt ihm ...?'. Negative: 'Das gefällt ihm nicht.'
target_language_example: Gefällt ihm das Buch?
native_language_example: Does he like the book?

meaning: 'my ... pleases (you/him/her/them)'; used to say that someone likes something of mine
additional_notes: Gefällt is the 3rd-person singular of gefallen (to please/be liked). German uses dative for the person who likes something: 'mir gefällt ...' (I like ... / ... pleases me), 'dir gefällt ...' (you like ...). With 'gefällt mein' the speaker refers to 'my' + noun that follows (e.g. 'mein neues Album', 'mein Drehbuch'). Word order often: [Person in dative] gefällt mein(en) + noun. The person who likes can be du/er/sie/ihnen/etc.; the thing liked is nominative.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dir gefällt mein Geschenk.
native_language_example: I hope you like my present.

meaning: 'he/she/it likes his' or 'pleases his' as a fragment (this exact two-word sequence is not a correct standalone phrase in German)
additional_notes: This sequence pairs gefällt (3rd person singular of gefallen, 'to please' / 'to like' in the sense 'X pleases Y') with the possessive seine ('his'). In grammatical German the words would normally be separated by other elements or appear in a larger clause (e.g., 'gefällt seine Freundin ihm' would still be awkward — the natural order is 'Seine Freundin gefällt ihm'). The two-word sequence 'gefällt seine' can appear within a longer sentence when followed by a noun in nominative: e.g., 'Das gefällt seine Mutter' is ungrammatical; correct forms are 'Das gefällt seiner Mutter' (That pleases his mother) or 'Seine Mutter gefällt ihm' (He/it pleases his mother). If you mean 'he likes his ...', use 'er mag sein ...' or 'ihm gefällt sein ...'.
target_language_example: Wenn ihm gefällt seine neue Uhr, freut er sich.
native_language_example: If he likes his new watch, he is happy.

meaning: to vaccinate (someone) against the flu; to get vaccinated against the flu
additional_notes: Commonly used in reflexive form with sich (sich gegen Grippe impfen lassen) to mean 'to get a flu shot'. In questions and everyday speech you'll hear the perfect or present forms asking whether someone has already had the vaccination. 'gegen' indicates 'against' and 'impfen' is 'to vaccinate'.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mich dieses Jahr gegen Grippe impfen lassen.
native_language_example: I want to get vaccinated against the flu this year.

meaning: 'against this' — expresses opposition toward a specific (neuter) thing or idea.
additional_notes: Gegen = against. Dieses is the demonstrative pronoun/adjective for neuter nouns in nominative/accusative (this/this one). Use 'gegen dieses' when referring to a specific neuter noun previously mentioned or obvious from context (e.g., 'gegen dieses Medikament', 'gegen dieses Gesetz'). If the noun is feminine or masculine, the demonstrative changes: 'gegen diese' (fem./pl.) or 'gegen diesen' (masc.).
target_language_example: Viele sind gegen dieses Vorhaben.
native_language_example: Many are against this project.

meaning: 'against you' (addressing a group, informal plural 'you')
additional_notes: Used to indicate opposition, hostility, complaint, or prejudice directed at a group of people you address as 'euch' (informal plural). Common in phrases like 'nichts gegen euch' (nothing against you) or 'gegen euch sein' (to be against you). 'Euch' is the informal plural dative/accusative form of 'ihr'.
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts gegen euch, aber ich stimme nicht zu.
native_language_example: I have nothing against you, but I don't agree.

meaning: to be against (something); to oppose or disapprove of something
additional_notes: Used to express opposition or disagreement with an idea, plan, person, or action. Often followed by a noun or a pronoun (gegen etwas sein) or by a clause introduced with 'dass' or an infinitive with 'zu'. Conjugate 'sein' as usual (ich bin gegen, du bist gegen, er/sie ist gegen, wir sind gegen...).
target_language_example: Ich bin gegen sein Vorhaben.
native_language_example: I am against his project/plan.

meaning: 'against his' (masculine singular possessive)
additional_notes: Combines the preposition 'gegen' (against) with the possessive pronoun 'seine' referring to a masculine or plural noun in accusative or nominative depending on context. Use 'seine' when the owner is 'he' (er) and the noun it modifies is feminine singular (acc.), plural (acc./nom.), or masculine/neuter if grammar requires. In many contexts 'gegen seine' is followed by a noun (e.g. 'gegen seine Idee', 'gegen seine Leute'). The phrase order is typical: 'gegen' + possessive + noun.
target_language_example: Wir müssen gegen seine Entscheidung protestieren.
native_language_example: We have to protest against his decision.

meaning: opposite/facing (the) — indicates location across from something or, in abstract use, 'toward' or 'in relation to'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a dative noun (der = feminine or dative masculine/neuter depending on article). In spatial contexts it means 'opposite' or 'across from' (e.g., a building opposite another). In non-spatial contexts it can mean 'toward' or 'in relation to' (e.g., gegenüber der Konkurrenz = in relation to the competition). Word order: 'gegenüber' can appear before or after the noun phrase (often after in modern German: 'das Haus gegenüber der Bibliothek').
target_language_example: Das Café liegt gegenüber der Post.
native_language_example: The café is located opposite the post office.

meaning: has eaten (perfect tense; used after subject in subordinate clauses or questions).
additional_notes: Part of the perfect tense of essen (to eat): 'hat gegessen'. In main clauses word order is Subject–Verb (Er hat gegessen), but in many subordinate clauses or after question words the past participle 'gegessen' comes before the auxiliary 'hat' (…dass sie gegessen hat) or at the end in questions (Weißt du, ob er gegessen hat?). Used to ask or state whether someone already ate, or what they ate.
target_language_example: Weißt du, ob sie schon gegessen hat?
native_language_example: Do you know if she has already eaten?

meaning: 'switch on' or 'start' (imperative/command form: go and turn on)
additional_notes: Geh an is composed of the verb gehen (imperative geh) + an (particle) and can be used colloquially to tell someone to switch something on or to start working/acting. Context matters: with appliances it means 'turn on' (e.g. Licht an → turn the light on). It can also appear in phrasing like "Geh an die Arbeit" (start working), but that construction more commonly uses other verbs; native speakers often say "mach an" for 'turn on' or "geh los" for 'start moving'.
target_language_example: Geh an das Licht!
native_language_example: Turn on the light!

meaning: imperative 'go to' (tell someone to go to a place).
additional_notes: Geh is the informal singular imperative of gehen (to go). Auf here combines with a noun to mean 'to' or 'onto' a location (e.g. 'auf dein Zimmer' = to your room). Used when speaking to one person you know well (du). For polite/formal or plural use, say 'gehen Sie auf...' or 'geht auf...'. Word order: imperative + preposition + object.
target_language_example: Geh auf dein Zimmer und bleib dort.
native_language_example: Go to your room and stay there.

meaning: a polite or emphatic request telling someone to 'go' (please go).
additional_notes: Geh is the informal imperative of gehen (to go). Bitte adds politeness or urgency. Used with du (informal singular). Can be soft/polite (
target_language_example: Geh bitte zum Arzt, wenn du Fieber hast.
native_language_example: Please go to the doctor if you have a fever.

meaning: I'm off / I'll go now (informal way to say you're leaving).
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'gehe dann' (from 'ich gehe dann'). Used when announcing departure or movement to another place (e.g., going inside, outside, downstairs). Common in spoken, casual German. Often followed by destination (rein, raus, runter) or used alone as a short farewell.
target_language_example: Okay, ich geh dann mal wieder.
native_language_example: Okay, I'm off again.

meaning: an informal imperative pattern meaning 'go and (do something to/for yourself)' used with reflexive verbs (colloquial: 'go and...').
additional_notes: This is a colloquial spoken structure where the imperative 'geh' (go) combines with a reflexive infinitive like 'amüsieren', 'entschuldigen', 'umziehen' plus the reflexive pronoun 'dich'. It roughly equals 'go and [verb]' in English: e.g. 'Geh dich umziehen' = 'Go change (your clothes).' It is common in some dialects/colloquial German; the more standard alternatives are 'Geh dich amüsieren' → 'Geh dich amüsieren' is already colloquial, or more standard: 'Geh dich umziehen' → 'Geh dich umziehen' (note: in standard German many speakers would say 'Geh dich umziehen' less often and prefer 'Zieh dich um' for 'change your clothes' or 'Entschuldige dich bei Tom' for 'apologize to Tom'). Use with 'du' (informal 'you').
target_language_example: Geh dich bei ihm entschuldigen — es ist wichtig.
native_language_example: Go and apologize to him — it's important.

meaning: go and (do something)
additional_notes: Colloquial imperative construction using gehen + reflexive/ dative pronoun dir to tell someone to go and perform an action (often followed by verb with anziehen, angucken, die Zähne putzen, etc.). Very common in spoken German with children or informal commands: 'Geh dir die Zähne putzen' = 'Go and brush your teeth.' Use 'geh' (singular informal du). For plural or formal: 'geht euch ...' or 'gehen Sie ...'.
target_language_example: Geh dir jetzt die Schuhe an und komm runter.
native_language_example: Go and put your shoes on now and come downstairs.

meaning: Get out of my way / get away from me (rude, forceful).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to move away or leave you alone. Often followed by 'dem Weg', 'dem Gesicht' or 'dem Haus' (e.g. 'geh mir aus dem Weg' = 'get out of my way'). Can be rude or angry — tone matters. Common in spoken German; may include expletives in examples.
target_language_example: Geh mir aus dem Weg, ich muss hier durch.
native_language_example: Get out of my way, I have to get through here.

meaning: go to
additional_notes: Informal imperative or conversational form of gehen + nach (often followed by a place or direction). Used to tell someone to go to a specific location (geh nach Hause = go home) or to indicate movement toward a direction (geh nach rechts = go to the right). In standard grammar you might see full forms like "geh nach Hause" or "geh nach vorne." For polite/formal commands use "gehen Sie nach..." or the infinitive construction.
target_language_example: Geh nach Hause, es ist spät.
native_language_example: Go home, it's late.

meaning: just go / I'm just going (used to downplay or limit the action).
additional_notes: Geh nur is informal spoken German (geh = imperative or colloquial short form of 'gehe' or present 'ich geh'). 'Nur' softens or limits the action: 'just', 'only', or 'briefly'. Can be used to explain a small purpose (Ich geh nur kurz...), to reassure (Ja, geh nur = go ahead / suit yourself), or to emphasize that nothing else will happen. Common in everyday conversation; tone and context determine whether it's literal, minimizing, or sarcastic.
target_language_example: Ich geh nur kurz einkaufen, ich bin gleich zurück.
native_language_example: I'm just going shopping quickly; I'll be right back.

meaning: I like to go / I enjoy going (somewhere or doing an activity).
additional_notes: Used with 'gehen' + activity or place to say you enjoy going or doing that activity. 'gern' (or 'gerne') expresses liking; word order: 'Ich gehe gern ...'. Common collocations: auf Konzerte gehen, spazieren gehen, essen gehen, schwimmen gehen. 'Gern' can be moved: 'Ich gehe gerne nachmittags schwimmen.'
target_language_example: Ich gehe gern am Wochenende wandern.
native_language_example: I like to go hiking on weekends.

meaning: I like to go / I enjoy going
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (gehen + place or infinitive) to say you enjoy going somewhere or doing something. 'Gerne' expresses liking; word order: subject + verb (gehe) + gerne + destination/activity. Can be used with fixed destinations (in die Stadt, zur Schule) or with an infinitive (ich gehe gerne spazieren).
target_language_example: Ich gehe gerne am Wochenende im Wald spazieren.
native_language_example: I like to go for a walk in the forest on weekends.

meaning: go with
additional_notes: Used to say you accompany someone or that someone accompanies you. Often appears with a dative pronoun or noun (mit + person). In questions like "kommst du mit?" it means "are you coming along?" Tense/verb changes apply: ich gehe mit (I go with / I'm going with), er geht mit (he goes with), wir gehen mit (we go with).
target_language_example: Ich gehe mit Maria ins Kino, willst du mit?
native_language_example: I'm going to the cinema with Maria — do you want to come along?

meaning: 'I only go' / 'just go' (adds limitation or reassurance to 'go')
additional_notes: Used with a verb (gehen) to indicate limitation (only/just) or to soften/reassure (e.g., 'just go' / 'go ahead'). Depending on word order and context, it can mean 'I only go to...' (limitation) or 'go ahead, don't worry' (imperative sense in spoken German: 'Gehe nur!' → 'Go on!'). Often followed by a destination or a time expression.
target_language_example: Ich gehe nur kurz zur Bank.
native_language_example: I'm just going to the bank briefly.

meaning: I often go / I go often
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gehen (to go) in first person singular (ich gehe) plus the adverb oft (often). Used to say you frequently do an activity or visit a place. Word order: oft commonly appears after the verb or before the rest of the sentence (Ich gehe oft ins Kino / Oft gehe ich ins Kino). Replace ich with other subjects and conjugate gehen (du gehst, er geht, wir gehen…).
target_language_example: Ich gehe oft am Wochenende ins Café.
native_language_example: I often go to the café on weekends.

meaning: '(we/they) all go' or 'everyone goes' — states that all members of a group go somewhere or are affected together. Depending on context it can be literal (everyone goes somewhere) or emphatic/idiomatic (everyone suffers or is doomed).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gehen (to go) and the quantifier alle (all/everyone). Word order can vary by sentence; in short clauses the verb may appear before the subject/pronoun and 'alle'. Context determines person (wir, sie, etc.). Can be used literally or in exclamations (e.g., 'wir gehen alle drauf').
target_language_example: Ich sage, wir gehen alle, dann können wir aufeinander aufpassen.
native_language_example: I say we all go, then we can look out for each other.

meaning: to go to work; to go and do paid work (leave home to work).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone is going to their job or starting work. Often conjugated with gehen + infinitive (e.g., Ich gehe arbeiten). Can be used for regular jobs or temporary shifts. Less formal alternative: 'zur Arbeit gehen'.
target_language_example: Ich gehe arbeiten, bis später.
native_language_example: I'm going to work now, see you later.

meaning: 'they go' or 'do they go' — literal use of gehen with the pronoun 'die' (they/these) depending on context
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb gehen (to go) used with the pronoun die (they or these). Meaning depends on context and word order: 'Gehen die ...?' is a question ('Do they go/Do those ... go?'); 'gehen die' in a main clause can be part of an imperative/statement ('Either they go or I [leave]!' = 'Entweder gehen die oder ich!'). 'Die' can refer to people or things (those). Watch word order: in questions the verb comes first. Informal register is fine.
target_language_example: Gehen die morgen zusammen ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are they going to the cinema together tomorrow?

meaning: to like to go / to enjoy going (somewhere or doing an outing).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'gehen' (to go) with 'gerne' (gladly/prefer to). Used to say someone enjoys going somewhere or doing an activity. Word order: 'gehen gerne' often appears with destination or activity after (e.g. 'gehen gerne spazieren', 'gehen gerne aus'). 'Gerne' can also follow the verb: 'gehen gerne' or 'gehen ... gerne'. Tense/person change as usual (e.g. 'gehen' → 'geht', 'gingen').
target_language_example: Wir gehen gerne am Wochenende ins Kino.
native_language_example: We like to go to the cinema on weekends.

meaning: we/they are going now; let's go now. (indicates leaving or starting to go immediately)
additional_notes: Common combination of the verb gehen (to go) with jetzt (now). Word order in full sentences usually places jetzt after the verb or elsewhere for emphasis (Wir gehen jetzt = We're going now). Can be used declaratively or as an imperative-like prompt (Let's go). Context shows leaving a place or starting an action immediately.
target_language_example: Okay, wir gehen jetzt zum Spielplatz.
native_language_example: Okay, we're going to the playground now.

meaning: to be able to go / to be able to walk (depending on context).
additional_notes: Combines the verb gehen (to go / to walk) with the modal verb können (can/to be able to). Used to express ability or possibility to go or to walk. Context determines whether it means 'be able to go' (e.g. leave or attend) or 'be able to walk' (physical ability). In conditional or past contexts you'll often see forms like hätte gehen können (would have been able to go) or würde gehen können (would be able to go).
target_language_example: Nach der Operation hoffe ich, bald wieder gehen können zu sein.
native_language_example: After the operation I hope to be able to walk again soon.

meaning: to let go / to allow (someone) to leave; to let (someone) do something
additional_notes: A separable verb phrase: gehen is the verb and lassen is the infinitive that together mean 'to allow (someone) to go/leave' or more generally 'to let/allow'. Word order separates in main clauses (e.g. Ich lasse ihn gehen → Ich habe ihn gehen lassen in perfect). Can be used transitively with a person (jemanden gehen lassen) or with an action (etwas geschehen lassen). Context decides whether it means 'release', 'permit to leave', or 'allow'.
target_language_example: Warum hast du ihn gehen lassen?
native_language_example: Why did you let him go?

meaning: must go / have to go (indicates necessity or obligation to go)
additional_notes: ‘gehen müssen’ combines the verb gehen (to go) with the modal verb müssen (must/have to). In German, müssen is conjugated and often appears in the sentence’s finite form while the main verb (gehen) appears in the infinitive at the end of the clause (especially in subordinate clauses or with auxiliary/modal constructions). It expresses necessity, obligation, or inevitability about going somewhere. Word order can vary (e.g., 'Er muss gehen.' or 'Er wird gehen müssen.' for future/obligation).
target_language_example: Morgen werde ich früh gehen müssen.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll have to leave early.

meaning: to go to bed / to go to sleep.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used to say you are going to bed or going to sleep. Conjugate gehen as usual and combine with schlafen; e.g. Ich gehe schlafen (I'm going to bed). Can be used both literally (physically going to bed) and figuratively to indicate going to sleep soon.
target_language_example: Ich werde jetzt gehen schlafen.
native_language_example: I'm going to bed now.

meaning: literally ‘go should’; expresses that someone should go — used to report advice, instruction, recommendation, or to express wondering whether someone ought to go.
additional_notes: Combination of gehen (to go) and soll (from the modal verb sollen). Common in subordinate clauses and reported speech (…dass er gehen soll), in questions about advice (soll er gehen?), and in expressions of uncertainty (ob ich gehen soll). Tone depends on context: can be directive (command), consultative (asking for advice), or speculative. Word order changes in direct questions and subordinate clauses: ‚Soll ich gehen?‘ vs. ‚ob ich gehen soll.‘
target_language_example: Wenn ich gehen soll, sag’s einfach!
native_language_example: If I should leave, just tell me!

meaning: should go / ought to go (expresses recommendation, obligation, or uncertainty about going)
additional_notes: Combines the infinitive gehen (to go) with the modal-like past-tense form sollte (from sollen). Used to express advice, obligation, or doubt about where or whether someone should go. In many contexts German speakers use a different word order (e.g., 'wohin er gehen sollte' or 'ob ich gehen sollte'). Can appear in reported speech or subordinate clauses. Tone is neutral; not informal.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, ob ich zum Arzt gehen sollte.
native_language_example: I don't know whether I should go to the doctor.

meaning: 'want to go' (second person singular, informal: you want to go).
additional_notes: Combines the infinitive gehen (to go) with the modal-like construction wollen in the 2nd person singular (du willst). Used to talk about someone's desire or intention to go somewhere or to leave. Common in statements, questions, and conditional clauses (Wenn du gehen willst...). Informal because it uses du. Word order: in subordinate clauses the verb cluster may appear at the end (…gehen willst).
target_language_example: Wenn du gehen willst, kannst du jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: If you want to go, you can go now.

meaning: Conditional or future-in-the-past form of the verb gehen — 'would go' or 'would/was going to go' in reported speech.
additional_notes: Formed with the conditional auxiliary würde + infinitive gehen. Used for hypothetical actions (conditional) and for reported or future-in-the-past constructions (indirect speech). Word order can vary within a sentence; the sequence 'gehen würde' appears when the infinitive precedes the auxiliary in subordinate clauses or in certain poetic/colloquial structures (e.g., als-clauses).
target_language_example: Tom erzählte mir, dass er heute früh nach Hause gehen würde.
native_language_example: Tom told me that he would go home early today.

meaning: You're annoying me / You're getting on my nerves.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to tell someone they are bothering or irritating you. Often followed by objects like 'den Sack', 'den Wecker', 'die Nerven' or colloquial vulgarities ('die Eier') — these emphasize annoyance. Use with caution: can be rude depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Du gehst mir auf die Nerven — hör auf zu reden!
native_language_example: You're getting on my nerves — stop talking!

meaning: 'when it comes to' / 'as for' (introduces a topic or subject)
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Wenn es um X geht, ist ...' or 'Wenn es um X geht, ist Y ...' Used to introduce a topic and then make a statement about it. Can also appear as 'Wenn es um X geht' or simpler 'Wenn es um X geht, ...'. In other contexts the verbs keep their literal meanings ('gehen' = to go, 'sein' = to be), but together in this pattern they form a fixed phrase meaning 'when it comes to'.
target_language_example: Wenn es um Musik geht, ist sie die Expertin.
native_language_example: When it comes to music, she's the expert.

meaning: imperative phrase: 'everyone go' or 'all of you go'.
additional_notes: Used as an imperative addressing a group (ihr or alle) to tell everyone to leave, go out, go home, or take their positions. Tone depends on context — can be neutral (directions, orders) or firm/abrupt. In everyday speech you might also hear 'geht alle raus', 'geht alle nach Hause' or simply 'geht raus' when addressing a group. The verb 'geht' is the 2nd-person plural imperative form of 'gehen' (go), and 'alle' emphasizes 'everyone'.
target_language_example: Geht alle jetzt nach Hause, bitte.
native_language_example: Everyone go home now, please.

meaning: everything goes / everything is happening (in a certain way) — used to describe how things are proceeding or that everything is affected.
additional_notes: Common in colloquial and neutral contexts. Often follows a subject or conditional clause and describes the overall course or result (e.g., 'geht alles zugrunde' = 'everything is ruined'). Can express general state ('everything is fine' with different adjectives) or outcome ('everything goes wrong'). The literal components 'geht' (goes) + 'alles' (everything) are transparent.
target_language_example: Wenn wir zusammenarbeiten, geht alles viel leichter.
native_language_example: If we work together, everything goes much more easily.

meaning: part of the phrase used to ask or say how someone (female or feminine noun) or something (feminine noun) is doing/feeling
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences with dative feminine nouns/pronouns, e.g. 'Wie geht es der Frau?' (How is the woman?). Common full patterns: 'Wie geht es der ...?' (How is the ...?), 'Geht es der ... gut?' (Is the ... well?). If referring to a male person use 'geht es dem', plural use 'geht es den'.
target_language_example: Wie geht es der Freundin heute?
native_language_example: How is the (female) friend today?

target_language_multi_word_term: geht fünf (Minuten) nach / geht fünf (Minuten) vor
meaning: to be fast/slow by five (minutes).
additional_notes: Used about clocks/watches. 'geht ... nach' means the clock is slow (shows a time later? actually 'nach' = 'slow' shows time later than true time? Wait: In German, 'geht fünf Minuten nach' = is five minutes slow (i.e., shows a time 5 minutes later than it should) — for learners: 'nach' = slow (behind true time), 'vor' = fast (ahead of true time). Structure: 'Die Uhr geht [time] nach/vor.' Can also use other time amounts. Note: 'Tom geht fünf Tage die Woche in die Schule.' uses 'geht' as the verb 'goes' (not about clocks) — same verb but different meaning.
target_language_example: Meine Uhr geht fünf Minuten nach; ich muss sie stellen.
native_language_example: My watch is five minutes slow; I need to set it.

meaning: Used to indicate that something happens fully, completely, or very quickly/entirely, depending on context; 'geht' is form of gehen used in constructions (impersonal 'es geht' = 'it goes/is'), and 'ganz' intensifies meaning ('completely/very').
additional_notes: Flexible phrase: in 'Es geht ganz schnell' it means 'it happens very quickly.' In 'Er geht ganz in seinem Beruf auf' the construction is 'geht ... auf' (sich in etwas aufgehen) meaning 'is completely absorbed in,' with 'ganz' intensifying to 'completely.' Can appear in imperative/elliptical uses like 'Geht ganz schnell.'
target_language_example: Es geht ganz schnell.
native_language_example: It happens very quickly.

meaning: 'is going' or 'is walking' (present progressive sense: 'is ... right now')
additional_notes: Combines the verb gehen (to go/walk) with gerade (right now/at the moment). Used to describe an action happening right now. Depending on context, 'gehen' can mean 'walk', 'go', or more figuratively 'sink' (as in 'untergehen' = go under/sink) — note sentence 1 uses 'geht ... unter' where 'geht' is part of the separable verb 'untergehen'. Pay attention to word order: 'gerade' commonly appears after the conjugated verb or before the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Er geht gerade zum Bäcker.
native_language_example: He is going to the bakery right now.

meaning: Are you (all) going/are you (all) ... today? (asking about plans or actions of 'ihr')
additional_notes: Uses the verb gehen (to go) with the pronoun ihr (you plural). Common in questions about where or when a group will go somewhere or do something today. Context determines the rest of the sentence (e.g. 'ins Bett' = to bed, 'nach Hause' = home, 'in den Pub' = to the pub). In spoken German, 'heute abend' (this evening) often follows: 'Geht ihr heute abend ...?'.
target_language_example: Geht ihr heute ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you (all) going to the cinema today?

meaning: always (does something) / is always the case
additional_notes: Common phrase used with a verb to say someone regularly or habitually does something. Word order: subject + geht immer + (rest) is natural when the verb is 'gehen' (to go) or in idiomatic uses. Can be used for habits (Sie geht immer spät ins Bett) or repeated actions (Tom geht immer zu Fuß). Not limited to 'gehen'—'immer' follows the verb in simple present statements.
target_language_example: Er geht immer früh joggen.
native_language_example: He always goes jogging early.

meaning: adds emphasis or confirmation like '...after all' / 'you know' / 'indeed', often to point out something obvious
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. 'ja' here is a modal particle that changes the tone of a sentence; it doesn't mean 'yes'. 'geht ja' often appears in statements like 'Das geht ja nicht' ('That really won't work') or 'Das geht ja gut' (sarcastic/positive depending on context). The exact translation depends on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Das geht ja nicht — so kann ich das nicht machen.
native_language_example: That really won't work — I can't do it like that.

meaning: Okay; will do; that's fine.
additional_notes: Informal, conversational phrase used to agree, confirm that something is understood, or that a request will be done. Common in spoken German: can stand alone („Geht klar.“) or follow a name/person. Tone ranges from neutral to casual; not formal enough for business letters.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bis morgen erledigen? — Geht klar.
native_language_example: Can you finish that by tomorrow? — Okay, will do.

meaning: one/people go; how/where one goes; (impersonal) people/you/one do(s) something
additional_notes: "geht man" is an impersonal or general way to talk about what people do (similar to English "one/you/people go" or "one/you/people do"). Context determines translation: it can describe walking (geht man zu Fuß = one walks), ask about common behavior (Wie geht man mit ...? = How does one deal with ...?), or ask where people go (Wo geht man hin?). It often appears in general statements or instructions.
target_language_example: Wenn es regnet, geht man besser nicht spazieren.
native_language_example: When it rains, one/you/people better not go for a walk.

meaning: 'is/are not only' or 'it's/they're not just' (used to say something has other aspects besides the one mentioned)
additional_notes: Common phrase built on 'es geht um' (= 'it's about') or 'es geht mir' (= 'I'm concerned/affected'). Use 'geht nicht nur' to deny that only the mentioned thing matters — e.g. 'Es geht nicht nur ums Geld' = 'It's not just about the money.' Can appear with 'um' + noun (um X) or with a dative pronoun (mir).
target_language_example: Es geht nicht nur um Arbeit, sondern auch um Freizeit.
native_language_example: It's not just about work, but also about free time.

meaning: literally 'nothing goes'; used in different expressions meaning 'nothing works/left', 'nothing beats', or 'nothing goes out/sent'.
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed single idiom; meaning depends on the full sentence. Common patterns:
- 'Es geht nichts mehr.' = nothing works anymore / nothing is left / it's impossible now.
- 'Es geht nichts über ...' = nothing beats ... / ... is the best.
- 'Es geht nichts schief.' (with 'hoffentlich') = hopefully nothing goes wrong. Often used with verbs after 'geht'.
- In technical contexts: 'es geht nichts raus' = nothing is going out/sending fails.
Use the whole sentence to understand the intended meaning.
target_language_example: Es geht nichts über einen guten Kaffee am Morgen.
native_language_example: Nothing beats a good coffee in the morning.

meaning: 'never goes' or 'never (does something)' — used to say someone never does a particular action.
additional_notes: Combines the verb gehen (to go) in third person singular with nie (never). In these examples gehen is used in a general sense for actions (go somewhere, leave the house, date someone, go to sleep). You can replace gehen with other verbs: er macht nie (he never does), sie isst nie (she never eats). Word order: nie usually comes after the verb in simple statements.
target_language_example: Sie geht nie ohne Mantel aus dem Haus.
native_language_example: She never leaves the house without a coat.

meaning: nobody goes / nobody answers / nobody does (depending on context) — 'niemand' is the subject and 'geht' is the verb 'to go' or used in idiomatic constructions.
additional_notes: Literally 'goes nobody', but in natural English: 'nobody …'. The verb can change meaning with context: 'geht niemand ran' = 'nobody answers (the phone / door)', 'geht niemand raus' = 'nobody goes outside', 'geht niemand zu Fuß' = 'nobody walks'. Word order: in statements the verb comes second (Geht niemand? is a question). Useful to replace with 'niemand geht' in some contexts, but German often places verb first in questions.
target_language_example: Bei dem Sturm geht niemand raus.
native_language_example: Nobody goes out in the storm.

meaning: 'is/are only' or 'it's just about' depending on context
additional_notes: Used in different ways: 1) as part of a sentence meaning 'only' or 'only in this way' (e.g. 'Aber es geht nur so' = 'But it only works this way'). 2) with a verb to mean 'only (does something)' (e.g. 'Er geht nur nachts raus' = 'He only goes out at night'). 3) with 'um' to mean 'it's only about' or 'it's just about' (e.g. 'Es geht nur ums Geld' = 'It's just about the money'). Common in spoken and written German. Word order and prepositions determine the exact English translation.
target_language_example: Es geht nur um die Arbeit, nicht um persönliche Dinge.
native_language_example: It's only about work, not personal matters.

meaning: 'is about' or 'is a matter of' (often: concerns, is at stake).
additional_notes: Used to say what something concerns or what is at stake. Common construction: 'es geht um + Akk.' = 'it's about...' or 'it's a question of...'. Can express urgency ('es geht um Leben und Tod' = 'it's a matter of life and death'). Note: 'gehen' appears in other contexts (e.g. 'jemand geht um' meaning 'someone walks around' or 'Tom geht um zehn Uhr dreißig zu Bett' where 'geht' is part of 'zu Bett gehen') — those senses are different and not covered by this entry, which focuses on the impersonal construction 'es geht um'.
target_language_example: Es geht um die Zukunft der Firma.
native_language_example: It's about / The matter concerns the future of the company.

meaning: goes to / is going to (someone or something)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb gehen (to go, to walk) + the preposition zu (to). Used to indicate movement toward a person, place, or thing. Can be literal (physically going somewhere) or metaphorical/spiritual (e.g., 'seelisch zu jemandem/etwas gehen'). Word order and case: zu takes the dative (e.g., zu dem → zum). In commands or narrative it can appear in contexts like 'Er geht zu Boden' (= he falls to the ground).
target_language_example: Sie geht zu ihrem Freund und spricht mit ihm.
native_language_example: She goes to her boyfriend and talks to him.

meaning: goes/go to the (masculine or neuter noun); 'geht zum' = 'goes to the' or imperative 'go to the' (plural informal: 'Geht zum...').
additional_notes: Combines the verb gehen (to go) with the contracted preposition zum = zu + dem (to the). Used for movement toward a specific masculine or neuter place or person (zum Hof, zum Arzt, zum Parkplatz). Can be present tense (er geht zum = he goes to the) or imperative plural 'Geht zum ...!' = 'Go to the ...!' In contexts like 'Geht zum Rauchen auf den Balkon' it's a command telling a group to go to the balcony to smoke. Use 'zur' (zu + der) for feminine nouns and 'zum' for masculine/neuter.
target_language_example: Sie geht zum Supermarkt, um Milch zu kaufen.
native_language_example: She goes to the supermarket to buy milk.

meaning: is starting/going to start very soon
additional_notes: Used to say that an event or action will begin in a moment. Common in spoken and informal contexts. Often follows the subject (Das Spiel geht gleich los = The game is about to start). Can be used with activities (Vorstellung, Sitzung) or situations (z. B. Fahrt).
target_language_example: Der Film geht gleich los, nimm bitte Platz.
native_language_example: The movie is starting in a moment, please take a seat.

meaning: to belong to; to be part of or owned by someone or something.
additional_notes: Used with dative objects (to whom/what something belongs). Can indicate ownership (these belong to me), membership (I belong to a group), or being part of a category. Conjugates like gehören (gehöre, gehörst, gehört, gehören...). Use 'zu' + dative noun/pronoun: 'zu mir', 'zu ihm', 'zu der Gruppe'. Word order: the verb gehören appears conjugated and the preposition zu follows the verb in infinitive structures or in separable contexts the components remain together as a multi-word verb.
target_language_example: Die gehören zu mir.
native_language_example: Those belong to me.

meaning: Does this belong (to someone)? / Is this theirs?
additional_notes: Used to ask about ownership of an object. Word order can change (e.g., "Gehört das Ihnen?" or "Gehört das ihr?"). Formal address: use "Ihnen"; informal: "dir" or "ihr". You can also ask "Wem gehört das?" (Who does this belong to?).
target_language_example: Gehört das Ihnen, Herr Müller?
native_language_example: Does this belong to you, Mr. Müller?

meaning: belongs in / should go into (a place or category).
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone should be placed somewhere, stored somewhere, or belongs in a certain category or institution. Can be literal (objects: 'belongs in the drawer') or figurative (people: 'belongs in a hospital' or 'belongs in German hands'). Often followed by a noun with a preposition (in + accusative: in die Schublade, in ein Krankenhaus).
target_language_example: Das Handy gehört in die Schublade.
native_language_example: The phone belongs in the drawer.

meaning: have heard (you) — second person singular, perfect/subordinate clause form
additional_notes: Used in clauses referring to something the listener heard. Combines the past participle 'gehört' (heard) with the auxiliary 'hast' (you have). Common in questions and statements: 'Was du gehört hast' = 'what you heard' or 'what you have heard'. Word order follows German subordinate/clausal patterns.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, ob du das richtig gehört hast.
native_language_example: I don't know whether you heard that correctly.

meaning: had heard / would have listened (depends on context) — either past perfect in indirect speech ('had heard') or subjunctive II in unreal past/conditional constructions ('would have listened' or 'had listened' as in 'had followed advice').
additional_notes:
Formed from the past participle gehört (from hören) + auxiliary hätte (Konjunktiv II of haben). Common uses:
1) Indirect/reported past: expresses that someone said they had heard something (e.g. Sie hat gesagt, daß sie Schüsse gehört hätte).
2) Unreal past/conditional/regret: used with auf + jemanden hören to mean 'would have listened / had listened' (e.g. Wenn ich doch nur auf Ihren Rat gehört hätte!).
Word order varies in full clauses; the sequence gehört hätte must appear together when embedded or in certain word orders (especially in subordinate clauses or reported speech).
target_language_example: Sie hat gesagt, daß sie Schüsse gehört hätte.
native_language_example: She said that she had heard shots.

meaning: ‘I came to (you) to…’ — introduces the purpose of coming to someone (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with the perfect/past verb kommen (here: Ich bin gekommen) plus „um … zu“ + infinitive to state the purpose of coming to the person addressed (dir = to you). Common in spoken and written German for polite or direct purposes: giving, telling, thanking, congratulating, wishing, etc.
target_language_example: Ich bin gekommen, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I came to help you.

meaning: have come to (do something) — indicates purpose: 'I came to [do something] to/for you (plural/informal)'.
additional_notes: This is the perfect tense form of kommen + infinitive clause with 'um ... zu' to express purpose. 'Euch' is the informal plural or familiar direct/indirect object (you all). English word order often: 'I came to congratulate you' or 'I've come to tell you...'. Use with an infinitive at the end (e.g. gratulieren, sagen, suchen, töten).
target_language_example: Ich bin gekommen, um euch zu helfen.
native_language_example: I came to help you (all).

meaning: 'to have cost' (perfect tense of 'kosten' — to cost).
additional_notes: Used in the perfect tense to say something was expensive for someone or that something has cost a certain amount. Often appears with modal verbs like 'müssen' to express a strong assumption: 'Das muss dich ein Vermögen gekostet haben.' Word order: the thing that cost is often expressed as a noun phrase ('ein Vermögen', 'viel Geld'); the person affected is in the accusative ('dich', 'ihn', 'uns').
target_language_example: Das muss dich ein Vermögen gekostet haben.
native_language_example: That must have cost you a fortune.

meaning: he succeeded (in doing something) / it succeeded for him (often used in negative: 'he didn't succeed')
additional_notes: From the verb gelingen (to succeed, to work out). 'Es gelang ihm' is an impersonal construction: literally 'it succeeded to him' — in English we normally say 'he succeeded' or 'he managed (to...)'. Commonly used with 'nicht' to say someone failed: 'es gelang ihm nicht' = 'he didn't succeed / he couldn't'. The subject of the action is often an infinitive clause or a noun phrase earlier in the sentence.
target_language_example: Es gelang ihm schließlich, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: He finally succeeded in solving the problem.

meaning: I managed / I succeeded (in doing something) — used to say that something was achieved (or not).
additional_notes: Phrase is the past-tense form of 'gelingen' with the dative pronoun 'mir' ('to me'). Commonly used with an infinitive or clause: 'Es gelang mir, ...' or 'Es gelang mir nicht.' Often translated as 'I managed to...' or 'I succeeded in...'. Use 'nicht' to negate: 'Es gelang mir nicht.'
target_language_example: Es gelang mir, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: I managed to solve the problem.

meaning: has left (somewhere); left behind (perfect form used to indicate someone left something or left something in a certain state)
additional_notes: Perfect (Perfekt) form of the separable verb lassen (participle: gelassen) used with haben; appears in subordinate clauses and reported questions where auxiliary comes at the end (…gelassen hat). Often used to ask or state where someone left an object or who left something in a certain state (e.g. offen gelassen = left open). Not to be confused with the adjective gelassen meaning 'calm.'
target_language_example: Ich weiß, wo Tom seinen Regenschirm gelassen hat.
native_language_example: I know where Tom left his umbrella.

meaning: to be left alone / to be left as is
additional_notes: Passive form of 'gelassen' (from 'lassen' = to let/leave). Used when something or someone is not to be changed, touched, or disturbed. Context decides whether it's physical (leave it alone), emotional (let someone be), or procedural (leave something as it is). Common in commands or descriptions: 'Das darf so gelassen werden' = 'That may be left as is.'
target_language_example: Lass das bitte gelassen werden.
native_language_example: Please leave that alone.

meaning: to allow or permit (someone) to do something; to let (someone) be
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'gelassen' (from lassen) used with 'zu' + infinitive or with an object implied. Often appears in constructions like 'jemanden etwas gelassen zu tun' or 'etwas gelassen zu werden' to express allowing or leaving something/someone alone. It's more common to see 'jemanden etwas lassen' or 'lassen + zu' separately (e.g. 'zu lassen' in infinitive). In spoken German you'd more often hear 'lassen' forms ('ich lasse dich') rather than 'gelassen zu'.
target_language_example: Er hat mich gelassen zu gehen.
native_language_example: He allowed me to go.

meaning: has learned (something) — perfect tense (3rd person singular) indicating that someone learned or acquired knowledge/skill.
additional_notes: Perfect tense (Perfekt): past participle 'gelernt' + auxiliary 'hat' (3rd person singular). Common in spoken and written German to state completed actions. Appears in main clauses and subordinate clauses; word order may vary (e.g., subordinate clause with verb-final). Can follow question words or clauses (e.g., 'wo ... gelernt hat'). Can combine with activities/nouns like 'Auto fahren'/'Autofahren'.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, wo Tom wohl Französisch gelernt hat.
native_language_example: I wonder where Tom learned French.

meaning: to be loved (in an infinitive construction).
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'geliebt' + infinitive marker 'zu' used in German infinitive clauses (often after verbs like 'sein', 'werden', or expressions with 'es ist ... zu'). It appears in passive-like constructions meaning 'to be loved' (e.g., 'geliebt zu werden' = 'to be loved'). You will commonly see the full phrase 'geliebt zu werden' or 'geliebt zu sein'.
target_language_example: Geliebt zu werden ist sehr wichtig für viele Menschen.
native_language_example: To be loved is very important for many people.

meaning: the relative clause 'die ... gemacht' (lit. 'that/who ... made/did') used to refer back to a feminine/plural noun and describe an action done to/by it.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but an example of a past participle (gemacht = made/done) combined with a relative pronoun (die) introducing a relative clause. 'Die' agrees in gender/number with the noun it refers to (die Nudeln, die Bücher, or plural people). In English it usually becomes 'that/which/who ... made/did' or '... that I/you/we/they made/did'. Word order in the relative clause places the past participle at the end when using perfect tense with an auxiliary (e.g. 'die wir gerade gegessen haben' — 'that we just ate').
target_language_example: Hast du die Kekse gemacht, die auf dem Tisch sind?
native_language_example: Did you make the cookies that are on the table?

meaning: would have done / had done (past conditional or reported speech expressing hypothetical or uncertain past actions)
additional_notes: Compound of the past participle gemacht + the subjunctive/conditional auxiliary hätte (from haben). Used for the past conditional (would have done) and in indirect/reported speech to express that a past action was hypothetical, contrary-to-fact, or considered uncertain. Translation into English depends on context: commonly 'would have done' or 'had done'. Word order may vary in subordinate clauses and direct speech contexts.
target_language_example: Tom fragte mich, was ich so gemacht hätte.
native_language_example: Tom asked me what I would have done.

meaning: how something is done; how it is made (passive phrasing).
additional_notes: Passive construction: 'wie ... gemacht wird' is used to ask or state the method or way something is done. Common in reported questions and instructions. Structure: 'wie' + object + 'gemacht wird' (present passive). Can be replaced with active phrasing ('wie man ... macht') in many contexts.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir zeigen, wie das gemacht wird?
native_language_example: Can you show me how that is done?

meaning: exactly at / precisely at (a place or point); exactly (with memory of something) when used with verbs like erinnern.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize precision of location or moment (genau an + Dativ: genau an der Stelle, genau an diesem Ort) or precision in remembering (sich genau an etwas erinnern). Often appears with articles/pronouns showing the place/time: genau an der/dieser/stelle. Word order: 'genau' before 'an'.
target_language_example: Wir standen genau an der Ecke des Parks.
native_language_example: We stood exactly at the corner of the park.

meaning: exactly toward / directly at (or exactly on/top of, depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion or impact to mean 'directly toward' someone/something (geh genau auf mich zu = come straight toward me) or with verbs indicating contact/impact to mean 'precisely on' or 'right on' (genau auf den Mund getroffen = hit me right on the mouth). Often followed by a noun phrase with a preposition (auf mich zu, auf uns zu, auf den Mund).
target_language_example: Der Ball flog genau auf das Tor zu.
native_language_example: The ball flew straight toward the goal.

meaning: to do exactly that / to do exactly what (was said).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to follow instructions precisely. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'was' (what) or a direct instruction. 'Genau' emphasizes precision; 'das' refers to the action previously mentioned or what follows. Polite and informal forms depend on the pronoun and verb conjugation (du/ihr/Sie).
target_language_example: Du musst genau das tun, was ich dir gesagt habe.
native_language_example: You must do exactly what I told you.

meaning: strictly speaking; more precisely; to be exact
additional_notes: Used to correct, refine or qualify a previous statement. Often placed at the start of a sentence or clause. Can soften a correction or add precision (e.g., 'actually', 'in fact', 'strictly speaking').
target_language_example: Genau genommen ist das nicht meine Aufgabe.
native_language_example: Strictly speaking, that's not my job.

meaning: exactly in / right in (indicates a precise location or moment).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize precision of place or time. Often appears before a noun with a preposition (in der Mitte, in dem Moment) or in short exclamations (Genau in die Mitte!). Can be followed by accusative or dative depending on the preposition phrase that follows (e.g. in die Mitte — direction/accusative; in der Mitte — location/dative).
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel steckt genau in der Tasche.
native_language_example: The key is exactly in the pocket.

meaning: 'exactly do/want' — used to ask for more precise information about someone's intentions or plans.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions (often with 'was', 'wie', 'woher', etc.). 'Genau' adds emphasis: you're asking for specific details or clarification. Word order: 'genau' directly before the verb or question word group (e.g. 'Was genau willst du?').
target_language_example: Was genau willst du von mir?
native_language_example: What exactly do you want from me?

meaning: the same size; equally big
additional_notes: Used to compare sizes or extents. Often appears in comparisons with wie (genauso groß wie = as big as) or to say two things are equally large: 'Das Haus ist genauso groß.' Can also be used more broadly for 'just as ...' when paired with adjectives (genauso + adjective).
target_language_example: Mein Auto ist genauso groß wie deins.
native_language_example: My car is just as big as yours.

meaning: just as well; equally well; might as well
additional_notes: Used to compare ability or likelihood (equal degree) — e.g. 'just as good as'. Also used in hypothetical or modal phrases to mean 'might as well' or 'it could equally be' (often followed by a verb or clause). Context determines whether it's a literal comparison (ability) or a suggestion/hypothetical.
target_language_example: Du kannst genauso gut morgen kommen.
native_language_example: You might just as well come tomorrow.

meaning: has taken / took (perfect tense form using past participle 'genommen' with auxiliary 'hat' of the verb nehmen).
additional_notes: This is the auxiliary-plus-past-participle construction used to form the Perfekt (present perfect) of nehmen for third-person singular and formal contexts with 'hat'. Context-dependent: literal (took something), reflexive (sich nehmen = to take for oneself; e.g., sich eine Frau nehmen), or idiomatic (sich das Leben nehmen = to take one's own life). Word order: appears as part of the verb phrase or clause (e.g., in subordinate clauses the auxiliary may follow the participle: ...genommen hat).
target_language_example: Ich habe gesehen, wie er es genommen hat.
native_language_example: I saw how he took it.

meaning: enough of it / tired of it / had enough
additional_notes: Used to say you have had enough of something or are fed up. Context determines if it refers to quantity (enough of it) or to being fed up (I've had enough of it). Often stands after verb: Ich habe genug davon. Can be followed by a clause with 'zu' + infinitive or 'dass'.
target_language_example: Ich habe genug davon, jeden Abend aufzuräumen.
native_language_example: I've had enough of tidying up every evening.

meaning: just (doing something) / right at (a place or activity) — indicates something happening just now or at the moment, often before a verb or noun.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. 'gerade' = 'just/right now'. 'am' is a contraction of 'an dem' and often combines with nouns (am Bahnhof, am Strand) or with verb-noun constructions in colloquial German (am Essen sein = eating). Use to say someone is currently at a place or in the middle of an activity. Word order: 'gerade am' usually appears before the noun or activity. Not used with all verbs; many activities use 'gerade' + verb (ich esse gerade) or 'gerade dabei, ...' alternatively.
target_language_example: Er ist gerade am Kochen.
native_language_example: He is just cooking / he is cooking right now.

meaning: 'just/currently on the' (used before a masculine or neuter dative noun)
additional_notes: Combines 'gerade' (just/right now) + prepositional phrase 'auf dem' (on the). Used to describe something happening right now or just recently while located 'on' something. 'Dem' is dative masculine or neuter, so the noun after it will be in dative (e.g. 'gerade auf dem Weg', 'gerade auf dem Tisch'). Common in spoken and written German to indicate immediate action or current location.
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade auf dem Weg.
native_language_example: I'm just on the way / I'm on my way right now.

meaning: to have just learned that / I just found out that
additional_notes: Used to say you have only just been informed of some fact. "gerade" = just/recently, "erfahren" = to learn/find out, "daß" (modern spelling: "dass") introduces the new information. Common in both formal (Sie) and informal (du/ihr) contexts. Tense in the sentence is usually present perfect (haben + past participle erfahren).
target_language_example: Ich habe gerade erfahren, daß du nach Berlin gezogen bist.
native_language_example: I just found out that you moved to Berlin.

meaning: 'to be about to leave' or 'to be just leaving'
additional_notes: Used to say someone was on the point of leaving or had just decided to leave when something else happened. Often appears with the past tense (wollte gerade gehen) to express an interrupted action. 'gerade' here means 'just/about to' rather than 'just now'.
target_language_example: Ich wollte gerade gehen, da klingelte das Telefon.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when the phone rang.

meaning: just; exactly at this moment (often combined with verbs or directions) — 'just now' / 'just to/toward'.
additional_notes: ‘gerade’ means 'just' or 'exactly'; when followed by a direction/place with verbs of motion it can mean 'just to/toward' (e.g. 'gerade nach Rom' = 'just to Rome'). In other contexts 'gerade' + verb indicates something happening right now or recently ('gerade nach dir gesucht' = 'just looked for you'). Pay attention to word order: the phrase may separate across the sentence (e.g. 'ist gerade nach Boston zurückgekommen'). It is compositional and not informal.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn gerade nach dem Weg gefragt.
native_language_example: I just asked him for directions.

meaning: just (barely) / only just / at the last moment
additional_notes: Used to say something happened only narrowly or was only just enough. Can describe barely managing to do something (Ich habe den Zug gerade noch erreicht), or that something is still missing or sufficient (Uns fehlen gerade noch Sie und Ihr Kind; Dafür reicht es gerade noch). Also used in narrative to emphasize a recent action (Ich hab gerade noch mit ihm gesprochen). Tone is neutral and common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus gerade noch erwischt.
native_language_example: I just barely caught the bus.

meaning: just/at the moment + 'very' (emphasizes current degree or timing).
additional_notes: Combines gerade (meaning 'just' or 'right now') with sehr ('very'). Often used to describe someone's current state or to soften/ironically downplay a quality (e.g., 'nicht gerade sehr...' = 'not exactly very...'). Placement: gerade usually goes before adjectives or adverbs to mark the present moment.
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade sehr müde.
native_language_example: I am very tired right now.

meaning: 'something just/just now' or 'something happening right now' (informal spoken German)
additional_notes: Common in colloquial German. 'gerade' = 'just/at the moment'; 'was' = 'something' (informal). Used to ask if someone heard/said something just now, or to say that something is currently happening or coming. In more formal German you'd use 'etwas' instead of 'was' ('gerade etwas'). Word order and context decide whether it refers to a recent event ('just now') or an ongoing action ('right now').
target_language_example: Hast du gerade was gesehen?
native_language_example: Did you just see something?

meaning: to get out of (a state) / to fall into (a different, often negative, state) — used with nouns like Kontrolle, Fassung, Zeitplan (e.g. 'außer Kontrolle geraten' = to get out of control).
additional_notes: This is part of the separable verb geräten (past: geriet) + an adverbial phrase 'außer' + a noun. In German you usually see the full phrase 'außer + noun + geraten' (present: gerät außer ... / past: geriet außer ...). It describes something moving into an undesirable or unexpected condition (außer Kontrolle, außer Fassung, außer Plan). Common collocations: außer Kontrolle geraten, außer Fassung geraten, außer Zeit geraten/außer Plan geraten. Use past tense 'geriet außer' for simple past narrative; present perfect is 'ist außer ... geraten.'
target_language_example: Die Party geriet außer Kontrolle.
native_language_example: The party got out of control.

meaning: 'to like (to) ...' when used with verbs like erinnern (sich an) or with locations/activities: 'to enjoy' or 'to like being/doing (something)'.
additional_notes: Gern (also written gerne) means 'gladly' or 'to like doing something'. When combined with verbs that require 'an' (e.g. sich erinnern an = to remember), 'gern an' appears in sentences like 'sich gern an ... erinnern' = 'to fondly remember ...'.
