'eine' agrees with a feminine noun or a noun phrase introduced by 'eine/solche/so...' (e.g. eine Giraffe, eine so schreckliche Geschichte, eine solche Verschwendung). Replace 'eine' with other articles for different genders/numbers (z. B. 'einen' for masculine accusative, 'ein' for neuter).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie eine Oper live gehört.
native_language_example: I've never heard an opera live.

meaning: 'have (for) a long time' — used to say you haven't done/received/seen something for a long time
additional_notes: This phrase is part of the present perfect construction (Ich habe ...). 'schon lange' emphasizes a long period. Often appears with negative words (kein/nie/nichts/keine mehr/nichts mehr) to mean 'haven't ... for a long time' or 'haven't heard/seen/used ... in a long time.' Word order and endings may change (e.g. Ich habe schon lange nichts mehr gehört).
target_language_example: Ich habe schon lange keine Briefe von meinen Eltern bekommen.
native_language_example: I haven't received any letters from my parents for a long time.

meaning: 'have (something) for' or 'have (done) something for (someone/price/consideration)'.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'haben' (here as part of a perfect tense) + object 'sie' + preposition 'für'. Depending on context, 'für' can indicate recipient ('for someone'), purpose/intended person ('for Tom'), price/exchange ('for ten dollars'), mistaken identity ('considered/held for'), or value ('for almost nothing'). In English translations you may need to change word order: e.g. 'I wrote it for Tom', 'I bought them for everyone', 'I thought she was a prostitute', 'I got it for almost nothing', 'I sold it for ten dollars.'
target_language_example: Ich habe sie für meine Freundin gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought them for my girlfriend.

meaning: I saw/called/met her yesterday (part of a past-tense sentence: 'I have/ I did ... her yesterday').
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself but a common phrase fragment in the Perfekt (present perfect) construction: 'Ich habe ... gestern ...' + past participle (e.g. angerufen, getroffen, gesehen). 'Sie' can mean 'her' (accusative) or the formal 'you' (Sie) depending on context, but in these examples it means 'her'. Use it to say you contacted or met someone yesterday.
target_language_example: Ich habe sie gestern im Park getroffen.
native_language_example: I met her in the park yesterday.

meaning: have (met/visited/heard) her in/at (a place).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a past-tense sentence using the present perfect (Perfekt) with 'haben' + past participle; 'sie' = her/they (context-dependent, here 'her'). 'in' introduces a location (country, city, building, room) and may combine with an article or place name: e.g. 'in Australien', 'in Paris', 'in der Bibliothek', 'in ihrem Zimmer'. The full sentence needs a past participle verb later (kennengelernt, besucht, getroffen, gehört).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie in Barcelona getroffen.
native_language_example: I met her in Barcelona.

meaning: 'have not (seen/done) her/it' — the present perfect (or subjunctive perfect) negation used with 'ich/er/sie' + object 'sie'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines a form of 'haben' (habe) + object pronoun 'sie' + negation 'nicht'. Depending on context it can mean 'I haven't seen her/it' or 'he hasn't (done something to) her'. In reported speech German can use the Konjunktiv I perfect (er habe sie nicht …) to report what someone said (e.g. 'Tom sagt, er habe sie nicht töten wollen' = 'Tom says he did not want to kill her'). Word order may change (e.g. 'Ich habe sie nicht gesehen'). 'Sie' can mean 'her' or 'them' or formal 'you' depending on context; here examples use 'her'.
target_language_example: Ich habe sie nicht gesehen, als ich nach Hause kam.
native_language_example: I didn't see her when I came home.

meaning: I never have/I've never (her/it).
additional_notes: Common fragment meaning 'I never [verb] her/it' when used with a past participle: 'Ich habe sie nie gesehen' = 'I never saw her/it' (perfect tense). 'Sie' can mean 'her' (accusative) or 'you' formal in other contexts, but here it's 'her/it'. 'Nie' = never; word order: subject + auxiliary (habe) + object (sie) + nie + past participle or main verb (depending on tense).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie nie wieder angerufen.
native_language_example: I never called her again.

meaning: I happened to meet her / I ran into her by chance.
additional_notes: Combines the auxiliary 'habe' (from 'haben' used in the present perfect) + object 'sie' (her) + adverb 'zufällig' (by chance). Used to say you met a female person unexpectedly. Word order may change in different tenses or with pronouns (e.g. 'Ich traf sie zufällig' or 'Ich habe ihn zufällig getroffen' for 'him').
target_language_example: Ich habe sie zufällig gestern im Café getroffen.
native_language_example: I happened to meet her in the café yesterday.

meaning: 'have forgotten' — first-person singular perfect construction (literally 'have forgotten'); used to indicate that someone has forgotten something or to have failed to do something
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to say you forgot an object or to perform an action. Appears as part of the Perfekt (present perfect) with an object or infinitive clause, e.g. 'Ich habe vergessen, das Licht auszumachen.' Can be used in polite apologies or explanations. Note that 'habe vergessen' is specific to first person singular; other persons use forms like 'hast vergessen', 'hat vergessen', 'haben vergessen'.
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, meinen Schlüssel mitzunehmen.
native_language_example: I have forgotten to take my key. / I forgot to take my key.

meaning: I forgot to ... (followed by an action/object).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Ich habe vergessen, das ... zu ...' or 'Ich habe vergessen, das ...' + infinitive/participle. Use to say you forgot to do something or forgot an action (e.g., close the window, turn off the light). In spoken German the comma is often omitted and word order can vary: 'Ich habe das vergessen' (I forgot that/it) vs. 'Ich habe vergessen, das Fenster zu schließen' (I forgot to close the window).
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, das Fenster zu schließen.
native_language_example: I forgot to close the window.

meaning: 'I overslept' (present perfect: 'I have overslept' → used as 'I overslept').
additional_notes: Common way to say you slept longer than intended and missed something (alarm, bus, class). Often used in the perfect tense with 'ich habe verschlafen'. Can stand alone as a short explanation or apology.
target_language_example: Ich habe verschlafen und bin deswegen zu spät zur Arbeit gekommen.
native_language_example: I overslept and was therefore late for work.

meaning: I understand / I have understood (I got it).
additional_notes: Common phrase to confirm comprehension. Standalone 'Habe verstanden.' is an informal/neutral short way to say 'Got it.' In full sentences use 'Ich habe verstanden.' to indicate you understood something said or explained. Can be used in spoken or written communication (messages, commands).
target_language_example: Habe verstanden, ich komme um 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: Got it, I'll come at 6 PM.

meaning: have heard a lot about / have learned a lot from
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'viel von + jemandem/etwas haben' can mean either 'to have heard a lot about (someone)' or 'to have learned a lot from (someone)'. With 'gehört' it means 'heard about' (reputation). With verbs like 'gelernt' it means 'learned from' (experience or lessons). Common in polite introductions and when praising someone's influence or reputation.
target_language_example: Ich habe viel von Ihnen gehört, deshalb freue ich mich auf die Zusammenarbeit.
native_language_example: I have heard a lot about you, so I'm looking forward to working together.

meaning: I ... the day before yesterday (present perfect with time expression).
additional_notes: Combines the auxiliary verb 'habe' (I have) with the time expression 'vorgestern' (the day before yesterday). In German, actions in the recent past are often expressed with the present perfect (Perfekt): 'Ich habe ... gesehen/gekauft/besucht.' Use 'vorgestern' to indicate the action happened two days ago. Replace the past participle (gesehen, gekauft, besucht) as needed.
target_language_example: Ich habe vorgestern ein Buch gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a book the day before yesterday.

meaning: have too much / have done too much (of something).
additional_notes: Used after a personal subject with a past participle (Perfekt) or with another verb to say you did something excessively (e.g., eaten, drunk, talked, slept). Common structure: Ich habe zu viel + past participle (gegessen, getrunken, geredet). Can also be used in present-like statements: Ich habe zu viel (gegessen).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe zu viel Kaffee getrunken.
native_language_example: I think I drank too much coffee.

meaning: 'what I have is' / structure: 'What I have is...' or 'What I want/need to say is...'
additional_notes: This is a common German sentence structure combining a relative clause with the verbs haben (here: 'habe' in first person) and sein ('ist'). It often appears as 'Alles, was ich habe, ist ...' (Everything I have is ...) or 'Was ich (ihnen/euch) zu sagen habe, ist ...' (What I have to tell you is ...). The relative clause (Was ich ... habe) comes before the main clause with 'ist'. Use appropriate pronouns/cases (ich, Ihnen, euch).
target_language_example: Was ich dir sagen habe, ist kurz und wichtig.
native_language_example: What I have to tell you is short and important.

meaning: to be afraid of / to fear (something).
additional_notes: Used with the accusative after 'vor' (e.g. vor Schlangen, vor dem Sterben). Conjugate 'haben' for person: ich habe Angst vor..., du hast Angst vor..., er/sie hat Angst vor... Formal subjunctive (Konjunktiv I) can appear in reported speech (e.g. er habe Angst vor...). Common for fears of people, animals, situations, or abstract things.
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor Spinnen.
native_language_example: I am afraid of spiders.

meaning: 'have (to) you' in formal address — part of sentences meaning 'I have (something) for you' or 'I have (nothing) to tell you'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a verb (habe) plus the formal dative pronoun Ihnen (you, polite). You will see it in sentences like 'Ich habe Ihnen etwas mitzuteilen' (I have something to tell you) or 'Ich habe Ihnen nichts zu sagen' (I have nothing to say to you). 'Ihnen' is formal (Sie → Ihnen). Word order and endings depend on the rest of the sentence (e.g. perfect: 'Ich habe Ihnen... mitgeteilt').
target_language_example: Ich habe Ihnen morgen die Informationen geschickt.
native_language_example: I will have sent you the information tomorrow.

meaning: I have the impression that / it seems to me that
additional_notes: Used to express a personal feeling, guess or tentative opinion about something; softer than a direct statement. Common in spoken and written German. Structure: 'Ich habe den Eindruck, dass ...' + subordinate clause with verb at the end.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Eindruck, dass das Wetter morgen besser wird.
native_language_example: I have the impression that the weather will get better tomorrow.

meaning: 'have' (form of haben) combined with the particle doch; used to add pleading/urgency in commands or to add expectation/reassurance in statements (English: 'please have', 'do have', 'after all', 'you know')
additional_notes: 'habe' is the first-person singular indicative and also appears in more formal/archaic imperatives; in spoken imperative the form is usually 'hab doch'. 'Doch' is a modal particle with multiple functions: (1) in pleas/commands it softens or urges (Habe doch Erbarmen mit mir! = Please have mercy on me!/Do have mercy on me!), (2) in statements it conveys expectation, reassurance or contradiction (Ich habe doch alles, was ich brauche, bei mir. = I do have everything I need with me/After all, I have everything I need). Translate according to context.
target_language_example: Habe doch Erbarmen mit mir!
native_language_example: Please have mercy on me. / Do have mercy on me.

meaning: have three
additional_notes: A short sequence showing possession of three of something. In German, the verb (haben) must be conjugated for the subject (ich habe = I have). 'habe drei' alone is not a complete sentence in formal writing without the subject, but appears naturally after the subject or in replies (e.g. 'Ich habe drei.'). Use with a noun: 'Ich habe drei Hunde.'
target_language_example: Ich habe drei Bücher.
native_language_example: I have three books.

meaning: have a
additional_notes: A basic, compositional combination of haben + ein, meaning to have something. In direct speech, habe usually means I have. In reported speech, as in er habe ein ... or sie habe ein ..., it can be Konjunktiv I and mean he has a / she has a. Also note that ein is used here with singular neuter nouns; with feminine nouns you would use eine, and with masculine accusative nouns usually einen.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Handy.
native_language_example: I have a new phone.

meaning: have a few / I have a few
additional_notes: Common phrase meaning 'I have a small number of...' or 'there are a few ... that I (or someone) have'. In sentences it's usually followed by a noun (Dinge, Fragen, Freunde). 'Ein paar' means 'a few' (countable, more than one but not many). Verb form changes with subject (ich habe, du hast, wir haben).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein paar Bücher, die du dir ausleihen kannst.
native_language_example: I have a few books you can borrow.

meaning: I have a few friends in (a place).
additional_notes: This is part of a sentence used to say you know a few people who live or are located in a particular city, country, company, etc. You normally finish the phrase with the place: e.g. 'habe ein paar Freunde in Berlin'. 'Ein paar' means 'a few' (small number). Verb 'habe' is first-person singular of 'haben' (to have).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein paar Freunde in Berlin.
native_language_example: I have a few friends in Berlin.

meaning: I have a wife and… (start of a sentence listing more information)
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: the speaker says they have a wife and then continues with another clause (e.g., describing her, saying what she does, or adding another fact). 'habe' is the first-person singular of 'haben' (to have). In full sentences you’ll usually see the subject 'Ich' explicitly: 'Ich habe eine Frau und ...' The phrase is neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Frau und zwei Kinder.
native_language_example: I have a wife and two children.

meaning: have a surprise (for someone) — used to say you have something unexpected planned or a gift for someone.
additional_notes: Common phrase in sentences like "Ich habe eine Überraschung für dich." Use with a person pronoun (für dich, für Sie, für euch). Can be used casually or formally (Sie). The verb form changes with subject: Ich habe, Du hast, Er hat. In reported speech or subjunctive (er sagte, er habe...) the form may change. Often followed by reveal or invitation (Komm, ...).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Überraschung für dich.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

meaning: 'have some' or 'I have a few'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb haben (here in 1st person singular: ich habe) + the quantifier einige meaning 'some' or 'a few'. Used to state possession of a non-specific plural amount. Context determines exact translation: 'some', 'a few', or 'several'. Followed by a plural noun. Word order can change with different subjects (e.g., 'wir haben einige').
target_language_example: Ich habe einige Bücher, die ich dir leihen kann.
native_language_example: I have some books I can lend you.

meaning: have enough (I have enough...)
additional_notes: Used to say you possess a sufficient amount of something (money, time, etc.). In sentences it's usually part of 'Ich habe genug ...' or 'Du hast genug ...'. Can be followed by a noun or an infinitive clause with 'um ... zu' (e.g. 'genug Geld, um es zu kaufen').
target_language_example: Ich habe genug Zeit, um ins Kino zu gehen.
native_language_example: I have enough time to go to the cinema.

meaning: literally 'have good' — used to say you possess something positive (news, chances, friends, reasons, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the verb haben ('to have') + adjective 'gut(e)' used before a noun. Common patterns: 'Ich habe gute Neuigkeiten' (I have good news), 'Ich habe gute Chancen' (I have good chances), 'Ich habe gute Freunde' (I have good friends). Remember to match adjective ending (gute/guten) to the noun's gender, number, and case.
target_language_example: Ich habe gute Neuigkeiten für dich.
native_language_example: I have good news for you.

meaning: I always have a (something). — used to say you regularly carry or wear an item.
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Ich habe immer einen/eine/immer + noun + dabei/auf' or simply 'Ich habe immer einen ...' to express a habit of carrying or wearing something for safety or convenience. Choose gender/ending to match the noun (einen for masculine accusative). If the item is carried, 'dabei' often appears (e.g. 'immer einen Schirm dabei').
target_language_example: Ich habe immer einen Regenschirm dabei.
native_language_example: I always have an umbrella with me.

meaning: have barely / have hardly (very little of something).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'ich habe kaum + Noun' or 'ich habe kaum + noch + Noun/energy'. 'kaum' weakens the amount — almost none. Use to say you nearly lack something. Word order: 'kaum' comes before the thing you lack. Can be used with other persons (e.g. 'er hat kaum...').
target_language_example: Ich habe kaum Zeit, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I have hardly any time to help you.

meaning: 'have more' (I have more ...)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb haben (to have) in the 1st person singular (ich habe) plus 'mehr' (more). Used to compare quantities with 'als' (than): ich habe mehr X als Y = I have more X than Y. Adjust noun and pluralization as needed. In other persons use 'hast/hat/ haben'.
target_language_example: Ich habe mehr Zeit als du.
native_language_example: I have more time than you.

meaning: have nothing
additional_notes: A short combination often used in sentences like "Ich habe nichts" (I have nothing) or "Ich habe nichts zu sagen" (I have nothing to say). In spoken German the full subject is usually included (ich, du, er/sie/es, etc.). Depending on context it can mean 'have nothing' (possession) or 'did nothing' when used in perfect/periphrastic constructions with past participles (less common without context).
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts Zeit verloren.
native_language_example: I have lost no time.

meaning: I still have one year (left).
additional_notes: Used to say there is one year remaining until something happens (end of school, graduation, a deadline). Often appears in patterns like 'Ich habe noch ein Jahr [X] vor mir' or 'Ich habe noch ein Jahr bis (zum) ...'. 'noch' emphasizes that the time remains.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch ein Jahr bis zur Prüfung.
native_language_example: I still have one year until the exam.

meaning: I still have one / I still have (something).
additional_notes: Common fragment used with a feminine or feminine-looking noun (eine) or with expressions like ‚eine Menge‘ (a lot). ‚Ich habe noch eine…‘ means you still possess or have remaining something (time, appointment, etc.). Complete the phrase with the noun or phrase: ‚eine Menge Zeit‘ (a lot of time), ‚eine Verabredung‘ (an appointment/date).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch eine Stunde.
native_language_example: I still have one hour.

meaning: only have
additional_notes: A common combination of the verb haben (to have) + nur (only). Used to say you possess or have available only a limited thing or amount. Word order: nur typically comes after the verb or before the noun/phrase it restricts. Can appear with other persons (hast nur, habt nur, haben nur).
target_language_example: Ich habe nur fünf Euro.
native_language_example: I only have five euros.

meaning: literally 'have only one' — used to say you possess a single item or only one of something
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short fragment you'd hear in a sentence (subject + verb + 'nur ein' + noun). You need the noun (and correct article/case) after 'ein' to complete the thought: e.g. 'Ich habe nur ein Buch.' For feminine or plural nouns the article changes: 'Ich habe nur eine Schwester.' / 'Ich habe nur zwei.' (note: 'nur zwei' because plural doesn't use 'ein').
target_language_example: Ich habe nur ein Fahrrad.
native_language_example: I only have one bicycle.

meaning: 'have bad' — part of phrases meaning 'I have bad (something)' (e.g. bad mood, bad news).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself but the start of sentences like "Ich habe schlechte Laune/Neuigkeiten/Nachrichten." It means you possess or are experiencing something negative (a bad mood, bad news, bad feelings). Common follow-ups: Laune (mood), Neuigkeiten/Nachrichten (news). In English you would usually say "I have bad..." or more naturally "I have bad news" / "I'm in a bad mood."
target_language_example: Ich habe schlechte Neuigkeiten für dich.
native_language_example: I have bad news for you.

meaning: I already have a (feminine/singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (eine) to say you already possess or have arranged something. Often appears in full sentences with different nouns: Arbeitsstelle (job), Eintrittskarte (ticket), Familie (family), Idee (idea), Verabredung (appointment/plan). In spoken German you might also hear 'hab schon eine' (colloquial). If the noun is masculine or neuter, 'eine' changes to 'einen' or 'ein' (e.g. 'ich habe schon einen Termin', 'ich habe schon ein Ticket').
target_language_example: Ich habe schon eine Wohnung.
native_language_example: I already have an apartment.

meaning: plan to
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (zu + verb or bare infinitive) to express a plan or intention. Often appears as 'ich habe vor, ...' followed by a comma and an infinitive clause (e.g. 'ich habe vor, nächstes Jahr zu reisen') or 'ich habe vor zu ...' without comma. Equivalent to 'be going to' or 'intend to' in English.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, im Sommer nach Spanien zu fahren.
native_language_example: I plan to go to Spain in the summer.

meaning: have something / there's something (informal, spoken).
additional_notes: A colloquial, abbreviated way to say 'habe etwas' (have something). Used in many contexts: possession (I have something that belongs to you), obligations (I have something to do), plans (I have something planned), bodily issues (I have something stuck between my teeth), or vague statements (Yes, I have something). In the subjunctive example ('er habe was damit zu tun') it's part of a subordinate clause and means 'has something to do with'. 'was' is an informal substitute for 'etwas'.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht — ich habe was zu erledigen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't — I have something to take care of.

meaning: I have little / I have few (something).
additional_notes: Common construction: 'ich habe wenig + noun' to say you have a small amount of something (money, experience, knowledge, chance, etc.). 'Wenig' is used with uncountable or mass nouns (wenig Geld, wenig Erfahrung). For countable nouns you'd use 'nur wenige' (e.g. 'nur wenige Freunde'). Word order follows normal German: verb second (Ich habe wenig Zeit.).
target_language_example: Ich habe wenig Zeit, aber ich helfe dir trotzdem.
native_language_example: I have little time, but I'll help you anyway.

meaning: have fewer / have less
additional_notes: Used to compare quantity with someone or something (comparative). 'Weniger' can mean 'fewer' (countable nouns) or 'less' (uncountable nouns). The verb changes with subject (ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat). Common structure: [subject] + habe/has + weniger + [noun] + als + [comparison].
target_language_example: Ich habe weniger Zeit als du.
native_language_example: I have less time than you.

meaning: have two
additional_notes: Combines the verb haben (to have) in the first-person singular (ich habe) with the number zwei (two). Used to state possession or quantity. In full sentences you usually include the subject ich (I) as in the examples, but in short answers you can omit ich and say "habe zwei" in informal spoken German (e.g., when responding to a question). Word order and endings may change in different grammatical contexts (e.g., questions: "Hast du zwei?"; past tense: "ich hatte zwei").
target_language_example: Ich habe zwei Katzen.
native_language_example: I have two cats.

meaning: 'to have' + 'your' (formal) — auxiliary verb + formal possessive pronoun (third person plural or formal 'Sie' construction).
additional_notes: In German, haben is the verb 'to have' used here as an auxiliary or main verb. Ihr (capitalized) in these examples is the formal possessive pronoun meaning 'your' when speaking politely to one person or a group (Sie). Note: In sentence-initial position 'Sie' (subject) and 'Ihr' (possessive) are different words; examples show constructions like 'Sie haben Ihr ...' = 'You (formal) have your ...'. The capitalization of Ihr indicates the polite form in some contexts; when not formal, 'ihr' can mean 'her' (possessive) or 'you (plural)'. Pay attention to word order: subject (Sie) + haben + Ihr + noun.
target_language_example: Sie haben Ihr Gepäck am Flughafen vergessen.
native_language_example: You (formal) forgot your luggage at the airport.

meaning: Have you started / When did you start...?
additional_notes: Polite/formal question (Sie) asking when someone began an activity. Often followed by an infinitive clause with 'zu' (e.g., 'zu lernen') or a verb without 'zu' after a comma. Use 'Wann haben Sie angefangen, ...?' to ask about the start time of a habit, activity, or relationship.
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie angefangen, Deutsch zu sprechen?
native_language_example: When did you start speaking German?

meaning: 'when did you last' or 'when was the last time (you) ...'
additional_notes: Polite/formal question form using the formal 'Sie'. Used to ask when someone last did a particular activity. Followed by a verb in the perfect tense (e.g., geduscht) or an infinitive phrase. For informal/familiar speech use 'hast du das letzte Mal'.
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Urlaub gemacht?
native_language_example: When did you last go on holiday?

meaning: used to ask how long someone needed to do something (How long did you take to...?)
additional_notes: This phrase uses the perfect tense with gebraucht (past participle of brauchen in the sense of 'to need/take time') plus the infinitive clause introduced by um ... zu. Common question: "Wie lange haben Sie gebraucht, um + verb (zu + infinitive)?" Can be used with informal 'hast du gebraucht, um' for du-form. Not to be confused with 'gebraucht' meaning 'used' (as in second-hand) — here it refers to time needed.
target_language_example: Wie lange haben Sie gebraucht, um Deutsch zu sprechen?
native_language_example: How long did you need to speak German? / How long did it take you to speak German?

meaning: Did you know (formal)?
additional_notes: Formal, slightly old-fashioned or more formal past-participle question form of 'wissen' used to ask whether someone knew something (often followed by 'daß'/'dass' + clause). In modern spoken German you'd often hear 'wussten Sie' or 'haben Sie gewusst' (note spelling: 'gewusst' is more common). Use 'Sie' for the formal 'you'.
target_language_example: Haben Sie gewußt, daß Tom in Australien geboren wurde?
native_language_example: Did you know that Tom was born in Australia?

meaning: a part of questions/statements meaning 'have (you) ... to' or 'said/said to / invited to' depending on context; often appears in perfect tense or questions about what someone said/did toward someone.
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the verb haben followed by the formal 'Sie' and the preposition/particle 'zu' used in different constructions. Common uses in the examples: (1–3) with a past participle (Das haben Sie zu mir gesagt) it refers to something you said to me (i.e. 'you said that to me'); (2–3) as a question 'Was haben Sie zu ... gesagt?' = 'What did you say to ...?'; (4) 'Wie viele Leute haben Sie zu Ihrer Feier eingeladen?' uses 'zu' with 'einladen' (to invite to) — here 'haben Sie ... zu Ihrer Feier eingeladen' = 'have you invited ... to your party'. Pay attention to word order: in questions the finite verb (haben) comes before Sie, and the past participle goes to the end. 'Sie' is formal 'you'.
target_language_example: Was haben Sie zu mir gesagt, als ich nicht da war?
native_language_example: What did you say to me when I wasn't there?

meaning: 'have all' or 'all have' depending on word order — often used to say that everyone/ everything has done or been affected (English: 'all have' / 'have all [something]')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb haben plus the quantifier alle. Word order matters: 'haben alle' (verb before 'alle') appears in sentences like 'Die Wildschweine haben alle unsere Kartoffeln gefressen' — here 'alle' modifies the object ('all our potatoes'). In 'Wir haben alle Eltern angeschrieben' the same structure means 'we have written to all parents' — 'alle' modifies 'Eltern'. In other cases 'alle haben' (subject 'alle') means 'everyone has' (e.g., 'Alle haben Hunger' = 'Everyone is hungry'). Pay attention to what 'alle' refers to (subject or object) and to case (nominative for subjects, accusative for direct objects).
target_language_example: Wir haben alle Tickets verkauft.
native_language_example: We have sold all the tickets.

meaning: 'to have the game' — used in German as part of perfect tenses: 'to win/lose the game' when combined with a past participle (e.g. gewonnen/verloren).
additional_notes: The verb 'haben' here is an auxiliary used to form the present perfect (Perfekt). You won't say 'haben das Spiel' alone to mean 'won' or 'lost' — you need the past participle after it: 'haben das Spiel gewonnen' (have won the game) or 'haben das Spiel verloren' (have lost the game). In spoken German Perfekt often replaces the simple past for events: 'Wir haben das Spiel gewonnen.' = 'We won the game.'
target_language_example: Wir haben das Spiel gestern klar gewonnen.
native_language_example: We won the game clearly yesterday.

meaning: The verb 'haben' (to have) followed by the masculine accusative indefinite article 'einen' — a grammatical pattern used when the direct object is a singular masculine noun. It appears in constructions expressing possession, completed actions (with a past participle), experiences, or actions performed on a masculine noun.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a common compositional pattern. Word order varies in subordinate clauses and questions. 'Einen' marks a masculine singular accusative noun (e.g. 'einen Tag', 'einen Fehler', 'einen Hund'). The meaning depends on context (possession, experience, completed action).
target_language_example: Wir haben einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: We made a mistake.

meaning: 'have' + 'almost' — used with a verb phrase to mean 'almost (did/have)'.
additional_notes: In German, 'fast' (almost) often appears after the auxiliary 'haben' or before a verb phrase to indicate that an action nearly happened or was nearly completed. Word order can vary: e.g. 'haben fast alle mitgemacht' = 'almost all took part' and 'haben fast den Bus verpasst' = 'almost missed the bus'. Translate according to the main verb (past actions with 'haben' usually form the perfect).
target_language_example: Wir haben fast das Spiel gewonnen.
native_language_example: We almost won the game.

meaning: have just
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haben + past participle) or with 'gerade' to indicate that an action happened a very short time ago. In English often translated as 'have just' or simply 'just' + past action. 'gerade' can also emphasize 'right now' in some contexts (we're doing it right now), but here with 'haben' it usually means 'just did'.
target_language_example: Wir haben gerade zu Abend gegessen.
native_language_example: We have just eaten dinner.

meaning: 'we are closed' (used by shops/businesses to say they are closed)
additional_notes: Common phrase used by store staff, on signs, or when answering calls to indicate a business is not open. Literally 'have closed' (perfect tense), but functions like the English present 'are closed'. Can be said firmly or politely with 'Tut mir leid' or 'Ruf später an'.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wir haben geschlossen. Kommen Sie morgen wieder.
native_language_example: Sorry, we are closed. Please come back tomorrow.

meaning: have their
additional_notes: not a fixed expression. It is the verb haben ('to have') plus the possessive pronoun ihr. In these examples, ihr means 'their' before a singular noun like Haus, Auto, or Leben. If written as Ihr, it can also mean polite 'your'.
target_language_example: Die Kinder haben ihr Zimmer schon aufgeräumt.
native_language_example: The children have already cleaned their room.

meaning: 'have ... for a long time' — used with a past participle to say that an action lasted a long time (we have/had been ... / we ... for a long time).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the verb 'haben' plus the adverb 'lange' to indicate duration. In the examples it's used with past participles (discussiert, gesprochen, gesucht, gewartet, überlegt) to form the perfect tense: 'Wir haben lange diskutiert' = 'We discussed for a long time' / 'We have discussed for a long time.' Can be used in present or perfect: 'Wir diskutieren lange' (we discuss for a long time) vs. 'Wir haben lange diskutiert' (we discussed for a long time).
target_language_example: Wir haben lange auf den Bus gewartet.
native_language_example: We waited for the bus for a long time.

meaning: have never (to me) / never ... me (have)
additional_notes: A word order chunk showing the present perfect or simple perfect auxiliary 'haben' + indirect object 'mir' + adverb 'nie' (never). Commonly appears in sentences like 'Sie haben mir nie ...' meaning 'You/They have never ... to me' or 'They never ... me'. The pronoun 'mir' indicates the action affected 'me'. Word order can change depending on tense and emphasis: e.g. 'Sie haben mir das nie gesagt.'
target_language_example: Sie haben mir nie die Wahrheit gesagt.
native_language_example: They have never told me the truth.

meaning: did they ... that
additional_notes: A common word order in German for questions and subordinate clauses uses haben (as auxiliary) + sie (they/you formal) + das (that/it). Context decides translation: in questions like "Wie haben sie das gemacht?" it means "How did they do that?" In statements like "Als Kinder haben sie das gespielt." it means "They played that as children." "Sie" can be formal 'you' or plural 'they' — capitalization in German distinguishes them in writing (Sie vs. sie).
target_language_example: Haben sie das gestern gesehen?
native_language_example: Did they see that yesterday?

meaning: "have they (her/them/it)" — used in questions or statements about people or things someone else has done or obtained.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the auxiliary verb haben (in past tenses or questions) with the pronoun sie (third-person plural or formal 'you') and the object pronoun sie (third-person singular feminine or plural). In spoken/written German word order and capitalization matter: 'Haben sie sie ...?' = 'Have they found/seen/caught her/them?' In statements like 'Da haben sie sie geholt.' = 'There they fetched her/them.' Context tells whether the first 'sie' is 'they' or formal 'you' (Sie). Pronunciation tends to run the words together, so pay attention to context to know who is subject and who is object.
target_language_example: Haben sie sie gestern in der Stadt gesehen?
native_language_example: Did they see her/them in town yesterday?

meaning: 'have' + reflexive 'us' + preposition 'on/at' — part of past tense phrases meaning 'we met/attacked on/at (a place)'.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in the Perfekt (present perfect) with a reflexive verb (kennenlernen: 'wir haben uns kennengelernt') or with other verbs (angreifen: 'haben uns angegriffen') plus a location introduced by auf (on/at). The word order separates the reflexive pronoun (uns) from the auxiliary (haben) and places the location phrase (auf ...) later: e.g. Wir haben uns auf der Straße kennengelernt = We met each other on the street. 'Auf' requires the correct case (auf der Straße).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns auf dem Festival kennengelernt.
native_language_example: We met each other at the festival.

meaning: 'we ... each other / ourselves in ...' — the auxiliary verb haben + reflexive pronoun uns + location preposition im (in dem). Used in perfect tense with a reflexive verb and a location.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common word order chunk: haben (perfect auxiliary) + uns (reflexive pronoun) + im (in + dem, 'in the') before a location noun. The main verb (seen, met, got lost, etc.) appears at the end in the past participle: e.g. Wir haben uns im Wald verirrt. = We got lost in the forest. 'Uns' indicates a reciprocal or reflexive action (we each other / ourselves). Change the pronoun for different persons (hast dich, haben uns, haben euch).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns im Park getroffen.
native_language_example: We met each other in the park.

meaning: 'have' (perfect tense) + reflexive 'ourselves' + 'with' — used to say you did something together/with someone in the past (e.g. became friends with, talked with, had fun with).
additional_notes: This is the perfect-tense construction of verbs that use the reflexive pronoun 'sich' plus the preposition 'mit' (e.g. sich anfreunden mit, sich unterhalten mit, sich amüsieren mit). In English it's often translated as 'we became friends with', 'we talked with', 'we had fun with'. The exact meaning depends on the main verb (anfreunden, unterhalten, amüsieren). Word order: haben + uns + past participle + mit + someone (or with someone can appear before participle depending on verb).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns mit den Nachbarn gut verstanden.
native_language_example: We got on well with the neighbors.

meaning: 'we only (did) ...' — used to say that something was limited or nothing more happened.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'haben' with the reflexive pronoun 'uns' (we/us) and the particle 'nur' (only). It appears in perfect tenses (e.g. 'Wir haben uns nur geküsst' = 'We only kissed'). 'Nur' limits the action (nothing more, just that). The exact meaning depends on the main verb that follows (geküsst, unterhalten, getroffen). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns nur kurz verabschiedet.
native_language_example: We only said goodbye briefly.

meaning: have many
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. 'viele' means 'many' and is used with plural countable nouns. In many sentences like your examples, 'haben' is just the auxiliary of the perfect tense, so English often translates it with the simple past: 'Wir haben viele Tiere gesehen' = 'We saw many animals.'
target_language_example: Wir haben viele Freunde in Berlin.
native_language_example: We have many friends in Berlin.

meaning: Not a standard fixed German phrase. On its own it's ungrammatical or a fragment. It could arise from combining the verb phrase 'haben vor' (to intend/plan) with the time expression 'vor drei' (before three), but correct sentences separate them (e.g. 'Ich habe vor, vor drei zu gehen' or 'Ich habe vor, um drei zu gehen'). Literally: 'to have plan before three' (awkward).
additional_notes: 'Haben vor' is used with an infinitive to mean 'to intend' (Ich habe vor, ...). 'vor drei' is a time phrase meaning 'before three' (o'clock) or 'three [units] ago' in some contexts. The sequence 'haben vor drei' without punctuation or additional words is not grammatical; you must insert a comma and an infinitive or re-order: e.g. 'Ich habe vor, vor drei zu gehen' (I plan to leave before three). Watch word order and commas.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor drei zu gehen. (nonstandard/colloquial omission of the comma — grammatically should be: 'Ich habe vor, vor drei zu gehen.')
native_language_example: I plan to leave before three.

meaning: 'to want to have' or 'to want (something)'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb haben (to have) with wollen (to want). Used to say you want something (to possess or receive it) or that you don't want it. Word order and endings change with subject and tense (e.g., ich will haben, wir wollten haben). In spoken German you may also hear contractions like 'haben wollen' in perfect constructions (e.g., 'ich habe das haben wollen' — rare). Here it's the simple idea 'to want to have/own/receive.'
target_language_example: Welche Tasche haben Sie haben wollen?
native_language_example: Which bag did you want to have?

meaning: we all have our ... (used to introduce something everyone possesses)
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a clause meaning 'we each possess' or 'we all have' followed by a noun (e.g. Fehler, Geheimnisse). It's used to acknowledge a common human trait or shared experience. Structure: Wir haben alle unsere + [plural noun]. Often followed by a plural noun referring to faults, stories, problems, roots, etc.
target_language_example: Wir haben alle unsere Erinnerungen.
native_language_example: We all have our memories.

meaning: also have
additional_notes: Combination of the verb haben (to have) with the adverb auch (also/too). Used to add that someone/something has something in addition to others or to point out a shared/extra situation. Word order follows normal German sentence structure: verb (haben) conjugated, then other elements; auch can appear after the verb, before or after the object depending on emphasis. Not an idiom—just two separate words.
target_language_example: Wir haben auch ein Problem.
native_language_example: We also have a problem.

meaning: to have the same (something) — used when two or more people share the same person, thing, or attribute.
additional_notes: Followed by a noun in the accusative (e.g. 'denselben Freundeskreis'). 'Denselben' is the masculine/neuter accusative singular form of 'derselbe' (the same). Use different forms for gender/number: dieselbe (fem. acc.), dieselben (plural). Common in everyday speech to say you share someone (friend, doctor, hairdresser) or something (name, preference).
target_language_example: Wir haben denselben Reiseführer.
native_language_example: We have the same guidebook.

meaning: have (with the particle doch adding emphasis, reassurance, contradiction, or expectation)
additional_notes: Combines the verb haben with the modal particle doch. Doch can indicate surprise, contrast, reassurance, or an appeal to shared knowledge (e.g., 'after all', 'of course', 'surely', or used in confirmation questions). Not a fixed idiom — translation depends on context and intonation. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Sie haben doch kurz Zeit.
native_language_example: You do have a moment, don't you?

meaning: to have something
additional_notes: Directly translates as "to have something." Used both for possession (e.g., "we have something to eat") and for idiomatic uses like "have something in mind" or "have something in common." Meaning depends on context and the words that follow (e.g., "etwas gemeinsam haben" = "to have something in common"). Word order in German often places "etwas" after the verb in spoken or emphatic structures.
target_language_example: Wir haben etwas Zeit, also können wir bleiben.
native_language_example: We have some time, so we can stay.

meaning: to have enough (of something); to be sufficient
additional_notes: Used with a noun (Geld, Zeit, Platz, Wasser, etc.) to say there is a sufficient amount. In statements the finite verb (haben) is conjugated and placed according to German word order (e.g. Wir haben genug Zeit). Can be used with pronouns or in questions (Haben Sie genug?). "Genug" can appear before or after the noun for slight emphasis: genug Zeit / Zeit genug (both common).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, wir haben genug Zeit.
native_language_example: I think we have enough time.

meaning: to have just / to currently have / to be doing something right now (depending on context)
additional_notes: Gerade is an adverb meaning 'just now', 'at the moment' or 'currently'. With haben it indicates a current state or recent occurrence: e.g. 'haben gerade Ferien' = 'are currently on vacation'; 'haben gerade Zeit' = 'have time right now'. Not every combination translates literally as 'have just'. Context decides whether it means 'just' (recently) or 'right now/at the moment'.
target_language_example: Wir haben gerade keine Termine und können helfen.
native_language_example: We don't have any appointments right now and can help.

meaning: to have (something) big / to be greatly affected by (something).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the verb haben + adjective große (feminine/ plural noun follows). Literally 'have big ...'. Common in sentences like 'haben große Angst' (are very afraid) or 'haben große Ohren' (have big ears). Remember adjective agrees with the noun: große Angst (die Angst), große Ohren (die Ohren).
target_language_example: Die Kinder haben große Freude an dem Spiel.
native_language_example: The children have great/enjoyment in the game.

meaning: always have
additional_notes: This is the verb haben (to have) followed by immer (always). In examples it expresses habitual or general truths (e.g. "they always have" or "they are always [doing/saying something]"). English translation depends on context: often "always have" (possession) or simply "always" when describing a repeated action or characteristic. Word order in German places immer after the verb or after the object, so you may also see "haben immer" as in the examples.
target_language_example: Wir haben immer Zeit für dich.
native_language_example: We always have time for you.

meaning: the verb 'haben' (to have) plus the particle 'ja' used to add emphasis or remind someone of a known fact (»after all«, »you know« or »remember that«).
additional_notes: Ja here is a modal particle (not the question word) that softens or emphasizes a statement and signals that the information should be obvious or already known to the listener. Common in spoken German. Placement: it follows the verb or appears elsewhere in the clause (e.g., 'Wir haben ja genug Zeit' = 'We have, after all, enough time'). Not every sentence with 'haben' uses 'ja'—it's optional and conveys attitude, not a literal meaning.
target_language_example: Du musst dich nicht beeilen, wir haben ja Zeit.
native_language_example: You don't have to hurry, we have time after all.

meaning: to not have time for (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are too busy or unwilling to deal with something/someone. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or verb in the infinitive (often introduced with 'zum' or 'für' + noun; e.g., keine Zeit für dich / keine Zeit zum Lesen). Common in everyday speech; verb 'haben' conjugates (e.g., ich habe, du hast).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit für ein Treffen.
native_language_example: I don't have time for a meeting today.

meaning: to have no other choice / to have no alternative
additional_notes: Used to say someone must do something because there is no viable alternative. Often appears with a subject: Wir/Ich/Er haben/habe keine andere Wahl. Can be used in past or conditional contexts (e.g., 'hatten keine andere Wahl', 'würden keine andere Wahl haben'). Formal and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir haben keine andere Wahl, als das Angebot anzunehmen.
native_language_example: We have no other choice but to accept the offer.

meaning: to be allowed to have / to be able to have (possibility or permission to possess something).
additional_notes: A combination of haben (to have) and können (can/able to). Used when talking about the possibility or permission to have/receive something. Context determines whether it means physical ability, possibility, or permission. In many cases native speakers prefer alternative constructions (z. B. 'etwas bekommen können' for 'to be able to get something'), but 'haben können' appears in sentences like 'Er konnte das Auto haben' (He could have the car) or in modal perfect forms ('hätten haben können' in complex tenses).
target_language_example: Wenn du sparst, kannst du bald ein eigenes Fahrrad haben können.
native_language_example: If you save, you may soon be able to have your own bike.

meaning: to have nothing to (do/say/lose/eat/etc.) — expresses lack of something (an action, item, reason, etc.).
additional_notes: Structure: haben (conjugated) + nichts + zu + infinitive or noun. Commonly followed by an infinitive (zu + Verb) — e.g. zu verlieren, zu tun, zu sagen, zu befürchten — or by a noun in spoken usage (e.g. zu essen). Neutral in register; context determines formality. Word order and verb conjugation change with subject (Wir haben nichts zu verlieren; Sie haben nichts zu sagen).
target_language_example: Wir haben nichts zu verlieren.
native_language_example: We have nothing to lose.

meaning: to still have one (something); to have one more / another
additional_notes: Combines the verb haben (to have) with noch (still/another) and the indefinite article ein. Used to say you still possess one of something, have one left, or can offer one more. Word order can change depending on sentence (e.g., 'Wir haben noch ein Zimmer' = 'We still have one room/We have one more room'). The noun that follows ein must match gender and case (ein/ eine/ einen...).
target_language_example: Wir haben noch ein Buch, das du ausleihen kannst.
native_language_example: We still have one book you can borrow.

meaning: to still have (one/something) / to have something remaining
additional_notes: Common structure meaning 'we still have [something]'. The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows (e.g. Gemeinsamkeit = a similarity, Menge = a lot, Rechnung offen = an unpaid bill, letzte Chance = last chance). 'haben noch' expresses that something remains or is left to do/resolve. Word order can change with different nouns or plural forms (e.g. 'wir haben noch viele Fragen').
target_language_example: Wir haben noch eine Frage.
native_language_example: We still have one question.

meaning: to still have; to continue to have (a state, feeling, or condition)
additional_notes: 'noch immer' = 'still' or 'even now' (slightly more formal/neutral than 'noch'). Used after the conjugated verb or after the object to indicate a continuing state. Common structure: haben (conjugated) + noch immer + noun, adjective, or clause. Works with questions and statements.
target_language_example: Die Leute haben noch immer Angst, aus dem Haus zu gehen.
native_language_example: The people still have fear of leaving the house.

meaning: to often have; frequently experience or possess something.
additional_notes: Combines the verb haben (to have) with the adverb oft (often). Used to say that someone frequently has a feeling, characteristic, possession, or situation. Word order: subject + haben + oft + object/compliment (often 'Angst haben' = to be afraid). Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Viele Menschen haben oft keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Many people often have no time.

meaning: 'already have enough' or 'we/they already have enough of (something)'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used with 'wir', 'ich', 'sie' etc. to say you already have enough of something and don't need more. 'Schon' here means 'already' or 'enough already' (adds emphasis). Often followed by a noun (Arbeit, Fotos, Probleme) or a clause. Can express refusal or that no more are needed.
target_language_example: Wir haben schon genug Essen für die Party.
native_language_example: We already have enough food for the party.

meaning: to be supposed to have (done) / ought to have (done)
additional_notes: Combines the perfect-infinitive auxiliary 'haben' with the modal 'sollen'. Used to talk about obligations or expectations in relation to a completed action (i.e., that someone was supposed to have done something). Often appears in contexts like reported requirements, expectations that something was already done, or mild criticism. English equivalents: 'should have (done)', 'was supposed to (have)'.
target_language_example: Du hättest das Buch längst haben sollen.
native_language_example: You should have had the book a long time ago.

meaning: have our / have ours (depends on sentence) — combination of the verb haben (to have) with the possessive pronoun unsere (our/ours).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the verb haben + the possessive unsere. Depending on context, unsere can be followed by a noun (unsere Pflichten = our duties) or stand alone as a pronoun (Die haben unsere = They have ours). Word order and endings change with gender, number and case (unser, unsere, unser, unseren).
target_language_example: Wir haben unsere Entscheidung getroffen.
native_language_example: We have made our decision.

meaning: to have a lot to (do) — used to say someone is very busy or has many tasks.
additional_notes: This phrase is followed by an infinitive verb (often 'tun', 'erledigen', 'machen' or similar) or the verb can be implicit when context makes it clear. Commonly used to describe being busy: e.g. 'Wir haben viel zu tun.' Neutral register, suitable for everyday speech and formal contexts. Not slang.
target_language_example: Ja, wir haben viel zu tun.
native_language_example: Yes, we have a lot to do.

meaning: to have something / to be related to something (colloquial)
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase: 'was' = 'something'. Meaning depends on context: can indicate relation ('have to do with'), possession ('have something'), or an obligation/activity ('have something to do'). Often shortened spoken form of 'etwas haben' or 'etwas zu tun haben'. Word order may change in full sentences (e.g. 'Wir haben etwas gemeinsam' → 'Wir haben was gemeinsam').
target_language_example: Viele Jobs haben was mit Technik zu tun.
native_language_example: Many jobs have something to do with technology.

meaning: to have little (few); to not have much of something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with nouns to say there is a small amount or few of something (time, money, options, etc.). Word order: subject + haben + wenig + noun (e.g. Wir haben wenig Zeit). Can be used in urgent commands (e.g. Fang an, wir haben wenig Zeit).
target_language_example: Wir haben wenig Zeit, also beeil dich bitte.
native_language_example: We have little time, so please hurry.

meaning: 'we have a' (used to say there is/are something for us — often 'we have a problem').
additional_notes: Literal word order is 'haben wir ein' as part of a clause (subject 'wir' + verb 'haben' + indefinite article 'ein' + noun). Commonly used in the fixed phrase 'haben wir ein Problem' meaning 'we have a problem' or 'this is a problem for us'. Can express discovery (Anscheinend haben wir ein...), a consequence (Dann haben wir ein...), a conditional warning (Wenn du lügst, haben wir ein...) or simple statement of possession. In the last example it appears in a locational sentence ('in Jurjewetz haben wir ein Zimmer' = 'in Yuryevets we have a room'), showing normal usage with other nouns.
target_language_example: Wenn das nicht klappt, haben wir ein Problem.
native_language_example: If that doesn't work, we have a problem.

meaning: to want to have; to desire to possess
additional_notes: A modal construction: haben (to have) + wollen (to want) expresses wanting to possess something. Used with objects or people (often in colloquial contexts). In German word order, wollen is the finite verb and haben appears as the infinitive or in perfect/subjunctive forms (e.g., 'haben wollen', 'hätte haben wollen' often surfaces as 'hätten ... haben wollen' or with auxiliary in compound tenses). Can express a present desire, past hypothetical desire, or necessity that someone insists on having something.
target_language_example: Sie wird das neue Auto haben wollen.
native_language_example: She will want to have the new car.

meaning: have/has (not) at all; used to emphasize complete absence of something.
additional_notes: Combine 'haben' with 'überhaupt' plus a negation (kein/keine/keinen) to stress that something is completely lacking or someone has no idea/sense of something. Often appears as 'haben überhaupt keinen/keinen ...' or 'haben überhaupt keine Ahnung.' Tone is neutral; common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Wir haben überhaupt keinen Kaffee mehr.
native_language_example: We don't have any coffee at all anymore.

meaning: 'do you (plural) have/think about it' or 'are you (plural) thinking about it/considering it' (depending on context)
additional_notes: A phrase combining the verb 'habt' (2nd person plural of 'haben') + pronoun 'ihr' (you plural) + prepositional object 'daran' ('on/about/it'). Commonly used in questions: e.g. asking whether a group has something on them ('habt ihr daran?' = 'do you have it with you?') or whether they are thinking about/considering something ('habt ihr daran gedacht?' = 'did you think about it?'). The meaning depends on the verb and tense around it ('habt ihr daran' alone is incomplete — often followed by a past participle like 'gedacht' or a noun).
target_language_example: Habt ihr daran gedacht, die Tickets zu kaufen?
native_language_example: Did you (all) think about buying the tickets?

meaning: 'did you need' or 'have you needed' (informal plural) — asking whether a group needed or used something.
additional_notes: This is the present perfect/question form using the verb brauchen with habt (2nd person plural of haben) + gebraucht (past participle). It addresses a group (ihr). Context determines tense/nuance: can ask about a past need ('did you need') or recent experience ('have you needed'). Formal address would be 'haben Sie gebraucht'. Note: In some contexts German uses 'gebraucht' to mean 'used' (as in second-hand), so context matters: 'habt ihr gebraucht' could also be part of 'habt ihr [etwas] gebraucht gekauft?' ('did you buy [something] used?').
target_language_example: Habt ihr gebraucht, was ihr wolltet? — Habt ihr gebraucht
native_language_example: Did you need what you wanted? — Have you needed

meaning: 'how long did you take to' / 'how long did it take you to' (do something).
additional_notes: Common question structure using the verb gebraucht (from brauchen in past tense: gebraucht haben) + 'um ... zu' + infinitive. Ask about the duration needed to complete an action. 'Habt ihr' is plural (you all). For singular polite/formal use 'haben Sie gebraucht, um...', for one person informal use 'hast du gebraucht, um...'.
target_language_example: Wie lange habt ihr gebraucht, um das Auto zu reparieren?
native_language_example: How long did it take you (all) to repair the car?

meaning: a question phrase: 'have you (plural) in the...?', asking whether a group saw/did something inside a specific feminine noun (dative).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (ihr = you plural) about something that happened or was done inside a location introduced by a feminine noun (die → der in dative). The verb following this phrase often is gesehen (seen), nachgesehen (looked), Bescheid gesagt (informed), geschrieben (written), etc. Word order: 'Habt ihr in der + [noun in dative] + [past participle/verb]?'
target_language_example: Habt ihr in der Garage nachgesehen?
native_language_example: Did you (all) check in the garage?

meaning: 'do you (plural) have anything else' or 'anything else with you/for you?'.
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking a group (informal 'ihr') if they have anything more — items, questions, requests, problems, etc. 'Sonst' here means 'else' or 'otherwise'. Word order may change in a full sentence (e.g. 'Habt ihr sonst noch Fragen?'). Informal because it uses 'ihr' (plural you).
target_language_example: Habt ihr sonst noch Fragen?
native_language_example: Do you (all) have any other questions?

meaning: 'you (plural) never (to) me' — expresses that a group of people never did something to or for the speaker (e.g. never told, never believed, never trusted me).
additional_notes: habt is the 2nd-person plural present form of haben (you have). In perfect or past constructions it's part of 'ihr habt mir nie ...' meaning 'you (all) never ... me'. mir is the dative pronoun 'to me' or 'me' in English indirect-object sense. nie means 'never'. Common verbs used with this phrase: glauben (to believe), sagen (to tell), vertrauen (to trust). Context: addressing a group (ihr), informal plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Ihr habt mir nie die Wahrheit gesagt.
native_language_example: You (all) never told me the truth.

meaning: you (plural) have a (masculine accusative) ...
additional_notes: Second-person plural present of 'haben' (ihr habt) followed by the indefinite article 'einen' (accusative masculine). Used when addressing a group (you all) about possessing or having someone or something that is masculine in grammatical gender. For feminine nouns use 'habt eine', for neuter 'habt ein', and for plural 'habt (keine/unsere/etc.)' or no article depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, ihr habt einen Reisepass.
native_language_example: I assume you (all) have a passport.

meaning: 'have no' (plural 'you' form) — used with Ihr to say that you (plural) do not have something
additional_notes: 'habt' is the second-person plural (ihr) form of 'haben' (to have). 'keine' is the negative determiner used before plural nouns or feminine/unspecified nouns (and as the plural of 'kein'). Together 'ihr habt keine ...' = 'you (all) have no ...' or 'you don't have any ...'. In commands or reassurance (Habt keine Angst) the verb can appear without 'ihr' and still addresses 'you' plural. Word order may change with emphasis: 'Ihr habt keine Chance' = 'You have no chance.'
target_language_example: Ihr habt keine Zeit, also beeilt euch.
native_language_example: You have no time, so hurry up.

meaning: 'you (plural) are right' or 'you're right' (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Present-tense phrase using ihr (informal plural 'you'). Common reply to agree with others. Can stand alone as short agreement. If speaking formally or to one person, use 'Sie haben recht' (formal) or 'du hast recht' (singular informal). Note capitalization: 'Recht' is not capitalized here.
target_language_example: Ihr habt recht, wir sollten früher losgehen.
native_language_example: You're right, we should leave earlier.

meaning: helped the (something) — past tense of helfen with dative article 'den' (plural or masculine dative).
additional_notes: Half is the simple past (preterite) of helfen (to help). Helfen takes the dative case, so the thing or people helped appear in dative (here 'den' can be the dative plural article or dative masculine singular in older usage, but in modern German 'den' + noun with -n is the dative plural: e.g. den Menschen → to the people). Use 'half' when speaking/writing in the past simple (written narratives); in spoken German the Perfekt form 'hat geholfen' is more common. Example sentences show 'half den Tisch decken' (helped set the table), 'half den Armen' (helped the poor), 'half den Menschen' (helped people).
target_language_example: Sie half den Nachbarn beim Umzug.
native_language_example: She helped the neighbors with the move.

meaning: literal: 'half of her' or 'half of their' — a fragment meaning half belonging to 'her' or 'them' (feminine or formal plural possessive form 'ihrer'), often part of larger phrases like 'halb ihrer ...' or 'die Hälfte ihrer ...'.
additional_notes: 'half ihrer' as written mixes English 'half' with German 'ihrer' and is nonstandard in German. Correct German forms are 'halb ihrer ...' or 'die Hälfte ihrer ...'. If you mean English 'half of her/their' used within German text, it's a code-switch. 'ihrer' is the genitive (or dative plural) possessive of 'sie' (she/they) or the formal 'Sie'. The phrase is a fragment and requires a noun or clause after it to be complete (e.g., 'halb ihrer Zeit').
target_language_example: halb ihrer Zeit arbeitet sie von zu Hause aus.
native_language_example: half of her time she works from home.

meaning: an informal/colloquial imperative meaning 'stop (it)' or 'stop that' (tell someone to stop a vehicle or an object).
additional_notes: Used in spoken German as a short command. 'Halt' here is the imperative of 'halten' (to stop/hold) and 'das' is a neuter pronoun referring to the thing to be stopped (e.g., das Auto, das Ding, das Licht). In full sentences you will often hear the object named (»Halt das Auto an!«). The negative is formed with 'nicht' (»Halt das Auto nicht an.«). This phrase is colloquial but common; in more formal contexts you might hear 'Halten Sie das Auto an.'
target_language_example: Halt das Fahrrad an, bitte.
native_language_example: Stop the bicycle, please.

meaning: 'hold that' or 'keep that (secret)'.
additional_notes: Literal imperative phrase using halten (to hold). Can mean physically hold something (Halte das fest! — 'Hold this tightly!') or tell someone to keep something secret (Bitte halte das geheim — 'Please keep this secret'). With context it can also be an exclamation like 'Halte das!' meaning 'Hold on!' or in 'Ich halte das nicht aus' it's part of a different construction meaning 'I can't stand/endure that' (there the verb is conjugated for 'ich' and 'das' is the object). 'Halte das mal!' is a colloquial, softer imperative. Tone and context determine whether it's physical, secret-keeping, or emotional.
target_language_example: Halte das bitte kurz, ich mache die Tür auf.
native_language_example: Please hold this briefly, I'll open the door.

meaning: I consider that / I regard that as...
additional_notes: Used to state your opinion about something mentioned before (das = that/it). Followed by a noun phrase with appropriate case (often accusative after 'für' — e.g. 'eine Lüge', 'einen Fehler') or an adjective ('für unangebracht', 'für offensichtlich'). Common in statements like 'Ich halte das für + (article) + noun' or 'Ich halte das für + adjective'.
target_language_example: Ich halte das für einen Fehler.
native_language_example: I consider that to be a mistake.

meaning: imperative form 'hold/keep the' (informal singular or plural imperative depending on context).
additional_notes: Halte is the imperative of halten (to hold/keep). 'Halte die' is followed by a feminine or plural noun in accusative (die Augen, die Hand, die Ohren, die Streichhölzer). It can mean 'keep the [something]' or 'hold the [something]' or be part of fixed expressions like 'Halte die Ohren steif!' (stay strong). In sentence 5 the verb 'halte' is used in a declarative present (Ich halte...) not an imperative, so watch the difference in meaning depending on subject and punctuation.
target_language_example: Halte die Tür bitte offen.
native_language_example: Please keep the door open.

meaning: think/regard something as (e.g. 'I consider it ...').
additional_notes: Used with an adjective, noun phrase or clause to say what you consider or judge something to be. Structure: subject + halte es für + [adj./noun/clause]. Common in formal and neutral contexts. Followed by 'besser', 'falsch', 'das Beste' or a full clause with 'wenn'/'zu...'.
target_language_example: Ich halte es für gefährlich, nachts allein spazieren zu gehen.
native_language_example: I consider it dangerous to walk alone at night.

meaning: Hold him (physically); stop him.
additional_notes: Imperative or present-tense phrase using halten (to hold/stop) + accusative pronoun ihn (him). Depending on context it can mean 'hold him' (physically grasp or keep someone) or 'stop/detain him' (e.g. in commands). Can be softened with 'mal' (Halte ihn mal). In conversational contexts 'Ich halte ihn nur' means 'I'm just holding him' or 'I'm only keeping him (for a moment)'.
target_language_example: Halte ihn bitte fest, bis die Polizei kommt.
native_language_example: Please hold him firmly until the police arrive.

meaning: consider him (to be) / think him (to be).
additional_notes: Verb phrase using halten + accusative + für + noun/adjective. Used to express an opinion about someone: 'I consider him to be ...' or 'I think he's ...'. Change pronouns/forms as needed (halte sie für, halte dich für, halte ihn für ...). Often followed by a noun or adjective: halte ihn für zuverlässig / halte ihn für einen Freund. In spoken German the 'für' is necessary to connect the opinion to the classification.
target_language_example: Ich halte ihn für zuverlässig.
native_language_example: I consider him to be reliable.

meaning: hold it/her
additional_notes: Two different uses depending on context: 1) Literal: imperative or present tense of halten + object pronoun sie = 'hold it/her' (physical action). Example 1 shows a physical command. 2) Idiomatic: in expressions like 'jemanden für etwas halten' meaning 'to consider/regard someone as ...' — then 'ich halte sie für...' = 'I consider her (to be)...' Example 2 and 3 show this meaning. Word order and punctuation can mark reported speech or subjunctive (e.g. 'er halte sie für...' in reported speech).
target_language_example: Ich halte sie für zuverlässig.
native_language_example: I consider her reliable.

meaning: 'what do you think of that?' or 'how do you feel about that?'.
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrase used to ask someone's opinion or reaction to an idea, plan, person, or action. Often appears as a full question: "Was halten Sie davon?" (What do you think about that?). Use 'Was hältst du davon?' for informal (du) address. Can be followed by a clause: "Was halten Sie davon, ...?" (How about ...?).
target_language_example: Was halten Sie davon, morgen einen Ausflug zu machen?
native_language_example: What do you think about going on a trip tomorrow?

meaning: 'to think of' or 'what do you think of' (asking for someone's opinion)
additional_notes: Formal / polite form using Sie. Often appears in questions: 'Was halten Sie von ...?' = 'What do you think of ...?' Can be followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g. 'dem Film', 'der Idee', 'mir'). For informal use with friends, use 'Was hältst du von ...?'.
target_language_example: Was halten Sie von dem neuen Restaurant?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new restaurant?

meaning: should/must hold (something) / are supposed to hold (someone/something); expresses obligation or expectation to hold
additional_notes: Combines the verb halten (to hold) with the modal verb sollen (should/ought to). Use in contexts where someone is expected or obligated to hold, keep, or maintain something or someone. Word order and tense follow normal German rules for modal verbs (e.g., in perfect tense the main verb goes to the infinitive form at the end: 'hat halten sollen' or more commonly 'hätte halten sollen' for conditional). Depending on context, it can mean physical holding (e.g., hold a baby) or more abstract holding (e.g., keep a promise, maintain a position).
target_language_example: Du sollst das Kind während der Fahrt halten sollen? → Du sollst das Kind während der Fahrt halten.
native_language_example: You are supposed to hold the child during the ride.

meaning: 'to keep ourselves' or 'to hold ourselves' — used in various reflexive expressions like 'keep to', 'stay', 'hold on to', or 'keep away from'.
additional_notes: This is the reflexive form of halten (halten + uns). The exact meaning depends on the rest of the phrase: • 'sich an etwas halten' = to stick to/obey (rules, plan). • 'sich bereit halten' = to be ready. • 'sich fernhalten (von)' = to keep away from. • 'jemand hält uns mit Gewalt fest' = someone holds us (physically). Pay attention to word order: the conjugated verb (halten) appears in second position and 'uns' usually comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Wir halten uns an die Abmachung.
native_language_example: We stick to the agreement.

meaning: 'hold/stop her/them' or 'keep her/them' (imperative, plural familiar)
additional_notes: Plural imperative of halten + pronoun sie (her/them). Used to tell a group (you all) to hold, stop, keep, or keep awake a female person or multiple people/objects (context decides if 'sie' = she or they). Meaning depends on the verb phrase: 'haltet sie auf' = stop them, 'haltet sie fest' = hold them tight, 'haltet sie wach' = keep her awake. Informal familiar address (ihr).
target_language_example: Haltet sie fest, bis die Polizei kommt!
native_language_example: Hold them tight until the police arrive!

meaning: a happy ending; a positive, satisfying conclusion (often of a story, film, or situation).
additional_notes: Borrowed from English and used in German with the same meaning. Common in everyday speech and media reviews. Can describe fictional plots or real-life situations that conclude well. Plural: happy Ends or Happy Ends (both seen). Pronunciation like English but with German stress.
target_language_example: Der Film hatte ein richtiges happy End — alle Probleme wurden gelöst.
native_language_example: The movie had a real happy ending — all problems were solved.

meaning: 'hate this' (present tense: 'I hate this') or reported/ subjunctive: 'he said he hates/hated this'.
additional_notes: hasse = first-person present of hassen (ich hasse = I hate). In reported speech German often uses the subjunctive I (Konjunktiv I) form 'er habe/er hasse' to report someone else's words: 'Er sagte, er hasse dieses Buch.' means 'He said he hates this book.' For simple statements use 'Ich hasse dieses Buch.' Word order: object (dieses Buch) can come after the verb.
target_language_example: Ich hasse dieses Buch; es ist langweilig.
native_language_example: I hate this book; it's boring.

meaning: 'I hate my...' — used to say you strongly dislike something you possess or someone close to you.
additional_notes: Hasse is the first-person singular of 'hassen' (to hate). 'Meine' is the feminine/ plural/possessive form 'my' that agrees with the following noun (e.g. meine Arbeit, meine Eltern, meine Wohnung). This phrase expresses strong negative feeling; in many situations 'nicht mögen' (don't like) is softer and more polite. Watch informal tone — 'hassen' can sound harsh in conversation.
target_language_example: Ich hasse meine alte Jacke — sie hat viele Löcher.
native_language_example: I hate my old jacket — it has many holes.

meaning: 'I hate my...' (expressing strong dislike toward a male person or masculine noun)
additional_notes: Contains the verb hassen (to hate) in the first person singular (ich hasse) plus the possessive meinen (my, masculine accusative). Use meinen when the noun is masculine and in the accusative (e.g. meinen Bruder, meinen Chef). For feminine nouns you would say 'hasse meine' (e.g. Ich hasse meine Schwester). This is a strong/emphatic phrase — avoid in polite contexts; choose mag nicht or nicht leiden for milder dislike.
target_language_example: Ich hasse meinen Kollegen nicht — er ist nur oft laut.
native_language_example: I don't hate my colleague — he's just often loud.

meaning: do they hate / they hate her/them (depends on capitalization and context).
additional_notes: Lowercase 'sie' after a verb is typically the 3rd-person plural pronoun 'they' (sie hassen = they hate). Capitalized 'Sie' is formal 'you' (Hassen Sie? = Do you hate?). In questions word order inverts: 'Hassen sie?' can mean 'Do they hate...?' if 'sie' is lowercase, or 'Do you hate...?' if 'Sie' is formal and capitalized. Also 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they' or formal 'you' depending on context; look for capitalization and surrounding words to tell which.
target_language_example: Warum hassen sie ihn?
native_language_example: Why do they hate him?

meaning: ‘you did say’ — used to remind or confirm something the other person previously said
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase. The particle doch adds emphasis or contradiction (meaning roughly ‘after all’ / ‘as I thought’). Used when reminding someone of their past statement or pointing out inconsistency. It appears in informal and neutral contexts. You can substitute other persons/verb forms (z. B. „du hast doch gesagt“, „er hat doch gesagt“, „hast du doch gesagt?“).
target_language_example: Du hast doch gesagt, du kommst später.
native_language_example: You did say you'd come later.

meaning: 'have you thought about/considered (it)' or 'do you have it in mind'
additional_notes: Common fragment used in questions. Often followed by a noun or clause (e.g. 'hast du daran gedacht?' = 'did you think of that?'; 'hast du daran gedacht, ...' = 'have you considered ...'). 'daran' is a combination of 'da' + 'an' meaning 'about/of it' or 'on that'. Can be used in both present ('hast du daran gedacht?') and past contexts. Useful in informal and formal speech; tone depends on verb and context.
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, die Schlüssel mitzunehmen?
native_language_example: Did you think about taking the keys with you?

meaning: Did you pay attention to that / did you notice that?
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone noticed or paid attention to a specific detail mentioned or implied (darauf = to that/about that). Often followed by a clause introduced with an interrogative (um wieviel Uhr, was, wo, etc.). Can be formal or neutral; word order may change in other tenses (z. B. "Hast du darauf geachtet?").
target_language_example: Hast du darauf geachtet, wo ich meine Tasche hingestellt habe?
native_language_example: Did you notice where I put my bag?

meaning: 'did you need' or 'have you needed' (informal, second person singular).
additional_notes: A question phrase using the auxiliary 'hast' + past participle 'gebraucht' (from brauchen) forming the present perfect to ask whether someone needed something. Often used with an object or additional context: e.g. 'Hast du gebraucht, dass...?' is uncommon; more natural with an object: 'Hast du das gebraucht?'. Used with 'du' (informal). For present-tense questions Germans more commonly use 'Brauchst du ...?'; 'Hast du gebraucht' refers to a completed need in the past or present perfect context.
target_language_example: Hast du gebraucht
native_language_example: Did you need (it)?

meaning: 'how long did you need to... / how long did it take you to...'
additional_notes: Commonly used in questions with the perfect tense (hast du gebraucht) + infinitive clause introduced by 'um ... zu' to ask how much time someone needed to do something. Word order: 'Wie lange hast du gebraucht, um + [infinitive phrase] zu + verb'. Informal/formal: neutral, everyday spoken and written German.
