target_language_example: Ich hatte mir den Urlaub schöner vorgestellt.
native_language_example: I had imagined the vacation would be nicer.

meaning: had not
additional_notes: Past tense (past perfect / simple past-like depending on context) negation: 'hatte' is the past form of 'haben' and 'nicht' negates the verb or clause. In English this usually becomes 'had not' or in conversational translation 'didn't' + verb (e.g. 'hadn't understood' → 'didn't understand'). Often used to say you did not expect, think, wait, etc., before another past event.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nicht gedacht, dass er uns helfen würde.
native_language_example: I hadn't thought that he would help us.

meaning: 'had never' — expresses that something did not happen before a certain past time or experience.
additional_notes: Combines the past tense auxiliary 'hatte' (preterite of 'haben' used in past perfect contexts) with 'nie' (never). Often appears in past perfect (Plusquamperfekt) or narrative past contexts to say someone had never done or experienced something up to that past point. English equivalents: 'had never (done/seen/expected...)' or 'never before'.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nie zuvor so etwas gesehen.
native_language_example: I had never seen anything like that before.

meaning: was hungry
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of 'Hunger haben' — describes being hungry at a specific time in the past. Common in storytelling or recounting past events. In spoken German, the Perfekt ('hat Hunger gehabt') is also often used; 'hatte Hunger' is the simple past form.
target_language_example: Ich hatte Hunger und Durst.
native_language_example: I was hungry and thirsty.

meaning: had the (masculine/neuter singular accusative) — common past tense phrase meaning 'had the' or 'had' with a specific masculine/neuter object.
additional_notes: ‘hatte’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of ‘haben’ (to have). ‘den’ is the masculine/neuter accusative definite article used when the direct object is masculine (or certain masculine nouns) or when fixed expressions use ‘den’. Together they introduce the thing someone possessed, felt, experienced, or had to do. Used in many contexts: possession (Tom hatte den ganzen Campingplatz), attributes/ambitions (Er hatte den Ehrgeiz...), tasks/orders (Ich hatte den Auftrag...), appearances (Es hatte den Anschein...). Word order after this phrase often continues with the object phrase or an infinitive clause introduced by ‘zu’ or ‘als’.
target_language_example: Sie hatte den Wunsch, zu reisen.
native_language_example: She had the desire to travel.

meaning: had something / was somewhat (depending on context)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past tense of haben (hatte) with etwas (something/somewhat). Depending on context it can mean: 1) literally 'had something' (possession: someone possessed an object), 2) 'had something in [one's] hand/under coat' (specific object), 3) 'had something to object' or 'had an objection' (hatte etwas einzuwenden), 4) idiomatically 'was somewhat' or 'had something about them' (Maria hatte etwas Geheimnisvolles an sich = she seemed a bit mysterious), or 5) 'who benefited?' (Wer hatte etwas davon? = Who got something out of it?). The meaning is determined by the rest of the sentence. Useful verbs/phrases to learn with it: etwas damit zu tun haben (to have something to do with it), etwas an sich haben (to have a certain quality), etwas davon haben (to benefit).
target_language_example: Sie hatte etwas Geld in ihrer Tasche.
native_language_example: She had some money in her bag.

meaning: an emphatic combination of the past-tense verb 'hatte' (had) + 'ganz' (very, completely, quite); used to intensify a past state or action
additional_notes: ‘Hatte’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of ‘haben’ or used as an auxiliary; ‘ganz’ intensifies an adjective, adverb, or past participle that follows (very/completely/quite). In different contexts it can mean 'very' (hatte ganz rote Wangen), 'completely/entirely' (hatte ganz vergessen), 'certainly' (ganz bestimmt), or 'simply' (ganz einfach). Word order: 'hatte' comes before 'ganz' and the adjective/participle follows.
target_language_example: Sie hatte ganz vergessen, den Schlüssel mitzunehmen.
native_language_example: She had completely forgotten to take the key.

meaning: adds emphasis or mild surprise to 'I had' — often means 'I really had' / 'I didn’t (know) after all' depending on context.
additional_notes: The particle 'ja' here doesn't translate directly; it softens or emphasizes the statement and can express surprise, reminding the listener of a known fact, or justify the speaker's attitude. Common in spoken German. Often used with 'keine Ahnung' (no idea): 'Ich hatte ja keine Ahnung' = 'I really had no idea' / 'I didn't know (as you probably know)'.
target_language_example: Ich hatte ja keine Ahnung, dass das Konzert ausverkauft ist!
native_language_example: I really had no idea that the concert is sold out!

meaning: 'used to have' or 'once had' (indicates past possession, relationship, job, injury, or experience).
additional_notes: Combines the simple past of 'haben' (hatte) with 'mal', which softens/generalisizes the statement or indicates a past occasion. Very common in spoken German. Can express habitual past or a single past instance. Often translated as 'I once had' or 'I used to have.' Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: Ich hatte mal einen gebrochenen Arm.
native_language_example: I once had a broken arm.

meaning: still had
additional_notes: Common past-tense phrase using haben (hatte) + noch. Usually means 'still had' (something remaining) or in negative contexts 'had not ... yet' when followed by words like keine/keine Zeit/keine Gelegenheit. Context determines whether 'noch' emphasizes continuation ('still') or incompletion ('yet'). Example structures: 'Ich hatte noch Zeit' = I still had time. 'Ich hatte noch keine Zeit' = I hadn't had time yet.
target_language_example: Ich hatte noch genug Geld, also bezahlte ich das Taxi.
native_language_example: I still had enough money, so I paid for the taxi.

meaning: 'had too much' (usually followed by a noun like Angst = 'had too much fear' → 'was too afraid')
additional_notes: Commonly appears with Gefühle (emotion) nouns, especially 'Angst' (fear). Structure: hatte zu große + [NOUN] + (um ... zu ... / als dass ...). Means the person felt such a strong degree of the noun that they could not do something. Use past tense (hatte).
target_language_example: Sie hatte zu große Angst, das Haus allein zu verlassen.
native_language_example: She was too afraid to leave the house alone.

meaning: 'did you have' or 'had you' (polite/formal past tense question to 'Sie')
additional_notes: Polite/formal second-person plural/singular (Sie) past tense of 'haben' used to form questions about past states or actions. Common in formal speech or when addressing someone respectfully. Word order: verb (hatten) comes first in yes/no questions. In subordinate clauses or past perfect contexts, word order differs (e.g., 'Sie hatten ... gehabt').
target_language_example: Hatten Sie gestern Zeit, ins Büro zu kommen?
native_language_example: Did you have time to come to the office yesterday?

meaning: had it
additional_notes: Usually just the regular combination of hatten ("had") and es ("it"). It is compositional rather than a fixed idiom, and it often appears in the pluperfect with a past participle, e.g. hatten es erwartet = "had expected it" or hatten es geschafft = "had managed it" / "had made it".
target_language_example: Wir hatten es erwartet.
native_language_example: We had expected it.

meaning: they had
additional_notes: Usually means 'they had'. In questions or with inverted word order, it can also correspond to 'had they'. It can be the simple past of haben ('they had something') or part of the past perfect with a past participle, as in hatten sie gesagt = 'they had said'. If written as Sie with a capital S, it can also mean formal 'you had'.
target_language_example: Vor dem Umzug hatten sie ein kleines Haus.
native_language_example: Before the move, they had a small house.

meaning: 'had a' — past tense plural (or polite past for formal singular) of haben + the indefinite article ein; indicates possession, experience, or occurrence in the past
additional_notes: Combination of the simple past plural (wir/sie) or polite past (Sie) form of haben (hatten) with the indefinite article ein. Used before a noun to say that people had something in the past. Remember to match the article to the noun's gender/case (ein/eine/einen) and adjust verb form for other subjects (ich hatte, du hattest, er/sie/es hatte, ihr hattet).
target_language_example: Alle hatten ein Fahrrad.
native_language_example: Everyone had a bicycle.

meaning: had no idea / didn't know
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum or Perfekt context) of 'keine Ahnung haben' — used to say someone did not know something. 'Hatten' is the 3rd person plural past of 'haben' (they had/no one had). Can refer to people or things like 'wir hatten keine Ahnung' (we had no idea). Common in everyday speech. To make it present: 'haben keine Ahnung'.
target_language_example: Wir hatten keine Ahnung, dass das Treffen abgesagt wurde.
native_language_example: We had no idea that the meeting was canceled.

meaning: had nothing / didn't have anything (past tense)
additional_notes: Combination of the past-tense verb 'hatten' (we/they/you formal had) and 'nichts' (nothing). Used to say someone lacked something in the past or that there was nothing (to do, to say, to lose, etc.). Word order can change with other elements (e.g. 'nichts zu verlieren', 'nichts gemeinsam'). Common in simple past descriptions or narratives.
target_language_example: Wir hatten nichts Interessantes zu sehen.
native_language_example: We had nothing interesting to see.

meaning: 'you were right' (past tense, singular informal 'du')
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (du) they were correct about something. Commonly followed by a clause or prepositional phrase introduced with 'mit' (about) or 'zu' (to + infinitive). Informal/personal — addresses one person you know well (du).
target_language_example: Du hattest Recht, ich hätte vorsichtiger sein sollen.
native_language_example: You were right; I should have been more careful.

meaning: 'you were right' (past tense, singular informal 'du' form)
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (du) that what they said or thought was correct. 'Hattest' is the simple past of 'haben' for 'du'; 'recht haben' = to be right. Can appear alone as a short reply. Formal or plural would be 'Sie hatten recht' / 'ihr hattet recht'.
target_language_example: Du hattest recht, das Wetter wurde besser.
native_language_example: You were right, the weather got better.

meaning: A Nazi salute meaning 'Hail Hitler' (greeting/support for Adolf Hitler and Nazism).
additional_notes: Extremely offensive, explicitly tied to Nazi ideology and crimes. Illegal to display or use in many countries (including Germany) except in historical, educational, or artistic contexts. Do not use — it's hate speech. If you need to refer to it, explain its historical context or quote it only when necessary for study.
target_language_example: In Geschichtsbüchern wird oft erklärt, warum Parolen wie ‚Heil Hitler!‘ verboten sind.
native_language_example: History books often explain why slogans like 'Heil Hitler!' are banned.

meaning: to marry and ... (used to link 'marry' with another action or result)
additional_notes: Heiraten means 'to marry'. When followed by 'und' it connects marriage to another verb or consequence (e.g. 'heiraten und sich niederlassen' = 'marry and settle down'). The second action is usually in the infinitive or reflexive form. Common in advice, plans, or describing motives. Not idiomatic on its own—needs the rest of the sentence to complete the idea.
target_language_example: Wir wollen heiraten und nach Spanien ziehen.
native_language_example: We want to get married and move to Spain.

meaning: 'we will marry' or 'we marry' (first-person plural, often used to propose marriage or state intention to marry)
additional_notes: Heiraten is the verb 'to marry'. In the form 'heiraten wir' it uses inverted word order typical for yes/no questions or emphatic statements in German (e.g., as a question: 'And then do we get married?'; as a statement: 'Then we get married.'). Context shows it can be an offer, a decision, or a question about marriage. For beginner learners: note difference in tone by intonation—question vs. statement—since written form can be identical except punctuation.
target_language_example: Wenn du bereit bist, heiraten wir nächstes Jahr.
native_language_example: If you are ready, we'll get married next year.

meaning: It's hot here. / It's hot in here.
additional_notes: Used to comment on the temperature of the current place (room, car, outside spot). Can be a full sentence (Es ist heiß hier) or shortened/informal (Heiß hier drin, nicht?). 'drin' or 'drinnen' specify 'inside'. Commonly used to complain or note warmth; tone can be neutral, surprised, or annoyed.
target_language_example: Ist es heiß hier drin!
native_language_example: It's so hot in here!

meaning: hot chocolate; a warm chocolate drink (often with milk).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for a warm chocolate beverage. Used when offering, ordering, or talking about the drink. Gender: die Schokolade (feminine); adjective agrees: heiße Schokolade. Can be served in a cup (Tasse).
target_language_example: Möchtest du eine heiße Schokolade?
native_language_example: Would you like a hot chocolate?

meaning: 'is called that' / 'is named that' (used to ask or state the name of something).
additional_notes: Used with objects, people or places to ask for or give their name. In questions it appears in phrases like "Wie heißt das...?" (What is that called?/What's the name of that?). In statements it can follow a noun: "So heißt das Schiff..." (That's the name of the ship...). The verb "heißen" means "to be called"; "das" is the demonstrative pronoun "that" or the neuter definite article used to refer to the thing in question.
target_language_example: Wie heißt das Restaurant dort?
native_language_example: What's the name of that restaurant over there?

meaning: 'What is the capital (called)?' (used to ask the name of a country's capital)
additional_notes: Common question phrase: put before the country name with von/der (e.g. "Wie heißt die Hauptstadt von Frankreich?" or "Wie heißt die Hauptstadt der Schweiz?"). Literal parts: heißt = 'is called', die Hauptstadt = 'the capital'. Use in spoken and written German to ask for a capital city.
target_language_example: Wie heißt die Hauptstadt von Japan?
native_language_example: What is the capital of Japan called?

meaning: 'doesn't mean' or 'is not equivalent to'
additional_notes: Used to deny that one fact or situation implies another. Common pattern: 'Dass ... heißt nicht, dass ...' (That ... does not mean that ...). Can also appear in informal contexts with nouns/pronouns ('du heißt nicht Tinte' = 'you are not called/are not...'), though that use involves 'heißen' as 'to be called' rather than the idiomatic implication meaning.
target_language_example: Dass wir es versuchen, heißt nicht, dass es klappt.
native_language_example: That we try it doesn't mean that it will work.

meaning: to help (me) with this / to help (someone) do this.
additional_notes: „helfen, dieses“ isn't a fixed phrase; it's the verb helfen followed by a direct object indicated by dieses (this). In German you often say helfen + zu + infinitive (e.g. helfen, dieses ... zu tun) or helfen + bei + noun. In requests use polite forms: Kannst du mir helfen, dieses ... zu + Infinitiv? (Can you help me to ... this?). Formal: Können Sie mir helfen, dieses ... zu + Infinitiv? Plural informal: Könnt ihr mir helfen. Use appropriate pronoun (mir/dir) and gender/case for dieses depending on the noun (dieses for neuter nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen, dieses Paket zur Post zu bringen?
native_language_example: Can you help me take this package to the post office?

meaning: to help (someone) stop smoking.
additional_notes: Used to offer or describe assistance for quitting smoking. German commonly uses helfen + (jemandem) + dabei/blank + infinitive clause with 'aufhören' (mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören). 'dabei' is optional and emphasizes 'in that process'. Pronouns change: Ihnen (formal), dir (informal singular), euch (informal plural).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir dabei helfen, mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören.
native_language_example: I can help you stop smoking.

meaning: ‘help (you) if you’ — a combination used to express conditional help depending on the other person's action or willingness.
additional_notes: Combines the verb helfen with a conditional clause beginning with wenn du (...). Common in offers or hypothetical statements: Ich kann dir helfen, wenn du ...; Maria würde dir helfen, wenn du ... . In the wenn-clause the finite verb goes to the end (e.g. wenn du mich lässt). Can be used with different persons and tenses (kann, würde, könnte).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir helfen, wenn du mich lässt.
native_language_example: I can help you if you let me.

meaning: ‘will help’ — future tense of 'helfen' (to help).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone helping in the future or to ask whether they will help. In German the verb 'helfen' is dative (e.g. 'jemandem helfen'). Here 'wird' is the future auxiliary (3rd person singular). Word order and context change with questions and subordinate clauses: e.g. 'ob er uns helfen wird' (whether he will help us), 'dass er uns helfen wird' (that he will help us).
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass Anna uns morgen helfen wird?
native_language_example: Do you think Anna will help us tomorrow?

meaning: to want to help; to be willing to help
additional_notes: A modal construction: helfen (to help) + wollen (to want). In German it expresses the intention or willingness to help someone. Conjugate wollen to match the subject and put helfen in the infinitive (e.g. Ich will helfen, Wir wollen helfen). Often used with dative objects: Ich will dir helfen. Word order can vary in subordinate clauses (…dass ich helfen wollen würde).
target_language_example: Ich will dir morgen beim Umzug helfen wollen.
native_language_example: I want to want to help you move tomorrow. (used to illustrate the exact phrase; in normal speech one would say "Ich will dir morgen beim Umzug helfen.")

meaning: 'would help' — conditional/ subjunctive-like form of 'helfen' using the auxiliary 'würde' to express a hypothetical, polite, conditional action, or reported speech
additional_notes: Combines the verb helfen with the conditional auxiliary würde. Used in reported speech (Er sagte, er würde helfen), to express expectation or surprise about a past conditional (Ich hatte nicht gedacht, dass er helfen würde), or to make polite/conditional offers (Ich sagte, ich würde helfen). Word order follows German rules: in subordinate clauses the auxiliary often appears near the end. Tone can be neutral or polite depending on context.
target_language_example: Er versprach, dass er uns helfen würde.
native_language_example: He promised that he would help us.

meaning: 'to be after' (following/pursuing) or in time expressions 'ago' (indicating how long ago something happened)
additional_notes: This phrase has two main uses: 1) Combined with a locative/agent phrase like 'hinter ... her sein' it means to follow or pursue someone (e.g. 'Er ist hinter Ihnen her' = 'He is after you / following you'). 2) In temporal expressions (often with 'Wie lange' or 'Das ist ... her') it expresses how long ago something occurred (English 'ago'). Word order: 'her' often appears at the end of the clause; 'sein' is the verb. Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Meinen Sie, dass er hinter Ihnen her sein könnte?
native_language_example: Do you think he could be after you / following you?

meaning: hervor: 'out' or 'out from' (movement out of/from something); und: 'and'.
additional_notes: In the examples 'hervor' is part of separable verbs or adverbial particles meaning movement out of or appearing from somewhere (e.g. 'hervorkommen', 'herausholen' / ‚etwas hervorholen‘). Here 'hervor' + verb indicates pulling or coming out from under/inside something. 'und' simply connects actions (and). Beginners will more often learn 'hervor' attached to the verb (separable prefix) or as an adverb; in everyday sentences you usually see the full verb (e.g. 'kam hervor', 'holte hervor').
target_language_example: Die Katze kroch aus der Kiste hervor und sprang auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: The cat came out of the box and jumped onto the table.

meaning: Congratulations (warm/heartfelt).
additional_notes: A common way to congratulate someone in German. Often used for birthdays, achievements, weddings, exams, etc. The adjective 'herzlichen' (heartfelt) makes it more warm than just 'Glückwunsch'. You can also say the shorter 'Glückwunsch' or the full sentence 'Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!' to be specific.
target_language_example: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zur Beförderung!
native_language_example: Congratulations on the promotion!

meaning: this evening
additional_notes: Refers to the evening of today. It's commonly used for plans, events, or situations happening later the same day. Depending on context, English may use either "this evening" or "tonight."
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Abend zu mir?
native_language_example: Are you coming over to my place tonight?

meaning: this evening to (the) ... / tonight for ... (used to say you're going somewhere or inviting someone for an activity, often 'zum Essen' = for dinner).
additional_notes: A time phrase + preposition: 'heute Abend' = 'this evening/tonight'. 'zum' = contraction of 'zu dem' and introduces the place or purpose (e.g. 'zum Essen' = for dinner, 'zum Inder' = to the Indian restaurant). Common in invitations and plans. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Zum Essen heute Abend?').
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Abend zum Abendessen vorbei?
native_language_example: Are you coming by for dinner tonight?

meaning: tonight; this night (the coming or current night)
additional_notes: Used to refer to the ongoing or upcoming night (same day-night period as 'tonight' in English). Can describe events that happened earlier this night or will happen later tonight. Word order: 'heute Nacht' is common, but you may also see 'heute Nacht' = 'in der heutigen Nacht' (more formal).
target_language_example: Heute Nacht wird es wahrscheinlich regnen.
native_language_example: It's likely to rain tonight.

meaning: today in the (specific) + time/place phrase (literally: 'today at/on the').
additional_notes: Used to say something happened 'today' combined with a following time or place expression introduced by 'am' (a contraction of 'an dem'). Common with times of day (am Morgen), locations (am Strand), or parts of the day (am Nachthimmel here poetic). In questions it can refer to people 'today at the ...' (e.g. "heute am Flughafen"). Word order: 'heute am' + [time/place].
target_language_example: Ich habe heute am Abend einen Film gesehen.
native_language_example: I watched a movie this evening.

meaning: today I am
additional_notes: Heut(e) bin is the start of a present-tense clause meaning 'today I am...'. It's used to state one's current role, identity, age, condition, or situation today. The verb follows (e.g. ich bin, du bist) — here the examples show first person singular 'ich bin'. 'Heute bin ich...' can introduce a temporary or current state ("today I'm X") or a more permanent fact stated in the present ("what I am today").
target_language_example: Heute bin ich müde, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
native_language_example: Today I am tired, so I'm staying home.

meaning: today all day / the whole day today
additional_notes: Used before a time noun (usually 'Tag') to say that something lasted or happened for the entire day today. Common structure: 'heute den ganzen Tag ...' (e.g. 'heute den ganzen Tag gearbeitet'). You can also use other time words (e.g. 'heute den ganzen Abend'), but 'Tag' is most frequent. Word order: 'heute' (today) + 'den ganzen' + time noun in accusative.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute den ganzen Tag Deutsch gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied German all day today.

meaning: 'to have' used with 'heute' (today) to talk about events, plans, classes, or the current day/date (literally: 'today have').
additional_notes: This combination appears when German speakers say what they have or what is happening today (e.g., classes, meals, events) or when asking/answering about the current day. Context determines the subject: often used with wir (we) — »Heute haben wir …« — or in questions like »Welchen Tag haben wir heute?« It is literal in structure but English often uses 'today we have' or simply 'we have (today)'.
target_language_example: Heute haben wir um neun Uhr Schule.
native_language_example: Today we have school at nine o'clock.

meaning: today in / today at (used to locate something in time or place together with a following noun or phrase).
additional_notes: Combines heute (today) with a preposition (here: in) that belongs to the phrase following it. 'Heute in' is not a fixed idiom by itself — meaning depends on the noun or phrase that follows: e.g. 'heute in der Schule' = 'in school today', 'heute in der Zeitung' = 'in the newspaper today', 'heute in einem Monat' is unusual (use 'in einem Monat' for 'in a month'); watch word order: in questions you may see 'War Tom heute in der Schule?' (Was Tom in school today?).
target_language_example: Warst du heute in der Bibliothek?
native_language_example: Were you in the library today?

meaning: today is / it is today
additional_notes: A common phrase used to state the date, day, weather, or general condition of the current day. 'Heute' = today, 'ist' = is. Often followed by a noun (Heute ist Dienstag), an adjective + noun (Heute ist ein schöner Tag), or 'es' + adjective (Heute ist es kalt). Useful for simple statements about today's situation.
target_language_example: Heute ist ein schöner Tag zum Spazierengehen.
native_language_example: Today is a nice day for a walk.

meaning: 'not ... today' or 'no ... today' — negates something happening or available today
additional_notes: Combination of heute (today) + keine (the negation 'no' for feminine/plural/neutral nouns in accusative/nominative depending on context). Used to say that something (e.g., school, time, event) does not occur or is not available today: 'Heute keine Schule?' = 'No school today?'. Word order can vary (e.g., 'Wir haben heute keine Schule.' or question forms like 'Habt ihr heute keine Schule?').
target_language_example: Hast du heute keine Arbeit?
native_language_example: Don't you have work today? / You have no work today?

meaning: to come today / to arrive today.
additional_notes: Combines the adverb 'heute' (today) with the verb 'kommen' (to come). Used to talk about someone arriving or attending on the current day. Tense and mood change meaning: could be future (will come), conditional (would come), permission (can come), or instruction (should come). Word order: in full sentences the verb inflects and may move (e.g. 'Tom kann heute kommen' — 'kann' is conjugated).
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass er heute kommen wird?
native_language_example: Do you think he will come today?

meaning: today (for a change) / why not today — adds a casual, tentative tone to a suggestion or decision.
additional_notes: Combines heute (today) with mal (a softening/temporary particle). Used to propose doing something today, try something once, or indicate a slight change from the usual. Common in spoken German. Tone: informal to neutral; not urgent. Can be translated as “maybe today,” “why don’t (we) today,” or “today for a change.”
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollte ich heute mal einen Kuchen backen.
native_language_example: Maybe I should bake a cake today.

meaning: depends on context: 'today to' (motion toward a place) or 'today feel like' when part of 'mir ist heute nach ... zumute' (I feel like ... today).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — 'heute' means 'today' and 'nach' is a preposition used for direction ('to' a city/country/place: heute nach Berlin/Boston) or as part of expressions. In sentence 2, the structure is 'mir ist heute nach [etwas] zumute' meaning 'I feel like [doing something] today' (colloquial). In sentence 6, 'nach' appears in the sequence 'nach der Verleihung' meaning 'after the award ceremony' — here 'nach' means 'after', not 'to'. Pay attention to the word(s) that follow 'nach' to choose the correct translation.
target_language_example: Ich fahre heute nach München.
native_language_example: I'm going to Munich today.

meaning: 'today at' (used to give a specific time on the current day)
additional_notes: Combine 'heute' (today) with 'um' + a clock time to say when something happens (e.g. 'heute um Mitternacht', 'heute um 8 Uhr'). 'Um' is the preposition used with exact times. Note: 'heute um' can also start a sentence like 'Mein Bruder kümmert sich heute um sie' only if 'um' is part of a different construction (here 'sich um jemand/etwas kümmern' = 'look after'); in that case 'um' is not the time preposition.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns heute um 19 Uhr.
native_language_example: We'll meet today at 7 PM.

meaning: 'today (exactly) ... ago' — used to say that something happened a certain time before today (e.g. 'today one year ago').
additional_notes: Commonly combined with a time expression introduced by 'einem', 'fünf', etc. + unit (Jahr, Tag, Wochen) to mean '... ago, on this date X years/months/days ago'. Word order: 'Heute vor einem Jahr ...' Also note a different use: in sentence 5 ('heute vor Mittag') 'vor' means 'before' (so 'today before noon'). Context tells which meaning applies: 'heute vor + [time span] + (haben/ereignete...)' = '... ago'; 'heute vor + [time point]' = 'today before ...'.
target_language_example: Heute vor drei Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Three years ago today I moved to Berlin.

meaning: used to talk about something that will happen today (future action).
additional_notes: Combines 'heute' (today) with the auxiliary verb 'werden' to form a future meaning ('will ... today'). In German, 'werden' plus an infinitive expresses the future tense: 'Heute werden wir Pfannkuchen backen.' = 'Today we will bake pancakes.' You can also use the present tense for near future (e.g., 'Heute backen wir Pfannkuchen.').
target_language_example: Heute werden wir ins Kino gehen.
native_language_example: Today we will go to the cinema.

meaning: today, really / really today (adds emphasis or surprise about 'today')
additional_notes: Combines heute (today) with wirklich (really) to add emphasis, surprise, doubt, or affirmation about something happening today. Use at the start, middle, or end of a sentence: questions often use it to express disbelief (Ist heute wirklich Montag?), while statements use it to stress that something actually happened today (Wir haben heute wirklich etwas geschafft). Word order is flexible depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Willst du heute wirklich so früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Do you really want to get up that early today?

meaning: 'today to' or 'today at/to (someone's place)'.
additional_notes: Combines the time word 'heute' (today) with the preposition 'zu' (to). In many examples 'zu' indicates going to someone's home or place (e.g. 'zu jemandem gehen' = go to someone's place). In sentence 2 ('heute zu Hause') the phrase 'zu Hause' is a fixed expression meaning 'at home' (note the capital H in 'Hause' in older/formal usage, modern everyday writing uses 'zu Hause'). Word order can vary: 'heute zu dir' = 'to you today', and 'noch heute zu ihr' = 'to her still today' (meaning: we can go to her place today).
target_language_example: Kannst du heute zu mir kommen?
native_language_example: Can you come to my place today?

meaning: today to the (feminine or dative noun); used to say you are going/bringing something to a place or event today
additional_notes: Heute = 'today'. Zur is the contraction of 'zu der' (to the) and is used before feminine nouns or nouns requiring dative. Common in everyday speech: 'heute zur Bank' (to the bank today), 'heute zur Feier/Party' (to the party today), or 'heute zur Inspektion' (for inspection today). Followed by a noun (event/place) in dative. Word order: time (heute) often comes before the destination (zur ...).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute zur Bibliothek.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library today.

meaning: A casual way to start a question meaning 'hey, are (you)...' or 'hey, are you...'.
additional_notes: Informal spoken greeting + question using the verb 'bist' (2nd person singular of 'sein' = to be). Used to get someone's attention before asking about identity, profession, condition, or opinion. Common in casual conversation; follow with a noun, adjective, or clause (e.g. 'du Chema?', 'du verletzt?').
target_language_example: Hey, bist du müde?
native_language_example: Hey, are you tired?

meaning: held/kept the (masculine or neutral noun in accusative); part of past tense of halten + article den.
additional_notes: «hielt den» is the simple past (Präteritum) form of halten (to hold/stop/keep) followed by the masculine or neuter accusative article den. Meaning depends on the verb's sense and context: e.g. hielt den Zug auf = 'stopped/delayed the train'; hielt den Atem an = 'held (one's) breath'. The noun after den is in accusative. For plural or feminine nouns the article changes (die/das/den etc.).
target_language_example: Sie hielt den Ball fest.
native_language_example: She held the ball tightly.

meaning: past tense of 'hält die' — 'held the' (feminine/plural object follows).
additional_notes: ‘hielt’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of halten (to hold, stop, keep). 'die' is the definite article for feminine singular or plural accusative. Together 'hielt die ...' means 'held the ...' or 'stopped/kept the ...' depending on the object and context (e.g. held the nose, held the hands up, stopped/held the passersby). In questions about duration (Wie lang hielt die Beziehung?) it means 'How long did the relationship last?' — here 'hielt ...' is used figuratively for 'lasted'.
target_language_example: Er hielt die Tür für mich offen.
native_language_example: He held the door open for me.

meaning: 'held her' / 'stopped her' / 'considered her' (past tense of halten + pronoun 'sie')
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) form of the verb halten combined with the object pronoun sie. Meaning depends on context: halten can mean to hold (physically), to stop/keep (prevent someone), to consider/judge (halten für), or to keep someone from doing something (halten von/abhalten). The pronoun sie can be 'her' (feminine singular) or 'them' or formal 'you' depending on context, but in these examples it's 'her'.
target_language_example: Er hielt sie lange am Arm fest, bis sie sich beruhigte.
native_language_example: He held her tightly by the arm until she calmed down.

meaning: a polite way to suggest or propose something: 'what would you think if we...' / 'how would you feel about us...'
additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or proposal in a tentative, polite way. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) or simple past for hypothetical actions (e.g. bestellten, gingen). Common in spoken and written German when asking for someone's opinion about doing something together.
target_language_example: Was hieltest du davon, wenn wir morgen zusammen kochten?
native_language_example: What would you think if we cooked together tomorrow?

meaning: 'here, isn't it?' — a colloquial tag question using hier (here) combined with nicht or nicht wahr to ask for confirmation about being or being present here.
additional_notes: Used as a question tag to request confirmation or agreement about someone's presence or location. In German you commonly say 'Du bist neu hier, nicht?' or 'Du warst gestern Abend auch hier, nicht wahr?' — 'nicht' and 'nicht wahr' are interchangeable; 'nicht wahr' is slightly more formal. Word order: the statement comes first, then the tag 'nicht?' or 'nicht wahr?'.
target_language_example: Du kennst ihn doch hier, nicht?
native_language_example: You know him here, don't you?

meaning: a spoken way to link two clauses with 'here, and...' or 'here — and...'; used to continue, add information, or point to a consequence or contrast.
additional_notes: This combination appears in colloquial speech or informal writing where the speaker mentions 'here' (hier) then adds another clause introduced by 'und' (and). It often marks continuation, a consequence, contrast, or additional detail about the situation. Punctuation and intonation can vary (comma, pause, or dash). Not a fixed idiom — just two common words used together.
target_language_example: Ich bleibe hier, und morgen helfe ich dir weiter.
native_language_example: I'll stay here, and tomorrow I'll help you further.

meaning: help here; asking or saying that assistance is needed at this place.
additional_notes: Common short phrase used to indicate that help is required now or at the current location. Can be used in informal and formal contexts; word order often appears in sentences like 'Ich brauche hier Hilfe' or as a call for help 'Hier Hilfe!'. You can also say 'Wir brauchen hier Hilfe' (we need help here) or use 'benötigen' for a more formal tone.
target_language_example: Hier Hilfe! Die Maschine ist kaputt.
native_language_example: Help here! The machine is broken.

meaning: 'your' (formal) with 'here' — used to point to a place where the listener should enter or place something (literally: 'here your').
additional_notes: Common in forms, instructions, or when pointing to an object/place: 'hier Ihr' + noun (often capitalized 'Ihr' formal pronoun). 'Ihr' is the formal 'your' (Sie). Use when addressing someone formally. Word order: 'hier Ihr [Noun]' or 'Ist das hier Ihr [Noun]?'. Not a single fixed phrase but a combination of adverb ('hier') and possessive pronoun ('Ihr').
target_language_example: Bitte legen Sie hier Ihr Ticket auf den Scanner.
native_language_example: Please place your ticket here on the scanner.

meaning: 'here too' or 'also here'.
additional_notes: Used to add that something applies to the current location or situation as well. Can be placed after a noun or clause (Das hier auch — 'this one here too') or within a sentence (Endlich ist hier auch der Winter angekommen — 'the winter has arrived here too'). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Bei uns hat es geschneit — hier auch.
native_language_example: It snowed where we are — here too.

meaning: here (at this place) — used with the verb 'warten' (to wait) to mean 'wait here (for someone)'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears with verbs that take the preposition 'auf' (e.g. warten auf = to wait for). 'Hier' indicates the location (here) and 'auf' is the preposition that links to the person or thing being waited for. Word order in German often places the person/thing after 'auf' (Warte hier auf mich = Wait here for me).
target_language_example: Warte hier auf mich, ich bin in fünf Minuten zurück.
native_language_example: Wait here for me, I'll be back in five minutes.

meaning: from here; originating from here (spoken about a person or thing)
additional_notes: Used to indicate origin or location relative to the speaker: 'hier' = here, 'aus' = from/out of. Common in phrases like 'Ich komme hier aus' (I come from here) or 'Die Blumen sind hier aus dem Garten' (The flowers are from here/in the garden). Word order can change in full sentences (e.g. 'Ich komme aus hier' is incorrect; use 'Ich komme hierher' or 'Ich komme von hier' or 'Ich komme hier aus' colloquially). 'hier aus' is conversational and often appears in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich bin hier aus der Stadt.
native_language_example: I'm from this city.

meaning: from here one can / you can see from here
additional_notes: Used to say what is visible or possible from the current location. Often appears as 'Von hier aus kann man ...' meaning 'From here you can ...'. 'man' is the impersonal 'one/you/people' and is common in spoken and written German to make general statements.
target_language_example: Von hier aus kann man die ganze Stadt sehen.
native_language_example: From here you can see the whole city.

meaning: from here to the train station (distance/time between current location and the station).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the distance or travel time between the speaker's current location ('hier') and 'der Bahnhof' (the train station). Often followed by a verb about duration (dauert, braucht man, ist es) and a time expression (z. B. zehn Minuten, eine halbe Stunde). Can be used with different modes of travel (zu Fuß, mit dem Auto, mit dem Bus).
target_language_example: Von hier bis zum Bahnhof braucht man zu Fuß etwa zwanzig Minuten.
native_language_example: From here to the train station it takes about twenty minutes on foot.

meaning: adds emphasis of puzzlement or frustration: 'what on earth/what the heck is happening here' or 'what on earth am I doing here'.
additional_notes: Placed after or near a question word or phrase to express surprise, confusion, irritation, or strong curiosity. 'Bloß' here is not literal ('only') but intensifies the question (like 'on earth' / 'the heck'). Common in spoken German. Tone can be exasperated, worried, or simply curious depending on context.
target_language_example: Was mache ich hier bloß?
native_language_example: What on earth am I doing here?

meaning: someone here / anyone here (informal reference to a person present)
additional_notes: Used to refer informally to an unspecified person present in the location. Often appears in questions or statements like 'Ist hier einer ...?' (Is there anyone here ...?) or in clauses specifying who does something ('Wenn hier einer ...,' meaning 'if anyone here ...'). Tone can be casual; context determines exact translation (someone/anyone/one of us).
target_language_example: Wenn hier einer Hilfe braucht, soll er es sagen.
native_language_example: If anyone here needs help, they should say so.

meaning: to find something here / to be able to find (someone/something) in this place
additional_notes: Common phrase pairing the adverb 'hier' (here) with the verb 'finden' (to find). Used in statements and questions to say that something exists/is located here or that someone can locate something/someone here. Formality depends on the verb form (Sie, wir, du). Word order: 'hier finden Sie ...' or 'finden wir hier ...?'.
target_language_example: Hier finden Sie alle wichtigen Informationen.
native_language_example: Here you will find all the important information.

meaning: there was/there were here (past tense)
additional_notes: Combines 'hier' (here) + 'gab' (preterite of geben used in existential sentences: 'es gab' = 'there was/were'). Used to say that something existed or was located at this place in the past. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (e.g. 'hier gab es einen Laden' = 'there used to be a shop here').
target_language_example: Hier gab es früher einen schönen Park.
native_language_example: There used to be a nice park here.

meaning: 'found here' (something was discovered or obtained at this place)
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to say that the item was discovered/obtained 'here' (at this location or context). Common in spoken German: word order can vary (e.g., 'die habe ich hier gefunden' or short form 'die hier gefunden'). Can refer to physical location or to something seen/mentioned in the current context (e.g., online, in a shop, in this conversation).
target_language_example: Die Tasche habe ich hier gefunden.
native_language_example: I found the bag here.

meaning: enjoy living/being here; 'like it here'.
additional_notes: Combines 'hier' (here) with 'gerne' (with pleasure). Used to ask or state whether someone likes living, growing up, or being in a place. Common in questions: 'Lebst du hier gerne?' = 'Do you like living here?'. Not formal or slang—neutral everyday language.
target_language_example: Ich bin hier gerne aufgewachsen.
native_language_example: I liked growing up here.

meaning: happy here; content in this place or situation.
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) + glücklich (happy). Used to say someone feels happy in the current place, situation, or life circumstance. Can appear in different tenses and moods (indicative, subjunctive) in reported speech: e.g. Er sagte, er sei hier glücklich (reported). Common in everyday and formal speech.
target_language_example: Sie bleibt, weil sie hier glücklich ist.
native_language_example: She is staying because she is happy here.

meaning: to here / to this place (movement toward where the speaker is or toward a specific spot nearby).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or placement toward a location near the speaker or a specific spot. Often combined with verbs of motion or placement (kommen, stellen, setzen). In spoken German you may also hear 'hierhin' written as one word. Contrast with 'hier' (at/to here, often static) and 'dahin' (to there).
target_language_example: Stell den Koffer hier hin.
native_language_example: Put the suitcase here (toward this spot).

meaning: 'this/these (here) is/are for' — used to point to something nearby and say who it's intended for.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German when handing or pointing to an object. Word order in full sentences often varies: e.g. "Das hier ist für dich." or simply "Hier, das ist für dich." The demonstrative (das/diese/der) and person (dich/Sie/uns) change with gender/number and formality.
target_language_example: Das hier ist für dich.
native_language_example: This here is for you.

meaning: 'no ... here' / 'there is no ... here' (negation placed after location)
additional_notes: Combine 'hier' (here) with 'kein' to negate a noun at a location. Word order: 'hier' (or other location) + 'kein' + noun. Used to say that something does not exist or is not allowed here. In spoken German you might also hear 'hier nicht' with verbs (e.g. 'hier nicht rauchen'), while 'kein' negates nouns (e.g. 'hier kein Platz').
target_language_example: Hier kein Alkohol!
native_language_example: No alcohol here!

meaning: 'here no' — used to say that something (person, thing, action) does not exist or is not allowed here
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) + keinen (negative accusative/masculine or general negation depending on context). Common in sentences denying existence, permission, presence, or wanting to avoid something: e.g. keine Gefahr, keinen Zutritt, keinen Streit. Word form (keinen) changes with gender/case/number: you may also see hier keine, hier kein, hier keinen/keine/kein depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Du hast hier keinen Zutritt.
native_language_example: You have no access here.

meaning: to leave something/someone here; to leave (behind) in this place.
additional_notes: Used to indicate leaving an object or person at the current location. Common with direct objects (die Tasche hier lassen, das Rad hier lassen) or with pronouns (die hier lassen). Can be used as a suggestion, permission, or instruction. Context (tone, verb form) shows whether it's a question, permission, or command.
target_language_example: Du kannst die Koffer hier lassen.
native_language_example: You can leave the suitcases here.

meaning: lives here / is alive here (depending on context).
additional_notes: Usually part of a clause with a subject: 'hier lebt man' (one lives well here), 'jemand, der hier lebt' (someone who lives here). Can also appear in exclamations: 'Der Kopf hier lebt noch!' meaning 'is still alive' (less common, dramatic). Use context to tell whether it means 'to live/reside here' or 'is alive here.'
target_language_example: Kennst du jemanden, der hier lebt?
native_language_example: Do you know someone who lives here?

meaning: 'here is' / 'here lies' (indicates something is located or present here)
additional_notes: Used to point out the location or presence of a person or thing. Can be literal (an object/person is physically lying/located here) or figurative (e.g., 'here lies the power' = 'the real power is here'). Often followed by a noun or clause. In formal/technical contexts it can appear in passive-like constructions (e.g., 'hier liegt ein Fehler vor' = 'there is an error here').
target_language_example: Hier liegt mein Schlüssel.
native_language_example: Here is my key.

meaning: to do/make (something) here — refers to actions taking place at this location or in this situation.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a verb's object or as part of a question/comment about an activity at the current place or context. Word order can vary (e.g., 'was wir hier machen' = 'what we are doing here'). 'Hier' = here; 'machen' = to do/make. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Können wir das hier machen?
native_language_example: Can we do this here?

meaning: 'nothing here' / 'not ... here' (used to say that something is not present, doesn't help, or is not allowed in this place)
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) + nichts (nothing). Common in negative statements: can mean 'there is nothing here', 'this doesn't help here', or 'you don't belong here' depending on context. Word order may change in full sentences (e.g. 'es nützt hier nichts' or 'hier hat sich nichts verändert').
target_language_example: Mit Drohungen erreichst du hier nichts.
native_language_example: With threats you won't get anywhere here.

meaning: have no business being/doing something here; don't belong here.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed phrase 'hier nichts zu suchen' (literally 'to search nothing here') meaning someone/something does not belong here or must leave. Used to tell people to go away or to say something is out of place. Tone can be strong or rude depending on context; common in warnings or commands.
target_language_example: Du hast hier nichts zu suchen — geh bitte weg.
native_language_example: You have no business being here — please go away.

meaning: nobody here / no one here
additional_notes: Used to say that there are no people in a place or that no one does something in this context. Often appears in questions (Ist hier niemand…?) to express surprise or annoyance. Word order can change in a sentence (e.g., Hier hält niemand an; Mir sagt hier niemand was).
target_language_example: Ich klopfe — hier niemand antwortet.
native_language_example: I knock — nobody here answers.

meaning: up here; here above (in this higher place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location at a higher position relative to speaker or reference point (e.g., upstairs, on a hill, on a platform). Can be used alone ('Hier oben bin ich!') or with verbs to describe seeing, staying, placing someone/something. Common in everyday speech; neutral register.
target_language_example: Hier oben ist die Aussicht wunderschön.
native_language_example: Up here the view is beautiful.

meaning: here often / often here
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) + oft (often). Used to ask or say that something happens frequently at this place. Word order: oft can appear before or after hier (e.g. 'hier oft' or 'oft hier'), but 'hier oft' is natural in many contexts. Common in questions (Schneit es hier oft?) and statements (Tom frühstückt hier oft.).
target_language_example: Kommst du hier oft?
native_language_example: Do you come here often?

meaning: already here; here for (a period of time) — indicates that something is already true at this place or has been happening here for some time.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs to say someone/something is already present or has been at this location for a duration. With stative verbs (leben, sein, stationiert sein) it often pairs with a time expression: 'Wie lange sind Sie hier schon?' In contexts like sentence 1 it emphasizes that actions (e.g. arrests) have already taken place here. Word order: 'hier schon' can appear after the verb or object.
target_language_example: Wir wohnen hier schon seit drei Jahren.
native_language_example: We have been living here for three years already.

meaning: are here
additional_notes: A literal combination of hier ('here') and seid, the ihr-form of sein ('to be'). In the examples, it is understood with ihr: ihr hier seid = 'you all are here / you're here'. In subordinate clauses, German often puts seid at the end, as in dass ihr hier seid.
target_language_example: Schön, dass ihr heute hier seid.
native_language_example: It's nice that you're here today.

meaning: 'here looks' — used to describe how something appears in this place or situation.
additional_notes: Commonly part of phrases like 'Das hier sieht ... aus' or 'Hier sieht ... aus'. 'sieht' is from sehen (to see) and with 'aus' forms 'aussehen' (to look/appear). Use to comment on appearance, condition, or impression of a place, thing, or situation. Word order: 'Das hier sieht nach ... aus' = 'This here looks like ...'; 'Hier sieht es besser aus' = 'Here it looks better.'
target_language_example: Das hier sieht nach einem guten Plan aus.
native_language_example: This here looks like a good plan.

meaning: Not a correct standalone phrase in German; an ungrammatical sequence mixing plural verb form 'sind' with singular indefinite article 'ein'. Likely an incorrect attempt to say 'here is/are a ...'.
additional_notes: This sequence is ungrammatical and should be avoided. Correct alternatives: 'Hier ist ein ...' (singular: 'Here is a ...'), 'Hier sind ...' (plural: 'Here are ...'), or adjust article/gender: 'Hier ist eine ...' for feminine nouns. The error often comes from confusing verb number (sind vs. ist) with the noun's number and gender.
target_language_example: Hier sind ein Fehler und viele Missverständnisse.
native_language_example: Here are an error and many misunderstandings.

meaning: to stand here / to be standing here
additional_notes: Used both as a literal description (physically standing in this place) and figuratively (being in a situation or position). Common in commands (Bleiben Sie bitte hier stehen), descriptions (Die Leute, die hier stehen...), and reflections (wie Sie heute hier stehen). Word order: hier = here, stehen = to stand.
target_language_example: Ich kann jetzt nicht weg — ich muss hier stehen.
native_language_example: I can't leave now — I have to stand here.

meaning: 'meet here' or 'meet (at this place)'
additional_notes: Used to indicate that people meet at this place. Often appears with a reflexive verb: 'sich hier treffen' (to meet each other here). Can refer to a planned meeting (e.g. 'Wir treffen uns hier um 18 Uhr') or an accidental encounter (e.g. 'Ich treffe dich hier zufällig'). Word order can vary in sentences (e.g. question, exclamation).
target_language_example: Gut, dass wir uns hier treffen.
native_language_example: Good that we are meeting here.

meaning: down here; here below (in this place or area below).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location that is lower, below, or within the current area (physically or metaphorically). Common in spoken German. Can refer to being downstairs, in a lower part of a ship/building, underground, or in a disadvantaged situation ('being down here' emotionally). Often follows the verb or noun phrase (e.g., 'wir hier unten', 'ist es hier unten').
target_language_example: Ich fühle mich sehr wohl hier unten.
native_language_example: I feel very comfortable down here.

meaning: "here a lot" / "a lot here" — used to describe a large quantity, frequency, or degree in the current place or situation
additional_notes: Combines hier (here/at this place or in this situation) with viel (much/many/a lot). Common in statements about quantity, frequency, or degree related to the current location or context. Often appears in constructions with modifiers (e.g., viel zu + adjective = far too ...). Word order can vary (e.g., Im Frühling regnet es hier viel); when both words appear together as 'hier viel' the emphasis is on location plus quantity.
target_language_example: Im Frühling regnet es hier viel.
native_language_example: It rains a lot here in spring.

meaning: here becomes / here it/one/this is becoming (something); indicates a change or result happening 'here'.
additional_notes: Combines the adverb 'hier' (here) with the verb 'werden' (to become). Used to say that something is becoming true or occurring at this place or in this situation. The subject after 'wird' can be explicit or impersonal: 'es wird' (it becomes / it gets), 'man wird' (one becomes), or a noun ('dieser Koffer wird ...'). Often used with adjectives (gefährlich) or clauses introduced by 'was'. Context determines the subject and English translation: 'here it gets/ becomes...', 'here one becomes...', or 'this will serve as...'.
target_language_example: Hier wird es schnell sehr laut.
native_language_example: Here it quickly becomes very loud.

meaning: here, really / is it really like this here? (adds emphasis or doubt about 'here')
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) + wirklich (really). Used to emphasize or question the truth, intensity, or surprise about something related to the location 'here'. Can appear in questions or statements. Word order may change (e.g. 'Würdest du hier wirklich wohnen wollen?').
target_language_example: Bist du hier wirklich glücklich?
native_language_example: Are you really happy here?

meaning: here (I/we/they) wonder — adds a sense of wondering or guessing about 'here'.
additional_notes: Combines hier (here) with wohl, which softens statements and expresses speculation, curiosity or expectation. Often used in questions to mean 'I wonder whether/what/if... here'. Common in spoken and written German. Context, intonation, and sentence structure determine whether it's polite curiosity, mild surprise, or speculation.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, wie es hier wohl ist.
native_language_example: I wonder what it's like here.

meaning: here (to this place) and... — used to invite or command someone to come here and then do something, or in the fixed phrase 'Bis hierher und nicht weiter' meaning 'this far and no further'.
additional_notes: The phrase combines hierher (to here) with und (and). In commands it appears before another verb: 'Komm hierher und ...' = 'Come here and ...' — common in spoken and written German. In sentence 1 it appears as part of the idiom 'Bis hierher und nicht weiter' (literal: 'up to here and no further') meaning 'this is as far as it goes / stop right there.'
target_language_example: Komm hierher und hilf mir, das Regal aufzubauen.
native_language_example: Come here and help me build the shelf.

meaning: helps everyone / helps anybody (who asks).
additional_notes: Present-tense phrase from the verb helfen (to help) + jedem (dative of "everyone/anyone"). Often used with a relative clause: ‚hilft jedem, der ...‘ meaning 'helps anyone who...'. Dative construction: jemandem helfen. Formality: neutral; suitable for everyday use.
target_language_example: Er hilft jedem, der ihn um Hilfe bittet.
native_language_example: He helps anyone who asks him for help.

meaning: back and forth; to and fro
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or motion in two directions repeatedly (physical movement: walking, swinging) or figurative/reciprocal actions (e.g. exchanging messages, indecision). Common in everyday speech. Can appear with verbs like gehen, laufen, schwingen, schreiben.
target_language_example: Sie lief in der Wohnung hin und her und suchte die Brieftasche.
native_language_example: She paced back and forth in the apartment looking for her wallet.

meaning: now and then; from time to time; occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens irregularly but more than rarely. Common in spoken and written German. Can appear at the start of a sentence (followed by inversion) or within a sentence without changing word order.
target_language_example: Hin und wieder besuche ich meine Großeltern am Wochenende.
native_language_example: Every now and then I visit my grandparents on the weekend.

meaning: behind bars; put in prison
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to imprison someone. Often used in passive or with verbs like bringen (to bring) or gehören (belongs) to imply someone should be jailed. Colloquial but common in spoken and written German. 'Gitter' literally means 'bars' (as in jail bars).
target_language_example: Wenn du das noch einmal machst, bringe ich dich hinter Gitter.
native_language_example: If you do that again, I'll put you behind bars.

meaning: beyond the horizon; out of sight or unknown
additional_notes: Used literally to say something is physically beyond the visible horizon (e.g., a ship, the sun) or figuratively to indicate something unknown, mysterious, or in the future. Usually follows the noun it describes and requires dative case: 'hinter dem Horizont'.
target_language_example: Was passiert hinter dem Horizont, weiß niemand.
native_language_example: What happens beyond the horizon, nobody knows.

meaning: behind me; (in set phrase) to get something done/over with (bring it behind me).
additional_notes: Used literally to mean ‘behind me’ (position) and idiomatically in the set phrase 'etwas hinter sich bringen' meaning to finish or get something over with. In your examples, 1–2 show the idiomatic use (Ich will es hinter mich bringen = I want to get it over with). Examples 3–4 use the literal spatial meaning (stand/move behind me). Word order changes in the idiom: the full idiom is 'etwas hinter sich bringen' (note 'sich' instead of 'mich' in standard reflexive form); 'hinter mich' as in examples 1–2 is colloquial/informal speech.
target_language_example: Ich möchte die Prüfung hinter mich bringen.
native_language_example: I want to get the exam over with.

meaning: please leave (a message); leave (formal you).
additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative using the verb 'hinterlassen' (to leave, e.g. a message or note) with the formal 'Sie' (addressing one or more people politely). Common in phone prompts and polite requests: 'Hinterlassen Sie eine Nachricht' = 'Please leave a message.' Word order can vary: 'Bitte hinterlassen Sie...' or 'Hinterlassen Sie bitte...'.
target_language_example: Hinterlassen Sie bitte eine Nachricht auf dem Anrufbeantworter.
native_language_example: Please leave a message on the answering machine.

meaning: to deceive or trick someone (literally: to lead someone behind the light).
additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning to mislead, cheat, or fool someone. Often used with a direct object: 'jemanden hinters Licht führen' = to deceive someone. Can be used in contexts from mild trickery to deliberate fraud. Synonyms: 'täuschen', 'betrügen'.
target_language_example: Er hat mich hinters Licht geführt, als er mir falsche Angaben machte.
native_language_example: He deceived me and gave false information.

meaning: 'how high is the' / 'how much is the' (asking about an amount, price, size, probability, etc.)
additional_notes: Used in questions with 'wie' at the start: 'Wie hoch ist die ...?' Common for asking about prices (Miete, Rechnung), measurements, levels, or probabilities. Word order: 'Wie hoch ist die + noun?'. You can replace 'die' with other articles/pronouns (den/das/der/sein/etc.) depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Wie hoch ist die Temperatur heute?
native_language_example: How high is the temperature today?

meaning: 'I hope that...' or 'I hope this/that...'
additional_notes: A common way to express hope or wish about something. In German you often say 'Ich hoffe, dass...' with 'dass' (that) or shorten to 'Ich hoffe, das...' when referring to a nearby clause or thing (spoken/written). Followed by a clause (subject + verb) or by a phrase referring to a thing (this/that). Use formal 'dass' in writing; the shortened 'das' is common in speech and informal writing when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, das klappt morgen.
native_language_example: I hope that works tomorrow.

meaning: 'I hope that you' (formal) or 'I hope that he/she/they/you (formal)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or expectation about something. 'Sie' with a capital S is the formal 'you' and requires verb conjugation in the subordinate clause (verb to the end). Can also refer to third person plural in written contexts if context indicates, but in most everyday use with capitalization it addresses someone formally. In informal speech to a friend use 'hoffe, dass du'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass Sie schnell wieder fit sind.
native_language_example: I hope that you get well quickly.

meaning: I hope that it/that... (expressing a wish about something).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Ich hoffe, dass ...' + clause. 'es' often refers to a situation, weather, someone's mood, or an event (it/that). Use subjunctive optionally for politeness but indicative is normal in speech. You can replace 'es' with a noun or pronoun (e.g. 'hoffe, dass du kommst').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass es morgen nicht regnet.
native_language_example: I hope that it doesn't rain tomorrow.

meaning: I hope that I ... (used to express a wish or expectation about something the speaker will do or experience).
additional_notes: Common construction: hoffe, dass + clause with ich. Use it to express the speaker's hopes about their own actions or outcomes. In spoken German, ‘dass’ can sometimes be dropped after hoffe (e.g. „Ich hoffe, ich sehe dich bald“) but in written German include 'dass' for clarity. Tense and verb position follow normal German word order (subordinate clause: verb goes to the end).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass ich dir morgen helfen kann.
native_language_example: I hope that I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: I hope that you (plural).
additional_notes: Used to express the speaker's wish or expectation about something concerning 'ihr' (you plural, informal). Common in everyday speech and writing. 'Hoffe' is first person singular of 'hoffen'; 'dass' introduces a subordinate clause (verb goes to the end). For formal/respectful 'you' use 'Sie' (hoffe, dass Sie ...).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass ihr heute Abend Zeit habt.
native_language_example: I hope that you (all) have time this evening.

meaning: 'I hope that we...' — used to express a wish or expectation about something involving 'we'.
additional_notes: Common phrase starter in German for expressing hopes or wishes about future actions or outcomes involving the speaker and others. 'Hoffe' is the first‑person singular of 'hoffen' (to hope). The clause after 'dass' uses the verb at the end (subordinate clause word order): e.g. 'dass wir uns wiedersehen' (that we see each other again).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass wir bald wieder zusammen essen können.
native_language_example: I hope that we can eat together again soon.

meaning: I hope that + (noun phrase starting with 'der' — i.e. 'I hope the ...').
additional_notes: This is a clipped/oral way to show the clause 'Ich hoffe, der ...' meaning 'I hope the ...' followed by a noun phrase or a relative clause beginning with the masculine/feminine/neuter nominative article 'der' (here 'der' is the definite article or a relative pronoun). Common in spoken or written German when the speaker comments about a person or thing (e.g. 'der Richter', 'der Block'). Use it to express a wish or hope about that specific person/thing. The comma after 'hoffe' marks the start of the dependent clause.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, der Zug kommt pünktlich.
native_language_example: I hope the train arrives on time.

meaning: I hope that (introduces a clause; 'die' = that).
additional_notes: This is the structure of a sentence where the speaker says 'I hope that ...' — in German: 'Ich hoffe, (dass) ...'. Informally or in speech, 'dass' can be omitted and a comma plus a pronoun like 'die' (those/those things) or a clause follows. In your examples 'die' refers back to a feminine or plural noun mentioned earlier (e.g. 'die Dinge' or 'die Straße' as context). More common and explicit is 'Ich hoffe, dass ...'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, die Prüfung läuft gut.
native_language_example: I hope that the exam goes well.

meaning: 'I hope he ...' — expresses the speaker's hope about something a male person will do or that will happen to him.
additional_notes: This is the first person singular of hoffen followed by a subject pronoun (er). It's used to state what the speaker wishes or expects regarding a male person or masculine noun. In German word order the verb (hoffe) can come first in sentences like questions or exclamations, but in normal statements you'd usually see 'Ich hoffe, er ...'. The clause after the comma is a subordinate content clause describing the hoped-for outcome. Tone can be neutral, positive, or even negative/ironic depending on context (e.g. 'Ich hoffe, er bricht sich das Genick.' is hostile).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, er findet seinen Weg nach Hause.
native_language_example: I hope he finds his way home.

meaning: I hope (that) they ... (used to express the speaker's wish about what 'they' will do).
additional_notes: This is the verb 'hoffen' (to hope) with the subject 'ich' implied and a following clause that begins with 'sie' (they). In German spoken style, you often hear 'Ich hoffe, sie ...' or shortened in writing to 'hoffe, sie ...' to express a wish, expectation, or sometimes a hope for something negative or violent (as in example 1). Use with a comma before the clause. The clause after 'sie' follows normal word order for subordinate or main clauses depending on whether 'dass' is included (e.g. 'Ich hoffe, dass sie kommen' vs 'Ich hoffe, sie kommen').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, sie helfen uns morgen.
native_language_example: I hope they help us tomorrow.

meaning: imperative 'get it' or 'fetch it' (tell someone to go and bring or take something)
additional_notes: Casual spoken imperative of holen + es (to fetch/get it). Often used with dative reflexive 'dir' (hol es dir = get it for yourself) or with a location (vom Dachboden, aus dem Wasser). Can be commanding or encouraging. Tone depends on context — can be firm or helpful. Common in everyday spoken German.
target_language_example: Hol es vom Dachboden, bitte.
native_language_example: Get it from the attic, please.

meaning: 'get/bring/fetch that' (I will get that)
additional_notes: Informal everyday phrase using holen (to fetch/get). 'Hole das' is a short command or statement meaning 'I'll get that' or 'get that' depending on context. Word order can change: in full sentences you often see subject (ich) before holen: 'Ich hole das.' Can refer to money, luggage, an item, etc. If addressing someone directly as an instruction, tone and context determine whether it's a promise ('I'll fetch it') or an imperative.
target_language_example: Ich hole das Gepäck vom Auto.
native_language_example: I'll get the luggage from the car.

meaning: I/I'm getting (the) ...; I'll fetch/pick up the ...
additional_notes: Present-tense form of holen used in conversational sentences. 'Hole' is first person singular ('ich hole') or imperative-like in colloquial speech. The direct object follows (die Sachen, die Zeitungen, die Unterlagen, die Papiere, die Unterschrift, die Dame, die Polizei). 'Abholen' (abholen) appears in some examples — 'hole ... ab' = pick up (and bring back). Can be used to volunteer to fetch something, to collect someone, or to threaten to summon (e.g. 'ich hole die Polizei' = I'll get/call the police). Word order: subject often omitted in spoken German ('Hol deine Sachen' = (You) get your things / literally: Get your things).
target_language_example: Ich hole die Schlüssel aus dem Auto.
native_language_example: I'll get the keys from the car.

meaning: I'm just getting/grabbing (something).
additional_notes: Used to say you are only fetching or picking up one thing or doing a quick action — minimizes importance or time. Common in spoken German. 'Hole' = (I) get/fetch, 'nur' = only/just. Variations: 'Ich hole nur noch ...' adds 'just quickly' or 'just before leaving'.
target_language_example: Ich hole nur schnell die Post.
native_language_example: I'm just quickly getting the mail.

meaning: 'fetch/get that' or 'bring that out' (imperative or present tense of holen + object 'das')
additional_notes: Holt is the 3rd person plural present or imperative (addressing 'ihr' or 'you all') of holen (to fetch/get). 'Das' is the neutral pronoun 'that/it'. Use when asking or telling two or more people to fetch, bring out, or remove something. Context determines exact English verb: 'fetch', 'get', 'bring (out)', or 'remove'. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Holt das raus!' = 'Bring that out!').
target_language_example: Holt das Buch von dem Tisch!
native_language_example: Get that book from the table!

meaning: to count to one hundred (to be able to count up to 100).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like 'können' and the preposition 'bis' (bis hundert) to ask or say whether someone can count up to 100. Common in questions about basic number skills (children, language ability). You can replace 'hundert' with other numbers (bis zehn, bis zwanzig).
target_language_example: Kannst du bis hundert zählen?
native_language_example: Can you count to one hundred?

meaning: 'holds a' (third person singular of halten + indefinite feminine noun)
additional_notes: Used with er/sie/es (e.g., er hält, sie hält) + feminine noun in accusative (eine ...). 'halten' can mean physically holding something, keeping/maintaining (e.g., a diet), or giving (e.g., a speech with different structure). The noun following 'eine' must be feminine; for masculine/neuter you'd see 'einen' or 'ein'.
target_language_example: Sie hält eine Tasse.
native_language_example: She is holding a cup.

meaning: literally 'holds her' or 'does she think' depending on context; often part of the verb 'halten' used in questions like 'Für wen hält sie sich?' = 'Who does she think she is?'.
additional_notes: Hält is the 3rd-person singular of 'halten' (to hold). With a direct object it can mean 'holds her/it' (e.g. 'Wen hält sie an der Hand?'). In idiomatic questions about opinion or self-image it appears in constructions like 'Für wen hält sie sich?' (Who does she think she is?) or 'Was hält sie von ...?' (What does she think of ...?). Pay attention to word order: the verb comes second in statements but appears first in yes/no and question forms. The pronoun 'sie' can mean 'she' or 'they' or formal 'you' depending on context, but here it means 'she'.
target_language_example: Was hält sie von dem neuen Lehrer?
native_language_example: What does she think of the new teacher?

meaning: you consider yourself (to be)... / you think you're...
additional_notes: Second-person singular informal (du) form of the reflexive verb construction 'sich für etwas halten' meaning 'to consider oneself (something)'. It is followed by an adjective or noun (usually without an article): 'du hältst dich für clever' = 'you think you're clever'. Often used critically or sarcastically in the examples.
target_language_example: Du hältst dich für wichtig, aber keiner hört zu.
native_language_example: You think you're important, but nobody listens.

meaning: 'what do you think of it' / 'how do you feel about it' (asking someone's opinion about something)
additional_notes: This is the informal 2nd-person singular of the phrase 'halten von' used in the question form 'Was hältst du davon?' or shortened in conversation to 'Hältst du davon...?' or 'Was hältst du davon?' Use 'du' for someone you know well (friends, family). For polite/formal situations use 'Was halten Sie davon?'. Often followed by a noun, clause, or reference to something just mentioned.
target_language_example: Was hältst du davon, wenn wir morgen ins Kino gehen?
native_language_example: What do you think of it if we go to the cinema tomorrow?

meaning: 'what do you think of' or 'how do you feel about' (asking someone's opinion about something).
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to ask for an opinion. It is always followed by an object or topic (e.g. 'dem Plan', 'der Idee', 'mir'). Word order: 'Was hältst du von ...?' for 'What do you think of ...?'. Formal: use 'halten Sie von' for polite form. Often appears as question.
target_language_example: Was hältst du von diesem Film?
native_language_example: What do you think of this movie?

meaning: 'what do you think of the' (asking for someone's opinion about a feminine noun or feminine phrase introduced by 'der').
additional_notes: Part of the question phrase 'Was hältst du von ...?' meaning 'What do you think of ...?'. 'Von der' is the preposition von + feminine definite article in dative (or could be dative for feminine nouns). Use 'von dem' (wonach 'vom') for masculine/neuter, and 'von der' for feminine nouns or for feminine noun phrases (e.g. 'der Regierung', 'der Firma'). For plural use 'von den'. Common in spoken and written German when asking opinions.
target_language_example: Was hältst du von der neuen Idee?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new idea?

meaning: to leave someone hanging / to leave something unfinished or neglected; also to dump or stand someone up (informal)
additional_notes: Context-dependent phrasal verb. Can mean: 1) to leave a person waiting or without help (leave someone hanging or stand someone up), 2) to leave something unfinished or neglected (e.g. a task, a coat left hanging), or 3) to abandon a relationship (informal). Often used informally. Conjugates like a separable verb (ich lasse ihn hängen → he is left hanging).
target_language_example: Du kannst mich nicht einfach hängen lassen – ich brauche deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: You can't just leave me hanging – I need your help.

meaning: would have everything
additional_notes: Combination of the subjunctive auxiliary 'hätte' (would have) with 'alles' (everything). Used in conditional or counterfactual statements. Translation depends on context: can mean 'would have made everything...' (with a following past participle implied or stated) or 'would have done everything' (when referring to actions). Common in phrases expressing hypothetical results or regrets.
target_language_example: Das hätte alles verhindert.
native_language_example: That would have prevented everything.

meaning: 'would have' or 'should have' + listened/paid attention to / waited for (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) form of 'haben' (hätte) used in perfect conditional or reported past; often appears with verbs like 'hören' (to listen), 'warten' (to wait) or in passive/reported constructions ('jemand hätte auf ... geschossen' = someone allegedly shot at ...). In many examples 'auf ... hören' means 'to listen to/heed someone' and 'hätte auf ... hören sollen' = 'should have listened to...'. Word order: 'hätte' + past participle later in the clause (hätte ... gehört). 'Hätte auf' by itself is incomplete; understand together with the rest of the verb phrase (e.g., 'hätte auf euch hören sollen').
target_language_example: Ich hätte auf deinen Rat hören sollen.
