native_language_example: If you are right, I must admit: I am wrong.

meaning: I have time / I'm free (available).
additional_notes: Used to say you are available or have time for something. Can be used for short or longer periods depending on context. Formality: neutral; suitable in spoken and written German. You can also say "ich habe keine Zeit" (I don't have time). To ask someone else if they have time, use "Hast du Zeit?" or formally "Haben Sie Zeit?"
target_language_example: Ich habe Zeit am Nachmittag, wir können uns treffen.
native_language_example: I have time in the afternoon, we can meet.

meaning: I have three times as (much/many) / I have it three times that way.
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete sentence on its own; it typically appears in comparative statements like ‚ich habe dreimal so viel/groß/teuer‘ meaning 'I have three times as much/large/expensive'. Native speakers often say ‚dreimal so viel wie...‘ or ‚dreimal so groß wie...‘ to compare quantities or sizes. You may also hear shortened colloquial uses where the noun/adjective is understood from context (e.g. ‚Ich habe dreimal so.‘ = 'I have three times that').
target_language_example: Ich habe dreimal so viel Geld wie du.
native_language_example: I have three times as much money as you.

meaning: 'I have a question.'
additional_notes: A polite, common way to signal you want information or to ask something. Use when raising a hand, interrupting, or starting a question in conversation or class. You can add 'an dich', 'an euch', or 'an Sie' to specify the person/group you're addressing (e.g. 'Ich habe eine Frage an Sie.').
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe eine Frage zum Text.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question about the text.

meaning: "I have a friend whose..." (introduces a relative clause describing the friend's possession or relation)
additional_notes: Use to link a main clause about 'I have a friend' with a relative clause that describes something belonging to or related to that friend. 'Dessen' is the masculine/neuter genitive relative pronoun meaning 'whose'. It agrees with the gender of the antecedent (here 'Freund' — masculine). In spoken German, genitive forms like 'dessen' are common in written and formal speech; in casual spoken German people sometimes prefer constructions with 'von dem' (e.g. 'ich hab einen Freund, von dem der Vater ...').
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Freund, dessen Schwester in Berlin wohnt.
native_language_example: I have a friend whose sister lives in Berlin.

meaning: I have had enough / I have enough.
additional_notes: Can mean either 'I've had enough' (fed up, tired of something/someone) or 'I have enough' (sufficient amount) depending on context. When followed by 'von' + someone/something (Ich habe genug von ...), it expresses annoyance or that you're fed up. Alone (Ich habe genug) can mean you're done or you have enough of something. With 'zu tun' it means you have enough to do. Tone and context determine whether it's emotional (fed up) or literal (sufficient).
target_language_example: Ich habe genug von den ständigen Ausreden.
native_language_example: I've had enough of the constant excuses.

meaning: I have no money / I don't have any money.
additional_notes: Used to say you lack money. Can appear alone as a short statement or followed by a reason/purpose using 'um ... zu', 'für', or a clause. 'kein' negates the noun 'Geld'. Formality: neutral, everyday language.
target_language_example: Ich habe kein Geld, um das Ticket zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I don't have any money to buy the ticket.

meaning: "I don't feel like it" / "I don't want to" (expressing lack of desire or motivation).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase to say you don't want to do something or aren't in the mood. Can be used alone as a short reply (Ich habe keine Lust.) or followed by an infinitive with zu (Ich habe keine Lust, aufzuräumen.) or by auf + noun (Ich habe keine Lust auf Kaffee.). Tone can range from casual to slightly rude depending on context; soften with Bitte or adding a reason.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, heute Abend auszugehen.
native_language_example: I don't feel like going out tonight.

meaning: I don't have time / I'm too busy.
additional_notes: A common, direct way to say you cannot do something because of lack of time. Can be followed by a prepositional phrase with für + noun (für ...), or by a comma + infinitive clause (keine Zeit, ... zu ...). Tone is neutral; can sound curt depending on context. Useful for declining requests or explaining why you can't do an activity.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, dir beim Umzug zu helfen.
native_language_example: I don't have time to help you move.

meaning: I do not have the (intention/time/etc.) — used to deny possession of intention, time, or similar nouns that follow.
additional_notes: This phrase begins a negative statement where the speaker negates having something (Absicht = intention, Zeit = time, etc.). In German you often say 'Ich habe nicht die Absicht...' to mean 'I have no intention...' or 'Ich habe nicht die ganze Nacht Zeit' for 'I don't have the whole night (available)'. The noun that follows is usually definite (die Absicht, die Zeit). You can replace 'die' with other articles/genders as needed (z. B. 'ich habe nicht den Mut', 'ich habe nicht das Geld').
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht die Energie, heute auszugehen.
native_language_example: I don't have the energy to go out today.

meaning: 'I intend' or 'I plan to' (followed by an infinitive clause).
additional_notes: Used to express a personal intention or plan. It is followed by a comma and an infinitive clause with 'zu' (e.g. ich habe vor, ... zu ...). More formal alternatives: 'ich plane' or 'ich habe die Absicht'. Can be used for neutral, positive, or negative actions depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, nächste Woche einen Sprachkurs zu machen.
native_language_example: I intend to take a language course next week.

meaning: 'I' + auxiliary 'have' + reflexive 'ourselves' — this exact word order is incorrect in German; the correct forms are shown in notes.
additional_notes: The sequence 'ich haben uns' is not grammatically correct. In German, the auxiliary verb agrees with the subject and the reflexive pronoun follows the conjugated verb (or appears in its usual object position). For first person singular use 'ich habe mich' (I have myself / I met with someone — but note meaning depends on the verb). In the example sentences the subject is plural (Tom und ich = we), so the correct auxiliary is 'haben' with 'uns' as the reflexive/plural object: 'Tom und ich haben uns früher an jedem Wochenende getroffen.' 'Wir haben uns getrennt.' 'Tom und ich haben uns über Australien unterhalten.' If the subject were 'ich' alone, use 'habe' and 'mich': e.g. 'Ich habe mich gestern mit ihm getroffen.'
target_language_example: Tom und ich haben uns gestern im Café getroffen.
native_language_example: Tom and I met each other at the café yesterday.

meaning: 'we ... together' — indicates that the speaker and someone else did something together (correct German: "Tom und ich haben zusammen ..." or simply "Wir haben zusammen ...").
additional_notes: The phrase as written ('ich haben zusammen') is not grammatical. In German you cannot use 'ich' with the verb form 'haben' (it should be 'ich habe'). When referring to the speaker plus another person, use either 'Tom und ich haben zusammen ...' or the pronoun 'wir haben zusammen ...'. 'Zusammen' means 'together' and usually follows the verb or the direct object: e.g. 'Wir haben zusammen Kaffee getrunken.'
target_language_example: Tom und ich haben zusammen in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: Tom and I lived together in Berlin.

meaning: 'I hate you.'
additional_notes: A strong, direct expression of hatred toward someone. Very strong and often offensive — use only in fiction, dramatic situations, or when you deliberately want to be rude. Can be intensified with additions (e.g., 'wie die Pest', 'über alles'). In German word order: subject (ich) + verb (hasse) + object (dich).
target_language_example: Ich hasse dich nicht — ich mag nur nicht, wie du lügst.
native_language_example: I don't hate you — I just don't like how you lie.

meaning: I had no other (choice/options).
additional_notes: Commonly completed by 'Wahl' (choice) or followed by 'als' + infinitive clause (meaning 'except/to do X'). Used to explain that there was no alternative. Can stand alone (Ich hatte keine andere.) to mean 'I had no other option.' Tone is neutral; often used to justify a decision.
target_language_example: Ich hatte keine andere Wahl, als das Angebot anzunehmen.
native_language_example: I had no other choice but to accept the offer.

meaning: I had nothing / I didn't have anything (to ...).
additional_notes: Commonly used as the start of a sentence meaning you did not have something (e.g., intention, something to add, something else to say, or anything to do). Usually followed by an infinitive phrase (z. B. 'im Sinn', 'hinzuzufügen', 'zu tun') that completes the idea. In past tense (Präteritum) and polite/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nichts Wichtiges zu sagen.
native_language_example: I had nothing important to say.

meaning: I was so (____) / I had such (____).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun (Angst, Schmerzen, Probleme) or a clause starting with dass to express strong intensity. In English you can translate as “I was so (afraid)” or “I had such (fear)”. In spoken German you might also hear the contracted form ich hatte so (without -che) before an adjective or noun. Often used to describe a past emotional or physical state.
target_language_example: Ich hatte solche Angst, dass ich nicht atmen konnte.
native_language_example: I was so afraid that I couldn't breathe.

meaning: my name is
additional_notes: Common way to introduce yourself in German. Literally 'I am called'. Use to say your name (Ich heiße Maria). Can also be used in expressions of approval/disapproval with 'das heiße ich nicht' meaning 'I don't approve of that' (less common). Formal alternatives: 'Ich bin Maria' or 'Mein Name ist Maria.'
target_language_example: Ich heiße Alex und du?
native_language_example: My name is Alex — and you?

meaning: I thought/considered it (to be)... / I kept it (in a certain state) — past tense of 'halten' in contexts like thinking or keeping.
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'ich hielt es' can mean 'I considered it' (often followed by 'für' + noun/adjective: e.g. 'ich hielt es für wichtig' = 'I considered it important') or a physical/continuative sense 'I kept/held it' (e.g. 'ich hielt es in der Hand' = 'I held it in my hand'). It's the simple past (Präteritum) first-person form of 'halten'. In spoken German, the Perfekt ('ich habe es gehalten' or 'ich habe es für ... gehalten') is more common for past events, but 'ich hielt es für ...' is a standard written/neutral expression.
target_language_example: Ich hielt es für eine gute Idee, früher zu gehen.
native_language_example: I considered it a good idea to leave earlier.

meaning: I really hope (that)...
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the speaker's hope or wish about something. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'dass' (that) or a verb in the infinitive with modal constructions. Tone: sincere; can express optimism or a polite wish.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe wirklich, dass das Wetter morgen schön wird.
native_language_example: I really hope that the weather will be nice tomorrow.

meaning: I hungry — a reduced fragment indicating the speaker is hungry; not a complete standard sentence in German.
additional_notes: Standard full forms are 'Ich bin hungrig.' or more commonly 'Ich habe Hunger.' The fragment 'ich hungrig' appears in informal notes, telegram-style speech, headlines, or in ellipsis where the verb is omitted but understood (e.g., reported speech or shorthand). It is grammatical as a fragment but not a complete finite sentence in standard written German.
target_language_example: Tom schrieb in der Nachricht nur: „ich hungrig“, damit alle wissen, dass er essen will.
native_language_example: Tom wrote in the message just: "I hungry", so everyone knows he wants to eat.

meaning: I would not have / I wouldn't
additional_notes: Part of the conditional/subjunctive II form of 'haben' used to talk about hypothetical or unreal situations in the past or present. Often appears in longer sentences: e.g. 'Ich hätte nicht so viel gesagt' (I wouldn't have said so much) or with 'ge...' to form perfect conditional: 'Ich hätte nicht gegessen' (I wouldn't have eaten). In spoken German it can be contracted (’ich hätt’ nicht’).
target_language_example: Ich hätte nicht so viel Geld ausgegeben, wenn ich das gewusst hätte.
native_language_example: I wouldn't have spent so much money if I had known that.

meaning: i would have a
additional_notes: An incomplete phrase that normally needs a noun after it, such as a drink, item, or other thing. Literally it means 'I would have a', but in everyday German it is often used politely to mean 'I'd like a ...', especially when ordering or requesting something.
target_language_example: Ich hätte ein Wasser, bitte.
native_language_example: I'd like a water, please.

meaning: 'I heard' or (with 'auf') 'I stopped' (simple past).
additional_notes: Ich hörte is the simple past (Präteritum) form of hören. Alone it means 'I heard' (e.g. Ich hörte ein Geräusch = I heard a noise). In the example sentences it appears with 'auf' + infinitive (hörte auf ... zu + Inf.), meaning 'I stopped (doing something)'. German often uses 'hörte auf' to express stopping an action; in spoken German Perfekt (Ich habe aufgehört) is more common.
target_language_example: Ich hörte gestern das neue Lied.
native_language_example: I heard the new song yesterday.

meaning: 'I ... him the ...' — a word order fragment showing a sentence where 'ich' (I) is subject, 'ihm' (to him) is the dative object, and 'die' (the) begins a feminine/plural accusative direct object or nominative plural.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence but a common word-order fragment in German: subject (ich) + dative pronoun (ihm) + definite article (die) for the direct object. In a full sentence a verb and a noun will appear as well (e.g. ich ihm die Blume gebe in subordinate/verb-final contexts or Ich gebe ihm die Blume in main-clause word order). 'Ihm' is dative (to him), so the thing after 'die' is the thing being given or referred to. Word order can change in questions, subordinate clauses, or with multiple objects.
target_language_example: ich ihm die Blume gebe (as in: dass ich ihm die Blume gebe).
native_language_example: that I give him the flower.

meaning: ‘I told him’ — a chunk from German past-tense constructions showing the subject (ich), indirect object in dative (ihm = to him), and the past participle (gesagt = told). It appears in sentences with auxiliary verbs (haben) or in subordinate clauses where the auxiliary may be elsewhere.
additional_notes: Not a complete standalone sentence in main clauses without the auxiliary. Commonly appears in word-order variations: main clause perfect uses auxiliary before the subject (Ich habe ihm gesagt...), subordinate clauses and embedded questions may separate the auxiliary (..., was ich ihm gesagt habe). Recognizing this chunk helps when parsing spoken or written past-tense statements with indirect objects.
target_language_example: Er tat genau, was ich ihm gesagt hatte.
native_language_example: He did exactly what I had told him.

meaning: Portion of the phrase used in negative constructions meaning 'I (don't) like him / I (can't) stand him' when completed (e.g. with modal verb and negation). By itself it's incomplete.
additional_notes: This three-word sequence is not a standalone sentence in German. It commonly appears inside full sentences such as "ich kann ihn nicht leiden" (I can't stand him) or in colloquial variants. The verb "leiden" in this context means 'tolerate' or 'stand', not 'suffer'. Use the complete construction when speaking or writing.
target_language_example: Wenn ich ihn sehe, denke ich: ich ihn leiden — aber natürlich müsste man sagen: "ich kann ihn nicht leiden".
native_language_example: When I see him I think: I (don't) like him — but of course you would have to say: "I can't stand him."

meaning: A sequence of common German words meaning literally 'I him already' — not an idiom but a fragment that appears in sentences where the speaker refers to having already seen, known, or found 'him' (e.g., 'I have already seen him').
additional_notes: 'ich ihn schon' is not a standalone sentence in German; it occurs within larger sentences with a verb and proper word order (e.g., after a conjunction or in subordinate clauses the verb may come later). Typical uses: to state prior experience ('ich habe ihn schon gesehen'), prior knowledge ('ich wusste, dass ich ihn schon früher gesehen hatte'), or counterfactuals ('Sonst hätte ich ihn schon gefunden'). 'schon' means 'already' or 'earlier'. The fragment is compositional: each word keeps its usual meaning and function (ich = I, ihn = him (accusative), schon = already).
target_language_example: Da ich ihn schon einmal gesehen hatte, erkannte ich ihn sofort.
native_language_example: Since I had already seen him once, I recognized him immediately.

meaning: a common sequence meaning 'I always (have) a/one ...' — used when the speaker says they always do or have something (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a frequent word order in German: subject (ich) + adverb of frequency (immer) + indefinite article (eine) + noun. It appears when you state a habitual action involving a singular feminine noun (eine) or any noun requiring 'eine' in that context. Replace 'eine' with 'einen', 'ein', 'zwei', etc., as needed for other nouns. Word order: frequency adverb often comes after the subject.
target_language_example: Ich immer eine Tasse Kaffee trinke? → Morgens trinke ich immer eine Tasse Kaffee.
native_language_example: I always drink a cup of coffee.

meaning: a short sequence: 'I' (ich) followed by the masculine/neuter accusative article 'in den' meaning 'into the' or 'to the' (used with movement into or entering a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase—just the pronoun ich + the preposition in with the definite article den (accusative masculine/neuter). Used when the speaker describes themselves entering or going into a place or joining something (e.g. in den Park, in den Bus, in den Krieg). Word order may vary in subordinate clauses (e.g. Dass ich in den Krieg zieh). Translate depending on context as 'I go into the...', 'I got on the...', or 'Should I join the...'.
target_language_example: Gestern ging ich in den Park spazieren.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went for a walk in the park.

meaning: 'I have ever seen' (used to say something is the best/worst/most ... you've seen)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in relative clauses after superlatives or comparatives (das beste, der süßeste, einer der schlechtesten). 'Je' here means 'ever'. In full sentences you often see the verb at the end: 'das ich je gesehen habe.' Can be used with past tense (habe gesehen) and in short forms like 'die besten, die ich je gesehen habe.'
target_language_example: Das ist das interessanteste Buch, das ich je gesehen habe.
native_language_example: That is the most interesting book I have ever seen.

meaning: I, at least; as for me (emphasizing your own stance or opinion).
additional_notes: Used to highlight or contrast the speaker's personal position or feeling. Often appears in replies or disagreements (e.g., 'Not me' / 'As for me, ...'). Can be moved in the sentence (e.g., start or end). Tone is neutral; common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich jedenfalls gehe heute nicht mit.
native_language_example: As for me, I'm not going along today.

meaning: when I was young / when I was a child.
additional_notes: A time phrase used to introduce a past habit, state, or experience from one's youth. Often followed by a verb in the past tense (Perfekt or Präteritum). 'Als' here means 'when' for a single time period in the past (not repeated events – for repeated events use 'wenn').
target_language_example: Als ich jung war, bin ich jeden Sommer zu meinen Großeltern gefahren.
native_language_example: When I was young, I went to my grandparents every summer.

meaning: 'I' + 'younger' used in hypothetical phrases (part of conditional sentences meaning 'if I were younger')
additional_notes: This sequence appears in conditional structures about wishing or imagining being younger (e.g., 'Wenn ich jünger wäre...' or inverted 'Wäre ich jünger...'). Alone 'ich jünger' isn't a complete sentence; you need a conditional verb form (wäre, würde ... sein) or a full clause. Common in wishes (subjunctive II / Konjunktiv II) to talk about unreal or hypothetical situations.
target_language_example: Wenn ich jünger wäre, würde ich um die Welt reisen.
native_language_example: If I were younger, I would travel around the world.

meaning: when I was younger
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period of one's life (younger age). Often appears with verbs in the past tense (Perfekt, Präteritum) or with 'früher' and can introduce habits or states that no longer apply. Commonly used with 'als' — 'Als ich jünger war' = 'When I was younger.'
target_language_example: Als ich jünger war, bin ich jeden Sommer mit dem Fahrrad gefahren.
native_language_example: When I was younger, I rode my bike every summer.

meaning: I can teach you how (to)...
additional_notes: Used to offer to teach someone a skill or how to do something. Follows with a verb phrase introduced by 'man' in examples (impersonal 'one') or directly with an infinitive phrase: Ich kann dich lehren, wie man X macht / wie man X tut. More natural alternatives: 'Ich kann dir beibringen, wie...' or 'Ich kann dir zeigen, wie...'. 'Dich' is the informal singular accusative 'you'.
target_language_example: Ich kann dich lehren, wie man Fahrrad fährt.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to ride a bike.

meaning: I can (the...) / I am able to (the...).
additional_notes: This is the start of sentences where 'ich kann' (I can/am able to) is followed by a feminine or plural accusative noun with the article 'die' (or a demonstrative). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows: e.g. inability ('ich kann die Dinger nicht mehr sehen' = 'I can't stand those things anymore'), ability to fix ('ich kann die Sache ... in Ordnung bringen'), or ability to find ('ich kann die Seite ... nicht finden'). Use 'ich kann' for ability or possibility; 'die' is the direct object article here.
target_language_example: Ich kann die Aufgabe bis morgen erledigen.
native_language_example: I can finish the task by tomorrow.

meaning: I can teach you how (to)...
additional_notes: Used to offer instruction. Follows with an infinitive clause introduced by 'man' or a verb in the infinitive: e.g. 'wie man kocht' or 'wie man schwimmt'. 'Dir' is the dative 'to you' — change for other persons (ich kann ihm/ihr beibringen, wie...). Polite form: 'ich kann Ihnen beibringen, wie...'.
target_language_example: Ich kann dir beibringen, wie man eine Bewerbung schreibt.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to write an application.

meaning: 'I can never' (I am never able to / it's never possible for me)
additional_notes: Used to say that something is impossible or you are never able to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g. ich kann nie pünktlich sein) or by a clause introduced with '...weil...'/'...wenn...'. Tone can be neutral or emphatic depending on context. For present-tense statements about habitual inability or impossibility.
target_language_example: Ich kann nie pünktlich sein, wenn der Bus Verspätung hat.
native_language_example: I can never be on time when the bus is delayed.

meaning: I can't go on / I can't do it anymore / I'm exhausted.
additional_notes: Used to say you are physically or emotionally unable to continue, exhausted, overwhelmed, or at the limit. Tone can be dramatic, pleading, or literal (e.g., too tired to continue). Often used alone as an exclamation. Context clarifies whether it's temporary (tired) or extreme (desperate).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mehr, ich brauche eine Pause.
native_language_example: I can't go on, I need a break.

meaning: I knocked (past tense of 'klopfen').
additional_notes: Used to say you knocked (on a door, window, etc.) in the past. 'Klopfen' means to knock or tap. Sentence structure: often followed by 'an' + accusative or dative ('an die Tür' / 'an der Tür') or used alone with context. Formal past simple (Präteritum) — commonly used in written narratives; in spoken German people may prefer 'ich habe geklopft' (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Ich klopfte an die Tür, bis jemand öffnete.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door until someone opened.

meaning: 'I come from' / 'I'm from' (to say where you are from)
additional_notes: Use this phrase to state your origin (country, city, region). Commonly followed by a place name: country (Spanien), city (Medford), state/region (Minnesota, Limburg). Can be shortened in conversation to "ich komme aus + place" or replaced by "ich bin aus + place" in informal speech, but "ich komme aus" is standard and clear.
target_language_example: Ich komme aus Deutschland, aber jetzt wohne ich in Berlin.
native_language_example: I'm from Germany, but now I live in Berlin.

meaning: 'I come to' / 'I arrive at'; can introduce a result or conclusion ('I come to the conclusion'); with an infinitive it can mean 'I manage to' or 'I get around to' doing something.
additional_notes: Depends on context. As physical movement it can mean 'I arrive at' (e.g. ich komme zu dir — I arrive at your place). Used to introduce a result: ich komme zu dem Schluss — I come to the conclusion. With an infinitive (ich komme zu + Infinitiv) it can mean 'I find the time to' or 'I manage to' (e.g. ich komme zu lesen — I get around to reading). Word order and following words determine precise meaning; in spoken German contractions or alternative verbs (ankommen, gelangen) may be used for arrival.
target_language_example: Ich komme zu dir, sobald das Meeting vorbei ist.
native_language_example: I will come to your place as soon as the meeting is over.

meaning: I could (do) that / I was able to (do) that.
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of 'können' used to say you were able to do something or managed to do it. 'das' refers to a previously mentioned thing or action (it/that). In spoken German, the Perfekt ('ich habe das gekonnt' is rare) or 'ich konnte' is common in narration. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause: e.g. 'ich konnte das Buch finden' or 'ich konnte das nicht'.
target_language_example: Ich konnte das Problem schnell lösen.
native_language_example: I was able to solve that problem quickly.

meaning: 'may I ... with you for a moment' — part of polite requests to speak briefly with someone
additional_notes: This fragment appears in polite questions like "Darf ich kurz mit Ihnen sprechen?" or "Kann ich kurz mit dir reden?" Use a modal verb (darf/kann/könnte) + "ich kurz mit" + person (dir/Ihnen) + verb (sprechen/reden). "kurz" means briefly; "mit" introduces the person you're addressing. Formal: "Ihnen" (capitalized). Informal: "dir".
target_language_example: Darf ich kurz mit dir sprechen?
native_language_example: May I speak with you for a moment?

meaning: I would come
additional_notes: Konjunktiv II form of kommen. It often expresses a hypothetical or polite idea ('I would come'). In reported speech, especially after a past-tense verb, dass ich käme can mean 'that I was coming' or 'that I would come'. It can look similar to English 'I came', but it usually does not mean the simple past.
target_language_example: Ich käme gern mit, aber ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: I would gladly come along, but I have to work.

meaning: I could
additional_notes: Used mainly in reported speech as the Konjunktiv I form of können, often after verbs like sagte, meinte, or hat gesagt. It usually reports what someone said was possible or allowed for me to do.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, ich könne morgen früher gehen.
native_language_example: She said I could leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: 'I could get into' / 'I could be in' (expresses a possible situation or hypothetical entering into a state or place).
additional_notes: Ich könnte is the conditional of können ('could'). When followed by in + noun it often means 'I could get into' (e.g. trouble: in Schwierigkeiten). It can also be followed by a time or place (in einer Stunde, in so einem Haus) to indicate possible timing or being in/at a place. Used for hypotheticals, polite suggestions, or imagining possibilities.
target_language_example: Ich könnte in Schwierigkeiten kommen, wenn ich lüge.
native_language_example: I could get into trouble if I lie.

meaning: I could her/it/them
additional_notes: Ich könnte is the conditional form of ich kann (I can) and expresses possibility or hypothetical ability. sie can mean 'her', 'it' (feminine), or 'them' depending on context; word order and surrounding words determine the exact meaning. Common continuations: ich könnte sie anrufen (I could call her/them), ich könnte sie fragen (I could ask her/them), ich könnte sie reparieren (I could fix it).
target_language_example: Ich könnte sie morgen anrufen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: I could call her/them tomorrow if you want.

meaning: I take care (of it / someone).
additional_notes: Used with 'mich' plus 'um' + object (ich kümmere mich um ...). Means to handle, look after, or deal with something. Common in promises or refusals (I'll take care of it / I won't deal with him). Often followed by 'darum' (about it) or a noun/pronoun. Conjugate 'kümmere' as needed: ich kümmere, du kümmerst, er/sie kümmert, wir kümmern.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, gib mir die Unterlagen und ich kümmere mich darum.
native_language_example: Don't worry, give me the documents and I'll take care of it.

meaning: 'I live for' — used to say that someone or something gives your life meaning or is the main reason you live.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a person, activity, or cause (e.g., 'sie', 'meine Kunst', 'die Musik'). Often expresses strong emotional commitment or devotion. Can be literal (someone depends on you) but usually figurative (someone/something gives purpose). Tone can be romantic, passionate, or emphatic.
target_language_example: Ich lebe für die Musik; ohne sie wäre ich unglücklich.
native_language_example: I live for music; without it I would be unhappy.

meaning: I love you
additional_notes: A direct, strong expression of romantic or deep affection. Used in intimate contexts (romantic partners, close family in some cases). Not casual—use only when you mean it. Word-for-word: ich (I) + liebe (love) + dich (you).
target_language_example: Ich liebe dich sehr — für immer.
native_language_example: I love you very much — forever.

meaning: literally 'I lie' — the verb phrase 'to lie' used with the subject 'I'.
additional_notes: This exact form 'ich lügen' is grammatically incorrect in standard German. In German, verbs must be conjugated to match the subject. The correct first-person singular form is 'ich lüge' (I lie / I am lying / I would lie in some contexts uses conditional). Many example sentences use modal verbs or subjunctive constructions (soll, sollte) where the infinitive 'lügen' appears after the modal: e.g. 'Soll ich lügen?' (Should I lie?) or 'Deswegen muss ich lügen.' (Therefore I must lie.) So you will see either the conjugated form 'ich lüge' or the infinitive after another verb/modal: 'ich muss lügen', 'soll ich lügen?'.
target_language_example: Deshalb muss ich lügen.
native_language_example: That's why I have to lie.

meaning: I like you.
additional_notes: A straightforward, friendly way to say you like someone (romantically or platonically depending on context). 'Mag' is from mögen (to like). Intensifiers like 'sehr' (very) or 'wirklich' (really) add emphasis. Not as strong as 'ich liebe dich' (I love you). Word order: subject 'ich' + verb 'mag' + object 'dich'.
target_language_example: Ich mag dich sehr, aber ich bin noch nicht bereit für eine Beziehung.
native_language_example: I like you very much, but I'm not ready for a relationship yet.

meaning: I mean it / I am serious about what I just said.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize sincerity or seriousness about a statement. Often followed by 'ernst' (serious) or an explanation (e.g. 'ich meine es nur gut' = I mean well). Common in both formal and informal contexts depending on pronoun (du/Ihnen).
target_language_example: Ich meine es ernst, ich werde dir helfen.
native_language_example: I mean it—I'll help you.

meaning: 'I report' / 'I'll report' or 'I'll get in touch' depending on context.
additional_notes: Verb 'melden' has several uses: to report or notify (someone) — e.g. "Ich melde das dem Sicherheitsdienst"; to sign someone up/register (with an object) — "Ich melde Sie an"; and reflexive 'ich melde mich' means I'll contact/get back to you or volunteer ("Ich melde mich später", "Ich melde mich freiwillig"). Tense and endings change with subject and formality.
target_language_example: Ich melde mich morgen bei dir.
native_language_example: I'll get in touch with you tomorrow.

meaning: 'I ... on' — fragment appearing when 'ich' (I) is subject, 'mich' is the reflexive accusative pronoun, and a verb takes the preposition 'auf'. The full meaning depends on the verb and the rest of the sentence (e.g. 'ich mich auf die Suche begeben' = I set out in search of; 'ich mich auf jemanden verlassen' = I rely on someone; 'ich mich auf etwas freuen' = I look forward to).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but a common sequence in sentences with a reflexive verb that uses the preposition 'auf'. Word order varies: in main clauses the conjugated verb is second and the reflexive pronoun appears close to the verb (e.g. 'begab ich mich auf...'), in questions or subordinate clauses order can change. The meaning depends entirely on the verb and its object/prepositional phrase. Note that some example usages are idiomatic and some combinations (e.g. 'mich auf das Sofa legen') normally appear without the reflexive pronoun ('ich lege mich auf das Sofa' or more commonly 'ich lege mich aufs Sofa').
target_language_example: Als Bürger von Zhao verkleidet begab ich mich auf die Suche nach ihnen.
native_language_example: Disguised as a citizen of Zhao, I set out in search of them.

meaning: 'I ... for' — the sequence ich + reflexive pronoun mich + preposition für appears when the speaker refers to themselves (ich/mich) in constructions with verbs that take 'für' to mark the object/beneficiary or topic (e.g. sich für etwas/jemanden bewerben, entschuldigen, freuen). Translations depend on the verb: e.g. 'sich für einen Job bewerben' = 'to apply for a job (oneself)', 'sich für jemanden entschuldigen' = 'to apologize for someone', 'sich für jemanden/etwas freuen' = 'to be happy for someone/something'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the sequence showing the first-person subject (ich) and the reflexive accusative pronoun (mich) followed by the preposition für. Word order varies in questions and subordinate clauses (e.g. 'Würde ich mich für ... bewerben?' or 'Weil ich mich für ... interessiere'). The pronoun may move after auxiliaries/modals: 'Ich würde mich für ... bewerben.'
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich mich für den Job bewerben.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would apply for the job.

meaning: 'I (to) myself that' — part of sentences where the speaker says they will do/receive/experience something for themselves (literal: 'I ... myself that').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common German word order where the speaker uses ich + dative pronoun mir + das (or another object). Mir marks the indirect object ('to/for me'); das is a neuter direct object or a demonstrative pronoun ('that/it'). English translations vary by context: 'I will listen to that myself', 'May I borrow that book?', 'I have to share that room', 'Can I borrow that car?'. Pay attention to verb and sentence context to translate correctly.
target_language_example: Darf ich mir das Handy kurz ansehen?
native_language_example: May I look at that phone for a moment?

meaning: A common sequence showing first-person subject (ich) + dative reflexive pronoun (mir) + masculine accusative indefinite (einen). It appears in constructions meaning “I [for myself] a/one …” used with verbs where the action is done to/for the speaker (putting on, getting, buying, taking, borrowing, etc.). The exact English wording depends on the verb (e.g. “I put on a sweater,” “I bought myself a computer,” “May I get myself a dog?”).
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed idiom but a syntactic pattern: ich (nominative) + mir (dative reflexive/personal pronoun) + einen (masculine accusative indefinite). The dative pronoun mir indicates the action is done for/affects the speaker. The accusative item’s gender/number may change (einen → eine/ein/die/den etc.) depending on the object. Word order can vary (e.g. in subordinate clauses or with auxiliaries): the pronouns keep their cases. Translation is verb-dependent. Informal/formal register depends on verb and context.
target_language_example: Da ich fror, zog ich mir einen Pullover an.
native_language_example: Because I was cold, I put on a sweater.

meaning: This exact word order is not standard German; it is missing the conjugated verb (normally 'bin') in the reflexive construction 'sich (Dat.) sicher sein'. The intended meaning is usually 'I'm sure' (ich bin mir sicher).
additional_notes: Beginners should use 'ich bin mir sicher' to say 'I'm sure' or 'ich bin mir nicht sicher' for 'I'm not sure.' The phrase 'ich mir sicher' by itself is ungrammatical — it's a verbless fragment often resulting from speech errors, typos, or omitted words. If you encounter it, supply the correct form: 'Ich bin mir sicher, dass...' or a question: 'Bist du dir sicher?'.
target_language_example: Ich mir sicher zu fühlen, ohne es auszusprechen, ist ungewöhnlich.
native_language_example: Feeling 'ich mir sicher' without saying the verb is unusual.

meaning: the pronoun 'ich' (I) followed by the preposition 'mit' + the definite article 'der' (dative feminine). Used when the speaker (I) is involved with or doing something 'with' a feminine noun in the dative case.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom—it's a compositional sequence: ich + mit + der (feminine dative). Use when the noun governed by mit is feminine (die → der in dative). Appears in various word orders (e.g., clause-initial, subordinate clauses). Examples include references to people (Ärztin, Person), institutions (Schule), objects (Torte) or abstract nouns (Arbeit).
target_language_example: Wenn ich mit der Schule fertig bin, werde ich im Ausland studieren.
native_language_example: When I am finished with school, I will study abroad.

meaning: 'I' followed by 'with a' (feminine or dative/neuter context) — part of phrases meaning 'May I pay with a...?', 'what do I do with a...?', or 'I am with a...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a sequence showing the pronoun ich (I) plus the preposition mit (with) and the indefinite article einer. Einer here can be the feminine nominative/accusative or the dative of 'one/a' depending on context: after mit, the following noun takes the dative, so einer is the dative feminine (einer Freundin) or dative feminine/neuter form for some pronouns. Common uses: asking how to use or pay with something (Darf ich mit einer Kreditkarte bezahlen?), asking what to do with an object (Was mache ich mit einer leeren Kiste?), or saying you are accompanied by someone (Ich bin mit einer Freundin unterwegs). Note for beginners: focus on mit + dative; learn the dative articles (einer for feminine singular).
target_language_example: Darf ich mit einer Fahrkarte einsteigen?
native_language_example: May I get on with a ticket?

meaning: Can I come along? / May I come with you?
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to join someone or go along to an activity. In correct German you'd usually say the question as 'Darf ich mitkommen?' or 'Kann ich mitkommen?'. 'Ich mitkommen' alone is not a full sentence — include a modal verb (darf/kann) or use future/ability context. Common in informal and polite situations.
target_language_example: Darf ich mitkommen zum Park?
native_language_example: May I come along to the park?

meaning: I still have to (do something) — start of a sentence fragment meaning you must still do one more thing
additional_notes: This is a fragment often used before naming a task or a short action. 'Ich muss noch' = 'I still have to' or 'I have one more thing to...' Adding 'ein' before a noun can indicate 'one (more) [item/action]'. In many cases a full sentence would continue with a noun or infinitive: e.g. 'Ich muss noch ein Formular ausfüllen' or 'Ich muss noch eins machen.' Informal spoken German often shortens or leaves out the rest when context is clear.
target_language_example: Ich muss noch ein Formular ausfüllen.
native_language_example: I still have to fill out one form.

meaning: I have to (go) to the/for the...
additional_notes: Common way to say you need to go somewhere. 'Zum' is the contraction of 'zu dem' and is used before masculine or neuter nouns with the dative (e.g. 'zum Büro', 'zum Flughafen', 'zum Zahnarzt'). The verb after 'ich muss' can be implicit (Ich muss zum Bahnhof. = I have to go to the station.) or explicit (Ich muss zum Arzt gehen.).
target_language_example: Ich muss zum Supermarkt, ich habe nichts zu essen.
native_language_example: I have to go to the supermarket; I have nothing to eat.

meaning: I was tired.
additional_notes: A simple past tense clause (past descriptive) using 'war' (was). Commonly used after conjunctions like 'da' or 'weil' to give a reason: 'Da ich müde war...' = 'Because I was tired...'. Word order: when starting a sentence with 'Da...' the verb of the main clause follows the subject (e.g., 'Da ich müde war, bin ich gleich ins Bett gegangen.').
target_language_example: Da ich müde war, bin ich früh ins Bett gegangen.
native_language_example: Because I was tired, I went to bed early.

meaning: I took / I participated (past tense of 'nehmen' used with 'an ... teilnehmen' = 'to take part').
additional_notes: Ich nahm is the simple past (Präteritum) first-person singular of nehmen. In the example sentences it's used with the separable verb teilnehmen (ich nahm ... teil) to mean 'I took part in' or 'I attended' an event or occasion. For spoken German beginners, the present perfect (ich habe teilgenommen) or present (ich nehme teil) are more common in conversation. Word order: the prefix 'teil' moves to the end: Ich nahm am Treffen teil.
target_language_example: Ich nahm letztes Jahr an einem Sprachkurs teil.
native_language_example: I took part in a language course last year.

meaning: I called / I named (past tense of 'nennen').
additional_notes: Used to say you named something or called someone a certain name or described/gave details. 'nennen' can mean 'to name' (give a name) or 'to mention'/'to state' (give details). 'ich nannte' is the simple past (Präteritum), common in written narration; in spoken German Perfekt ('ich habe genannt') is more frequent.
target_language_example: Ich nannte das Buch 'Die Reise'.
native_language_example: I called/named the book 'The Journey'.

meaning: 'I' + negation + preposition 'in' — a fragment used in various constructions meaning 'I am not in/at/into ...' or 'if I am not in ...' depending on context and clause type.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a compositional fragment: ich (I) + nicht (not) + in (in/into) begins clauses like 'I am not in [a place/state]' or negates an action that takes 'in' with an object (e.g., 'in die Brieftasche schauen' = 'look into the wallet'). Word order and exact meaning depend on clause type (main vs. subordinate) and surrounding verbs: in main clauses the finite verb usually appears in second position (Ich bin nicht in...), while in subordinate/conditional clauses the verb often moves to the end (...dass ich nicht in der Stadt bin / ...falls ich nicht in einer Stunde zurück bin).
target_language_example: Dann sagen Sie mir, woher Sie wussten, dass ich nicht in die Brieftasche schaue.
native_language_example: Then tell me how you knew that I am not looking into the wallet.

meaning: 'I'm not so...' / 'I wasn't so...': a fragment used to downplay or qualify a degree, quality, or manner referring to oneself (not that / not as / not so much / not in that way).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but a common sequence: pronoun ich + negation nicht + so. It appears inside larger sentences and normally requires additional words to complete the idea (e.g., viel, allein, sein wie, schwach gewesen). It can express comparison, diminished capacity, lesser degree, or negation of a manner. Word order may change when combined with auxiliary verbs or objects, but the exact sequence ich nicht so can occur in spoken/written German as shown in examples.
target_language_example: Als ich sagte, dass ich nicht so viel Zeit habe, fing sie an zu weinen.
native_language_example: When I said that I don't have that much time, she began to cry.

meaning: 'I (would) not have expected (that) from (someone)' / 'I haven't heard from (someone)' — depends on context; uses 'nicht von' with a pronoun to say something negative about that person or that you have not received news from them.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common combination: 'ich nicht von + jemandem' can express surprise/disappointment (Das hätte ich nicht von ihm gedacht — I wouldn't have thought that of him) or lack of contact (Ich habe nicht von ihr gehört — I haven't heard from her). The exact meaning comes from the verb and sentence. Word order and verb forms change: e.g. 'hätte ich nicht von ihnen gedacht' (conditional past), 'habe ich nicht von ihr gehört' (present perfect).
target_language_example: Das hätte ich nicht von dir gedacht.
native_language_example: I wouldn't have expected that from you.

meaning: 'I will not allow' / 'I won't permit' (when part of a longer verb phrase like 'das lasse ich nicht zu') or in modal constructions 'I don't need to' (as in 'ich brauche nicht zu') depending on context.
additional_notes: This word group isn't a fixed phrase by itself — it appears when 'ich' is the subject and 'nicht' negates an infinitive or separable verb construction with 'zulassen' or with modal-like constructions (e.g. 'brauche nicht zu'). Most common: 'das lasse ich nicht zu.' = 'I won't allow that.' In other examples it can be part of 'ich brauche nicht zu + Inf.' = 'I don't need to...'. Pay attention to the full verb: 'zulassen' (to allow/permit) vs. 'zu' + infinitive after verbs like 'brauchen' or 'sein zu' (formal).
target_language_example: Das lasse ich nicht zu.
native_language_example: I won't allow that.

meaning: depends on context: (A) 'I was still a...' (when followed by a noun like Kind/Junge) or (B) 'May I have another...' (asking for one more of something).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in two common uses. 1) Time/age: 'als ich noch ein Kind/Junge war' = 'when I was still a child/a boy' — 'noch' here means 'still'. 2) Requests/offers: 'Darf ich noch ein Stück Kuchen haben?' = 'May I have another piece of cake?' — 'noch ein' means 'one more/another'. Word order and the following word determine the meaning. Not an idiom; composed of common words.
target_language_example: Könnte ich noch ein Glas Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Could I have another glass of water?

meaning: 'I have never seen' (spoken fragment: 'I have never seen [this/that/person]').
additional_notes: This is a clipped spoken fragment in German where the auxiliary verb (usually habe) is omitted in casual speech or in short answers. The complete written form is Ich habe ... noch nie gesehen. Use the full form in formal writing or complete sentences; the fragment ich noch nie gesehen is common in conversation or as a reply.
target_language_example: Ich noch nie gesehen — als kurze Antwort auf die Frage, ob man etwas schon gesehen hat.
native_language_example: I've never seen it — as a short reply to the question whether you've seen something.

meaning: adds emphasis or gives a reason about 'I' — 'I, you see' / 'as for me' / 'I (indeed)'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or contrast the speaker's role, behavior, opinion or to give an explanatory remark about oneself. Often appears mid-sentence or as a short response. Tone can be friendly, defensive, or explanatory depending on context. Not formal or slang — common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich nämlich gehe morgen früher nach Hause.
native_language_example: As for me, I'm going home earlier tomorrow.

meaning: I personally; expressing your own opinion or preference.
additional_notes: Used to stress that what follows is the speaker's personal view, preference, or experience. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the verb/phrase. Polite and common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich persönlich finde dieses Buch besser als den Film.
native_language_example: I personally find this book better than the movie.

meaning: I (am) on time / I will be on time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate you arrive or will arrive at the agreed time. In standard German the verb is normally included (e.g. 'ich bin pünktlich', 'ich komme pünktlich', 'ich werde pünktlich sein/ankommen'), but the fragment 'ich pünktlich' can appear in headlines, notes, or elliptical speech. Prefer full sentences in conversation.
target_language_example: Dank dir kam ich pünktlich an, ich pünktlich war keine Sorge.
native_language_example: Thanks to you I arrived on time; I being on time was no worry.

meaning: 'ich' + 'richtig' — uses 'richtig' as an adverb to emphasize or intensify the speaker's feeling, ability or state (I really / I truly / I was really). It can strengthen adjectives, adverbs or verbs in colloquial and neutral contexts.
additional_notes: 'Richtig' here functions as an intensifier: before adjectives (Ich bin richtig müde = I'm really tired), after modal/ability expressions (Das kann ich richtig gut = I can do that really well) or after verbs in colloquial speech (Ich habe das richtig gemerkt = I really noticed that). Word order varies: 'ich richtig' appears together when 'richtig' follows the subject directly in structures like 'Ich richtig eifersüchtig' only in reduced or emphatic colloquial fragments; more commonly 'richtig' follows the verb or accompanies an adjective (Ich war richtig eifersüchtig). The literal translation 'I right' is not used in English; translate as 'I really' or 'I was really.'
target_language_example: Das kann ich richtig gut.
native_language_example: I can do that really well.

meaning: I said it.
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) first-person form of sagen + object pronoun 'es' (it). Used to report that you already said something. In spoken German, Perfekt ("ich habe es gesagt") is more common in many regions, but Präteritum is natural in writing or for some verbs. Word order: subject – verb – object. Tone depends on context (neutral statement or irritated).
target_language_example: Ich sagte es dir schon gestern.
native_language_example: I said it to you yesterday.

meaning: I can do it / I can manage it (or: I can't — with 'nicht').
additional_notes: Common phrase to say you are (or are not) able to do or manage something. 'Schaffen' here means 'to manage/cope' or 'to succeed in doing' rather than 'to create'. To negate, place 'nicht' after 'schaffe' (Ich schaffe das nicht = I can't do/manage it). Can be used for practical tasks or emotional/mental challenges.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich schaffe das.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I can do it.

meaning: I closed / I shut (past tense of 'schließen').
additional_notes: ‘Ich schloss’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of schließen. It can mean physically closing something (eyes, door) or completing/closing an action (e.g., to conclude a deal or place a bet: eine Wette abschließen). For everyday spoken German, the present perfect (ich habe ... geschlossen / ich habe ... abgeschlossen) is often used instead, but the simple past appears frequently in writing and storytelling.
target_language_example: Ich schloss das Fenster, bevor es zu regnen begann.
native_language_example: I closed the window before it started to rain.

meaning: I have always (wanted/been)... / I've always...
additional_notes: Used to express a long-standing desire, intention, or feeling about something. Often appears with verbs like wollen (to want), sehen (to see), hassen (to hate), verreisen (to travel). Can be followed by 'mal' for a casual tone (e.g., 'schon immer mal' = 'always wanted to (once)'). It emphasizes that the feeling or wish existed for a long time up to now.
target_language_example: Dieses Konzert wollte ich schon immer sehen.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to see this concert.

meaning: 'I shouted' or 'I screamed' (simple past of schreien).
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the verb schreien (to shout/scream). Common in written or narrative contexts; in spoken German people often use 'ich habe geschrien' (Perfekt). Use for loud vocal expressions, either anger, pain, surprise or fear.
target_language_example: Als das Licht ausging, ich schrie vor Schreck.
native_language_example: When the light went out, I screamed in fright.

meaning: 'it's my fault' / 'I am to blame' (phrase using 'ich' + 'schuld' to express guilt)
additional_notes: This construction appears in spoken or written German when the speaker says they are to blame. More fully correct forms are "ich bin schuld" or "an ... bin ich schuld" (e.g. "Daran bin ich schuld" = "I'm to blame for that"). You can use it in questions: "Bin ich schuld?" = "Am I to blame?". Common verbs with Schuld: "schuld sein" (to be at fault) and "jemandem die Schuld geben" (to blame someone).
target_language_example: Daran bin ich schuld, und es tut mir leid.
native_language_example: I'm to blame for that, and I'm sorry.

meaning: I pregnant / I am pregnant (used to indicate that the speaker is pregnant).
additional_notes: The grammatically correct full phrase in German is normally "Ich bin schwanger." "Ich schwanger" by itself is nonstandard or fragmentary and may appear in informal notes, headlines, or ellipsis where the verb is omitted. Use appropriate verb forms for tense/mood (e.g. "Ich war schwanger", "Ich wäre schwanger").
target_language_example: Weil ich schwanger bin, muss ich mich ausruhen — nicht: "ich schwanger" allein in formalem Kontext.
native_language_example: Because I am pregnant, I need to rest — not: "ich schwanger" alone in a formal context.

meaning: I look (like) / I appear (like).
additional_notes: Used with 'wie' + someone/something to say you resemble or look like them (physical appearance, clothing, or impression). 'aussehen' is a separable verb: in present tense the prefix 'aus' moves to the end of the clause (Ich sehe ... aus). Can also be used without 'wie' to mean 'I look' + adjective (Ich sehe müde aus = I look tired).
target_language_example: Ich sehe aus wie meine Mutter.
native_language_example: I look like my mother.

meaning: I am (supposedly)
additional_notes: A subjunctive (Konjunktiv I) construction used to report what someone else said or to express doubt/skepticism about a statement. Often appears after verbs like 'glauben', 'denken', 'sagen' (e.g. 'Er sagt, ich sei ein...') or in exclamations to dispute an accusation. In spoken informal German, the indicative ('ich bin') is frequently used instead. The phrase literally means 'I be a' but functions as 'that I am' or 'I am (allegedly)'.
target_language_example: Glauben Sie wirklich, ich sei ein Betrüger?
native_language_example: Do you really believe that I am a fraud?

meaning: I (should) [do something] to/for you with them/it (pronoun order: I — them — to you).
additional_notes: This string shows typical German pronoun order in a sentence: subject (ich) + accusative pronoun (sie = her/them/it) + dative pronoun (dir = to you). The exact meaning depends on the verb: e.g. erzählen (tell them to you), schneiden (cut them for you), zeigen (show them to you). In sentence 4, überlass ich sie dir means 'I'll leave them to you' or 'I'll hand them over to you.' Word order can change in questions or subordinate clauses, but the pronoun case roles remain (sie = accusative, dir = dative).
target_language_example: Soll ich sie dir schicken?
native_language_example: Shall I send them to you?

meaning: 'I [do something] her/them for' — fragment used when the speaker is saying they consider, take, keep, or do something with 'sie' (her/them/you formal) and uses 'für' (for/as).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a common sequence: ich (I) + sie (her/them/you formal) + für (for/as). Meaning depends on the verb in the full sentence. Common uses: "für ... halten" = to consider/think someone is (e.g. 'ich hielt sie für verrückt' = I thought she was crazy), "für ... nehmen" = to take someone for (to mistake someone for), "für ... aufbewahren" = to keep something for someone, and in perfect/compound tenses pronouns and prepositions appear in this order. 'sie' can be accusative ('her' or 'them') or dative/accusative depending on verb; context tells you which.
target_language_example: Anfangs hielt ich sie für verrückt.
native_language_example: At first I thought she was crazy.

meaning: a fragment meaning 'I saw her/them' (perfect tense: 'I have seen her/them').
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own but a common word order fragment in German perfect tense: subject (ich) + object (sie) + past participle (gesehen) often appears inside a clause. 'Sie' can mean 'her' (accusative singular) or 'them' depending on context. In full sentences the auxiliary verb 'habe' appears (e.g. 'Ich habe sie gesehen.'), but in subordinate clauses or when words are moved, you can find 'ich sie gesehen' separated by other words: e.g. 'mit denen ich sie gesehen habe.'
target_language_example: Gestern im Park habe ich sie gesehen.
native_language_example: Yesterday in the park I saw her.

meaning: 'I ... her/them/it still' — a fragment showing the pronoun 'ich' (I), object pronoun 'sie' (her/them/you formal depending on context), and 'noch' meaning 'still' or 'yet'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common word order fragment in German sentences. 'Sie' can be feminine singular 'her', plural 'them', or formal 'you' (Sie) depending on context and capitalization. 'Noch' often means 'still' (continuing situation) or 'yet' (in questions). Word order and verb position matter: the verb usually appears after the subject ('ich') or in second position in questions. Pay attention to context to know which meaning of 'noch' and which 'sie' is intended.
target_language_example: Manchmal vermisse ich sie noch.
native_language_example: Sometimes I still miss her.

meaning: I (would) anyway / I (would) in any case
additional_notes: Used to say that the speaker would do or feel something regardless of other factors. Often appears in sentences like "Das wollte ich sowieso machen" (I was going to do that anyway) or to emphasize inevitability (e.g. "kann ich sowieso nicht mehr schlafen"). "sowieso" can modify verbs, statements, or attitudes and is common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Das hätte ich sowieso gesagt.
native_language_example: I would have said that anyway.

meaning: 'I found/realized' (simple past of 'feststellen' — to notice, realize, find out).
additional_notes: Used to report a discovery or realization in the past. Often appears as 'ich stellte fest, dass ...' meaning 'I realized that ...' or 'I found that ...'. 'stellte' is the Präteritum (simple past); in spoken German you'd often hear 'ich habe festgestellt' (present perfect).
target_language_example: Ich stellte fest, dass die Tür offen war.
native_language_example: I realized that the door was open.

meaning: I'm disturbing (you) / I interrupt (you).
additional_notes: Used when apologizing for interrupting or bothering someone. Often appears in polite phrases: "Es tut mir leid, wenn ich störe" (Sorry if I'm disturbing) or "Ich hoffe, ich störe dich nicht" (I hope I'm not disturbing you). The object (dich/Sie) is often omitted when context is clear. Verb tense is present; choose formal "ich störe Sie nicht" when speaking to someone formally.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung — ich störe kurz, habe eine Frage.
native_language_example: Excuse me — I'm interrupting briefly, I have a question.

meaning: 'I stepped' or 'I entered' (past tense of 'treten').
additional_notes: Ich trat is the simple past (Präteritum) of treten. Depending on context it can mean 'I stepped', 'I kicked', 'I entered' (e.g. joined an organization using 'ein' as a separable prefix: 'ein|treten' → 'eintrat' or in spoken/written simple past 'trat ... ein'), or 'I moved' (e.g. stepped aside 'zur Seite treten'). The separable verbs place the prefix at the end in sentences (e.g. 'Ich trat in die Luftwaffe ein.').
target_language_example: Ich trat zur Seite, damit sie durchgehen konnte.
native_language_example: I stepped aside so she could pass through.

meaning: 'I (am) sad' — a brief/telegraphic expression indicating the speaker's sadness; grammatically it omits the copula 'bin'.
additional_notes: This sequence pairs the pronoun 'ich' (I) with the adjective 'traurig' (sad). Standard German requires a verb: 'Ich bin traurig.' Omitting the verb occurs in colloquial, poetic, or telegraphic contexts (e.g., headlines, captions, messages, song lyrics) or as part of reduced clauses. Use to indicate feelings; in full sentences include 'bin' for correctness.
target_language_example: Wenn ich traurig bin, schreibe ich manchmal 'ich traurig' in mein Tagebuch.
native_language_example: When I'm sad, I sometimes write 'ich traurig' in my diary.

meaning: I would do
additional_notes: Konjunktiv II of tun. It is used for hypothetical, unreal, or polite statements. In everyday German, speakers often prefer 'ich würde ... tun' or simply another verb instead. In some expressions, English may translate it more naturally without 'do', for example 'ich täte besser daran ...' = 'I'd better ...'.
target_language_example: Ich täte dir gern helfen, wenn ich könnte.
native_language_example: I would gladly help you if I could.

meaning: 'I forgive (you)'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone you forgive them. Often followed by 'dir' (ich vergebe dir) when forgiving a person. Can be simple forgiveness (Ja, ich vergebe dir) or conditional/partial (Ich vergebe dir, aber ...). Tone can be serious or casual depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich vergebe dir für das Missverständnis.
native_language_example: I forgive you for the misunderstanding.

meaning: I don't understand / I don't get it.
additional_notes: Use to say you do not understand what someone said or the reason for something. Polite/formal version: same phrase works with Sie (e.g. "Ich verstehe nicht, was Sie meinen"). Can be followed by a clause introduced by "was", "wieso", "wovon", etc., or used alone as a brief response.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, warum das so teuer ist.
native_language_example: I don't understand why that is so expensive.

meaning: 'I (heard/know/thought) from him' — a sequence indicating that the speaker's information, impression or action relates to a male person; exact meaning depends on surrounding verbs and context.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — it's a combination of the subject pronoun 'ich' and the prepositional phrase 'von ihm' (dative of 'er'). Often appears in larger sentences where a verb is present or implied (e.g. 'Ich habe von ihm gehört', 'Das wusste ich von ihm'). In colloquial speech ellipsis may lead to fragments like 'Ich — von ihm.' 'Von' can mean 'from' (source) or 'about' depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Als er gefragt wurde, sagte ich von ihm nichts.
native_language_example: When he was asked, I said nothing about him.

meaning: I (a short while ago) / I earlier (today) — indicates the speaker referring to something they did or noticed a short time before now.
additional_notes: "Vorhin" means 'a short time ago' or 'earlier (today)'. Combined with a pronoun like "ich" it marks that the speaker themself did or experienced something recently. Common in everyday speech (neutral, not slang). The phrase "ich vorhin" typically appears within a larger clause (e.g., "Das habe ich vorhin nicht erwähnt").
target_language_example: Das habe ich vorhin nicht erwähnt, oder?
native_language_example: I didn't mention that a little while ago, did I?

meaning: 'I woke' (simple past of 'aufwachen' — I woke up).
additional_notes: Used to say you woke up (often followed by 'auf' as separable verb: 'ich wachte auf' or more commonly in spoken German 'ich bin aufgewacht'). The sentences show time or reason clauses (when the phone rang, at sunrise, at five in the morning). In everyday speech Germans usually use the perfect: 'ich bin aufgewacht.'
target_language_example: Ich wachte spät auf und hatte keine Zeit zum Frühstück.
native_language_example: I woke up late and didn't have time for breakfast.

meaning: I was (at/in/on/connected to) ... — depends on context.
additional_notes: The phrase 'ich war an' combines the verb 'war' (was) with the preposition 'an' and needs a noun or noun phrase to complete its meaning. 'An' can indicate responsibility ('an allem schuld sein' = to be to blame for), location ('an dem Ort' or 'an der Universität' = at the place/university), or time/manner in some contexts ('an dem Abend' = on that evening). Choose the correct prepositional phrase following 'an' (often 'an + dem' becomes 'am' in spoken/written German: 'ich war am Abend').
target_language_example: Ich war an dem Projekt beteiligt.
native_language_example: I was involved in the project.

meaning: I was (for) three (units of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long you were somewhere or in a state: combine with a time unit (Jahre, Tage, Wochen, Monate). Often includes 'lang' or 'mit [person]'/prepositional phrase: e.g. 'Ich war drei Jahre lang im Gefängnis.' For durations with activities you can also use 'drei Tage damit beschäftigt ...'. English equivalents: 'I was in prison for three years', 'I was married to Tom for three years.'
target_language_example: Ich war drei Monate in Spanien.
native_language_example: I was in Spain for three months.

meaning: I was sad.
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of 'sein' (to be) used to describe a past emotional state. Commonly used in telling stories or describing how you felt at a specific time. For everyday spoken German, many speakers use the perfect ('ich bin traurig gewesen'), but 'ich war traurig' is perfectly natural and common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Als das Konzert abgesagt wurde, ich war traurig, aber dann traf ich alte Freunde.
native_language_example: When the concert was cancelled, I was sad, but then I met old friends.

meaning: "I refuse" (first-person singular of weigern, used with a reflexive pronoun: ich weigere mich).
additional_notes: German verb weigern is normally reflexive when saying 'I refuse' — you say "ich weigere mich (zu ... / dagegen)". Alone, "ich weigere" is incomplete and uncommon in standard German. More natural alternatives: "ich weigere mich" (I refuse), or "ich lehne ab" (I decline/refuse). Use "zu + infinitive" to say what you refuse to do: "Ich weigere mich, zu unterschreiben."
target_language_example: Ich weigere mich, das Formular zu unterschreiben.
native_language_example: I refuse to sign the form.

meaning: I know / I'm aware / I'm informed.
additional_notes: Used to say you have the necessary information or understand a situation. Can be a short reply (like 'I know') or reassure someone you’ll take action when informed. Tone can be neutral or a bit curt depending on context. Literal parts: 'weiß' = know, 'Bescheid' = information/notification.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich weiß Bescheid und kümmere mich darum.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I know and I'll take care of it.

meaning: I don't (know) any more / I no longer know (something).
additional_notes: Used to say that you no longer know or remember something, or that you're out of ideas/at a loss (e.g., 'Ich weiß nicht mehr weiter' = 'I don't know what to do next'). Context determines whether it's about memory (who/what/when) or about being unable to continue/solve a problem. 'Mehr' here means 'anymore' or 'any longer.'
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht mehr, wo ich das Buch hingelegt habe.
native_language_example: I don't know anymore where I put the book.

meaning: I will do (something).
additional_notes: Ich werde + verb (infinitive) is the simple future construction in German. However, 'ich werde tun' by itself is uncommon and feels incomplete; native speakers usually include an object or a specific verb infinitive, e.g. 'ich werde es tun' or 'ich werde das machen/erledigen/versuchen'. In everyday speech Germans often use the present tense with a future time expression (e.g. 'Ich mache das morgen').
target_language_example: Ich werde tun, was nötig ist.
native_language_example: I will do what is necessary.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase; these three words can appear together within a larger sentence. Literally: 'ich' = I, 'wieder' = again, 'zu' = to/at (meaning depends on context).
additional_notes: This sequence is incomplete by itself and typically requires additional words (especially a verb or noun phrase) before or after to form a grammatical sentence. It can occur when the verb or noun appears elsewhere in the sentence or is implied. Examples of completions include 'Ich komme wieder zu ...' (I come back to ...), 'Ich bin wieder zu Hause.' (I am home again) — note word order for 'zu Hause'. Beginners should look for the missing element that completes the clause.
target_language_example: Ich wieder zu sagen, wäre unhöflich.
native_language_example: Saying 'I again to' would be rude.

meaning: 'I want that' or 'I want it'.
additional_notes: A direct, strong way to say you want something. 'Das' can refer to a specific thing previously mentioned or pointed at (that/it). In polite requests, use 'ich möchte das' or add 'bitte'. Context and tone matter: can sound demanding. Word order can change with emphasis (e.g. 'Das will ich.').
target_language_example: Ich will das Buch dort, bitte.
native_language_example: I want that book over there, please.

meaning: 'I don't want (any) more' or 'I can't/don't want to continue (with this)'
additional_notes: Common phrase to refuse something (e.g., more food, drinks) or to say you no longer want to continue an activity or situation. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be polite refusal, tired/frustrated complaint, or a stronger emotional statement. If used alone it often implies 'I've had enough' or 'I can't take it anymore.'
target_language_example: Danke, ich will nicht mehr. Ich bin satt.
native_language_example: Thanks, I don't want any more. I'm full.

meaning: 'I lived' (simple past / narrative past of wohnen).
additional_notes: Used to say where you lived in the past. 'Wohnen' = to live/reside (more like 'be living' or 'reside' than 'have a home'). 'Ich wohnte' is the Präteritum (simple past) and is common in written/narrative German; in spoken German people often say 'ich habe gewohnt' or use 'wohnte' in stories. Can be followed by locations (in, neben, am) or by a place (Hotel, Stadt).
target_language_example: Ich wohnte früher in einem kleinen Haus am Fluss.
native_language_example: I lived earlier in a small house by the river.

meaning: I knew it (after all) / I told you so — expresses that the speaker's previous suspicion or expectation was correct.
additional_notes: Used when something the speaker suspected or predicted turns out to be true. 'Doch' adds emphasis — a sense of 'after all' or 'see, I was right'. Common in spoken German. Can be followed by a subordinate clause with 'dass' or by a statement. Tone can be reassuring, triumphant, or slightly reproachful.
target_language_example: Ich wusste doch, dass er gelogen hat.
native_language_example: I knew it — that he lied.

meaning: I didn't know (at all); I had no idea.
additional_notes: Used to express surprise about new information. Often followed by 'dass' + clause (that ...). 'Gar' emphasizes negation (completely/not at all). Polite and common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich wusste gar nicht, dass du heute Geburtstag hast.
native_language_example: I had no idea that it's your birthday today.

meaning: I would be more / I would rather be more (context-dependent)
additional_notes: This phrase uses the subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) of sein: 'wäre'. On its own it is incomplete and typically followed by an adjective, adverb, prepositional phrase, or clause that specifies what 'more' refers to (e.g., 'ich wäre mehr überzeugt', 'ich wäre mehr dabei'). It expresses a hypothetical increase in some quality, degree, or involvement. Context is required to make the idea specific.
target_language_example: Ich wäre mehr, wenn ich deine Unterstützung hätte.
native_language_example: I would be more if I had your support.

meaning: I'd like to know / I would like to find out.
additional_notes: Polite, slightly formal or tentative way to ask for information. Uses Konjunktiv II (wüsste) to soften the question—similar to 'ich möchte gern wissen'. Common in spoken and written German. Followed by a clause introduced by ob, was, wie, etc.
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gern, ob das Meeting verschoben wird.
native_language_example: I'd like to know whether the meeting will be postponed.

meaning: I open / I'm opening.
additional_notes: First-person singular present of öffnen (to open). Used to say you are opening something now or will open it. Can be followed by a direct object (die Tür, die Luke, sie) or stand alone in response (e.g., 'Gut, ich öffne.' = 'Okay, I'll open.').
target_language_example: Ich öffne das Fenster, damit frische Luft hereinkommt.
native_language_example: I open the window so fresh air can come in.

meaning: I it
additional_notes: shortened form of ich es. It is mainly used in speech and informal writing when ich and es come directly next to each other, often in subordinate clauses or after inversion, as in wenn ich’s weiß or dann sage ich’s. In more formal writing, ich es is usually preferred. English normally would not translate this as a fixed unit; it simply means ich + es.
target_language_example: Wenn ich’s sehe, sage ich dir Bescheid.
native_language_example: If I see it, I’ll let you know.

meaning: with him when / at the time that
additional_notes: Combines 'bei ihm' (at/with him; indicates presence near a male person) with 'als' (when/as — used for a single past event). Used to say who was present at a specific moment in the past (e.g., when someone died, saw something, fled). 'Als' here is temporal and refers to one occasion; for repeated actions use 'wenn'. Word order: 'bei ihm, als ...' or 'Sie waren bei ihm, als er ...'.
target_language_example: Sie waren bei ihm, als er die Nachricht bekam.
native_language_example: They were with him when he received the news.

meaning: 'to him, it' — two short pronouns used together to refer to a person (ihm = to him) and a neutral thing or statement (es = it/that).
additional_notes: Common in German when reporting things to someone or explaining something to a third person: first the indirect object (ihm = 'to him'), then the neutral pronoun es ('it' or 'that') which refers to the information, object or situation. Word order is flexible in German, but this paired form often appears in spoken and written instructions or requests (e.g. "Sag ihm, es ist dringend" = "Tell him it's urgent"). The pronouns can refer to clauses (es = 'that...') as well as nouns. Formal address uses "Sagen Sie ihm, ...".
target_language_example: Sag ihm, es ist wichtig.
native_language_example: Tell him it's important.

meaning: A short way to report speech: 'tell him (that) I…' — used to introduce what you want the other person to say to him on your behalf.
additional_notes: This is a spoken/informal pattern: two clauses linked by a comma, where the speaker instructs someone to tell a third person (ihm) what the speaker (ich) says or wants. Often used with imperatives (Sag ihm..., Ruf ... an) followed by the content starting with 'ich' (e.g. 'ich nehme…', 'ich will…'). In English you would say 'tell him I...' or 'tell him that I...'.
target_language_example: Sag ihm, ich kann heute Abend nicht kommen.
native_language_example: Tell him I can't come tonight.

meaning: to him, not — used to indicate advising or referring negatively about 'him'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's just the dative pronoun 'ihm' (to/for him) or 'because of him' in some contexts, followed by 'nicht' (not). In examples 1, 3–6 'ihm, nicht' appears in reported advice constructions: someone advised him not to do something (e.g., 'riet ihm, nicht zu rauchen' = 'advised him not to smoke'). In example 2 ('Es ist wegen ihm, nicht?') 'ihm' is the object of a preposition ('wegen ihm' — because of him) and 'nicht?' is a question tag meaning 'right?'. Word order and punctuation in German normally: 'ihm nicht' (no comma) within a sentence; when introducing an infinitive clause after a verb of advising, use a comma: 'riet ihm, nicht ...'.
target_language_example: Die Mutter riet ihm, nicht so spät nach Hause zu kommen.
native_language_example: The mother advised him not to come home so late.

meaning: part of several separable verb constructions; generally means 'to (him) —' as the dative object used with verbs that separate (e.g. sich anfreunden mit, ankommen, anstehen, ansehen).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the words 'ihm an' often appear when a separable or reflexive verb with the prefix 'an-' is used and 'ihm' is the dative pronoun (to/for him). The exact English translation depends on the verb: 'mit ihm anfreunden' → 'become friends with him'; 'kurz nach ihm ankommen' → 'arrive shortly after him'; 'mit ihm anstehen' → 'stand in line with him' or 'wait with him'; 'sieht man ihm an' (sehen + an) → 'you can tell by looking at him'. Pay attention to word order: in perfect or main clauses the prefix 'an' often appears at the end (separable verb).
target_language_example: Man sieht ihm an, dass ihn die Reise erschöpft hat.
native_language_example: You can tell (by looking at) that he is exhausted from the trip.

meaning: to him as well / also to him
additional_notes: Combines the dative pronoun 'ihm' (to him) with the adverb 'auch' (also). Used to indicate that something applies additionally to 'him' — e.g. someone receives/experiences something in addition to others. Word order can vary depending on sentence; 'auch' can come before or after 'ihm' ('auch ihm') with little change in meaning.
