Often followed by a clause (comma + clause). Tone can be neutral to dramatic. Polite/formal pronouns (Sie/Ihnen) or informal (du/dir) appear depending on context.
target_language_example: Was ich dir jetzt sage, ist ehrlich gemeint.
native_language_example: What I'm about to tell you now is meant honestly.

meaning: now be
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to adopt a different attitude or behavior immediately (e.g., 'be serious', 'be quiet', 'don't be silly'). Often followed by an adjective or phrase (sei nicht so, sei still, sei ernst). 'Jetzt' adds urgency ('now' / 'come on'). Common in spoken German; tone can be firm, pleading, or admonishing depending on context.
target_language_example: Jetzt sei bitte ruhig und hör zu.
native_language_example: Now be quiet please and listen.

meaning: 'now I understand' (short for 'jetzt verstehe ich')
additional_notes: Used to show that you have just realized or understood something. Often appears in the shortened form 'jetzt verstehe (ich)' in informal speech or notes; full sentence is 'jetzt verstehe ich'. Can be used alone as a reaction (like 'I see' or 'now I get it').
target_language_example: Ah, jetzt verstehe ich, warum du gestern spät warst.
native_language_example: Ah, now I understand why you were late yesterday.

meaning: now much / now a lot (used to intensify a change compared to before).
additional_notes: Combines jetzt (now) + viel (much/a lot) to emphasize that something is noticeably more or better than before. Common in comparisons: 'jetzt viel besser' = 'now much better'. Not a fixed idiom—grammar depends on the adjective, adverb, or verb it modifies (e.g. besser, hübscher, fleißiger, geht es ... besser).
target_language_example: Seit der Kur geht es ihm jetzt viel besser.
native_language_example: Since the treatment, he is now much better.

meaning: 'now (something)' — used in casual speech to mean 'now' + an unspecified small action or thing (e.g. have something to eat/drink/ do something now).
additional_notes: Informal spoken German. 'Was' here is vague and means 'something' or 'a little'. Common in phrases like 'jetzt was trinken/essen/kriegen' = 'to have/get something to drink/eat/now'. Often used when suggesting or stating a short, immediate action. Word order: 'jetzt was' can appear before the verb (Gehen wir jetzt was trinken?) or before the noun (Ich will jetzt was essen).
target_language_example: Wollen wir jetzt was spazieren gehen?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a (short) walk now?

meaning: now (what) next / now continue
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell what comes next or to tell someone to continue. Can appear in commands (Gehen Sie jetzt weiter! — Keep walking/Move on now), in transitional phrases in speech or text (und jetzt weiter im Text — and now back to the text), or in questions about the next step (Wie geht es jetzt weiter?). Tone is neutral; context determines whether it's an instruction, a transition, or a question.
target_language_example: Wir haben die Einladung geschrieben — und jetzt weiter zum Einladungsversand.
native_language_example: We have written the invitation — and now on to sending the invitations.

meaning: 'now you know' (beginning of a sentence addressing 'du')
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used to tell someone they are informed or have learned something just explained. Usually followed by du/du's/du es/du Bescheid/warum, etc. Often used conversationally to confirm understanding or to close a topic. Tone can be neutral, reassuring, or slightly dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Jetzt weißt du, wie man das Formular ausfüllt.
native_language_example: Now you know how to fill out the form.

meaning: now (we/they/you) will... — used to introduce an action that will happen next
additional_notes: Combines jetzt (now) with the auxiliary werden (will/become) to form a future or imminent action. Context and subject determine who will do it (we/you/they). Often followed by an infinitive: "Jetzt werden wir ... + Infinitiv." Can also be emphatic, announcing a next step or consequence. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Jetzt werden wir das Problem lösen.
native_language_example: Now we will solve the problem.

meaning: now I/you/he/she/etc. want(s) to (do something) — introduces what someone intends or is about to say/do
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to announce an intention, decision, or upcoming statement. Often followed by a verb or a clause (e.g., 'jetzt will ich…', 'jetzt will sie…'). Can be emphatic or confrontational depending on tone and context (e.g., 'Jetzt will ich dir mal was sagen' = 'Now I'm going to tell you something' — could be friendly or scolding). In sentence 6 the structure 'will mir ... erzählen' shows a dative pronoun and a negative/irritated tone ('...will mir erzählen').
target_language_example: Jetzt will ich endlich Urlaub machen.
native_language_example: Now I want to finally go on vacation.

meaning: 'now (you/we) want to' — used to introduce what someone wants to do or to start an action (often colloquial).
additional_notes: Combine jetzt (now) + wollen (to want). Used to state someone's desire or to prompt/shift to an action. Context determines the subject (Sie, wir, du) and tone: can be confrontational (example 1), curious/judging (example 2) or encouraging/suggesting (example 3). Common in spoken German. Verb agreement with the subject follows in the sentence (e.g., jetzt wollen Sie, jetzt wollen wir).
target_language_example: Jetzt wollen wir endlich anfangen zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: Now we want to finally start working.

meaning: 'now to' or 'now heading to' (used before a feminine or dative place/event noun with the article contracted: zu + der → zur).
additional_notes: Combines jetzt (now) + zur (contraction of zu + der). Used to say someone is going or moving toward a place or event right now. The noun after 'zur' is usually feminine (e.g. Trauung, Uni as short for Universität) or a dative singular feminine noun; context determines the exact English translation (going to, heading to, off to, must now do...).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt zur Bibliothek.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library now.

meaning: ‘is young’ — third-person singular form of the verb sein (to be) with the adjective jung (young).
additional_notes: Simple adjective + verb combination used to state that someone or something is young. Appears in predicate position after the subject (e.g. "Sie ist jung"). Word order may change in questions or with emphasis (e.g. "Ist er jung?"). Not idiomatic; purely descriptive. Can combine with adverbs or contrasting conjunctions (e.g. "jung ist er zwar, aber..." for contrast).
target_language_example: Wenn man jung ist, lernt man schnell.
native_language_example: When one is young, one learns quickly.

meaning: used with 'sein' or other verbs to say 'to be young' (young to be...).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own — 'jung' (young) combines with an infinitive construction using 'zu' when forming certain infinitive phrases (e.g. 'zu sein' = 'to be'). In sentences like 'scheint jung zu sein' the structure is: verb (scheint) + adjective (jung) + zu + infinitive (sein). Beginners can treat 'jung zu sein' as 'to be young' when it follows verbs like 'scheinen', 'finden', 'glauben', etc. Also appears in statements like 'jung zu sterben' = 'to die young' (here 'sterben' is the infinitive after 'zu').
target_language_example: Sie scheint jung zu sein.
native_language_example: She seems to be young.

meaning: 'so cold that' — introduces a result clause showing the effect of cold.
additional_notes: Used with 'so/so... dass' (often 'so kalt, dass' or 'so ... dass') to connect a cause (very cold) and its consequence. In German word order the verb of the 'dass' clause goes to the end. Commonly the comma is placed before 'dass'. You can also say 'es war so kalt, dass...' or 'ich bin so müde, dass...'.
target_language_example: Draußen war es so kalt, dass die Wasserleitungen einfrieren.
native_language_example: It was so cold outside that the water pipes froze.

meaning: 'cold here' — used to say that the current place feels cold.
additional_notes: A simple way to comment on the temperature of the place you're in. Commonly used with 'es ist' (Es ist kalt hier.). Can be modified with adverbs: sehr (very), besonders (particularly), tierisch (colloquial: extremely). Can be used both as an observation and as a prompt to change the situation (e.g., ask someone to close a window or add wood to a fire).
target_language_example: Es ist kalt hier, kannst du das Fenster schließen?
native_language_example: It's cold here, can you close the window?

meaning: cold in (used to say a place or time is cold)
additional_notes: Used to describe that it was cold at/in a location or during a time. Commonly appears with Es war/Es wurde/War es/ Ist dir + kalt in + [place or time]. When asking about a person’s feeling use 'Ist dir kalt in ...?' (Are you cold in ...?). 'Kalt in' is compositional and literal: 'kalt' = cold, 'in' = in/at.
target_language_example: Es war kalt in der Wohnung.
native_language_example: It was cold in the apartment.

meaning: 'kam ... an' is the simple past (Präteritum) form of the separable verb 'ankommen' used in constructions where the finite verb 'kam' appears and the separable particle 'an' moves to the clause end; 'kam der' occurs when 'kam' is followed immediately by a determiner 'der' (masculine or genitive/relative uses) as part of the subject or noun phrase.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself—it's a fragment of the past-tense separable verb construction 'kam ... an' (ankommen). The particle 'an' goes to the end of the clause: e.g. 'kam der Scherz ... an'. 'Ankommen' can mean 'to arrive' (physical) or 'to be received/liked' (idiomatic). Word order depends on sentence structure; here 'der' begins the following noun phrase (e.g., 'der Scherz', 'der Mann').
target_language_example: Wie es aussah, kam der Scherz bei Sarkozy nicht gut an.
native_language_example: As it seemed, the joke was not well received by Sarkozy.

meaning: a simple past phrase meaning 'a ... came' or 'arrived' (something/someone arrived).
additional_notes: ‘kam’ is the past tense of kommen (to come). When followed by the indefinite article ‘ein’ it introduces that something (a thing or person) arrived or was received: e.g. 'kam ein Brief' = 'a letter came' / 'a letter arrived'. Common in describing mail, news, rumors, or arrivals. Word order can vary (subject may be omitted): 'Heute kam ein Buch in der Post.'
target_language_example: Gestern kam ein Paket mit neuen Schuhen an.
native_language_example: Yesterday a parcel with new shoes arrived.

meaning: 'he came' or 'he arrived' (simple past of kommen for 'er').
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) form of kommen used with the pronoun 'er' (he). In German, 'kam er' often appears when the verb precedes the subject (e.g., in questions, subordinate clauses with verb-first placement, or after adverbials). Depending on context, kommen can mean 'come' (approach) or 'arrive' (often with an additional particle like 'an' or an adverbial). Example contexts: questions ('Wann kam er hier an?'), narrative past tense ('Als ich gerade gehen wollte, kam er an.'), or idiomatic uses ('Und selbstverständlich kam er auch auf mich.' meaning 'And of course he also came to me/approached me').
target_language_example: Wann kam er hier an?
native_language_example: When did he arrive here?

meaning: came/arrived as (in the role/state of) or came in a certain order (e.g., as first/last).
additional_notes: Used with 'als' to indicate the role, status, or change someone had when arriving (e.g. 'als Lehrer' = 'as a teacher'), or with superlatives/ordinal expressions to state arrival order (e.g. 'als Erste/Letzte' = 'came first/last'). Context and grammar determine meaning: for roles it usually refers to a temporary or stated capacity; for order it refers to sequence. Verb tense will change ('kommt als', 'ist als ... gekommen').
target_language_example: Sie kam als Erste ins Zimmer.
native_language_example: She came into the room first.

meaning: past tense of 'kommen' + preposition 'in' with a time/place phrase: 'came in/at/during' or 'arrived in/at/during' (he came/arrived in ...).
additional_notes: Kam im is the simple past form (er kam) of kommen followed by the preposition in used with a time expression (im Juni, im Morgengrauen, im letzten Jahr) or with a noun phrase indicating manner/place (im Bademantel = wearing a bathrobe). In English the preposition choice varies (in, at, during, wearing). Use 'im' = in + dem (masculine/neuter dative) for months, parts of day, years (im letzten Jahr), and clothing/conditions (im Bademantel).
target_language_example: Er kam im Dezember spät nach Hause.
native_language_example: He came home late in December.

meaning: 'came/arrived' or 'managed' + 'only/just' — expresses limitation or qualification (e.g. only came, just came, merely managed).
additional_notes: kam is the past (simple) form of kommen (to come). nur means only/just/merely. Together they limit or qualify the action: 'came only', 'just came', 'only managed to'. Context determines exact translation: temporal ('just a moment late'), exclusivity ('only Tom came'), or difficulty ('only just managed').
target_language_example: Ich kam nur kurz vorbei, um das Paket zu bringen.
native_language_example: I only stopped by briefly to bring the package.

meaning: 'came' or 'arrived' + 'very' (past tense of kommen with intensifier)
additional_notes: kam = simple past (preterite) of kommen (to come/arrive). sehr is an adverb meaning 'very' and modifies adjectives or adverbs (e.g., sehr spät = very late; sehr zufrieden = very satisfied). In sentences the order is subject + kam + sehr + adjective/phrase. Common in narrative or reports about arrival times or states.
target_language_example: Sie kam sehr müde nach Hause.
native_language_example: She came home very tired.

meaning: arrived/returned at (a specific time).
additional_notes: Past tense of 'ankommen' or 'zurückkommen' when giving the time someone arrived or returned. Common structure: 'kam um + [time]' (e.g. 'kam um sechs Uhr zurück' = 'returned at six o'clock'). Often followed by place (nach Hause, aus der Bibliothek). Not to be confused with 'umkommen' (to die).
target_language_example: Sie kam um acht Uhr nach Hause.
native_language_example: She came home at eight o'clock.

meaning: 'came' or 'arrived' (past of 'vorkommen'/'ankommen' depending on context) — often used to mean 'came/arrived (at/after/of a time)' or 'came before' in legal phrasing.
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) form of verbs used in different constructions: - as part of 'vorkommen' (to occur/happen) or legal phrase 'vor Gericht kommen' = 'to come before a court / be brought to court'; - as past of 'ankommen' in colloquial contexts meaning 'to come/arrive' or 'to return' (e.g. 'kam nach Hause' = 'came home'); - used with time expressions: 'vor drei Jahren' = 'three years ago' (literal: 'came before three years'). Context tells the exact verb sense. Not informal.
target_language_example: Ich kam vor drei Jahren nach Deutschland.
native_language_example: I came to Germany three years ago.

meaning: arrived (somewhere) / was late (came late).
additional_notes: Past-tense form of 'kommen' + adverb/particle 'zu' in these examples means 'to arrive' (often with 'zu spät' = 'too late' / 'late'). Common pattern: 'zu spät kommen' = 'to be late'. 'kam zu' appears in sentences like 'kam zu spät' or 'kam zu [Ort]'. Use with time expressions or places: 'kam zu spät zur Schule', 'kam zu Hause' (less common).
target_language_example: Er kam zu spät zur Arbeit, weil der Bus verspätet war.
native_language_example: He arrived late to work because the bus was delayed.

meaning: 'came to' or 'came into' (used before a noun to indicate arrival or that something began/was used).
additional_notes: Past tense of kommen + the preposition 'zu'. Common patterns: 'kam zum Einsatz' = 'was put into use/was used', 'kam zum Spielen' = 'came to play' (i.e. arrived to play), 'kam zum richtigen Zeitpunkt' = 'arrived/appeared at the right time'. After 'zum' a noun (often with a verbal noun or fixed phrase) follows. Literal translation is possible but exact English phrasing varies.
target_language_example: Die Hilfe kam zum richtigen Zeitpunkt.
native_language_example: The help came at the right time.

meaning: came/arrived on (a day) or at (a place) — past tense of 'ankommen' with a time or location introduced by 'am'.
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) form of 'ankommen' (sie kamen = they arrived) followed by the preposition 'am' (= an + dem). 'Am' is used before days (e.g. am Montag) and before certain locations with articles (e.g. am Fuße des Berges = at the foot of the mountain). Use 'kamen am' for plural subjects or formal past narration; for conversational past you might hear 'sind am ... angekommen'.
target_language_example: Wir kamen am Abend am Bahnhof an.
native_language_example: We arrived at the train station in the evening.

meaning: they came
additional_notes: Past tense of kommen with lowercase sie = "they." In German, the verb can come before the subject after another element or in questions: "Dann kamen sie" = "then they came," "Wann kamen sie?" = "when did they come?" If it appears with a separated prefix, the full meaning may change, for example "kamen sie frei" from freikommen = "they were released."
target_language_example: Um neun Uhr kamen sie endlich nach Hause.
native_language_example: They finally came home at nine o'clock.

meaning: we came / we arrived / we got (somewhere) — simple past (Präteritum) of 'kommen' for 'wir'.
additional_notes: Used to describe past arrival or movement of 'we'. Context decides exact English: 'came', 'arrived', 'got', or 'managed to'. In narratives it's common to use Präteritum (kamen wir) rather than Perfekt (sind wir gekommen). Word order: verb first in past narrative clauses (e.g. 'Dann kamen wir...') or after a clause element ('Nachdem wir ... gekommen waren' uses Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Stunden kamen wir am Bahnhof an.
native_language_example: Two hours ago we arrived at the station.

meaning: Combination of the modal verb 'kann' (from können — can / be able to) with the relative/interrogative pronoun 'was' (what / that which). Used in subordinate clauses or embedded questions to mean 'can ... what' / 'can ... that/what' (e.g., 'can see what', 'can do what').
additional_notes: 'kann, was' is not a fixed idiom but a common sequence where 'kann' appears before or near 'was' in subordinate clauses or indirect questions. Word order: in subordinate clauses the conjugated modal often appears toward the end of the clause (e.g., 'sehen kann, was...'), and in main clauses the modal precedes the verb. 'Was' refers to things or actions (not persons). Examples often contain commas when introducing subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur jemanden gesucht, der sehen kann, was ich sehe.
native_language_example: I was only looking for someone who can see what I see.

meaning: can (speak/understand/use) French; 'kann' = can (able to).
additional_notes: This combines the modal verb 'kann' (ich/er/sie/etc. form of 'können') with the noun 'Französisch' (the French language). It expresses ability, possibility, permission, or capacity regarding the French language. Context determines the exact verb after 'kann' (e.g. lesen, verstehen, unterrichten) or it can be used alone to mean 'can speak French'. Word order: verb (kann) + language (Französisch) + infinitive or object. Examples with 'nicht' negate the ability (Ich kann Französisch nicht leiden = I can't stand French).
target_language_example: Ich kann Französisch sprechen, aber nicht sehr gut.
native_language_example: I can speak French, but not very well.

meaning: can your
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. In the examples, kann means 'can' and Ihren means the formal 'your' (used with Sie) before a masculine noun in the accusative, such as Computer or Rechner. Ihren is capitalized because it refers to formal Sie.
target_language_example: Die Software kann Ihren Browser verlangsamen.
native_language_example: The software can slow down your browser.

meaning: 'cannot (you) [formal]' — used to express inability with the formal pronoun 'Sie' (you).
additional_notes: Formed from the modal verb 'können' in the present tense ('kann') + the formal object pronoun 'Sie' + negation 'nicht'. Often followed by an infinitive or complement later in the sentence (e.g. verstehen, mitnehmen, retten, loben). Context determines exact English rendering (e.g. 'I cannot understand you', 'I cannot take you with me').
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber ich kann Sie nicht verstehen.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I cannot understand you.

meaning: "can everyone" or "can all" depending on context; literally 'can all' — used when a subject (he/she/it/I/etc.) is able to do something for or to everyone/all (or when 'alle' is the object meaning 'everything'/'all').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb 'kann' (can) plus the pronoun/determiner 'alle' (all/everyone). Meaning depends on sentence context: 'alle' can be people (everyone) or things (everything/all). Word order and case matter: with people 'alle' is usually nominative (everyone) or accusative (everyone as object). In spoken or written German you'll more often see full subjects (e.g. 'Er kann alle...') or different pronouns ('ich kann alle...').
target_language_example: Er kann alle Kinder unterrichten.
native_language_example: He can teach all the children.

meaning: can stay / may stay (is allowed or able to remain)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'kann' (can/may) with the verb 'bleiben' (to stay). Used to indicate permission ('may stay') or ability/possibility ('can stay'), depending on context and intonation. Often follows a subject (e.g. 'Der kann bleiben' = 'He/that one may stay'). Common in spoken and written German; word order and subject pronoun affect form (kann vs. kannst/können).
target_language_example: Er kann bleiben.
native_language_example: He can/may stay.

meaning: 'can (your) ...' — the modal verb 'kann' (can) + the possessive pronoun 'deine' (your, feminine/plural or informal).
additional_notes: Used when saying someone is able to do something about or related to something owned by 'du' (informal you). 'Deine' agrees with a feminine singular or plural noun (e.g. deine Frage, deine Eltern) and appears before the noun. In questions, word order changes: 'Kann deine Schwester ...?' means 'Can your sister ...?'.
target_language_example: Ich kann deine Nachricht lesen.
native_language_example: I can read your message.

meaning: literally 'can the human...' — part of a clause meaning 'is able to (do) the human ...' (e.g. 'can imitate the human ...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the beginning of a verb clause: 'kann' (can/is able to) + object 'die menschliche ...' (the human ...). Commonly appears with verbs like 'imitieren' or 'nachmachen' (imitate/mimic): 'kann die menschliche Stimme imitieren' = 'can imitate the human voice.' Useful to recognize the structure: subject + kann + (object) die menschliche + noun + verb (infinitive) at the end in German main clauses with modal verbs.
target_language_example: Der Papagei kann die menschliche Stimme sehr genau nachmachen.
native_language_example: The parrot can imitate the human voice very accurately.

meaning: 'can' or 'is able to' + 'through' (ability to go/see/pass/etc. through something).
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'kann' (from 'können' = can/able to) and the preposition/adverb 'durch' (through). Used to express the ability to move, pass, see, or travel through something or a space. Word order and complements vary: verb may be repeated (Ich kann durch Sie durchgehen) or followed by a noun phrase (durch die Zeit). Common in literal and figurative contexts.
target_language_example: Er kann durch die Tür gehen.
native_language_example: He can go through the door.

meaning: 'can (it) to you' — used to say you are able to do/say/explain something to someone (informal 'du' form).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the modal verb 'können' (kann) with the object pronoun 'es' (it) and the indirect object 'dir' (to you, informal). It's followed by an infinitive or past participle depending on the verb: e.g. 'kann es dir sagen' (can tell you), 'kann es dir nicht geben' (cannot give it to you). Use 'dir' for someone you address with 'du'. For formal speech use 'Ihnen' instead of 'dir'.
target_language_example: Ich kann es dir morgen erklären.
native_language_example: I can explain it to you tomorrow.

meaning: 'can [do] for me' or 'can I afford/allow myself' depending on context
additional_notes: This fragment appears in different constructions. Common uses: 1) with 'leisten' (kann es mir leisten) = 'I can afford it / allow myself it' (money or luxury). 2) with verbs like 'zum Vorwurf machen' (kann es mir zum Vorwurf machen) means 'he can blame me for it' (ability/permission in a rhetorical sense). The literal words are 'can it me', so the full meaning depends on the verb that follows or precedes. For beginners, learn the fixed phrase 'kann es mir leisten' = 'I can afford it'.
target_language_example: Ich kann es mir nicht leisten, Urlaub zu machen.
native_language_example: I can't afford to go on vacation.

meaning: "I can (for) you the..." — offers or ability to do something for a group (informal plural 'you').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short sequence: 'kann' (can) + 'euch' (informal plural 'you', dative) + definite article 'die' (feminine plural accusative or nominative plural depending on the noun). It appears before a direct object (e.g., 'die Bilder', 'die Flasche'). Use when offering to do or show something to multiple people you address informally. Word order can change in questions or with modal verbs; the key parts are the modal verb 'kann' + dative/accusative pronoun 'euch'.
target_language_example: Ich kann euch die Tür aufhalten.
native_language_example: I can hold the door open for you (all).

meaning: 'can almost' or 'is almost able to'
additional_notes: Used to say someone is nearly able to do something or nearly as (adjective/adverb) as someone/something else. 'kann' is the verb 'can/to be able to'; 'fast' modifies it to mean 'almost' or 'nearly'. Common in comparisons (fast genauso, fast so gut) and with verbs (fast jede... fahren = can almost drive any...). Word order: 'kann fast' appears before the verb or adjective phrase.
target_language_example: Sie kann fast so schnell lesen wie ihr Bruder.
native_language_example: She can almost read as fast as her brother.

meaning: can do something equally (as well/fast/stubbornly) — expresses ability at the same level as someone/something else.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb + 'wie' to compare abilities or qualities (kann genauso + [adverb/adjective] + wie + person). Often followed by verbs in infinitive (kann genauso schnell rennen wie...). 'Genauso' means 'just as' or 'equally'.
target_language_example: Ich kann genauso gut kochen wie meine Schwester.
native_language_example: I can cook just as well as my sister.

meaning: used to ask what you can do for someone; 'can I do for' — used when offering help, service, or asking how you can assist someone.
additional_notes: Typically appears in questions like 'Was kann ich für dich tun?' The person or pronoun follows 'für' (dich, Sie, euch, sie, die Damen, etc.). Formality depends on the pronoun (du = informal, Sie = formal). Often combined with words like 'Was' (what) or 'etwas' (something).
target_language_example: Was kann ich für dich tun?
native_language_example: What can I do for you?

meaning: How can I help you? / What can I do for you?
additional_notes: Polite, formal way to offer help or ask what someone needs. Uses formal 'Sie' (capitalized) — appropriate for strangers, customers, or in service situations. Often appears at the start of conversations (phone, reception, shops). You can make it less formal by using 'dir' and inversion: 'Was kann ich für dich tun?'.
target_language_example: Guten Tag. Was kann ich für Sie tun?
native_language_example: Good day. How can I help you?

meaning: 'can I (see/forget/give) her/it/them' — a polite question beginning meaning 'may I' or 'can I' followed by the pronoun 'sie'.
additional_notes: Used to ask permission or ability. 'kann' is the modal verb 'can/may', 'ich' = 'I', 'sie' can mean 'her', 'it' or 'them' depending on context (and can also be the formal 'you' = 'Sie' but here lowercase 'sie' = third person). Word order: modal verb first in yes/no questions ('Kann ich sie...?'). Context determines translation: 'sehen' → 'see her/it/them', 'schenken' → 'give it/them to someone', 'vergessen' → 'forget her/it/them'.
target_language_example: Kann ich sie fragen?
native_language_example: Can I ask her?

meaning: 'cannot' or 'am/are/is not able to' + negation of a noun or noun phrase (no/none/no ... able to)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'kann' (can/cannot) with the negating article 'kein' to say someone is unable to do something or that something is impossible; 'kein' negates a noun (kein Deutsch = no German / cannot speak German). Word order: 'kann' is conjugated for the subject, and 'kein' directly precedes the noun. Use 'kann nicht' to negate verbs (e.g., ich kann nicht schwimmen = I cannot swim).
target_language_example: Ich kann kein Auto fahren.
native_language_example: I cannot drive a car.

meaning: cannot (do) any / cannot (do) [something]; expresses inability or impossibility with a negative object (female form 'keine' depends on noun).
additional_notes: This combines the modal verb 'kann' (can/cannot) with the negative determiner 'keine' (no/none). It appears before a noun or verb phrase (often with an infinitive omitted in casual speech). Use 'keine' for feminine/plural/neutral contexts depending on case; word order follows normal German: 'kann keine' + noun (e.g. 'kann keine Kinder bekommen') or 'kann keine' + plural noun. In some sentences 'keine' negates a noun (I can't give any details) or is used idiomatically to mean 'cannot stand' (Ich kann keine Kommunisten leiden = I can't stand communists).
target_language_example: Ich kann keine Schokolade essen.
native_language_example: I can't eat any chocolate.

meaning: cannot (have/do) any; 'cannot' with a negated direct object (masculine/neuter accusative), often meaning 'there is no' or 'is unable to'.
additional_notes: Used when the verb is modal (kann) and the direct object is negated with keinen (masculine or mixed/neuter in accusative). Context decides translation: 'kann keinen Hunger haben' = 'cannot be hungry' (i.e. it's impossible), 'kann keinen Wein trinken' = 'is unable to drink any wine' (e.g. for health/religion). With abstract nouns it can mean 'there can be no...' (Es kann keinen Fortschritt geben = There can be no progress). Word order may vary; gender/case matters (use keine for feminine/plural).
target_language_example: Sie kann keinen Kaffee trinken, weil sie allergisch ist.
native_language_example: She cannot drink any coffee because she is allergic.

meaning: can (do something) for a long time; may take a long time
additional_notes: Used with verbs to express ability or possibility over a long duration (e.g., endure, wait, keep). Context determines whether it means 'is able to do something for a long time' (ability/endurance) or 'something may take a long time' (possibility). Often followed by verbs like auskommen, dulden, aufbewahrt werden, warten.
target_language_example: Er kann lange ohne Schlaf auskommen.
native_language_example: He can go a long time without sleep.

meaning: 'can remember' (literally: 'can myself to') — used with erinnern an + accusative: 'I can remember (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb sich erinnern an (to remember). In sentences you will see a form of können + reflexive pronoun + an + accusative object (person, thing, time). Word order: subject + kann + mich + an + [accusative]. Sometimes used negatively (kann mich an niemanden erinnern = I can't remember anyone). Also appears with specific time clauses (an den Tag, an das erste Mal).
target_language_example: Ich kann mich an das Konzert letztes Jahr erinnern.
native_language_example: I can remember the concert last year.

meaning: ‘can hardly’ or ‘can barely’ (with a reflexive verb: I can hardly ... myself).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs like erinnern (to remember) or bewegen (to move) to say you are barely able to do something. Word order: 'Ich kann mich kaum + verb infinitive' or in present: 'Ich kann mich kaum erinnern / bewegen.' 'Kaum' weakens the ability (almost not).
target_language_example: Ich kann mich kaum an den Unfall erinnern.
native_language_example: I can hardly remember the accident.

meaning: 'kann' (can/able to) + 'mit' (with) — a combination that appears when a modal verb 'kann' is used together with a verb or prepositional phrase containing 'mit'. It can indicate ability or permission involving 'with', be part of separable verbs (e.g. mitkommen, mitgehen) or constructions with the preposition 'mit' governing a dative object (e.g. mit jemandem umgehen = to get along with/handle someone).
additional_notes: Depends on context: often occurs before a separable-prefix verb (e.g. er kann mitkommen → er kann mit kommen in spoken/colloquial segmentation) or with 'mit' as a preposition + dative (kann mit jemandem umgehen). Word order and meaning depend on whether 'mit' is part of a separable verb, a prepositional phrase, or used adverbially ('mitgehen', 'mitkommen', 'mitmachen'). Non-literal translations vary: sometimes literal translation 'can with' is unnatural in English and should be rendered according to the full clause meaning (e.g. 'can come with us', 'can get along with').
target_language_example: Tom kann mit uns kommen, wenn er mag.
native_language_example: Tom can come with us if he wants.

meaning: 'can tomorrow' — indicates someone is able to do something the next day (can + tomorrow).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to say someone is available or able to do something the following day. 'kann' is the 3rd-person singular (he/she/it) or 1st-person singular/formal 'kann' for 'I can' (ich kann). Combine with an infinitive verb at the end: e.g. 'kann morgen kommen' = 'can come tomorrow'.
target_language_example: Sie kann morgen mit uns essen.
native_language_example: She can eat with us tomorrow.

meaning: cannot (do something) as (well/early/etc.) — used to make comparisons or soften inability.
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb + wie to compare abilities/qualities (e.g. so gut wie = as well as) or before adverbials (so früh) to say someone cannot be that [adjective/adverb]. Often appears in full phrase 'kann nicht so gut ... wie ...' (can't ... as well as ...). Word order: 'Ich kann nicht so gut X wie Y.'
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht so schnell laufen wie du.
native_language_example: I can't run as fast as you.

meaning: 'can't see anything' — I am unable to see.
additional_notes: A simple present-tense phrase used to say you cannot see (something) at all. Commonly used literally (poor light, blocked view, glare) and can be exclaimed. You can change the subject or tense (z. B. ich konnte nichts sehen = I couldn't see). To specify what you can't see, add an object: 'Ich kann das Poster nichts sehen' is incorrect — use 'Ich kann das Poster nicht sehen.'
target_language_example: Dreh die Lampe an, ich kann nichts sehen.
native_language_example: Turn on the lamp, I can't see anything.

meaning: 'can do without' or 'cannot live/do without' when negated; expresses ability to exist or function without something or someone.
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'kann ohne ... nicht ...' (cannot do/live/exist without ...) or 'kann ohne ...' in positive contexts when describing that something is possible without X. Followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. 'Salz', 'dich', 'euch', 'Brille'). Word order and negation: German often places 'nicht' after the phrase, e.g. 'kann ohne dich nicht bestehen' = 'cannot exist without you.'
target_language_example: Er kann ohne Kaffee nicht arbeiten.
native_language_example: He cannot work without coffee.

meaning: can + his/its (used when the direct object is masculine/neuter and possessed by 'he' or 'it')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the modal verb 'können' (in present tense 'kann') followed by a possessive pronoun 'seine' agreeing with a feminine or plural noun (or masculine/neuter in accusative depending on noun). In the examples, 'kann seine' introduces what someone is able or unable to do with something that belongs to 'er' (he/it). Word order: subject + kann + seine + noun + (rest). English translations usually use 'can/able to' + verb or 'can + his…' depending on context (e.g., 'He can change his mind', 'I can't stand his arrogance').
target_language_example: Er kann seine Meinung ändern.
native_language_example: He can change his mind.

meaning: can (one) + his/one's (masculine/neuter accusative); used to say someone/one is able to do something involving a masculine or neuter direct object (or reflexive idea like 'one's').
additional_notes: kann is the 3rd-person singular of können (can/be able to). seinen is the accusative masculine/neuter possessive (his/one's) for er/sie/es or the impersonal man (one). In English you often translate the phrase depending on context: 'one/you/he can [do something to] one's/his...' or simply 'can [verb] ...'. The noun that follows determines the exact translation (e.g. seinen Kuchen = one's cake; seinen Rücken = one's back).
target_language_example: Man kann seinen Hund nicht immer schützen.
native_language_example: You/One cannot always protect one's dog.

meaning: can/able to do something like that; expresses ability or (in negative sentences) disbelief that someone did something like that.
additional_notes: Literally 'can something like that'. Often used to talk about possibility, ability, or to express surprise/disbelief (especially with negation or questions). Context decides if it means ability ('can do') or contradiction ('X couldn't have done that'). 'so etwas' = 'something like that'.
target_language_example: Das kann so etwas nicht passieren!
native_language_example: Something like that can't happen!

meaning: can (do) both / is able to ... as well as ...
additional_notes: Used to introduce two items or actions that someone is able to do. Usually appears with 'als (auch)' or 'als auch' later in the sentence: 'kann sowohl X als auch Y'. Emphasizes that both options apply. Word order: 'sowohl' comes before the first element and 'als auch' before the second.
target_language_example: Sie kann sowohl Klavier spielen als auch singen.
native_language_example: She can both play piano and sing.

meaning: 'can (do) better' or 'is better at (something)' — used to compare ability or skill.
additional_notes: Used with a verb or language/topic to say someone has greater ability than someone else or than expected. Often appears in comparisons: 'als' (than) for comparing two people/things, or 'als du denkst' (than you think). Word order: subject + kann besser + [verb/object], e.g. 'Sie kann besser Englisch.'
target_language_example: Er kann besser schwimmen als ich.
native_language_example: He can swim better than I can.

meaning: can't do it / I cannot (do) it.
additional_notes: Common short phrase used to say you are unable to do something. Usually follows a verb or stands alone with context — subject often implied (Ich kann es nicht = I can't do it). 'Es' refers to the task or situation already mentioned. Use appropriate verb form for other subjects (du kannst es nicht, er/sie kann es nicht).
target_language_example: Ich will ihm helfen, aber ich kann es nicht.
native_language_example: I want to help him, but I can't.

meaning: I can't right now / I'm not able to at the moment.
additional_notes: Used to politely or firmly refuse or postpone something because of a current inability or lack of time/availability. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be neutral, apologetic, or impatient. Often followed by a brief reason (e.g., 'muss los' = 'have to go').
target_language_example: Sorry, ich kann jetzt nicht, ich bin gerade beschäftigt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't right now, I'm busy at the moment.

meaning: is not to blame; it's not (their) fault.
additional_notes: Common short form of 'kann nichts dafür' meaning someone is not responsible for something. Used to defend or excuse a person. Often follows a subject (er/sie/Tom) and can be said emphatically (e.g., with 'Lasst ihn in Ruhe'). Not a literal modal meaning — it's idiomatic.
target_language_example: Sie kann nichts dafür, dass das Wetter schlecht ist.
native_language_example: It's not her fault that the weather is bad.

meaning: you can also / you could also (used to offer an alternative, give permission, make a suggestion, or add emphasis — can be friendly, casual, or sharp depending on context and intonation)
additional_notes: Used with the second-person singular 'du' (kannst) + 'auch'. Tone depends on context and intonation: friendly (Du kannst auch die andere haben), casual (Du kannst auch locker bleiben), or sharp/rude (Du kannst auch verschwinden!). Often appears after a conjugated verb or as part of a clause offering an alternative or suggestion.
target_language_example: Du kannst auch die andere haben.
native_language_example: You can also have the other one.

meaning: 'you can rely/count on' (informal singular 'you')
additional_notes: Part of the separable verb 'sich auf jemanden/etwas verlassen' (to rely on someone/something). 'Kannst dich auf ... verlassen' uses the informal singular 'du' form. Put the person or thing after 'auf'. In full sentence: 'Du kannst dich auf X verlassen.'
target_language_example: Du kannst dich auf mich verlassen.
native_language_example: You can rely on me.

meaning: you cannot (yourself) / you can't
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'du kannst dich nicht ...' used to say someone is unable to do something (often followed by a verb or phrase). 'Dich' is the accusative reflexive pronoun for 'du' and must appear when the verb is reflexive (e.g., 'sich erinnern', 'sich verstecken', 'sich einschließen'). In questions or negatives you may see 'kannst du dich nicht ...?' or 'du kannst dich nicht mehr ...' (no longer).
target_language_example: Du kannst dich nicht einfach abwenden.
native_language_example: You can't just look away.

meaning: Can you dare to do it? / Are you willing to risk it?
additional_notes: A question asking if someone is brave or willing to take a risk. Uses the verb wagen (to dare/risk). Tone can be encouraging or challenging depending on context. You can replace 'du' with other pronouns (kann ich es wagen, können wir es wagen). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Wenn du den Job wirklich willst, kannst du es wagen, dich zu bewerben.
native_language_example: If you really want the job, you can dare to apply.

meaning: literally 'can you in' — part of questions asking what someone can do or where/how many of something they can do or be in; used when forming questions with 'können' + a prepositional phrase starting with 'in'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common word order chunk in questions: 'kannst du' (can you) followed by a prepositional phrase starting with 'in' (e.g. in einem Wörterbuch, in der Hölle, in einem Monat, in deinem Aquarium). Translate whole sentence naturally into English (e.g. 'Can you look that up in any dictionary?'). Pay attention to case after 'in' (dative or accusative depending on meaning) and word order: verb second in statements but verb-first inversion in questions.
target_language_example: Kannst du in diesem Buch nachsehen?
native_language_example: Can you check/look that up in this book?

meaning: informal way to ask what someone can do, how well they can do something, or whether they can do something like that (can you...)
additional_notes: Used colloquially after a verb or alone to mean 'are you able to do that / do you do that / how well can you do that'. Context determines exact sense: after a verb (Kannst du so fahren?) = 'Can you drive like that?'; alone or with a question word (Und was kannst du so?) = 'So what can you do (approximately)?'; with 'ungefähr' it asks for an approximate amount or level (Wie viele Kanji kannst du so ungefähr?). Often heard in speech; tone and context give nuance.
target_language_example: Kannst du so kochen?
native_language_example: Can you cook like that? / Can you cook?

meaning: you can't (it) / you are not able to (do) it.
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'kannst du es nicht' or used after 'du' as in spoken German. 'Es' refers to some object or action from context. Use to say someone cannot do, understand, lift, explain, etc. In full questions/negations you may also see 'du kannst es nicht' or the tag question 'kannst du es nicht?'.
target_language_example: Du kannst es nicht öffnen, ohne den Schlüssel.
native_language_example: You can't open it without the key.

meaning: you might as well / you could just as well
additional_notes: Used to suggest an alternative action that is as reasonable (or as pointless) as the one mentioned. Often implies resignation, indifference, or that two options are equally possible. Common in spoken German. Follows the informal 'du' form here; structure: 'Du kannst genauso gut + verb...' or 'Du kannst genauso gut + infinitive phrase.'
target_language_example: Du kannst genauso gut jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: You might as well leave now.

meaning: you can't (do something) here / you are not allowed or able to here
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the 2nd-person singular of 'können' (kannst), the adverb 'hier' (here) and 'nicht' (not). Used to say someone cannot or is not allowed to do a specific action at this place. The full sentence normally contains the action verb (e.g. 'ausbrechen', 'bleiben', 'schwimmen'). Can express inability (cannot physically/mentally) or prohibition (not allowed). Word order may change in different tenses or with modal emphasis (e.g. 'Du darfst hier nicht...').
target_language_example: Du kannst hier nicht rauchen.
native_language_example: You can't smoke here.

meaning: you can't him / you cannot (do something to/with) him
additional_notes: This is the informal second-person singular (du) + modal verb construction meaning "you cannot" regarding a male person (ihn = him). In English you'd usually translate the whole sentence depending on context: "you can't insult him...", "you can't see him", "you can't hold him back". Word order in German places the modal verb (kannst) before the object (ihn) and 'nicht' negates the action. Use with different verbs after or before for full meaning.
target_language_example: Du kannst ihn nicht einfach anrufen und erwarten, dass er kommt.
native_language_example: You can't just call him and expect him to come.

meaning: a soft or sometimes ironic suggestion/observation using 'you can' (you could / you might as well / you know), often adding a comment or concession
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'kannst' (you can) with the particle 'ja'. 'Ja' here doesn't mean 'yes' but adds emphasis, conveys obviousness, resignation, suggestion, mild reproach, or permission depending on context and tone. Common in spoken German. Translate depending on meaning: 'you could (just)...', 'you might as well...', 'after all, you can...', or simply 'you know, you can...'.
target_language_example: Du kannst ja im Wohnzimmer warten, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: You could wait in the living room, if you want.

meaning: 'you can now' (informal singular): permission or ability to do something at this moment.
additional_notes: Used with du (informal singular). Indicates that the person is allowed or able to do something right now. Word order in full sentences: 'Du kannst jetzt ...' (You can now ...). To make it negative, add 'nicht' after 'jetzt' or before the verb phrase: 'Du kannst jetzt nicht ...' (You cannot/are not allowed to ... right now). For formal or plural use, use 'können Sie jetzt' or 'könnt ihr jetzt'.
target_language_example: Du kannst jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: You can go now.

meaning: you can ... me
additional_notes: Usually part of the pattern du kannst mich + infinitive. kannst is the 2nd-person singular form of können ('can'), and mich means 'me'. The main action verb usually comes later in the sentence, e.g. Du kannst mich anrufen. = 'You can call me.'
target_language_example: Du kannst mich später anrufen.
native_language_example: You can call me later.

meaning: you can't just / you can't simply (do that).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that an action is not acceptable or not allowed — often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g. 'aufstehen', 'herkommen'). Tone can be firm or corrective. In English it corresponds to 'you can't just...' or 'you can't simply...'.
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht einfach die Tür aufmachen und reingehen.
native_language_example: You can't just open the door and go in.

meaning: You can (do) it — said to encourage, remind, or insist that someone is able to do something (often with expectation or mild reproach).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'kannst' (can) with 'du' (you) and the particle 'doch', which adds certainty, insistence, encouragement, or contradiction of a previous doubt. Tone depends on context and intonation: can be encouraging ("You can do it!"), slightly reproachful ("You could do better"), or used to contradict someone who said they can't. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Komm schon, das kannst du doch!
native_language_example: Come on, you can do that!

meaning: knew her/them
additional_notes: Past tense of kennen (to know). ‚sie' can mean 'her' (singular) or 'them' (plural) depending on context. Use for familiarity or acquaintance (I knew her/them), not for facts or skills (use wissen for knowing facts). Example 4 uses a time expression: ‚Ich kannte sie schon zehn Jahre, als ...' = 'I had known her for ten years when ...' (English may use past perfect).
target_language_example: Ich kannte sie kaum, bevor wir zusammenarbeiteten.
native_language_example: I hardly knew her before we worked together.

meaning: 'is broken' (describing something that doesn't work or is damaged).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or in subordinate clauses to state that an object is broken or not functioning. Common with weil/wenn clauses (e.g. 'weil das ... kaputt ist' = 'because the ... is broken'). 'Kaputt' is an adjective; 'ist' is the 3rd-person singular of 'sein' (to be). Informal register: 'kaputt' is casual but widely used.
target_language_example: Weil das Telefon kaputt ist.
native_language_example: Because the phone is broken.

meaning: to be able to buy / could buy (ability or possibility to buy).
additional_notes: Combines kaufen (to buy) with the modal verb können (can/could). Used to express ability or possibility in present (can buy) or past/subjunctive (could have bought, would have been able to buy). In sentences with hätte/würde + kaufen können it often indicates a missed opportunity or hypothetical ability.
target_language_example: Wenn ich das Geld gehabt hätte, hätte ich das Auto kaufen können.
native_language_example: If I had had the money, I could have bought the car.

meaning: hardly any / almost no (used before a singular noun or with expressions like 'Wort' to mean 'hardly a...').
additional_notes: Often used to say that something is very rare or almost never happens. With countable nouns it means 'hardly any' (e.g. 'kaum ein Drittel' = 'hardly a/only about a third'). With words/actions (e.g. 'kaum ein Wort') it means 'hardly a word' or 'barely spoke'. Word order: 'kaum ein' precedes the noun. Formal and common in both written and spoken German.
target_language_example: Er sagte während des Treffens kaum ein Wort.
native_language_example: He hardly said a word during the meeting.

meaning: hardly any / almost no (feminine or singular noun)
additional_notes: Used to say that there is very little or almost none of something. 'Kaum' means 'hardly' or 'barely'; 'eine' agrees with a feminine noun or can appear before singular nouns in general statements. Often followed by a noun (e.g., 'kaum eine Rede', 'kaum eine Arbeit') or by a verb phrase meaning 'hardly do X'.
target_language_example: Er findet kaum eine Lösung für das Problem.
native_language_example: He finds hardly any solution for the problem.

meaning: hardly anything; very little
additional_notes: Used to say that there is very little of something or that something barely happens/is possible. Often followed by a verb or past participle. Can modify objects (kaum etwas gegessen), ability/perception (kaum etwas sehen/verstehen) or quantities (kaum etwas geladen).
target_language_example: Heute habe ich kaum etwas geschlafen.
native_language_example: Today I hardly slept / I slept very little.

meaning: no (single) sheet/leaf; used in expressions to mean 'not a bit' or 'not at all' depending on context
additional_notes: Alone 'kein Blatt' literally means 'no leaf' or 'no sheet'. It's often part of idiomatic expressions (e.g. 'kein Blatt vor den Mund nehmen' = 'to not mince words'). By itself it can appear in contexts like 'kein Blatt Papier' (no sheet of paper) or be used poetically to mean nothing at all. Pay attention to the full expression to get the exact idiomatic meaning.
target_language_example: Ich habe kein Blatt Papier dabei.
native_language_example: I don't have a sheet of paper with me.

meaning: to speak very openly; to not hold back; to be blunt.
additional_notes: Literal image: 'not to take a leaf in front of (one's) mouth' — idiomatic German meaning someone says exactly what they think without softening it. Commonly used in present/past forms: 'nimmt kein Blatt vor den Mund', 'nahm kein Blatt vor den Mund'. Usually followed by direct speech or about a person's style of speaking. Can be used as an imperative: 'Nimm kein Blatt vor den Mund!'.
target_language_example: Sie nimmt kein Blatt vor den Mund und sagt sofort ihre Meinung.
native_language_example: She doesn't mince her words and says her opinion immediately.

meaning: no photo / not a photo (of someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that a photo does not exist or is not available. Often appears with von + person/object (kein Foto von ihr = no photo of her) or in questions expressing surprise (Wie, kein Foto?). 'Kein' negates the noun (Foto).
target_language_example: Ich habe leider kein Foto von meinem Großvater.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I don't have a photo of my grandfather.

meaning: to have no money; to be broke
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you don’t have any (or enough) money. Used with a person or subject: Ich habe kein Geld / Er hat kein Geld. For emphasis, speakers may say 'kein Geld mehr haben' (to have no money left) or use colloquial alternatives like 'pleite sein' or 'kein Geld auf der Tasche haben'.
target_language_example: Ich werde dieses Wochenende kein Geld haben, also kann ich nicht mitkommen.
native_language_example: I will have no money this weekend, so I can't come along.

meaning: no more money / out of money
additional_notes: Used to say someone has run out of money or no longer has any money. Can refer to past, present, or general situations depending on context. Word order: 'kein Geld mehr' usually follows the subject and verb (e.g., 'Ich habe kein Geld mehr').
target_language_example: Ich habe gerade kein Geld mehr, kannst du mir helfen?
native_language_example: I have no money left right now; can you help me?

meaning: not a boy / no boy (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used to negate 'Junge' (boy). Can mean 'not a boy' (identity: I'm not a boy) or 'no boy' (absence: there is no boy who...). Word order and sentence context determine meaning. In comparisons or statements about class membership, it often translates as 'no boy' or 'no boy in the class...'. In identity/age contexts it translates 'not a boy' or 'no longer a boy'. 'Kein' agrees with gender and case of the noun it negates.
target_language_example: Ich bin kein Junge, ich bin ein Mann.
native_language_example: I'm not a boy, I'm a man.

meaning: not a teacher / no teacher (negation of 'ein Lehrer')
additional_notes: Kein is the negative form used with nouns (without an article) and agrees with gender/case. 'Kein Lehrer' negates 'ein Lehrer' — used to say someone is not a teacher. In questions, tone or word order can check for confirmation (e.g. 'Sind Sie kein Lehrer?').
target_language_example: Sie ist kein Lehrer, sie arbeitet als Ingenieurin.
native_language_example: She is not a teacher; she works as an engineer.

meaning: no idea; I don't know.
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to say you don't know or have no plan/idea about something. Often used on its own as a short answer (e.g. "Kein Plan.") or in sentences like "Ich habe keinen Plan." Literal words: kein = no, Plan = plan/idea.
target_language_example: Kein Plan, was ich heute machen soll.
native_language_example: No idea what I should do today.

meaning: No problem; that's fine / not an issue.
additional_notes: Used to say something is not a problem, to agree, to reassure, or to accept an invitation/offer. Common in spoken and informal contexts but also widely used politely. Can reply alone ("Kein Problem.") or within a sentence ("Ich habe kein Problem damit.").
target_language_example: Ja, gern—kein Problem.
native_language_example: Yes, gladly—no problem.

meaning: nobody / not a soul (colloquial, somewhat rude)
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to emphasize that no one is present, watching, or doing something. Literally 'no pig', but it means 'nobody' and can sound coarse or blunt; avoid in very polite contexts.
target_language_example: Wir spielen in London, und kein Schwein ist da.
native_language_example: We're playing in London, and nobody is there.

meaning: no more words / not another word (keep quiet about it).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop talking about something or to keep a secret. Can be a command (Not another word!) or a statement meaning 'don't mention it again' or 'no more of that.' Tone can be firm or warning; context determines whether it's about stopping discussion or keeping silence.
target_language_example: Kein Wort mehr darüber, verstanden?
native_language_example: Not another word about it, understood?

meaning: no wonder; not surprising
additional_notes: Used to say that something is unsurprising or expected. Can stand alone as an exclamation ("Kein Wunder!") or introduce a clause with a comma ("Kein Wunder, ..."). Tone ranges from neutral to mildly critical or resigned depending on context.
target_language_example: Kein Wunder, dass er müde ist — er hat die ganze Nacht gearbeitet.
native_language_example: No wonder he's tired — he worked all night.

meaning: not a coincidence; no accident
additional_notes: Used to say that something was intentional, expected, or has an explanation rather than being random. Often appears in phrases like 'Das kann kein Zufall sein' or 'Es ist kein Zufall, dass...'.
target_language_example: Es ist kein Zufall, dass du und ich dieselben Interessen haben.
native_language_example: It's not a coincidence that you and I have the same interests.

meaning: no idea
additional_notes: Used informally in many contexts to say you don't know something or to criticize someone's lack of knowledge. Can be a short standalone answer ("Keine Ahnung.") or part of a sentence ("Du hast keine Ahnung"). Tone can be neutral or rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Keine Ahnung, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: No idea how that works.

meaning: I had no idea that... / I didn't know that...
additional_notes: Used to express that one was unaware of a fact or situation. Combines the phrase 'keine Ahnung' (no idea) with the conjunction 'daß' (older spelling of 'dass') followed by a subordinate clause. Note: modern German orthography uses 'dass' instead of 'daß', but 'daß' still appears in older texts. In subordinate clauses the conjugated verb moves to the end (e.g. 'dass Maria deine Tochter ist').
target_language_example: Ich hatte keine Ahnung, daß Maria Ihre Tochter ist.
native_language_example: I had no idea that Maria is your daughter.

meaning: to have no idea / not to know
additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase used to say you don't know the answer to a question or are unsure about something. Often used in spoken German: 'Ich habe keine Ahnung.' Synonyms/variants: 'keinen Schimmer haben' (more informal). Conjugate 'haben' as needed: 'Er hat keine Ahnung', 'Hast du keine Ahnung?'.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Ahnung haben ist hier grammatisch falsch; korrekt: Ich habe keine Ahnung.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my key is.

meaning: 'no question' / 'no doubt' / 'of course' (used to confirm something or say something is certain).
additional_notes: Used both as a short answer meaning 'no question' or 'of course' (e.g. 'Keine Frage!' = 'No doubt!' / 'Of course!') and within sentences to say that something is certain or beyond dispute ('ist keine Frage' = 'is beyond question'). Can also introduce a concessive clause: 'Keine Frage, ...' = 'No question, ...' / 'Granted, ...'.
target_language_example: Keine Frage, du wirst es schaffen.
native_language_example: No doubt, you'll make it.

meaning: no opinion
additional_notes: Used to say you don't have an opinion about something. Commonly appears with verbs like haben (haben keine Meinung) or in questions asking others if they have an opinion. Can be strengthened with words like überhaupt (at all).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Meinung zu dem Film.
native_language_example: I have no opinion about the movie.

meaning: no mother / not a mother (she/they have no mother).
additional_notes: A negative noun phrase: 'keine' negates the feminine noun 'Mutter'. Used to say someone lacks a mother (e.g., orphaned) or to question/express surprise ('Hast du keine Mutter?' / 'Keine Mutter?'). Word order and pronouns/context determine exact translation (she has no mother = 'Das Mädchen hat keine Mutter').
target_language_example: Das kleine Mädchen hat keine Mutter.
native_language_example: The little girl has no mother.

meaning: to not matter; to be irrelevant
additional_notes: Used to say that something has no importance or influence on a situation. Commonly appears in negative constructions: 'Das spielt keine Rolle.' You can also specify the subject or context: 'Für mich spielt das keine Rolle.'
target_language_example: Für mich spielt das keine Rolle.
native_language_example: For me, that doesn't matter.

meaning: no (female) sister; not a sister
additional_notes: Used to say someone does not have a sister (possession) or to deny that someone is a sister (identity/role). Keine is the negation for feminine nouns in singular (nominative/accusative) and goes with Schwester. Context determines translation: "keine Schwester haben" = "to have no sister"; standalone exclamation ("Du bist keine Schwester!") denies that someone is a sister.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Schwester, aber einen Bruder.
native_language_example: I have no sister, but a brother.

meaning: You're welcome; don't mention it (used to reply to thanks).
additional_notes: Common polite reply after someone says 'danke'. Literally 'no cause' — i.e. there was no need to thank. Can be used in casual and formal contexts. Tone may vary with intonation; often short and friendly. Not used to refuse an offer.
target_language_example: A: Danke für die Hilfe! B: Keine Ursache.
native_language_example: A: Thanks for the help! B: You're welcome.

meaning: to not have time / to be too busy
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used to say you are unable to do something because you're busy or lack time. Can be used for short-term unavailability (today, now) or more general busy periods. Often appears with an activity: 'keine Zeit für ...' or with infinitive: 'keine Zeit, ... zu ...'.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit haben, deswegen kann ich nicht mitkommen.
native_language_example: I don't have time today, so I can't come along.

meaning: no time to (do something)
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say you don't have time to do an action. Often appears in sentences like "Ich habe keine Zeit zu ..." or shortened in speech as "Keine Zeit, zu ..." Can be followed by verbs with "zu" (e.g. zu arbeiten, zu kommen) or replaced by a clause: "keine Zeit, weil..."
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit zu kochen.
native_language_example: I have no time to cook today.

meaning: not a very / not much of a (used to downplay or qualify someone or something)
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun to say something is not impressive, important, or significant. Tone can be dismissive, modest, or ironic depending on context. Forms change with gender, number, and case of the following noun (e.g., kein großer Freund, keine große Hilfe, keine großen Aussichten). Often appears in phrases like "keine große Hilfe/Leistung/Ehre/Vergangenheit/Band."
target_language_example: Er ist vielleicht klug, aber keine große Hilfe.
native_language_example: He may be smart, but not much help.

meaning: to have no idea; to not know at all
additional_notes: Informal expression used to say you don't know something. Often used in first person (Ich habe keinen Schimmer) or as a short reply (Keinen Schimmer!). Equivalent to English 'I have no clue.'
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Schimmer, wo mein Schlüssel ist. — Ich habe keinen Schimmer.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my key is. — I have no clue.

meaning: nobody has / no one has (used to say that no one possesses, wants, or is willing)
additional_notes: Keiner means 'no one' or 'nobody'. Combined with hat (from haben) it states that no person has something or is willing/able to do something. Common in everyday speech. Depending on context, it can mean 'nobody wants to' (Keiner hat Lust) or 'nobody has time' (Keiner hat Zeit). Word order may change (Keiner hat ... / Hat keiner ...?) and regional variants may use 'niemand hat'.
target_language_example: Keiner hat Interesse, am Samstag zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: Nobody is interested in working on Saturday.

meaning: I know all (of them).
additional_notes: Combines the verb kennen (to know, be familiar with) in first person singular (ich kenne) with alle (all/every). Used to say you know all members of a group: songs, rules, people, secrets, etc. Pay attention to possessive pronouns after alle (e.g., alle deine Geheimnisse = all your secrets). For other persons change the verb (du kennst alle, er/sie kennt alle).
target_language_example: Ich kenne alle deine Bücher.
native_language_example: I know all your books.

meaning: I know your ... (familiar with someone or something belonging to 'you')
additional_notes: A first-person singular form of the verb kennen (to know) followed by a masculine or neutral singular accusative possessive dein + noun (deinen). Used to say you are familiar with a person or thing that belongs to 'you'. Word order: 'Ich kenne deinen Bruder.' Note that kennen means to be acquainted with (people, places, things), not to 'know how to' (which is wissen or können + infinitive). The accusative masculine/neuter form of 'dein' is 'deinen' when the noun is masculine; for feminine nouns you'd say 'deine' (Ich kenne deine Mutter).
target_language_example: Ich kenne deinen Nachbarn seit zwei Jahren.
native_language_example: I've known your neighbor for two years.

meaning: I know these / I am familiar with these.
additional_notes: A form of the verb kennen (to know, be familiar with) in the first person singular (ich kenne) plus the demonstrative diese (these/these ones). Used to say you recognize or are familiar with people, things, places, statements, etc. Word order can change: e.g. "Ich kenne diese Leute" or in questions/clauses "Glaubst du etwa, ich kenne diese Anschuldigungen nicht?" Not used for knowing facts or skills (use wissen or können).
target_language_example: Ich kenne diese Straße sehr gut.
native_language_example: I know this street very well.

meaning: 'I know this' (masculine/neuter singular object) — used to say you are familiar with a person, place, thing, name, etc.
additional_notes: Kenne is the first‑person singular of kennen (to know, be familiar with). Diesen is the accusative masculine/neuter demonstrative for 'this' when the noun is masculine (der) or can appear before certain nouns (e.g. Blick, Lehrer, Ort, Teil). For feminine nouns you would say 'kenne diese' (e.g. 'kenne diese Frau') and for plurals 'kenne diese' as well. Use 'kenne diesen' to refer to something specific you recognize or have experience with.
target_language_example: Ich kenne diesen Ort sehr gut.
native_language_example: I know this place very well.

meaning: I don't know any / I don't know (someone) — masculine or general.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of knowing (kennen) to say you don't know a person or thing. 'Keinen' is the accusative masculine singular form of 'kein' and agrees with a masculine noun (or when speaking generally about 'any' person). For feminine use say 'kenne keine' (e.g. Ich kenne keine Anna). For plural use 'kenne keine' as well (e.g. Ich kenne keine Politiker). Common in statements like 'Ich kenne keinen X' meaning 'There isn't any X I know.'
target_language_example: Ich kenne keinen netten Nachbarn in diesem Haus.
native_language_example: I don't know any nice neighbor in this building.

meaning: 'know only' / 'only know (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb kennen (to know, be familiar with) in the first person singular (ich kenne) with the adverb nur (only). Used to say you are familiar with just one person/place/thing or only have limited knowledge. Word order: nur usually follows the verb or the thing it restricts (Ich kenne nur das Zentrum / Ich kenne nur ihn).
target_language_example: Ich kenne nur ein paar Wörter Deutsch.
native_language_example: I only know a few words of German.

meaning: 'kenne viele' = 'know many' (I know many ...).
additional_notes: Phrase combines the verb kennen (to know/be acquainted with) plus 'viele' (many). Used when talking about knowing/being familiar with a large number of people, songs, jokes, places, etc. In German, word order can change (e.g., 'Ich kenne viele Leute' or 'Viele Leute kenne ich' in emphasis). Use 'kennen' for familiarity or acquaintance (people, songs, places), not for facts — for facts use 'wissen'.
target_language_example: Ich kenne viele Cafés in dieser Stadt.
native_language_example: I know many cafés in this city.

meaning: to know (something/the ...).
additional_notes: Kennen is the verb 'to know' used for people or things you are familiar with. 'Den' is the masculine accusative definite article ('the') used here because the direct object is a masculine noun (den Ablauf, den Ausdruck, den Grund, den Verfasser, den Unterschied, den Treffpunkt). In English you usually translate as 'know the ...' or 'know (about) the ...'. The phrase appears in sentences like 'Sie kennen den Ablauf ja' = 'You/They know the procedure, after all.'
target_language_example: Wir kennen den Plan schon.
native_language_example: We already know the plan.

meaning: to get to know (someone); to meet and become acquainted
additional_notes: Used when meeting someone and beginning to know them (often reflexive: sich kennen lernen / uns kennen lernen). Common in spoken and written German. Can be separated in conjugated forms (ich lerne ihn kennen). The reflexive form emphasizes mutual getting-to-know (wir lernen uns kennen).
target_language_example: Wir sollten uns nächste Woche kennen lernen.
native_language_example: We should get to know each other next week.

meaning: ‘is clear’ or part of the phrase ‘that is clear’ (used to say something should be/ is understood).
additional_notes: Used in subordinate clauses like 'dass das klar ist' or 'damit das klar ist' to emphasize that a fact should be understood or is obvious. Often appears with verbs like 'sein' or expressions 'ich möchte nur, dass das klar ist' (I just want that to be clear). Not a fixed idiom on its own; meaning depends on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass das klar ist: Ich helfe nur einmal.
native_language_example: I want that to be clear: I'm only helping once.

meaning: clearly; plainly (used to emphasize clarity when followed by another adjective like 'deutlich').
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the fixed pair 'klar und deutlich' (= 'clear and distinct/clearly'). Used to emphasize that something is easy to perceive, hear, understand, or proven. Common in spoken and formal contexts (e.g., during announcements, testimony, or phone calls). The phrase 'klar und' by itself is typically followed by another adjective (most often 'deutlich').
target_language_example: Sag es bitte klar und deutlich.
native_language_example: Please say it clearly and distinctly.

meaning: Sure; of course; certainly (affirmative, sometimes slightly emphatic or friendly).
additional_notes: Used to give a positive answer or agreement. Tone ranges from friendly/enthusiastic to mildly ironic depending on context and intonation. Common in spoken German. Can replace simpler 'klar' or 'doch' to strengthen agreement.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? — Klar doch!
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? — Sure!

meaning: little boy; a young male child.
additional_notes: Adjective + noun phrase. 'kleine' is the feminine/weak inflected form used before a masculine noun in the nominative singular only when using weak declension? Actually: correct form for nominative singular masculine is 'kleiner Junge'. However, 'kleine Junge' appears in spoken or in different cases (e.g., accusative plural) or in contexts with determiner. Beginners should know 'kleiner Junge' (a little boy) and that 'kleine' changes with gender, case and number. Commonly used to describe a young boy; can be combined with articles: 'der kleine Junge', 'ein kleiner Junge'.
target_language_example: Der kleine Junge lacht laut.
native_language_example: The little boy laughs loudly.

meaning: little finger; pinky (the smallest finger on the hand).
additional_notes: Refers to the fifth finger on the hand. Common in literal contexts (body, injury) and sometimes used idiomatically (e.g., to indicate someone 'told me' something jokingly, as in example 1). Use 'der kleine Finger' with articles; plural 'kleine Finger'.
target_language_example: Mein linker kleiner Finger tut weh.
native_language_example: My left little finger hurts.

meaning: smaller and (used to connect two descriptions or actions about the same subject)
additional_notes: This phrase combines a comparative adjective (kleiner = smaller) with und (and) to add a second comment about the same person or thing (often another comparative or consequence). Common in sentences like 'X ist kleiner und ...' or 'Wir werden kleiner und ...' Note that 'kleiner' is the comparative of 'klein'. The second part after 'und' can be another verb phrase, adjective phrase, or an adverbial phrase. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Das Baby ist kleiner und schläft länger als sein Bruder.
native_language_example: The baby is smaller and sleeps longer than his brother.

meaning: a small gift; a little present
additional_notes: Common phrase for a modest or inexpensive present given on various occasions (birthday, thank-you, small favor). 'kleines' is the accusative/nominative singular of 'klein' matching the neuter noun 'Geschenk'. You can change the adjective ending for case/number (z. B. ein kleines Geschenk, zwei kleine Geschenke).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein kleines Geschenk für dich.
native_language_example: I have a small gift for you.

meaning: a small gift for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to present or mention a modest/polite gift intended for a specific person. ‚kleines Geschenk‘ emphasizes that the gift is small or simple; ‚für + dative pronoun/noun‘ shows the recipient (für Sie, für dich). Formality: use ‚Sie‘ for formal, ‚dich/dir‘ for informal.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein kleines Geschenk für dich mitgebracht.
native_language_example: I brought a small gift for you.

meaning: knocks on the (female) — i.e. 'knocks on the door.'
additional_notes: Klopft an die is the present-tense, third-person singular form of 'an die klopfen' when referring to a feminine noun with the article 'die' (most commonly 'die Tür' = the door). In German you normally say 'an die Tür klopfen' or more commonly 'an die Tür klopfen' with the verb either before or after the object: 'Er klopft an die Tür.' For other persons or numbers the verb changes (ich klopfe, du klopfst, wir klopfen). If the noun is masculine/neuter or plural, the article changes (an den, ans/ an das, an die).
target_language_example: Sie klopft an die Tür, bevor sie hereinkommt.
native_language_example: She knocks on the door before coming in.

meaning: literally "clever/smart and" — used to link 'klug' (smart/clever) with another adjective or quality.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in descriptions listing two or more traits (e.g., "klug und hübsch" = "smart and pretty"). The coordinating conjunction 'und' simply connects qualities; word order typically places 'klug' before 'und' when you want to emphasize intelligence first. Can be used in positive character descriptions. Not an idiom — literal composition.
target_language_example: Er ist klug und freundlich.
native_language_example: He is smart and friendly.

meaning: Come out / come here from that place (imperative).
additional_notes: Informal command using 'kommen' (come) + 'da' (there/that place). Often followed by a direction word (raus = out, runter = down) or stands alone to tell someone to come out of or away from a specific spot. Used in spoken, everyday German; tone can be urgent or commanding depending on context.
target_language_example: Komm da raus, ich helfe dir!
native_language_example: Come out of there, I'll help you!

meaning: come (to) me
additional_notes: Komm mir appears in several idiomatic uses. Literally it can mean 'come to me' (e.g. komm mir nach / komm mir hinterher). More often in colloquial speech it forms part of phrases like 'komm mir nicht so' or 'komm mir nicht mit ...', meaning 'don't act/come at me like that' or 'don't start with me about ...' — used to reject, warn, or distance oneself. Tone can be informal and sometimes slightly confrontational. Word order and particles (nach, hinterher, so, nicht mit ...) change the meaning.
target_language_example: Komm mir nicht mit Ausreden.
native_language_example: Don't come at me with excuses.

meaning: Phrase built from kommen ('to come') + hier ('here'). Depending on context and inflection it can mean 'I come/come here', 'I will be here', or appear within colloquial/imperative expressions.
