As written ('komme hier' using first-person singular stem), it most naturally appears inside larger first-person sentences (e.g. 'Ich komme hier ...').
additional_notes: 'Komme hier' by itself is not the standard imperative for 'du' (that would be 'Komm hier!'). Used in full sentences it usually reflects first-person present or near-future (Ich komme hier in einer Stunde wieder vorbei = I'll come by here in an hour). In colloquial speech stronger or coarse expressions can include this sequence (beware of offensive language). Word order, particles, and case determine exact meaning; the phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Ich komme hier in einer Stunde wieder vorbei.
native_language_example: I'll come by here again in an hour.

meaning: I'll come/arrive later; I'll be there later.
additional_notes: Common phrase to say you'll come at a later time or that you'll do something later. Often used alone as a short reply ("Ich komme später.") or with a destination ("Ich komme später rüber/zu dir/zum Unterricht"). Use polite form with "zu Ihnen" for formal situations. Can imply a short delay or coming back later depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich komme später zu dir, wir können dann essen.
native_language_example: I'll come to your place later; we can eat then.

meaning: 'I'll come back' / 'I'll be back' (I return).
additional_notes: First-person singular present of kommen + wieder. Used to say you will return or regain consciousness/awareness (context matters). Can be literal (I will come back/return) or figurative (I come to/come around: regain consciousness). Common in promises or dramatic statements. To avoid repetition in German, speakers sometimes say 'Ich komme zurück' (same meaning).
target_language_example: Ich komme wieder, ich verspreche es.
native_language_example: I'll be back, I promise.

meaning: 'I feel' (literally 'come to myself' — used with adjectives to say how one feels or appears to oneself)
additional_notes: Used with adjectives or adjective phrases and the reflexive pronoun 'mir' plus 'vor' (often omitted in the prompt examples? — here examples include 'komme mir ... vor'). Structure: 'Ich komme mir + (adjective) + vor' = 'I feel (adjective)'. Common in self-evaluations (e.g. feeling foolish, helpless, sick, lonely). Do not translate word-for-word; translate the whole phrase as 'I feel/ I find myself'.
target_language_example: Ich komme mir heute komisch vor.
native_language_example: I feel strange today.

meaning: 'arrive' (we) — used to ask or say when/where 'we' will arrive
additional_notes: Kommen wir is the verb kommen (to come) conjugated for 'wir' (we). In these examples it appears with the separable prefix an at the end (ankommen = to arrive). Word order: in questions the time/place often comes after 'kommen wir' and 'an' goes to the end of the clause. Use for talking about arrival times or places for a group that includes the speaker.
target_language_example: Wann kommen wir in Berlin an?
native_language_example: When do we arrive in Berlin?

meaning: How do you come to that conclusion? / What makes you say that?
additional_notes: Polite/formal (Sie). Used to question someone's assumption, belief or statement — often expresses surprise or doubt about how they reached that idea. Can be shortened to "Wie kommen Sie darauf?" Informal equivalent: "Wie kommst du darauf?"
target_language_example: Wie kommen Sie darauf, daß das wirklich passiert ist?
native_language_example: How do you come to that conclusion that it really happened?

meaning: 'come (into/at) / come (in)'.
additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative or request using Sie (formal 'you'). Depending on context, 'kommen in' can mean 'enter (into)' (e.g., 'Kommen Sie in mein Büro' = 'Come into my office'), or it can be part of time expressions meaning 'come in (after) [time]' or 'come back in [time]' (e.g., 'Kommen Sie in einer Stunde' = 'Come in an hour' / 'Come back in one hour'). Word order may vary (e.g., 'Kommen Sie in zwei Tagen wieder' = 'Come back in two days').
target_language_example: Kommen Sie in zehn Minuten wieder.
native_language_example: Come back in ten minutes.

meaning: they all come / all of them come (or are from...).
additional_notes: Used with a plural subject or names to say that every person in the group does something or shares a trait (e.g., comes from a place or will come). Word order: verb (kommen) before 'alle' in many spoken constructions: 'Die drei Männer kommen alle aus Boston.' Can be used with time (kommen morgen alle) or as an invitation/confirmation (Es kommen alle mit = Everyone is coming along).
target_language_example: Die Schülerinnen und Schüler kommen alle pünktlich zur Klasse.
native_language_example: All the students arrive on time for class.

meaning: to get along / to do well (in a certain way); 'kommen gut miteinander aus' = to get along well with each other; 'kommen gut voran' = to make good progress.
additional_notes: Kommen combines with different adverbs/particles to change meaning. Common uses: 'gut miteinander auskommen' = to get along well (with each other); 'gut ohne jemand zurechtkommen' = to manage well without someone; 'gut vorankommen' = to make good progress. Word order and particles (miteinander, ohne, zurecht, voran) are important. For beginners, learn the full phrases rather than translating 'kommen' alone.
target_language_example: Wir kommen gut miteinander aus.
native_language_example: We get along well with each other.

meaning: 'How do you come to that?' → 'Why do you think that?' or 'What makes you say that?'
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for the reason, evidence, or basis for a statement or assumption. Common in spoken German. Often appears as a question: "Wie kommst du darauf?" You can add the clause being questioned: "Wie kommst du darauf, dass ...?"
target_language_example: Wie kommst du darauf, dass er krank ist?
native_language_example: Why do you think he's sick? / What makes you say that?

meaning: 'you don't come' / 'you are not coming' (2nd person singular, present tense, negative)
additional_notes: Used with 'du' (informal you). Context determines nuance: can deny origin (du kommst nicht aus...), refuse permission or exclude (du kommst nicht in meine Gang / du kommst nicht nach...), or be used to ask/confirm someone's attendance or participation (Heißt das, du kommst nicht? / Du kommst nicht mit?). Word order and particles may vary in questions or emphatic sentences.
target_language_example: Heißt das, du kommst nicht zur Party?
native_language_example: Does that mean you are not coming to the party?

meaning: 'you never come' (second-person singular informal + 'never')
additional_notes: This is the present tense of kommen (to come) with the negation nie (never). It uses the du form kommst. Common in sentences like 'Du kommst nie pünktlich' (You never arrive on time). Tone can be complaining or reproachful. For polite/formal address use 'kommen Sie nie'.
target_language_example: Du kommst nie zu unseren Treffen.
native_language_example: You never come to our meetings.

meaning: depends (on it); short for 'kommt darauf an' = 'it depends'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say that the outcome or answer varies depending on something else. Often appears as the full phrase 'kommt darauf an' or shortened in casual speech to 'kommt darauf an' or 'kommt darauf'. Use with 'wie', 'wer', 'wann' etc. to specify the condition (e.g. 'kommt darauf an, wie...').
target_language_example: Kommt darauf an, wie viel Zeit du hast.
native_language_example: It depends on how much time you have.

meaning: Come on, let's ... (invitation/command to a group including the speaker)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used to urge others to do something together. 'Kommt' is the 2nd-person plural imperative of 'kommen' (you all come), but here it functions like English 'come on' or 'let's' + verb. Often followed by a verb phrase: 'Kommt, wir gehen' = 'Come on, let's go.' Used with friends, family, or groups; not formal.
target_language_example: Kommt, wir probieren das neue Café aus.
native_language_example: Come on, let's try the new café.

meaning: come, everybody / everyone come (imperative invitation).
additional_notes: A short, colloquial way to call a group to come closer or join in. It's the verb kommen in imperative form addressing a group: 'kommt' (ihr-form imperative) + 'alle' (everyone). Common in spoken German: e.g. a teacher, friend or parent calling multiple people. Depending on context it can mean 'come here, everyone' or 'everybody come along'.
target_language_example: Kommt alle her, das Essen ist fertig!
native_language_example: Everyone come here, the food is ready!

meaning: 'come (you) all' / 'everyone come' (imperative or statement addressing a group)
additional_notes: Used with ihr or as an imperative call to a group. In statements it means 'you all come from...' (ihr kommt alle). In commands it shortens to 'Kommt alle!' or 'Kommt alle her!' meaning 'Everyone come!' or 'Come here, everyone!'. Informal, used in spoken German. Word order: kommt = (you plural) come; alle = everyone/all.
target_language_example: Kommt alle bitte in den Raum.
native_language_example: Everyone please come into the room.

meaning: 'so' / 'therefore' / conversational filler showing a conclusion or reaction (lit. 'comes so')
additional_notes: In spoken German, 'also' is a versatile filler word. After a verb like 'kommt' it often signals that the speaker draws a conclusion, expresses surprise, confirms information, or reacts to what was just said. Translate depending on context: 'so', 'then', 'therefore', 'so I/we/you ...', or simply leave it as a conversational 'well'. Word order note: 'kommt also' is the verb 'kommt' followed by the particle 'also' and appears in contexts like rhetorical questions, surprised statements, or conclusions about someone's action or origin.
target_language_example: Er kommt also sturzbetrunken nach Hause und macht Feuer.
native_language_example: So he comes home stone-drunk and starts a fire.

meaning: literally 'comes the/that' — used to ask or say that something is coming, arriving, or originates from somewhere; also used when adding an item (with 'dazu').
additional_notes: Usage depends on context and word order. As a statement with 'Da kommt das ...' it points out that something is arriving or appearing (e.g., food being served, a flow of liquid). As a question 'Kommt das ...?' it can ask whether something is included (Kommt das Gemüse dazu? = Is the vegetable included?) or about origin (Kommt das Hühnchen hier aus der Region? = Does the chicken come from this region?). 'Das' refers to the specific item mentioned; verb 'kommt' is 3rd person singular of kommen.
target_language_example: Kommt das Brot noch mit zur Bestellung?
native_language_example: Is the bread included with the order?

meaning: 'how come' / 'how is it that' (asks for an explanation or reason)
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask why something is the case. Often appears in the fixed phrase 'Wie kommt es (dass ...)?' — interchangeable with 'Wie kann das sein?' or 'Warum...?' but slightly more conversational/formal. Word order: 'Wie kommt es, dass ...' or short 'Wie kommt es?'.
target_language_example: Wie kommt es, dass er gestern nicht gekommen ist?
native_language_example: How come he didn't come yesterday?

meaning: used in questions to ask 'how is it that you...' or 'how come you...'
additional_notes: Formal/neutral phrase often used to ask why or how something happened or why someone has a certain fact/ability. Common pattern: "Wie kommt es, dass + clause?" followed by the person (du/er/sie) and verb. Equivalent to English "How come..." or "How is it that..." — asks for an explanation or reason.
target_language_example: Wie kommt es, dass du so gut Deutsch sprichst?
native_language_example: How is it that you speak German so well?

meaning: comes/reaches fresh; indicates something arrives or is delivered in a fresh/new state (e.g., food just prepared, newly received goods)
additional_notes: Literal phrase; not a fixed idiom. Commonly used in contexts describing freshness or recent arrival. Often part of longer phrases (e.g., 'kommt frisch aus der Küche'). Tone neutral; context determines whether it refers to food, produce, or newly arrived items.
target_language_example: Das Brot kommt frisch in die Bäckerei geliefert und wird sofort verkauft, sobald es kommt frisch.
native_language_example: The bread is delivered fresh to the bakery and is sold immediately as soon as it comes fresh.

meaning: has just come from (the) — used to say someone recently arrived from a place or institution.
additional_notes: Common informal phrase in spoken German. 'frisch' emphasizes 'just' or 'recently'. 'von der' is feminine or dative because the following noun (e.g. Uni = die Universität) is feminine; form changes with different nouns (z. B. 'kommt frisch vom Krankenhaus'). Often used to introduce someone's background (job, school, institution).
target_language_example: Er kommt frisch von der Uni und kennt sich mit aktueller Forschung aus.
native_language_example: He has just come from the university and knows about current research.

meaning: 'gets along (well)'.
additional_notes: Used with 'mit' + someone to mean 'to get along well with someone' (kommt gut mit ... aus). Also appears in the imperative plural 'Kommt gut nach Hause!' meaning 'Get home safely / have a good trip home.' Context determines if it's part of the separable verb 'auskommen' (kommt ... aus) or an imperative of 'kommen' ('come' home).
target_language_example: Sie kommt gut mit ihren Nachbarn aus.
native_language_example: She gets along well with her neighbors.

meaning: 'How do you come to that?' / 'How did you get that idea?'.
additional_notes: Used to question someone's assumption or conclusion — asking why they think or believe something. Common in the plural/informal address (ihr). Can be followed by a clause introduced by dass/daß or a question word. Tone can be neutral or skeptical depending on context.
target_language_example: Wie kommt ihr darauf, dass ich das wollte?
native_language_example: How did you get the idea that I wanted that?

meaning: how does one get from (a place) / how do you get from
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions or how to get from one location to another. Common structure: 'Wie kommt man von [Ort A] (zum/zur) [Ort B]?' or shorter 'Wie kommt man von hier zum/zur ...?' 'man' is impersonal (one/you). Use 'zum' for 'zu dem' (masculine/neuter), 'zur' for 'zu der' (feminine).
target_language_example: Wie kommt man von hier zur Bank?
native_language_example: How do you get from here to the bank?

meaning: comes with; comes along; comes into contact with (depends on context)
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'kommt mit' is the 3rd-person singular present of the separable verb mitkommen or a phrase meaning 'comes with' or 'comes into contact with'. Uses: 1) 'comes with' in the sense of accompanying something (Der Appetit kommt mit dem Essen). 2) 'comes into contact with' (kommt mit ... in Kontakt). 3) 'comes along' or 'goes with' (Tom kommt mit uns). 4) As part of an address: 'Kommt mit!' is the imperative for ihr. Note that word order and case vary with sentence structure; the infinitive/separable form is 'mitkommen'.
target_language_example: Der Appetit kommt mit dem Essen.
native_language_example: The appetite comes with the food.

meaning: never arrives (to/for).
additional_notes: Form of kommen + nie + zu (often followed by a noun like 'einem Date', 'einer Verabredung' or an implicit place/event). Used to say someone never arrives late or never shows up for something. Context determines whether 'zu' links to a specific appointment/event ('zu einer Verabredung') or is part of a phrase like 'zu spät kommen' (in examples the full idea is 'kommt nie zu spät' = 'is never late').
target_language_example: Sie kommt nie zu unseren Treffen; sie ist immer pünktlich.
native_language_example: She never arrives at our meetings; she's always punctual.

meaning: 'is/are still coming' or 'will still happen/arrive'; can mean 'else' in questions (who else is coming) or 'there's more to come'.
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: 1) To say someone/something is still on the way or will arrive (e.g. 'Der Pudding kommt noch' = the pudding is still coming). 2) To ask if something else will happen (e.g. 'Kommt noch Regen?' = will it still rain?). 3) In questions about additional people, it means 'else' or 'also' (e.g. 'Wer kommt noch?' = Who else is coming?). Can be used conversationally and covers present/future sense.
target_language_example: Wartet kurz, mein Bruder kommt noch.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, my brother is still coming.

meaning: something's coming / something's going to happen; (colloquial) is something on (TV)?
additional_notes: Colloquial phrasing: 'kommt was' is a shortened, informal way to say that something is coming or will happen soon. Context decides meaning: it can refer to an event (Da kommt was = Something's coming) or to programming on TV (Kommt was im Fernsehen? = Is anything on TV?). Often used with surprised or anticipatory tone.
target_language_example: Da kommt was – schnell, schaut hin!
native_language_example: Something's coming — quick, look!

meaning: 'seems familiar to me' or 'rings a bell'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, name, place, or situation seems familiar. Literally: 'comes to me known'. Often appears as 'kommt mir bekannt vor' (with 'vor'). Common in spoken and written German. You can replace 'mir' with another pronoun (e.g. 'kommt dir bekannt vor').
target_language_example: Der Ort kommt mir bekannt vor.
native_language_example: The place seems familiar to me.

meaning: 'could/was able to (do) that' or 'couldn't/wasn't able to (do) that' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the past (preterite) form of 'können' + the pronoun 'das'. Use to say someone was able (or unable) to do something, or to ask how something could happen. Context and word order determine whether it's a statement or a question and whether it's positive or negative (e.g., 'konnte das nicht' = couldn't do that). In questions 'Wie konnte das passieren?' = 'How could that happen?'.
target_language_example: Ich konnte das gestern nicht reparieren.
native_language_example: I couldn't fix that yesterday.

meaning: could you
additional_notes: A sentence fragment, not a complete expression by itself. konnte is the simple past of können ('could' / 'was able to'), and dich means singular informal 'you' as the object. It is usually completed by another verb later in the sentence, for example: Ich konnte dich nicht finden = 'I couldn't find you.'
target_language_example: Ich konnte dich nicht hören.
native_language_example: I couldn't hear you.

meaning: 'could (not) myself' — used with reflexive verbs to mean 'I could (not) [do something]' or 'I was (unable to) [do something]'.
additional_notes: Konnte is the past (simple) form of können (could/was able to). Mich is the reflexive pronoun for 'myself' (accusative). Together they appear in sentences with reflexive verbs (e.g., sich beherrschen, sich zurückhalten, sich verabschieden) or in constructions like sich verständlich machen. Often used to say you were able or unable to do something in the past: 'Ich konnte mich nicht ...' = 'I couldn't ...'. Word order follows normal German rules (verb second in main clauses; the past modal preceding the reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: Ich konnte mich gestern nicht konzentrieren.
native_language_example: I couldn't concentrate yesterday.

meaning: the past (could) + reflexive 'to myself' — used to say you were able/unable to do or allow something for yourself (I could / I couldn't ... for myself).
additional_notes: Commonly appears with verbs like leisten, verkneifen, rufen, entgehen or with objects (das nicht leisten, das Lachen nicht verkneifen). 'Konnte' is simple past of können; 'mir' is the dative reflexive/pronominal object meaning 'to/for me'. Translate according to context: ability (I could), inability (I couldn't), or 'I could afford' (ich konnte mir das nicht leisten = I couldn't afford that).
target_language_example: Ich konnte mir den Urlaub trotz allem nicht leisten.
native_language_example: I couldn't afford the vacation despite everything.

meaning: could already / was already able to
additional_notes: Combination of the past tense of 'können' (konnte) with 'schon' to say someone was already able to do something (or already felt a certain way) at a past time. Use with an action or quality: e.g. 'konnte schon mit vier lesen' = was already able to read at four. Context decides tense/person; 'konnte' is simple past (preterite).
target_language_example: Er konnte schon mit sechs Fahrrad fahren.
native_language_example: He could already ride a bike at six.

meaning: 'how could you do/know/forget that' (expressing surprise, disbelief, or criticism)
additional_notes: Commonly used in questions beginning with 'Wie konntest du ...?' to express strong surprise, disappointment, or accusation about someone's action or omission. Tone can be accusatory or incredulous. The verb konntest is the past (imperfect) of können and refers to ability/possibility; context determines whether it asks how someone could have done, known, remembered, or failed to do/know something.
target_language_example: Wie konntest du das nur tun?
native_language_example: How could you do that (to me)?

meaning: to be/ stay concentrated; used with verbs meaning to force oneself to concentrate (e.g. sich zwingen, sich bemühen).
additional_notes: This phrase is not a standalone verb; 'konzentriert' is an adjective/participle and 'zu' appears because it connects to an infinitive clause (e.g. 'zwang sich dazu, konzentriert zu bleiben' = 'forced himself to stay concentrated'). Common structures: 'sich (dazu) zwingen, + zu + Infinitiv' or 'sich bemühen, + zu + Infinitiv.' It describes directing attention or focus. Word order: the infinitive clause often comes after the main verb and comma.
target_language_example: Ich zwinge mich dazu, konzentriert zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: I force myself to work in a focused way.

meaning: 'no matter the cost' / 'whatever it takes' (used in phrases like "koste es, was es wolle").
additional_notes: Alone, "koste es" is part of the fixed expression "koste es, was es wolle" meaning 'whatever it costs, no matter what'. It is used to stress determination to achieve something regardless of expense or consequences. Not typically used alone without the rest of the phrase. "koste es, was es wolle" is somewhat formal/literary but common in speech for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich werde das Projekt fertigstellen, koste es, was es wolle.
native_language_example: I will finish the project, whatever it takes.

meaning: no matter the cost; at any cost
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something regardless of the expense, effort, or consequences. Strong, emphatic phrase — can be used seriously or hyperbolically. Often follows or precedes an action. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Ich werde das tun, koste es, was es wolle.').
target_language_example: Ich muss den Vertrag bekommen, koste es, was es wolle.
native_language_example: I must get the contract, no matter the cost.

meaning: 'how much does the (masculine) ... cost' or 'what's the price of the ...' (masculine noun)
additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns (der) or when asking about a specific item. More generally you'll hear 'Was kostet ...?' or 'Wie viel kostet ...?' — use 'kostet der' within a question like 'Was kostet der Kuchen?' The noun following 'der' must be masculine (der Schinken, der Kuchen, der Computer, der Spaß, der Hut). For feminine use 'kostet die', for neuter 'kostet das', and plural 'kosten die'.
target_language_example: Was kostet der Apfel?
native_language_example: How much does the apple cost?

meaning: ‘costs the’ or 'how much is the…' (used to ask or state the price of a specific feminine or definite noun).
additional_notes: The verb 'kosten' means 'to cost'. 'kostet die' is the present tense singular (er/sie/es kostet) combined with the feminine or definite article 'die' (or plural 'die'). In questions use 'Was kostet die…?' or 'Wie viel kostet die…?' to ask the price of a specific item (e.g., die Fahrkarte, die Flasche). In statements you can say e.g. 'Die Suppe kostet zehn Euro.' Note word order: in questions the verb comes second ('Was kostet die Fahrkarte?').
target_language_example: Was kostet die Jacke dort?
native_language_example: How much is the jacket over there?

meaning: 'how much does one (cost)' — used to ask the price of a single item (feminine or when using 'eine' as indefinite article).
additional_notes: Common in questions about price. 'kostet' is the verb (from 'kosten' = to cost). 'eine' is the indefinite article for feminine nouns (e.g. 'eine Karte', 'eine Dose') or for counting one item. For masculine/neuter nouns you would hear 'kostet ein' or 'kostet ein(e)?' depending on gender: e.g. 'Was kostet ein Brot?' (masculine/neuter). Often appears in phrases like 'Was kostet eine Fahrkarte?' or 'Wie viel kostet eine Dose Bier?'.
target_language_example: Was kostet eine Eintrittskarte?
native_language_example: How much does one admission ticket cost?

meaning: I'm/It makes me sick; I'm/I'm really annoyed by (very strong, rude).
additional_notes: Colloquial and vulgar: from the verb 'kotzen' (to puke). Used to express strong irritation, disgust or anger toward a person, thing or situation. Commonly appears as 'Das kotzt mich an' (That pisses me off) or 'Du kotzt mich an' (You annoy me). Avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Das Verhalten deiner Kollegen kotzt mich an.
native_language_example: The behavior of your colleagues really pisses me off.

meaning: 'are sick' (second-person singular, informal — part of the verb phrase 'krank sein')
additional_notes: This is the present tense, informal 'du' form of 'krank sein' (to be sick). Used to talk about someone's current state of illness. In sentences it appears after a subject (Du bist krank) or in questions/inversions (Wie krank bist du?). For formal or plural you would use 'krank sind Sie' (formal) or 'krank seid ihr' (plural informal).
target_language_example: Wie krank bist du heute? — Ich fühle mich ein bisschen fiebrig.
native_language_example: How sick are you today? — I feel a bit feverish.

meaning: to make (someone) sick; to cause illness; also used figuratively to mean to disgust, distress, or exhaust someone.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'to make sick.' Commonly used with a person as object (mich, dich, ihn, sie, uns). Can refer to causing physical illness or strong negative feelings (e.g., disgust) or extreme fatigue. Conjugation follows 'machen' (e.g., macht krank, machte krank, hat krank gemacht). In casual speech the phrase is informal when used figuratively ('Das macht mich krank' = 'That makes me sick').
target_language_example: Der Gestank kann einen wirklich krank machen.
native_language_example: The smell can really make you sick.

meaning: to be sick
additional_notes: Common verb + adjective construction meaning someone is unwell. Frequently used with modal verbs (muss krank sein = must be sick) to express deduction. Can describe temporary illness. Use with personal pronouns: Ich bin krank (I'm sick).
target_language_example: Sie war gestern zu Hause, weil sie krank sein könnte.
native_language_example: She was home yesterday because she might be sick.

meaning: are sick / are ill.
additional_notes: Combination of the adjective krank (sick) with the verb sein (to be) in the plural third-person form sind. Used to state or wonder that people (they, names, soldiers) are ill. Can appear after conjunctions like dass (that), ob (whether/if), vielleicht (maybe). Replace sind with bin/ist/sind depending on subject (ich bin krank, er ist krank, wir sind krank).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass sie nicht mehr krank sind.
native_language_example: I hope that they are not sick anymore.

meaning: extremely worried about (literally: 'sick with' worry).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning to be very worried or anxious about someone or something. Commonly used with 'Sorge' (Sorge um + person/thing) or just 'krank vor Sorge'. It's somewhat emphatic but not slang. Word order: 'krank vor Sorge (um ...)' or 'krank vor + noun'.
target_language_example: Ich war krank vor Sorge um meine Mutter.
native_language_example: I was sick with worry about my mother.

meaning: 'to get sick' or 'to become ill'.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: werden (to become) + adjective krank. Used to say someone becomes ill now or in the future. Can be used with modal verbs and time expressions (könnte, wird, darf nicht). Neutral, everyday language.
target_language_example: Wenn du dich nicht warm anziehst, wirst du krank werden.
native_language_example: If you don't dress warmly, you'll get sick.

meaning: would be sick / might be sick (conditional or reported possibility).
additional_notes: Combines the adjective 'krank' (sick) with the subjunctive/conditional form 'wäre' of 'sein'. Used to express hypothetical situations (If I weren't sick...) or reported/uncertain information (someone is said or believed to be sick). English equivalents include 'would be sick', 'might be sick', 'was said to be sick', or 'would have been sick' depending on context and tense. Word order can vary in subordinate clauses and reported speech.
target_language_example: Darauf steht, dass seine Schwester krank wäre.
native_language_example: It says there that his sister might be sick.

meaning: (typically part of a larger construction) 'sick to' or 'to be sick (with)'; often appears before an adjective or infinitive to describe being ill enough to...
additional_notes: Alone 'krank' means 'sick' and 'zu' is a preposition/infinitive marker. 'krank zu' by itself is uncommon; you usually see it in phrases like 'krank zu Hause' (sick at home) or in constructions 'krank zu sein' (to be sick) or 'krank zu werden' (to become sick). For beginners, learn 'krank sein' = to be sick and 'krank werden' = to get sick. 'zu' often links to an infinitive (krank zu sein) or to a location/description when combined with other words. Do not treat 'krank zu' as a fixed standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Ich möchte krank zu Hause bleiben, wenn ich mich nicht besser fühle.
native_language_example: I want to stay sick at home if I don't feel better.

meaning: 'get/receive it' or in contexts with 'hin' = 'we'll manage/handle it'
additional_notes: Kriegen = colloquial verb meaning 'to get' or 'to receive'. With 'das' it can mean 'get/receive that/it' (Die kriegen das zurück = They'll get it back). When used with 'hin' (kriegen das hin) it is an informal way to say 'manage/handle/figure it out' (Wir kriegen das hin = We'll manage it). Tone: casual, common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — wir kriegen das hin.
native_language_example: Don't worry — we'll manage it.

meaning: 'they get' / 'they'll get (someone/you/me)' or idiomatic 'they'll catch/receive/experience it' depending on context.
additional_notes: Kriegen is a colloquial verb meaning 'to get', 'to receive', 'to catch', or 'to obtain'. With sie (they) it often means 'they will get/catch (someone)' or 'they will hear about it / experience consequences' in threats. Context determines the object (who or what is gotten). Note word order: in full sentences the verb form changes (e.g. 'kriegen sie mich' = 'they catch me'). Capitalization: 'Sie' (formal you) differs from 'sie' (they). The examples use 'sie' = they.
target_language_example: Mach kein Geräusch, sonst kriegen sie dich.
native_language_example: Don't make a sound, otherwise they'll catch you.

meaning: gets/receives it; manages/handles it (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common colloquial use of kriegen (to get/receive or to manage). With objects (e.g., "kriegt das, was du willst") it means 'gets/receives it'. With verbs or situations (e.g., "Ihr kriegt das hin") it means 'you'll manage/figure it out' or 'you can do it'. Informal; 'bekommt' and 'schafft' are more neutral alternatives depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ihr kriegt das hin.
native_language_example: Don't worry, you'll manage it.

meaning: used in a sentence pattern 'zu kurz, um ...' meaning 'too short to ...' or 'too brief to ...'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of the structure 'zu kurz, um + zu + infinitive' (or 'zu kurz, um + reflexive/accusative phrase') and expresses that there is not enough time or it's not worth spending time on something. Literal translation: 'too short to...'. Common in sentences about life, time, deadlines, or not worrying about small things.
target_language_example: Das Wochenende ist zu kurz, um alles zu erledigen.
native_language_example: The weekend is too short to get everything done.

meaning: shortly after; soon after that.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened a short time after a previously mentioned event. It can appear at the beginning or middle of a sentence. Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Wir sprachen über den Film, und kurz darauf gingen wir nach Hause.
native_language_example: We talked about the movie, and shortly after we went home.

meaning: about to; on the verge of; very close to doing something
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or "zu" + infinitive to say someone or something is almost doing or about to do an action (e.g., "kurz davor, zu beginnen" or "kurz davor, aufzugeben"). Can describe a present or past near-action (use past tense with "war kurz davor"). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich war kurz davor, das Projekt abzubrechen.
native_language_example: I was about to abandon the project.

meaning: in short; briefly; to sum up
additional_notes: Used to introduce a concise summary or conclusion. Often appears at the start of a sentence to compress earlier or longer information into a short statement. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Kurz gesagt, ich kann nächsten Monat nicht kommen.
native_language_example: In short, I can't come next month.

meaning: 'shortly after' or 'just after' (a short time following something).
additional_notes: Used with times or events to say something happened a short time after another event. Often followed by a noun with the dative (e.g., 'der Geburt') or a time expression ('acht', 'Mittag'). Can also appear in colloquial placement like 'kurz nach nebenan' meaning 'just next door' (note: there the structure is slightly different).
target_language_example: Er kam kurz nach dem Meeting an.
native_language_example: He arrived shortly after the meeting.

meaning: just before; shortly before (in time) or a short distance before (in place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens a short time earlier than another event (e.g., kurz vor dem Ende, kurz vor Tagesanbruch) or a short distance/time before a location (e.g., kurz vor der Küste). Often followed by a noun in dative (kurz vor der Küste) or a time expression (kurz vor Ende, kurz vor dem Schlafengehen).
target_language_example: Wir kamen kurz vor Sonnenaufgang an.
native_language_example: We arrived just before sunrise.

meaning: briefly; for a short time (often combined with a verb like zuhören, warten, winken); 'kurz zu' itself is part of separable verbs or expressions meaning 'briefly + [verb]'.
additional_notes: In German, kurz often comes before a separable verb particle (zu) or before verbs to mean 'briefly' or 'for a moment'. Examples: 'kurz zuhören' (listen briefly), 'kurz warten' (wait briefly), 'kurz zuwinken' (give a brief wave). Word order depends on the verb and sentence (imperative: Hör mal kurz zu! = 'Listen briefly!'). 'Um es kurz zu machen' is a fixed phrase meaning 'to make a long story short'.
target_language_example: Kannst du kurz zuhören?
native_language_example: Can you listen for a moment?

meaning: to fight/struggle with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing introduced by mit (dative). Can mean physically fight or struggle/contend with a problem or opponent. Commonly conjugated (ich kämpfe, du kämpfst, er kämpft). Context determines literal (physical) vs. figurative (struggle, cope).
target_language_example: Sie kämpfen mit ihren eigenen Ängsten.
native_language_example: They are struggling with their own fears.

meaning: could (oneself)
additional_notes: This is a combination of the subjunctive form 'könne' (Konjunktiv I, used for reported speech) and the reflexive pronoun 'sich'. It appears in indirect/reported speech (e.g. He says he could/was able to...) and with reflexive verbs like 'sich erinnern' or the fixed expression 'sich auf jdn/etw verlassen' (to be able to rely on someone). For beginners: interpret it as 'could' or 'would be able to' referring back to the subject (he/she/one/they).
target_language_example: Er sagte, er könne sich an den Weg erinnern.
native_language_example: He said he could remember the way.

meaning: How dare you (do that)? — an outraged question challenging someone's action.
additional_notes: Polite-form (Sie) used here but expresses strong indignation or shock. Often followed by an infinitive clause introduced with ‚zu‘ or a direct object/action. Common in formal or dramatic contexts; tone is confrontational. For familiar/informal address use „kannst du es wagen“. Not literally asking ability — it's rhetorical.
target_language_example: Wie können Sie es wagen, das ohne meine Erlaubnis zu tun?
native_language_example: How dare you do that without my permission?

meaning: 'everyone can' or 'all (of them) can'.
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb können (can/be able to) and the determiner/pronoun alle (everyone/all). Used to say that every person in a group is able to do something or that the whole group shares a quality or possibility. Word order and subject pronoun may change (e.g. 'Wir können alle...' = we all can; 'Sie können alle...' = they/you can all).
target_language_example: Wir können alle heute Abend kommen.
native_language_example: We can all come tonight.

meaning: they can
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb können and the pronoun die (they). Word order in German sentences can place the verb first for questions ("Können die...?" = "Can they...?") or after the subject for statements ("Die können..." = "They can..."). In casual speech, 'die' may refer to people or groups; context determines meaning. Use 'können die' when talking about what a group is able to do or asking whether they are able to do something.
target_language_example: Vielleicht können die uns morgen helfen.
native_language_example: Maybe they can help us tomorrow.

meaning: 'can' or 'are able to' + 'this' (demonstrative in accusative masculine or temporal 'this' for days) — indicates ability/possibility regarding a specific object, event, time, or day.
additional_notes: This combines the modal verb 'können' (to be able to/can) with the demonstrative 'diesen' (accusative masculine singular or temporal accusative for days). 'Diesen' must agree in case and gender with the noun it modifies (e.g., diesen Test, diesen Film, diesen Donnerstag). Word order depends on clause type: in main clauses the finite verb form of 'können' appears second. The full phrase will normally include the noun after 'diesen'.
target_language_example: Sie können diesen Donnerstag kommen.
native_language_example: You can come this Thursday.

meaning: 'can' or 'able to' + 'this' (modal verb + demonstrative pronoun)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the modal verb 'können' (can/be able to) followed by the demonstrative pronoun 'dieses' (this) and a noun. Word order in German: modal verb conjugated for the subject, then the object (here 'dieses' + noun). 'Dieses' must match the gender/case of the noun (e.g., dieses Buch (neuter), diese Tür (feminine), diesen Stuhl (masculine accusative)).
target_language_example: Wir können dieses Problem gemeinsam lösen.
native_language_example: We can solve this problem together.

meaning: 'may/might/are allowed to go' or 'can go' (ability or permission to leave/go)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb können (can/may) with gehen (to go). Depending on context it expresses permission ('you may go'), ability ('we can go'), or possibility ('you can go where you want'). Word order: können conjugates for the subject; gehen stays in infinitive at the end of the clause. Formal or informal meaning depends on context and tone.
target_language_example: Sie können gehen, wenn Sie möchten.
native_language_example: You may go if you like.

meaning: 'can (do something) well' — expresses ability plus that the action is done well
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb können (to be able to/can) with the adverb gut (well). Used to say someone has the ability to do something and does it well. Word order: subject + können (conjugated) + gut + verb (infinitive) when describing a specific action (e.g. Sie können gut singen). Can also describe interpersonal compatibility (wir können gut miteinander auskommen). Conjugate können to match the subject (ich kann, du kannst, er/sie kann, wir/Sie können, ihr könnt).
target_language_example: Affen können gut klettern.
native_language_example: Monkeys can climb well.

meaning: cannot do anything / are unable to do anything
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb können (can) with nichts (nothing). Used to say someone is unable to act or that something has no effect. Common word orders vary with sentence structure (e.g., 'Wir können nichts tun.' or 'Sie können nichts bauen.'). Frequent in spoken and written German. Equivalent English forms: 'can't do anything', 'are unable to...'.
target_language_example: Wir können nichts tun.
native_language_example: We can't do anything.

meaning: can only / are only able to
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'können' (to be able to/can) with the adverb 'nur' (only). Used to limit possibilities or actions — i.e. saying that nothing else can be done or that the action is the only option. Word order: 'nur' usually follows the verb or the element it restricts (e.g. 'Wir können nur warten' = 'We can only wait').
target_language_example: Wir können nur unser Bestes geben.
native_language_example: We can only do our best.

meaning: can do it
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb können (can/be able to) plus the pronoun das (that/it). Used to say someone is able to do something—often with the verb omitted because context makes it clear. Word order and conjugation change with subject (e.g., ich kann das, wir können das).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, du kannst das schaffen — wir können das zusammen üben.
native_language_example: I think you can do it — we can practice that together.

meaning: 'could stay at' / 'might (do something) at/with' depending on context (polite or hypothetical possibility + preposition 'bei' = at someone's place or in/at something).
additional_notes: Könnte is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of 'können' and is used to express possibility or polite requests/offers. Bei is a preposition meaning 'at/with' (e.g., at someone's home, at an event, in a course). Together 'könnte bei' often appears when saying you could stay at someone's place (könnte bei dir übernachten) or that something might happen in/at a situation (könnte bei dem Kurs durchfallen = I might fail in that course). Word order and pronoun form change the politeness (du/dir, ihr/euch, Sie/Ihnen).
target_language_example: Ich könnte bei meiner Freundin übernachten, wenn das okay ist.
native_language_example: I could stay at my girlfriend's place if that's okay.

meaning: could be a
additional_notes: The phrase combines the modal verb könnte (could) + the indefinite article eine. Use 1) to express possibility: 'could be a ...' (Das könnte eine Lösung sein). 2) to say you could do or make something when the object is feminine or when talking about 'a' thing: 'I could make/do a ...' (Ich könnte eine Ausnahme machen). The exact English translation depends on the verb or noun that follows. Typical in conditional or tentative statements; often followed by a noun or verb phrase.
target_language_example: Das könnte eine gute Idee sein.
native_language_example: That could be a good idea.

meaning: could help / might be able to help
additional_notes: Conditional form: 'könnte' is the Konjunktiv II (subjunctive II) of 'können' and expresses possibility, ability in hypothetical or polite contexts. Often used to offer help (Ich könnte helfen) or to express wish/regret (Ich wünschte, ich könnte helfen). Tone can be tentative, polite, or regretful depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich denke, ich könnte helfen.
native_language_example: I think I could help.

meaning: 'could' or 'might' + 'today' — expresses possibility or ability in the present day (conditional/subjunctive).
additional_notes: Könnte is the Konjunktiv II (or conditional) form of können. With 'könnte heute' you either indicate something that might happen today (possibility) or something you would be able to do today (ability/wish). Context (e.g., following verbs or wishes like 'ich wünschte') shows whether it's possibility (Es könnte heute regnen = It might rain today) or a hypothetical ability/desire (Ich wünschte, ich könnte heute mitkommen = I wish I could come along today).
target_language_example: Ich könnte heute früher gehen, wenn das für dich passt.
native_language_example: I could leave earlier today if that suits you.

meaning: ‘I could (to) you’ — polite/offering possibility: 'I could (do something) for you' or 'could I (do something) for you?'.
additional_notes: Used to offer help, make a polite suggestion, or state a hypothetical ability. Often followed by an infinitive or an object (e.g. helfen, geben, welches leihen). In questions word order can be 'Könnte ich dir helfen?' (Could I help you?). 'Dir' is the dative 'to you'. Tone can be polite and tentative.
target_language_example: Könnte ich dir morgen beim Umzug helfen?
native_language_example: Could I help you move tomorrow?

meaning: could him
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb 'könnte' (conditional/polite 'could' or 'might') and the pronoun 'ihn' (accusative 'him'). Used before a verb or in ellipsis to indicate possibility, ability, hypothetical action, or politeness about something done to 'him'. Word order: in full sentences the main verb often goes to the end (Ich könnte ihn noch gebrauchen → I could still use him). Tone depends on context (neutral, hypothetical, polite, or strong/threatening).
target_language_example: Ich könnte ihn morgen anrufen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: I could call him tomorrow if you want.

meaning: could be in the (feminine or dative) / might be inside the
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'könnte' (could/might) + prepositional phrase 'in der' (in the + feminine noun in nominative/accusative? Actually 'in der' is used for feminine nouns in dative or for feminine nouns in nominative/accusative with the fixed phrase; most commonly 'in der' = 'in the' with a feminine noun in dative after motion or location). Use when speculating about something being located inside or within a feminine noun (or in dative case). Example contexts: 'Es könnte in der Tasche sein' (It might be in the bag). Word order: 'könnte in der' is usually followed by a noun (e.g. 'Tasche') or a pronoun ('könnte in der sein' often needs a noun omitted but understood).
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel könnte in der Tasche sein.
native_language_example: The key could be in the bag.

meaning: could be now / could be right now (expresses possibility or wish in the present)
additional_notes: Used with the modal verb 'können' in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) to indicate a present possibility (e.g. 'he might be now') or a present unreal wish/desire (e.g. 'I wish I could be there now'). 'Jetzt' means 'now' and simply places the action in the present moment. Tone can be speculative ('might') or hypothetical ('could/wish').
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich könnte jetzt mit dir am Strand sitzen.
native_language_example: I wish I could be sitting with you on the beach right now.

meaning: could more / wish I could have more (usually: more time, money, etc.).
additional_notes: Used in wishes or hypothetical statements with *ich wünschte, (dass) ...* or *wünschte sich*, expressing regret about not having enough of something. *könnte* is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of *können*. Commonly followed by what is lacking (e.g., Zeit, Geld, Mut).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich könnte mehr Ruhe haben.
native_language_example: I wish I could have more peace / quiet.

meaning: one might think / you could think (used to introduce an impression or ironic remark).
additional_notes: Common impersonal phrase (often with 'Man') to express a possible impression, usually followed by a clause describing what that impression would be. Can be used literally or sarcastically. Tenses: often uses Konjunktiv II ('könnte') for tentativeness. Word order: 'Man könnte meinen, ...'.
target_language_example: Man könnte meinen, das hier ist ein Museum.
native_language_example: One might think this is a museum.

meaning: 'I could' or 'I might' (reflexive: with 'mich' = myself).
additional_notes: Könnte is the subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) form of 'können' used for possibility, uncertainty, polite requests or wishes. When combined with the reflexive pronoun 'mich', it indicates the speaker performing the action on themselves (e.g. 'I might be mistaken', 'I wish I could join'). Word order can change depending on sentence structure (verb at end in subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: Ich könnte mich irren.
native_language_example: I could be mistaken.

meaning: could never / would never (be able to); expresses that something is impossible or someone would not do something.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'könnte' (Konjunktiv II of 'können', used for hypothetical or polite statements) with 'nie' (never). Used to say that something would/ could not happen or that someone would never do/feel something. Context determines whether it's a hypothetical impossibility (could never happen) or a strong moral/psychological statement about someone (would never do/feel).
target_language_example: Ich könnte nie so früh aufstehen.
native_language_example: I could never get up that early.

meaning: could still / might still (indicates a possibility that continues or remains).
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'könnte' (conditional of 'können') with 'noch' (still/yet). Used to express that something is still possible, may happen, could continue to be true, or that someone could do something additionally. Tone is neutral; context and word order determine nuance (possibility, permission, offer, or suggestion).
target_language_example: Das könnte noch interessant werden.
native_language_example: That could still become interesting.

meaning: might be; could be (expresses possibility or uncertainty).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is possible but not certain. Common in short replies (even stand-alone: "Könnte sein.") and in clauses with 'dass/daß' to state a hypothesis. Tone can be neutral or noncommittal; context often determines whether it's polite, doubtful, or dismissive.
target_language_example: Es könnte sein, dass wir zu spät kommen.
native_language_example: We might be late.

meaning: used to express possibility: 'it could be that' / 'maybe'.
additional_notes: A cautious, polite way to say something is possible but not certain. Common in spoken and written German. Often followed by a clause with a verb at the end (subordinate clause introduced by 'dass'). Can be contracted in speech to 'könnte sein, ...' or replaced by 'vielleicht' for a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Es könnte sein, dass ich etwas später komme.
native_language_example: It could be that I'll arrive a bit later.

meaning: could just as well / might as well
additional_notes: Used to suggest that one option is about as good as another, or that something is a reasonable or acceptable alternative. Often part of phrases like "könnte so gut ... sein/heißen" or "könnte so gut...tun". Tone can be neutral or slightly casual; context clarifies whether it's hypothetical or a suggestion.
target_language_example: Wir haben keinen besseren Vorschlag, es könnte so gut dieser sein.
native_language_example: We don't have a better suggestion; this one could just as well be it.

meaning: could also / might also (suggesting an additional possibility)
additional_notes: Combines the conditional/modal verb 'könnten' (could/we might) with 'auch' (also). Used to propose an alternative or additional possibility, often politely or tentatively. Followed by an infinitive or clause. Tone can be suggestive (Let's.../We could...) or speculative (They could also...).
target_language_example: Wir könnten auch ins Café gehen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: We could also go to the café, if you want.

meaning: you could (yourself) / you might (yourself) — polite/conditional possibility referring to the person.
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular conditional form of 'können' plus the reflexive pronoun 'dich'. It expresses a possible action or outcome that could happen to the listener (e.g., get infected, get hurt, get lost). In English it often translates as 'you could...' or 'you might...'. Use appropriate verb after 'könntest dich' (e.g., 'anstecken', 'verletzen', 'verirren').
target_language_example: Du könntest dich erkälten, wenn du ohne Jacke rausgehst.
native_language_example: You could catch a cold if you go out without a jacket.

meaning: could (you) for me — polite or hypothetical request/suggestion using the conditional (Konjunktiv II) with the dative pronoun 'mir' (to me).
additional_notes: Used when asking or suggesting that someone do something for the speaker. 'Könntet' is the second-person plural (ihr) or formal 'Sie' form of the conditional of 'können'. In context the subject can be 'ihr' (you plural) or polite 'Sie'. Common in polite requests and hypothetical statements: e.g. 'Ihr könntet mir helfen' (You could help me) or 'Könnten Sie mir sagen...?' (Could you tell me...?). 'Mir' is the dative pronoun meaning 'to me'. Word order can vary (verb-first in questions or subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: Ich hatte gehofft, ihr könntet mir sagen, wo Tom sich befindet.
native_language_example: I had hoped you could tell me where Tom is.

meaning: you care / you take care (reflexive) — 'you are concerned' or 'you look after' depending on context.
additional_notes: From the verb sich kümmern um. With 'du kümmerst dich (um ...)' it can mean either 'you take care of/look after' (someone/something) or 'you worry/are concerned about' (something). The object after 'um' shows which sense: e.g. 'um die Kinder' = you take care of the children; 'um die Meinung der anderen' = you worry about others' opinions. Informal everyday phrase; the verb requires the reflexive pronoun (dich for du).
target_language_example: Du kümmerst dich um deine Schwester, während ich einkaufe.
native_language_example: You take care of your sister while I go shopping.

meaning: artificial intelligence (AI).
additional_notes: Refers to computer systems or software that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence (learning, reasoning, pattern recognition). Often shortened in speech/text to 'KI' (abbreviation). Used in technical and everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Künstliche Intelligenz hilft Ärzten bei der Diagnose.
native_language_example: Artificial intelligence helps doctors with diagnosis.

meaning: '(he/she) kissed me on the' (introduces the body part or location kissed).
additional_notes: This is the imperfect/subjunctive form 'küsste' (often used in narratives or conditional/indirect speech). In simple past you'd say 'küsste' only in Konjunktiv II; more commonly for past narration use 'küsste' may appear in reports — however in everyday past narration you'd more often see 'küsste' replaced by 'küsste' only in hypotheticals. The structure 'auf die + [body part in accusative]' is used for 'on the [body part]'. Common complete phrase: 'Er küsste mich auf die Wange.' = 'He kissed me on the cheek.'
target_language_example: Sie küsste mich auf die Stirn.
native_language_example: She kissed me on the forehead.

meaning: 'laughed and' — used to connect an action of laughing with another action
additional_notes: This is simply the past tense of lachen (lachte) plus the conjunction und (and). It links two actions the same person did in sequence or together (e.g. laughed and kissed, laughed and hugged). Very common in narrative. Word order after und follows normal German rules (verb second or at end depending on clause).
target_language_example: Sie lachte und winkte ihrem Freund zu.
native_language_example: She laughed and waved to her friend.

meaning: past tense of 'liegen' with the feminine or plural noun/pronoun 'die' (was lying / lay).
additional_notes: ‘Lag’ is the simple past (Präteritum) of liegen (to lie, be situated, or lie down). When you see 'lag die', the subject after 'die' is typically feminine singular (die Stadt) or plural (die + plural noun), or 'die' can be the definite article for a feminine noun. Context decides whether it means 'was located' (Dort lag die Stadt Thal = There lay/was located the town Thal) or 'was lying/was in bed' (Er lag die ganze Woche krank im Bett uses 'lag' with a masculine subject; note in these examples 'lag die' appears only in the locational/feminine case in sentence 1 — for sentences with people you will usually see 'er/sie/ich lag'). Use 'lag' for past simple descriptions of position or state.
target_language_example: Früher lag die kleine Kirche mitten im Dorf.
native_language_example: In the past, the small church lay in the middle of the village.

meaning: he/it lay; he was lying (past tense of 'liegen' for 'er').
additional_notes: Simple past word order: subject 'er' after the verb in many clauses (Verb-second in main clauses yields 'Lag er' only in questions or narrative inversion; here examples show narrative: 'Als er wieder zu sich kam, lag er ...' — 'lag' is the simple past (Präteritum) of 'liegen' meaning 'to lie' (be in a horizontal position). Use for describing where someone or something was positioned in the past. Not reflexive. English equivalent usually 'he was lying' or 'he lay'.
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall lag er noch eine Weile bewusstlos auf dem Boden.
native_language_example: After the accident he lay unconscious on the floor for a while.

meaning: 'was (lying) with' or 'was due to' (past of 'liegen mit' / 'liegen an' depending on context)
additional_notes: This is the past tense form (Präteritum) of a verb phrase using liegen + mit. Alone, 'lag mit' is uncommon without context. It can mean someone/something 'was lying with' (physically located with someone) or, in some contexts, 'it was due to' when used like 'es lag an' (but note the difference). You will most often see 'lag bei' (to be at/amount to) or 'lag an' (to be due to) instead. Pay attention to the rest of the sentence to know the meaning.
target_language_example: Das Buch lag mit den anderen auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The book was lying with the others on the table.

meaning: to continue or last (for a certain length of time); 'for ... (time)'.
additional_notes: Often used with a duration (eine Stunde, drei Wochen) placed before or after 'lang' + 'an' to say something continued for that time. 'anhalten' is the base verb (to stop/continue) and when split into 'lang an' it emphasizes duration: e.g. 'drei Tage lang anhalten' = 'to last for three days'. Can be used with actions like 'stehen' or verbs of perception with 'an' as a separable prefix (e.g. 'sah ... an' = looked at) plus 'einige Augenblicke lang' to indicate how long.
target_language_example: Das Konzert hielt zwei Stunden lang an.
native_language_example: The concert continued for two hours.

meaning: for ... (duration) in/at (somewhere); indicates how long someone stayed somewhere or in a state.
additional_notes: Combines the duration word 'lang' (meaning 'long' as in duration) with a following prepositional phrase introduced by 'in' + dative (e.g. im Bett, im Krankenhaus, im Gefängnis, im Ausland). Word order in examples: duration (eine Woche/ drei Jahre) + lang + im + place/state. You can also say 'für ... lang' or put 'lang' after the time expression (e.g. 'drei Monate lang').
target_language_example: Sie blieb zwei Wochen lang im Hotel.
native_language_example: She stayed in the hotel for two weeks.

meaning: not ... for (a period of time); 'haven't ... for' (used with a duration)
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone did not do, see, or experience something during a specified length of time. Often appears as '<DURATION> lang nicht' before or after the verb phrase (e.g. 'eine Woche lang nicht zur Arbeit kommen'). Common colloquial short form in greetings: 'Na, lang nicht gesehen.' Usually used with perfect, modal, or infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Na, lang nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: Well, long time no see.

meaning: a long trip or long drive (in time or distance).
additional_notes: Used to describe journeys that take a long time or cover a large distance. Can refer to car drives, train trips, bus rides, or general travel. Often used with verbs like haben (eine lange Fahrt haben), sein (es war eine lange Fahrt), or fahren (wir hatten eine lange Fahrt).
target_language_example: Die lange Fahrt gestern war sehr anstrengend.
native_language_example: The long trip yesterday was very tiring.

meaning: to work for a long time / to work long hours
additional_notes: Used to say someone spends a long time working or has long work hours. Can refer to a single long work session or regularly working late. "lange" modifies duration; common with subjects like ich, wir, er/sie. Often appears with time expressions (z. B. 'seit', 'bis', 'heute Abend').
target_language_example: Ich muss heute lange arbeiten.
native_language_example: I have to work long hours today.

meaning: to stay up late
additional_notes: Used to advise or tell someone not to remain awake late into the night. Common with modal verbs (sollen, dürfen) and negation: nicht so lange aufbleiben = 'not stay up so long'. 'aufbleiben' is separable (ich bleibe lange auf).
target_language_example: Ich sollte heute nicht so lange aufbleiben.
native_language_example: I shouldn't stay up so late today.

meaning: 'how long have you been (doing/being) ...' — asks about the duration up to now
additional_notes: Used to ask how long someone has been in a state, job, relationship, location, or activity. Often follows 'Wie' as in 'Wie lange bist du schon ...?'. The verb and preposition change depending on context (e.g., 'Verkäufer' uses no preposition, 'auf Reisen', 'im Ausland', 'mit Maria befreundet', 'von zu Hause weg').
target_language_example: Wie lange bist du schon in Deutschland?
native_language_example: How long have you been in Germany?

meaning: 'how long it takes' or 'how long will it take'
additional_notes: Common fragment used in questions about duration. Often appears in full questions like "Wie lange dauert es?" (How long will it take?) or with an object: "Wie lange dauert es bis zum Bahnhof?" (How long until we reach the station?). Use 'Wie' at the start to form the question. Can be used in present or future sense depending on context.
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es, bis der Bus kommt?
native_language_example: How long will it take until the bus arrives?

meaning: 'how long it will take' (duration of something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the expected duration of an action or event. Often appears in questions with verbs like wissen, haben (eine Ahnung) or wissen/kennen. Common structure: (Wie) lange es dauern wird? In direct questions use 'wie lange wird es dauern?' or embedded clauses like 'weißt du, wie lange es dauern wird?'.
target_language_example: Weißt du, wie lange es dauern wird, bis der Zug ankommt?
native_language_example: Do you know how long it will take until the train arrives?

meaning: a long time ago; it's been a long time
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened a long time in the past or that too much time has passed since an event. Often appears in sentences like "Es ist (viel) zu lange her" or exclamations "Ist das lange her!" Can be followed by context (e.g. what happened) or used alone as a comment.
target_language_example: Mein Gott, das ist ja wirklich lange her!
native_language_example: My God, that really was a long time ago!

meaning: how long ago it was that / how long has it been since
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the time passed since a past event. Common in questions: 'Wie lange ist es her, dass ...?' = 'How long has it been since ...?' Can be followed by a clause with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum). Formality: neutral, suitable for spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Wie lange ist es her, dass du das letzte Mal in Deutschland warst?
native_language_example: How long has it been since you were in Germany last?

meaning: to live a long time; long-lived
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something lives/has lived for many years. Can be used as a verb phrase (Er will lange leben) or in exclamations/wishes: 'Lange lebe ...!' (Long live ...!). As an adjective-like concept German more commonly uses 'langlebig' or 'langlebig(er)' for durable objects, but 'lange leben' is natural for beings or in wishes.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche mir, dass ich lange leben kann.
native_language_example: I wish that I can live a long time.

meaning: How long have you been living (here/there/doing that)?
additional_notes: Common informal question asking about the duration someone has lived in a place or done something. Often used in conversation with context (e.g., 'Wie lange lebst du schon hier?' or 'Wie lange lebst du schon in Deutschland?'). The full question normally includes 'wie' at the start: 'Wie lange lebst du schon ...?'. Without 'wie' it can be heard in casual speech, but learners should use the complete form.
target_language_example: Wie lange lebst du schon in Berlin?
native_language_example: How long have you been living in Berlin?

meaning: 'how long have you been learning' (asking duration of someone's study of a language or activity).
additional_notes: This is part of the question pattern 'Wie lange lernst du schon ...?' Use to ask how long someone has been studying or doing something. 'Wie lange' = how long (duration); 'lernst du' = you learn/are learning; 'schon' emphasizes that the action started in the past and continues now. For formal situations use 'lernen Sie' instead of 'lernst du'.
target_language_example: Wie lange lernst du schon Spanisch?
native_language_example: How long have you been learning Spanish?

meaning: for a long time looking for a (something); 'lange nach einem Parkplatz suchen' = to search a long time for a parking space.
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'lange' (for a long time) + 'nach' (looking for) + an indefinite noun with the dative/accusative as required (here 'einem Parkplatz' = a parking space). It appears inside the verb phrase 'lange nach ... suchen' meaning to spend a long time searching for something. Word order can change with auxiliary verbs (e.g. perfect tense). Use with verbs like suchen (to search) or fragen (to ask) in similar patterns.
target_language_example: Sie mussten lange nach einem guten Restaurant suchen.
native_language_example: They had to search for a good restaurant for a long time.

meaning: 'not for a long time' or 'haven't ... in a long time' (used with verbs).
additional_notes: Typically appears as part of a sentence like 'Ich habe lange nichts gehört' (I haven't heard anything for a long time). 'Lange' (for a long time) + 'nichts' (nothing) combine to say that nothing has happened or been done during a long period. Common with perfect and present tenses. Word order follows normal German sentence structure (verb often second or auxiliary + past participle at end).
target_language_example: Ich habe lange nichts von dir gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from you in a long time.

meaning: 'how long have you (plural) been...?'
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of a state or situation for 'ihr' (you plural). Commonly begins with 'Wie' as in 'Wie lange seid ihr schon ...?'. Can refer to being in a place, having a status (e.g. vegetarian), or being in a relationship. If speaking to one person formally use 'Wie lange sind Sie schon ...?' and for one informal person use 'Wie lange bist du schon ...?'.
target_language_example: Wie lange seid ihr schon in Deutschland?
native_language_example: How long have you (all) been in Germany?

meaning: "How long have you been..." (formal "you")
additional_notes: Use to ask about the duration of a state, job, relationship, habit, etc., addressed formally (Sie). Put the rest of the sentence after this phrase (e.g. Single, Vegetarier, Verkäufer, mit Ihrer Freundin zusammen). For informal 'du' use "wie lange bist du schon". Often used with present perfect/continuous meaning in English.
target_language_example: Wie lange sind Sie schon in Deutschland?
native_language_example: How long have you been in Germany?

meaning: 'How long have you been in ...?' (formal)
additional_notes: Used to ask how much time someone (formal 'Sie') has spent in a place. Fill in the place after 'in' (country, city, etc.). Common in introductions and polite conversation. Informal alternative with friends: 'Wie lange bist du schon in ...?'. You can also use past-focused versions (e.g. 'Wie lange waren Sie in ...?') for completed stays.
target_language_example: Wie lange sind Sie schon in dieser Stadt?
native_language_example: How long have you been in this city?

meaning: as long as possible / for as long as possible
additional_notes: Used to say you want something to continue for the maximum possible time. Often follows a verb or phrase (e.g., bleiben, weitermachen, leben). Can be shortened in speech to 'so lange wie möglich' or simply 'so lange wie möglich' is common.
target_language_example: Ich möchte so lange wie möglich hier bleiben.
native_language_example: I want to stay here for as long as possible.

meaning: slowly (doing something with a direct object or a specific path/motion).
additional_notes: langsam = 'slowly'. In the examples it appears before a noun with a verb of motion or action: 'langsam die Treppe hinunter' (slowly down the stairs), 'langsam die Augen' (slowly the eyes → slowly opened the eyes), 'Zieh langsam die Socken aus' (slowly take off the socks). The phrase order in German often places langsam before the object or path. You can use langsam with many verbs to indicate a slow pace or deliberate action.
target_language_example: Sie ging langsam die Treppe hinunter.
native_language_example: She walked down the stairs slowly.

meaning: slowly into / slowly in (indicates gradual movement or change toward something)
additional_notes: Combines langsam (slowly) with the preposition in to show gradual motion into a place or gradual change into a state. Used with verbs of motion (e.g., schmelzen, sinken, fahren) or change (verwandeln, kommen). Word order and separable verbs: with separable verbs (einfahren) the particle may appear elsewhere (e.g., 'fuhr ... in den Bahnhof ein'). Context decides case and preposition phrase (in + accusative for movement into).
target_language_example: Die Kerze brannte langsam in die Wachsform hinein.
native_language_example: The candle slowly melted into the wax mold.

meaning: “slowly and…” — used to link two adverbs or adjectives, often describing how something is done (e.g. slowly and clearly, slowly and passionately).
additional_notes: Commonly used to join two qualities or manners (adverbs or adjective phrases). In imperative or instructive contexts (e.g. Sprechen Sie langsam und deutlich) it's a polite request to do something slowly and in another specified way. Word order: both parts usually describe manner; the second element can be an adjective used predicatively (langsam und deutlich) or another adverbial phrase (langsam und aufmerksam).
target_language_example: Geh bitte langsam und vorsichtig die Treppe runter.
native_language_example: Please go down the stairs slowly and carefully.

meaning: so boring that... (introduces a result or consequence)
additional_notes: Use when describing something as very boring and then stating the consequence or result (often with 'so ... that' in English). In German the structure is typically: [Es/Das/Die ...] war so langweilig, dass + clause (verb goes to the end of the clause). Can be used with different subjects and tenses.
target_language_example: Die Vorlesung war so langweilig, dass ich nach zehn Minuten eingeschlafen bin.
native_language_example: The lecture was so boring that I fell asleep after ten minutes.

meaning: 'read the' (past tense, singular subject: he/I/he-name read the ...).
additional_notes: Combines the simple past (Präteritum) form of lesen (las) with the definite article den (accusative masculine singular). Used to say someone read a specific masculine noun (e.g., Artikel, Brief, ganzen Morgen as temporal phrase with direct object). In English you usually translate as 'read the ...' (past). The subject can be ich, er, or a name (Tom) depending on context—German uses las for ich/er/sie/es in Präteritum. Pay attention to the noun that follows den (it must be masculine accusative).
target_language_example: Sie las den Brief gestern Abend.
native_language_example: She read the letter last night.

meaning: Enjoy your meal / Hope it tastes good to you.
additional_notes: A common phrase said to someone who is about to eat. Polite and friendly; similar to 'Guten Appetit' but more colloquial and literally 'let it taste to you'. Can be used warmly, teasingly, or sarcastically depending on tone and context (see example 3).
target_language_example: Lass es dir schmecken, setz dich und iss in Ruhe.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal, sit down and eat in peace.

meaning: Let go of / leave my ... (imperative; telling someone to stop touching or bothering something/someone of mine).
additional_notes: Combines the imperative 'lass' (from lassen) with the possessive 'meine' (my, feminine/plural). Used to tell someone to stop touching, bothering, or involving the speaker's person or belongings. The noun that follows will determine gender/number (meine for feminine singular or any plural). Colloquial and direct — can sound strong depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Lass meine Tasche in Ruhe!
native_language_example: Leave my bag alone!

meaning: leave me alone; don't bother me.
additional_notes: Common imperative phrase used to tell someone to stop bothering, interrupting or annoying you. Usually appears as the full fixed phrase "lass mich in Ruhe" (leave me in peace). Can be strong or rude depending on tone and context; add 'bitte' to soften. 'Lass mich in' by itself is incomplete — learners should memorize the full phrase with 'Ruhe'.
target_language_example: Lass mich in Ruhe, ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: Leave me alone, I have to work.

meaning: leave me
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own. With lassen + mir, the exact meaning depends on what follows. In commands, it can mean 'leave me ...' ('Lass mir mein Brot!'). In other patterns, it can mean 'I won’t let ... happen to me' or be part of an idiom, such as 'sich etwas einfallen lassen' = 'to think of something'. Also, 'ich lass' is a common spoken short form of 'ich lasse'.
target_language_example: Lass mir bitte den letzten Keks.
native_language_example: Leave me the last cookie, please.

meaning: 'I let myself' / 'I allow myself' or in set phrases 'I won't let (something) happen to me' (often used to say you permit or refuse to tolerate something).
additional_notes: Form: first-person singular of lassen + dative reflexive pronoun mir. Often appears in fixed expressions: 'ich lasse mir das nicht gefallen' = 'I won't put up with that'. Can also mean 'I make sure' or 'I arrange for myself' (e.g. 'ich lasse mir den Eid abnehmen' = 'I have the oath administered to me'). Context decides whether it's permissive (allowing) or reflexive/tolerating (refusing to tolerate).
target_language_example: Ich lasse mir das nicht gefallen.
native_language_example: I won't put up with that.

meaning: leave her/them
additional_notes: From lassen + sie. Depending on context, it can mean either leaving someone/something somewhere or letting someone do/be something. sie can mean her or them (and sometimes formal you, though not in these examples). lasse is either 1st-person singular present ("I leave/let") or a more literary/formal imperative form of lass ("leave/let").
target_language_example: Ich lasse sie in Ruhe.
native_language_example: I leave her alone.

meaning: to have something done; to arrange for someone to do something for you (using lassen + machen as a causative phrasing)
additional_notes: A causative construction: lassen + machen indicates arranging or commissioning an action to be performed by someone else. In practice speakers more often use lassen + infinitive without 'machen' (e.g., etwas reparieren lassen), but the sequence 'lassen machen' appears in contexts like 'lassen machen' with a following noun or clause (e.g., 'ein Regal lassen machen' = 'have a shelf made'). Conjugate lassen according to the subject (ich lasse, du lässt, er/sie/es lässt, wir lassen, ihr lasst, sie/Sie lassen).
target_language_example: Ich lasse mir ein neues Regal machen lassen.
native_language_example: I am having a new shelf made for me.

meaning: let us be / allow ourselves to
additional_notes: This is the reflexive or middle-voice use of lassen with wir/uns (or Sie/uns). It can mean 'let ourselves do X' (allow ourselves) or, more commonly in passive-causing constructions, 'have/get something done' (we arrange for someone to do something for us). Context determines whether it's permissive ('we allow ourselves to...') or causative ('we get/have...'). With verbs like 'scheiden' (sich scheiden lassen) it forms a fixed reflexive phrase meaning 'to get divorced'.
target_language_example: Wir lassen uns das Auto reparieren.
native_language_example: We are getting the car repaired.

meaning: 'let ourselves go' (relax/behave freely) or 'allow ourselves to leave' depending on context
additional_notes: This is a reflexive construction built from lassen + uns + gehen. Context and word order determine meaning. Common uses: 1) 'uns gehen lassen' or 'lassen uns gehen' in subordinate clauses can mean to relax/lose inhibitions (e.g. at a party). 2) Rarely, in permissive sense it can mean 'allow ourselves to leave' when combined with other verbs or modals. Pay attention that standard finite forms usually adjust: e.g. 'wir lassen uns gehen' (present), 'ließen uns gehen' (past).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende lassen uns die Freunde gehen und wir vergessen den Alltag.
native_language_example: On the weekend our friends let us go and we forget everyday life.
