(The only thing that ... does is ...), "Was ... macht, ist ..." (What ... does is ...). Can introduce a relative clause (was ... macht) meaning "what someone does" or function in spoken phrases like "der Typ, der die Pässe macht, ist..." where "macht" = 'makes/does/produces'. Context shows "macht" can mean 'do/make' and "ist" links to the focused information. Word order: the verb of the relative clause appears before "ist" in these cleft sentences.
target_language_example: Was sie macht, ist beeindruckend.
native_language_example: What she does is impressive.

meaning: adds emphasis, reassurance, mild urging, or softens commands depending on context (roughly: 'do/does/it — come on/after all/it's OK').
additional_notes: A versatile phrase: with 'nichts' it reassures ('that's OK' / 'never mind'); with imperatives it softens or urges action ('do something,' 'come on, do it,' 'don't do that'). 'Doch' can add contradiction or emphasis. Tone and context determine whether it's comforting, encouraging, or scolding.
target_language_example: Macht doch bitte die Fenster zu.
native_language_example: Please just close the windows.

meaning: 'makes him' or 'does something to him' (literal: makes him); used both literally and in idiomatic expressions
additional_notes: Literally from machen (to make/do) + ihn (him). Common in combinations where an action affects 'him' (e.g., macht ihn fertig = 'ruins/finishes him' or 'exhausts him'). Context determines meaning: can be neutral (makes him something), causative (causes him to feel/ become), or idiomatic (macht ihn fertig = defeats/overwhelms; macht ihn alle = colloquial 'gets rid of him' or 'kills him' depending on context; macht ihn dort fest = 'secure him there'). Often appears in spoken German.
target_language_example: Der Stress macht ihn müde.
native_language_example: The stress makes him tired.

meaning: 'what do you do with...' or 'what are you doing with...'
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone (ihr = you plural/informal) does with a person or object. Often appears as a question: 'Was macht ihr mit ...?' Can refer to current action (what are you doing with it/them now) or general handling/disposal (what do you do with them). 'Ihr' is plural informal (you all).
target_language_example: Was macht ihr mit dem Hund?
native_language_example: What are you doing with the dog?

meaning: 'always does' or 'keeps doing' (habitual action).
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'macht' (does/makes) with 'immer' (always). Used to describe repeated or habitual actions—can be neutral, positive, or negative depending on context and tone. In English often translated as "always [does]" or "keeps [doing]". The subject and object determine the full sentence meaning (e.g. "macht immer Witze" = "always makes jokes").
target_language_example: Er macht immer seine Hausaufgaben pünktlich.
native_language_example: He always does his homework on time.

meaning: 'doesn't (do) any' / 'doesn't (do)' depending on context
additional_notes: Literally 'makes no'. In German 'macht keine' can start different expressions: 1) with a noun it means 'doesn't make/do any' or 'doesn't (do) [that kind of thing]' (Die Natur macht keine Sprünge = Nature doesn't make leaps → no sudden changes). 2) As an imperative with 'Macht keine ...!' it is a warning: 'Don't ...!' (Macht keine Gefangenen! = 'Take no prisoners!' or figuratively 'be ruthless'; Macht keine Scheiße! = 'Don't screw up!'). Context determines whether it's descriptive (third-person) or an instruction/warning (addressing people).
target_language_example: Macht keine Fehler bei der Prüfung.
native_language_example: Don't make mistakes on the exam.

meaning: 'never mind', 'it's okay', or 'doesn't matter'.
additional_notes: Common short phrase. Used to say something is not a problem, to dismiss a mistake, or to indicate that something has no effect. Can be a full sentence on its own (Macht nichts!). In sentence 1 it literally means 'does nothing' (compositional); in conversational use it means 'no problem/never mind'. Tone can be casual or polite depending on context.
target_language_example: Oh, du hast die Tasse zerbrochen? Macht nichts, ich kaufe eine neue.
native_language_example: Oh, you broke the cup? Never mind, I'll buy a new one.

meaning: 'does something' or colloquially 'do something about it / take action' depending on context.
additional_notes: Literal words: macht (does), was (what/something). Used in different ways: 1) indicates someone is doing something (Jeder macht was = Everyone does something/does what they want). 2) informal urging to interact or take action regarding someone or something (Macht was mit ihm! = Do something with him / get involved with him). 3) can be used in questions about someone's actions (Und dein Vater macht was? = And your father, what does he do?). Tone is informal; context and word order affect nuance. Verb form may change (Mach was! = Do something!).
target_language_example: Jeder macht was er will.
native_language_example: Everyone does what they want.

meaning: opened/closed the
additional_notes: This is the past tense (simple past) of machen + the definite article die. In these examples it appears in common constructions: "die Tür aufmachen/zumachen" (to open/close the door), "die Augen zumachen" (to close one's eyes), and "jemanden auf etwas aufmerksam machen" (to draw someone's attention to something). Translate the verb according to the separable verb or idiom: e.g. machte die Tür auf = opened the door; machte die Zuhörer auf ... aufmerksam = drew the listeners' attention to .... Word order in German often places the separable prefix (auf, zu, aufmerksam) at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Sie machte die Fenster auf, weil es warm war.
native_language_example: She opened the windows because it was warm.

meaning: made her
additional_notes: This is the past tense (simple past) form of machen + the feminine/plural possessive ihre. Meaning depends on the object that follows: with tasks or chores (e.g. Hausaufgaben) it translates as "did her..."; with emotions or states (e.g. Mutter froh) it translates as "made her...". "Ihre" could refer to "her" (feminine singular possessor) or "their/your formal" depending on context, but in these examples it refers to something belonging to a female (her). Word order: verb (machte) before possession (ihre).
target_language_example: Sie machte ihre Hausaufgaben nach dem Abendessen.
native_language_example: She did her homework after dinner.

meaning: 'joined in' or 'participated' (simple past/Präteritum of 'mitmachen'); in some contexts can mean 'continued' when combined with other elements (e.g., 'mit etwas weitermachen')
additional_notes: 'Machte mit' is the Präteritum (simple past) form used for narration or writing; in spoken German Perfekt ('hat mitgemacht') is more common. Context decides exact sense: usually 'mitmachen' = to join in/participate. Rarely, depending on sentence structure, it can appear in constructions implying continuation (e.g., 'Ich machte mit meinem Lesen weiter.') or other actions when combined with additional verbs. Pay attention to separable verb behavior: 'mitmachen' separates in some tenses (er macht mit) but in Präteritum the components appear together as 'machte mit'.
target_language_example: Ich machte mit meinem Lesen weiter, obwohl es spät war.
native_language_example: I continued with my reading, although it was late.

meaning: 'doesn't like' or 'doesn't want to' (expresses dislike or refusal)
additional_notes: Derived from the verb mögen (to like/want) in the 3rd person singular or polite form; with 'nicht' it negates the liking or willingness. Can indicate dislike (She doesn't like public speaking) or refusal/unwillingness (I don't want to be watched). Context and subject determine whether it's more 'doesn't like' or 'doesn't want to'. When used with infinitives (e.g. 'mag nicht beobachtet werden') it expresses not wanting to be done to or not wanting something to happen. In sentence 4, 'mag' is used in the sense 'likes' (Tom not only likes Maria, but also Elke).
target_language_example: Er mag nicht alleine reisen.
native_language_example: He doesn't like to travel alone.

meaning: 'like that' or 'like it' (literal parts: 'mag' = like, 'das' = that/it).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the verb mögen (to like). 'Mag das' on its own is not a fixed phrase — it combines the conjugated verb (ich mag, er mag, etc.) with the demonstrative pronoun 'das' referring to a thing or idea. Can be used with or without 'nicht' to negate (Ich mag das nicht = I don't like that). Often followed by a noun or a verb nominalized (das Skifahren = skiing).
target_language_example: Ich mag das langsame Tempo dieses Liedes.
native_language_example: I like the slow tempo of this song.

meaning: I/Do (you) like your… ("mag" = like; "deine" = your, feminine/plural/ informal).
additional_notes: Used with the verb mögen (to like). "Ich mag deine..." = "I like your...". "Mag deine...?" is a question form (Do [you] like your...?) when verb-first addressing or context-dependent. "Deine" is the informal second-person possessive (du) and matches feminine or plural nouns (deine Mutter, deine Bücher, deine Katzen). For masculine/neuter singular nouns use "deinen" or "dein" depending on case (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich mag deine Küche sehr.
native_language_example: I like your kitchen a lot.

meaning: 'I like your' (masculine or masculine/neuter singular accusative noun follows).
additional_notes: Combines the verb mögen (ich mag = I like) with the possessive deinen (your) in the masculine/neuter singular accusative form. Use deinen when the noun that follows is masculine (den Bart, den Hund, den Hut, den Laster, den Spiegel) or for some neuter nouns that take accusative with diesen patterns; for feminine nouns use deine (ich mag deine Tasche) and for plural use deine (ich mag deine Freunde). The verb may be followed by a noun or a noun phrase (Ich mag deinen Unterricht = I like your class/teaching).
target_language_example: Ich mag deinen Stil.
native_language_example: I like your style.

meaning: 'like this' or 'like this one' (first person singular + demonstrative).
additional_notes: Combines the verb mögen in the present (ich mag = I like) with the demonstrative diesen (masculine accusative or generic for 'this one' when referring to a masculine noun). Use würden/gern/gerne to add emphasis (e.g. ich mag diesen Sänger sehr gerne). The form of 'this' changes with gender/case: diesen (masculine accusative), diese (feminine), dieses (neuter), diese (plural).
target_language_example: Ich mag diesen Film.
native_language_example: I like this film.

meaning: 'likes classical' (short for 'mag klassische Musik')
additional_notes: This is a clipped phrase: 'mag' is the verb 'to like' (from mögen) in 3rd person singular; 'klassische' is the adjective 'classical' used before a noun (here implied: 'Musik'). You will often see it in informal contexts or notes where the noun is omitted because it's clear from context (e.g., talking about music). For full sentences use 'Er/Sie mag klassische Musik.'
target_language_example: Sie mag klassische Musik, besonders Klavierstücke.
native_language_example: She likes classical music, especially piano pieces.

meaning: A casual way to start a question: 'tell me, are you...?' or 'say, are you...?'
additional_notes: "Sag mal" or "Hör mal" are common spoken fillers used to get attention or soften/introduce a direct question. In the examples the speaker then asks a blunt or surprised question (bist du ...?). Use in informal, conversational contexts. You can drop the verb (e.g. "Sag mal, ...?") or use other attention-getters like "Hey" or "Hör mal."
target_language_example: Sag mal, bist du müde?
native_language_example: Say, are you tired?

meaning: A combination of the particles 'mal' and 'das' used in colloquial speech to draw attention, soften commands, or point something out — roughly 'just/hey, that...' or 'look, that...'.
additional_notes: Here 'mal' is a softening/attention-getting particle (colloquial) attached to imperatives or interjections (sagen mal, hör mal, schau mal, probier mal, überleg mal). 'Das' then refers to something the speaker points out or comments on. Used to make requests less direct or to draw attention to a fact. Common in spoken German. Tone and exact translation depend on context (e.g. 'Hör mal, das ist Richie.' = 'Listen — that's Richie.').
target_language_example: Hör mal, das solltest du dir ansehen.
native_language_example: Hey, look — you should take a look at that.

meaning: The particle 'mal' used in casual or softening expressions; here shown with 'es' (it) to soften commands, draw attention, or make statements less direct.
additional_notes: mal is a common conversational particle with many uses: 1) Soften commands or requests (e.g., 'Fühl mal' = 'feel it' / 'have a feel' in a friendlier tone). 2) Draw attention ('Sieh mal' / 'Seht mal' = 'look!'). 3) Make suggestions or hypothetical statements less direct ('Sagen wir mal' = 'let's say' / 'suppose'). 4) Fillers in speech to sound more natural. It does not translate directly in all cases; translate according to context (imperative softener, 'look', 'let's say', etc.).
target_language_example: Sieh mal, es regnet!
native_language_example: Look, it's raining!

meaning: A casual way to start a question or get someone's attention before asking 'is...?', similar to 'hey, is...?' or 'say, is...?'
additional_notes: This pair shows two common conversational starters: 'Sag mal', 'Sagen Sie mal', 'Sagt mal', 'Schauen Sie mal' followed by a question starting with 'ist...'. 'mal' softens or makes the request more casual/polite; the verb form ('Sag/Sagen/Sagt/Schauen') changes with person and formality. Use 'Sie' for formal, 'du' forms (sag) for informal singular, and 'ihr' form (sagt) for informal plural. It's not translated word-for-word in English—translate the whole phrase as a polite/casual 'hey/please look, is...?' or 'tell me, is...?'.
target_language_example: Sag mal, ist das richtig so?
native_language_example: Hey, is that correct?

meaning: A spoken softening particle 'mal' combined with the formal accusative possessive 'Ihren' (Sie → Ihren), used to make polite or less direct requests involving 'your' (formal).
additional_notes: 'mal' here functions like 'just/for a moment/please' to soften or casualize a request. 'Ihren' is formal (Sie) accusative; choose 'Ihre/Ihren/ihrem' by gender/case as required. Common in everyday spoken and polite contexts: e.g. asking to see or hand over something. For informal 'du' use 'mal deinen' or 'mal deine'.
target_language_example: Darf ich mal Ihren Führerschein sehen?
native_language_example: May I see your driver's license for a moment?

meaning: a softening particle combined with the separable verb prefix 'ab' (used with different verbs); here it means 'just/for a moment' or 'go ahead and.../take off' depending on the verb.
additional_notes: In German 'mal' is a colloquial particle that softens commands or requests (like 'just' or 'for a moment'). 'Ab' is a separable prefix that changes the meaning of verbs (e.g., 'abwarten' = wait, 'abnehmen' = take off / remove). Together in examples you see different uses: 'frag mich mal ab' (colloquial imperative: 'try to question me' or 'quiz me'), 'warte mal ab' (wait and see), 'nimm mir das mal ab' (take that off me / remove it for me), 'nehmen Sie ... ab' (polite command: take off the hat). The exact translation depends on the main verb and context.
target_language_example: Warte mal ab, dann siehst du, was passiert.
native_language_example: Just wait, then you'll see what happens.

meaning: a casual way to address everyone at once; 'all of you' or 'everyone' (often with the softening particle mal).
additional_notes: Combines the particle 'mal' (softens commands or makes requests less direct) with 'alle' (everyone). Common in spoken German to get attention or make a suggestion: e.g. 'Hört mal alle her' = 'Everyone listen (for a moment)'. Use in informal or neutral contexts; not highly formal. The particle 'mal' doesn't translate directly but makes the phrase sound friendlier or less abrupt.
target_language_example: Kommt mal alle kurz her, bitte.
native_language_example: Everyone come here for a moment, please.

meaning: 'have/look/check briefly on the (masculine/neuter dative) — used with verbs like bleiben, sein, schauen, sehen to mean 'for a moment' or 'on/at the (dative)'.
additional_notes: This is a combination of the particle 'mal' (a casual soften/briefly/once) + the prepositional phrase 'auf dem' (on/at + masculine/neuter dative). It appears before a noun in dative (e.g., Boden, College, Fahrplan, Rücksitz). In commands or requests (Bleib mal..., Schau mal..., Sieh mal...) 'mal' makes the tone more casual/friendly. With verbs like 'auf dem Boden der Tatsachen bleiben' it means 'stay grounded'; with 'auf dem Fahrplan nachsehen' it means 'check the schedule'.
target_language_example: Guck mal auf dem Tisch nach, ob mein Buch da liegt.
native_language_example: Have a quick look on the table to see if my book is there.

meaning: to stop (doing something) — used to tell or ask someone to quit a repeated or annoying action.
additional_notes: mal softens the command, making it less harsh (like 'please' or 'could you just'). Often used in imperatives: 'Kannst du mal aufhören...?' = 'Could you stop...?' Used for annoying habits, repeated actions or ongoing behaviors.
target_language_example: Kannst du mal aufhören, so laut zu atmen?
native_language_example: Could you stop breathing so loudly?

meaning: a softened/colloquial way to ask someone to give, show, or do something (like 'could you/pass me/let me see that').
additional_notes: mal adds politeness/softness and makes the request less direct; 'das' refers to a specific item just mentioned or pointed at. Common in spoken German. Word order can vary (e.g. 'Reich mir mal das Brot', 'Kann ich mal das Buch haben?'). Not a fixed idiom—it's the particle mal + the demonstrative das.
target_language_example: Gib mir mal das Buch, bitte.
native_language_example: Give me that book, please.

meaning: a casual way to say 'your' (with 'mal' adding a softening or casual tone like 'just' or 'for a moment').
additional_notes: Used in informal spoken German. 'Mal' here doesn't change the possessive meaning but makes requests or statements sound friendlier/more casual ('Can I just borrow your...?', 'Give me your...'). In contexts like 'das war ja mal dein Laden' it emphasizes or comments on something (e.g. 'that used to be your shop' with a colloquial tone). Use 'dein' for singular informal 'your' (du).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mal dein Buch geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me your book for a moment?

meaning: a casual/softening way to ask someone to do or look at something (imperative softener + direct object 'the ...').
additional_notes: mal is a colloquial modal particle that makes commands or requests sound less harsh or more casual (like 'just' or 'go ahead and' in English). Here it appears before the direct object (die + noun) in spoken German: e.g. 'Gib mir mal die Banane' = 'Give me the banana, please/just give me the banana'. Common in informal speech. Use with familiars (du/ihr) or friends; not very formal.
target_language_example: Schau dir mal die Fotos an.
native_language_example: Just take a look at the photos.

meaning: a casual way to say 'once' or 'give (something) a try' with a masculine accusative noun (e.g. 'mal einen Blick' = 'take a quick look').
additional_notes: Informal conversational filler: 'mal' softens or makes the request/suggestion less direct; 'einen' is the masculine accusative article and depends on the noun that follows. Common in phrases like 'mal einen Blick werfen' (take a quick look), 'mal einen Versuch starten' (give it a try), or 'mal einen Kaffee trinken' (have a coffee). Use with appropriate verb and noun; not a complete phrase by itself.
target_language_example: Komm, wir trinken mal einen Kaffee.
native_language_example: Come on, let's have a coffee (for once / let's grab a coffee).

meaning: used to ask for or suggest checking/looking more closely; 'let's take a closer look' or 'exactly/precisely (now)'.
additional_notes: Often appears in questions or commands to prompt someone to look more closely, think carefully, or check details. 'mal' here softens the request (makes it more casual). Can be placed before verbs (e.g. 'schau mal genau') or used in questions like 'Was ist das mal genau?' depending on context.
target_language_example: Kannst du dir das mal genau ansehen?
native_language_example: Can you take a closer look at this?

meaning: 'met' or 'encountered' once / 'met by chance' (literal: 'met once')
additional_notes: A short phrase using the adverb 'mal' (colloquial softener meaning 'once' or 'just') with the past participle 'getroffen' of 'treffen' (to meet). Common in spoken German to say you met someone (or were hit/affected) casually: e.g. 'Ich habe ihn mal getroffen' = 'I met him once' or 'Ich wurde mal getroffen' (less common) could mean 'I was hit once'. Context determines if it means meeting a person or being struck/affected. 'mal' makes the statement less formal and more casual.
target_language_example: Ich habe sie letzte Woche mal getroffen.
native_language_example: I met her once / I ran into her last week.

meaning: 'once' / 'sometime' when suggesting or briefly doing something; here 'mal' softens the suggestion or action and 'ins' is a contraction of 'in das' (into the).
additional_notes: mal is a colloquial particle used to make requests, suggestions or descriptions less direct (like 'sometime', 'give it a try', or 'just'). 'ins' = in + das and indicates movement into something (into the café, into the room, into the fire). Together 'mal ins' appears when you say you'll go/peek/put something into (a place) sometime or once: e.g. 'mal ins Café' = 'sometime to the café' or 'drop into the café'. In sentence 1 it describes a one-time action into (into the fire).
target_language_example: Komm mal ins Büro, ich muss dich kurz sprechen.
native_language_example: Come into the office for a moment, I need to speak to you briefly.

meaning: come (here) / come by / come around (used to request or indicate someone should come sometime).
additional_notes: Mal softens requests or statements, making them more casual/polite ('could you come?','we should come sometime'). Used in imperatives/questions: 'Können Sie mal kommen?' = 'Could you come (here) for a moment)?' In statements it can mean 'at some point' or 'eventually' ('jemand mal kommen würde' = 'someone would come at some point'). Not strongly formal.
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte mal kommen?
native_language_example: Could you come here for a moment, please?

meaning: happens once/in the past (colloquial) — 'it happened' / 'if it happens (once)'
additional_notes: Combines mal (here meaning 'once' / 'ever' / 'at some point') with passiert ('happened'/'occurs'). Used in everyday speech to say that something happened (often unexpectedly) or to ask if it ever happened to someone. Context decides tense: can refer to a single past event (»Es ist nun mal passiert« = 'It just happened') or a hypothetical/occasional occurrence (»wenn es mal passiert« = 'if it ever happens').
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — wenn es mal passiert, helfe ich dir sofort.
native_language_example: Don't worry — if it ever happens, I'll help you right away.

meaning: let's see
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase. Can mean 'let's see' when considering something or 'have a look' when asking to see an object. 'mal' softens the request or makes the phrase more casual. Used frequently in questions and informal statements.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das Foto mal sehen lassen?
native_language_example: Can you let me have a look at that photo?

meaning: once/for a moment; (used to soften commands or statements) just/for now
additional_notes: Often follows verbs or phrases like 'mach mal so' or 'lass mal so' to make requests or suggestions less direct and more casual. 'mal' alone is very common and adds a colloquial, softening, or momentary sense; combined with 'so' it can mean 'like this' or 'this way for now'. Usage is informal and frequent in spoken German.
target_language_example: Mach das mal so, dann sehen wir weiter.
native_language_example: Do it like this for now, then we'll see.

meaning: a casual/softening phrase used before a direction or suggestion meaning 'just to' or 'maybe to' (often part of phrases like 'mal zur Toilette' = 'just to the toilet').
additional_notes: Informal, spoken German. 'mal' here softens the statement or makes it less direct; 'zur' is the contraction of 'zu der' (to the). Together they commonly appear before nouns with feminine gender or in fixed phrases: e.g. 'mal zur Toilette', 'mal zur Sicherheit', or 'mal zur Kontrolle'. Used to suggest a quick or casual action ('I'll just go to...').
target_language_example: Ich gehe mal zur Toilette.
native_language_example: I'll just go to the bathroom.

meaning: the impersonal pronoun 'man' (one/people/they) + formal dative 'Ihnen' (you, formal); used to say that people in general do/say something to you (formal).
additional_notes: 'man' is an impersonal subject used for general statements; verbs agree with 'man' (third person singular). 'Ihnen' is the formal dative pronoun. Common in reported speech and descriptions: »man sagt Ihnen…«, »man hat Ihnen…«, »das sieht man Ihnen an«. Word order follows normal German syntax: 'man' (nominative) often appears before the verb or in subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Das sieht man Ihnen an.
native_language_example: You can tell (by looking at) that about you.

meaning: a general phrase meaning 'one/you/people (can) do everything' or 'all the things people...'; used to talk about things people do or can do in general.
additional_notes: Man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one', 'you' (general), or 'people'. 'Man alles' often appears in sentences like 'Hier kann man alles machen' (You can do anything here) or in exclamations about surprising things people do: 'Komisch, was man alles tut...' ('Funny what people do...'). The exact nuance depends on context (ability, surprise, general statement).
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt kann man alles erleben, was man sich wünscht.
native_language_example: In this city you can experience everything you wish for.

meaning: 'one/people of it' or 'about it' depending on context; often part of the phrase 'was hat man davon' (what do you get/benefit from it) or 'davon essen' (eat of it) and 'davon träumen' (dream about it).
additional_notes: Man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one/people/you' (general subject). Davon means 'of it' or 'about it' and refers back to something mentioned. Together they are used in different idiomatic ways: literally (e.g. 'man davon essen' = 'one could eat from it'), as 'dream about it' (träumen davon), as 'what do you get from it' (Was hat man davon?), or 'people talked about it' (man sprach davon). Context determines whether 'davon' is translated as 'of it', 'about it', or omitted in natural English.
target_language_example: Was hat man davon, jeden Tag Überstunden zu machen?
native_language_example: What do you get out of working overtime every day?

meaning: how one (you) does this; 'how to' for the thing mentioned.
additional_notes: Combines the impersonal pronoun man ('one/you/people') with dieses ('this' — masculine/neuter accusative). Used when asking or explaining how to do or use a specific thing mentioned in context. In English often translated as 'how you/one ... this' or more naturally 'how to ... this/that'. In spoken German the question often drops man and uses 'wie macht man das?' or 'wie ... man das?'.
target_language_example: Weißt du, wie man dieses Gerät einschaltet?
native_language_example: Do you know how to turn this device on?

meaning: 'man' (impersonal 'one/you/people') + 'durch' (through) — a common structure where the impersonal pronoun 'man' is used with the preposition 'durch' to indicate that people in general go through, experience, or accomplish something by/through something.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a frequent compositional pattern: man + verb + durch + (object). Used to describe general actions, means, causes, or physical passage. Word order follows normal German syntax (e.g. Man geht durch die Tür; Manche Hindernisse kann man durch Gewalt nicht beseitigen).
target_language_example: Man durchquert den Tunnel — aber man durch den Tunnel gehen kann man auch zu Fuß.
native_language_example: One traverses the tunnel — but one can also go through the tunnel on foot.

meaning: 'one' or 'people' (impersonal subject) + 'you' (plural, accusative/dative) — used when speaking about actions done to or involving 'you' by unspecified people.
additional_notes: man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one/people/they' (no specific subject). euch is the informal plural 'you' (accusative or dative). Together they appear in contexts like 'what have people told you?', 'have people followed you?', or 'what have they done to you?'. Use when the doer is unknown or general. Word order: man usually comes before euch in these examples.
target_language_example: Warum hat man euch das verschwiegen?
native_language_example: Why did people hide that from you?

meaning: The impersonal pronoun 'man' (one/people/you in general) combined with the dative pronoun 'ihnen' (to/for them). Used when an indefinite subject acts toward 'them'.
additional_notes: 'Man' is an impersonal subject meaning 'one', 'people', or 'you' (general/indefinite people). 'Ihnen' is dative plural or formal singular meaning 'to them' or 'to you' (formal). Together 'man ihnen' appears in sentences where an indefinite subject performs an action directed at 'them' (dative). Translate depending on context: 'one/people can trust them', 'people tell them', 'one helps them', 'what do people accuse them of?'.
target_language_example: Bis zu einem gewissen Grad kann man ihnen vertrauen.
native_language_example: To a certain extent one/people can trust them.

meaning: the impersonal pronoun man ('one/people/they') used with the dative pronoun ihr ('to her'/'her'), indicating that something was done to or about a female person by unspecified people or in general.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a common grammatical combination: man + dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). Use to report actions, statements, or general opinions affecting a female person when the agent is unspecified. Context determines translation (e.g., 'someone/people told her', 'one gives her', 'you have to admit to her').
target_language_example: Als sie nach ihm fragte, sagte man ihr, er sei weggelaufen.
native_language_example: When she asked about him, someone told her that he had run away.

meaning: 'to do' or 'to make' when used with the impersonal pronoun 'man' (one/you/people).
additional_notes: Combines the impersonal pronoun 'man' (meaning 'one', 'you' in general, or 'people') with the verb 'machen' (to do/make). Used to talk about actions in general, e.g. things one can do or mistakes one can make, or rhetorically (Was soll man machen? = What can you do?). Translate according to context as 'one/you/people do' or idiomatically 'you can/you should/what can you do'.
target_language_example: Was soll man machen, wenn das Geld fehlt?
native_language_example: What can you do when the money is missing?

meaning: there's nothing one can do / nothing can be done
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used to express resignation or that a situation is unavoidable. Often appears in exclamations: "Da kann man nichts machen!" Can be used neutrally or with mild frustration. "man" is the impersonal pronoun (one/people/you).
target_language_example: Da kann man nichts machen, wir müssen warten.
native_language_example: There's nothing you can do, we have to wait.

meaning: 'one often' / 'people often' / 'you often' (general, impersonal 'one/people')
additional_notes: Man is the impersonal pronoun used to talk about people in general (like English 'one' or informal 'you/people'). Placed before or after adverbs: 'man oft' (common in examples) or 'oft trifft man' — word order can change depending on emphasis. Use to make general statements or observations.
target_language_example: In Deutschland trinkt man oft Kaffee am Nachmittag.
native_language_example: In Germany one often drinks coffee in the afternoon.

meaning: used to mean 'one could say' or 'you could say' — a tentative comment or generalization.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German to soften or hedge a statement. Often appears as 'Das kann man sagen' ('You could say that') or 'könnte man sagen' ('one could say'). 'Man' is the impersonal 'one/you/people'. Use when giving an opinion without asserting it strongly.
target_language_example: Das ist, könnte man sagen, eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: That is, one could say, a good idea.

meaning: A construction using the impersonal pronoun 'man' (one/people/you) with the possessive 'seine' meaning 'one's' or 'your' (general). It expresses that something belongs to or is associated with people in general rather than a specific person.
additional_notes: 'Man' is impersonal and does not refer to a specific person. 'Seine' agrees in gender/number with the (usually masculine or neuter) noun it modifies. In many contexts English equivalents are 'one's' or the generic 'your'. Depending on context and register, speakers may instead use other possessives (e.g., 'seine/ihre') or rephrase to avoid ambiguity. Note: gender/number agreement of the possessive can change (e.g., 'man seine Freunde' → 'seine' for plural as written here is common in colloquial usage; prescriptively one may see 'man seine Freunde' colloquially, while standard written German often rephrases to avoid this ambiguity).
target_language_example: Angesichts der Kürze des Lebens sollte man seine Zeit nicht vergeuden.
native_language_example: In view of life's brevity, one should not waste one's time.

meaning: a combination of the impersonal pronoun 'man' (one/you/people) with 'so' (like/that way) used to talk generally about people or a general situation ('one/you/people ... like that').
additional_notes: Use 'man' to make general statements (like 'one' or informal 'you/people') and 'so' to mean 'like that' or 'in that way/degree'. Together they appear in casual spoken German: Das könnte man so sagen = You could put it that way. Context often determines whether 'man' translates as 'one', 'you', or 'people'. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wenn man so gestresst ist, sollte man eine Pause machen.
native_language_example: When you're that stressed, you should take a break.

meaning: one does / people do (general, impersonal 'you' or 'we').
additional_notes: Man is the impersonal pronoun used to talk about people in general (like 'one', 'you', or 'people' in English). 'Tut' is the third-person singular of 'tun' (to do). Together 'man tut' expresses general actions or truths: 'one does', 'you do', or 'people do'. Use for general statements, proverbs, instructions or observations.
target_language_example: Man tut sein Bestes und hofft auf das Beste.
native_language_example: One does one's best and hopes for the best.

meaning: 'man' = impersonal 'one/people/they/you'; 'uns' = 'us'. Together: 'one/they/people/you us' → used to talk about what people (in general) do/think to/with us (English: 'they/people/one (will) ... us' or more naturally 'we will be ...' / 'they will ... us').
additional_notes: ‘man’ is the German impersonal pronoun used to make general statements (like English 'one' or passive/general 'they/people'/'you'). When combined with a personal pronoun (uns = 'us') it says what people in general do to 'us' (e.g. 'they will catch us', 'people will look for us'). Often translated more naturally into English as 'they/people/will...' or using passive constructions ('we will be ...'). Context decides whether 'they', 'people', 'one' or a passive translation fits best.
target_language_example: Was, wenn man uns erwischt?
native_language_example: What if they catch us?

meaning: 'one/people/you' + 'a lot/much' — used to say that people in general do something a lot or experience something much
additional_notes: Man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one', 'people' or conversational 'you'. Combined with an adverb or quantity like viel it expresses a general statement about many people or people in general (e.g. 'people do X a lot'). Use with verbs: 'man macht', 'man geht', 'man lernt'. Word order: 'man viel' will typically appear as part of a larger phrase (e.g. 'man viel lernt' or 'man viel zu Fuß geht'); ensure correct placement of verbs and particles in full sentences.
target_language_example: Da wird man viel schneller mit dem fertig.
native_language_example: There you get finished with that much faster.

meaning: 'one/you/people (in general) [have/do] a lot (of)'.
additional_notes: man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one', 'you' or 'people' (general statements). 'viel' means 'much' or 'a lot (of)'. Together they express that people in general experience/need/have a large amount of something. English translations vary (one/you/people often) depending on context.
target_language_example: In den Bergen hat man viel Schnee.
native_language_example: In the mountains one has a lot of snow.

meaning: you never know; one never knows.
additional_notes: A common German phrase used to express uncertainty about the future or outcomes. 'Man' is the impersonal pronoun equivalent to English 'one' or informal 'you'. Can stand alone as a short comment ("Man weiß nie.").
target_language_example: Man weiß nie, ob das Meeting ausfällt.
native_language_example: You never know if the meeting will be canceled.

meaning: 'if one wants to' / 'if you want to' (general, impersonal conditional meaning)
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun man (one/you in general) + wollen (to want) in present tense to form a conditional: 'if one wants to' or 'if you want to.' Common in advice, general statements, and offers. Can be followed by a clause (Wenn man will, ...). Tone: neutral/colloquial; not personal 'I' or 'you (du)'.
target_language_example: Wenn man will, kann man jeden Tag spazieren gehen.
native_language_example: If you want to, you can go for a walk every day.

meaning: 'one/you/people become(s)' — impersonal passive-like expression meaning people in general grow/come to be ...
additional_notes: Man is an impersonal pronoun meaning 'one', 'you' or 'people' (general statements). 'Wird' is the present tense of werden ('to become'). Together they describe what generally happens to people (e.g., age, get tired, become something). Use for general observations; verb after 'man' stays in third person singular.
target_language_example: Man wird mit der Zeit ruhiger.
native_language_example: One becomes calmer over time.

meaning: 'one/you/people' to the (masculine/neuter) — impersonal way to say how to get to a place
additional_notes: man is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one', 'you' or 'people in general'. zum is the contraction of zu + dem (to the) used before masculine or neuter nouns. Together, man zum is used in questions and statements about how to reach or how long it takes to get to a specific place (e.g., Zum Flughafen, zum Bahnhof). It's common in directions and travel phrases. Replace zum with zur (zu + der) for feminine destinations.
target_language_example: Wie kommt man zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How does one/you get to the train station?

meaning: 'one/about' or 'people/about' — the impersonal pronoun man + preposition über, used to say what people in general say/know/ask about something.
additional_notes: Combines the impersonal subject man (meaning 'one', 'people', or 'you' in general) with the preposition über ('about' or 'across' depending on context). Use man über to talk about what people think, know, or ask about a topic (sentences 1–4,6). In direction/place contexts (sentence 5), über means 'across' ('how does one get across the river?'). The phrase is grammatical, not idiomatic; translate man as 'one', 'people', or 'you' depending on natural English.
target_language_example: Was sagt man über dieses Buch?
native_language_example: What do people say about this book?

meaning: sometimes (it/one/he/she/you) can...
additional_notes: Combines 'manchmal' (sometimes) with the modal verb 'kann' (can). The subject after 'kann' can be explicit (er, ich, man) or implied; meaning depends on context (ability, possibility, or polite suggestion). Common in spoken and written German to introduce that something is sometimes possible or happens.
target_language_example: Manchmal kann ein kleines Danke schon viel bewirken.
native_language_example: Sometimes a small 'thank you' can already make a big difference.

meaning: 'sometimes are' — the adverb 'manchmal' (sometimes) + the verb 'sind' (are)
additional_notes: Used to state that something is true occasionally. 'Manchmal' can appear before the verb, at the beginning of a sentence, or elsewhere; here it's followed by the verb 'sind' (3rd person plural of 'sein'). The rest of the sentence supplies the subject or complement. Useful for describing situations, states, or general truths that happen occasionally.
target_language_example: Manchmal sind Entscheidungen schwer, aber nötig.
native_language_example: Sometimes decisions are difficult but necessary.

meaning: more than enough; plenty
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is a large surplus of something. Can describe quantity, time, money, energy, etc. Often used in everyday speech for reassurance or emphasis (e.g., "Das ist mehr als genug" = "That's more than enough").
target_language_example: Wir haben für das Picknick mehr als genug Essen.
native_language_example: We have more than enough food for the picnic.

meaning: no longer (looking/stop paying attention to); 'try harder' when part of 'sich mehr anstrengen'.
additional_notes: The words 'mehr' + 'an' appear in different constructions here. 1) In sentences like "hält hier niemand mehr an" (verb + mehr anhalten), "mehr" means "anymore/no longer": 'nobody stops here anymore.' 2) In the imperative "Strengt euch mehr an", the phrase is part of the separable verb "sich anstrengen" (to make an effort) — here it means 'try harder.' 3) In "sieht einen kein Mensch mehr an" the structure is a verbal phrase with "ansehen" (to look at): "keinen mehr ansehen" = 'no one looks at you anymore.' Pay attention to the verb: the meaning changes with different verbs (anhalten, sich anstrengen, ansehen).
target_language_example: Du musst dich bei der Arbeit mehr anstrengen.
native_language_example: You have to try harder at work.

meaning: more from / get more out of (used to say getting greater benefit, value, or results from something)
additional_notes: Often appears as part of phrases like "mehr aus etwas machen" (to make more of something) or "mehr aus etwas herausholen" (to get more out of something). Used to compare a higher amount, quality, or benefit than before. Context determines exact translation: can mean 'more of' (quantity) or 'more out of' (benefit/result).
target_language_example: Wir sollten mehr aus der Gelegenheit machen.
native_language_example: We should make more of the opportunity.

meaning: more about/with it; (to be) more concerned with it
additional_notes: Used after a verb or phrase to indicate increased attention, effort, interest, or emphasis on 'it' (daran = da + an = about/at/on that). Common in constructions like 'arbeiten mehr daran' (work more on it), 'denken mehr daran' (think more about it). 'Mehr' modifies the degree. 'Daran' refers back to something previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Wir müssen mehr daran arbeiten.
native_language_example: We need to work more on it.

meaning: no longer the same as it used to be; not what it once was
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a place, institution, medium, ability, etc.) has changed, declined, or lost its former qualities. Commonly appears in structures like "X ist nicht mehr das, was es (einmal/mal) war." Tone ranges from neutral observation to nostalgic or critical. Can be used with temporal markers (früher, vor zehn Jahren) or qualifiers (einmal, mal).
target_language_example: Das Deutschland von heute ist nicht mehr das, was es vor zehn Jahren war.
native_language_example: Germany today is no longer what it was ten years ago.

meaning: more of it / more of that
additional_notes: Used to ask for or state that you want a larger quantity or repetition of something just mentioned or shown. Common in spoken and informal contexts. Can refer to countable things (cakes), uncountable things (time, fun), or abstract actions (ideas). Often follows a noun or demonstrative: "Ich möchte mehr davon."
target_language_example: Der Kuchen ist lecker — ich möchte mehr davon.
native_language_example: The cake is delicious — I want more of it.

meaning: 'more than' or 'more ... than ever' (used to strengthen a comparison — often equivalent to 'more than ever').
additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison. Often appears in constructions like 'mehr denn je' (more than ever). Can link nouns or clauses (e.g. 'mehr denn Wohlstand' = values X more than wealth). Formal or neutral register; common in written and spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich vermisse ihn mehr denn je.
native_language_example: I miss him more than ever.

meaning: 'there is more' or 'there are more' (used within phrases like "es gibt mehr")
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the phrase "es gibt mehr (als)..." meaning "there is more (than)..." or "there are more..." Alone, the sequence "mehr gibt" can occur in subordinate clauses or after verbs (e.g. "wenn mehr gibt" is ungrammatical without "es" in many contexts; typical correct forms include "wenn es mehr gibt" or "mehr gibt es nicht").
target_language_example: Wenn mehr gibt, sage mir Bescheid.
native_language_example: If there is more, let me know.

meaning: no longer / not ... anymore (followed by a feminine or dative noun phrase introduced by 'in der')
additional_notes: mehr ... in der appears in negative statements to say that something is no longer present or no longer happening inside/at a specific feminine/dative place (e.g. 'in der Flasche', 'in der Luft', 'in der Kiste', 'in der Schule'). Word order: 'kein/keine/keinen ... mehr in der...' or 'nicht mehr in der...' depending on the verb and negation. 'mehr' here means 'anymore' or 'no longer'.
target_language_example: Es ist kein Saft mehr in der Flasche.
native_language_example: There is no juice in the bottle anymore.

meaning: do more; make (something) more / any longer (in 'no longer make sense' uses).
additional_notes: Context-dependent phrase: 'mehr machen' often means 'do more' or 'do additional things' (e.g., Ich kann mehr machen = I can do more). In sentences like 'Das würde keinen Sinn mehr machen' the word 'mehr' pairs with 'machen' to mean 'no longer' or 'any longer' (i.e., 'would no longer make sense'). Pay attention to context to choose the correct English translation.
target_language_example: Ich kann noch mehr machen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: I can do more if you want.

meaning: 'anymore/any longer with' — used to say someone no longer does something with someone or something.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in negative statements: 'niemand mehr mit ... reden' or 'nicht mehr mit ... sprechen'. 'Mehr' here means 'anymore' and 'mit' means 'with'. Word order follows German: 'nicht mehr mit + person' or 'niemand mehr mit + person'. Can also be used with objects (e.g. 'mehr mit dem Gewicht arbeiten' = 'work more with the weight').
target_language_example: Ich spreche nicht mehr mit ihm.
native_language_example: I don't speak with him anymore.

meaning: more or less; roughly; to some extent.
additional_notes: Used to say something is approximately true or partly true. Can be a short response (like 'more or less?') or part of a sentence to soften a statement. Very common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich spreche Deutsch, mehr oder weniger.
native_language_example: I speak German, more or less.

meaning: to say more / to add more (words or information).
additional_notes: Used when talking about adding further information, continuing to speak, or implying there is nothing left to add. Context determines whether it's a question (Do I need to say more?) or a statement (he wanted to say more). 'Mehr' modifies the amount of speech or content.
target_language_example: Musst du noch mehr sagen, oder sind wir fertig?
native_language_example: Do you need to say more, or are we done?

meaning: 'more about' / 'more (concerned) with' — indicates increased attention, care or importance given to something or someone
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sorgen (sich sorgen um), kümmern (sich kümmern um) or gehen (es ging um) to show that someone gives greater concern, care, or priority to a person or thing. Often follows a comparative idea ('more than before' or 'more than something/someone else') and is followed by a noun or pronoun in the accusative (um + Akk.).
target_language_example: Sie kümmert sich jetzt mehr um die Kinder als früher.
native_language_example: She now takes more care of the children than before.

meaning: more further / any more (used with negation to mean 'no more' or 'any more')
additional_notes: This exact combination 'mehr weiter' is not a standard fixed phrase in German. More common are 'nicht mehr' (no longer, no more) or 'weiter' alone (further, continue). In some dialects or colloquial speech you might hear 'nicht mehr weiter' as part of a sentence meaning 'no longer further' or 'can't continue any further' (e.g. 'Ich kann nicht mehr weiter'). Don't use 'mehr weiter' by itself in standard German.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mehr weiter.
native_language_example: I can't go on any more / I can't continue.

meaning: 'to know more' or 'want to know more' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (to have greater knowledge) or in phrases meaning 'want to hear more' or 'don't want to hear more about something' (e.g. 'davon nichts mehr wissen' = 'don't want to hear about it anymore'). Often appears with modal verbs (möchten, wollen) or negation. Word order and context determine whether it's about wanting information or stating relative knowledge.
target_language_example: Möchtest du mehr wissen?
native_language_example: Do you want to know more?

meaning: 'anymore' or 'no longer' (used with verbs or infinitives to indicate that something stops happening or is no longer the case).
additional_notes: Often appears before infinitives (mit zu + Infinitiv) or with verbs to express cessation: 'nicht mehr' = 'no longer/not anymore'. Word order can vary: 'mehr zu tun' = 'to do more' versus 'nicht mehr zu tun' = 'to no longer do'. In sentences like 'Kein Parkplatz ist mehr zu haben' it means 'no longer available'.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr zu warten.
native_language_example: I have no more time to wait. / I can't wait anymore.

meaning: more back / further back (depends on context: can mean 'give back more' or 'move/put back further')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's a combination of 'mehr' (more) and 'zurück' (back). Meaning depends on the verb or situation around it. Possible uses: asking for a larger refund or repayment (e.g. 'Geben Sie mir mehr zurück' = 'Give me more back'), or telling someone to move something further back (e.g. 'Stell das mehr zurück' = 'Push it further back'). For beginners: pay attention to the verb and word order — German often places the verb between these words (e.g. 'Kannst du mir mehr zurückgeben?').
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mehr zurückgeben? Ich habe zu viel bezahlt.
native_language_example: Can you give me more back? I paid too much.

meaning: 'my brother and' — the start of a phrase that adds another person or action connected to 'my brother'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the possessive phrase 'mein Bruder' followed by the conjunction 'und' (and). You will see it when someone lists things or people, e.g. "mein Bruder und ich" (my brother and I) or "mein Bruder und seine Frau" (my brother and his wife). Be careful: word endings and possessive forms change with gender, case and number (e.g. 'meine Schwester' for sister, or 'meinem Bruder' in dative).
target_language_example: Mein Bruder und ich gehen morgen ins Kino.
native_language_example: My brother and I are going to the cinema tomorrow.

meaning: Oh my God; an exclamation expressing surprise, shock, emotion, or emphasis.
additional_notes: Common spoken expression used alone or before a sentence. Can show surprise, disbelief, worry, admiration, frustration, or strong feeling depending on context and tone. Can be used seriously (literal religious address) in prayers or dramatically (e.g., "Mein Gott, was hast du getan?") but most everyday uses are equivalent to English "Oh my God." Avoid overuse in formal writing or very polite situations.
target_language_example: Mein Gott, was hast du getan?
native_language_example: Oh my God, what have you done?

meaning: my house is located / my house is situated
additional_notes: Used to say where your house is. Commonly appears with 'sich befinden' (reflexive) to mean 'to be located' and is followed by a location phrase (am Rande der Stadt, gegenüber, hier, etc.). You can omit 'mein Haus' and say 'befindet sich' with other subjects. Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Mein Haus befindet sich in einer ruhigen Straße.
native_language_example: My house is located on a quiet street.

meaning: 'my plan is' — used to state or compare what your plan/idea is or to say it's better than someone else's.
additional_notes: Simple, neutral phrase. Common in comparisons (e.g., mein Plan ist besser = my plan is better). Can be followed by adjectives, clauses, or explanations. The possessive mein agrees with the speaker; for formal 'your' use Ihrer, for plural 'your' use eurer. Useful in arguments or making proposals.
target_language_example: Mein Plan ist realistisch und günstiger.
native_language_example: My plan is realistic and cheaper.

meaning: my older (male); used before a noun to say someone is older than you
additional_notes: ‘älterer’ is the comparative adjective of ‚alt‘ and agrees with a masculine noun here. Use ‚meine ältere‘ for a feminine noun (my older sister) and ‚mein älteres‘ for a neuter noun. In spoken German you may also hear ‚mein älterer Bruder‘ shortened to ‚mein großer Bruder‘ in some contexts, but ‚älterer‘ specifically emphasizes age (older).
target_language_example: Mein älterer Bruder wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in Berlin.

meaning: my job/task is; it's my responsibility to…
additional_notes: Used to say what someone’s responsibility, duty or role is. Often followed by 'es' + infinitive clause (meine Aufgabe ist es, ... zu + verb) or by a noun/phrase explaining the task. Common in both formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Meine Aufgabe ist es, dafür zu sorgen, dass alle sicher sind.
native_language_example: My job is to make sure that everyone is safe.

meaning: my questions.
additional_notes: A possessive phrase: 'meine' (my) + plural noun 'Fragen' (questions). Used when referring to questions the speaker asked or has. Change 'meine' for other possessives (deine, seine, unsere) and adjust noun pluralization if needed. Pronunciation tip: 'meine' sounds like 'MY-nuh' and 'Fragen' like 'FRAH-gen'.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte meine Fragen beantworten?
native_language_example: Can you please answer my questions?

meaning: an exclamation like "oh my goodness" or "goodness me" expressing surprise, annoyance, or emphasis.
additional_notes: Common, mildly emotional interjection used to react to something surprising, frustrating, impressive, or painful. Can be used alone or with a sentence. Polite and not strong profanity; suitable in most situations. Often appears with 'ach, du' or 'oh'.
target_language_example: Meine Güte, das war aber laut!
native_language_example: Oh my goodness, that was loud!

meaning: my teachers
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: 'meine' is the feminine/plural form of 'mein' used with plural nouns; 'Lehrer' (teachers) is plural here. Use 'mein Lehrer' for one male teacher, 'meine Lehrerin' for one female teacher, and 'meine Lehrerinnen' for multiple female teachers. Word order: possessive comes before the noun.
target_language_example: Meine Lehrer helfen mir beim Lernen.
native_language_example: My teachers help me with studying.

meaning: my people; my team; the people I am responsible for or associated with.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group connected to the speaker — staff, team, family, followers, or associates. Context determines tone: can be neutral (team, staff), protective (family, close group), or imply authority (boss talking about subordinates or associates). Not literal 'people' only; often means 'people who work for me' or 'my crew.'
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, meine Leute regeln das.
native_language_example: Don't worry, my people will handle that.

meaning: my plans
additional_notes: A simple possessive phrase: 'meine' (my) + plural noun 'Pläne' (plans). Used to talk about intentions, arrangements, projects, or goals. Can refer to short-term or long-term plans depending on context. Common verbs with it: machen, ändern, aufgeben, haben, verfolgen, zunichte machen.
target_language_example: Ich muss meine Pläne für das Wochenende noch bestätigen.
native_language_example: I still have to confirm my plans for the weekend.

meaning: my speech (a prepared talk) or my statement.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a speech given at an event or a prepared spoken statement. Can mean the text of the speech (Hast du meine Rede gelesen?) or the act of giving it (Ich halte jetzt meine Rede.). Polite/neutral; common in formal and informal contexts depending on setting.
target_language_example: Ich muss noch meine Rede vorbereiten.
native_language_example: I still have to prepare my speech.

meaning: in my direction / toward me (or toward my destination).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement toward the speaker (or toward the speaker's destination). Context decides whether it means 'toward me' (physical direction) or 'toward my route/destination' (e.g. asking if someone is driving the same way). 'Richtung' is feminine: 'in meine Richtung' is correct when referring to 'meine (route)'; when emphasizing 'toward me' you might also hear 'auf mich zu'.
target_language_example: Fährst du in meine Richtung, kannst du mich mitnehmen?
native_language_example: If you're going in my direction, can you give me a lift?

meaning: my school
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: 'meine' is the feminine/neuter/plural possessive for 'my' used with 'Schule' (feminine). Use to say where you study, which school you attend(d), or to talk about the school's location. For past attendance Germans often say 'auf meine Schule gehen' (colloquial regional usage) or more commonly 'auf meine Schule gegangen sein' / 'auf die Schule gehen'.
target_language_example: Meine Schule liegt in der Nähe des Bahnhofs.
native_language_example: My school is near the train station.

meaning: 'my concern' / 'my worry' (something I am worried about or will take care of).
additional_notes: Used to say something is your concern (worry) or to tell someone to leave an issue to you (Lass das meine Sorge sein = leave that to me). Can express worry (Meine Sorge ist, dass...) or responsibility (Das lassen Sie meine Sorge sein = let that be my responsibility). Tone is neutral; context decides whether it's about worry or responsibility.
target_language_example: Lass das meine Sorge sein — ich kümmere mich darum.
native_language_example: Leave that to me — I'll take care of it.

meaning: 'mine is' (referring to a feminine noun in German)
additional_notes: Used as a short answer where the speaker refers back to a previously mentioned feminine noun (e.g., Tasche, Uhr, Uhrzeit not—use feminine nouns like Lampe, Jacke, Tasche, Kamera (die Kamera)). The possessive pronoun 'meine' agrees with a feminine noun in nominative case; 'ist' is the verb 'is'. For other genders you would say 'meiner ist' (masculine), 'meins ist' (neuter/informal), or 'meine sind' (plural).
target_language_example: Meine ist blau und funktioniert noch gut.
native_language_example: Mine is blue and still works well.

meaning: I think / I mean (followed by 'he' clause).
additional_notes: A spoken/written pattern where the speaker introduces their opinion or belief about 'he'. 'Ich meine' softens a statement (like 'I think' or 'I mean'). It can introduce facts, guesses, impressions, or suggestions. Often followed by a clause with 'er' + verb. Tone is neutral; not informal slang.
target_language_example: Ich meine, er hat das ruhig erklärt.
native_language_example: I think he explained that calmly.

meaning: 'I mean' (followed by what is meant) — used to clarify or emphasize what someone intends to say.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'meinen' (to mean) used with a clause introduced by 'was' ('what'). In natural German you would usually say 'Ich meine, ...' + statement or question (without a comma before 'was' in many cases). Use to introduce clarification, emphasis, or to restate what you mean. Examples in the input show both statements and questions that follow 'Ich meine, was ...' — in conversational English this corresponds to 'I mean, what ...' or 'I mean what I say.'
target_language_example: Ich meine, was ich sage — das ist mein Angebot.
native_language_example: I mean what I say — that's my offer.

meaning: I mean that / I intend that (what I say is sincere or intended).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the speaker's intention or seriousness about a previous statement. Often appears as 'Ich meine das' followed by a noun phrase (e.g. 'als Kompliment') or an adjective/adverb (e.g. 'ernst', 'ganz aufrichtig'). Can be used to correct misunderstanding or stress sincerity.
target_language_example: Ich meine das wirklich ernst.
native_language_example: I really mean that seriously.

meaning: in my eye / inside my eye.
additional_notes: Dative case of 'mein Auge' (das Auge). Used to say something is in or happened to the speaker's eye (e.g., an object, irritation, or a burst blood vessel). Common in everyday situations like eye discomfort; literal meaning.
target_language_example: Etwas steckt in meinem Auge — ich muss es rausnehmen.
native_language_example: Something is in my eye — I need to take it out.

meaning: 'my success' (dative case)
additional_notes: This is the dative form of 'mein Erfolg' used after verbs or prepositions that require the dative; common with 'zu' as in 'zu meinem Erfolg' = 'for/at my success' or 'congratulated me on my success.' 'mein' changes ending based on gender (Erfolg = masculine) and case (dative singular -> 'meinem').
target_language_example: Alle haben mir zu meinem Erfolg gratuliert.
native_language_example: Everyone congratulated me on my success.

meaning: ‘there is/are at my house’ or 'at my house is' (location: something is located in front of/behind my house).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of 'mein Haus' (meinem Haus) used with verbs of location like 'ist' (is) to say where something is relative to your house: e.g. 'Hinter meinem Haus ist ein Garten' = 'Behind my house there is a garden.' Word order in German often places the location phrase first, followed by 'ist' and the thing that exists.
target_language_example: Neben meinem Haus ist eine Bushaltestelle.
native_language_example: Next to my house there is a bus stop.

meaning: to my best (as in 'to my best friend'); dative form meaning 'my best' when referring to someone close.
additional_notes: This is the dative singular masculine or neuter form of 'mein bester' and appears before a noun like 'Freund' (friend). Common in phrases meaning 'to my best friend' or 'with my best friend' (e.g. 'mit meinem besten Freund'). Word order can change (Meinem besten Freund kann ich alles sagen). Use dative verbs or prepositions (mit, zu, für) with this form.
target_language_example: Ich habe meinem besten Freund zum Geburtstag ein Buch geschenkt.
native_language_example: I gave my best friend a book for his birthday.

meaning: my seat / my place (position or spot).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical seat or a specific spot/position that belongs to or was occupied by the speaker. Can also be used metaphorically for a role or position (e.g., in a hall or organization). In sentences with verbs like 'nehmen', 'wegnehmen', 'setzen (auf)', the phrase indicates whose place is affected.
target_language_example: Bitte setz dich nicht auf meinen Platz.
native_language_example: Please don't sit in my seat.

meaning: to (do something) to/for my father — part of an infinitive clause with a verb at the end (e.g. 'to meet/my father', 'to say goodbye to my father').
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete phrase by itself: it combines the accusative object 'meinen Vater' (my father) with the particle 'zu' that introduces or connects to an infinitive clause in German word order (common after verbs like 'gehen, kommen, bleiben' + 'um ... zu' for purpose, or with verbs that require 'zu' before an infinitive). In English you usually translate the whole clause (e.g. 'to meet my father', 'to say goodbye to my father', 'to avenge my father'). Pay attention to case: 'meinen Vater' is accusative (male).
target_language_example: Ich fahre nach Hause, um meinen Vater zu besuchen.
native_language_example: I'm going home to visit my father.

meaning: in my presence; while I am present.
additional_notes: Literally 'my presence' (Gegenwart = presence). Used to say that something happens or should/shouldn't happen when the speaker is there. Often appears in the fixed phrase 'in meiner Gegenwart' followed by a verb (e.g. 'nicht verstellen', 'sich unwohl fühlen', 'weinen'). Formality: neutral to slightly formal; common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Bitte iss nicht in meiner Gegenwart, ich habe gerade gegessen.
native_language_example: Please don't eat in my presence; I just finished eating.

meaning: with my help
additional_notes: Used to say that the speaker provided assistance. Commonly appears after verbs with 'mit' (mit meiner Hilfe = with my help). Can be used in different word orders: 'Tom hat es mit meiner Hilfe geschafft' or 'Mit meiner Hilfe hat Tom es geschafft.' Tone is neutral; not possessive in the sense of owning something, but indicates the help came from 'me'.
target_language_example: Ohne deine Unterstützung, aber mit meiner Hilfe hat sie das Projekt beendet.
native_language_example: Without your support, but with my help she finished the project.

meaning: in my opinion; from my point of view.
additional_notes: A common phrase to state your opinion. Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence (Meiner Meinung nach ...) but can also appear elsewhere (Ich denke, meiner Meinung nach ...). Formal and neutral — safe to use in conversations, emails, and discussions. Use with verbs in normal word order after the phrase.
target_language_example: Meiner Meinung nach sollten wir früher anfangen.
native_language_example: In my opinion, we should start earlier.

meaning: to/for my party (dative case of 'meine Party').
additional_notes: Used when talking about attending, coming to, or inviting people to a party you are hosting. 'meiner' is the dative feminine singular form of the possessive pronoun 'mein' (because Party is feminine and verbs like 'kommen zu' and prepositions like 'zu' take the dative). Choose 'meine Party' in nominative/accusative contexts (e.g. 'Ich organisiere meine Party').
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Abend zu meiner Party?
native_language_example: Are you coming to my party tonight?

meaning: 'in my place' / 'if you were me' (used to ask what someone would do in your situation)
additional_notes: Used in the construction 'an meiner Stelle' (literally 'at my place') to ask for advice or imagine someone taking your position. Common in questions: 'Was würdest du an meiner Stelle tun?' — 'What would you do if you were me?'. Can be adapted to other persons (an deiner Stelle, an seiner Stelle).
target_language_example: An meiner Stelle würde ich das Angebot annehmen.
native_language_example: If I were you / In my place, I would accept the offer.

meaning: to my surprise / much to my surprise
additional_notes: Used with 'zu' as in 'Zu meiner Überraschung' to introduce something unexpected. Common in past and present contexts. It literally means 'to my surprise' and is a fixed expression; use dative 'meiner' (feminine noun 'Überraschung').
target_language_example: Zu meiner Überraschung hat sie das Konzert genossen.
native_language_example: To my surprise, she enjoyed the concert.

meaning: mine is / mine (one) is
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a previously mentioned noun without repeating it. 'Meiner' is the masculine or neutral possessive pronoun (or nominalized adjective) meaning 'my one' or 'mine' and agrees with the implied noun; followed by a form of 'sein' (here 'ist') to say what the speaker's item is like. Common in comparisons (Meiner ist größer = Mine is bigger) and simple statements (Meiner ist schwarz = Mine is black).
target_language_example: Dein Rucksack ist schwer, aber meiner ist leicht.
native_language_example: Your backpack is heavy, but mine is light.

meaning: 'as far as I know' / 'to my knowledge'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that the speaker is giving information based on their knowledge or belief, not claiming absolute certainty. Polite and common in both spoken and written German. Often followed by 'ist' or a clause. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: Meines Wissens beginnt der Kurs um neun Uhr.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the class starts at nine o'clock.

meaning: 'mine is' — used to say that something belongs to me or to describe my thing.
additional_notes: Meins is a short possessive pronoun meaning 'mine'. In sentences with sein (ist), 'meins ist' can mean 'mine is [something]' or 'my one is...'. Common in spoken German. Word order: you can also say 'Das ist meins' ('That is mine'). When referring to specific objects, meins agrees in meaning but not in gender/number (meins stays the same).
target_language_example: Meins ist neu, aber deins sieht besser aus.
native_language_example: Mine is new, but yours looks better.

meaning: I/they meant that (the intended meaning of something said).
additional_notes: Used to clarify or emphasize the intended meaning of a previous statement. 'Meinte' is the past tense (Präteritum) of 'meinen' (to mean/intend). 'Das' refers to 'that' (what was said). Depending on subject, translate as 'I meant that', 'she meant that', 'Tom meant that', etc. Common in phrases like 'Ich meinte das als Kompliment' (I meant that as a compliment) or 'Ich meinte das nicht so' (I didn't mean it that way).
target_language_example: Ich meinte das wirklich ernst.
native_language_example: I really meant that.

meaning: I meant (that) / I meant it.
additional_notes: Past tense of meinen (to mean). Used to clarify or correct what you intended to say. Often appears in phrases like "Das meinte ich" (That's what I meant) or with a negation: "Das meinte ich nicht" (I didn't mean that). Can introduce an explanation: "Das meinte ich, als..." (That's what I meant when...).
target_language_example: Das meinte ich nicht — ich wollte dich nicht verletzen.
native_language_example: I didn't mean that — I didn't want to hurt you.

meaning: 'most men' or 'the majority of men'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what the majority of men do, think, or are like. Usually appears as 'die meisten Männer' (with the definite article 'die') in standard German. Can be followed by verbs, complements, or prepositional phrases. Use 'die meisten' to mean 'most (of a group)'.
target_language_example: Die meisten Männer arbeiten an Werktagen.
native_language_example: Most men work on weekdays.

meaning: most of my / the majority of my
additional_notes: Used to say that the majority of a group that belongs to the speaker has a certain property. Often appears as part of a noun phrase: 'Die meisten meiner + [plural noun]'. English equivalents: 'most of my friends', 'most of my bills'.
target_language_example: Die meisten meiner Bücher stehen im Wohnzimmer.
native_language_example: Most of my books are in the living room.

meaning: 'remember' (formal imperative) — telling someone politely to notice or to memorize something.
additional_notes: Formal (Sie) imperative of merken. Used to instruct or ask someone politely to remember something (merken Sie sich = remember/keep in mind) or to notice/realize (merken Sie? = do you notice?). Often followed by 'sich' when meaning 'remember' (merken Sie sich das).
target_language_example: Merken Sie sich bitte die PIN-Nummer.
native_language_example: Please remember the PIN number.

meaning: 'dass' ('daß' in older orthography) used after a phrase containing 'mich' to introduce a subordinate clause meaning 'that' (English).
additional_notes: This entry shows the pattern where a clause or expression with 'mich' (e.g. 'freut mich', 'erinnere mich', 'freue mich') is followed by 'dass' (older spelling 'daß') to introduce a subordinate clause. Note: modern German uses 'dass' (double s). In subordinate clauses the finite verb typically moves to the end. The comma before 'dass' is required. Examples below use older orthography with 'daß' to match the requested term.
target_language_example: Freut mich, daß Sie die Blumen bekommen haben.
native_language_example: I'm pleased that you received the flowers.

meaning: 'me' and 'you' (informal singular) used as object pronouns in phrases meaning 'I'm glad to see/meet you'.
additional_notes: Mich = accusative 'me'; dich = accusative informal singular 'you'. Common fixed phrases: "Es freut mich, dich zu sehen/kennenzulernen" = "I'm pleased/glad to see/meet you." In polite/formal situations use "Sie" (e.g. "Es freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen"). Word order often: "Es freut mich, dich ..." or shortened "Freut mich, dich kennenzulernen."
target_language_example: Es freut mich, dich hier zu haben.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have you here.

meaning: Used in infinitive constructions with verbs of emotion or refusal: 'to ... me, to see you' — as in 'It pleases me to see you' / 'I refuse to pay attention to you.'
additional_notes: This pattern appears when a verb (often reflexive like freuen sich, weigern sich) is followed by an object (mich, dich etc.) and an infinitive clause introduced by zu. In modern spoken German, with verbs of perception or emotion it's more common to say 'Es freut mich, dich zu sehen' or 'Ich freue mich, dich zu sehen.' The comma before the infinitive clause is optional in informal writing but often used. 'mich' and 'dich' are objects (me / you).
target_language_example: Es freut mich, dich zu treffen.
native_language_example: I'm pleased to meet you.

meaning: 'mich' = me / 'dir' = to you (informal singular).
additional_notes: These are two separate personal pronouns used together in sentences with verbs that take an accusative object (mich) and a dative object (dir). 'Mich' is the accusative form of 'ich' (me). 'Dir' is the dative form of 'du' (to/for you, informal singular). Common verbs: freuen (sich freuen + über/auf + accusative; or sich freuen + dative person with infinitive), helfen, zuhören, sagen (someone asks/tells someone). Word order follows German rules: pronouns often come early; dative pronoun can come before or after accusative depending on emphasis, but typically dative before accusative when both are pronouns (e.g., 'mir ihn' vs 'mich dir'—note: standard order is dative then accusative: 'mir ihn' but with both short forms it's usually 'mir ihn' → 'Sie gab mir ihn' rare; learners should follow examples). 'Dir' is informal; for formal you would use 'Ihnen'.
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, dir helfen zu können.
native_language_example: I'm happy to be able to help you.

meaning: 'me' as the object plus the preposition 'with' (i.e. 'asked/urged/etc. me to come with / to do something with someone)'.
additional_notes: This shows the combination of the accusative pronoun 'mich' (me) and the preposition or particle 'mit' (with). In the example sentences 'mit' often begins an infinitive clause with another person (e.g. 'mit ihr zu reden' = 'to talk with her', 'mit ihnen mitzukommen' = 'to come along with them'). Word order: the pronoun 'mich' stays before the comma and the infinitive clause after the comma. Common verbs that appear here: bitten (ask), überreden (persuade), bezichtigen (accuse).
target_language_example: Sie forderten mich, mit ihnen zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: They asked me to work with them.

meaning: uses of 'mich' (accusative 'me') combined with 'nicht' (not); commonly appears when negating actions or making contrasts involving 'me', and in short tag-like phrases. Not a fixed idiom but a frequent combination in different syntactic patterns.
additional_notes: Typical patterns: 1) verb + mich + nicht: negating an action toward 'me' (Ich bemühte mich, nicht einzuschlafen = I tried not to fall asleep). 2) contrast/clarification where 'nicht' excludes an alternative (Sie küsste mich, nicht ihn. = She kissed me, not him). 3) short/colloquial confirmation or surprise: 'Mich, nicht wahr?' or 'Sie war sogar ein wenig eifersüchtig auf mich, nicht wahr?' 4) contrast with nouns/places: 'Nein, er hasst mich, nicht Amerika.' Word order note: 'mich' is accusative and usually appears where objects go; 'nicht' can negate the verb, the object, or serve to contrast depending on placement.
target_language_example: Ich bemühte mich, nicht einzuschlafen.
native_language_example: I tried not to fall asleep.

meaning: 'I wonder whether/if it...' (used to express curiosity or doubt about something).
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside the sentence: Ich frage mich, ob es ... — literally 'I ask myself whether it ...'. Use it to introduce a yes/no clause (ob) about a situation (es = it/that). Commonly followed by verbs in various tenses. In spoken German you can also say 'Ich frage mich, ob...' without the pronoun 'es' when context makes the subject clear.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, ob es heute klappt.
native_language_example: I wonder whether it will work today.

meaning: 'me, and' — the accusative object pronoun 'mich' followed immediately by the conjunction 'und' connecting to the next clause.
additional_notes: Appears when 'mich' is the direct object in the preceding clause and the speaker continues with another clause beginning with 'und'. Often written with a comma before 'und' if the first clause is complete. Example sentences may place a verb or other elements before or after 'mich, und'.
target_language_example: Er liebt mich, und ich liebe ihn auch.
native_language_example: He loves me, and I love him too.

meaning: literally 'myself, what' — used in the structure 'frage mich, was...' meaning 'ask me what...' or 'I wonder what... (when reflexive: 'ich frage mich, was...')
