meaning: I'd like to know / I would like to know
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information. 'Möchte' is the subjunctive/conditional of 'mögen' and makes the request softer. 'Gerne' adds politeness/emphasis. Often followed by a question word (warum, was, wie, wo, wie lange) or a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass' or omitted. Use formal 'Sie' or informal 'du/ihr' as needed.
target_language_example: Ich möchte gerne wissen, wann der Bus ankommt.
native_language_example: I'd like to know when the bus arrives.

meaning: 'would like to (stay/be/sit) here' — expresses a polite desire to be or remain in this place.
additional_notes: Möchte is the polite subjunctive form of mögen (to like) used to express wishes or desires. Hier means 'here'. Together they are followed by verbs or phrases that complete the desire (e.g. bleiben, sein, sitzen, rauskommen). Common in polite requests and statements. Word order: möchte + hier + (additional info) or möchte + (verb) + hier (both are possible depending on sentence).
target_language_example: Ich möchte hier noch eine Stunde bleiben.
native_language_example: I would like to stay here for one more hour.

meaning: 'I would like to' + reflexive 'myself' (used with reflexive verbs): expresses a polite desire to do something with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Möchte is the polite conditional form of mögen (would like). Many German verbs are reflexive and require 'mich' (myself) for the first person singular (e.g. sich bedanken, sich entschuldigen, sich spiegeln, sich einmischen). You must pair 'möchte' with the full infinitive at the end of the sentence: Ich möchte mich entschuldigen = I would like to apologize. Word order: 'möchte' (conjugated) + reflexive pronoun (mich) + ... + infinitive (ent-schuldigen) at the end.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mich bei Ihnen entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I would like to apologize to you.

meaning: 'would not like to' / 'do not want to' (polite negative desire)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'möchte' (polite form of 'mögen' used to express desire/wish) with 'nicht' to negate the desire. Use to politely say you don't want something or don't want someone to do something. In subordinate clauses place comma + 'dass' as needed: Ich möchte nicht, dass... For stronger or more direct refusal, Germans might use 'will nicht' (less polite) or 'möchte nicht, dass...' remains polite.
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht, dass du dir Sorgen machst.
native_language_example: I would not like you to worry / I don't want you to worry.

meaning: 'would like nothing' / 'do not want anything' (expressing desire to have/ do none of something)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'möchte' (polite form of 'want') with 'nichts' (nothing). Used to say you don't want anything, don't want to do something, or prefer that nothing happens. Can appear with objects (Ich möchte nichts essen) or with verbs/clauses (Ich möchte nichts davon vergessen). In sentences like 'Tom möchte nichts mehr mit dir zu tun haben' it means 'Tom doesn't want anything more to do with you.'
target_language_example: Ich möchte nichts kaufen, danke.
native_language_example: I don't want to buy anything, thanks.

meaning: 'would like to know' or 'want to know' (polite)
additional_notes: Möchte is the subjunctive/polite form of mögen used to express a wish or polite desire. 'möchte wissen' is commonly used to ask for information politely (I would like to know...). Use with an object or clause: 'Ich möchte wissen, ...' or in questions: 'Möchten Sie wissen, ...?'. For informal speech you can also use 'will wissen' (stronger).
target_language_example: Ich möchte wissen, wann der Zug ankommt.
native_language_example: I would like to know when the train arrives.

meaning: 'would like to (go/speak) to' or 'wants to (go/speak) to' — expresses a polite desire directed toward a person or place.
additional_notes: Möchte is the polite conditional form of mögen (would like). Zu + dative indicates direction toward a person, place, or group (e.g., zu Ihnen, zu dem Laden, zu uns). In many cases English uses 'to' (go to, speak to) or 'see' (see someone). Word order: 'möchte zu' is followed by a dative noun or pronoun. For movement to a location use 'möchte zu + place' or more commonly 'möchte in + place' / 'möchte in das Hotel' depending on the destination.
target_language_example: Ich möchte zu dem Arzt gehen.
native_language_example: I would like to go to the doctor.

meaning: 'would like a' (polite request for a singular feminine or indefinite noun)
additional_notes: Möchte is the subjunctive of mögen used to make polite requests or express desires. 'eine' is the indefinite article for feminine nouns (or any noun in contexts where 'eine' appears due to gender). Use 'möchte ein' for masculine/neuter nouns, and adjust number/article accordingly (e.g. 'wir möchten', 'ich möchte zwei'). Common in offers and ordering (e.g. at a café or when offering food).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine Tasse Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I would like a cup of coffee, please.

meaning: 'would like a' (masculine or neuter singular accusative object)
additional_notes: Möchte is the polite conditional form of mögen (to like) used to make requests or express desires. Einen is the masculine (and for some neuter nouns with adjective endings) accusative indefinite article 'a'/'an'. Use möchte + accusative noun to say you would like something: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. For feminine nouns use 'eine' (Ich möchte eine Tasse). For plural use 'möchte + (keine/keine) or 'möchte + (plural noun)' without 'einen'.
target_language_example: Ich möchte einen Salat, bitte.
native_language_example: I would like a salad, please.

meaning: 'would like' (polite way to express a wish or desire)
additional_notes: Common polite phrase used to request or express a desire. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (möchte gern einen Kaffee / möchte gern gehen). 'Gern' (or gerne) adds a friendly tone but isn't necessary: 'ich möchte' and 'ich möchte gern' are both polite; 'möchte gern' is slightly softer. Conjugate 'möchte' with the subject (ich möchte, er/sie möchte).
target_language_example: Ich möchte gern ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: I would like a piece of cake.

meaning: 'would like (that)...' — used to express a polite desire or request that someone do something.
additional_notes: Möchten is the subjunctive form of mögen used for polite requests. Followed by a comma and 'dass' + clause with a verb at the end (standard German word order). Often used to soften commands: 'Wir möchten, dass du...'. For polite address use Sie: 'Wir möchten, dass Sie...'.
target_language_example: Wir möchten, dass du pünktlich bist.
native_language_example: We would like you to be on time.

meaning: would you like
additional_notes: Usually written as "möchten Sie" with a capital S when addressing someone formally. It is a polite way to ask what someone wants, would like to drink, talk about, do, etc. "möchten" is softer and more polite than a direct "want."
target_language_example: Möchten Sie einen Kaffee?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee?

meaning: would you like anything else / otherwise?
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants anything more or anything else in addition. Often followed by 'noch' (noch etwas) or a verb phrase. Polite, informal (du-form). Common at the end of a service interaction, meal, meeting, or before leaving.
target_language_example: Möchtest du sonst noch etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like anything else to drink?

meaning: 'like the' or 'like those' (verb 'mögen' + definite plural article 'die')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb mögen ('to like') followed by the definite plural article 'die'. It appears when talking about liking specific plural nouns (e.g., die Leute, die gleichen Dinge). Word order and endings depend on the noun that follows. For polite/formal 'you' use mögen as in sentence 1 (Wenn Sie versuchen... mögen die Leute es nicht = people don't like it).
target_language_example: Wir mögen die neuen Filme.
native_language_example: We like the new movies.

meaning: to like (to do) something; to enjoy something.
additional_notes: Common structure: mögen + es + infinitive (often without 'zu' in spoken German) or mögen + es + noun. 'Es' is a placeholder (dummy pronoun) referring to the activity. Negation: 'nicht' comes after 'es'. Formality: neutral. For beginners, learn 'mögen' (to like) and this construction to say you like doing something.
target_language_example: Wir mögen es, am Wochenende spazieren zu gehen.
native_language_example: We like to go for walks on the weekend.

meaning: to like him (object: 'him').
additional_notes: Mögen is the verb 'to like'. In these examples it's conjugated for plural subjects (Sie, wir, alle). 'Ihn' is the accusative pronoun 'him'. Word order: subject + mögen + object in simple statements (Wir mögen ihn). In questions you may see inversion (Mögen Sie ihn?) or tag questions (Sie mögen ihn, nicht?).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, die Nachbarn mögen ihn.
native_language_example: I think the neighbors like him.

meaning: like me
additional_notes: Derived from the verb mögen (to like). In these sentences it means that people have a positive feeling or liking toward the speaker. Word order here is object pronoun after the verb (mögen mich); in normal statements pronouns often come before the verb (sie mögen mich / mögen mich? — note: in subordinate clauses or questions order can change). Can be used with different subjects: alle, die Leute, meine Lehrer, etc. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Viele meiner Kollegen mögen mich.
native_language_example: Many of my colleagues like me.

meaning: used with an infinitive to mean 'possible to' or 'to be able to (do something)'; often in set phrases like 'möglich zu machen' or 'so ... wie möglich zu + infinitive' = 'as ... as possible to + verb'.
additional_notes: Occurs with an infinitive (zu + verb). Common patterns: 'möglich zu + Inf.' (possible to ...), 'so + Adjektiv/Adverb + wie möglich zu + Inf.' (as ... as possible to ...), and 'etwas möglich machen' (to make something possible). Used to express ability/possibility or striving for the best/maximum degree.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, so schnell wie möglich zu antworten.
native_language_example: I try to answer as quickly as possible.

meaning: 'so tired that' — introduces a result clause explaining what tiredness caused.
additional_notes: Used to connect a cause ('müde' with an intensifier like so/so much/so) to its consequence; in German the verb moves to the end of the 'dass' clause (e.g., 'dass er einschlief'). Commonly appears as 'so müde, dass...' or 'so müde, dass ich/...'.
target_language_example: Ich war so müde, dass ich sofort eingeschlafen bin.
native_language_example: I was so tired that I fell asleep immediately.

meaning: too tired to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is too tired to perform an action. Structure: [subject] + ist/sind + zu müde, um zu + infinitive. 'zu müde' can be replaced by other adjectives (z. B. 'zu krank, um zu...'). The verb after 'um zu' stays in the infinitive form. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich bin zu müde, um zu kochen.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to cook.

meaning: used before an infinitive to mean 'too tired to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Combine with an infinitive verb: 'müde zu' expresses that someone is too tired to perform the action. In German you normally say 'zu' + infinitive (often with 'sein'): e.g. 'Ich bin zu müde, um zu ...' or more simply 'zu müde zu + Infinitiv' after an adjective. Common pattern: 'zu müde, um ... zu + Infinitiv' or in shortened speech 'zu müde zu + Infinitiv'.
target_language_example: Ich bin zu müde zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: I am too tired to work.

meaning: too tired to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive phrase introduced by 'zum' + noun or verb-noun (e.g., 'zum Laufen', 'zum Sprechen') to express that someone is too tired to perform that activity. More common alternatives: 'zu müde, um ... zu + infinitive' (e.g. 'zu müde, um zu laufen') or 'zu müde, um ...' with infinitive clause. 'Zum' here is a contraction of 'zu dem' used with nominalized verbs (gerund-like) or activity nouns.
target_language_example: Ich bin zu müde zum Kochen.
native_language_example: I am too tired to cook.

meaning: expresses that something must or should happen/has to be the case (often in past forms: 'should have known/acted that...').
additional_notes: This construction combines the modal verb 'müssen' with a subordinate clause introduced by 'dass'. In present it means 'must/has to'; in past modal forms (hätte wissen müssen, hätten verhindern müssen) it often translates as 'should have known/should have prevented' or 'would have had to'. Word order: the verb of the subordinate clause goes to the end. Common in regrets, obligations, and deductions.
target_language_example: Ich hätte wissen müssen, dass er lügt.
native_language_example: I should have known that he is lying.

meaning: Used in the structure 'Alles, was Sie ... müssen, ist ...' meaning 'All you have to ... is ...' or 'All you need to do is ...'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common sentence pattern combining a relative clause with müssen and the verb sein. Structure: 'Alles, was (du/Sie) [verb] müssen, ist [zu + infinitive / infinitive clause]' or with a finite clause. It expresses the single necessary action. Pronouns (du/Sie/er/etc.) can vary. Word order: the verb müssen appears in the relative clause; ist links to the following clause. Commas before 'ist' are optional in informal usage but often written.
target_language_example: Alles, was Sie machen müssen, ist, diesen Satz auswendig zu lernen.
native_language_example: All you have to do is memorize this sentence.

meaning: you must (your)
additional_notes: A combination of the modal verb müssen (must / have to) with the possessive pronoun Ihre (your, formal or plural). Commonly appears before a noun or verb phrase: "Sie müssen Ihre + [NOUN] + VERB" or "Sie müssen Ihre + VERB" when referring to something belonging to or related to 'you' (formal Sie or plural). In spoken/written German, word order matters: after müssen the verb or noun phrase follows (e.g. "Sie müssen Ihre E-Mail-Adresse bestätigen" = "You must confirm your email address"). Use Ihre (capital I) for formal singular/plural; informally with du you'd say "musst deine". "Sie müssen Ihre" is formal/polite.
target_language_example: Sie müssen Ihre Unterlagen bis Freitag einreichen.
native_language_example: You must submit your documents by Friday.

meaning: 'must' or 'have to' + (followed by a prepositional phrase with an)
additional_notes: This is the modal verb müssen combined with the preposition an. 'müssen' expresses obligation or necessity. 'an' requires an object and forms a prepositional phrase (e.g. an der Security vorbei = past 'by/through' security; an dem Treffen teilnehmen = participate in the meeting; an sich selbst glauben = believe in oneself). Word order and verb agreement follow normal German rules: the conjugated form of müssen matches the subject (ich muss, du musst, er/sie/es muss, wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie/Sie müssen). In examples with 'Entweder ... oder ...' the verb usually agrees with the nearer subject in spoken German, but formal writing may prefer agreement with the subject closer to the verb.
target_language_example: Wir müssen an der Kontrolle vorbei.
native_language_example: We have to go past the checkpoint.

meaning: 'must (do something) by' — expresses an obligation with a deadline
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (must/have to) with bis (by/until) + a time expression. Use to say someone is required to finish or be somewhere before a certain time or date. Word order: bis + time typically follows the verb phrase or appears before the main infinitive clause (e.g., Sie müssen bis Monatsende fertig sein). Time phrases can be a date, day, or phrases like 'Monatsende' or 'nächsten Montag'. The construction is compositional: müssen conveys obligation and bis specifies the deadline.
target_language_example: Sie müssen bis Monatsende mit dieser Arbeit fertig sein.
native_language_example: You must be finished with this work by the end of the month.

meaning: must (do) that; expresses obligation or necessity regarding something referred to as 'das' (that/this).
additional_notes: Phrase combines the modal verb müssen (to have to/must) with the demonstrative pronoun das (that/this). Appears in larger clauses; word order may change depending on tense and clause type (e.g., infinitive at sentence end). Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on pronoun and verb form.
target_language_example: Martha, Sie müssen das der Polizei sagen.
native_language_example: Martha, you must tell that to the police.

meaning: must do it
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb müssen (must/have to) with the pronoun das (that/it). Used to say that someone is obliged or required to do something; word order in German places the verb earlier in main clauses (Sie müssen das ...). Context supplies what "das" refers to. Can be used for necessities, obligations, or necessities accepted as unavoidable.
target_language_example: Wir müssen das Formular heute abschicken.
native_language_example: We have to send the form today.

meaning: 'must' or 'have to' with an added sense of expectation, insistence, or reassurance (like 'surely must' / 'we really have to').
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (must/have to) with doch, a particle that adds emphasis, surprise, objection, or reassurance depending on context. Here doch softens or strengthens the obligation — often translated as 'surely', 'after all', 'you must', or 'we really have to'. Common in spoken German. Tone can be persuasive ('we should really...') or mildly reproachful ('you must...').
target_language_example: Wir müssen doch heute etwas unternehmen.
native_language_example: We really have to do something today.

meaning: must have seen
additional_notes: Used to make a strong guess or logical conclusion about the past. In this construction, müssen expresses probability rather than obligation. The exact form changes with the subject: for example, ich muss gesehen haben, er muss gesehen haben, wir/sie/Sie müssen gesehen haben.
target_language_example: Sie müssen gesehen haben, wie er das Haus verlassen hat.
native_language_example: They must have seen how he left the house.

meaning: must/need to (do something) here; have to (be) here.
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'müssen' (must/need to) with the adverb 'hier' (here). Depending on sentence, 'müssen hier' can mean: something/someone must be here (existence), or an instruction/necessity to do something at this location (we must stay/leave/wait here). Word order and context determine whether an action follows ('Sie müssen hier aussteigen' = you must get off here) or the verb refers to being located here ('Die müssen hier drin sein' = they must be in here).
target_language_example: Wir müssen hier kurz warten.
native_language_example: We have to wait here for a moment.

meaning: must him
additional_notes: This is the verb müssen (must / have to) followed by the accusative pronoun ihn (him). In English you would usually say "must/have to + verb + him" — e.g. "We must warn him" or "You must know him well." Word order in German puts the conjugated verb in its normal position and the object (ihn) after it when appropriate. Context determines the full English translation; translate the whole sentence (e.g. "Sie müssen ihn ganz schön gut kennen." → "You must know him quite well.").
target_language_example: Wir müssen ihn heute warnen.
native_language_example: We must warn him today.

meaning: must always / have to always
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (must/have to) with immer (always). Used to say that something is required or necessary at all times or on every occasion. Word order depends on sentence; the finite verb (müssen) normally appears in second position in main clauses: 'Wir müssen immer pünktlich sein.' In subordinate clauses the verb goes to the end: '..., weil wir immer pünktlich sein müssen.' The form 'müssen immer' can appear when referring to third person or plural (e.g., 'sie müssen immer...') or in infinitival constructions where 'müssen' is adjacent to 'immer'.
target_language_example: In diesem Kurs müssen immer alle Teilnehmer pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: In this course, everyone must always be punctual.

meaning: must learn; need to learn (to do something)
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb müssen (must/need to) and lernen (to learn). Often followed by an infinitive clause introduced by a comma and 'zu' (e.g. müssen lernen, etwas zu tun) or a reflexive infinitive. Commonly used for advice, moral instruction, or stating necessity for personal or collective change.
target_language_example: Wir müssen lernen, einander zu respektieren.
native_language_example: We must learn to respect one another.

meaning: 'need to' / 'should' (colloquial, softening or casual tone)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen ('must/need to') with the colloquial particle mal, which softens or makes the statement less direct. Used in spoken German to express necessity, a suggestion, or a request that something be done (often soon or at some point). Common word order: subject + müssen + mal + verb (infinitive) or fixed phrases like 'Wir müssen mal reden' (We need to talk). Tone is informal; avoid in formal writing.
target_language_example: Wir müssen mal reden.
native_language_example: We need to talk.

meaning: must/need to (do something) tomorrow.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (must/need to) with the time expression morgen (tomorrow). Use with an infinitive verb or an implied action: e.g. ‚Wir müssen morgen fahren/aufstehen.‘ Word order: the finite verb (müssen) is in second position and the main infinitive goes to the end (Wir müssen morgen fahren). Commonly appears with time adverbs like früh or bei Tagesanbruch to specify when tomorrow.
target_language_example: Wir müssen morgen fahren.
native_language_example: We have to drive/leave tomorrow.

meaning: must get out / have to get out (leave a place)
additional_notes: Colloquial combination of the modal verb 'müssen' + separable particle 'raus' (short for 'heraus'/'hinaus'). Used to say someone needs to leave a location or escape a situation. Can be used with different subjects: 'Ich/Wir/Sie müssen raus.' Context determines urgency (from simple necessity to strong emotional/urgent push).
target_language_example: Wir müssen raus, bevor der Regen kommt.
native_language_example: We have to get out before the rain comes.

meaning: need to (do something) quickly; must hurry
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (must/need to) with the adverb schnell (quickly). Used to express urgency — that an action must be done fast. Word order in German: schnell typically follows the verb or appears after the object depending on sentence structure (e.g., "Wir müssen schnell handeln" = we must act quickly). In casual speech you might also hear contractions like "wir müssen uns beeilen" (we must hurry).
target_language_example: Wir müssen schnell die Tür schließen, bevor der Regen kommt.
native_language_example: We need to quickly close the door before the rain comes.

meaning: must they
additional_notes: This is context-dependent. sie can be the subject "they" (for example, Müssen sie gehen? = "Must they go?") or the object "her/them" after müssen (for example, Wir müssen sie suchen = "We must look for her/them"). Capitalized Sie means formal "you," so capitalization matters.
target_language_example: Wir müssen sie jetzt anrufen.
native_language_example: We have to call them now.

meaning: 'must' or 'have to' + reflexive 'ourselves' + preposition 'on' — used to say we need to focus on, prepare for, or agree on something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common construction: müssen (we must) + reflexive pronoun uns + auf + noun/phrase. It can mean 'we must focus on', 'we must prepare for', or 'we must agree on', depending on the following noun or verb (often an infinitive or noun phrase). Word order and case: the object after 'auf' typically takes the accusative. Use with verbs like 'konzentrieren (auf)', 'vorbereiten (auf)', 'einigen (auf)'.
target_language_example: Wir müssen uns auf die Prüfung vorbereiten.
native_language_example: We must prepare ourselves for the exam.

meaning: we must/need to (do something to) our ... (first-person plural obligation + masculine/neuter accusative possessive)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb müssen (we must/need to) with the possessive unseren (our, masculine or neuter singular in accusative). Used when the subject 'wir' has an obligation to do something to a specific noun that is masculine or neuter (e.g., Haushalt, Kamin, Plan, Wagen). Change unseren to unsere/euren etc. depending on the gender/case of the noun.
target_language_example: Wir müssen unseren Garten gießen.
native_language_example: We must water our garden.

meaning: must be careful / need to be careful
additional_notes: A short construction combining the modal verb 'müssen' (must/to have to) with the adjective 'vorsichtig' (careful). In natural sentences you normally include a subject and appropriate verb form (e.g. 'Wir müssen vorsichtig sein'). Used for warnings or instructions.
target_language_example: Wir müssen vorsichtig sein, wenn wir die Treppe runtergehen; also müssen vorsichtig handeln.
native_language_example: We must be careful when we go down the stairs; so we need to act carefully.

meaning: must know; need to know (that/what/who/etc.). Expresses that information is required or necessary to be known.
additional_notes: Used with conjugated müssen + wissen; commonly followed by a clause introduced by question words (warum, was, wer, wie) or by a declarative clause. Formal and informal contexts possible depending on pronoun and tone (Sie vs. du/ihr).
target_language_example: Wir müssen wissen, warum du das getan hast.
native_language_example: We need to know why you did that.

meaning: have to go (leave) now / must be off
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase combining the modal verb müssen + los (los meaning 'away'/'off'). Used to express the need to leave immediately. In actual usage you normally conjugate müssen for the person (e.g., Ich muss los, Wir müssen los). The bare infinitive phrase 'müssen los' appears in contexts like reported speech, notes, headlines, or fragments (e.g., 'Wir müssen los'). Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Wir müssen los, wenn wir den Zug nicht verpassen wollen.
native_language_example: We have to go if we don't want to miss the train.

meaning: must do it
additional_notes: Second-person plural (ihr) form of müssen + object pronoun es. Used when talking to a group (you all) telling them they must/ have to do something. Word order: in statements with a pronoun object, 'müsst' (verb) comes second and 'es' follows (or can appear later depending on sentence). The subject 'ihr' (you plural) is implied by 'müsst'.
target_language_example: Ihr müsst es bis morgen fertig machen.
native_language_example: You (all) must finish it by tomorrow.

meaning: you (plural, informal) must / have to (reflexive: something you do to yourselves)
additional_notes: Combination of 'müsst' (2nd-person plural of 'müssen' = must/have to) + reflexive pronoun 'euch' (yourselves). Used when addressing more than one person informally (ihr). The verb that follows is reflexive or requires 'euch' (e.g. euch beeilen, euch Sorgen machen, euch fragen). Word order: in main clauses 'müsst' is the verb in second position and the reflexive pronoun usually comes after the verb or later depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Ihr müsst euch beeilen, sonst verpasst ihr den Bus.
native_language_example: You (plural) must hurry, otherwise you'll miss the bus.

meaning: 'you (plural) only have to' / 'you just need to' (instructional)
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'müssen' (second-person plural: ihr müsst) and 'nur' meaning 'only' or 'just'. Used to give simple instructions or to minimize effort/requirements. Directed at 'ihr' (you all/informal plural). For formal or singular forms, verbs change (Sie müssen nur / du musst nur).
target_language_example: Ihr müsst nur die Tür schließen.
native_language_example: You just have to close the door.

meaning: would have to / should (he) — expresses conditional necessity or probability about 'he'.
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) of 'müssen'. Common in conditional sentences or to indicate a probable assumption. Word order: verb form 'müsste' before the subject 'er' (inversion can appear depending on sentence). Often appears with if-clauses (hätte..., würde...) or to soften a statement (polite/uncertain).
target_language_example: Wenn er die Regeln kennt, müsste er Bescheid wissen.
native_language_example: If he knows the rules, he should/would have to know.

meaning: you (plural, informal) must/need to (do something) — second person plural of 'müssen' with the reflexive pronoun 'euch'.
additional_notes: Formed from the modal verb 'müssen' (ihr müsst) plus the reflexive pronoun 'euch'. Used when addressing a group of people informally (ihr). The verb is reflexive in sentences that require a reflexive object (e.g., beruhigen, beeilen, anstrengen). Spelling note: modern orthography prefers 'müsst' with 'ss' (Ihr müsst euch), but 'müßt' (with ß) appears in older texts or certain keyboards. Word order follows normal German rules (verb second in main clauses, verb-final in subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: Ihr müßt euch beeilen, wenn ihr noch vor dem Dunkelwerden zu Hause sein wollt.
native_language_example: You (all) must hurry if you want to be home before it gets dark.

meaning: you (plural, informal) must / have to (your ...).
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb müsst (older spelling müßt) for ihr (you plural informal) + the possessive eure (your, plural). It precedes a noun (e.g. eure Pflicht, eure Zeit) and is used to give instructions or state obligations addressed to a group. In contemporary standard German spelling, 'müsst' or 'müsst' with umlaut is correct (informal spoken/written may show 'müsst' or older 'müßt'). Use full sentence order (e.g. 'Ihr müsst eure ...') or drop 'ihr' in imperatives for direct commands to a group ('Müsst eure ...' is nonstandard).
target_language_example: Ihr müßt eure Zeit irgendwie besser nutzen.
native_language_example: You (all) must somehow use your time better.

meaning: well
additional_notes: A conversational filler used to show mild hesitation, doubt, resignation or to soften a statement. Tone and context determine exact nuance (acceptance, understatement, reluctant agreement). Often written colloquially as 'naja'.
target_language_example: Na ja, das war nicht perfekt, aber in Ordnung.
native_language_example: Well, that wasn't perfect, but it's okay.

meaning: "of course" / "sure" (used to agree or confirm)
additional_notes: Informal, friendly way to give a positive answer or show agreement. Can be used alone as a short reply (like "sure") or in a sentence (e.g., "Na klar, ich helfe dir"). Tone can range from enthusiastic to slightly sarcastic depending on intonation.
target_language_example: Na klar helfe ich dir mit den Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: Of course I'll help you with the homework.

meaning: 'so what?' / 'and?' — a dismissive or challenging response expressing indifference or that something is no problem.
additional_notes: Used to react when someone points out something you don't care about or to challenge an accusation. Tone can be dismissive, annoyed, or defiant depending on context and intonation. Common in colloquial speech. Can be followed by a question mark or used rhetorically (no answer expected).
target_language_example: Du hast den Bericht nicht gelesen? Na und?
native_language_example: You didn't read the report? So what?

meaning: 'home' or 'to (one's) home' (motion toward or arrival at home).
additional_notes: Colloquial/idiomatic variant of 'nach Hause' used in everyday spoken German and some regional dialects. It indicates movement toward home ('go home') or arriving at home ('came home'). In standard written German, 'nach Hause' is preferred. Examples can appear with different verbs and tenses (gehen, kommen, bringen).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt nach Haus.
native_language_example: I'm going home now.

meaning: home
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion to show direction toward home: going, coming, driving, etc. It means movement to home, not being there. Compare with "zu Hause" = "at home."
target_language_example: Wir fahren jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: We're going home now.

meaning: toward (someone's) home / to go to someone's home
additional_notes: Used when indicating movement to a home (often with a verb of motion). Commonly appears as 'nach Hause' (to home) or 'zu + person' (to someone's place). 'nach Hause zu' combines both and is followed by a person or pronoun: e.g. 'Ich gehe nach Hause zu dir' (I'm going to your place/home). Native speakers more often say 'zu dir nach Hause' or 'zu Hause' depending on emphasis and word order.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend nach Hause zu dir.
native_language_example: I'm going to your place/home this evening.

meaning: about you / for you / after you (depends on context); often 'asking about you' or 'looking for you'.
additional_notes: Literal preposition 'nach' + polite pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal 'you'). Meaning changes with context: 'nach Ihnen suchen' = to look for you; 'sich nach Ihnen erkundigen' / 'nach Ihnen gefragt' = to ask about you; 'nach Ihnen sehen' = to check on you; 'nach Ihnen lesen' = to read aloud after you or read following your example (rare). Used with formal Sie (Ihnen).
target_language_example: Die Nachbarn haben sich nach Ihnen erkundigt.
native_language_example: The neighbors asked about you.

meaning: after all those (years/events); after so many (things/time).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a long period of time or many occurrences already passed (often followed by a noun like ‚Jahren‘). Common in spoken and written German to express that something has happened or changed because much time has passed. Word order: ‚nach all den + [noun in dative plural]‘ (e.g. ‚nach all den Jahren‘).
target_language_example: Nach all den Jahren kenne ich dich besser.
native_language_example: After all those years I know you better.

meaning: to (over) there; toward that place.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward a place that is farther away from the speaker. 'Dort' means 'there' (a specific place a bit farther away). In many contexts German speakers prefer 'dorthin' or just 'dort' or 'nach' + place name (e.g. 'nach Hause', 'nach Berlin'). 'Nach dort' is less common and can sound a bit marked or emphatic; 'nach dort und dort' lists multiple destinations. For distance expressions, 'von hier bis dorthin' or 'von hier bis dort' are more natural than 'von hier bis nach dort', but all can be understood.
target_language_example: Geh nicht nach dort allein.
native_language_example: Don't go over there alone.

meaning: outside
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement to the outside or being outdoors. Often appears with verbs of motion (gehen, müssen) or as an instruction (Geh nach draußen!). 'Draußen' can stand alone meaning 'outside'; 'nach draußen' emphasizes direction/movement toward the outside.
target_language_example: Wir gehen jetzt nach draußen, es ist schönes Wetter.
native_language_example: We're going outside now, the weather is nice.

meaning: inside; into the inside (movement toward the interior).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement from outside to the inside (into a building/room). Common with verbs of motion (gehen, kommen, laufen). 'Nach drinnen' emphasizes direction; you can also say 'reingehen' (colloquial) or 'hineingehen'. Formal polite form: 'Sind Sie nach drinnen gegangen?'.
target_language_example: Wir sollten jetzt nach drinnen gehen, es wird kalt.
native_language_example: We should go inside now; it's getting cold.

meaning: after/for something; looking or searching for something (usually 'for something').
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs of searching or moving (suchen nach, graben nach, auf der Suche nach). Here 'etwas' means 'something' (unspecified). Word order: verb + nach + etwas (or in questions: Sucht er nach etwas?). Can also mean 'after' in spatial/temporal senses but in these examples it means 'for' or 'in search of.'
target_language_example: Sie fährt in die Stadt, weil sie nach etwas Schönem sucht.
native_language_example: She is going to town because she is looking for something nice.

meaning: 'to the back' / 'backwards' (movement or direction toward the rear)
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position toward the back or rear. Common in commands (e.g., telling someone or something to move back) and descriptions (e.g., leaning/backward movement). Context determines whether it's physical movement ('move backwards') or position ('toward the back').
target_language_example: Geh ein Stück nach hinten, bitte.
native_language_example: Step back a bit, please.

meaning: to backfire; to have the opposite (usually negative) effect than intended.
additional_notes: Idiomatic phrasal expression used when a plan, action, or remark ends up causing problems or producing the opposite result. Often used with 'könnte' or other modal verbs to warn that something may backfire. Not literal (doesn't mean 'go backwards').
target_language_example: Sei vorsichtig — das könnte nach hinten losgehen.
native_language_example: Be careful — that could backfire.

meaning: inward; toward the inside (movement or direction).
additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction into an interior or toward the center. Can be literal (e.g., a door opens inward, someone runs inside) or more figurative (looking inward, introspection). Often contrasts with "nach außen" (outward). Common in everyday speech and neutral register.
target_language_example: Er ging nach innen, weil es draußen regnete.
native_language_example: He went inside because it was raining outside.

meaning: after every meal (used in instructions like 'after every meal, the...').
additional_notes: This phrase commonly appears before a body part or action in instructions: e.g. 'nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne putzen' = 'brush your teeth after every meal.' Grammatically: 'nach jeder Mahlzeit' = 'after each/ every meal'; the definite article 'die' introduces the following noun (here 'Zähne'). In everyday speech you may hear shortened forms like 'nach jeder Mahlzeit Zähne putzen' but including 'die' is natural.
target_language_example: Du solltest nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne putzen.
native_language_example: You should brush your teeth after every meal.

meaning: 'to the left' / 'leftwards' (direction)
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the left side. Common in commands (Dreh nach links!), descriptions (Der Fluss biegt nach links) and navigation (nach der Ecke nach links). Often follows verbs of movement or position. Literal translation to English is possible.
target_language_example: Bieg an der Ampel nach links.
native_language_example: Turn left at the traffic light.

meaning: up; upstairs; upwards (movement toward a higher place or direction).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward a higher position or floor. Can mean 'go upstairs' (movement into an upper floor) or simply 'look up' when combined with verbs like 'schauen'. Context decides whether it's physical (stairs, ladder) or directional (look up, move up). Common and neutral.
target_language_example: Komm bitte nach oben, das Essen ist fertig.
native_language_example: Please come upstairs, the food is ready.

meaning: to the right; rightwards; turn/move to the right.
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward the right side. Common with verbs of motion (gehen, fahren, bewegen) and as an imperative (commands). Can mean 'turn right' in driving/walking contexts or 'move something to the right' for objects.
target_language_example: Gehe die Straße entlang und biege nach rechts.
native_language_example: Walk along the street and turn right.

meaning: according to his (or its) — used to say something is done following someone's ideas, abilities, needs, etc.
additional_notes: Nach + dative indicates 'according to' or 'in accordance with'. 'Seinen' is the dative masculine/neuter or accusative plural form depending on the phrase; here it's part of fixed expressions like 'nach seinen Ideen' (according to his ideas) or 'nach seinen Fähigkeiten' (according to his abilities). Common in constructions like 'jeder nach seinen Fähigkeiten' (each according to his abilities). Choose the pronoun gender/number to match the noun that follows (z. B. 'nach ihren' for plural/feminine).
target_language_example: Die Möbel wurden nach seinen Wünschen ausgewählt.
native_language_example: The furniture was chosen according to his wishes.

meaning: after/after such; used to talk about time passed or to comment on amount/appearance (e.g. "after so many years" or "doesn't sound like that much").
additional_notes: Commonly appears in two patterns: "nach so vielen Jahren" = "after so many years" (time elapsed), and "klingt nicht nach so viel ..." = "doesn't sound like that much ..." (assessment of quantity/quality). "nach" here means "after" or "like", and "so" intensifies ("so many", "that much"). Word order: "nach" + "so" + amount or clause.
target_language_example: Nach so kurzer Zeit hast du viel gelernt.
native_language_example: After such a short time you have learned a lot.

meaning: down; downward; downstairs.
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward a lower place or position. Can describe physical movement (going downstairs, descending) or gaze/direction (looking down). Common and neutral; often follows verbs like gehen, schauen, fahren. Can pair with 'nach oben' (up).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt nach unten.
native_language_example: I'm going down now.

meaning: forward; to the front; toward the front
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the front or ahead. Common with verbs of motion (gehen, rücken, fallen, beugen) and as an instruction (Schau nach vorne!). Can mean physically moving to the front of a room, leaning forward, or advancing in position. Word order: 'nach vorne' usually follows the verb or object.
target_language_example: Stell dich bitte nach vorne.
native_language_example: Please stand at the front.

meaning: used in fixed expressions to mean 'after' or 'according to' when combined with another word (e.g. 'nach und nach' = 'gradually').
additional_notes: Alone, 'nach und' does not form a complete phrase; it appears as part of longer fixed expressions (most commonly 'nach und nach'). 'Nach und nach' means 'gradually', 'little by little'. Other combinations are rare. 'Nach' is a common preposition meaning 'after' or 'to', and 'und' means 'and'.
target_language_example: Wir lernen nach und nach mehr Vokabeln.
native_language_example: We learn more vocabulary little by little.

meaning: gradually; little by little; step by step.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes or happens slowly over time. Can be placed at the beginning or in the sentence. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Nach und nach lernte sie, dem neuen Tagesablauf zu folgen.
native_language_example: Little by little she learned to follow the new daily routine.

meaning: still; as before; continuing to be the same
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation or state remains unchanged. Similar to 'immer noch' but slightly more formal or emphatic. Common in written and spoken German. Often placed before the adjective or verb phrase it modifies.
target_language_example: Der Laden ist nach wie vor geschlossen.
native_language_example: The shop is still closed.

meaning: 'this/this afternoon with' — used to say you'll do something in the afternoon together with someone or ask if someone will join/help you in the afternoon.
additional_notes: nachmittag (lowercase: nachmittag or Nachmittag) means 'afternoon'. When combined with mit + pronoun or noun, it indicates doing something together or expecting someone's help 'in the afternoon'. Word order in German often places time expressions (heute nachmittag / morgen nachmittag) early in the sentence: 'Heute nachmittag mit mir ...'. Use appropriate verb forms depending on pronoun and sentence structure.
target_language_example: Heute nachmittag mit mir ins Kino kommen?
native_language_example: Come to the cinema with me this afternoon?

meaning: an invitation or suggestion: 'swim with us in the afternoon' (literally: 'afternoon swim with us' / 'swim with us in the afternoon').
additional_notes: This is a short informal phrase made of simple words: 'Nachmittag' (afternoon), 'mit uns' (with us), 'schwimmen' (to swim). It can be used as a suggestion or plan: e.g. 'Wollen wir Nachmittag mit uns schwimmen?' — however, the more natural German order would be 'nachmittags mit uns schwimmen' or 'am Nachmittag mit uns schwimmen' (add a verb like 'gehen' or 'wollen'). Use 'nachmittags' (adverb) or 'am Nachmittag' (time phrase) when speaking naturally.
target_language_example: Kommst du am Nachmittag mit uns schwimmen?
native_language_example: Will you come swim with us in the afternoon?

meaning: at night (it is)... — used to talk about how things are during the night.
additional_notes: Nachts = 'at night' (general time expression). Combined with 'ist' (is), it begins statements describing conditions or states that occur at night (e.g., temperature, noise, light). Common in simple observational sentences: 'Nachts ist es ...'. 'Es' often follows 'ist' to refer to weather, temperature, darkness, etc.
target_language_example: Nachts ist es oft sehr ruhig hier.
native_language_example: At night it is often very quiet here.

meaning: not at night; don't (do something) at night
additional_notes: Uses 'nachts' (at night) with 'nicht' to negate an action occurring at night. Common in instructions or statements about inability to do something during nighttime. Word order: 'nachts nicht' typically follows the verb or object it negates in a clause (e.g., 'er soll nachts nicht ...').
target_language_example: Bitte nachts nicht so laut Musik hören.
native_language_example: Please don't play music so loudly at night.

meaning: took something / removed something (simple past).
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of nehmen + etwas. Used to say someone took, removed, or picked up an unspecified object. Common in storytelling and descriptions of actions. In spoken German, the Perfekt (hat etwas genommen) is often used instead of nahm etwas.
target_language_example: Sie nahm etwas aus der Schublade und zeigte es mir.
native_language_example: She took something out of the drawer and showed it to me.

meaning: she took
additional_notes: Past tense of nehmen (to take). Meaning depends on context and the direct object: 'took' (physically grabbed), 'accepted' (received), or in some expressions 'took under her care' / 'took into protection'. Word order 'nahm sie' shows past simple (Präteritum) with a feminine or plural third-person object pronoun 'sie' (her/them) or subject 'sie' can be subject only in different order—here it's the verb + object. English translation often needs adjustment (e.g. 'took her under her wing', 'took pity on her', 'accepted the banknote').
target_language_example: Wortlos nahm sie das Paket entgegen.
native_language_example: She accepted the package without a word.

meaning: 'of course' or 'naturally' followed by 'I' — used to introduce what the speaker is saying about themselves
additional_notes: natürlich means 'of course' or 'naturally'. When followed by ich it often emphasizes the speaker's certainty, reaction, or a contrast (e.g. 'Of course I remember', 'Of course I feel guilty'). In spoken German the comma may be omitted and intonation conveys the pause: 'Natürlich ich ...' or more commonly 'Natürlich habe ich ...'. Useful for starting a sentence about yourself with emphasis.
target_language_example: Natürlich, ich helfe dir gern.
native_language_example: Of course, I'll help you.

meaning: of course (it/he/she/they) was / naturally was
additional_notes: Natürich war is the adverb 'natürlich' (meaning 'of course' or 'naturally') followed by the past-tense verb 'war' (was). It is used to emphasize that something was true or to accept/blame something. The subject (er, es, sie, etc.) may follow or be obvious from context. Word order can change depending on the sentence (e.g., 'Natürlich war es deine Schuld' or 'Es war natürlich deine Schuld').
target_language_example: Natürlich war er damals nervös.
native_language_example: Of course he was nervous back then.

meaning: next to you (used colloquially/idiomatically to indicate position toward or beside someone; grammatically non-standard in many contexts)
additional_notes: Standard German uses the dative after positional prepositions: 'neben dir' for location ('beside you'). 'Neben dich' uses accusative and can appear colloquially to indicate movement toward a position next to someone (direction). However, many native speakers would still prefer constructions like 'Ich setze mich neben dich' only in casual speech; prescriptive grammar recommends 'Ich setze mich neben dich' → more standard: 'Ich setze mich neben dich' is often avoided — correct standard forms: location: 'Er steht neben dir.'; movement/direction: 'Stell den Stuhl neben dich.' For beginners: learn 'neben dir' for 'next to you' (static). Use 'neben dich' only when context clearly marks direction and in informal speech; otherwise avoid.
target_language_example: Komm her und stell dich neben dich!
native_language_example: Come here and stand next to you! (colloquial/non-standard German)

meaning: beside him / next to him (positioning someone or yourself next to a male person).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location next to a male person (accusative pronoun 'ihn' after preposition 'neben' when movement toward or placement is implied). With static location you might hear 'neben ihm' (dative). Common with verbs of sitting, standing, kneeling, or placing (setzen, stellen, knien).
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich neben ihn und begann zu lesen.
native_language_example: She sat down next to him and began to read.

meaning: next to his (masculine or plural object in accusative).
additional_notes: A preposition phrase: 'neben' (next to/beside) + the possessive pronoun 'seinen' in accusative. Use when the thing next to which someone sits/is placed is masculine singular or plural and the verb requires the accusative (e.g., setzen, stellen, legen). Gender and case matter: for feminine it would be 'neben seine' (rare; usually 'neben seineN' isn't correct), for neuter 'neben sein', and for dative after some verbs or contexts you would use 'neben seinem'.
target_language_example: Tom setzte sich neben seinen Bruder.
native_language_example: Tom sat down next to his brother.

meaning: 'next to us' or 'beside us' (indicates something or someone located adjacent to the speaker and others).
additional_notes: Used to describe physical proximity. Can refer to a person, object, or place next to the speaker (singular/plural context depends on who 'uns' includes). Common with verbs like stehen, wohnen, sitzen. Word order: 'neben uns' usually follows the verb or noun phrase (e.g., 'Er wohnt neben uns', 'Direkt neben uns').
target_language_example: Der Laden ist direkt neben uns.
native_language_example: The shop is right next to us.

meaning: I accept your ... (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: A first-person present form of 'annehmen' (ich nehme ... an) followed by the possessive 'deine' (your, feminine/plural or informal). Used to accept something someone offers (conditions, apology, challenge). The full phrase requires a noun: e.g. 'nehme deine Entschuldigung an'. To refuse, add 'nicht' before 'an' or after the noun: 'Ich nehme deine Entschuldigung nicht an.'
target_language_example: Ich nehme deine Einladung an.
native_language_example: I accept your invitation.

meaning: I take her/it/them (depending on context).
additional_notes: ‘Nehme’ is first-person singular present of nehmen (to take); ‘sie’ can mean she, her, they/them, or formal you (less common) depending on context. Word order may change with particles: e.g. ‘Ich nehme sie an.’ (I accept/assume it), ‘Ich nehme sie mit.’ (I take her/it along), ‘Ich nehme sie zurück.’ (I take it back). Pay attention to separable verbs (mitnehmen → 'nehme ... mit').
target_language_example: Ich nehme sie mit zum Park.
native_language_example: I'll take her/it along to the park.

meaning: take the
additional_notes: Literally 'take the ...'. 'nehmen' is 'to take'; 'den' is the masculine accusative definite article ('the') and can also appear before masculine nouns or in set phrases. German word order may separate verb and article in sentences (e.g., imperative or with modal verbs). Examples show choosing a means of transport or a route: 'wir nehmen den Bus' = 'we take the bus'; 'nehmen den Weg' = 'take the way/route'. Can also appear in imperatives: 'Nehmen den Bus!' (colloquial: 'Wir nehmen den Bus, Idiot.').
target_language_example: Wir nehmen den Zug um 8 Uhr.
native_language_example: We'll take the train at 8 o'clock.

meaning: 'take the' (informal plural command or suggestion) referring to a masculine noun in accusative.
additional_notes: Nehmt is the imperative (or present-tense ihr-form) of nehmen for 'ihr' (you plural). Used to give a command or suggestion to multiple people (e.g., 'take the car/bus/rum'). Den is the masculine singular accusative article, so it's used before masculine nouns (der Wagen, den Zug, den Bus, den Rum). For a single person use 'nimm den' (du), for polite/formal use 'nehmen Sie den'.
target_language_example: Nehmt den Bus zur Haltestelle.
native_language_example: Take the bus to the stop.

meaning: imperative plural 'take the' (command to multiple people).
additional_notes: Nehmt is the informal plural imperative of nehmen (to take). Used when speaking to more than one person (ihr). 'Die' is the definite article matching the noun that follows (plural or feminine singular depending on case). Common in set phrases (e.g. "Nehmt die Beine in die Hand" = hurry up). Tone is informal; for formal address use 'nehmen Sie'.
target_language_example: Nehmt die Jacken mit, es wird kalt.
native_language_example: Take the jackets with you, it's going to be cold.

meaning: take me / include me / believe me (depends on context)
additional_notes: Nehmt mich is the 2nd-person plural (ihr) imperative or statement form of 'nehmen' + 'mich' (me). Meaning changes with context: as a question or command it can mean 'Are you taking me (with you)?' or 'Take me (along)!' In ironic or conversational contexts (e.g., 'Ihr nehmt mich wohl nicht ernst') it can mean 'you consider me / you take me (seriously)'. Tone and punctuation (question, command, flat statement) determine whether it's a request, demand, or complaint.
target_language_example: Wenn ihr in den Park geht, nehmt mich bitte mit.
native_language_example: If you go to the park, please take me with you.

meaning: 'take her/it/them' or 'grab her/it/them' (informal plural imperative)
additional_notes: Nehmt is the imperative (command) form for ihr (you plural) of nehmen (to take). Sie can mean 'her', 'it', or 'them' depending on context; capitalization (Sie) would mean formal 'you'. Use when speaking to a group you address as 'ihr'. Common in commands like 'take them!' or 'catch her!'
target_language_example: Nehmt sie bitte nicht zu leicht.
native_language_example: Please don't take them too lightly.

meaning: No, thanks (polite refusal).
additional_notes: A common, polite way to decline an offer or invitation. Can be used alone or followed by a short explanation (e.g., reason). Tone depends on context and intonation — very direct but still polite. Not rude by itself.
target_language_example: Nein danke, ich habe schon gegessen.
native_language_example: No thanks, I've already eaten.

meaning: to call oneself; to be called (used for names or labels people/groups use for themselves).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb construction (nennen + sich). Often used to report what someone or a group calls themselves: 'Sie nennen sich ...' = 'They call themselves ...' Can also be used with a name or label: 'Er nennt sich Arzt' (He calls himself a doctor). In informal speech you may also hear 'sich nennen' in similar contexts. Word order: the name follows the verb.
target_language_example: Sie nennen sich Die Freiwilligen.
native_language_example: They call themselves the volunteers.

meaning: 'they call (her/him/you/them)'.
additional_notes: A form of the verb nennen (to call/name). 'Nennen sie' here is the third-person plural present indicative (they call). Context decides the object (sie can be 'her' or 'them' depending on capitalization and previous context). Use with a direct object or a name/nickname: 'Die Leute nennen sie Ratten' = 'The people call them rats.'
target_language_example: Die Nachbarn nennen sie immer Maria.
native_language_example: The neighbors always call her Maria.

meaning: 'we call' or 'we name' (used to say what we call someone or something).
additional_notes: Present tense, first-person plural of 'nennen' (to call/name). Common in suggestions (Wie nennen wir...?) and statements about established names (nennen wir ihn...). Often followed by a direct object (e.g. jemanden/etwas + Akkusativ). Can be used for temporary or conventional names.
target_language_example: Nennen wir das Buch 'Abenteuer'.
native_language_example: Let's call the book 'Adventure'.

meaning: 'nice and' — used to link two positive qualities or to politely request someone to do something (with 'so nett und' = 'be so kind as to').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in two patterns: 1) as part of a description: "nett und + adjective" (e.g. "nett und freundlich" = "nice and friendly"); 2) in polite requests with "so nett und + verb" meaning "be so kind as to..." (e.g. "Seien Sie so nett und..." = "Please be so kind as to..."). The phrase is neutral and polite. Word order and formality change with the verb and subject (Sei/Seien/Sie etc.).
target_language_example: Seien Sie so nett und schließen Sie bitte das Fenster.
native_language_example: Please be so kind as to close the window.

meaning: the new house
additional_notes: This is the phrase for 'new house' but grammatically it should be 'neues Haus' (neuter noun 'Haus' takes the adjective ending -es in nominative/accusative singular). You will hear 'neue Haus' sometimes in casual speech or dialect, but use 'neues Haus' in standard German. Use appropriate endings for other cases (e.g. 'des neuen Hauses', 'im neuen Haus').
target_language_example: Ich freue mich auf das neue Haus.
native_language_example: I'm looking forward to the new house.

meaning: new teacher(s)
additional_notes: 'neue Lehrer' is the plural form meaning 'new teachers'. The corresponding singular is 'neuer Lehrer' (masculine) or 'neue Lehrerin' (feminine). Adjective endings change with gender, number, and case (e.g., 'der neue Lehrer' vs. 'ein neuer Lehrer'). In plural nominative with a definite article: 'die neuen Lehrer'.
target_language_example: Die neue Lehrer hatten am Montag ein Treffen mit der Schulleitung.
native_language_example: The new teachers had a meeting with the school administration on Monday.

meaning: new language
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to a language that is new (to someone) or newly created. Can mean a language someone wants to learn (eine neue Sprache lernen) or an invented/novel way of writing/speaking (eine neue Sprache schaffen). 'Neue' agrees in gender/case with 'Sprache' (feminine).
target_language_example: Ich lerne eine neue Sprache: Spanisch.
native_language_example: I'm learning a new language: Spanish.

meaning: new world; a new place, situation, or way of life (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Can be used literally (e.g., discovery of unknown lands) or figuratively to describe discovering a new culture, experience, or perspective. In contexts like the examples it means encountering a different culture or way of life. Word order: adjective before noun; adjective takes appropriate endings in sentences.
target_language_example: Durch das Auslandssemester öffnete sich für ihn eine neue Welt.
native_language_example: The semester abroad opened up a new world for him.

meaning: to introduce (someone) — specifically to introduce a new boyfriend or a new male friend.
additional_notes: Used when you present a new friend/boyfriend to other people (family, friends, colleagues). Context determines whether 'Freund' means 'friend' or 'boyfriend' (romantic). To say 'introduce a new female partner', use 'neue Freundin vorstellen'. Common constructions: 'Ich möchte dir meinen neuen Freund vorstellen.'
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir meinen neuen Freund vorstellen.
native_language_example: I want to introduce my new boyfriend to you.

meaning: to (do something) with/to a new car — used in infinitive constructions about getting, driving, or using a new car
additional_notes: This fragment appears inside different infinitive phrases (e.g. 'mir ein neues Auto zu kaufen', 'mein neues Auto zu fahren'). It isn't a stand-alone phrase; the verb and any dative/accusative pronouns around it determine the full meaning. Common verbs: kaufen (to buy), fahren (to drive), überzeugen (to persuade). Word order: German often uses an infinitive at the end of the sentence with 'zu' before the infinitive (zu kaufen, zu fahren).
target_language_example: Er plant, sich nächstes Jahr ein neues Auto zu kaufen.
native_language_example: He plans to buy himself a new car next year.

meaning: from nine to (used to give the time range '9 to ...').
additional_notes: Used with times to indicate a time span starting at nine (o'clock). Commonly appears as 'von neun bis (fünf)' = 'from nine to five'. Can be combined with full times (neun Uhr) or parts of the hour (halb sechs = 5:30). In speech, 'neun' alone often implies 'neun Uhr'.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite von neun bis fünf.
native_language_example: I work from nine to five.

meaning: not when / not at the time that; used to deny something about a specific time or situation
additional_notes: Often appears in spoken or literary German to say that something was not true at a particular moment or under a particular condition. Depending on sentence structure it can mean 'not when', 'not as', or 'not even when'. Commas often separate 'nicht' and 'als' in written examples. It is not a fixed idiom but a combination used to negate a clause introduced by 'als'.
target_language_example: Ich war nicht, als sie anrief, zu Hause.
native_language_example: I wasn't at home when she called.

meaning: used to introduce a consequence or alternative when something is not the case (if not, then...).
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written German. Often appears as 'Wenn nicht, dann...' or simply 'Nicht, dann...' after a negative clause to introduce what should happen next, a consequence, an alternative option, or resignation. Can be used emphatically: 'Wenn nicht, dann eben...'.
target_language_example: Wenn nicht, dann versuchen wir es später noch einmal.
native_language_example: If not, then we'll try again later.

meaning: a spoken correction or rejection meaning 'no, that's not so' or 'not that' (used to deny or correct something just said).
additional_notes: This is an informal, conversational way to contradict or correct a statement. Word order and punctuation in examples suggest a short interjection: 'Nicht, das ...' or 'Ich war das nicht' (I wasn't the one). In the second example the comma separates a negation from an explanation; native speakers might more commonly say 'Nein, das tut weh' (No, that hurts) or 'Das tut nicht weh' (That doesn't hurt). Use when quickly denying responsibility or correcting a claim.
target_language_example: Nicht, das habe ich nicht gesagt.
native_language_example: No, I didn't say that.

meaning: a structure meaning 'not that the...' used to introduce a clause expressing negation of a statement about a masculine noun (der).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common word order: 'nicht, dass' (or 'nicht dass') negates the following subordinate clause. 'der' is the masculine definite article/relative word starting the subordinate clause (e.g. 'der Krieg', 'der Soldat'). In English: 'not that the...' or 'I don't think that the...'. Often appears with verbs of thinking/believing (denken, glauben) or in direct speech to correct or warn. Word order: main clause + ',' + subordinate clause beginning with 'dass'.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass der Hund gefährlich ist.
native_language_example: I don't think that the dog is dangerous.

meaning: 'don't' or 'not', used in negative sentences followed by a familiar vocative (my ...).
additional_notes: This pair appears when a negative imperative or statement uses a vocative address with a possessive noun like meine Liebe, meine Mädchen, meine Süße, meine Cousinen. In English you'd usually translate the whole phrase as 'don't...my [dear ones]' or 'not...my [relatives]', e.g. 'Don't cry, my dear.' The comma shows direct address (vocative). The word order in German often places 'nicht' before the verb or clause element being negated; the vocative (meine + noun) simply calls the person(s).
target_language_example: Weine nicht, meine Liebe.
native_language_example: Don't cry, my dear.

meaning: negation plus reflexive/object pronoun: 'not me' or 'don't ... me' depending on word order and verb (used to negate an action related to 'me').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of 'nicht' (not) and the pronoun 'mich' (me). Word order matters: 'Bitte zögern Sie nicht, mich zu kontaktieren' = 'Don't hesitate to contact me' (imperative/infinitive structure). 'Ich schaff es nicht, mich zu binden' = 'I can't manage to commit myself' (reflexive). 'Vergiss nicht, mich ...' = 'Don't forget to ... me'. Use 'mich' as the accusative (direct object). In commands/requests with infinitives it's common to place 'nicht' before the infinitive clause or before the verb to negate the action.
target_language_example: Vergiss nicht, mich anzurufen, wenn du angekommen bist.
native_language_example: Don't forget to call me when you have arrived.

meaning: used to negate a clause with a prepositional object introduced by 'mit' (not with / don't know with whom).
additional_notes: This pattern appears when negating verbs that take a 'mit' + person/thing (mit wem, mit jemandem, mit jemand anderem). Word order in German often places 'nicht' before the prepositional phrase or clause element being negated. In spoken/written German you will more commonly see forms like "nicht mit" directly followed by the relevant pronoun or noun (e.g. "nicht mit ihm/mit jemandem/mit wem").
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, mit wem ich fahren soll.
native_language_example: I don't know who I should go with.

meaning: 'not what that/this is' or 'I don't know what that is/means'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of sentences like "ich weiß nicht, was das (ist)" or "ich höre nicht, was das ist". It expresses lack of knowledge or understanding about something (what something is, means, or intends). In natural German you will usually say "ich weiß nicht, was das ist" or "ich weiß nicht, was das soll". Word order: the clause "was das" (what that/this) follows verbs like wissen, hören, verstehen. The comma in the input separates the negation "nicht" from the subordinate clause; in normal writing you would place "nicht" before the verb or omit the comma: "ich weiß nicht, was das ist."
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was das soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what that's supposed to mean.

meaning: used in questions/statements meaning 'don't (you) know who I am' or 'you/they don't know who I am'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in sentences with different pronouns and verb forms: 'Du weißt nicht, wer ich bin.' (informal you singular), 'Wisst ihr nicht...'(informal plural), 'Wissen Sie nicht...'(formal you), and in questions the word order changes: 'Weißt du nicht, wer ich bin?' It combines 'nicht' (negation) with an embedded question clause 'wer ich bin' ('who I am'). Common in contexts where the speaker expects the other to recognize or respect them.
target_language_example: Du weißt nicht, wer ich bin, also sei vorsichtig.
native_language_example: You don't know who I am, so be careful.

meaning: 'not (know) how it (is/was/comes about)'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like wissen to say you don't know what something is like or how something happened. Often appears in phrases: "Ich weiß nicht, wie es ist, ..." (I don't know what it's like to ... ) or "Ich weiß nicht, wie es dazu kam." (I don't know how that came about). The clause after "wie es" can describe a state (ist), an event (kam), or continue with "... zu + infinitive".
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wie es ist, alleinerziehend zu sein.
native_language_example: I don't know what it's like to be a single parent.

meaning: 'not your' or 'not you' (formal 'Ihr').
additional_notes: Combines the negation 'nicht' with the formal possessive/pronoun 'Ihr' (capitalized 'Ihr' = formal 'you' or 'your' in written German). Depending on context it can mean 'not your' (e.g. not your son, not your master) or part of an expression 'Das kann doch nicht Ihr Ernst sein' = 'You can't be serious' (formal). In questions like 'Ist das nicht Ihr Ernst?' it addresses someone formally. Watch capitalization: 'Ihr' capitalized usually indicates the formal 'you'.
target_language_example: Das ist nicht Ihr Auto.
native_language_example: That is not your car.

meaning: not old; fairly young or recent
additional_notes: A simple negation of 'alt' (old). Can describe people, things, or time (e.g., a person is not old, a building is not old, an event was not long ago). Tone is neutral. Context may require specifying what 'not old' means (young in age vs. new/recent).
target_language_example: Das Haus ist nicht alt, es wurde vor zwei Jahren gebaut.
native_language_example: The house is not old; it was built two years ago.

meaning: negation with the prepositional phrase 'an der' (not at/on the).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the negation 'nicht' with the preposition + feminine/dative article 'an der'. It negates being at or involved with a location or position (e.g. not at the bus stop, not at the meeting) or can appear in set phrases like 'nicht an der Reihe' (not your turn). Word order can change depending on sentence structure; in many contexts 'nicht' negates the following prepositional phrase or the verb phrase. Pay attention to gender/case: 'an der' specifically is used with feminine nouns in the dative (e.g. die Bushaltestelle → an der Bushaltestelle).
target_language_example: Er war gestern nicht an der Schule.
native_language_example: He was not at the school yesterday.

meaning: 'not to' or 'not onto' when used with verbs like gehen/anrufen — here used in the phrase 'nicht ans Telefon gehen' meaning 'not to answer the phone' or 'not to pick up'.
additional_notes: This is a combination of negation 'nicht' and the contraction 'ans' (an + das/den). In spoken German 'ans Telefon gehen' / 'ans Handy gehen' is common for 'to pick up/answer the phone'. 'Nicht ans Telefon gehen' means to not answer. 'Ans' can also mean 'onto' or 'to the' in other contexts (e.g. 'ans Fenster treten' = 'step to the window'), so look at the verb and context. Use 'ans' when referring to masculine/neuter nouns with the preposition 'an' plus the definite article.
target_language_example: Sie geht gerade nicht ans Telefon.
native_language_example: She isn't answering the phone right now.

meaning: 'to not look at' / 'to not watch' (refusing or unable to view something).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronoun (sich etwas ansehen) meaning 'to watch/look at something'. With 'nicht' it expresses inability, prohibition, or unwillingness to look/watch. Context decides whether it's 'can't', 'mustn't', or 'doesn't want to'. Often followed by a direct object (e.g. einen Film, das Foto, sie).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mir das Video nicht ansehen.
native_language_example: I don't want to watch the video.

meaning: 'not onto/to the' (negative + contraction of 'auf das')
additional_notes: A negative phrase formed from 'nicht' + 'aufs' (contraction of auf + das). 'aufs' means 'auf das' and is used before neuter or masculine nouns with definite article in accusative in contexts where English uses 'onto', 'on the', or 'to the'. 'Nicht aufs' tells someone not to do something onto/to that specific thing (e.g. not onto the ship, not on the radio, don't look onto the track). Placement follows normal German negation rules. Context and the noun that follows determine the best English translation (not onto, not on, not to).
target_language_example: Schau nicht aufs Handy während der Fahrt.
native_language_example: Don't look at/on the phone while riding.

meaning: not from the / not out of the (part of a larger phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own but a sequence that appears inside larger sentences. 'nicht' negates a following verb or phrase. 'aus' means 'from' or 'out of' and usually takes the dative case; 'den' is the dative plural or accusative masculine definite article depending on context. Together 'nicht aus den ...' typically means 'not from the ...' or 'not out of the ...' and will be followed by a noun phrase (e.g. 'nicht aus den Fehlern lernen' — 'not learn from the mistakes'). Pay attention to case and the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Er hat nicht aus den Fehlern gelernt.
native_language_example: He did not learn from the mistakes.

meaning: 'not keep' or 'didn't keep' (to not retain something or someone)
additional_notes: Used to say you did not keep or will not keep something (e.g., a phone number, an object, or a person/animal). Context determines whether it's past (didn't keep) or present/future (will not keep). Can refer to permission/ownership (not allowed to keep). Often follows a direct object.
target_language_example: Ich habe deine Telefonnummer nicht behalten.
native_language_example: I didn't keep your phone number.

meaning: not with / not at / not in (depends on context)
additional_notes: A two-word combination where nicht negates a following prepositional phrase with bei. Meaning changes with context: 'nicht bei + person' = not with someone (physically or in possession), 'nicht bei + event/place' = not at (an event or organization), 'nicht bei jedem' = not for everyone. Common in colloquial speech. Choose translation based on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Willst du echt nicht bei mir schlafen?
native_language_example: Do you really not want to sleep at my place?

meaning: 'not receive' or 'not agree with' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'to not receive' (e.g. a message, letter, answer). In some contexts (especially with food/health) bekommen can mean 'to suit' or 'to agree with' someone; 'nicht bekommen' then means something had a negative effect on someone (e.g. a meal made someone feel sick). Pay attention to context to choose the right translation.
target_language_example: Ich habe deine E-Mail nicht bekommen.
native_language_example: I did not receive your email.

meaning: do not use / not to use
additional_notes: A negated verb phrase: 'nicht' + verb 'benutzen' (to use). Common on signs and in instructions (imperative or modal contexts). Can be used with different subjects and with modal verbs (dürfen, können) to forbid or say inability to use something.
target_language_example: Bitte dieses Gerät nicht benutzen.
native_language_example: Please do not use this device.

meaning: 'not used' / 'unused' (something is not being used or was not used)
additional_notes: Commonly describes that an object, device, or service is not in use now or was not used by someone. Can appear as a description (Gegenwärtig nicht benutzt = currently not used) or in statements about past actions (Warum hat er sie dann nicht benutzt? = Why didn't he use them?).
target_language_example: Die Küche ist neu und bisher nicht benutzt.
native_language_example: The kitchen is new and has not been used yet.

meaning: 'not ready' or 'not willing/prepared to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not ready, prepared, or willing to do something. Context determines whether it means 'not physically ready' (e.g. not prepared) or 'not willing/ready to accept' (e.g. not willing). Often followed by 'zu' + infinitive (nicht bereit sein, zu ...). Common in questions and statements about readiness or willingness.
target_language_example: Sie ist nicht bereit, das Projekt zu übernehmen.
native_language_example: She is not ready to take on the project.

meaning: cannot prove; to be unable to demonstrate something as true or factual.
additional_notes: Used to say that a fact, claim, or accusation cannot be proven. Often follows or precedes clauses with 'dass', 'es', or a question word. Common in legal, scientific, and everyday contexts. Word order: the verb 'beweisen' moves to the end in subordinate clauses (e.g. '...dass du es nicht beweisen kannst').
target_language_example: Ich kann dir nicht beweisen, dass es so war.
native_language_example: I cannot prove to you that it happened that way.

meaning: to not pay; to be unable or unwilling to pay
additional_notes: Used to indicate inability or refusal to pay money for something. Context and verb conjugation show who doesn't pay (e.g., ich kann das nicht bezahlen = I can't pay for that). Can express inability (can't afford) or unwillingness (won't pay) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich kann die Rechnung dieses Mal nicht bezahlen.
native_language_example: I can't pay the bill this time.

meaning: 'not paid' or 'didn't pay' (depends on tense/context).
additional_notes: A simple negation of 'bezahlen' (to pay). Used to say someone did not pay (past) or that something remains unpaid. Context and sentence tense determine exact English translation: 'didn't pay', 'hasn't paid', 'not paid' or 'unpaid'. Often follows the verb or is used in passive constructions (wurden nicht bezahlt = were not paid).
target_language_example: Die Rechnung ist noch nicht bezahlt.
native_language_example: The bill is not paid yet.

meaning: not stay; cannot or should not remain (somewhere or in a state).
additional_notes: Used to say someone cannot stay (physically or temporarily) or that staying is not appropriate. Can express inability (cannot stay) or advice/decision (should not stay). Context and tone clarify whether it's inability, refusal, or suggestion to leave.
