target_language_example: Wir haben nur wenig Zeit, wir können hier nicht bleiben.
native_language_example: We have little time, we can't stay here.

meaning: not to break; to refrain from breaking (can be literal — an object — or figurative — friendship, promise, law)
additional_notes: Frequently used with abstract nouns (Freundschaft, Versprechen) or rules (Gesetz). Context determines literal vs. figurative reading. Can express refusal or inhibition when used with reflexive or passive constructions (e.g. sich nicht brechen lassen).
target_language_example: Wir dürfen unser Versprechen nicht brechen.
native_language_example: We must not break our promise.

meaning: not the first (time); used to say something has happened before
additional_notes: Often used in sentences like 'Das ist nicht das erste Mal' (This is not the first time). It implies a repeated or familiar occurrence. Can be shortened in casual speech (e.g. 'Nicht das erste Mal'). Common with 'Mal' (time) but can be continued with other nouns.
target_language_example: Das ist nicht das erste Mal, dass er zu spät kommt.
native_language_example: This is not the first time that he has come late.

meaning: not get away with that / not avoid it / not talk about it (depending on context)
additional_notes:
A short phrase where 'davon' refers back to an action, topic, or consequence mentioned before. Common uses:
- To say someone won't get away without consequences: "So kommst du nicht davon." = "You won't get away with that." (idiomatic)
- To refuse to discuss something: "Können wir hier nicht davon reden?" = "Can we not talk about that here?"
- To tell someone not to run away: "Lauft nicht davon!" = "Don't run away!"
Meaning depends on the verb and context. 'nicht davon' itself isn't informal but appears in casual speech; it's compositional in the sense that 'nicht' = not and 'davon' = of/from that.
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht einfach weglaufen und dann davonkommen — so kommst du nicht davon.
native_language_example: You can't just run away and get away with it — you won't get away with that.

meaning: not yours / not your (something) — negates possession or association.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone does not own or is not responsible for something, or to express disbelief in fixed phrase 'Das ist nicht dein Ernst!' (= 'You can't be serious!'). 'Dein' is the informal singular 'your' (du). For formal or plural 'your' use 'nicht Ihr' or 'nicht euer'/ 'nicht eure' depending on number and gender/case.
target_language_example: Das ist nicht dein Fahrrad.
native_language_example: That is not your bike.

meaning: not the whole / not all (of something, e.g. day, way, summer)
additional_notes: Used before a time period or extent (Tag, Weg, Sommer usw.) to say you won't do or shouldn't do something for the entire duration. It often appears in full phrases like "nicht den ganzen Tag" (not the whole day) or "nicht den ganzen Weg" (not the whole way). Word order: "nicht" negates the following noun phrase (with accusative article "den" for masculine/neuter time expressions like "ganzen Tag"), so watch the case.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht den ganzen Abend bleiben.
native_language_example: I can't stay the whole evening.

meaning: not think; to be unable or not allowed to think (literal) — often used to say someone can't imagine or isn't allowed to have a thought
additional_notes: Literally 'not think'. Context determines meaning: it can mean 'cannot think' (unable to think), 'must not think' (prohibition), or colloquially 'can't imagine'/'can't bring oneself to think'. In some sentences it's reflexive (sich nicht denken = 'cannot imagine/visualize'). Useful for expressing inability to think, prohibition of a thought, or inability to imagine something.
target_language_example: Ich kann mir das nicht denken.
native_language_example: I can't imagine that.

meaning: not the whole / not the entire (used before a feminine or general noun phrase)
additional_notes: A negative phrase used to say something is not done for the entire time or not affecting the whole of something. 'Ganze' agrees in gender/number/case with the noun it modifies (here shown in feminine/accusative or general contexts). Common with time expressions (die ganze Nacht = the whole night) or abstract nouns (die ganze Geschichte = the whole story). Word order: 'nicht' comes before the noun phrase to negate it (nicht die ganze Nacht = not the whole night).
target_language_example: Wir bleiben nicht die ganze Zeit hier.
native_language_example: We won't stay here the whole time.

meaning: not directly; not immediately or not in a straightforward way.
additional_notes: Used to say something isn't done/said in a direct, straightforward, or immediate manner. Can refer to physical direction (not going straight to a place) or to indirectness in speech or action. Context determines whether it means 'not directly' (literal) or 'not exactly' / 'not really' (more idiomatic). Often used alone as a short reply: "Nicht direkt!"
target_language_example: Er ist nicht direkt zur Arbeit gegangen, sondern hat zuerst einen Umweg gemacht.
native_language_example: He didn't go directly to work; he took a detour first.

meaning: not to go there / not to go to that place (used with verbs like gehen).
additional_notes: Used in constructions with an infinitive (often gehen): 'jemanden bitten, nicht dorthin zu gehen' = to ask someone not to go there. Can appear in statements telling someone they don't need to go: 'Du brauchst nicht dorthin zu gehen.' Word order: 'nicht' negates the action; 'dorthin' indicates the destination.
target_language_example: Bitte mich morgen nicht dorthin zu schicken.
native_language_example: Please don't send me there tomorrow.

meaning: not on it / not about it / not going to (do it) — used colloquially to say someone is not involved, not thinking about it, or won't do something
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used after verbs like 'denken' or 'gewöhnen' or in commands: 'nicht dran denken' (don't think about it), 'nicht dran gewöhnen' (don't get used to it), 'lass ... nicht dran' (don't let someone touch it / don't let them be involved). Context decides exact translation: can mean 'not on it', 'not about it', 'don't think about it', or 'won't happen to (me)'. Often contracted speech.
target_language_example: Denk morgen nicht dran — wir reden darüber nächste Woche.
native_language_example: Don't think about it tomorrow — we'll talk about it next week.

meaning: not outside; indoors or not out in the open.
additional_notes: A simple negation phrase: nicht (not) + draußen (outside). Used to say something or someone is not outside — often implies they are inside or under cover. Can modify verbs or be used as a short answer: "Er ist nicht draußen." = "He is not outside."
target_language_example: Die Kinder spielen heute nicht draußen, weil es regnet.
native_language_example: The children are not playing outside today because it's raining.

meaning: not to turn / not to operate (a rotating machine); also: cannot film or shoot (in some contexts)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'not turn' or 'not spin'. Used when something cannot be turned, rotated, or operated (e.g., a mill, a machine, a knob). In contexts about film or media, drehen means 'to shoot/film', so 'nicht drehen' can mean 'cannot film'. Context determines whether it's physical turning or filming.
target_language_example: Die Maschine ist kaputt, wir können sie nicht drehen.
native_language_example: The machine is broken; we can't turn/operate it.

meaning: not earlier; sooner; not before (used to say something happened later than expected)
additional_notes: Used to apologize or express surprise that something wasn't done or said earlier. Often appears in subordinate clauses introduced by 'dass/daß' or questions (Warum ... nicht eher?). Similar to English 'not sooner' or 'not earlier' — common in apologies: 'Entschuldigung, dass ich es Ihnen nicht eher gesagt habe.'
target_language_example: Entschuldige, dass ich dir nicht eher geschrieben habe.
native_language_example: Sorry that I didn't write to you earlier.

meaning: 'not honest' / 'dishonest'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not truthful or trustworthy. Word order: 'nicht' negates the adjective 'ehrlich'. Can describe a person, behavior, or action. Tone can be accusatory depending on context.
target_language_example: Er war nicht ehrlich mit mir.
native_language_example: He was not honest with me.

meaning: not one / not a single one
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is not even a single person or thing (negation + focus). Often appears at sentence start for strong negation (e.g. "Nicht einer hat..." = "Not one [person] tried..."). Can also appear in questions or exclamations ("Fehlt da nicht einer?" = "Isn't one missing?").
target_language_example: Fehlt da nicht einer im Foto?
native_language_example: Isn't one missing in the photo?

meaning: not even
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen or is not true, often introducing an extreme or unexpected example (often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause). Can appear in negative contexts and with quantities/time (e.g., not even one).
target_language_example: Er hat nicht einmal angerufen.
native_language_example: He didn't even call.

meaning: to be unable to decide / not decide (in some contexts)
additional_notes: Often used with a reflexive pronoun (sich nicht entscheiden) meaning 'to be unable to choose/decide'. Can also appear in constructions meaning 'not to decide' (e.g. postpone a decision). Common with clauses introduced by ob (whether) or question words (wen, was).
target_language_example: Ich kann mich nicht entscheiden, welchen Film wir sehen sollen.
native_language_example: I can't decide which movie we should watch.

meaning: to not expect; to be unable to expect something (often used in negative statements: 'you can't expect...')
additional_notes: Used to say that something should not be assumed or hoped for. Common in phrases like 'Man kann nicht erwarten, dass...' (One cannot expect that...) or 'Ich hätte das nicht erwartet' (I wouldn't have expected that). Can be followed by a clause introduced by 'dass' or by an infinitive with 'zu' depending on sentence structure.
target_language_example: Man kann nicht erwarten, dass alles sofort perfekt ist.
native_language_example: You can't expect everything to be perfect right away.

meaning: not to tell; to not say (something to someone).
additional_notes: Common negative construction: 'nicht erzählen' is used when you choose or decide not to tell information. It often appears with indirect objects (wem) or direct objects (etwas). In spoken German you may hear shortened forms (e.g. 'Das musst du mir nicht erzählen' = 'You don't have to tell me that').
target_language_example: Sag ihm das bitte nicht erzählen.
native_language_example: Please don't tell him that.

meaning: 'not eat' / 'do not eat' (negation of the verb 'essen')
additional_notes: Used to negate the action of eating. Can appear in questions, permissions/rules (allowed to drink but not eat), warnings (do not eat this), or in modal/compound verb constructions (would not have had to eat). Word order follows German rules: 'nicht' typically negates the verb phrase and its position varies (before infinitives, after auxiliaries/objects, or before infinitive in subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: So etwas darfst du nicht essen.
native_language_example: You must not eat something like that. (Do not eat something like that.)

meaning: not your (plural/informal).
additional_notes: Combines the negation 'nicht' (not) with the possessive pronoun 'euer' (your, addressing multiple people informally). Use when denying possession, relationship, or describing something as not belonging to 'you' (plural). Word order: 'nicht' typically comes before the thing being negated or before the possessive phrase as in examples (e.g. 'nicht euer Freund', 'nicht euer Haus'). For formal or singular 'you', use 'nicht Ihr' (formal) or 'nicht dein' (singular informal).
target_language_example: Das ist nicht euer Problem.
native_language_example: That is not your problem.

meaning: 'not fall' or 'do not drop' (negative form used to say someone/something should not fall or be dropped).
additional_notes: Used to warn or ask that a person or object should not fall or be dropped. Often appears in commands with lass (let) or with verbs like stützen (support) and in constructions with damit (so that) + subjunctive. Can refer to people (don't let me fall) or objects (don't drop the eggs).
target_language_example: Lass das Glas nicht fallen!
native_language_example: Don't drop the glass!

meaning: not wrong; correct or acceptable (lit. 'not wrong')
additional_notes: Used to say something is correct, acceptable, or not mistaken. Can be a mild affirmation ("that's not wrong") or praise ("she's not wrong" meaning her view/choice is valid). Tone depends on context and intonation; sometimes used to soften agreement. Literal, easily understood from components.
target_language_example: Das Argument ist nicht falsch.
native_language_example: The argument is not wrong.

meaning: not be able to fly; to not fly
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something cannot fly (lack of ability) or simply does not fly. Can be literal (birds, planes, injured animals) or figurative/joking (I still can't fly). In questions or imperative forms it can appear with modal verbs (kann nicht fliegen, lassen fliegen) or word order changes. Common negative phrase: 'kann nicht fliegen' = 'cannot fly'.
target_language_example: Der Vogel ist verletzt und kann nicht fliegen.
native_language_example: The bird is injured and cannot fly.

meaning: not earlier; not sooner
additional_notes: Used to say that something did not happen at an earlier time or that someone did not do/say something sooner. Common in apologies, questions about timing, or comments about missed opportunities. Can be followed by verbs in perfect, past, or infinitive constructions (e.g., 'nicht früher gestellt', 'nicht früher geschrieben').
target_language_example: Warum hast du mir das nicht früher gesagt?
native_language_example: Why didn't you tell me that earlier?

meaning: not found
additional_notes: A simple negation of the past participle finden (to find). Used after a noun/pronoun or object to say something or someone wasn't found/found yet. Can appear in different tenses with auxiliary verbs (haben/hatten/hätten). Common in statements and questions.
target_language_example: Die Schlüssel wurden nicht gefunden.
native_language_example: The keys were not found.

meaning: didn't marry / did not get married
additional_notes: Negative form of the verb 'heiraten' (to marry). Used to say someone did not marry or to ask why they didn't marry. In spoken German you may also hear contractions (e.g. 'nicht geheiratet' remains the same, but tense changes with auxiliaries: 'hast ... nicht geheiratet', 'haben ... nicht geheiratet', or past perfect 'nicht geheiratet hätte').
target_language_example: Er hat sie nie geheiratet — sie haben nicht geheiratet.
native_language_example: He never married her — they did not get married.

meaning: 'not helped' (past participle 'helped' negated) — indicates someone did not help.
additional_notes: Used with a subject and an auxiliary (haben) in perfect tense or as part of a statement/accusation. Common in sentences like 'Du hast mir nicht geholfen' (You didn't help me) or questions 'Warum haben Sie mir nicht geholfen?'. Can be used in both informal (du) and formal (Sie) address depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Er hat mir gestern nicht geholfen.
native_language_example: He didn't help me yesterday.

meaning: not read; unread; cannot be read
additional_notes: Used either to say something hasn't been read (unread) or that something cannot be read (illegible / incomprehensible). Context and sentence structure determine meaning: with a passive construction (können nicht gelesen werden) it means 'cannot be read' (illegible/unreadable). As a short question or remark ("Nicht gelesen?") it can mean 'Not read?' or 'You haven't read it?'.
target_language_example: Der Brief liegt noch auf dem Tisch — er ist nicht gelesen.
native_language_example: The letter is still on the table — it is not read / unread.

meaning: not exactly; not certain/precisely.
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or lack of precision about facts, reasons, meanings, or actions. Can modify a verb or adjective (e.g., 'weiß nicht genau', 'nicht genau genug'). Common in spoken and written German for hedging or giving an approximate answer.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht genau, wann der Zug ankommt.
native_language_example: I don't know exactly when the train arrives.

meaning: not enough; insufficient
additional_notes: Used to say something is insufficient in quantity, quality, or degree. Can be used with nouns (nicht genug Zeit) or predicatively (Das ist nicht genug). With verbs it can appear in set phrases like "Ich kann dich/Sie nicht genug loben" meaning "I can't praise you enough." Tone is neutral; context determines emphasis.
target_language_example: Das Geld ist nicht genug für die Miete.
native_language_example: The money is not enough for the rent.

meaning: not dead / did not die
additional_notes: Used to say someone is alive or thankfully did not die. Common in past contexts (Perfekt or Präteritum) and as a reaction: Zum Glück/Glücklicherweise ist er nicht gestorben (Fortunately he didn't die). Word order may change with auxiliary verbs: ...ist nicht gestorben. Can be used literally or to soften bad news.
target_language_example: Zum Glück ist sie nicht gestorben.
native_language_example: Fortunately she didn't die.

meaning: 'not done' or 'didn't do (it)'.
additional_notes: Combines the negation 'nicht' with the past participle 'getan' of 'tun' (to do). Used to deny or state that something was not done. Common in perfect/periphrastic past forms (e.g. 'ich habe es nicht getan' = I didn't do it) and in subordinate clauses (word order may change: 'dass ich das nicht getan habe').
target_language_example: Ich habe es nicht getan.
native_language_example: I didn't do it.

meaning: to not win; to lose or be unable to win.
additional_notes: A simple negation of the verb gewinnen (to win). Used to say someone does not or cannot win, or that you must not let someone win (with lassen + gewinnen). Tense and modal verbs (können, dürfen, würden) change the meaning: e.g. können nicht gewinnen = cannot win; dürfen ... nicht gewinnen lassen = must not let ... win; würden nicht gewinnen = would not win. Word order follows German rules for negation (nicht usually comes before the verb in infinitive constructions or after auxiliaries).
target_language_example: Wenn wir so spielen, werden wir nicht gewinnen.
native_language_example: If we play like that, we will not win.

meaning: 'not the same' or 'not equal / not immediately' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can mean 'not the same' or 'not equal' (e.g. people, things, rights). In some contexts it can mean 'not immediately' (colloquial: 'not right now' or 'don't do that immediately') — context decides the sense. Common in comparisons: Wir sind nicht gleich = We are not the same / We are not equal. When used with verbs or actions it can convey 'not immediately' (Nicht gleich! = Don't do that yet / Wait!).
target_language_example: Nicht gleich! Warte kurz, ich muss noch etwas fertig machen.
native_language_example: Not yet! Wait a moment, I have to finish something.

meaning: not big; not large; small or not large enough
additional_notes: A simple negation of groß (big/large). Used to describe size or to say something is not big enough. Can modify nouns or be part of a comparison about suitability (e.g., 'nicht groß genug' = 'not big/large enough'). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Der Koffer ist nicht groß genug für meinen Laptop.
native_language_example: The suitcase is not big enough for my laptop.

meaning: not go there / don't go (there).
additional_notes: Direct negation of 'hingehen' (to go to a place). Used to tell someone not to go somewhere or to advise against attending. Can be polite when combined with modal verbs (solltest/sollten) and appears in spoken and written German. 'Hingehen' emphasizes movement toward a place; for general 'not go' you might also see 'nicht gehen' or 'nicht dorthin gehen.'
target_language_example: Wenn du nicht hingehen willst, bleib einfach zu Hause.
native_language_example: If you don't want to go there, just stay at home.

meaning: not up / not high / not enough (depending on context)
additional_notes: This phrase combines nicht (not) + hoch (up/high). Its exact meaning depends on the verb and context: 1) with motion verbs it can mean 'not up' or 'not upstairs' ('hier nicht hoch' = don't come up here); 2) in imperative forms it can be colloquial/emphatic ('kriegt euren Arsch nicht hoch' = you won't get off your butt); 3) as a suggestion it can mean 'let's go up' when used in a question with nicht (Warum gehen wir nicht hoch? = Why don't we go up?); 4) in the construction 'nicht ... hoch genug' it means 'not ... enough' (nicht hoch genug loben = cannot praise highly enough). Pay attention to word order and surrounding words to choose the correct translation.
target_language_example: Warum gehen wir nicht hoch? Da ist es ruhiger.
native_language_example: Why don't we go upstairs? It's quieter there.

meaning: not hungry.
additional_notes: Simple negation: nicht + adjective (hungrig). Used to say someone does not feel hunger. Can be used in different tenses (ist, war). 'Vermutlich' = 'probably' can modify it. Common everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht hungrig.
native_language_example: I'm not hungry today.

meaning: 'not pretty' or 'not attractive'.
additional_notes: Negation of hübsch (pretty). Used to say someone or something is not considered attractive. Common in everyday speech; tone can be blunt or rude depending on context. Word order: nicht usually comes before the adjective in simple statements (e.g., 'Sie ist nicht hübsch').
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie sei nicht hübsch, aber sehr sympathisch.
native_language_example: He said she is not pretty, but very likeable.

meaning: not alright / not OK; something is wrong
additional_notes: Used to say that something is malfunctioning, incorrect, or socially/problematic. Common in questions (Ist etwas nicht in Ordnung?) and statements (X ist nicht in Ordnung). Can refer to objects (machine), situations (behavior), or people's condition.
target_language_example: Die Lampe flackert — irgendetwas ist nicht in Ordnung.
native_language_example: The lamp is flickering — something is not right.

meaning: not into a / not into (a feminine or neuter noun in accusative) — used to say someone/something should not be transformed or put into (a state/place).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a common combination: 'nicht' (not) + 'in' (into) + the feminine or neuter singular accusative article 'eine'. It appears when negating actions like transforming, turning into, or putting someone/something into a place or state (e.g., 'in eine Klinik' = into a clinic; 'in eine Krähe' = into a crow). Gender and case matter: you'd use 'nicht in einen' for masculine accusative and 'nicht in ein' for neuter when the article differs.
target_language_example: Warum willst du ihn nicht in eine Therapie bringen?
native_language_example: Why don't you want to take him into therapy?

meaning: 'not every' / 'not every (one/thing)'.
additional_notes: Used to negate a general statement about people or things. Follows the noun (with appropriate article/gender) or precedes a noun phrase: e.g. "nicht jede Frau", "nicht jede Wahrheit". It means some but not all; contrasts with "jede" (every). Can be used with singular or plural concepts depending on context.
target_language_example: Nicht jede Lösung funktioniert für alle.
native_language_example: Not every solution works for everyone.

meaning: not every / not everyone
additional_notes: Used to say that a generalization does not apply to all members of a group or all instances. Followed by a noun (e.g., 'nicht jeder Tag' = not every day) or can imply people ('nicht jeder' = not everyone). Neutral, common phrasing for partial exceptions.
target_language_example: Nicht jeder hat Zeit, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: Not everyone has time to help you.

meaning: not every / not each
additional_notes: Used to negate a general statement about all members of a group. Follows the noun it modifies in word order (e.g. "Nicht jedes Buch...") and agrees in gender/number with the noun via the adjective ending (jedes for neuter/masculine singular in nominative). Common in everyday and written German.
target_language_example: Nicht jedes Auto ist elektrisch.
native_language_example: Not every car is electric.

meaning: 'do not know' — the negative form used with the verb kennen (to know someone or something); appears in contexts where the conjugated verb (kenne/kennst/kennt/kennen) combines with nicht to negate.
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase; compositional: verb kennen plus negation nicht. Word order can vary (e.g., 'ich kenne ihn nicht', subordinate clauses or certain constructions place the verb before nicht: '..., dass ich ihn nicht kenne'). The exact sequence 'nicht kenne' typically appears in subordinate clauses or after modal/auxiliary contexts where 'kenne' appears after the subject (e.g., '..., weil ich deinen Namen nicht kenne'). Register: neutral; can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on surrounding words.
target_language_example: Weil ich deinen Namen nicht kenne.
native_language_example: Because I do not know your name.

meaning: 'not clear' or 'can't handle/cope' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literally means 'not clear'. Used both for clarity (e.g. speech, meaning) and colloquially to say someone 'can't get along with' or 'can't handle' something/ someone (kommen nicht klar). Context decides meaning: with verbs like sprechen it means 'not clearly'; with kommen (z. B. 'nicht klar kommen') it means 'unable to cope/get along'.
target_language_example: Mit dem Lärm komme ich nicht klar.
native_language_example: I can't cope with the noise.

meaning: to not ring (be heard ringing); 'doesn't/didn't ring' or 'to not hear it ring' depending on sentence.
additional_notes: Literally 'not ring'. Often used with verbs of perception (hören) to say someone didn't hear a doorbell/phone/ alarm ring. Word order can vary in colloquial spoken German (infinitive vs. past participle after modal/perception verbs): e.g. 'Haben Sie es nicht klingeln gehört?' (perfect tense with past participle gehört) or 'Haben Sie es nicht klingeln hören?' (perfect with infinitive heard). Context determines whether it's about the object not ringing at all or the person not hearing it.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Telefon nicht klingeln gehört.
native_language_example: I didn't hear the phone ring.

meaning: 'not funny' or 'not strange' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'not funny'. In everyday German, "komisch" can mean either 'funny' (amusing) or 'strange/odd'. Context and intonation decide which meaning is intended. Examples with question forms (Ist das nicht komisch? / Kommt Ihnen das nicht komisch vor?) often mean 'Isn't that strange/odd?'. With a negative emphasis (Das ist wirklich nicht komisch.) it usually means 'That's really not funny' (someone is upset or offended).
target_language_example: Das Verhalten gestern fand ich nicht komisch.
native_language_example: I didn't find the behavior yesterday funny/it seemed strange to me.

meaning: not concentrate / not be able to focus
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verb sich konzentrieren (ich kann mich nicht konzentrieren). Common in sentences expressing inability to focus because of noise, stress, tiredness, etc. English equivalent: "I can't concentrate." Often appears with modal verbs (kann, konnte) and adverbs (leider, einfach).
target_language_example: Heute kann ich mich nicht konzentrieren, es ist zu laut.
native_language_example: Today I can't concentrate, it's too loud.

meaning: 'not sick' or 'not ill'.
additional_notes: Used to negate the adjective krank (sick). Can appear in different tenses and with different pronouns: e.g. present (Sie sind nicht krank = You/They are not sick), past (Sie waren nicht krank = You/They were not sick), perfect/modal (Er kann nicht krank gewesen sein = He cannot have been sick), question form (Warst du nicht krank? = Weren't you sick?/Weren't you ill?). Word order: nicht usually comes before the adjective it negates.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht krank, ich fühle mich gut.
native_language_example: I'm not sick today; I feel fine.

meaning: 'not fight' — to refuse, be unable, or be forbidden to fight (physically or in a contest).
additional_notes: Combines the negation 'nicht' with the verb 'kämpfen' (to fight). Used for physical fighting, combat, or figurative conflict (arguing, competing). Depending on context it can mean: refusing to fight, being unable to fight (e.g., due to injury), or being not allowed to fight. Word order changes in sentences with modal verbs or tense (e.g., 'wollten nicht kämpfen', 'würden nicht kämpfen', 'kann nicht kämpfen').
target_language_example: Ich will nicht kämpfen, ich will reden.
native_language_example: I don't want to fight, I want to talk.

meaning: to not be able to / cannot (lack ability, possibility, or capacity)
additional_notes: Used to indicate inability, lack of skill, or impossibility. Often appears with an infinitive verb after it (e.g. nicht können + Infinitiv) or in noun/phrase contexts. Can express genuine inability or be used as an excuse (contrast with 'nicht wollen' = not wanting). Word order depends on clause type: in main clauses the conjugated verb appears second and 'nicht' typically precedes the modal ('Sie können nicht kommen'); in nominal/infinitive phrases the sequence 'nicht können' can appear together (e.g. 'Dinge, die andere Kinder nicht können').
target_language_example: Dinge, die andere Kinder nicht können.
native_language_example: Things that other children cannot do.

meaning: not long ago; recently.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened a short time ago. Often appears in phrases like 'Es ist nicht lange her, dass...' (It's not long ago that...) or alone as a remark: 'Das ist nicht lange her.' Tone is neutral and common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Es ist nicht lange her, dass ich sie zuletzt gesehen habe.
native_language_example: I didn't see her long ago / I saw her not long ago.

meaning: not to work / not to go well; or not to run (physically) depending on context.
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) figurative: 'nicht laufen' = something doesn't work or won't go well (e.g., a plan, situation) — common in sentences like 'So wird es nicht laufen.' 2) literal: 'nicht laufen' = not to run (physically) or not allowed to run (imperative/permission), as in 'Ich kann nicht laufen' or 'Wir dürfen nicht laufen.' Context (modal verb, tone) tells which meaning applies. Wortstellung: often appears with modal verbs or negation 'nicht'.
target_language_example: Mit diesen Bedingungen wird das Projekt nicht laufen.
native_language_example: With these conditions the project won't work.

meaning: not easy; not likely/easily (to do or be)
additional_notes: Used to describe that something or someone is not easy, simple, or readily done. In front of adjectives (Er ist nicht leicht zufrieden) it means 'not easily [adjective]' or 'hard to be [adjective]'. Before verbs or nominal phrases it can express that something was/could be difficult to do (Voldemort ... nicht leicht gemacht haben). Tone is neutral; context determines exact translation (not easy, hard, not likely).
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe ist nicht leicht zu lösen.
native_language_example: The task is not easy to solve.

meaning: 'can't get rid of' / 'can't shake (off)'
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to say you can't get rid of, escape from, or stop thinking about something/someone. Common in phrases like 'den Gedanken nicht loswerden' (can't get rid of the thought) or 'man ist mich nicht los' (people won't leave me alone). Often appears as part of the separable verb 'loswerden' with 'nicht' negating it. Tone is neutral; can express annoyance, worry, or helplessness.
target_language_example: Den Ärger werde ich einfach nicht los.
native_language_example: I just can't get rid of the anger.

meaning: 'not do' / 'not allowed to do' / 'cannot be done' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Literally 'not do.' Can express prohibition (you must not do that), impossibility (that can't be done), or regret about a past action (shouldn't have done). Context and sentence structure determine meaning. Common with modal verbs (können, dürfen, lassen) and in spoken warnings.
target_language_example: Das darfst du nicht machen.
native_language_example: You must not do that.

meaning: not even
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that even the smallest, easiest, or most expected thing does not happen. It is a common shorter form of "nicht einmal" and is very common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Er hat nicht mal Hallo gesagt.
native_language_example: He didn't even say hello.

meaning: not bad / pretty good (surprised approval).
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to express pleasant surprise or mild praise. Often preceded by 'gar' or 'und' for emphasis (e.g. 'gar nicht mal schlecht' = 'actually not bad'). Tone can be approving or slightly teasing. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Gar nicht mal schlecht, das hast du gut gemacht!
native_language_example: Not bad at all, you did that well!

meaning: no longer
additional_notes: Used when something used to be true or happen before, but is now no longer true or happening. It can also mean something will not happen again. Very common with verbs: Ich wohne nicht mehr hier. Compare it with noch nicht, which means 'not yet'.
target_language_example: Ich wohne nicht mehr in Berlin.
native_language_example: I don't live in Berlin anymore.

meaning: not strange / not odd
additional_notes: Used to ask or state that something does not seem strange. Often appears in questions (Ist das nicht merkwürdig? = Doesn't that seem strange?) with different verb forms for person and number (Fandest du..., Fanden Sie..., Fandet ihr...). 'Merkwürdig' means 'strange' or 'remarkable'; 'nicht' negates it. Neutral, not informal.
target_language_example: Findest du das nicht merkwürdig?
native_language_example: Don't you find that strange?

meaning: not tired
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not tired or to ask whether someone is tired (often with a questioning tone: 'Bist du nicht müde?' = 'Aren't you tired?'). 'Nicht' negates the adjective 'müde'. Word order: verb + subject + 'nicht müde' in questions (e.g., 'Bist du nicht müde?').
target_language_example: Nach dem langen Spaziergang bin ich nicht müde.
native_language_example: After the long walk I'm not tired.

meaning: 'not nice' / 'not kind'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is unkind, rude or not pleasant. Can be used plainly (Er ist nicht nett = He's not nice) or rhetorically in questions/suggestions (Ist das nicht nett? = Isn't that nice?). Tone depends on context — can be critical, ironic or polite. 'Nett' is a common adjective; negation is simply 'nicht' before it.
target_language_example: Sei nicht so gemein — das ist wirklich nicht nett.
native_language_example: Don't be so mean — that's really not nice.

meaning: 'not only English, but (also...)' — used to say someone has more than one ability or quality, adding another item.
additional_notes: Structure: 'nicht nur X, sondern (auch) Y'. Use to contrast and add information. 'auch' (also) is optional but common. You can replace 'Englisch' with any noun/skill. Verb agreement and word order follow normal German rules (comma before 'sondern').
target_language_example: Er spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Spanisch.
native_language_example: He speaks not only English but also Spanish.

meaning: 'not open' / 'not receptive'.
additional_notes: Used both literally (e.g., a door not left open) and figuratively (a person not open/receptive to ideas or criticism). Context determines translation: for doors translate as 'don't leave (it) open'; for people translate as 'not open-minded' or 'not receptive'. Often appears with prepositions like 'für' (offen für = open to).
target_language_example: Sei bitte nicht offen für fremde Schlüssel—schließe die Tür.
native_language_example: Please don't leave the door open—lock it.

meaning: not often; rarely.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens seldom or infrequently. Can modify verbs or entire clauses. Tone is neutral; common in everyday speech. Word order: 'nicht' negates 'oft' (often).
target_language_example: Das passiert hier nicht oft.
native_language_example: That doesn't happen here often.

meaning: 'doesn't suit/agree/fit' or 'if (that) bothers you/you don't like it'.
additional_notes: Common in conditional phrases like "Wenn dir das nicht passt..." meaning "If you don't like/agree with that..." Used to tell someone they can leave, complain, or do something different. Can be neutral or slightly brusque depending on tone. Often follows a pronoun/object (das, dir, euch, Ihnen).
target_language_example: Wenn dir der Plan nicht passt, sag es jetzt.
native_language_example: If the plan doesn't suit you, say so now.

meaning: 'not really' / 'not quite' / 'uncertainly' depending on context
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or express doubt, hesitation, or lack of certainty. With verbs like wissen (ich weiß nicht recht) it means 'I'm not sure' or 'I don't really know.' In sentences like 'sie hat damit nicht recht' it can mean 'not right' or 'not correct' (i.e., 'she's not right about that'). Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht recht, ob ich heute Abend komme.
native_language_example: I'm not quite sure whether I'll come tonight.

meaning: 'not to speak' / 'don't speak' (negation of speaking)
additional_notes: Used either as a description that someone does not or cannot speak (e.g., due to noise or choice) or as an instruction/command telling someone to be quiet. Context, word order, and intonation determine whether it's a statement, question, or imperative. Can be neutral, firm, or rude depending on usage.
target_language_example: Du solltest hier nicht reden.
native_language_example: You shouldn't speak/talk here.

meaning: not down / don't go down (or don't fall down).
additional_notes: Combination of 'nicht' (not) + colloquial 'runter' (short for 'herunter' or 'hinunter' = down). Used to tell someone not to go down somewhere or to say you won't fall/down or won't go down. Context decides whether it's about going down (e.g., to the sea) or falling. Informal spoken language — 'runter' is casual.
target_language_example: Pass auf, fall nicht runter!
native_language_example: Careful, don't fall down!

meaning: not write / cannot write
additional_notes: Used to negate the verb schreiben (to write). Can mean 'would not write' (refusal or improbability) or 'cannot write' (lack of ability). Context and auxiliary/modal verbs determine whether it's ability (kann nicht schreiben) or conditional/negation (würde nicht schreiben). Often appears with other negations (nicht lesen, nicht sprechen).
target_language_example: Ich kann meinen Namen nicht schreiben.
native_language_example: I cannot write my name.

meaning: 'not beautiful' or 'not nice' (negation of 'schön').
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is not attractive, not pleasant, or not nice. Context determines tone: can be literal about looks, ironic, or used in expressions like a question tag (Sieht das nicht schön aus?) meaning 'Doesn't that look nice?'. Word order and intonation affect meaning (e.g., question vs. statement).
target_language_example: Das Bild ist nicht schön, aber es hat Charakter.
native_language_example: The painting is not beautiful, but it has character.

meaning: to not protect / cannot protect
additional_notes: Negation of schützen (to protect). Used to say someone or something is not protected or cannot be defended. Word order: nicht usually comes before the verb in infinitive constructions or before the object/adverb it negates; in simple sentences with a finite verb, nicht appears before the verb in subordinate or infinitive clauses (e.g., 'konnte ... nicht schützen' = 'could not protect').
target_language_example: Ich kann deine Daten nicht schützen.
native_language_example: I cannot protect your data.

meaning: doesn't see
additional_notes: Combination of nicht (not) + sieht (sees). Used to negate the verb 'sehen' in present tense (er/sie/es sieht). Can mean physically cannot see or figuratively does not perceive/notice. Word order follows German negation: nicht comes before the verb in short phrases like this when quoted or in relative clauses.
target_language_example: Er zeigt mir Dinge, die das Auge nicht sieht.
native_language_example: He shows me things that the eye doesn't see.

meaning: not so hungry / not very hungry
additional_notes: Used to soften or downplay how hungry someone is. Common in everyday conversation to describe reduced appetite compared with before or compared to others. Can be used with verbs: e.g. Ich bin nicht so hungrig (I am not very hungry) or as a comment: Ich bin nicht so hungrig wie du.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht so hungrig, ich esse nur eine Kleinigkeit.
native_language_example: I'm not very hungry today; I'll just eat a little something.

meaning: not proud; ashamed or not feeling pride about someone/something.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does not feel proud of a person, action or situation. Often followed by 'auf' + accusative (auf sich, auf ihn, auf die Kinder). Can express embarrassment or regret.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht stolz auf das, was ich damals gemacht habe.
native_language_example: I am not proud of what I did back then.

meaning: 'not constantly' / 'not all the time'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something does not happen continuously or should not be done all the time. Can express annoyance or request for less frequent action. Common in everyday speech; word order: 'nicht' negates 'ständig' (the adverb).
target_language_example: Du musst mich nicht ständig anrufen.
native_language_example: You don't have to call me all the time.

meaning: not sad; don't be sad.
additional_notes: A simple negation of the adjective traurig (sad). Commonly used to comfort someone — often at the start of an imperative (Sei nicht traurig) or as reassurance in a statement (Du darfst nicht traurig sein). Use 'nicht' before the adjective. Context tells whether it's a reassurance ('don't be sad') or a factual negation ('is not sad').
target_language_example: Sei nicht traurig, alles wird gut.
native_language_example: Don't be sad, everything will be fine.

meaning: 'not drink' / 'cannot drink' (to refuse or be unable to drink something)
additional_notes: Used to negate the verb trinken. Can express dislike/refusal (I don't want to drink that) or inability (I can't drink that because it's too hot/unsafe). Context and sentence structure determine whether it's refusal or physical impossibility. Common in negative statements and with modal verbs (kann nicht trinken).
target_language_example: Ich möchte das nicht trinken, das sieht schmutzig aus.
native_language_example: I don't want to drink that; it looks dirty.

meaning: 'not around' / part of the negative imperative 'dreh dich nicht um' meaning 'don't turn around' or in other contexts 'don't kill' when combined with a verb like 'bringen' (bringen ... um = kill).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase; meaning depends on the verb it accompanies. 1) With 'dreh dich nicht um' it is an imperative: 'don't turn around'. 2) With verbs like 'jemanden umbringen' (bringen ... um) it forms the negation of 'kill' → 'don't kill (someone)'. Word order matters: 'nicht um' usually appears split from the verb (separable verbs or verb+particle constructions).
target_language_example: Dreh dich jetzt nicht um!
native_language_example: Don't turn around now!

meaning: not for nothing; not without reason; you didn't do/experience that in vain.
additional_notes: Used to say that something had a purpose, value, or justified result. Can mean 'not for free' in some contexts (e.g. paid), but most commonly means 'not in vain' or 'there was a reason'. Tone depends on context—can be reassuring, defensive, or strong (e.g. about death or effort).
target_language_example: Du bist nicht umsonst hierhergekommen.
native_language_example: You didn't come here for nothing.

meaning: not impossible; doable or possible (often cautiously optimistic).
additional_notes: A double negative used to soften a statement: it says something isn't impossible, so it may be difficult but can be done. Common in spoken and written German to express cautious hope or qualification. Can be used alone as a short reply (e.g., "Aber nicht unmöglich.").
target_language_example: Russisch zu lernen ist schwierig, aber nicht unmöglich.
native_language_example: Learning Russian is difficult, but not impossible.

meaning: not under / not subject to (something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is not under a condition, influence, suspicion, charge, etc. Usually followed by a noun with the preposition 'unter' (e.g. 'unter Drogen', 'unter Verdacht', 'unter Anklage'). Context decides exact translation: 'not under drugs' → 'not on drugs', 'nicht unter Verdacht' → 'not under suspicion'.
target_language_example: Sie steht nicht unter Verdacht.
native_language_example: She is not under suspicion.

meaning: 'do not deserve' / 'did not deserve'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does not deserve something (usually something bad or good that happened). Common in spoken and written German. Word order: nicht negates verdient (the past participle) in sentences like 'Das habe ich nicht verdient' (I didn't deserve that). Can be used with different subjects and tenses: 'er hat das nicht verdient', 'sie verdienen das nicht'.
target_language_example: Du hast das nicht verdient.
native_language_example: You don't deserve that.

meaning: 'not sell' or 'to not sell' (negation of verkaufen).
additional_notes: Used to negate the verb verkaufen (to sell). Can mean someone refuses to sell (won't sell) or that something cannot be sold (won't sell / won't be able to be sold). Context determines whether it's about unwillingness (refusal) or impossibility/marketability. Word order follows German negation: nicht comes before the verb in infinitive constructions or before separable verb parts in clauses.
target_language_example: Er will das Fahrrad nicht verkaufen.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to sell the bike.

meaning: 'not lost' / 'not gone' — used to say something or someone hasn't been lost, destroyed, or is still recoverable or hopeful.
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun (e.g. Hoffnung, sie) to reassure that something still exists, is retrievable, or that hope remains. Can refer to people (not missing/lost), things (not lost/destroyed), or abstract things (hope, goodness). Tone can be comforting or factual depending on context.
target_language_example: Die Hoffnung ist nicht verloren — wir versuchen es weiter.
native_language_example: Hope is not lost — we'll keep trying.

meaning: ‘do not understand’ (second person singular — you don't understand).
additional_notes: A negative verb phrase: nicht + verstehst (from verstehen). Used when speaking to one person (du). In sentences it can appear in main clauses, subordinate clauses, or imperatives with conversational structures (e.g., Tu doch nicht so, als ob ...). For other persons or numbers, the verb form changes (ich verstehe nicht, wir verstehen nicht, Sie verstehen nicht).
target_language_example: Wenn du das nicht verstehst, frage bitte nach.
native_language_example: If you don't understand that, please ask.

meaning: 'not changed' or 'hasn't changed' (describing a person, thing or situation)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something remains the same. Common with verbs like 'sich verändern' (to change oneself) or in passive/neutral contexts (etwas ist nicht verändert). In spoken German you may also hear 'nicht verändert' to emphasize no change despite expectations.
target_language_example: Er ist seit Jahren nicht verändert.
native_language_example: He hasn't changed in years.

meaning: not many; few (i.e., a small number of people or things).
additional_notes: Used to say that the quantity of people or things is small. Common in everyday speech. Followed by nouns or verbs with impersonal constructions (Es sind/war/en nicht viele). Can be used with people (Tom mögen nicht viele = few people like Tom). Tone is neutral; context determines whether it's slightly negative.
target_language_example: Nicht viele haben zum Treffen geschafft.
native_language_example: Not many managed to make it to the meeting.

meaning: not introduced (to someone); not presented.
additional_notes: Used when someone has not been formally introduced or presented to another person or group. Common with reflexive or dative verbs: jemanden vorstellen (to introduce someone) or sich vorstellen (to introduce oneself). Context determines who is not introduced (e.g., 'du hast mir deinen Freund noch nicht vorgestellt' = you haven't introduced your friend to me). Can be used in passive-like constructions (e.g., 'nicht vorgestellt zu werden').
target_language_example: Du hast mich deinem Kollegen noch nicht vorgestellt.
native_language_example: You haven't introduced me to your colleague yet.

meaning: 'cannot imagine' or 'cannot picture (oneself/something)'.
additional_notes: Usually appears with a reflexive pronoun (sich) as 'sich nicht vorstellen' meaning 'to be unable to imagine/picture'. Used to express that something is hard to believe or to conceive mentally. Common constructions: 'Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen...' or 'Er kann sich nicht vorstellen, dass...'.
target_language_example: Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen, so weit zu reisen.
native_language_example: I can't imagine traveling that far.

meaning: isn't it
additional_notes: A common short tag question used to ask for confirmation or agreement. Can be added to the end of a statement (or used at the start) and corresponds to English question tags like "isn't it?", "right?", or "aren't you?" depending on context. Tone can be neutral, friendly, or slightly rhetorical. Word-for-word translation is "not true" but in usage it functions as a confirmation tag.
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen auch, nicht wahr?
native_language_example: You're coming tomorrow too, aren't you?

meaning: not away / don't take (it) away; not leaving
additional_notes: Used to negate verbs involving movement away or removing something. In requests it can mean “don’t take (it) away” (Bitte nehmt uns das nicht weg = Please don't take that away from us). In statements about location it means “I'm not leaving” or “I won't go away” (Ich gehe hier nicht weg = I'm not leaving here). Word order and context determine whether it refers to removing something or to not leaving a place.
target_language_example: Bleib hier und nimm mir das nicht weg.
native_language_example: Stay here and don't take that away from me.

meaning: to not hurt (someone) — i.e. not cause physical or emotional pain
additional_notes: Used to say you do not want to cause pain or that something shouldn't hurt. Can refer to physical pain or emotional hurt (e.g. feelings). Often appears with a subject and dative object (jemandem nicht wehtun / dir nicht wehtun). "Wehtun" is separable verb; in many tenses/word orders it splits (es tut nicht weh).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir nichts tun, ich will dir nicht wehtun.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt you, I don't mean to hurt you.

meaning: 'not far' / 'not far away' (distance or figurative closeness)
additional_notes: Used to describe short physical distance or to say someone/something is likely nearby. Can be used literally (location) or more loosely (e.g., 'not far' in time or degree). Often appears with 'von' + place (nicht weit von hier). Word order can vary in sentences (e.g., Sie sind nicht weit!).
target_language_example: Der Supermarkt ist nicht weit von meiner Wohnung.
native_language_example: The supermarket is not far from my apartment.

meaning: 'not far away' or 'not far from (here/there)' — used to say something is close by.
additional_notes: Common phrase to describe physical distance (e.g., a place or object). Can also be used figuratively to mean 'not far from (a certain situation or result)'. Often followed by a location expression: nicht weit entfernt von + Dativ (e.g., nicht weit entfernt von hier).
target_language_example: Der Bahnhof ist nicht weit entfernt von meinem Haus.
native_language_example: The train station is not far away from my house.

meaning: 'not less' / 'no less' — used to emphasize quantity or to mean 'just as' or 'no less than'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to emphasize surprising or noteworthy amounts (e.g. "nicht weniger als sieben" = "no less than seven"). It can also appear in comparisons meaning 'no less' or 'just as' (e.g. "Pflanzen brauchen Licht nicht weniger als Wasser" = "plants need light no less than water" i.e. they need it just as much).
target_language_example: Er hat nicht weniger als drei Bücher an einem Tag gelesen.
native_language_example: He read no less than three books in one day.

meaning: not like you; I'm different from you.
additional_notes: Used to contrast oneself with another person (often in personality, behavior, opinions). Common in brief replies or emphatic statements. Tone can be neutral, defensive, or dismissive depending on context and intonation. Can be used with or without a subject pronoun (e.g., "Ich bin nicht wie du" or just "Nicht wie du").
target_language_example: Ich weiß, dass du das anders machst, aber ich bin nicht wie du.
native_language_example: I know you do it differently, but I'm not like you.

meaning: 'not to (do something) again' — used with an infinitive to say someone should not repeat an action
additional_notes: This phrase appears before an infinitive (often at the end of the sentence): e.g. 'nicht wieder zu tun' = 'not to do (it) again'. Common in promises, requests, or warnings. Word order: the verb 'zu' + infinitive is placed at the end in German subordinate or infinitive constructions. Can be used with different subjects (du, ihr, Sie, names).
target_language_example: Versprich mir, das nicht wieder zu sagen.
native_language_example: Promise me not to say that again.

meaning: "not funny".
additional_notes: A common phrase to tell someone a joke, comment or action is not amusing or is inappropriate. Can be used in mild reproach or to stop behaviour. Tone depends on context and intonation (could be neutral, annoyed or serious).
target_language_example: Das ist nicht witzig, hör bitte auf.
native_language_example: That's not funny, please stop.

meaning: 'not show' or 'to refuse/not be willing to show'
additional_notes: Combines the negation 'nicht' (not) with the verb 'zeigen' (to show). Used to say someone does not or will not show something, or that something will not become apparent. Context determines whether it's refusal (She won't show it) or simple negation (it doesn't show). Word order follows normal German rules: 'nicht' usually comes before the verb in short answers or at the end of a clause when negating the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Sie will ihre Brüste nicht zeigen.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to show her breasts.

meaning: to not go too far; to avoid exceeding limits (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically not going too far) and figuratively (not exceeding social, moral, or practical limits). Common in advice or warnings about behavior, requests, or actions. Often appears with modal or temporal contexts: e.g. 'Ich möchte nicht zu weit gehen' or 'Lass uns nicht zu weit gehen.' Can be followed by an infinitive clause or stand alone in conversation.
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht zu weit gehen, aber das könnte problematisch werden.
native_language_example: I don't want to go too far, but this could become problematic.

meaning: by any chance (used to ask a question politely or tentatively)
additional_notes: Placed before a noun, name, question word, or clause to make a question less direct or to express surprise/guessing. Common in spoken German. Word-for-word it means "not accidentally," but functionally it's equivalent to English "by any chance" or "perhaps." Often paired with a question tag like "oder?"
target_language_example: Du heißt nicht zufällig Maria, oder?
native_language_example: Your name isn't Maria by any chance, is it?

meaning: didn't listen / wasn't listening
additional_notes: Past participle of 'zuhören' (to listen); used with haben (hat nicht zugehört) to say someone did not pay attention or failed to listen. Common in questions and complaints (e.g., 'Hast du mir nicht zugehört?').
target_language_example: Warum hast du mir nicht zugehört?
native_language_example: Why didn't you listen to me?

meaning: not to / didn't (do something) at (a place or institution) / not for (a purpose)
additional_notes: ‘nicht zur’ is not a fixed phrase on its own but a combination of the negation 'nicht' + the preposition 'zu' in dative form with the definite article 'der' (zur = zu + der). It appears before nouns to negate going to, doing something at, or referring to purpose (e.g. 'nicht zur Polizei gegangen' = did not go to the police). Word order and context determine exact translation; often it means 'didn't go to' or 'not to (the) ...'.
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern nicht zur Arbeit gegangen.
native_language_example: I didn't go to work yesterday.

meaning: not (necessary) to say/do something twice; 'don't tell me twice' or 'not twice' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used either as an idiom meaning 'you don't have to tell me twice' (i.e., I already understand or will comply), or literally to state that something does not occur twice (e.g., 'there aren't two of them' or philosophical statements like 'you cannot step into the same river twice'). Tone depends on context; common in everyday speech. Word order: 'nicht' negates 'zweimal' (twice).
target_language_example: Das musst du mir nicht zweimal sagen — ich kümmere mich darum.
native_language_example: You don't have to tell me twice — I'll take care of it.

meaning: not everywhere; not in all places/situations.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not available, true, or possible in every place or situation. Can refer to physical locations or to more general contexts (e.g., not common). Often follows the verb (e.g., 'kann man nicht überall finden').
target_language_example: So etwas sieht man nicht überall.
native_language_example: You don't see something like that everywhere.

meaning: not surprised; unsurprised.
additional_notes: Used to say someone did not feel surprise about something. Common with verbs like sein (sein nicht überrascht), werden, or constructions with von/über to indicate cause (z. B. 'nicht überrascht von'). Tone is neutral; can express expectation, resignation, or lack of shock.
target_language_example: Ich bin über die Nachricht nicht überrascht.
native_language_example: I am not surprised by the news.

meaning: nothing better to (do) — used to say someone has nothing better to do than X
additional_notes: Common phrase in German to express that someone has no more important or interesting activity; often followed by an infinitive (zu + verb) or implied activity. Tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive/sarcastic depending on context: e.g. „Ich hatte nichts Besseres zu tun“ = I had nothing better to do. In casual speech the ‚zu‘ may be left hanging when the verb is understood.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nichts Besseres zu tun, also half ich ihm beim Aufräumen.
native_language_example: I had nothing better to do, so I helped him clean up.

meaning: nothing but; only; merely.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is only or nothing more than what follows. Can express dismissal, minimization, or criticism (e.g., "nothing but a lie", "only trouble"). Often appears before nouns or noun phrases and can carry a negative tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Das war nichts als Zeitverschwendung.
native_language_example: That was nothing but a waste of time.

meaning: nothing else / no other thing
additional_notes: Used to say there is no alternative, no other option, or that only one thing has been seen/experienced. Can appear in full sentences ('Es bleibt mir nichts anderes übrig' = I have no choice) or in short replies ('Habe leider nichts anderes' = I don't have anything else).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute leider nichts anderes zu tun.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I have nothing else to do today.

meaning: to think of nothing else / to be unable to stop thinking about something
additional_notes: Used with verbs like können/konnte: 'an nichts anderes denken' means your thoughts are entirely occupied by one thing or person. Often appears as 'an nichts anderes denken als ...' (think of nothing else but ...). Common in present and past tenses.
target_language_example: Ich kann an nichts anderes denken als an den Urlaub.
native_language_example: I can think of nothing else but the vacation.

meaning: 'doesn't care about' / 'isn't interested in' (often used with 'sich nichts aus ... machen')
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the reflexive phrase 'sich (dat) nichts aus ... machen' meaning to not care about or not be interested in something. Can also be literal in contexts like 'nimm nichts aus ... mit' meaning 'don't take anything out of...'. Pay attention to context: with a reflexive pronoun it expresses indifference; in imperative or literal object contexts it can mean 'nothing from'.
target_language_example: Er macht sich nichts aus schnellen Autos.
native_language_example: He doesn't care about fast cars.

meaning: to get/receive nothing; to get very little (often used with 'fast' = 'almost nothing' or 'for almost nothing' meaning very cheaply).
additional_notes: Depending on context, 'nichts bekommen' can mean 'receive nothing' (no items, no response) or, with modifiers like 'für fast nichts' or 'fast nichts bekommen', it can mean 'got it for almost nothing' (= very cheaply) or 'received almost nothing'. Word order and prepositions matter: 'Ich habe es für fast nichts bekommen' = 'I got it for almost nothing' (price), while 'Ich habe fast nichts bekommen' = 'I received almost nothing'.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Fahrrad für fast nichts bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the bike for almost nothing.

meaning: 'No way!' / 'Not a chance!' (strong refusal or rejection).
additional_notes: Used as a short, emphatic refusal or to reject an idea or request. Tone ranges from firm to playful depending on context and intonation. Often stands alone or precedes a reason (e.g. "Nichts da, Geschäft ist Geschäft!"). Not polite — can sound blunt in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Nichts da, du gehst nicht ohne Jacke raus!
native_language_example: No way, you're not going out without a jacket!

meaning: 'nothing (of concern)/nothing special' or 'didn't think anything of it' depending on context
additional_notes: Used in several ways: (1) To say something is no big deal / nothing wrong (Es ist doch nichts dabei). (2) To say nothing resulted from something (Es kam nichts dabei heraus = nothing came of it). (3) In colloquial replies to excuse behavior: 'Nichts dabei, haben wir alle gemacht' = 'No big deal, we've all done it.' (4) To say someone doesn't feel anything about something (Sagen Sie nicht, dass Sie nichts dabei fühlen). (5) Used reflexively: 'Wir haben uns nichts dabei gedacht' = 'We didn't think anything of it.' Tone can be neutral or dismissive; suitable for spoken and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — ich habe mir nichts dabei gedacht.
native_language_example: Don't worry — I didn't think anything of it.

meaning: to not be able to do anything about it / to not be responsible
additional_notes: Used to indicate one is not to blame or could not change a situation. Commonly appears in first-person constructions like 'Ich kann nichts dafür' or with other subjects and infinitive constructions. Tone is neutral but can sound defensive depending on context.
target_language_example: Er kann nichts dafür, dass der Zug verspätet ist.
native_language_example: He can't do anything about the train being delayed.

meaning: to have nothing to do with (something/someone); to not be involved
additional_notes: Commonly used with a verb form like haben (hat nichts damit zu tun) to say someone/something is not involved or responsible. Structure: [Person/Thing] + hat/hatte nichts damit zu + (tun). Often followed by a clause or noun indicating the matter (e.g. 'was sie dir vorwerfen' or a noun phrase). Negative: expresses lack of connection or involvement.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nichts damit zu tun.
native_language_example: I had nothing to do with it.

meaning: 'I can't think of anything' / 'nothing comes to mind'.
additional_notes: Used in the common German impersonal construction 'mir fällt (et)was ein' — literally 'something falls to me' — to say that an idea, solution, name, etc. comes to mind. With 'nichts ein' it means that nothing comes to mind. Personal dative (mir/dir/ihm...) indicates who it comes to. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Mir fällt einfach nichts ein, wie wir das Problem lösen können.
native_language_example: I just can't think of any way to solve the problem.

meaning: 'not for' / 'not suitable for' / 'not my/your/etc. thing' (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to say something is not suitable, not preferred, or not someone's responsibility. Contexts: 1) Personal taste/suitability: "Das ist nichts für mich" = "That's not for me." 2) Strong content warning: "nichts für schwache Nerven" = "not for the faint-hearted." 3) Responsibility: "Ich kann nichts für Sie tun" = "I can't do anything for you / It's not something I can help with." Word order and meaning depend on surrounding words (e.g. "nichts für mich/uns/ihn/Sie" or set phrase "nichts für schwache Nerven").
target_language_example: Dieses Buch ist nichts für Kinder.
native_language_example: This book is not for children.

meaning: Don't take this the wrong way; no offense.
additional_notes: Polite phrase used before or after a critical or blunt remark to signal you don't mean to insult the person. Common in both spoken and written German. Tone can be apologetic or dismissive depending on context. Often followed by a comma and the critical comment (e.g., '...aber...').
target_language_example: Nichts für ungut, aber ich glaube, du hast einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: No offense, but I think you made a mistake.

meaning: 'nothing beats' / 'nothing compares to' (used to say something is the best) or in some contexts 'nothing goes wrong' (literal).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of the fixed expression "Nichts geht über ..." meaning "nothing beats/compares to ..." to praise something (e.g. food, drink, activity). Context matters: standalone "Nichts geht schief" uses a different meaning ('nothing goes wrong'). For beginners, learn the praise use: "Nichts geht über + [noun/gerund]".
target_language_example: Nichts geht über einen Spaziergang am Morgen.
native_language_example: Nothing beats a walk in the morning.

meaning: did nothing / haven't done anything
additional_notes: Common past‑tense phrase using 'nichts' (nothing) + past participle 'gemacht' of 'machen'. Used to say someone did not do any activity or to deny wrongdoing ('I didn't do anything!'). Can refer to a short incident or a whole period (e.g., all day, holidays).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern den ganzen Tag nichts gemacht.
native_language_example: I did nothing all day yesterday.

meaning: haven't heard from him anymore / no news from him since then.
additional_notes: Used to say there has been no contact or information about a male person since a certain time or event. Common in past or perfect tenses (haben + gehört). You can replace 'ihm' with other pronouns or names (z. B. 'nichts mehr von ihr', 'nichts mehr von Thomas').
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug habe ich nichts mehr von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: Since the move I haven't heard from him anymore.

meaning: nothing to do with; not related to
additional_notes: Used with dative objects (e.g., 'mit Ihnen', 'mit Politik') to say that something is unrelated or has no connection. Can also appear in separable contexts like 'nichts mit ... anfangen' meaning 'can't do anything with / can't relate to'. Common in statements denying responsibility, connection, relevance, or relation.
target_language_example: Das hat nichts mit dem Problem zu tun.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with the problem.

meaning: nothing to do with the / has nothing to do with the
additional_notes: Used to say that something is unrelated to or not caused by something else. Often followed by a noun phrase in dative (dem/der/den) or a pronoun (z. B. dem Kopf, dem Haus). Common in statements denying connection or responsibility.
target_language_example: Das hat nichts mit dem Unfall zu tun.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with the accident.

meaning: 'has nothing to do with me' / 'it's not my responsibility / I'm not involved'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as the full phrase 'nichts mit mir zu tun' or in variations like 'nichts mit mir zu tun haben'. Used to deny involvement, responsibility, connection, or relevance. Can be used about people (I'm not involved with them) or situations (this is not my fault/concern). Often followed by a comma and 'verstanden?' for emphasis.
target_language_example: Das hier hat nichts mit mir zu tun.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with me.

meaning: 'nothing without' — expresses that someone or something has no value, power, or meaning without someone/something else.
additional_notes: Used to say that a person, group, action, or thing depends completely on another person or thing. Often appears in sentences emphasizing dependence or loss of meaning/power. Word order: 'nichts ohne X' (X typically in accusative).
target_language_example: Ich bin nichts ohne dich.
native_language_example: I am nothing without you.

meaning: 'to see nothing' / 'to not see anything' (cannot see anything)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is unable to see anything (due to darkness, fog, obstruction, etc.). Commonly appears after a verb like sehen or with modal verbs (konnte nichts sehen = could see nothing / couldn't see anything). Word order: 'nichts' (nothing) before the verb in simple statements or after auxiliary/modal verbs (e.g., 'konnte nichts sehen').
target_language_example: Draußen war dicker Nebel; ich konnte nichts sehen.
native_language_example: Outside there was thick fog; I couldn't see anything.

meaning: to do nothing more / to do nothing else
additional_notes: Common phrase used to say someone won't take further action or nothing else happens. Can be used in statements about future action (won't do anything more) or descriptions of a situation (there's nothing else to do). Often appears in contexts like instructions, plans, or explanations.
target_language_example: Ich kann dir jetzt nicht helfen, ich kann nichts weiter tun.
native_language_example: I can't help you now; I can't do anything more.

meaning: 'nothing will' (used to say that nothing will do/stop/change something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears at the start of a clause to express certainty about the future or a general statement: 'Nothing will...'. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (with auxiliary 'wird' for future/passive) or used idiomatically (e.g. 'Nichts wird schiefgehen' = 'Nothing will go wrong'). Can be used in passive constructions ('nichts wird ... organisiert') or active future sense ('nichts wird ihn stoppen').
target_language_example: Nichts wird uns aufhalten.
native_language_example: Nothing will stop us.

meaning: never (any) money; used to say someone never has money or to emphasize never giving/using money
additional_notes: Literal words: 'nie' = never, 'Geld' = money. Often part of short exclamations or sentences: 'Du hast nie Geld!' (You never have any money!) or with verbs: 'Ich würde dir nie Geld leihen' (I would never lend you money). Can express habit (never has money) or a moral rule/refusal (would never give/steal money).
target_language_example: Ich gebe ihm nie Geld, weil er es nicht zurückzahlt.
native_language_example: I never give him money because he doesn't pay it back.

meaning: never (do something) — with separable verb 'abschließen/ablehnen/etc.'; 'nie' (never) + separable particle 'ab' indicates the verb's action is not done.
additional_notes: In German separable verbs split in main clauses: the prefix (here 'ab') goes to the end. 'nie ab' appears when 'nie' (never) sits before the separated particle to deny the action (e.g. 'nie ab' = 'never lock/never refuse' depending on the verb). You need the full verb to know the precise meaning: 'nie ab•schließen' = never lock/close; 'nie ab•lehnen' = never refuse. Word order can vary in subordinate clauses (particle may move).
target_language_example: Sie lässt die Haustür offen und schließt sie nie ab.
native_language_example: She leaves the front door open and never locks it.

meaning: never out of / never leave (something) — 'nie' = never; 'aus dem' is 'out of the' (masculine/neuter dative).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a combination: 'nie' (never) + prepositional phrase 'aus dem' (out of the). Used when talking about not leaving or not coming out of a place (e.g., Haus, Gefängnis). Word order can vary; in some sentences 'nie' may appear elsewhere (e.g., 'nie aus dem Haus gehen' or 'aus dem Haus nie gehen'). Pay attention to the noun's gender and case: 'aus dem' is used for masculine/neuter nouns in the dative (das Haus → aus dem Haus).
target_language_example: Er geht nie aus dem Büro vor 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: He never leaves the office before 6 pm.

meaning: never been there
additional_notes: Usually used with a form of sein to say that someone has never been at a place before, often as ich bin noch nie da gewesen = 'I've never been there before'. This separated form is literal and refers to a place. Be aware that the one-word form nie dagewesen can also mean 'unprecedented' in other contexts.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nie da gewesen.
native_language_example: I've never been there before.

meaning: 'never a' or 'never an' — the negative adverb 'nie' (never) + the indefinite article 'eine'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something never (does) a particular thing or never is a particular one. It appears before a feminine noun (eine) or in cases where English uses 'a'/'an'. Word order: 'nie' directly before the article/noun phrase (nie eine + noun). Can also appear with other articles (nie ein, nie einen, etc.) depending on gender/case.
target_language_example: Er hat nie eine Antwort gegeben.
native_language_example: He never gave an answer.

meaning: never heard (of it/them).
additional_notes: Common short reply when you want to say you have no knowledge or have never encountered something. Often used on its own in conversation (e.g. 'Nie gehört.') or with a subject: 'Ich habe davon nie gehört.' Tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Von dieser Band habe ich nie gehört.
native_language_example: I've never heard of this band.

meaning: never been kissed
additional_notes: Passive perfect construction: 'noch nie' = 'never (yet)'; 'geküsst worden' = past participle + 'worden' (passive of 'küssen'). Used to say someone has never experienced being kissed. Can appear with different subjects and auxiliary verbs (e.g. 'Er war noch nie geküsst worden' = 'He had never been kissed').
target_language_example: Ich war noch nie geküsst worden, bevor ich sie traf.
native_language_example: I had never been kissed before I met her.

meaning: never read
additional_notes: A past-participial construction used to say someone has never read something. Commonly appears with perfect tense (haben + gelesen) or simple past. 'Nie' (never) negates the action; 'gelesen' is the past participle of 'lesen' (to read). Use for books, articles, letters, etc.
target_language_example: Er hat den Brief nie gelesen.
native_language_example: He never read the letter.

meaning: never (in one's life); absolutely never
additional_notes: A strong, emphatic way to say 'never' in German. Often used to stress that something has never happened or will never happen. Can appear as 'nie im Leben', 'noch nie im Leben' (never yet/never before), or simply 'Nie im Leben!' as an emphatic exclamation meaning 'No way!' or 'Not a chance!'. Use in informal and formal contexts for emphasis, but be careful with tone—it's very forceful.
target_language_example: Nie im Leben würde ich so etwas tun!
native_language_example: I would never do something like that!

meaning: 'never crossed (one's) mind' / 'never occurred to (someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like kommen (kommen in den Sinn) to say that something never occurred to someone. The full idiom is "(es) kommt mir nie in den Sinn" or "mir ist nie in den Sinn gekommen." 'nie' = never; 'in den Sinn' = into the mind. Not all uses of 'nie' + 'in den' form an idiom — here it's the fixed expression about thoughts. Word order: the dative pronoun (mir) often appears before 'nie in den Sinn'.
target_language_example: Es ist mir nie in den Sinn gekommen, das zu fragen.
native_language_example: It never crossed my mind to ask that.

meaning: never again; no longer ever
additional_notes: Used to say that something will not happen any more in the future. Can express a one-time decision, a permanent change, or strong emotion (e.g. anger, sadness). Often appears alone for emphasis ("Nie mehr."). Can be followed by verbs in various tenses: "nie mehr + verb" (e.g. "nie mehr sehen", "nie mehr fischen").
target_language_example: Ich will dich nie mehr sehen.
native_language_example: I never want to see you again.

meaning: never with the (masculine or dative noun); 'never by/with the...'
additional_notes: A combination of 'nie' (never) + preposition 'mit' + dative article 'dem'. Used to say someone never uses/does something using a particular means or accompanied by something (e.g. never by the bus/train, never with the cigarette). The noun following 'dem' must be masculine or neuter in dative (or a demonstrative pronoun). Word order can vary: 'nie mit dem Bus' or 'mit dem Bus nie' (latter less common).
target_language_example: Sie fährt nie mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: She never goes to work by bicycle.
