Whether it means 'turned on' or 'turned off' depends on context and any prefixes (e.g., 'anschalten' = switch on, 'abschalten' = switch off). Common contexts: lights, devices, modes.
target_language_example: Er schaltete das Licht aus.
native_language_example: He switched the light off.

meaning: 'look into' / 'look in' / 'look at' (imperative, familiar form)
additional_notes: Informal imperative of schauen (du form: schau) + preposition in. Used to tell someone to look into/inside something or to direct their gaze (e.g. in a direction, into a mirror, into the camera, or metaphorically into the future). With a definite article or object after 'in' it means 'look in/into [the X]'; with a noun like 'alle Richtungen' it's 'look in/all directions'. Use 'schau' for informal singular (du). For formal or plural use: 'schauen Sie in...' or 'schaut in...'.
target_language_example: Schau in die Schublade, ob der Schlüssel dort ist.
native_language_example: Look in the drawer to see if the key is there.

meaning: 'look at me' (imperative/informal), or part of phrases meaning 'look/watch (for) me' depending on context.
additional_notes: Informal imperative form of schauen with a dative pronoun (mir = to/for me). Common uses: 'Schau mir in die Augen' = 'Look me in the eyes', 'Schau mir jetzt zu' = 'Watch me now'. In sentences like 'Ich schau mir die nicht so genau an' the verb is reflexive-ish: 'sich etwas anschauen' = 'to look at something' → 'I don't look at those that closely.' Use du-form (schau) in spoken/informal contexts; formal would be 'schauen Sie mir'.
target_language_example: Schau mir bitte in die Augen und sag die Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Please look me in the eyes and tell the truth.

meaning: 'don't look' or 'don't stare'.
additional_notes: Imperative negative form of schauen (to look). Used to tell someone not to look at something, not to look back, or not to glance in a certain direction. Tone can be neutral instruction or sharp warning depending on context and intonation. Can appear with direction phrases: 'schau nicht zurück' (don't look back), 'schau nicht hin' (don't look there), 'schau nicht so ...' (don't look so ...).
target_language_example: Schau nicht nach unten, das ist gefährlich.
native_language_example: Don't look down, that's dangerous.

meaning: to look at / to watch (something) — reflexive construction: schauen sich etwas an = to look at something or watch something.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (sich) and the separable particle an at the end. Conjugate the verb schauen and place the object before ‘an’ (e.g. wir schauen uns das Bild an). Common for watching films, plays, pictures, etc. English equivalents: 'look at', 'take a look at', 'watch'.
target_language_example: Jetzt schauen sich alle mal das Bild an.
native_language_example: Now everyone take a look at the picture.

meaning: watches; looks on/observes (third person singular/plural imperative of 'zuschauen').
additional_notes: From the verb zuschauen (to watch, to look on). 'schaut zu' can be: 1) present tense third person plural/second person plural formal: 'they/you (pl.) watch' depending on context; 2) imperative plural (Schaut zu!) meaning 'Watch!' or 'Look on!'. Often used when people observe an event without intervening (e.g., 'Die Welt schaut zu' = 'The world watches').
target_language_example: Schaut zu, dann könnt ihr Fragen stellen.
native_language_example: Watch, then you can ask questions.

meaning: 'looked at her' (past tense of 'anschauen'/'schauen')
additional_notes: Used to describe someone looking at a female person (sie = her). 'Schaute' is simple past (or conversational past in some contexts) of 'schauen' or part of the separable verb 'anschauen' when combined with 'an' (e.g. 'schaute ... an'). Word order can change: 'Er schaute sie an' = 'He looked at her.' Pronoun 'sie' could also mean 'you' (formal) or 'they' in other contexts—here it means 'her'.
target_language_example: Er schaute sie lange an, bevor er sprach.
native_language_example: He looked at her for a long time before he spoke.

meaning: to be destined/appointed to; to be allotted or turn out in a certain way (formal/literary usage)
additional_notes: This is an older or elevated verb construction: 'scheiden' here does not mean 'to divorce' but is used impersonally/intransitively (often with a dative) to indicate that something was allotted, destined, or befell someone (e.g. 'es schied ihm zu ...'). Rare in everyday modern German; modern alternatives include 'werden', 'zuteilwerden', 'sich erweisen als' or 'zuteilen'.
target_language_example: Es schied ihm zu, des Amtes würdig zu sein — so schieden ihm große Aufgaben zu.
native_language_example: He was destined/appointed to be worthy of the office — thus great tasks were allotted to him.

meaning: to get divorced (to have oneself divorced).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive construction with a reflexive pronoun: sich scheiden lassen = to have oneself divorced / to get divorced. Common in spoken and written German for talking about the decision or process of divorce. Use with a subject (e.g. Sie beabsichtigt, sich scheiden zu lassen). If you want present tense: sie lässt sich scheiden (she is getting divorced / she is having a divorce).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns entschieden, uns scheiden zu lassen.
native_language_example: We decided to get divorced.

meaning: to seem to; to appear to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express that something appears or seems likely (based on evidence or impression). Common with verbs like stimmen, wirken, frieren, glauben. Construction: scheinen + zu + infinitive (e.g., Die Gerüchte scheinen zu stimmen). Can express tentative or indirect statements or perceptions.
target_language_example: Die Gerüchte scheinen zu stimmen.
native_language_example: The rumors seem to be true.

meaning: 'to appear to be' or 'seem to be'
additional_notes: Used to express that something gives the impression of being a certain way, without certainty. Formed from the verb scheinen plus zu + infinitive (sein). Often followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or subordinate clause. Common in both spoken and written German; more formal than simply scheinen + adjective. Can be used with modal or evidential nuance.
target_language_example: Er scheint zu sein freundlich und hilfsbereit.
native_language_example: He seems to be friendly and helpful.

meaning: 'you seem to' (reflexive verb construction: 'you seem to yourself/you seem to ...')
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'scheinen' (to seem) with a reflexive pronoun 'dich' (you, accusative). Used when the action or state involves the subject reflexively (remembering, knowing oneself, injuring oneself). In English often translated as 'you seem to [verb]' or 'you seem to be [adjective]'. Followed by an infinitive or reflexive verb phrase (e.g. 'dich zu erinnern', 'dich verletzt zu haben').
target_language_example: Du scheinst dich gut an den Weg zu erinnern.
native_language_example: You seem to remember the way well.

meaning: 'it seems that he' / 'he appears to' (introduces a likely or perceived fact about 'he').
additional_notes: Used to express that something appears to be true based on evidence or impression, but with some uncertainty. 'Scheint' is impersonal here; 'dass er' introduces the clause about 'he'. You can replace 'er' with other pronouns/nouns (z. B. 'scheint, dass sie', 'scheint, dass Maria'). Often followed by verbs in various tenses (Präsens, Perfekt, Futur).
target_language_example: Es scheint, dass er heute nicht kommen kann.
native_language_example: It seems that he can't come today.

meaning: 'seems (that) everything' or 'everything seems (to...)'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'scheinen' (to seem) with 'alles' (everything). Use to say that everything appears a certain way. Word order can change: 'Das scheint alles sicher zu sein' (That seems to be all safe) or 'Irgendwie scheint alles schief zu laufen' (Somehow everything seems to be going wrong). Often followed by an adjective, infinitive clause with 'zu' or a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Nach dem Regen scheint alles wieder in Ordnung zu sein.
native_language_example: After the rain, everything seems to be fine again.

meaning: 'seems to' or 'appears to' (third-person singular of 'scheinen' + feminine/definite article 'die' or part of 'die Sonne').
additional_notes: Scheint is the 3rd person singular of the verb 'scheinen' (to seem; to shine). In the examples it appears both in the sense 'seems to' (e.g. jemand scheint etwas zu wissen / etwas zu sein) and in the literal sense 'shines' when used with 'die Sonne' (die Sonne scheint = the sun shines). When learning, treat 'scheint' as 'he/she/it seems' or 'he/she/it shines' depending on context. 'Die' here is either the definite article for feminine nouns like 'Sonne' or the article before a noun object (e.g. 'die Geschichte').
target_language_example: Der Hund scheint die Stimme seines Besitzers zu erkennen.
native_language_example: The dog seems to recognize his owner's voice.

meaning: 'seems to have' (used before a masculine accusative noun).
additional_notes: From the verb scheinen (to seem) + accusative object with the indefinite article 'einen' (masculine). Use when you judge or report that someone appears to possess or be experiencing something (e.g. a friend, a nightmare, a heart attack, a mistake). Word order: subject + scheint + einen + noun (+ verb/complement). For feminine/neuter nouns the article changes (scheint eine, scheint ein).
target_language_example: Sie scheint einen guten Plan zu haben.
native_language_example: She seems to have a good plan.

meaning: seems/appears now; indicates that something appears to be true at the present moment.
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'scheinen' (to seem/appear) with 'jetzt' (now). Used to express a current impression or appearance based on evidence or observation. Often followed by an adjective or an infinitive construction with 'zu' + verb (e.g., 'reich zu sein', 'beschäftigt zu sein'). Tone is neutral; can describe moods, states, or actions that seem to be happening now.
target_language_example: Er scheint jetzt müde zu sein.
native_language_example: He seems tired now.

meaning: seems not / does not seem to
additional_notes: Used to say that something appears unlikely or that the speaker judges (from evidence) that something is not the case. 'scheint' is the verb 'scheinen' (to seem) and 'nicht' negates it or the following infinitive/infinitive clause. Common structures: 'scheint nicht + zu + infinitive' (Er scheint nicht zu kommen) or 'scheint nicht + infinitive with modal/ability' (Er scheint nicht schwimmen zu können).
target_language_example: Sie scheint nicht glücklich zu sein.
native_language_example: She does not seem to be happy.

meaning: seems only / appears to only
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something appears to do or be something and nothing more; 'scheint' = 'seems/appears', 'nur' = 'only/just'. Often expresses an impression or guess (not a certainty). Can be followed by verbs, adjectives, or clauses.
target_language_example: Sie scheint nur müde zu sein.
native_language_example: She just seems to be tired.

meaning: seems to be rich; appears to be wealthy
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (sein) to express that someone appears or gives the impression of being rich. 'scheint' is the 3rd-person singular of 'scheinen' (to seem). Common structure: [Name/Pronoun] scheint reich zu sein. Can be used with other adjectives (e.g., 'scheint glücklich zu sein' = seems to be happy).
target_language_example: Die Frau mit dem teuren Mantel scheint reich zu sein.
native_language_example: The woman with the expensive coat seems to be rich.

meaning: seems that / appears so / looks like that
additional_notes: Used to express that something appears to be the case. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'als' or an adjective. Can stand alone as a short reply ('Ja, scheint so.') to agree that something appears true. 'scheint' is from 'scheinen' (to seem); 'so' emphasizes the appearance.
target_language_example: Ja, scheint so als hätten sie den Termin verschoben.
native_language_example: Yes, it seems like they postponed the appointment.

meaning: an informal way to say 'never mind', 'forget it' or 'screw it' (expresses dismissal or resignation).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar because of 'scheiß' (literally 'shit'). Used to dismiss something, to tell yourself or others not to worry about something, or to give up on a plan. Not appropriate for formal situations or with people you must respect. Can be softened in polite contexts by using alternatives like 'egal' or 'mach nichts'.
target_language_example: Das Spiel ist abgesagt? Scheiß drauf, dann machen wir etwas anderes.
native_language_example: The game is canceled? Screw it, then we'll do something else.

meaning: poured (for oneself); served oneself (a drink).
additional_notes: Reflexive past form of schenken + ein (sich etwas ein|schenken). Means to pour or serve a drink for oneself. Common with beverages (ein Glas, eine Tasse). Use present: 'schenkt sich ... ein'. Not to be confused with schenken meaning 'to give (as a gift)'.
target_language_example: Er schenkte sich noch ein Glas Wasser ein.
native_language_example: He poured himself another glass of water.

meaning: 'they send' or (formal) 'send it/them to you' depending on context; verb schicken (to send) + pronoun sie (they or formal you/it/them).
additional_notes: schicken is the verb 'to send'. sie can be lowercase 'sie' meaning 'they' or 'her/them', or capitalized 'Sie' meaning formal 'you'. Word order changes with questions: 'Warum schicken sie es nur an mich?' = 'Why do they only send it to me?'. In 'Wir schicken Sie Ihnen in einer Stunde.' Sie (formal you) vs. sie (they) and case of other pronouns (Ihnen = to you, dative) matter. Pay attention to capitalization to know whether 'sie' = they, she, or formal you.
target_language_example: Wir schicken sie morgen weg.
native_language_example: We will send them away tomorrow.

meaning: sent it (past tense, 3rd person singular or polite 2nd person).
additional_notes: From the verb schicken (to send) in simple past (Präteritum). 'schickte es' literally = 'sent it.' Could refer to er/sie/es schickte es (he/she/it sent it) or Sie schickten es (formal 'you' in past would be 'schickten', but polite past often uses 'hat es geschickt' instead). Common in storytelling or reports. For spoken German, Perfekt ('hat es geschickt') is more frequent than Präteritum.
target_language_example: Er schickte es gestern per Post.
native_language_example: He sent it by mail yesterday.

meaning: 'seemed to (do) that' — expresses appearance or impression that someone did/liked something.
additional_notes: Schien is the past (Imperfekt) of scheinen ('to seem'). 'Schien das zu ...' is used with an infinitive construction 'zu + verb' to report that something appeared or someone seemed to have a certain feeling or reaction. In English it often translates as 'seemed to...' or 'appeared to...'. Subject can be any person (er, sie, Tom, etc.).
target_language_example: Sie schien das Essen zu mögen.
native_language_example: She seemed to like the food.

meaning: 'it seemed' / 'it appeared' (past tense of erscheinen in impersonal use).
additional_notes: Used impersonally with 'es' to say that something appeared or seemed a certain way to someone (often followed by a dative person or an infinitive clause with 'zu' or 'zu + sein'). Common structure: 'schien es mir ...' = 'it seemed to me ...'. Past tense (Präteritum) of 'scheinen'.
target_language_example: Anfangs schien es eine leichte Aufgabe zu sein.
native_language_example: At first it seemed to be an easy task.

meaning: 'didn't seem' or 'did not appear (to be)'.
additional_notes: Past tense of 'scheinen' (to seem/appear) combined with negation 'nicht'. Used to describe someone's apparent state or attitude based on observation (e.g., not nervous, not pleased). Common in neutral descriptions. Word order: 'scheinen' is conjugated (schien = simple past) and 'nicht' negates the verb or the adjective phrase that follows.
target_language_example: Er schien nicht glücklich zu sein.
native_language_example: He didn't seem to be happy.

meaning: seemed surprised
additional_notes: Past tense/perfect of wirken/erscheinen: 'scheinen' + adjective means 'to appear/be seem [adjective]'. 'Schien' is the simple past (Präteritum) of 'scheinen'. Use to describe how someone looked or appeared emotionally.
target_language_example: Er schien überrascht, als er die Nachricht hörte.
native_language_example: He seemed surprised when he heard the news.

meaning: to go to sleep / to go to bed.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used to say you are going to bed or will go to sleep. Often used with personal pronouns and modal verbs (muss, will, müssen). Literally 'to go sleep' but functions as an English periphrasis 'go to sleep' or 'go to bed.'
target_language_example: Ich möchte jetzt schlafen gehen.
native_language_example: I want to go to bed now.

meaning: 'can sleep' or 'to be able to sleep' (infinitive schlafen + modal verb kann).
additional_notes: Used to express ability or possibility to sleep. Appears after a subordinating connector like 'damit' (so that) or in statements about being able/not able to sleep. Word order: the verb phrase 'schlafen kann' can appear at the end of a clause after words like 'damit' or 'dass' (…damit ich schlafen kann / …dass ich schlafen kann). In spoken German you may also hear other modal verbs (kannst, können) depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Ich mache das Fenster zu, damit ich besser schlafen kann.
native_language_example: I'll close the window so that I can sleep better.

meaning: in a bad mood; feeling grumpy or irritable.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's mood. Common in everyday speech to ask or state that someone is unhappy, annoyed, or not pleasant to be around. Can be used with estar-like verbs: 'sein' (ist/war) or verbs like 'wirkt/scheint'.
target_language_example: Warum bist du heute so schlecht gelaunt?
native_language_example: Why are you in such a bad mood today?

meaning: a poor loser; someone who reacts badly to losing.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who cannot accept defeat gracefully—may get angry, make excuses, or sulk. Common in informal speech; often used in imperative (Sei kein schlechter Verlierer) or as a comment about someone's behavior.
target_language_example: Sei kein schlechter Verlierer, wir spielen nur zum Spaß.
native_language_example: Don't be a poor loser, we're just playing for fun.

meaning: a guilty conscience; feeling guilty or remorseful
additional_notes: Used to describe feeling guilty about something you did or didn't do. Common in phrases like 'ein schlechtes Gewissen haben' (to have a guilty conscience) or 'jemandem ein schlechtes Gewissen machen' (to make someone feel guilty). Often used to explain why someone feels bad or apologetic.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil ich ihr nicht geholfen habe.
native_language_example: I have a guilty conscience because I didn't help her.

meaning: he slept (simple past: 'he was sleeping' / 'he slept').
additional_notes: This is the past tense (Präteritum) of schlafen used with the subject pronoun 'er' (he). Commonly used in narratives and written German. In spoken German, the perfect tense (er ist eingeschlafen/er hat geschlafen) is often used instead. The examples also show the separable verb einschlafen ('schlief er ein' = 'he fell asleep') vs. schlafen ('schlief er' = 'he slept').
target_language_example: Nach der langen Reise schlief er sofort.
native_language_example: After the long trip, he slept immediately.

meaning: past tense of 'schlafen' + preposition 'in' — 'slept in' (inside/at a location).
additional_notes: Used to say someone slept somewhere (inside or in/at a container/place). 'Schlief' is the simple past of 'schlafen'. 'in' is followed by the appropriate case (usually dative for locations: 'in der Hängematte', 'in der Scheune'). For speaking, Germans often use the present perfect 'hat geschlafen' or the past 'schlief' in narratives. Use word order: subject — schlief — in + place.
target_language_example: Er schlief in der Küche.
native_language_example: He slept in the kitchen.

meaning: 'slept very deeply' (often used as 'schlief tief und fest')
additional_notes: This phrase describes someone sleeping soundly; native speakers usually say the full fixed phrase "schlief tief und fest." Use for past tense (schlief) or change verb tense (schläft tief und fest, hat tief und fest geschlafen). It's idiomatic but literal: 'deep and firm' → 'deeply/soundly.'
target_language_example: Das Baby schlief tief und fest, also konnten die Eltern duschen.
native_language_example: The baby slept very soundly, so the parents could shower.

meaning: slept in (somewhere) — past tense plural of 'schlafen' + preposition indicating location
additional_notes: Used to say that 'they' or 'we' slept in a particular place (room, bed, tent, at night, etc.). 'Schliefen' is the simple past (Präteritum) for 'sie/wir' (they/we). The preposition 'in' is followed by the appropriate case (usually dative: 'in dem' → 'im') to name the location: e.g. 'im Zimmer' or 'in einem Zelt'. For spoken German, Perfekt ('haben/sein geschlafen') is more common, but simple past appears in writing.
target_language_example: Wir schliefen in einem alten Zelt.
native_language_example: We slept in an old tent.

meaning: to close (something) before (doing something else); used to ask or tell someone to close something before they leave or before another action.
additional_notes: Commonly used with windows/doors and with a subordinate clause introduced by bevor + subject + verb. Polite requests often use conditional forms (Könnten Sie..., Würden Sie bitte...). Word order: the verb of the main clause (schließen) appears before the comma; the subordinate clause with bevor comes after. You can change the verb and object (z. B. die Tür schließen, bevor du gehst).
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte die Tür schließen, bevor Sie gehen?
native_language_example: Could you please close the door before you leave?

meaning: 'to close' or 'to shut' (reflexive use for doors) / 'to join' or 'to attach oneself' (when used with people/groups); literal sense depends on context.
additional_notes: schließen sich is the reflexive/passive-like form of schließen. For doors it means 'the doors are closing' (Vorsicht, die Türen schließen sich = Watch out, the doors are closing). With people or groups, schließen sich + dative (e.g. euch, uns) means 'to join (you/us)'. In abstract contexts (Liebe und Freundschaft schließen sich gegenseitig aus) it means 'are mutually exclusive' or 'do not go together'. Word order and the dative object show the intended meaning.
target_language_example: Viele Freiwillige schließen sich dem Projekt an.
native_language_example: Many volunteers are joining the project.

meaning: 'worse is' or 'what is worse' (used to introduce something more serious/bad)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in sentences to contrast two things: first a bad point, then 'schlimmer ist' to introduce an even worse point. Can be followed by a clause (e.g. 'schlimmer ist, dass...'). Tone is neutral; used in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Er hat zu spät gearbeitet; schlimmer ist, dass er die Frist verpasst hat.
native_language_example: He worked too late; worse is that he missed the deadline.

meaning: 'locked herself in the bathroom' — used to say someone locked the bathroom door from the inside (often to be alone or to refuse to come out).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb construction: 'sich (irgendwo) einschließen' = to lock oneself in. Commonly used to describe intentionally isolating oneself in a room. The separable prefix 'ein' can appear at the end of the clause: 'schloss sich ... ein'. Often implies emotional reasons (upset, hiding) but can be neutral (seeking privacy). Use simple past 'schloss sich ... ein' (Präteritum) or present perfect 'hat sich ... eingeschlossen' (Perfekt). Can be used with different subjects and in different tenses.
target_language_example: Maria schloss sich im Badezimmer ein und fing an zu weinen.
native_language_example: Maria locked herself in the bathroom and began to cry.

meaning: 'sleeps on' or 'is sleeping on' (describes where someone is sleeping).
additional_notes: Used with a noun in the dative case to indicate the surface or place someone is sleeping (e.g. auf dem Bauch, auf dem Dachboden, auf Stroh). In present tense third person singular: schläft (from schlafen) + auf. Word order: schläft auf + [place].
target_language_example: Er schläft auf dem Sofa.
native_language_example: He is sleeping on the sofa.

meaning: 'he sleeps' or 'he is sleeping' (third-person singular of schlafen).
additional_notes: A simple present tense statement about a male or neuter subject (er = he). In German, present tense kann also mean 'is doing something now' or describe a near-future action (e.g. 'er schläft ein' = 'he falls asleep' / 'he is falling asleep'). Word order: subject (er) often follows the verb in yes/no questions or after certain adverbs; here it's the normal declarative order: verb + subject in subordinate clauses or after connectors.
target_language_example: Im Auto schläft er meistens während der Fahrt.
native_language_example: In the car he usually sleeps during the ride.

meaning: 'sleeps with' (literally: shares sleep/bed with someone or something).
additional_notes: Uses the verb schlafen (to sleep) + preposition mit (with). Can mean literally sleeping next to or together with someone/thing (e.g., a pet or object) or, in some contexts, imply an intimate/sexual relationship when used about people (e.g., 'Sie schläft mit ihrem Chef' can suggest a sexual relationship). Context determines whether it's literal/neutral or intimate. Verb must agree with the subject: er/sie/es schläft, wir schlafen.
target_language_example: Mein Hund schläft mit mir auf dem Sofa.
native_language_example: My dog sleeps with me on the sofa.

meaning: 'is she sleeping' / 'does she sleep' (third-person yes/no question or statement depending on word order).
additional_notes: This is the verb schlafen (to sleep) in the present tense with the pronoun sie (she). As a question, the verb can appear first: 'Schläft sie?' or with noch/immer for 'still' ('Schläft sie noch?'). In a statement the verb follows the subject: 'Sie schläft.' Word order matters: when the verb starts the sentence it's a yes/no question. 'schläft sie' can also refer to 'does she sleep' (habit) or 'is she sleeping' (now) depending on context and time words.
target_language_example: Schläft sie noch, oder soll ich reingehen?
native_language_example: Is she still sleeping, or should I go in?

meaning: 'sleeps deeply and...' used as part of the fixed phrase 'schläft tief und fest' meaning 'sleeps deeply'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common fixed expression 'schläft tief und fest' (literally 'sleeps deep and firm'), which means 'is sleeping very soundly' or 'is fast asleep'. You will usually see the full phrase; the provided fragment 'schläft tief und' by itself is incomplete and needs 'fest' to finish the idiom. Use it to describe someone who is in a deep, undisturbed sleep.
target_language_example: Das Baby schläft tief und fest.
native_language_example: The baby is fast asleep.

meaning: 'does it taste' (asked about a masculine or nominative subject), or part of a structure meaning '...tastes (to someone)'.
additional_notes: Used with the verb schmecken (to taste). In questions like "Schmeckt der Fisch?" it asks whether the food tastes good. Also appears in dative constructions: "Tom schmeckt der Kartoffelsalat" is unnatural — correct: "Der Kartoffelsalat schmeckt Tom" or "Tom schmeckt der Kartoffelsalat" (colloquial word order) meaning 'Tom likes the potato salad' (literally 'The potato salad tastes (good) to Tom'). Pay attention to word order and case: the thing that tastes is the grammatical subject (nominative), the person who experiences the taste is in the dative (Tom).
target_language_example: Schmeckt der Kuchen dir?
native_language_example: Does the cake taste good to you?

meaning: (formal) 'fasten' or 'buckle' (as an imperative to someone: 'please fasten/buckle (yourself)').
additional_notes: Used in the formal polite imperative with Sie + reflexive sich: 'schnallen Sie sich an' = 'please fasten your seatbelt.' Common on planes, buses, cars. Use polite/formal address (Sie). The reflexive verb is 'sich anschnallen'. Word order in questions or polite requests may vary: 'Bitte schnallen Sie sich an.'
target_language_example: Verehrte Passagiere, bitte schnallen Sie sich an.
native_language_example: Dear passengers, please fasten your seatbelt.

meaning: quickly to / quickly become used to (something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like (sich) gewöhnen an or anpassen an. It indicates that someone becomes used to or adapts to a new situation, condition, or environment quickly. The preposition an takes the accusative (das kalte Wetter, die neue Situation). Often appears as part of the reflexive verb sich gewöhnen an or as anpassen an.
target_language_example: Sie hat sich schnell an die neue Wohnung gewöhnt.
native_language_example: She quickly got used to the new apartment.

meaning: how fast can you... (asks about someone's speed doing an action)
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask how quickly someone can do a specific action. Usually followed by a verb (e.g. fahren, gehen, laufen). Word order: 'Wie schnell kannst du ...?' is the full question; 'schnell kannst du' appears inside that structure. Common in everyday and spoken German.
target_language_example: Wie schnell kannst du Fahrrad fahren?
native_language_example: How fast can you ride a bike?

meaning: to do something quickly / to hurry (to get something done quickly).
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say 'do/make something quickly' or 'hurry up' in German. Often used with a pronoun or object (e.g. 'das schnell machen' = 'do that quickly') or alone as an instruction ('Mach schnell!' = 'Hurry!'). Can be polite with 'können Sie das...?' or casual with 'du musst...'.
target_language_example: Können wir das schnell machen?
native_language_example: Can we do that quickly?

meaning: 'as fast/quick as' — used to compare speed (often with 'so ... wie' or alone in exclamations).
additional_notes: Usually appears in comparisons: 'so schnell wie' = 'as fast as'. Can be used with similes (schnell wie der Blitz) or in commands/exclamations to mean 'very quickly'. Often combined with adjectives/adverbs (so schnell wie möglich = as fast as possible). Word order and context matter: 'schnell wie' on its own may be part of a larger phrase.
target_language_example: Komm so schnell wie möglich zurück.
native_language_example: Come back as quickly as possible.

meaning: A colloquial urging or dismissal meaning roughly 'come on, that's...' used to encourage, downplay, or emphasize something.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. 'Komm schon, das ist ...' or 'Jetzt komm schon, das ist ...' is used to push someone, to reassure by minimizing a concern, or to express frustration. Tone and context determine whether it's encouraging (come on, it's nothing) or admonishing (come on, it's serious). 'Schon' here is informal/colloquial; the phrase often appears with ‚komm(s) schon‘ or ‚kommt schon‘.
target_language_example: Komm schon, das ist nur ein kleiner Fehler.
native_language_example: Come on, that's just a small mistake.

meaning: Come on (used to urge, encourage, or show impatience).
additional_notes: A colloquial phrase combining 'komm' (come) and 'schon' (adds emphasis). Used to prompt someone to act, hurry, agree, or to express frustration. Tone depends on context and intonation: friendly encouragement ('Come on, you can do it') or impatient urging ('Oh, come on!'). Often repeated for emphasis (e.g., 'Komm schon, komm schon!').
target_language_example: Komm schon, komm, das schaffen wir!
native_language_example: Come on, come on, we can do it!

meaning: already (felt) afraid; was getting worried
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like haben (hatte/schon) or bekommen to say you were already afraid or starting to feel fear/worry. In conversational German, schon here emphasizes that the feeling started earlier than expected. Often appears in past tense: 'ich hatte schon Angst' = 'I was already afraid/I was getting worried.'
target_language_example: Ich hatte schon Angst, dass der Zug Verspätung hat.
native_language_example: I was already afraid that the train would be late.

meaning: already (learning) French / for how long (have you been) learning French
additional_notes: In these examples the phrase appears in questions with 'seit wie vielen Jahren' or 'wie lange' + 'schon' to ask how long someone has been learning French. 'Schon' here emphasizes that the action started in the past and continues now (English: 'already' or in these questions often translated as 'for how long... already' or simply 'for how long'). The full verb phrase is usually 'lernen ... schon' (e.g. 'lernst du schon Französisch?').
target_language_example: Wie lange lernst du schon Französisch?
native_language_example: How long have you been learning French?

meaning: "already all" — used to ask or state whether everything/all of something is already done or completed.
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun (e.g., Weihnachtsgeschenke) or with a past participle to ask if all items/tasks are finished. In questions it often means "Have you already gotten/finished all... ?" Can be used in statements to say you've already done everything. Tone can be neutral; in colloquial use it may sound slightly blunt depending on context (e.g., "Schon alle Eingeweide aufgegessen?" is teasing or rude).
target_language_example: Hast du schon alle Aufgaben erledigt?
native_language_example: Have you already finished all the tasks?

meaning: already/just by (itself); emphasizing that something is possible or true by itself or for that reason alone.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something alone is enough or that just one factor/reason suffices. Can mean 'already on one's own' (ability to do something without help) or 'for that reason alone' (sufficiency). Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: Schon allein deshalb möchte ich dir danken.
native_language_example: For that reason alone I want to thank you.

meaning: a combination where 'schon' adds emphasis and 'an' is part of a verb phrase or prepositional construction; overall used to mean 'already' / 'even' / 'in itself' depending on context.
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed idiom by itself; 'schon' is an adverb ('already', 'indeed', or 'even') and 'an' can be a preposition or part of a separable verb or phrase. The exact translation depends on the sentence:
- 'schon an sich' = 'already in itself' / 'in itself' (emphasising that something is by itself remarkable).
- 'schon an die fünf Mal' = colloquial: 'around/close to five times already' ('an die' with numerals expresses an approximation).
- 'schon an ihren Schritten erkennen' = 'already/just by (her) steps recognize' (meaning: recognize someone from just their steps).
- 'schon an vielen Orten' = 'already/in many places' (here 'an' is the preposition 'in/at' with places). 
For learners: treat 'schon' and 'an' separately and pay attention to the structure (e.g. 'schon an sich', 'schon an die fünf', 'schon an [place]').
target_language_example: Man kann das Problem schon an den Symptomen erkennen.
native_language_example: You can already recognize the problem from the symptoms.

meaning: already on the (masculine/neuter dative) — used to say something is already located, happening, or present on/at something
additional_notes: This is a short sequence: 'schon' = already, 'auf' = on/at, and 'dem' is the dative definite article for masculine/neuter nouns. You will see it before a noun in dative (e.g. 'dem Tisch', 'dem Bildschirm', 'dem Weg'). It often appears in contexts like 'it's already on the table' (Es ist schon auf dem Tisch) or 'we're already on the way' (Wir sind schon auf dem Weg). Word order and case must match the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Das Buch liegt schon auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The book is already on the table.

meaning: already doing it / already on it / in the process (of doing something)
additional_notes: Used to say you are already engaged in an action or are about to start; context-dependent. In short replies it means "I'm on it" or "I'm already doing that." In sentences like "Ich bin schon dabei, mich zu ändern" it means "I'm in the process of..." Can also be used to downplay concern or question like "Was ist denn schon dabei?" = "What's the big deal?"
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — ich bin schon dabei, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: Don't worry — I'm already working on solving the problem.

meaning: 'already about it' — used to say someone has already heard about or been told something / 'already (of) it'.
additional_notes: Combine 'schon' (already) with 'davon' (about it/of it). Common in questions and statements: 'Hast du schon davon gehört?' = 'Have you already heard about it?' Use with verbs like erzählen (to tell) or hören (to hear). 'Davon' refers back to a topic previously mentioned. Word order: in questions with haben, 'schon davon' often comes after the subject.
target_language_example: Haben die Kinder schon davon gehört?
native_language_example: Have the children already heard about it?

meaning: 'for (already) the whole/entire' — used with a time period to say something has been happening for that duration (already).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'schon den ganzen... (Tag/Abend/Morgen/Nachmittag)' to emphasize that an action or situation has been going on for the entire indicated time. 'Schon' stresses that it has been happening for some time (often with mild surprise or impatience). 'Den' is the accusative article used with masculine time nouns like 'Tag', 'Morgen', 'Nachmittag', 'Abend' when combined with 'ganzen'.
target_language_example: Ich warte schon den ganzen Vormittag auf dich.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for you the whole morning.

meaning: already there
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is at a place earlier than expected or at the present moment. Can refer to past or present perfect context (e.g., 'was already there when I arrived') or to current state (e.g., 'you must already be there'). Common with time questions: 'Wie lange/oft ... schon dort?'
target_language_example: Als ich ankam, war sie schon dort.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was already there.

meaning: already a
additional_notes: Used when asking or stating whether someone already has/has arranged one of something (e.g. a plan, appointment, partner). 'schon' = already; 'einen' is the accusative masculine/neuter indefinite article used with masculine nouns (or generic 'one'). Word order may change depending on sentence. For feminine nouns you'd hear 'schon eine'.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einen Termin beim Arzt?
native_language_example: Have you already made an appointment with the doctor?

meaning: quite a few / a number of / several (already).
additional_notes: Used to say that there are several of something or that something has been happening for several units of time; 'schon' adds the sense 'already' or 'indeed'. Common with plural nouns and time expressions (Wochen, Monate, Tage) and with countable things (Falten). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Ich habe schon einige Bücher gelesen.
native_language_example: I have already read quite a few books.

meaning: 'have/has ... ever (the)' — used to ask if someone has ever experienced or done something (followed by a feminine/plural noun with 'die').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions: 'Hast du schon einmal ...?' or 'Habt ihr schon einmal ...?' Means 'have you ever ...?' The phrase 'die' is the definite article for feminine singular or plural nouns (e.g. die Alpen, die Sterne). Word order: 'schon einmal' emphasizes 'ever' or 'before'.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal die Alpen gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen the Alps?

meaning: have/has/have you ... ever in (a place or field).
additional_notes: Used in questions or statements to ask whether someone has ever had an experience in a particular place, institution, or area of work. 'schon einmal' = 'ever/before'; 'im' is the contraction of 'in dem' and is followed by a noun (e.g. Verkauf, Gefängnis, Zoo). Adjust verb and pronoun for person and formality (Sie/du/ihr).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal im Ausland gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you ever worked abroad?

meaning: have/has (someone) ever considered...
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask whether someone has ever thought about or considered a particular action or option. Usually appears as part of the phrase "schon einmal in Erwägung gezogen" (gezogen = considered). Formality: neutral — suitable for spoken and written German. Commonly followed by an infinitive clause (einen Therapeuten aufzusuchen, ein Kind zu adoptieren, etc.).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal in Erwägung gezogen, nach Deutschland zu ziehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever considered moving to Germany?

meaning: 'to cry (at least) once' in contexts like 'have you ever seen X cry?'.
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'jemanden schon einmal weinen sehen' = 'to have seen someone cry (ever)'. 'Schon einmal' = 'ever/once before' (experience), 'weinen' = 'to cry'. Used in questions asking whether someone has ever witnessed another person crying. Word order: 'Haben Sie ihn schon einmal weinen sehen?' (perfect or present with 'sehen' as perception verb).
target_language_example: Hast du deine Schwester schon einmal weinen sehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen your sister cry?

meaning: 'already found' (past participle construction indicating something has been found already).
additional_notes: Used with haben + gefunden to ask or say whether someone has located/found something yet. 'Schon' means 'already' and typically appears before the past participle or after the auxiliary in questions. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hast du den Ball schon gefunden?
native_language_example: Have you already found the ball?

meaning: already (have to) go / to leave already
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) with verbs like 'müssen' or in questions to ask or state that someone has to leave already (e.g. 'Müssen Sie schon gehen?'), and (2) in the phrase 'Das wird schon gehen' where 'schon' means 'it will be fine/it will work out' and 'gehen' means 'to work/turn out'. Context determines whether it means 'leave already' or 'it will be okay.'
target_language_example: Oh, du musst schon gehen? Dann bis bald!
native_language_example: Oh, you have to leave already? Then see you soon!

meaning: already written
additional_notes: Used with perfect or past contexts to say that something has been written already. Commonly appears in questions (Wie viele ... schon geschrieben?) and with personal pronouns. 'Schon' = already; 'geschrieben' = past participle of 'schreiben'. Word order follows German perfect/past constructions (e.g., 'Hat Tom den Brief schon geschrieben?').
target_language_example: Hast du den Bericht schon geschrieben?
native_language_example: Have you already written the report?

meaning: 'have already been' (perfect participle used to ask or say someone has visited/been somewhere before).
additional_notes: Used with forms of sein (bin/bist/ist/sind/seid) + schon gewesen to talk about past visits or experiences up to now. Common in questions about places or how often someone has been somewhere: e.g. 'In welchen Ländern seid ihr schon gewesen?' = 'Which countries have you already been to?' Not a fixed idiom—combines the adverb 'schon' (already) with the past participle 'gewesen' (been).
target_language_example: In welchen Ländern seid ihr schon gewesen?
native_language_example: Which countries have you already been to?

meaning: It's okay / never mind / that's fine (used to calm, reassure, or end a small disagreement).
additional_notes: A casual phrase used to tell someone not to worry or to accept/stop something. Tone can be soothing, dismissive, or resigned depending on context. Often used like 'Okay, it's fine' or 'Don't worry about it.' Not formal; common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Schon gut, du musst dich nicht entschuldigen.
native_language_example: It's okay, you don't need to apologize.

meaning: already/anyway (with 'hin' meaning 'there' or 'to that place'); often used in phrases meaning 'I'll manage it' or to ask 'where to' ('hin' = to there).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed single phrase but a combination: 'schon' (already/anyway/reassurance) + 'hin' (to there). Common usages: • reassuring ability: 'Das krieg ich schon hin' = 'I'll manage it / I'll fix it.' • telling someone to put/place something: 'Leg das Geld schon hin' = 'Go ahead and put the money there.' • asking where someone is going: 'Wo willst du ... hin?' with 'schon' adding surprise/emphasis: 'Where are you already going so early?' Tone and meaning depend on context and word order. Informal, frequently used in spoken German.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das mache ich schon hin.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll take care of it / I'll manage it.

meaning: always
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a long time or since the beginning (habit, condition, desire). Can be literal ('always') or emphatic ('all along', 'for as long as anyone can remember'). In some contexts it strengthens an exclamation (e.g. 'War sie schon immer!' — implying surprise about a long-standing trait).
target_language_example: Ich habe schon immer gern gezeichnet.
native_language_example: I've always liked drawing.

meaning: for a long time
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true for a long period up to now. Commonly appears with verbs of knowing, living, working, dating, etc. In casual speech can contract (e.g. 'schon lang'). Not to be confused with 'schon' alone (already) or 'lange' alone (long/for long).
target_language_example: Wohnst du schon lange hier?
native_language_example: Have you been living here for a long time?

meaning: already a long time ago / long since; something that should have happened or was true well before now.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that an action or state occurred much earlier than now or was overdue. Often appears with perfect or past context and can convey impatience, inevitability, or confirmation. Can be placed before or after the main verb phrase (e.g., 'schon längst weg' or 'hätte ... schon längst gemacht').
target_language_example: Ich hätte dir das schon längst sagen sollen.
native_language_example: I should have told you that a long time ago.

meaning: already
additional_notes: A common colloquial phrase used to indicate doing something now or in advance, often to prepare or start before something else happens. Context determines nuance: 'already' (something has been done), 'go ahead' or 'do X for now' (asking someone to begin or prepare). Often used in spoken German and with imperatives (e.g., 'mach schon mal...').
target_language_example: Ich mache schon mal das Licht aus.
native_language_example: I'll go ahead and turn off the light (for now).

meaning: already tired
additional_notes: Common phrase to say someone is tired earlier than expected or at the moment. 'schon' emphasizes that the state (tired) has occurred already — present, past or as a surprise. Can be used in statements, questions, formal (Sind Sie schon müde?) and informal plural (Seid ihr schon müde?).
target_language_example: Ich bin nach dem Spaziergang schon müde.
native_language_example: I'm already tired after the walk.

meaning: nothing / not anything (used to downplay or dismiss something)
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase in German. Often used to minimize importance, reject an offer, or say that nothing needs to be done or that nothing happened. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be casual reassurance (e.g. “it's nothing”) or a dismissive refusal (e.g. “no, really, nothing”). Common in combinations like “Das ist schon nichts” or as a short reply: “Schon nichts.”
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — das ist schon nichts.
native_language_example: Don't worry — it's nothing.

meaning: already often; many times before
additional_notes: Use to say something has happened repeatedly up to now. Common in present perfect (ich habe ... schon oft gesehen) or simple past contexts. 'schon' adds 'already' / prior occurrence; 'oft' means 'often'. Word order: 'schon oft' usually appears before the verb or participle phrase it modifies.
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Lied schon oft gehört.
native_language_example: I have heard this song many times before.

meaning: You’ll see; (used to warn, reassure, or predict something will happen or become clear).
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. When used with future tense (du wirst schon sehen) it often means “you’ll see” as a mild warning, promise, or prediction (‘wait and see’). With a noun like Ich kann schon sehen it can mean “I can already see.” Tone and context decide if it’s reassuring, threatening, or simply literal. Informal contractions drop the subject (Wirst schon sehen).
target_language_example: Du wirst schon sehen, dass alles gut wird.
native_language_example: You’ll see that everything will be fine.

meaning: already tried / have already tried
additional_notes: Used with verbs (often in perfect tense) to say that someone has already attempted something. 'Schon' = already; 'versucht' = tried (past participle of versuchen). Common in questions and statements: 'Hast du es schon versucht?' = 'Have you already tried it?'. Can be used with an infinitive clause: 'schon versucht, ...' (already tried to ...).
target_language_example: Hast du schon versucht, das Passwort zurückzusetzen?
native_language_example: Have you already tried resetting the password?

meaning: again (annoyance or surprise)
additional_notes: Used to express that something is happening again, often with annoyance, frustration or surprise. Context determines tone: can be simply factual ('again') or emphatic ('not again!'). Common in spoken German. Can appear at the start of a sentence (Schon wieder ...?) or before a verb/object.
target_language_example: Schon wieder hat er den Bus verpasst.
native_language_example: He missed the bus again.

meaning: already ten (years); indicates that ten years have passed or something has lasted ten years
additional_notes: Used with time expressions (usually 'Jahre') to say that an action or state has been true for ten years or that ten years have passed since something. Word order can vary: 'schon zehn Jahre' is common. Can be used in full sentences ('Schon zehn!') to express surprise about the number of years.
target_language_example: Wir kennen uns schon zehn Jahre.
native_language_example: We've known each other for ten years already.

meaning: already had lunch / already eaten lunch
additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone has eaten lunch yet. Often appears in questions and answers with verbs like essen (gegessen, gegessen haben). 'Schon' = already; 'zu Mittag' = at midday / for lunch. Common in present and past perfect contexts (e.g., Ich habe schon zu Mittag gegessen; Tom hatte schon zu Mittag gegessen...).
target_language_example: Hast du schon zu Mittag gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you already had lunch?

meaning: already back; returned already (used when someone or something has come back sooner than expected or has already returned).
additional_notes: Commonly used to ask or comment that a person (or item) has returned earlier than expected. Can be used as a short question (Schon zurück?) or in a full sentence (Er ist schon zurück?). Tone can be surprised or simply confirming. 'Schon' = already; 'zurück' = back/returned.
target_language_example: Er ist schon zurück vom Einkauf.
native_language_example: He's already back from shopping.

meaning: already more than / already over (a number); also used in questions meaning 'what does X already know about...?'
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) with numbers (often age) it means 'already over' or 'past' a certain amount (e.g. schon über vierzig = already over forty). 2) in questions or statements with 'was/wer/was weiß ... schon über ...' it expresses skepticism about how much someone knows — 'what does he/she really know about...?' Context determines meaning; 'schon' adds emphasis (already/really).
target_language_example: Sie ist schon über dreißig, fühlt sich aber jünger.
native_language_example: She is already over thirty, but feels younger.

meaning: he/she writes (a) — literally 'writes a' (used with a masculine or neuter noun like 'Buch').
additional_notes: This is the present tense (er/sie schreibt) plus the indefinite article 'ein'. It appears before a noun: 'schreibt ein Buch' = 'is writing a book.' For other subjects change the verb: ich schreibe ein, wir schreiben ein, du schreibst ein. With feminine nouns the article is 'eine' (schreibt eine Geschichte).
target_language_example: Sie schreibt ein Tagebuch.
native_language_example: She is writing a diary.

meaning: 'he writes' (third person singular of schreiben; 'er' = he).
additional_notes: A simple subject-verb phrase meaning 'he writes'. Word order varies in German: in statements it's usually 'er schreibt ...' but in yes/no questions or with sentence-initial elements the verb can come first as 'schreibt er ...?'. Here 'schreibt er' appears both in statements (e.g. 'schreibt er im Schlaf' = 'he writes ... effortlessly') and in questions ('Schreibt er das?' = 'Does he write that?'). Useful for forming questions about someone's writing or describing what he writes.
target_language_example: Schreibt er jeden Tag einen Brief?
native_language_example: Does he write a letter every day?

meaning: 'do you (plural) write' or 'are you (plural) writing'.
additional_notes: A present-tense question form using the verb schreiben (to write) addressed to 'ihr' (you plural). Use when asking a group or someone you address informally in plural. Word order: verb first in yes/no questions (Schreibt ihr...?); in open questions the question word comes first (Was schreibt ihr?). In German 'ihr' is the informal plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Schreibt ihr heute an eurem Projekt?
native_language_example: Are you (all) writing on your project today?

meaning: 'she writes' (present tense, simple statement or question word order when used in questions)
additional_notes: Literal present tense of schreiben (to write). Word order can be normal subject-verb (schreibt sie = she writes) or inverted in questions (Schreibt sie ...? = Does she write / Is she writing ...?). Used for general statements (Schreibt sie ihrem Sohn = She writes to her son) and questions about content, action or timing. Context determines whether it means 'writes' (composition), 'writes to' (corresponds with), or 'copies' (schreibt ... ab = copies down).
target_language_example: Schreibt sie jeden Tag eine E-Mail?
native_language_example: Does she write an email every day?

meaning: '(someone) screamed as loudly as (they) could.' — used to say someone shouted with all their strength.
additional_notes: This pattern combines the past tense verb 'schrie' (from 'schreien' = to scream/shout) with 'so ... (er/sie/ich) konnte' to indicate doing something as much/as loudly as possible. In spoken or written German you often see similar constructions with other verbs: 'rannte, so schnell er konnte' (ran as fast as he could). The subject pronoun changes to match the person (ich, er, sie, etc.).
target_language_example: Er schrie, so laut er konnte, um Hilfe zu holen.
native_language_example: He screamed as loud as he could to get help.

meaning: shouted/ screamed around/about (past tense of 'schreien'); 'schrie um' by itself is uncommon — usually part of a longer phrase like 'schrie um Hilfe' (shouted for help) or 'schrie um Aufmerksamkeit' (shouted for attention).
additional_notes: Schrie is the simple past (preterite) of schreien (to shout/scream). 'Um' is a preposition often used with nouns like 'Hilfe' (help) or 'Aufmerksamkeit' (attention) to form phrases: 'um Hilfe schreien' = to cry out for help. Word order in German can place 'schrie' before the object in narratives: 'Er schrie um Hilfe.' In spoken German, the perfect tense ('hat geschrien') is more common for past actions, but 'schrie' appears in written narration.
target_language_example: Sie schrie um Hilfe, als das Kind wegrannte.
native_language_example: She shouted for help when the child ran away.

meaning: to be to blame; to be at fault; (with a dative object) to owe (someone) something
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say someone is responsible or at fault for something (e.g. 'Er ist schuld' = 'He is to blame'). With a dative object (jemandem schuld sein) it can mean to owe someone something (less common). Can be used in questions and negatives: 'Wer ist schuld?' / 'Ich bin nicht schuld.' Tone is neutral; common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin schuld an dem Unfall; es tut mir leid, ich war schuld sein kann man hier nicht sagen—korrekt ist: "Ich bin schuld."
native_language_example: I am to blame for the accident; I'm sorry. Note: you cannot say "ich war schuld sein"—the correct form is "Ich bin schuld."

meaning: I owe you / I owe you (something).
additional_notes: Form of the verb 'schulden' used with the dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (formal 'you'). Commonly followed by a noun (e.g. Geld, Entschuldigung, Dank) or 'nichts'. Used to express obligation, debt, or owing thanks/apology. In everyday speech 'ich schulde dir' (informal) is used with friends/family.
target_language_example: Ich schulde Ihnen noch eine Erklärung.
native_language_example: I still owe you an explanation.

meaning: 'I owe you' (something to someone).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (what is owed) and the dative pronoun/phrase for the person owed (dir = to you). Common for money, favors, or figurative things (e.g., a favor, a meal). To say 'I owe you nothing' use 'Ich schulde dir nichts.' Past participle form: 'Ich habe dir ... geschuldet' or colloquially 'Ich schulde dir ...' is often used in spoken German with present tense.
target_language_example: Ich schulde dir ein Bier für deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: I owe you a beer for your help.

meaning: to be guilty; to be at fault; (colloquially) to owe (someone something)
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'to be guilty' or 'to be to blame' (for a crime or fault). In legal contexts it refers to legal guilt (e.g., Gericht erklärt jemanden für schuldig). Colloquially, used with a dative object to mean 'to owe' (jemandem etwas schuldig sein: Ich bin dir fünf Euro schuldig).
target_language_example: Er ist schuldig sein kann man ihm nicht vorwerfen.
native_language_example: He is guilty — you can't blame him for it.

meaning: 'to be guilty' or 'to be at fault' (used with an infinitive or as part of a clause).
additional_notes: Often appears in constructions like 'schuldig zu sein' (to be guilty) or 'jemandem Rechenschaft schuldig sein' (to owe someone an account/explanation). Used both for criminal guilt and for owing/being obligated. Commonly follows verbs like 'verdächtigen', 'gestanden' or appears in fixed phrases. Word order: 'schuldig zu sein' or 'als schuldig' + verb (e.g., 'überführen').
target_language_example: Die Jury erklärte ihn schuldig zu sein.
native_language_example: The jury declared him to be guilty.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people, organizations, or items to avoid or exclude
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone or something is banned, blocked, or not to be trusted. Can be literal (a list called 'black list') or figurative (e.g., a company blacklisting suppliers). Neutral to slightly negative; often used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Die Firma hat den Lieferanten auf die schwarze Liste gesetzt.
native_language_example: The company put the supplier on the blacklist.

meaning: black coffee (coffee without milk or cream).
additional_notes: Used to order or describe coffee served without milk, cream, or (sometimes) sugar. Grammatically, 'schwarzer' agrees with masculine noun 'Kaffee' (nominative). You may also hear 'schwarz' used after a verb: 'Ich möchte meinen Kaffee schwarz.'
target_language_example: Ich bestelle einen schwarzen Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I order a black coffee, please.

meaning: how difficult is it
additional_notes: Common part of questions asking about the difficulty of doing or obtaining something. Usually appears in the question pattern "Wie schwer ist es (für ...), X zu + infinitive?" or "Wie schwer ist es, etwas zu bekommen?" English equivalent: "How hard/difficult is it (to...)".
target_language_example: Wie schwer ist es für einen Anfänger, schwimmen zu lernen?
native_language_example: How difficult is it for a beginner to learn to swim?

meaning: a heavy blow; a severe shock or setback (emotional or practical)
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe news or events that hit someone hard emotionally or cause a serious setback. Can refer to physical blows but in these examples it means an emotional or reputational impact. Common collocations: 'ein schwerer Schlag für + jemanden'.
target_language_example: Die Kündigung war ein schwerer Schlag für die ganze Familie.
native_language_example: The dismissal was a severe blow for the whole family.

meaning: 'is difficult' (third-person singular of 'schwierig sein').
additional_notes: Used to say that something (it/that) is difficult. 'Schwierig' = difficult; 'ist' = is. Common in questions and statements. Word order can change (e.g. 'Wie schwierig ist das?'). Often follows a subject or introductory phrase: 'Dass Englisch schwierig ist.'
target_language_example: Wie schwierig ist das für dich?
native_language_example: How difficult is that for you?

meaning: to go swimming; to go for a swim.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase used to say you will go swimming (pool, lake, sea). Often used with a person or time (mit ... schwimmen gehen / diesen Sommer schwimmen gehen). It behaves like a separable verb construction when conjugated with gehen (e.g., wir gehen schwimmen / ich gehe schwimmen) but is commonly treated as a fixed phrase in speech.
target_language_example: Ich werde diesen Sommer viel schwimmen gehen.
native_language_example: I will go swimming a lot this summer.

meaning: to be able to swim / can swim.
additional_notes: A verb phrase: the infinitive schwimmen + modal verb können (ability). Used to say someone has the ability to swim or will have it in the future (with auxiliary or modal conjugation). Commonly appears with time expressions (bald) or necessity (Jeder sollte...). In German word order, können is conjugated and schwimmen remains in the infinitive at the end of the clause when used with modal verbs.
target_language_example: In ein paar Wochen wird sie schwimmen können.
native_language_example: In a few weeks she will be able to swim.

meaning: I swear to you / I promise you.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the truth of what you're saying or to promise something to the listener (informal singular 'dir'). Often appears as 'Ich schwöre dir' + clause. Tone can be serious, emotional, or emphatic. For formal or plural listeners use 'ich schwöre Ihnen' or 'ich schwöre euch'.
target_language_example: Ich schwöre dir, ich werde pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: I swear to you, I will be on time.

meaning: 'I am ashamed' or 'I feel ashamed'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular reflexive form of schämen (sich schämen). Used to express shame or embarrassment about something. Common patterns: 'Ich schäme mich (dafür), dass...'; 'Ich schäme mich + genitive/noun' (e.g. 'meines schlechten Englisch'). Can be negated: 'Ich schäme mich nicht...' Informal spoken emphasis may add 'eh' as in the example.
target_language_example: Ich schäme mich, dass ich zu spät gekommen bin.
native_language_example: I am ashamed that I arrived late.

meaning: 'are you ashamed' (informal question to one person)
additional_notes: A direct, sometimes confrontational question formed from the verb sich schämen (to be ashamed) in the second-person singular (du). Used to ask if someone feels shame or embarrassment — can be accusatory or reproachful depending on tone and context. Common in spoken German; with 'dich' (schämst du dich?) is the full reflexive form, but native speakers often shorten it to 'schämst du'.
target_language_example: Sag mal, schämst du dich nicht, das so zu sagen?
native_language_example: Tell me, aren't you ashamed to say that?

meaning: I felt ashamed / I was embarrassed.
additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of 'sich schämen' (to be ashamed/embarrassed). Used with 'für' or 'wegen' + noun to show the cause (e.g. für meinen Bruder / wegen meines Bruders) or with adverbial phrases (e.g. zu sehr, um ...). Common in personal statements: 'Ich schämte mich.' = 'I was embarrassed/ashamed.'
target_language_example: Ich schämte mich, als ich meinen Fehler bemerkte.
native_language_example: I was embarrassed when I noticed my mistake.

meaning: do you estimate / do you think (approximate or value someone/something)
additional_notes: From the verb schätzen. Can mean 'to estimate' (age, number) or 'to value/appreciate' (qualities of a person). Context decides meaning: with 'wie alt' it's 'estimate how old'; with 'an' + person it's 'what do you appreciate about...'. Common in questions. Verb is informal/neutral; 'schätzen Sie' is the formal form.
target_language_example: Was schätzt du an diesem Buch am meisten?
native_language_example: What do you appreciate most about this book?

meaning: Nice to... / It was nice to... (used to say you enjoyed doing something with someone).
additional_notes: This phrase is often followed by a verb in the infinitive with 'zu' or by a noun phrase indicating the activity (e.g. 'mit dir zu arbeiten', 'mit Ihnen zu reden', 'mit dir hier zu sitzen'). It expresses enjoyment or polite approval after an interaction. In casual speech the subject and auxiliary may be omitted (e.g. 'War schön, mit dir zu marschieren'). Use 'dir' for informal 'you' and 'Ihnen' for formal 'you'.
target_language_example: Schön, mit dir zu lernen.
native_language_example: Nice to study with you.

meaning: nice for; good for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is pleasant, fortunate, or beneficial for someone. Often appears in short exclamations (e.g., "Schön für dich!" or "Wie schön für dich!") to express sincere or sometimes sarcastic approval. Follows the person/recipient (dativ): "schön für dich", "schön für ihn/ihr/uns". Can be used in fuller sentences: "Ich will, dass es schön für dich ist."
target_language_example: Wie schön für dich, dass du das Meeting bestanden hast!
native_language_example: How nice for you that you passed the meeting!

meaning: nice/beautiful here; it's pleasant here.
additional_notes: Used to say a place is pleasant, attractive, or enjoyable. Common in simple statements (Es ist schön hier.) and in small talk or questions (Schön hier, oder?). Can be intensified with adverbs: sehr schön hier (very nice here).
target_language_example: Es ist wirklich schön hier am See.
native_language_example: It's really nice here by the lake.

meaning: 'nice and' used idiomatically to mean 'that's all well and good' or 'nice, but...' (introduces a contrasting reservation)
additional_notes: Common in the fixed expression 'Schön und gut' (or 'Ist ja schön und gut'), which means 'that's all well and good' and is used to politely or mildly disagree, add a restriction, or introduce a counterpoint. Alone 'schön und' can also appear in literal descriptions (e.g. 'schön und frisch' = 'nice and fresh'), but in the example sentences the idiomatic meaning is the relevant one. Use 'schön und gut' to soften criticism or signal that something is insufficient.
target_language_example: Schön und gut, aber wir brauchen noch mehr Informationen.
native_language_example: That's all well and good, but we still need more information.

meaning: 'schön auf' is not a fixed standalone phrase in German; it appears as the adverb 'schön' (nicely, beautifully, very) followed by a preposition or particle like 'auf' depending on context. Together they do not form a single idiomatic meaning.
additional_notes: Treat 'schön' and 'auf' separately. 'schön' is a common adverb/adjective meaning 'beautiful', 'nice', or (colloquially) 'very'/'really' before adjectives or participles (e.g. "schön groß" = "really big"). 'auf' is a preposition/particle with many uses (on, open, up, to). If you see 'schön auf' in a sentence, parse 'schön' as modifying an adjective or participle and 'auf' as beginning a prepositional phrase or particle of a separable verb. Example patterns: "schön aufgeräumt" (nicely/tidily cleaned/tidied up), "schön aufpassen" (colloquial: really pay attention) or "schön auf dem Tisch" (nicely on the table).
target_language_example: Das Zimmer ist schön aufgeräumt.
native_language_example: The room is nicely/very tidied up.

meaning: to know (someone) very well
additional_notes: A colloquial combination: schön (here meaning 'quite' or 'really') + gut kennen ('to know well'). Used to emphasize that you have strong familiarity or close relationship with a person. Appears with different subjects and object pronouns. Common in spoken German; not a fixed idiom but a natural emphatic phrase.
target_language_example: Du musst sie wirklich schön gut kennen, wenn du das gesagt hast.
native_language_example: You must know her really well if you said that.

meaning: the most beautiful girl (superlative).
additional_notes: A superlative phrase: schön (beautiful) → schöner → am schönsten; when used before a noun in definite form it becomes 'das schönste Mädchen' = 'the most beautiful girl'. Can describe one person as the most beautiful in a group, city, or ever seen. Gender: Mädchen is neuter in German (das Mädchen) even though it refers to a female person. Use appropriate context when speaking to avoid objectifying people.
target_language_example: Das ist das schönste Mädchen, das ich je gesehen habe.
native_language_example: That is the most beautiful girl I have ever seen.

meaning: 'bless you' (may God bless you).
additional_notes: Short, traditional phrase used to wish God's blessing on someone. Often appears in full as 'Gott segne dich' (God bless you). Can be used sincerely, formally, or in religious contexts; sometimes used idiomatically or warmly in everyday speech. Not the same as the one-word German response after sneezing ('Gesundheit' or informal 'Bless you' in English).
target_language_example: Gott segne dich, mein Freund.
native_language_example: God bless you, my friend.

meaning: see you
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of Standard German 'sehe dich' or the phrase 'ich sehe dich' (I see you) or 'ich sehe dich [morgen]' used as a casual 'see you' / 'I'll see you' or literal 'I see you'. Common in spoken, informal contexts. Context determines whether it's literal (I can see you) or used as a goodbye/appointment (see you tomorrow).
target_language_example: Ich seh dich morgen in der Schule.
native_language_example: I'll see you tomorrow at school.

meaning: I see (that) you... — introduces an observation about the listener.
additional_notes: Common phrase structure: 'Ich sehe, Sie ...' or shortened in speech to 'Ich seh', Sie ...'. It signals the speaker has noticed or realized something about the other person and is often followed by a statement about their status, behavior, or expectations. Can be neutral, sympathetic, mildly critical or ironic depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ich sehe, Sie haben lange gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I see (that) you have worked a long time.

meaning: I see that you... / I can tell that you...
additional_notes: Used to state an observation or impression about the other person. 'Sehe' is first-person singular of 'sehen' (to see). In spoken German you might also hear 'ich sehe, dass du...' or shorter 'ich seh, dass du...' The clause after 'dass' uses the normal word order for subordinate clauses (verb at the end). Common in both neutral and friendly contexts.
target_language_example: Ich sehe, dass du müde bist.
native_language_example: I can see that you are tired.

meaning: 'when I see (something), I remember' — a common clause pattern: sehe (see) + erinnere (remember)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a frequent combination of verbs in sentences with 'wenn'/'immer wenn'/'jedes Mal, wenn' ('when/whenever'). Word order: subordinate clause (wenn...) puts the conjugated verb at the end: 'Wenn ich das sehe, erinnere ich mich an ...'. 'Erinnere' normally appears with the reflexive pronoun 'mich' (erinnere mich). Useful for talking about memories triggered by sights.
target_language_example: Wenn ich das alte Lied sehe, erinnere ich mich an meine Kindheit.
native_language_example: When I see that old song, I remember my childhood.

meaning: 'I see it' or 'I consider it' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Sehe es is the first-person singular present of sehen (ich sehe) plus the pronoun es. It can mean the literal perception 'I see it' (e.g. visual or understanding: 'I get it') or be part of the construction 'ich sehe es als ...' meaning 'I consider/regard it as ...'. Word order may change in full sentences (e.g. 'Ich sehe es als wichtig an').
target_language_example: Ich sehe es als Chance.
native_language_example: I consider it a chance.

meaning: I see no reason (to)... / I don't see a reason (to)...
additional_notes: Used to say there is no reason or justification for something. Often followed by a clause with warum (why) or an infinitive/that-clause. Polite and neutral; common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich sehe keinen Grund, warum wir warten sollten.
native_language_example: I don't see any reason why we should wait.

meaning: see her
additional_notes: Present-tense first-person singular of sehen + object pronoun sie. Meaning depends on context: sie can be feminine singular 'her' or plural 'them'. Used for visual contact or meeting (I see/meet her/them). Word order can change (e.g. 'ich sehe sie' vs. 'sehe sie?' in questions).
target_language_example: Ich sehe sie heute Abend.
native_language_example: I see her/I'm seeing her tonight.

meaning: 'also look' / 'also appear' (used to add that someone or something appears a certain way in addition to something else).
additional_notes: Used when making an additional observation about appearance or expression. Note verb 'aussehen' (to look/appear) is separable: in many sentences the parts split (e.g. 'sehen ... aus'), so the contiguous sequence 'sehen auch' can occur when 'auch' follows the verb. Contexts: descriptions of mood, health, attractiveness. Formality: neutral; can be used in both formal and informal address depending on pronoun.
target_language_example: Sie sehen auch besorgt aus.
native_language_example: You also look worried.

meaning: 'to look' or 'to appear' (how someone or something seems/looks)
additional_notes: Separable verb construction: 'aussehen' is split in main clauses into 'sehen ... aus' (e.g., 'du siehst gut aus'). Common patterns: 'aussehen wie ...' (to look like ...), 'aussehen, als ...' (to look as if ...). Conjugate 'sehen' to match the subject: 'ich sehe aus', 'du siehst aus', 'er/sie/es sieht aus', 'wir sehen aus', 'ihr seht aus', 'sie sehen aus'.
target_language_example: Sie sehen aus wie wir.
native_language_example: They look like us.

meaning: to look good / to appear attractive or suitable
additional_notes: A common way to say that something or someone 'looks good' in German. Usually used with a subject (singular or plural) and often followed by 'aus' as in 'sehen gut aus'. In the examples the shortened form 'sehen gut' appears in context; learners should remember the full phrase 'sehen gut aus'. Can describe appearance (hair, clothes, items) or general suitability.
target_language_example: Deine neuen Schuhe sehen gut aus.
native_language_example: Your new shoes look good.

meaning: to not look/appear (a certain way); to not seem
additional_notes: Used with the verb sehen to state that someone or something does not have a certain appearance or does not seem a certain way. Often followed by adjectives or phrases (e.g., 'gut aus', 'so aus'). Word order commonly places 'sehen' before 'nicht' when negating the appearance (e.g., 'Sie sehen nicht gut aus'). Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on pronoun and verb form.
target_language_example: Sie sehen nicht gut aus.
native_language_example: They don't look well.

meaning: to appear/look + 'very' — used to intensify an adjective describing appearance (equivalent to 'look very' in English)
additional_notes: In German, sehen (in the construction sehen ... aus) combines with sehr placed before an adjective: sehen sehr + Adjektiv + aus. Use to describe how someone or something appears. Word order: Subject + sehen + sehr + Adjektiv + aus. The exact token sequence 'sehen sehr' appears when discussing or quoting the verb and intensifier together (e.g., in infinitive or explanatory contexts) or in contexts like reported speech or non-finite constructions.
target_language_example: Diese Äpfel sehen sehr frisch aus.
native_language_example: These apples look very fresh.

meaning: A sequence of two words ('sehen' = to see, infinitive or finite forms; 'ist' = is) that appears when a clause or infinitive phrase about seeing is followed by 'ist' to state or define something (e.g., 'What you see is ...' or 'To see X is ...'). It is not an idiom but a common syntactic pairing in explanatory or descriptive sentences.
additional_notes: Treat as two separate words rather than a fixed phrase. Frequently occurs in structures like 'Was ... sehen, ist ...' or '... zu sehen, ist ...'. Commas often separate the clause/infinitive from 'ist'. The exact surface sequence 'sehen, ist' can appear when the verb 'sehen' ends a subordinate clause or an infinitive phrase and is immediately followed by 'ist' in the main clause (comma present in German punctuation).
target_language_example: Den Sonnenaufgang von einem Berggipfel aus zu sehen, ist eine Wonne.
native_language_example: To see the sunrise from a mountain peak is a delight.

meaning: 'could see' (conditional/subjunctive: expressing a wish or hypothetical ability to see)
additional_notes: Combines the infinitive sehen (to see) with the subjunctive/conditional form könnte (from können). Used to express wishes, regrets, or hypothetical situations (e.g., 'If only someone could see that...'). Often appears in conditional sentences introduced by wenn or in exclamations ('Wenn sie dich doch jetzt nur sehen könnte!').
target_language_example: Wenn ich dich nur einmal sehen könnte!
native_language_example: If only I could see you once!

meaning: see you then / we'll see each other then
