additional_notes: Common informal way to say you'll meet again at a later time or place. Used when leaving or ending a conversation to confirm a future meeting (can be followed by a time or place: 'in Paris', 'morgen', etc.). Tone can range from friendly to sarcastic depending on context (example 3 shows a hostile/facetious use). Often shortened in speech to 'sehen wir uns dann' or simply 'bis dann'.
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns dann morgen um zehn.
native_language_example: We'll see each other tomorrow at ten.

meaning: we'll see each other in (place/time).
additional_notes: Used to say you'll meet again at a specific location or after a specific time. Word order in German: sehen uns in + place/time. It's an informal/friendly way to arrange a future meeting or say goodbye with a plan to meet later.
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns in drei Monaten.
native_language_example: We'll see each other in three months.

meaning: we'll see each other in (the)... — used to say where you'll meet someone or express 'see you in/at...'.
additional_notes: This is a common spoken structure: Wir sehen uns in der + place (dative feminine noun: z. B. 'Mittagszeit' is unusual but shows time). More natural: 'Wir sehen uns in der Schule' (we'll see each other at school) or 'Wir sehen uns in der Mittagspause'. It can also be used figuratively/angrily (e.g. 'Wir sehen uns in der Hölle') — tone matters. Use the correct article/case for the following noun (dative).
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns in der Schule morgen um neun.
native_language_example: We'll see each other at school tomorrow at nine.

meaning: 'see each other tomorrow' — a casual way to say you'll meet again the next day.
additional_notes: Common informal phrase used when arranging or confirming a meeting for the next day. Often used with 'wir' (we) as in 'Wir sehen uns morgen.' Subject pronoun can be omitted in spoken German: 'Sehen uns morgen.' Tone is friendly; can be used between colleagues, friends, or acquaintances. If you want to be more formal, use 'Wir sehen uns morgen' with a polite context or choose a more formal alternative like 'Wir treffen uns morgen.'
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen im Büro.
native_language_example: We'll see each other tomorrow at the office.

meaning: 'wants to see' (literally 'sees/wants'), typically 'wants to see (someone/something)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb sehen (to see) + the modal verb wollen (to want) in third person singular. Common in relative clauses (e.g., 'der dich sehen will') and statements about selective perception ('Jeder sieht nur, was er sehen will'). Word order may change in subordinate clauses; in conversational speech can appear in various contexts (questions, negatives).
target_language_example: Da ist ein Herr, der dich sehen will.
native_language_example: There is a gentleman who wants to see you.

meaning: 'look' (formal imperative; polite command or suggestion using Sie)
additional_notes: Used to give a polite order or suggestion to one or more people you address formally (Sie). Often appears with reflexive verbs like 'sich umsehen' (to look around): 'Sehen Sie sich um' = 'Look around.' Tone can be encouraging (Sehen Sie sich ruhig um) or emphatic (Sehen Sie sich nur um). Use 'sie' capitalized (Sie) to mark the formal 'you.'
target_language_example: Sehen Sie sich bitte im Wohnzimmer um.
native_language_example: Please look around the living room.

meaning: 'I long for' / 'I yearn for' (to strongly miss or desire something).
additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb 'sich sehnen nach' + accusative/dative object introduced by 'nach'. Use 'ich sehne mich nach ...' to express a deep desire or homesickness for people, places, situations, or experiences. Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (nach dem Sieg, nach meinem Volk) or by an infinitive phrase introduced with 'danach' (Ich sehne mich danach, ...).
target_language_example: Ich sehne mich nach dem Meer und der Ruhe.
native_language_example: I long for the sea and the peace.

meaning: very much that you / I/ we ... (used to intensify a hope, wish, or feeling about 'you').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the adverb 'sehr' (very/very much) placed before a subordinating clause introduced by 'dass du...' to strengthen emotional verbs (freuen, hoffen, wünschen, etc.). Used to emphasize how strongly the speaker feels about what follows. Word order: main clause + comma + 'dass' clause. In English you would often translate it as 'I'm very glad that you...', 'I very much hope that you...', or 'I really hope that you...'.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe sehr, dass du die Prüfung bestehst.
native_language_example: I really hope that you pass the exam.

meaning: something very important
additional_notes: Used to refer to an important piece of information or news. 'Wichtiges' is a nominalized adjective (neuter) and often follows verbs like 'sagen', 'mitteilen' or 'erzählen'. Capitalize 'Wichtiges'. The phrase is indefinite — it doesn't specify what the information is.
target_language_example: Er hat mir heute Morgen etwas sehr Wichtiges gesagt.
native_language_example: He told me something very important this morning.

meaning: very good
additional_notes: A common way to praise something or say it is of high quality. It is the straightforward combination of sehr + gut. It can describe things directly (Das war sehr gut.) and also appear in patterns like gut in/bei etwas sein (“to be good at something”), e.g. nicht sehr gut in Französisch = “not very good at French.”
target_language_example: Das Essen hier ist sehr gut.
native_language_example: The food here is very good.

meaning: very much about / very (worried) about — intensifier used with verbs like sorgen (sich sorgen um) or beneiden (beneiden um).
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase on its own; 'sehr' is an adverb meaning 'very' that modifies verbs with the preposition 'um' (e.g. sich sorgen um = to worry about; beneiden um = to envy for). Use with verbs that take 'um + accusative'. In many examples 'zu sehr um' (too much about) appears; both 'sehr um' and 'sich zu sehr um ... sorgen' are common. Word order: 'sich sehr um X sorgen' or 'X sehr um ... beneiden'.
target_language_example: Ich sorge mich sehr um deine Zukunft.
native_language_example: I am very worried about your future.

meaning: to suffer/feel greatly from something; to be strongly affected by (pressure, circumstances, noise, etc.).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like leiden (to suffer) or stehen (to be under) + a noun with 'unter' (e.g. 'unter Druck', 'unter dem Lärm'). 'Sehr' intensifies the degree. Common collocations: 'sehr unter Druck stehen', 'sehr unter etwas leiden'. It describes being strongly influenced, burdened, or harmed by something (not physical location).
target_language_example: Sie leidet sehr unter dem Stress bei der Arbeit.
native_language_example: She is suffering a lot from the stress at work.

meaning: a lot to (do); very much to (do/handle).
additional_notes: Used before verbs like tun (to do) or other infinitives implied — commonly in the phrase ‚sehr viel zu tun‘ meaning 'to have a lot to do'. It describes a large amount of tasks, work, or something to handle right now. Word-for-word: ‚sehr viel‘ = very much/a lot; ‚zu‘ links to the implied infinitive (often omitted in speech).
target_language_example: Im Büro habe ich heute sehr viel zu tun.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do at the office today.

meaning: 'very important that' — used to introduce a clause stating something essential or necessary.
additional_notes: Followed by a subordinate clause with the conjunction 'dass' + verb at the end. Common in formal and neutral contexts to emphasize importance (Es ist sehr wichtig, dass ...). Can be used with different subjects and verb forms (Sie, du, ihr, er, etc.).
target_language_example: Es ist sehr wichtig, dass du pünktlich kommst.
native_language_example: It is very important that you arrive on time.

meaning: 'be in' in reported speech using the subjunctive (Konjunktiv I) — used to report what someone said (he/she said they were in ...).
additional_notes: This is the present subjunctive (Konjunktiv I) form of 'sein' (er/sie sei) followed by a preposition + place (in ...). It's used in indirect/reported speech to report statements without asserting them as facts. Common in written German and formal speech. In everyday spoken German you may hear indicative forms instead (e.g. 'ist in'), or Konjunktiv II for distancing. Example sentences show it with locations (in den Fluss, in Tunesien, in Boston, dort, in jener Nacht).
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie sei in Italien gewesen.
native_language_example: He said she had been in Italy.

meaning: "be a" in reported speech or subordinate clauses (subjunctive/indirect speech).
additional_notes: Sei is the Konjunktiv I form of sein used for indirect speech (reporting what someone thinks/says) or in subordinate clauses expressing hearsay, doubt, or reported statements. "Sei eine" appears before feminine or unstressed noun phrases (eine + noun). In everyday spoken German, Konjunktiv II or normal word order may also be used, but Konjunktiv I is common in written/reported contexts. The literal translation is possible but the mood (reported/uncertain) should be conveyed in English (e.g. "he said it was a..." or "they thought it might be a...").
target_language_example: Er behauptete, es sei eine seltene Münze.
native_language_example: He claimed it was a rare coin.

meaning: be it
additional_notes: Usually used to introduce one or more possibilities, reasons, or examples, often in patterns like „sei es … oder …“ or „sei es …, sei es …“. It is somewhat formal and common in writing.
target_language_example: Viele Menschen helfen, sei es mit Geld oder mit Zeit.
native_language_example: Many people help, whether with money or with time.

meaning: 'be my...' (imperative: telling someone/something to be yours or take a role)
additional_notes: Combines the imperative form 'sei' (from 'sein' = to be) with the possessive 'mein' (my). Used to tell someone to be your X (e.g., 'Sei mein Freund!' = 'Be my friend!') or to ask/command someone to take on a role (e.g., 'Sei mein Zeuge!' = 'Be my witness!'). Context matters: in reported/subjunctive contexts (e.g., 'ich sagte ihr, er sei mein Freund') 'sei' can also appear as Konjunktiv I (reported speech) meaning 'he is my friend' (indirect speech), not an imperative. Not appropriate as a literal phrase with inanimate objects unless used stylistically or jokingly.
target_language_example: Sei mein Freund, bitte.
native_language_example: Be my friend, please.

meaning: please
additional_notes: Usually part of a polite request such as `sei so gut/freundlich/lieb und ...`, meaning 'please' or 'be so kind and ...'. By itself, `sei so` is incomplete in this use. In reported speech, though, `sei so ...` can also simply be the subjunctive form of `ist so ...`, as in `er sagte, es sei so schwer` = 'he said it was so heavy'.
target_language_example: Sei so gut und mach die Tür zu.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: 'please be' (addressing a group, informal plural)
additional_notes: Imperative form of 'sein' (to be) for 'ihr' (you plural). Used to politely ask a group to be in a certain state or to behave in a certain way. 'Bitte' softens the command. For formal or singular polite use, German uses 'seien Sie bitte' (formal) or 'sei bitte' (singular informal).
target_language_example: Seid bitte leise, der Film beginnt gleich.
native_language_example: Please be quiet, the movie is about to start.

meaning: you are really
additional_notes: Colloquial emphasis: seid (second-person plural of 'sein') + echt (really/for real). Used to emphasize a characteristic (often negative) about 'you' (plural). Tone can be critical, surprised, or teasing depending on context and intonation. In singular/informal you would say 'bist echt'.
target_language_example: Ihr seid echt frech.
native_language_example: You are really/seriously cheeky.

meaning: 'are you always' — second-person plural informal present of 'sein' combined with adverb 'immer' (always), used when asking if multiple people are consistently in a certain state or habitually do something.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person (informal). 'Ihr' is the informal plural 'you'. For formal address use 'Sind Sie immer...?'. Word order can vary depending on emphasis: in questions 'Seid ihr immer pünktlich?' or 'Seid ihr immer so freundlich?'. Can appear in negative or contrasting contexts: 'Seid ihr immer so laut?' (Are you always this loud?).
target_language_example: Seid ihr immer so pünktlich?
native_language_example: Are you always so punctual?

meaning: 'are you always so...' (used to ask why people are consistently a certain way)
additional_notes: A direct question phrase addressing a group (ihr = you plural). Followed by an adjective (e.g. aggressiv, beschäftigt). Often used to express annoyance or surprise at a repeated behavior or characteristic. Tone can be neutral or critical depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Warum seid ihr immer so ungeduldig?
native_language_example: Why are you always so impatient?

meaning: 'you are my' (plural informal/formal plural address), used to say someone belongs to you in a relational or figurative way.
additional_notes: Seid is the 2nd-person plural imperative or present-tense form of sein (ihr seid = you (pl.) are). In sentences like "Ihr seid meine Eltern" the full form is "Ihr seid meine..." meaning "You are my..." In the imperative "Seid meine Zeugen!" it means "Be my witnesses!" The phrase requires agreement in gender/number for the following noun (meine for feminine or plural nouns). For singular masculine nouns you would say "mein" (e.g. "Ihr seid mein Freund" for one male friend).
target_language_example: Ihr seid meine Freunde.
native_language_example: You are my friends.

meaning: 'you are so' (emphatic), used to intensify an adjective or comment about 'ihr' (plural you).
additional_notes: Used with the plural pronoun ihr (you all). Follows an adjective or comment to add emphasis — can be positive (nett, begabt, groß) or negative/insulting (blöd, inkompetent). In English it often corresponds to 'you are so...' or 'you guys are so...'. Tone depends on context and intonation; can be playful, admiring, or rude. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ihr seid so freundlich!
native_language_example: You are so friendly!

meaning: you (plural) are like / you are like
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'seid' (2nd person plural of 'sein' — 'to be') with 'wie' ('like' or 'as'). Used to compare a group of people to something or someone. In English it corresponds to 'you are like...' or in imperative contexts paired with exhortations ('seid wie Jesus') it means 'be like...'. Word order: 'Ihr seid wie ...' for statements; for commands to a group use the imperative 'seid' (same form), e.g. 'Seid wie Jesus!'
target_language_example: Ihr seid wie gute Freunde für mich.
native_language_example: You are like good friends to me.

meaning: 'you (plural) are really' — used to emphasize a quality of a group (you all).
additional_notes: Seid is the 2nd person plural form of 'sein' (to be). Wirklich means 'really', 'truly' or 'indeed' and adds emphasis. Used with ihr (you plural). Can express praise (Ihr seid wirklich gut.) or criticism (Ihr seid wirklich alle Dummköpfe.). In spoken German, the comma is not required between 'seid' and 'wirklich'.
target_language_example: Ihr seid wirklich freundlich.
native_language_example: You (all) are really friendly.

meaning: to dedicate/devote one's life to (something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun in the dative case introduced by der (e.g., der Wissenschaft, der Musik, der Lehre). Common verbs: widmen, (sich) verschreiben. Tone: neutral/formal. Typical structure: [Subject] + [verb] + sein Leben + der + [Dative noun] (or: [Subject] + sein Leben + der + [Dative noun] + verschreiben).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Leben der Lehre verschrieben.
native_language_example: He has devoted his life to teaching.

meaning: to love something very much; 'to really like' (strong preference)
additional_notes: Used after a verb to emphasize that someone really enjoys that activity. Literal parts ('sein Leben' = 'his life', 'gern' = 'gladly') don't translate directly — it's an idiomatic intensifier meaning 'for the life of him/her/them loves to...'. Common with verbs: essen, schwimmen, reden, reisen, etc. Grammar: appears as 'er/sie/es ... für sein Leben gern ...' or simply '... sehr gern ...'.
target_language_example: Er spielt für sein Leben gern Gitarre.
native_language_example: He absolutely loves playing guitar.

meaning: to keep one's promise; to do what one promised
additional_notes: Used when someone follows through on a commitment or promise. Commonly used with a person as subject (er/sie/du/ich). Often appears in finite forms (hält sein Versprechen) or perfect (hat sein Versprechen gehalten). Neutral register; appropriate in formal and informal contexts depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Er versucht, sein Versprechen zu halten, obwohl es schwierig ist.
native_language_example: He is trying to keep his promise, even though it's difficult.

meaning: to break one's word; to fail to keep a promise or go back on what one said.
additional_notes: Used when someone does not keep a promise or contradicts a previous commitment. Often used in past forms (er hat sein Wort gebrochen) or negated to express reliability (er würde sein Wort nicht brechen). Common in contexts discussing trust, agreements, or moral obligations.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er würde helfen, aber am Ende hat er sein Wort gebrochen.
native_language_example: He said he would help, but in the end he broke his word.

meaning: 'to keep one's word' — to do what you promised or agreed to do.
additional_notes: Used when someone fulfills a promise or commitment. Often used impersonally (er hält sein Wort) or in constructions referring to trust and reliability. Opposite: 'sein Wort brechen' or 'sein Versprechen nicht halten'.
target_language_example: Er hat versprochen zu helfen, und er versucht immer, sein Wort zu halten.
native_language_example: He promised to help, and he always tries to keep his word.

meaning: used to introduce a possibility or uncertainty about 'he' (that he ... / it may be that he ...).
additional_notes: This construction appears in phrases like "es kann sein, dass er...", "es mag sein, dass er...", or questions "Kann es sein, dass er...". It signals that something is possible, likely, or uncertain regarding a male subject (er). In the last example, "sicher sein, dass er..." means "to be sure that he..." — same structure but conveys certainty instead of possibility. Replace "er" with another pronoun or noun as needed (e.g. "dass sie", "dass Tom").
target_language_example: Es kann sein, dass er heute später kommt.
native_language_example: It may be that he will come later today.

meaning: uses of the verb sein ('to be') combined with the reflexive pronoun sich in various constructions (e.g. 'to be able to [do something to oneself]', 'to be about to [do something]', 'to be careful not to [do something]', 'to be surprised/wonder').
additional_notes:
This entry illustrates several common patterns where sein appears with a reflexive infinitive or reflexive pronoun:
- 'Muss toll sein, sich die Spieler aussuchen zu können.' — sein + infinitive clause expressing an opinion about an ability or situation.
- 'Tom und Maria schienen kurz davor zu sein, sich zu trennen.' — 'davor sein, ... zu' = 'to be about to ...' or 'to be close to ...'.
- 'Wenn man ein Messer wäscht, muß man vorsichtig sein, sich nicht zu schneiden.' — sein + adjective + reflexive infinitive expresses being careful/not to do something to oneself.
- 'Überrascht sein, sich wundern, heißt anfangen, zu verstehen.' — sein + adjective describes an emotional/state reaction; 'sich wundern' is a reflexive verb 'to wonder'.
Note for learners: 'sein, sich' is not a fixed phrase but a label showing how the copula sein can co-occur with reflexive constructions. Word order: the reflexive infinitive often appears at the end (… sich zu trennen).
target_language_example: Muss toll sein, sich die Spieler aussuchen zu können.
native_language_example: It must be great to be able to choose the players for oneself.

meaning: used to link a clause with another clause that continues or adds a related idea (literally 'be, and').
additional_notes: This combination appears when a verb or clause with 'sein' (to be) is followed by 'und' to connect a second clause. In English you often translate it simply as 'and' or with a rephrasing (e.g. 'and you shouldn't either', 'and it will be sad for him'). Word order and punctuation may vary; sometimes the second clause repeats the idea or adds a consequence. Not an idiom—just a normal conjunction after a verb phrase.
target_language_example: Er möchte freundlich sein, und die anderen sollten es auch sein.
native_language_example: He wants to be friendly, and the others should be too.

meaning: used to make comparisons with the verb 'to be' (… to be ... than ...).
additional_notes: Combine with an adjective or adverb to compare two things or people: 'X ist (adjective) als Y' often appears as 'X scheint (adjective) zu sein als Y' or with comparative forms: 'glücklicher als' = 'happier than'. In German the comparative adjective usually ends with -er (glücklicher) and is followed by 'als' to mean 'than'.
target_language_example: Tom scheint viel glücklicher zu sein als Mary.
native_language_example: Tom seems to be much happier than Mary.

meaning: to leave something as it is / to let something be; also 'to stop' or 'to give up (doing something)'.
additional_notes: Used in spoken and written German. Can mean: 1) don't change or don't touch something (leave it as is), 2) stop doing something or abandon an idea/plan (colloquial). Often appears with an object or as an imperative: 'Lass das sein!' (Stop that!). Context determines whether it's about leaving something alone or quitting an action. Can be separated in finite forms (e.g. 'ich lasse es sein').
target_language_example: Ich werde es sein lassen, das Projekt jetzt weiterzuverfolgen.
native_language_example: I'll leave it be / I'll stop pursuing the project now.

meaning: to have to be (somewhere / in a certain state) — expresses obligation or necessity using the verb 'sein'.
additional_notes: Combines the infinitive 'sein' (to be) with the modal verb 'müssen' (must/have to). Used when the thing you must do is to be somewhere or to be in a certain condition. Tenses and moods follow German auxiliary/modal constructions (e.g. wirst ... sein müssen, hättest ... sein müssen, werden ... sein müssen). Common in sentences about required presence or unavoidable states.
target_language_example: Morgen werde ich pünktlich sein müssen.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'll have to be on time.

meaning: literally 'wants to be' — used to express a desired or required state (often impersonal or modal), or that someone/something aims/intends to be in a certain way or place.
additional_notes: In German, 'sein will' combines the infinitive sein (to be) with wollen (to want). It appears in different constructions: 1) personal: 'er ist da, wo er sein will' = 'he is where he wants to be' (desire/intention). 2) impersonal/modal with passive-like sense: 'etwas will verstanden sein' = 'something needs to be understood' or 'ought to be understood' (expresses necessity or what is required). Context determines whether it means personal wanting or a general requirement.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht dort, wo ich sein will.
native_language_example: I am not where I want to be.

meaning: to want to be (something or somewhere); to wish to be
additional_notes: Combines the verb sein (to be) with wollen (to want). Used to express desire or intention about a state, role, profession, location, or hypothetical identity. Often appears in subordinate clauses introduced by wenn (if) or questions. Conjugate wollen for the subject: z. B. ich will sein, du willst sein, er/sie will sein; in infinitive constructions after modal verbs or in subordinate clauses the infinitive form is used (sein wollen).
target_language_example: Wenn ich Tier sein wollen würde, wäre ich ein Vogel.
native_language_example: If I wanted to be an animal, I would be a bird.

meaning: his teachers
additional_notes: Possessive phrase: 'seine' is the possessive determiner for 'his' (used with plural nouns like 'Lehrer'). Gender/number agreement matters: for 'his' with feminine singular use 'seine' as well (e.g., 'seine Mutter'), but contexts determine form (e.g., 'sein Lehrer' for singular). Commonly used to talk about the teachers someone has or had.
target_language_example: Er respektiert seine Lehrer.
native_language_example: He respects his teachers.

meaning: his people; his group/associates (people who work for or are loyal to him).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people associated with a man (employees, team, supporters, associates, or sometimes bodyguards). Context determines formality and exact meaning — can be neutral (staff, team) or imply loyal/connected associates. Pronoun agrees with owner (e.g., 'seine Leute' = his people).
target_language_example: Seine Leute haben das Treffen organisiert.
native_language_example: His people organized the meeting.

meaning: his love (someone he loves or his feeling of love).
additional_notes: Can refer to (a) a person he loves (e.g. "his beloved"), or (b) his feeling/affection for someone or something (often followed by "zu" + person). Context determines meaning: "seine Liebe zu Maria" = his love for Maria; standalone "seine Liebe" can mean "his beloved" or the emotion. Gender/possessive changes with the subject (seine = his).
target_language_example: Er schrieb ein Lied über seine Liebe zu Anna.
native_language_example: He wrote a song about his love for Anna.

meaning: His Majesty (formal title used for a king or emperor).
additional_notes: A formal, respectful way to refer to a male monarch (king, emperor). Used as a title or in the third person (e.g., 'Seine Majestät hat gebeten' = 'His Majesty has requested'). If referring to a queen, use 'Ihre Majestät' (Her Majesty). Often appears in formal contexts, historical texts, or polite speech.
target_language_example: Seine Majestät betritt den Saal.
native_language_example: His Majesty enters the hall.

meaning: his money / with his money (dative phrase).
additional_notes: A dative phrase using the possessive pronoun 'sein' (his) plus 'Geld' (money). Commonly appears in expressions like 'mit seinem Geld umgehen' (to deal with/spend his money) or 'machen, was er will' (do what he wants with his money). Adjusts for gender/number of possessor (mein Geld, ihrem Geld, etc.).
target_language_example: Er kann mit seinem Geld machen, was er will.
native_language_example: He can do what he wants with his money.

meaning: of/from his trip (genitive form indicating possession or origin)
additional_notes: Seiner Reise is the genitive form of 'seine Reise' (his trip) and often appears after verbs like 'berichten von', 'sprechen von', or with prepositions indicating origin (von). In the examples it appears with 'von' + dative (von seiner Reise) meaning 'about/from his trip'. Genitive alone (seiner Reise) can show possession (the trip belongs to him). English uses 'his trip' or 'from/about his trip' depending on context.
target_language_example: Sie erzählte begeistert von seiner Reise nach Japan.
native_language_example: She talked enthusiastically about his trip to Japan.

meaning: in his place; if you were him; instead of him.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone would do (or should have done) in another person's situation. Often appears as "an seiner Stelle" (literally "at his place") and is followed by a conditional or past conditional (e.g. "würde...", "hättest...", "täten..."). Can be adapted for other persons: "an meiner Stelle", "an deiner Stelle", "an ihrer Stelle".
target_language_example: An seiner Stelle würde ich das Angebot annehmen.
native_language_example: If I were him, I would accept the offer.

meaning: for three (units of time) / since three (o'clock).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions. 'seit drei' usually means 'since three o'clock' (point in time) or 'for three [hours/days]' when followed by a time unit (e.g. 'seit drei Stunden'). Alone, in spoken German, 'seit drei' typically implies 'since three o'clock'. To specify duration, add the unit: 'seit drei Stunden' = 'for three hours'. Can be followed by present-tense verbs to describe an action that started at that time and continues.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit drei.
native_language_example: I've been working since three o'clock.

meaning: for (the) past week / since one week ago.
additional_notes: Use to say something has been happening continuously or starting one week ago and still true now. Often followed by present tense in German (Perfekt or Präsens) to express ongoing state: e.g. 'Seit einer Woche ist Maria krank.' = 'Maria has been sick for a week.' Can also be used with verbs of continuing action or observation.
target_language_example: Seit einer Woche lerne ich täglich Deutsch.
native_language_example: I've been studying German every day for a week.

meaning: for half a (time unit) / since half a (time unit) ago
additional_notes: Used with a time unit (Stunde, Ewigkeit, etc.) to say something has been happening for half of that unit: e.g. seit einer halben Stunde = for half an hour / for thirty minutes. Typically followed by the time word in the genitive or dative construction (common: 'seit einer halben Stunde' or colloquially 'seit einer halben Stunde'). Often used with verbs in the present to indicate an action that started in the past and continues now.
target_language_example: Ich warte schon seit einer halben Stunde auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for the bus for half an hour.

meaning: for some time / for a while (ongoing, started in the past and continues)
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been happening for a period of time up to now. It implies the action or state began some time ago (not necessarily long) and is still relevant. Common in both formal and informal contexts. You can substitute 'seit einiger Zeit' with 'seit einiger Zeit schon' or with a specific duration (seit Wochen/Monaten/Jahren) for more precision.
target_language_example: Seit einiger Zeit habe ich Schwierigkeiten, gut zu schlafen.
native_language_example: I've had trouble sleeping for some time.

meaning: since yesterday; starting yesterday and continuing until now.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something began yesterday and still applies (duration up to the present). Often appears with verbs in present tense to express a continuing state (e.g., 'ich weiß seit gestern' = I've known since yesterday / I've been (not) sure since yesterday). Can also be used simply to say someone has been busy or learned something since yesterday.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit gestern Deutsch.
native_language_example: I've been learning German since yesterday.

meaning: since today; starting today.
additional_notes: Used to say that something began today or has been true from today onward. Often appears with a verb in present tense (e.g., 'ist seit heute ...') or alone as a short answer ('Seit heute.') to indicate the change happened today.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit heute in der neuen Abteilung.
native_language_example: I have been working in the new department since today.

meaning: for a long time; since long ago
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or state has been going on for a long period up to now. Often appears with verbs in the present tense plus 'schon' (schon seit langem) but 'seit langem' alone is also common. It answers 'how long?'.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn seit langem nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: I haven't seen him for a long time.

meaning: for a long time; for a long while
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true for a long period up to now, or that a long period has passed since something happened. Can describe past continuous situations (has been ... for a long time) or express that something is the first good/important thing in a long time (e.g. "der schönste Tag seit langer Zeit").
target_language_example: Ich habe sie seit langer Zeit nicht mehr gesehen.
native_language_example: I haven't seen her for a long time.

meaning: 'since when' — asks from what time something has been true or happening.
additional_notes: Common question phrase used to ask how long something has been the case (point in time or period starting then). Can be used in neutral or surprised contexts. Often followed by a clause with present perfect or present tense (e.g., 'bist du', 'wird... vermisst').
target_language_example: Seit wann lernst du Deutsch?
native_language_example: Since when have you been learning German?

meaning: used to ask 'since when have you been...' or 'how long have you been...?', asking about the starting time of a state or action.
additional_notes: Combines 'seit wann' (since when) with the verb 'bist' (you are/have been). Use with a location, state, or action: 'Seit wann bist du in Berlin?' or 'Seit wann bist du so nett?'. Common in spoken and written German. For other persons use different verb forms (z. B. 'seit wann ist er...', 'seit wann seid ihr...').
target_language_example: Seit wann bist du in Deutschland?
native_language_example: Since when have you been in Germany?

meaning: for more than (one) — indicates a period of time longer than one (unit)
additional_notes: Used with a time unit in the dative (e.g., Jahr, Monat) to say something has been happening or been true for more than one of that unit. Common structure: 'seit über einem Jahr/Monat/etc.' Often followed by a verb in the perfect or simple past to describe the ongoing state. Can stand alone as a short answer: 'Seit über einem.'
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit über einem Jahr in Berlin.
native_language_example: I have been living in Berlin for more than a year.

meaning: the same day
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more events happen on the identical calendar day. Often appears as "am selben Tag" (on the same day). Note: "selben" agrees with the noun; you'll also see forms like "am selben Tag" (dative) or "derselbe Tag" (nominative).
target_language_example: Wir sind am selben Tag angekommen.
native_language_example: We arrived on the same day.

meaning: 'at the same time' or 'simultaneously' (referring to when two or more events happen)
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used with dative (zur = zu + der). Often appears as 'zur selben Zeit', 'zur gleichen Zeit' or simply 'zur Zeit' (which means 'currently' and is different). Use to say people or events occurred together in time.
target_language_example: Wir sind zur selben Zeit angekommen.
native_language_example: We arrived at the same time.

meaning: 'not myself' / 'I myself don't (know/believe/recognize)'.
additional_notes: Selber is an emphatic/reflexive form of 'selbst' meaning 'oneself' or 'personally'. Paired with 'nicht' it negates that reflexive/emphatic idea: e.g. 'ich weiß selber nicht' = 'I myself don't know' or 'I don't even know myself' depending on context. Common in sentences about not knowing, not recognizing, not understanding, or not believing something about oneself. Word order: 'selber' usually comes before 'nicht' or before the verb complement.
target_language_example: Manchmal erkenne ich mich selber nicht mehr.
native_language_example: Sometimes I don't even recognize myself anymore.

meaning: to think for oneself; to consider one's own needs or make one's own decisions.
additional_notes: Used both for meaning 'think for yourself' (make your own judgments) and for 'think of yourself' (consider your own needs). Context determines whether it's about independent thinking or self-care. Common in advice, commands, or general statements. Conjugate verb 'denken' normally (du denkst selbst, er denkt selbst).
target_language_example: Du solltest öfter selbst denken und nicht nur anderen folgen.
native_language_example: You should think for yourself more often and not just follow others.

meaning: 'even a' (feminine/indefinite) — emphasizes that something applies also to/including one example (here with a feminine noun or indefinite noun phrase).
additional_notes: selbst = 'even' or 'oneself' depending on context. When used as 'selbst eine' it emphasizes that something applies to or is true of even one (female person or a noun introduced by 'eine') or highlights surprise. It can also appear with other genders/articles (z. B. 'selbst ein', 'selbst einen', 'selbst eine Fliege'). Word order: 'selbst' usually comes before the article. In some sentences 'selbst' can mean 'oneself' (reflexive) but with an article it typically means 'even'.
target_language_example: Selbst eine Schülerin hat die Antwort gewusst.
native_language_example: Even a student (female) knew the answer.

meaning: emphasis meaning 'oneself' or 'personally' often used before a phrase like 'die Hand' (to do something personally/oneself).
additional_notes: selbst is used for emphasis ('by oneself' / 'personally'). In the examples it appears in the common phrase 'selbst in die Hand nehmen' (to take something into one's own hands). 'selbst in' is not a fixed idiom by itself — it combines with a following noun phrase (e.g. 'selbst in die Hand nehmen', 'mir selbst in den Fuß geschossen' where 'selbst' emphasizes that the action affected the speaker). Use it to stress that someone did something personally, without help.
target_language_example: Ich werde das Problem selbst in Angriff nehmen.
native_language_example: I will tackle the problem myself.

meaning: literally 'even/oneself to' — used to emphasize that someone did something themselves or that the subject is the cause; often appears before a noun with 'zum' (to the) or before an infinitive construction.
additional_notes: selbst adds emphasis ('oneself', 'personally', 'even'). Combined with zum + noun it stresses that the person personally went or caused something (e.g. 'selbst zum Krankenhaus fahren' = 'personally go to the hospital'). With reflexive verbs it can emphasize that people cause something to themselves (e.g. 'sich selbst zum Aussterben bringen' = 'bring themselves to extinction'). Word order: selbst typically precedes the element it emphasizes.
target_language_example: Sie hat das Problem nicht gelöst, also musste ich selbst zum Laden gehen.
native_language_example: She didn't solve the problem, so I had to go to the store myself.

meaning: seldom/rarely (with a verb that follows 'zu' or as part of a verb phrase meaning 'rarely ...').
additional_notes: selten = 'rarely/seldom'. 'zu' here appears in different constructions: in sentences 1–4 'zu' is part of the verb 'zuhören' (Er hört nur selten zu) or the separable verb 'zustimmen' (ich stimme Ihnen selten zu) — in German separable verbs split in main clauses, so 'zu' moves to the end. In sentence 5 ('Tom ist selten zu spät') 'zu' is part of the adverbial phrase 'zu spät' meaning 'too late' but combined with 'selten' means 'is rarely late'. Pay attention to word order: for separable verbs the 'zu' goes to the end in present tense main clauses.
target_language_example: Sie stimmt ihren Kollegen nur selten zu.
native_language_example: She seldom agrees with her colleagues.

meaning: Put/Place them (or it/her) — imperative (informal 'du' form).
additional_notes: Informal command using the verb setzen (to set/put/place) + pronoun 'sie'. Context determines whether 'sie' means 'them', 'her', or formal 'you' (but here it's object, so usually 'them' or 'her'). Contraction of 'setze sie' to 'setz sie' is common in spoken and informal German. Often followed by a location word (hierher, drauf) or an indirect object (ihm).
target_language_example: Markl, setz sie hierher.
native_language_example: Markl, put them/here.

meaning: part of a reflexive verb construction plus a following accusative object introduced by 'den' (e.g. 'sich weigern, den ...' = 'to refuse to ... the ...').
additional_notes: This shows a reflexive verb with an infinitive clause introduced by a comma and 'zu' omitted in some contexts (here examples use infinitive without 'zu' after verbs like 'wehren/ wehren sich' or 'bemühen sich'). In the examples, 'sich weigern, den ...' means 'to refuse to (do) the ...' where 'den' is the masculine/neuter accusative article for the direct object. Beginners should learn the verb (e.g. 'sich weigern', 'sich bemühen') as reflexive and pay attention to word order: reflexive pronoun (sich) near the verb and the object after the comma/infinitive phrase.
target_language_example: Er weigerte sich, den Raum zu betreten.
native_language_example: He refused to enter the room.

meaning: Reflexive pronoun (sich) used with a first- or third-person subject plus an object (mich) meaning '... oneself' / 'me' — shows actions directed at the subject while also involving 'me'.
additional_notes: This pattern appears when a verb is reflexive (requires sich with er/sie/es or sich for formal/infinite forms) while the sentence also has a separate accusative object 'mich' (me). English often uses constructions like 'he made the effort to accompany me', 'he refused to acknowledge me', or 'she is happy to see me'. Verb forms: sich + infinitive/verb / plus explicit object. Word order: German places the reflexive pronoun where the verb expects it; 'mich' stays as the direct object. Watch verbs that are reflexive in German but not in English (sich freuen = to be happy).
target_language_example: Er freute sich, mich zu treffen.
native_language_example: He was happy to meet me.

meaning: Part of a reflexive construction with a dative object and an infinitive with zu: used with verbs like 'sich weigern' (to refuse) to indicate someone refuses to do something for/to someone (e.g. 'to refuse to help me' / 'to refuse me something').
additional_notes: This entry shows the pattern 'sich + dative pronoun + zu + infinitive'. 'Sich' is the reflexive pronoun that agrees with the subject (er/sie/ich/etc.). 'Mir' is the dative pronoun meaning 'to/for me'. The infinitive appears after 'zu' (often at the end of the clause). Common with verbs such as 'sich weigern' (to refuse). Word order examples: [Subject] weigerte sich, mir zu helfen. Or: [Subject] weigerten sich, mir zu sagen, ...
target_language_example: Er weigerte sich, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: He refused to help me.

meaning: negation applied to a reflexive verb or reflexive clause: 'not' used to negate an action expressed with a reflexive pronoun (sich).
additional_notes: In German many verbs are reflexive and use 'sich' (or other reflexive pronouns). To negate such verbs, 'nicht' is placed according to normal negation rules — often after the reflexive infinitive or at the end of the clause in perfect/infinite constructions: e.g. 'sich entscheiden, nicht ...' = 'to decide not to ...'. Word order depends on tense and clause type. The comma is sometimes used before 'nicht' when introducing an infinitive clause ('sich entschließen, nicht zu...').
target_language_example: Tom entschied sich, nicht zu warten.
native_language_example: Tom decided not to wait.

meaning: Two separate German items shown together: 'sich' (reflexive pronoun used as the object of reflexive verbs) and 'sein' (possessive pronoun meaning 'his' or 'its' when the possessor is masculine or neuter). Often appear together in sentences where the subject performs or experiences an action on/for themselves and also possesses something.
additional_notes: 'Sich' is the accusative or dative reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (e.g., sich bemühen, sich weigern, sich wünschen). 'Sein' is the possessive adjective that agrees in gender/number with the thing possessed (sein Buch, sein Ziel). Although shown together here, they are separate words with distinct grammatical roles; examples often place them close in a clause (e.g., sich weigern, sein X zu tun). For feminine possessor use 'ihr', for first person use 'mein', etc.
target_language_example: Der Demokrat bemühte sich, sein Ziel ganz allein zu erreichen. — hier stehen die Wörter 'sich, sein' im selben Satz.
native_language_example: The democrat endeavored to achieve his goal entirely alone. — here the words 'sich, sein' appear in the same sentence.

meaning: Reflexive pronoun 'sich' used with a verb + 'und' (and) to link two actions; often describes something happening to itself or a change of state, then another action follows.
additional_notes: In German many verbs use the reflexive pronoun 'sich' (e.g. sich öffnen, sich verdunkeln). Here examples show a clause with a reflexive verb + 'und' connecting a second clause. 'sich' marks the verb as reflexive or indicating a change of state; the second clause (after 'und') describes what happens next or as a result. Word order follows normal clause rules: verb in second position in the main clause, and the second clause also is a main clause starting with the conjugated verb after 'und'.
target_language_example: Die Tür schloss sich, und niemand war mehr draußen.
native_language_example: The door closed (lit. shut itself), and no one was outside anymore.

meaning: A combination of the reflexive pronoun 'sich' with the formal possessive 'Ihr' (your, formal) used in reflexive constructions: 'yourself' / 'your' (formal) in reflexive contexts.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but two words that can appear together in sentences where the verb is reflexive (requires 'sich') and the object/possessor is formal 'Ihr' (capitalized 'Ihr' = polite 'your'). Meaning depends on the verb and sentence: sometimes 'Ihr' is a possessive ('your') as in 'Ihr Pyjama' or 'Ihr Englisch'; sometimes the structure asks about spelling with 'sich ... schreiben' (Wie schreibt sich Ihr Nachname? is unusual — more common: 'Wie schreiben Sie Ihren Nachnamen?'). Watch word order and capitalization: 'Ihr' (formal you) is capitalized; 'ihr' lowercase can mean 'her' or 'their'.
target_language_example: Sie haben sich Ihr Geschenk verdient.
native_language_example: You have truly deserved your gift.

meaning: 'of you' / 'your' in reflexive or opinion phrases (part of larger reflexive or possessive constructions)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a combination of the reflexive pronoun 'sich' plus the formal/genitive/dative possessive 'Ihrer' (capitalized 'Ihr' = formal 'you'). Its meaning depends on the full sentence: it can appear in reflexive constructions like 'sich Ihrer Verantwortung entziehen' (to absolve oneself of your responsibility) or in opinion phrases 'sich Ihrer Meinung nach' (according to your opinion). In many examples 'Ihrer' is dative genitive or part of 'Ihrer Meinung nach' (meaning 'in your opinion'). Note capitalization: 'Ihrer' with capital I is formal; lowercase 'ihrer' has different meanings.
target_language_example: Meines Erachtens hat er sich Ihrer Hilfe nicht bedient.
native_language_example: In my opinion, he did not make use of your help.

meaning: to make an effort; to try hard
additional_notes: Reflexive construction with 'sich' + noun 'Mühe' + verb 'geben'. Commonly used to say someone is putting effort into something. Often appears with an infinitive: 'sich Mühe geben, etwas zu tun' or with an adjective/adverb describing the result (e.g. 'Er gibt sich große Mühe.'). Word order can vary in subordinate clauses and with separable elements.
target_language_example: Er versucht, sich Mühe zu geben und die Aufgabe sorgfältig zu erledigen.
native_language_example: He is trying to make an effort and complete the task carefully.

meaning: to worry; to be concerned (about something or someone).
additional_notes: Reflexive expression: use with a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch) and often phrased in infinitive or conjugated forms. Commonly followed by über + noun/accusative or um + noun to indicate the object of worry (e.g., sich Sorgen machen über die Prüfung / sich Sorgen um ihn machen). Conjugation example: ich mache mir Sorgen, du machst dir Sorgen, er macht sich Sorgen, wir machen uns Sorgen. Can be used in both formal and informal contexts depending on pronouns and tone.
target_language_example: Viele Eltern neigen dazu, sich Sorgen zu machen, wenn ihre Kinder spät nach Hause kommen.
native_language_example: Many parents tend to worry when their children come home late.

meaning: to take one's time; not to hurry
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase meaning to deliberately act slowly or allow oneself more time. Commonly used to tell someone not to rush or to pace oneself. Conjugates with the reflexive pronoun (ich lasse mir Zeit, du lässt dir Zeit, er/sie lässt sich Zeit). Can be used with oder without an explicit object or activity (e.g., ‚Lass dir Zeit.‘).
target_language_example: Er lässt sich Zeit bei der Entscheidung und will nichts überstürzen.
native_language_example: He is taking his time with the decision and doesn't want to rush anything.

meaning: to take one's time; to allow enough time for something
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase. Used when you deliberately spend more time on an activity or avoid rushing. Common in advice and polite suggestions: use with an activity or an infinitive (e.g. sich Zeit nehmen, etwas zu tun) or with für + noun (sich Zeit für etwas nehmen). Conjugate the reflexive pronoun to the subject (ich nehme mir Zeit, du nimmst dir Zeit, er nimmt sich Zeit...).
target_language_example: Nimm dir Zeit, dich für die richtige Wahl zu entscheiden — nimm dir Zeit.
native_language_example: Take your time to decide on the right choice.

meaning: to be alone / to feel alone; literally 'oneself alone'.
additional_notes: Used reflexively. Can mean physically alone or emotionally lonely. Commonly appears in phrases like 'auf sich allein gestellt sein' (to be left to cope on one's own). Context determines whether it's about being by oneself (no help) or feeling lonely.
target_language_example: Nach dem Umzug fühlte er sich allein in der neuen Stadt.
native_language_example: After the move he felt alone in the new city.

meaning: A reflexive prepositional phrase used with verbs like sich gewöhnen or sich anpassen meaning 'to get used to' or 'to adapt to' when followed by a neuter noun or a demonstrative pronoun (literally: 'to oneself to the').
additional_notes: Not a standalone verb — appears with a reflexive verb (e.g., sich gewöhnen an das, sich anpassen an das). Word order changes in subordinate clauses or with auxiliary/modal verbs (the reflexive pronoun and 'an das' can be separated). 'das' agrees with the following noun; if the noun has a different gender/case, 'das' changes to the appropriate article (an den, an die, an dem, etc.). Common translations: 'to get used to the (something)', 'to adapt to the (something)'.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mich schnell an das neue Arbeitsumfeld zu gewöhnen; ich will mich an das Klima hier anpassen.
native_language_example: I'm trying to get used to the new work environment quickly; I want to adapt to the climate here.

meaning: to keep something to oneself (not tell others); to keep a secret
additional_notes: Used reflexively with objects like 'ein Geheimnis' and often appears as 'für sich behalten' (to keep to oneself). It means not to share information. Common in sentences about secrets or private information. Conjugates with a reflexive pronoun: ich behalte es für mich, sie behält es für sich.
target_language_example: Er kann die Neuigkeit nicht für sich behalten.
native_language_example: He can't keep the news to himself.

meaning: both (of them) — reflexive use with 'sich' + 'beide' to indicate that two people (or things) each did or experienced something.
additional_notes: Used when referring to two people (or things) who each perform or experience an action reflexively. 'Sich' is the reflexive pronoun and must agree with the subject (e.g., 'wir haben uns beide', 'sie haben sich beide'). Word order can vary: 'sich beide' may appear after the verb or before it depending on clause structure. Common with verbs like 'entspannen' (relax) or 'schneiden' (cut). Example contexts: advice ('Sie sollten sich beide einfach entspannen.') or reporting injuries ('Tom und Mary haben sich beide an Glasscherben geschnitten.').
target_language_example: Sie sollten sich beide einfach entspannen.
native_language_example: You both should just relax.

meaning: 'just' / 'simply' (emphatic) or 'merely'; in warnings or imperatives with 'bloß' it can add strong emphasis meaning 'for heaven's sake, just don't' or 'don't you dare'.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb (sich + verb) to soften, limit, or emphasize the action as merely that—e.g. expressing that someone is simply feeling or doing something. In imperatives (e.g. 'Machen Sie sich bloß keine Gedanken') it intensifies the warning. Tone depends on context; not slang. 'bloß' can also be used without the reflexive pronoun.
target_language_example: Er freut sich bloß, zu Hause zu sein.
native_language_example: He's just happy to be home.

meaning: 'about it' / 'in doing so' / 'in that situation' (refers to something mentioned or the action being done)
additional_notes: Reflexive pronoun + adverbial 'dabei'. Used to refer back to a previously mentioned thing, situation, or action. Common in questions: 'worum handelt es sich dabei?' (what is it about?), 'Was haben Sie sich dabei gedacht?' (what were you thinking when you did that?). Can mean 'about it', 'while doing that', or 'in that situation' depending on context.
target_language_example: Was haben Sie sich dabei gedacht?
native_language_example: What were you thinking when you did that?

meaning: A reflexive pronoun (sich) + damit (da- + mit) meaning 'with that'/'about that'/'by that' — used with verbs to mean things like 'to agree to that', 'to be familiar with that', 'to struggle with that', etc.; exact translation depends on the verb and context.
additional_notes: sich is the reflexive pronoun and damit is da- + mit ('with that' / 'about that'). The phrase is compositional: it combines with many verbs to produce different meanings (e.g. sich damit einverstanden erklären = to agree to that; sich damit auskennen = to be familiar with that; sich damit abmühen = to struggle with that). Word order: sich usually appears near the finite verb (or as required by German word order), and damit refers to something mentioned earlier. Register is neutral; some verb phrases may be informal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Er erklärte sich damit einverstanden, auf sie zu warten.
native_language_example: He agreed to that / He agreed to wait for her.

meaning: to take one's own life; to commit suicide.
additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used with verbs like versuchen (to try) or vorhaben (to intend). Typical construction: [Person] + [verb] + versuchen/vorhaben + sich das Leben zu nehmen (or infinitive clause: versucht, sich das Leben zu nehmen). Very sensitive topic — use carefully. Formal/neutral; not slang. The verb nehmen (to take) completes the phrase; sometimes words like 'versuchen' or 'vorhaben' appear before the infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Sie hat versucht, sich das Leben zu nehmen.
native_language_example: She tried to take her own life.

meaning: to distance oneself from that / to get away from it (reflexive pronoun + 'davon' = 'from/of that').
additional_notes: 'Davon' refers to something previously mentioned (that thing, that situation). 'Sich davon' combines the reflexive pronoun with a prepositional adverb; full meanings depend on the verb used (e.g. 'sich davon fernhalten' = keep away from it, 'sich davonmachen' = leave quickly/get away). Word order and form change with imperative and infinitive constructions.
target_language_example: Halten Sie sich davon fern!
native_language_example: Keep away from that!

meaning: 'to be aware of the danger' (literally: 'to oneself of the danger (aware)')
additional_notes: This phrase appears with the reflexive pronoun 'sich' and the adjective 'bewusst' (often used as 'sich der Gefahr bewusst sein' = 'to be aware of the danger'). In German the dative 'der Gefahr' follows 'sich bewusst sein'. Use the correct reflexive form for the subject (ich bin mir der Gefahr bewusst, du bist dir ...). Commonly used to say someone recognizes a risk or danger.
target_language_example: Sie ist sich der Gefahr bewusst und geht vorsichtig vor.
native_language_example: She is aware of the danger and proceeds carefully.

meaning: to take the trouble / to bother (to do something)
additional_notes: Used reflexively with machen (sich die Mühe machen) to say someone made an effort or took the trouble to do something. Often followed by a verb phrase introduced by zu or an infinitive clause with zu + past participle (gemacht haben) or an infinitive (zu + verb). Can be used positively (appreciation) or neutrally/critically (nobody bothered).
target_language_example: Er hat sich die Mühe gemacht, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: He took the trouble to help me.

meaning: to make the effort; to bother to do something
additional_notes: Used when someone takes time or trouble to do something (often followed by zu + infinitive or a dass-clause). Can express appreciation or simply note that someone went to some trouble. Reflexive dative pronoun (mir/dir/sich/etc.) matches the subject. Common patterns: "sich die Mühe machen, etwas zu tun" or "sich die Mühe gemacht haben".
target_language_example: Er hat sich die Mühe gemacht, mir alles zu erklären.
native_language_example: He made the effort to explain everything to me.

meaning: 'oneself' + partitive/indefinite (used in contexts like 'sich einer Sache', 'sich einer Person', or in exclamations 'Sieh sich einer ... an') — often marks an indefinite person/thing or reflexive reaction; can be part of set phrases.
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed single phrase but a combination: 'sich' (reflexive) + 'einer' (indefinite/genitive/dative form of 'one'/'someone' or partitive). Usage varies by construction:
- 'sich einer Sache' (genitive) = to be aware of / to admit something (formal/old-fashioned). Example 1 uses a colloquial past passive-like structure 'Beschwerte sich einer …' meaning 'If someone complained…'.
- 'sich einer von euch zeigen' (example 2) uses 'einer' = 'one (of you)' in a subjunctive/conditional hope: 'that one of you would show up'.
- In the exclamation 'Sieh sich einer die an' the structure is idiomatic: 'Well, would you look at that' or 'Just look at that' (colloquial, often surprised or critical). 
Note for beginners: focus on recognizing 'einer' as 'someone/one (of...)' and that 'sich' makes verbs reflexive or forms fixed expressions like 'sich zeigen' or exclamations. Word order and case matter.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, sich einer von uns würde helfen.
native_language_example: I wish one of us would help.

meaning: a reflexive combination where 'sich' is used with 'einige' (some/several) to indicate that some people/objects are present or that someone takes some time/moments.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — appears in constructions with reflexive verbs (sich befinden, sich entschuldigen, sich Zeit nehmen, sich bilden). 'einige' means 'some', 'a few', or 'several'. Word order varies: often 'sich + verb + einige ...' (Es befanden sich einige Kinder...) or 'nahm sich einige Zeit' (took some time). Use cases: stating existence/location (befinden sich), forming apologies with time reference (entschuldigte sich einige Augenblicke später), or saying someone takes some time (nahm sich einige Zeit).
target_language_example: Auf dem Platz befanden sich einige Stände mit Essen.
native_language_example: There were several food stalls on the square.

meaning: to feel lonely
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: used with a reflexive pronoun (ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, er/sie fühlt sich, wir fühlen uns, ihr fühlt euch, sie fühlen sich). Commonly used to describe an emotional state (lonely, isolated, alone). Often combined with adjectives like verlassen (e.g., sich einsam und verlassen fühlen) or with temporal/place phrases (z. B. wenn Freunde weg sind).
target_language_example: Er fühlte sich einsam.
native_language_example: He felt lonely.

target_language_multi_word_term: sich etwas zu (e.g. sich etwas zu essen nehmen/zu tun wünschen)
meaning: a reflexive construction meaning to get/prepare/take something for oneself, or to wish/decide/intend to do something — exact sense depends on the main verb used (nehmen, kaufen, machen, wünschen, sagen, etc.).
additional_notes: Structure: 'sich' (reflexive pronoun) + 'etwas' (something) + verb (often with infinitive/zu or a noun phrase). Common examples: 'sich etwas zu essen nehmen/kaufen/machen' = get/make something to eat for oneself; 'sich etwas zu tun wünschen' = wish to do something; 'sich etwas zu sagen trauen' = dare to say something. Word order can vary (e.g., object placement, separable verbs). Use appropriate case: 'sich' is accusative (Maria hat sich etwas gekauft).
target_language_example: Maria hat sich etwas zu essen gekauft.
native_language_example: Maria bought herself something to eat.

meaning: to apologize for / to stand up for (depending on verb) — literally 'oneself for his/its'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a combination: the reflexive pronoun 'sich' + preposition 'für' + a possessive like 'sein'. The full meaning depends on the main verb used (e.g. 'sich entschuldigen für sein Benehmen' = to apologize for one's behavior; 'sich stark machen für sein Land' = to stand up for one's country). 'Sein' matches the subject (sein = his/its). Common verbs: entschuldigen (to apologize), stark machen (to support/defend).
target_language_example: Er entschuldigte sich für sein Verhalten.
native_language_example: He apologized for his behavior.

meaning: to say or give (something) about oneself; here 'von sich geben' = to utter/say (often something notable) and 'sich geben' = to behave or present oneself.
additional_notes: Two related uses appear in the examples: "von sich geben" (often reflexive + prep) means to utter or say something — often used for comments, statements, lies etc. Example: "Lügen von sich geben" = to tell lies. "ein Bild von sich geben" means to give a picture of oneself (i.e. hand or show a photo). Separately, "sich geben" (Wie hat sie sich gegeben?) means "how did she behave/come across?" or "how did she present herself?" Use context to tell which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Er hat gestern viele komische Sachen von sich gegeben.
native_language_example: He said a lot of strange things yesterday.

meaning: to feel happy; to consider oneself lucky (when used in idioms such as 'sich (etwas) glücklich schätzen')
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase with 'sich' (accusative reflexive pronoun). Used to describe an emotional state ('sich glücklich fühlen') or in idiomatic constructions ('sich glücklich schätzen' = to count oneself lucky). Conjugate 'sich' to the subject (ich fühle mich glücklich; du fühlst dich glücklich; er/sie fühlt sich glücklich).
target_language_example: Die meisten Menschen wollen sich glücklich fühlen.
native_language_example: Most people want to feel happy.

meaning: A reflexive construction with the separable particle 'heraus' used as part of various verbs to express movement or emergence 'out' or figurative meanings like 'to turn out' or 'to find out' depending on the main verb. 'sich heraus' by itself is not a standalone verb but appears in combinations (e.g. sich herausstellen, sich herausfinden).
additional_notes: 'heraus' is a separable particle: in main clauses it often appears at the end (e.g. Das stellt sich heraus.). In infinitives or subordinate clauses the particle can remain attached (z. B. sich herauszustellen). The meaning depends on the full verb: herausfinden = to find out, herausstellen = to turn out/prove to be, sich herausnehmen = to take the liberty. 'sich heraus' as given is compositional but must be combined with a verb root to convey a complete meaning.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mich heraus zu halten.
native_language_example: I'm trying to keep myself out of it.

meaning: reflexive pronoun + possessive (literally 'herself her...') used with reflexive verbs or reflexive constructions to indicate the subject is performing an action on or for themselves (e.g. put on her ... / earn her ...).
additional_notes: 'sich' is the accusative or dative reflexive pronoun for third-person singular/plural; the following possessive (ihren) agrees in gender/case/number with the noun that follows, not with the person. In the examples: "sich ihren Kopfhörer aufsetzen" (accusative) = put on her headphones; "sich ihren Mantel anziehen" (accusative) = put her coat back on; "sich ihren Lebensunterhalt verdienen" = earn her living (sich verdienen is idiomatic meaning to earn for oneself). Verb particles (auf/an) may split and go to the end: Maria setzte sich ihren Kopfhörer auf. Pay attention to case (accusative/dative) based on the verb and noun.
target_language_example: Anna wäscht sich ihren Hund nach dem Spaziergang.
native_language_example: Anna washes her dog (for herself) after the walk.

meaning: a reflexive phrase meaning 'oneself in this...' used to refer to actions, situations or knowledge that occur or apply in a particular place or context
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a combination of the reflexive pronoun 'sich' with the locative phrase 'in diesem' (in this + masculine/neuter noun). It appears in various constructions: with verbs like 'treffen' (meet), 'bestellen' (order), 'abspielen/abspielen' (happen, play out) or 'auskennen' (know one's way around). English equivalents depend on the verb: 'meet in this…', 'order for yourself in this…', 'happen in this…', 'be familiar with this…'. Remember to match gender/case of the noun after 'diesem' (dative).
target_language_example: Wer kennt sich in diesem Stadtteil besser aus?
native_language_example: Who knows this neighborhood better?

meaning: 'recently' or 'lately' when used with a reflexive verb; indicates something happening in recent times
additional_notes: The core phrase is 'in letzter Zeit' meaning 'lately'. When used with a reflexive verb, the reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject (e.g. ich habe mich in letzter Zeit gefühlt). The written form 'sich in letzter' is a citation form showing the reflexive infinitive plus the time phrase; in actual sentences you'll normally see the correct pronoun and full phrase (z. B. 'Ich habe mich in letzter Zeit...'). Placement: often before or after the verb phrase: 'In letzter Zeit habe ich mich ...' or 'Ich habe mich in letzter Zeit ...'.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich in letzter Zeit oft gefragt, ob das die richtige Entscheidung war.
native_language_example: I have often wondered lately whether that was the right decision.

meaning: 'ever' (used with reflexive verbs to ask if someone has ever done or felt something, or in negatives to mean 'ever/at any time')
additional_notes: je is an adverb meaning 'ever' or 'at any time'. When used with reflexive verbs, it appears after the reflexive pronoun (sich) in questions and negatives: Haben Sie sich je gefragt...? / Niemand hat sich je beklagt. Common in both questions ('Have you ever...') and negatives ('...never' in a literary or emphatic sense).
target_language_example: Haben Sie sich je gefragt, wie viele Sterne es im Himmel gibt?
native_language_example: Have you ever wondered how many stars there are in the sky?

meaning: Not a fixed phrase on its own; 'sich' is a reflexive pronoun and 'jeden' is the masculine accusative form of 'jeder' meaning 'every'. Together they can start reflexive constructions like 'sich jeden Tag ...' (to ... oneself every day).
additional_notes: 'Sich jeden' by itself is incomplete and must be followed by a noun or time expression (e.g., jeden Tag, jeden Morgen) and a reflexive verb construction. 'Sich' changes with person (mir, dir, sich, uns, euch) when used as an object pronoun. 'Jeden' agrees in case, gender and number; here it is masculine accusative and commonly used with time expressions (jeden Tag). Common patterns: 'sich jeden Abend entspannen', 'sich jeden Tag etwas ansehen'. Useful for forming routines or habitual actions that are reflexive.
target_language_example: Ich erinnere mich und sage mir: "Ich muss mich jeden Tag weiterbilden."
native_language_example: I remind myself and say: "I have to educate myself every day."

meaning: literally 'oneself everyone' — part of reflexive constructions meaning 'everyone can/does (something for themselves)' or 'everyone (feels)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence: 'jeder' (everyone) with a reflexive verb using 'sich' (accusative/dative reflexive). Commonly appears as 'kann sich jeder ...' (everyone can get/afford ...) or 'fühlt sich jeder ...' (everyone feels ...). Word order in German often places 'sich' before 'jeder' or after the verb depending on sentence structure. Translate according to the whole verb phrase (e.g. 'kann sich Bücher besorgen' = 'can get books for themselves', 'fühlt sich jeder manchmal' = 'everyone sometimes feels').
target_language_example: Heute kann sich jeder ein Handy leisten.
native_language_example: Today everyone can afford a mobile phone.

meaning: a reflexive construction with 'jedes' meaning 'every' or 'each' (as in 'each [one] ...'), used when the verb is reflexive or when something applies to every member of a group.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the combination of the reflexive pronoun 'sich' and the determiner 'jedes' (neuter accusative/genitive or masculine/neuter depending on context). 'Sich' marks reflexive verbs (e.g. 'sich leisten', 'sich häuten', 'sich erholen'), and 'jedes' means 'every'/'each' and agrees in gender/case with the noun it modifies (jedes Auto, jedes Jahr, jedes Mädchen). English translations often insert 'each' or 'every' and may require changing word order: e.g. 'sich jedes Auto kaufen' → 'buy every car for herself' or more naturally 'buy any car she wants.'
target_language_example: Sie kann sich jedes Buch kaufen, das sie will.
native_language_example: She can buy herself any book she wants.

meaning: to not worry (about something) — part of the reflexive expression used to reassure or indicate not being concerned
additional_notes: This string 'sich keine Sorgen zu' is incomplete on its own; it typically appears within larger constructions such as 'sich keine Sorgen zu machen' (to not worry), or before an infinitive/zu-infinitive clause (e.g., 'sich keine Sorgen zu machen' or 'sich keine Sorgen zu machen wegen ...'). It is reflexive: the pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch) must be conjugated to match the subject. Common everyday use: 'Mach dir keine Sorgen' = 'Don't worry.'
target_language_example: Er versucht, sich keine Sorgen zu machen, obwohl die Lage unsicher ist.
native_language_example: He tries not to worry, even though the situation is uncertain.

meaning: to afford (something) — to be able to pay for or permit oneself something.
additional_notes: Used reflexively with an object introduced by 'es' (es sich leisten) or directly with a noun (sich etwas leisten). Common construction: 'jemand kann es sich leisten, ...' (someone can afford to ...). Often followed by an infinitive clause (zu + infinitive) or a noun. Implies financial ability or allowance for a luxury/expense.
target_language_example: Sie können es sich leisten, einen neuen Computer zu kaufen.
native_language_example: They can afford to buy a new computer.

meaning: sometimes (with a reflexive verb) — 'sich' marks a reflexive action; 'manchmal' = sometimes
additional_notes: Use when the verb is reflexive (the action refers back to the subject). 'Sich' is the reflexive pronoun and changes form with the person (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch). Word order: 'manchmal' usually comes after the conjugated verb or before it in simple sentences (e.g. 'Er ruht sich manchmal aus.' or 'Manchmal ruht er sich aus.').
target_language_example: Er ruht sich manchmal im Garten aus.
native_language_example: He sometimes rests in the garden.

meaning: to take (for oneself); to accept or assume something (responsibility, blame, food, possession); to consume (food/medicine) when used in constructions like etwas zu sich nehmen.
additional_notes: A reflexive verb phrase with several uses depending on context and construction: - accept/assume responsibility or blame: die Schuld auf sich nehmen / die Verantwortung auf sich nehmen; - claim or take possession: jemanden/etwas an sich nehmen; - consume/eat/drink: etwas zu sich nehmen. Requires the appropriate reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich) and often additional particles (auf, an, zu) that change meaning.
target_language_example: Jemand muss die Schuld auf sich nehmen.
native_language_example: Someone has to take/assume the blame.

meaning: 'to feel unwell' or 'to not feel well' (physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase (sich fühlen). Use with appropriate reflexive pronoun: ich fühle mich nicht wohl, du fühlst dich nicht wohl, er/sie fühlt sich nicht wohl, etc. Can refer to mild illness, discomfort, or general unease. Common alternative: 'nicht gut fühlen' or synonym 'sich unwohl fühlen'. Politeness/formality neutral; can be used in casual and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich heute Morgen schlecht gefühlt und mich deshalb entschieden, mich nicht wohl zu fühlen ist keine Option — ich bleibe zu Hause.
native_language_example: I felt bad this morning and therefore decided that not feeling well is not an option — I'm staying home.

meaning: An emphatic combination used with reflexive verbs where 'richtig' intensifies the verb: meaning can be 'properly/correctly', 'really/truly', or 'with full effort/very' depending on context.
additional_notes: Used only with reflexive constructions (sich + verb). 'richtig' modifies the action: e.g. 'sich richtig verhalten' = behave properly, 'sich richtig anstrengen' = really make an effort, 'sich richtig gut bewegen' = move very well. Not a fixed standalone idiom; word order follows normal German reflexive patterns (er hat sich richtig ...). Translation depends on context and nuance.
target_language_example: Er hat sich richtig angestrengt.
native_language_example: He really made an effort.

meaning: used with reflexive verbs to mean 'feel free to' / 'go ahead' / 'be calm' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase appears with reflexive verbs (e.g. sich verhalten, sich Zeit nehmen, sich umsehen). Depending on context it can mean: 1) 'be calm/quiet' (sich ruhig verhalten = keep quiet), or 2) a polite encouragement 'feel free to' or 'go ahead' (Lassen Sie sich ruhig Zeit; Nehmen Sie sich ruhig die Zeit). It's not idiomatic on its own — it's always part of a reflexive verb phrase.
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie sich ruhig noch ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: Go ahead and take another piece of cake.

meaning: to feel guilty; to feel responsible or remorseful for something
additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: subject uses the reflexive pronoun (ich fühle mich, du fühlst dich, er/sie/es fühlt sich). Commonly used to describe an emotional state after doing something wrong or when feeling responsible for a negative outcome. Can be followed by a clause introduced by ‚weil/da‘ or a prepositional phrase with ‚wegen‘: Ich fühle mich schuldig, weil... / Ich fühle mich schuldig wegen...
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht aufhören, mich schuldig zu fühlen.
native_language_example: I can't stop feeling guilty.

meaning: 'to see each other' or 'to meet (each other)' in a planned or mutual way
additional_notes: A reflexive construction used when two or more people meet or expect to meet. 'Sich sehen' is the infinitive/reflexive dictionary form; in use replace 'sich' with the appropriate reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich). Common in spoken German as 'uns sehen' (Wir sehen uns). Often appears with time expressions or after modal verbs (z. B. 'Wir wollen uns sehen', 'Wir werden uns noch sehen').
target_language_example: Wir wollen uns morgen im Café sehen — wir haben uns schon lange nicht gesehen; wir hoffen, uns bald wieder sehen zu können.
native_language_example: We want to see each other at the café tomorrow — we haven't seen each other for a long time; we hope to be able to see each other again soon.

meaning: uses of 'sein' (his/its) with reflexive or impersonal constructions; appears in several patterns: reflexive possession (sich sein + body part/possessions), passive/impersonal 'sein' (to be), and possessive referring to someone (his/her).
additional_notes:
This is not a single fixed phrase. The examples show different uses where sich and sein appear together or near each other:
- Reflexive possession with a person: someone 'brach sich sein ...' = they injured their own ... (common in spoken German: reflexive dative + possessive = 'he broke his own...').
- Causative/allowing repair: 'hat sich sein Fahrrad reparieren lassen' = had his bike repaired (by someone else).
- Possessive reference: 'sich sein Mädchen ... stehlen zu lassen' = (about someone) letting his girl be stolen (possessive sein = his).
- Change of state with 'sich verschlimmern' uses 'sein' as possessive pronoun in following noun phrase: 'sich sein Zustand' is incorrect; correct is 'sein Zustand verschlimmert sich' (example 3 shows standard verb + sein).
- Location: 'sich ... befinden' with 'sein' as possessive: 'sagte, dass sich sein Wörterbuch in seiner Tasche befinde' = said that his dictionary was in his pocket.
For beginners: focus on patterns rather than a single phrase. Key useful patterns:
  - sich + dat. + Akk. (body part/possession) to say someone did something to their own body/thing: 'Tom brach sich sein Handgelenk.' = Tom broke his (own) wrist.
  - sich etwas reparieren lassen = to have something repaired for oneself.
  - sich befinden (reflexive verb) = to be located; 'sein' as possessive simply marks ownership: 'sein Wörterbuch' = his dictionary.
Watch word order and case: 'sein' is a possessive pronoun (his/its) and 'sich' is a reflexive pronoun (acc./dat.). They are separate words serving different roles.
target_language_example: Er ließ sich sein Auto in der Werkstatt reparieren.
native_language_example: He had his car repaired at the garage.

meaning: oneself
additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used to indicate the action refers back to the subject. Use the appropriate reflexive pronoun form (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch) in different persons; 'sich selbst' adds emphasis or clarity (e.g. 'he did it himself' or 'served himself'). Can be used for emphasis or to mean 'by oneself.'
target_language_example: Sie hat sich selbst geholfen.
native_language_example: She helped herself.

meaning: to be sure that / to be certain that
additional_notes: Reflexive construction: 'sich sicher sein, daß ...' expresses being certain about a fact or decision. Formal/informal forms: 'Sind Sie sich sicher, daß ...?' (formal) or 'Bist du dir sicher, daß ...?' (informal). Note: modern German orthography uses 'dass' (double s) instead of the older 'daß'.
