Tone is friendly or permissive. Examples: 'Halt sie ruhig.' (calm/hold them), 'Kommen Sie ruhig mit rein.' (please feel free to come in), 'Sie können sie ruhig anprobieren.' (go ahead and try them on), 'Nimm du sie ruhig!' (you can take them), 'Stellt sie ruhig!' (ask them — feel free to ask questions).
target_language_example: Komm ruhig mit — du kannst sie ruhig fragen.
native_language_example: Come along — you can feel free to ask them.

meaning: they manage / they create / they accomplish (depending on context)
additional_notes: Verb 'schaffen' has several meanings: 'to manage' or 'to succeed in doing something' (sie schaffen = they manage/succeed), and 'to create' or 'to produce' (sie schaffen = they create). Context (object, sentence) tells which meaning applies. Also 'schaffen' can mean 'to make it' (colloquial) or 'to accomplish/finish' a task. Pronunciation stress on first syllable: SCHAf-fen. Note: 'Sie schaffen' with capital 'Sie' can also mean 'you (formal) accomplish/manage' depending on capitalization in written German.
target_language_example: Sie schaffen es, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: They manage to solve the problem.

meaning: she looks / she is looking
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (she) looking, watching, or glancing. Can be followed by a direct object (sie schaut mich an = she looks at me), a prepositional phrase (auf ihr Smartphone = at her smartphone), or an activity (fern = TV; here 'fern schauen' = to watch TV). In present tense 'schaut' is the 3rd person singular of 'schauen'.
target_language_example: Sie schaut gerade aus dem Fenster.
native_language_example: She is looking out of the window right now.

meaning: 'they send' or 'you (formal) send' depending on context; here usually 'they send'.
additional_notes: Verb phrase made of subject pronoun 'sie' (they or formal you 'Sie') + verb 'schicken' (to send). In most everyday contexts 'sie schicken' means 'they send'. Context determines tense and object (what or whom is sent). Can also be used with infinitive (e.g. 'sie schicken uns heim' = they send us home). Watch capitalisation: 'Sie schicken' with capital S is formal 'you send'.
target_language_example: Sie schicken uns ein Paket aus dem Ausland.
native_language_example: They are sending us a package from abroad.

meaning: 'it/ she tastes' (i.e. something has a taste / tastes to someone).
additional_notes: Used to say how something (usually food or drink) tastes. 'Sie' can refer to 'die Suppe/das Torte' (feminine nouns) or more generally 'it' when talking about a feminine noun. Often followed by an adjective (gut, lecker, scheußlich) or the dative construction 'mir' to mean 'I like the taste' (Sie schmeckt mir = I like how it tastes). Context determines whether 'sie' means 'she' or 'it' — for beginners, treat it as 'it tastes' for food/drink.
target_language_example: Die Suppe? Sie schmeckt sehr gut.
native_language_example: The soup? It tastes very good.

meaning: she shot / she fired (past tense of 'schießen').
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of 'schießen' = to shoot/fire. Can mean shooting with a gun (auf jemanden schießen = to shoot at someone), hitting/striking (less common), or moving very quickly (colloquial: 'sie schoss durch das Haus' = she rushed through the house). Context tells whether it's literal shooting or fast movement.
target_language_example: Sie schoss aus dem Zimmer und rief nach Hilfe.
native_language_example: She rushed out of the room and shouted for help.

meaning: her/herself (emphatic); or 'them/themself' depending on context — emphasizes that the action is done by that person, not someone else.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the person referred to ('sie' = she/her/they depending on context) does the action themselves. Can mean 'ask her yourself', 'she herself', or 'he left her of his own will' (emphasis on 'herself' or 'herself/ herself's own decision'). Word order and context determine whether 'sie' is object (her) or subject (she). 'Selber' is slightly less formal than 'selbst' but both are common.
target_language_example: Frag sie selber, ob sie mitkommen will.
native_language_example: Ask her yourself whether she wants to come along.

meaning: she sets / she puts / she begins (depends on verb phrase that follows)
additional_notes: This is the third-person singular of the separable verb 'setzen' or part of various verb phrases. Meaning changes with the rest of the sentence: e.g. 'sich durchsetzen' (to assert oneself) — here 'setzt ... ihren Kopf durch' = 'gets her way'; 'die Segel setzen' (to set sail) — 'setzt die Segel' = 'sets sail'; 'sich in Szene setzen' (to show oneself off) — 'setzt sich in Szene' = 'likes to put herself on display'; 'etwas frei setzen' (to release something) — 'setzt Gefühle frei' = 'releases/emits strong feelings'; 'zum Schuss ansetzen' (to take aim/shoot) — 'setzt zum Schuss an' = 'prepares to shoot/starts the shot'. Watch for reflexive 'sich' and separable prefixes (e.g. 'an' in 'ansetzen').
target_language_example: Sie setzt sich beim Meeting immer durch.
native_language_example: She always gets her way in the meeting.

meaning: A sequence of pronouns + article commonly found in German reflexive constructions: 'sie' (they / formal you / she depending on context) + 'sich' (reflexive pronoun) + 'die' (definite article). The exact meaning depends on the verb and noun that follow (e.g., 'they gave themselves the...' or 'they should brush their...').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own but a frequent word-order pattern before a reflexive or body-part noun. 'sich' here is a reflexive pronoun whose case (dative or accusative) depends on the verb; in many common expressions with body parts it is dative (e.g. 'sich die Zähne putzen'). 'sie' must be interpreted from context (sie = they, she, or formal you). Watch agreement and case: 'die' can be article for feminine singular or plural nominative/accusative; in phrases like 'die Zähne' it is accusative plural.
target_language_example: Jeden Freitagabend gaben sie sich die Kante.
native_language_example: Every Friday evening they partied hard (literally: 'gave themselves the edge').

meaning: 'they/she/you (formal) ... for' depending on pronoun—part of the reflexive verb construction 'sich für (etwas) interessieren' meaning 'to be interested in (something)'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines a subject pronoun (sie = she/they/you formal) with the reflexive pronoun 'sich' and the preposition 'für'. It appears in the common verb phrase 'sich für etwas interessieren' (to be interested in something). Word order changes in questions and with different pronouns (e.g., 'Interessiert sie sich für mich?' = 'Is she interested in me?'). 'Sie' can mean she, they, or formal you—context and capitalization matter ('Sie' = formal you).
target_language_example: Interessieren sie sich für Musik?
native_language_example: Are they/she/formal you interested in music?

meaning: A sequence combining the subject pronoun 'sie' (she), the reflexive pronoun 'sich', and the preposition 'in'. It appears within reflexive verb constructions that take 'in' to indicate falling into/into someone, entering/hiding in a location, or becoming involved in a state or relationship (e.g. 'she fell in love with', 'she hid in', 'she became engaged in'). The full meaning depends on the verb it's attached to and should be translated as part of the whole verb phrase, not word-for-word.
additional_notes: This chunk is not a standalone fixed phrase but a common part of reflexive verb clauses. Word order can change with tense, mood, and sentence type (e.g. questions, subordinate clauses). In German sentences you will often see the full verb near this sequence (e.g. 'hat sie sich in ... verliebt', 'dass sie sich in ... versteckt hat'). Pay attention to case required after 'in' (accusative for movement into, dative for location).
target_language_example: Auf der Party hat sie sich in ihn verliebt und er in sie.
native_language_example: At the party she fell in love with him and he with her.

sie sich keine Sorgen zu machen

target_language_multi_word_term: sie sich keine Sorgen zu machen
meaning: that she doesn't need to worry / to tell her not to worry
additional_notes: This phrase appears as the content of reported speech or an infinitive clause after verbs like sagen (to tell). Literal structure: 'sie' = she, 'sich Sorgen machen' = to worry, 'keine' negates it. Commonly used to reassure someone about a woman or girl. In spoken/written German you may also hear: 'sich keine Sorgen machen muss' or shorter: 'sich keine Sorgen machen braucht' (regional/colloquial).
target_language_example: Sag ihr bitte, dass sie sich keine Sorgen zu machen braucht.
native_language_example: Please tell her that she doesn't need to worry.

meaning: 'sie' (she/they) + reflexive 'sich über' — not a single fixed phrase but the subject pronoun 'sie' together with reflexive constructions using 'sich über ...' which change meaning depending on the main verb. Common patterns: 'sich über etwas/jemanden freuen' = to be happy about something, 'sich über jemanden lustig machen' = to mock someone, 'sich über etwas/ jemanden informieren' = to inform oneself about, and literal/motion uses like 'sich über die Schulter werfen' or 'sich über die Stadt erheben' in descriptive contexts.
additional_notes: This entry focuses on the combination 'sie' + reflexive 'sich über', which appears when the subject is 'sie' (she or they) and the verb requires the reflexive 'sich' followed by the preposition 'über'. Meaning depends on the main verb: emotional reactions (freuen), mocking (lustig machen), motion/descriptive uses (sich über etwas erheben). Word order: in main clauses the reflexive pronoun usually follows the finite verb (e.g. 'Bestimmt freut sie sich über...'); in questions and subordinate clauses the order changes ('Hat sie sich über...?', '..., weil sie sich über...'). Note that 'sie' can be singular (she) or plural (they) — context determines which.
target_language_example: Bestimmt freut sie sich über den Besuch.
native_language_example: She is surely happy about the visit.

meaning: they are sitting / they sit
additional_notes: Present-tense form of sitzen with the pronoun sie (they). Used to describe people who are seated or who habitually sit (e.g., watching TV every evening). Context determines whether it means a current action (they are sitting) or a habitual/state (they sit/they sit every evening). Not to be confused with formal 'Sie sitzen' (you sit) when addressing one or more people politely — that has the same verb form but different capitalization/pronoun.
target_language_example: Sie sitzen jeden Abend zusammen auf dem Sofa.
native_language_example: They sit together on the sofa every evening.

meaning: to call/name it that way; to refer to it like that
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "sie so zu nennen/benennen" meaning "to call/name it that way". 'sie' refers to a feminine noun (e.g. 'die Sprache'); 'so' = 'like that'; 'zu' is part of the infinitive construction with verbs like 'reichen', 'genügen' or commands with 'aufhören' + 'sie so zu nennen'. The phrase is neutral and can be used in statements and imperatives.
target_language_example: Hör auf, sie so zu nennen!
native_language_example: Stop calling it that!

meaning: 'they die' or 'she dies' (depending on context; German verb form can mean 'they die' or the polite/formal 'you die' is different).
additional_notes: The verb sterben means 'to die'. 'Sie sterben' most commonly means 'they die' (third person plural). In some contexts (capitalized 'Sie') it could be formal 'you die', but that form would use 'sterben' with a capitalized pronoun and different meaning. Context (surrounding words, punctuation) decides whether 'sie' refers to 'she' (singular) or 'they'—note: singular 'she dies' is 'sie stirbt' (not 'sie sterben'). Also appears in different tenses: 'Dann wird sie sterben' = 'Then she will die.' 'Ich werd nicht zulassen, dass sie sterben' = 'I won't allow them to die.'
target_language_example: Ich werde nicht zulassen, dass sie sterben.
native_language_example: I will not allow them to die.

meaning: 'she dies' or 'she is dying'.
additional_notes: Simple present tense of sterben (to die). In German present tense can describe a general fact, a future event, or an action happening now (she dies / she is dying / she will die). Context decides exact nuance. 'sie' can mean 'she' (subject) — not to be confused with formal 'Sie' (you).
target_language_example: Wenn sie stirbt, werde ich sehr traurig sein.
native_language_example: If she dies, I will be very sad.

meaning: she studies / she is studying
additional_notes: Used to say what subject someone studies or that she is engaged in studying. 'Studieren' normally refers to university/college study or formal higher education, but can also mean 'to study' in a general sense. Word order: subject 'sie' + verb 'studiert'. To indicate duration, add time expressions (e.g. 'seit ein paar Jahren').
target_language_example: Sie studiert Biologie an der Universität.
native_language_example: She studies biology at the university.

meaning: they dance
additional_notes: Simple present of 'tanzen' with pronoun 'sie' (they). Can also be 'Sie tanzen' (formal you dance) depending on capitalization/context — here examples use lowercase 'sie' = they. Used for statements about people dancing or observed actions. In sentence 3 the structure 'Wir haben sie tanzen gesehen' uses a bare infinitive after a perception verb: 'we saw them dancing.'
target_language_example: Abends im Park sie tanzen zu sehen macht mich glücklich.
native_language_example: Seeing them dance in the park in the evening makes me happy.

meaning: she/they are dead (a clipped or colloquial short form implying 'sie ist tot' or 'sie sind tot').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a sequence of pronoun + adjective 'tot' ('dead'). Context determines whether 'sie' is singular 'she' or plural 'they' (or formal 'Sie' vs. lowercase 'sie'). Grammatically complete sentences normally include a verb: 'Sie ist tot.' / 'Sie sind tot.' The clipped form 'sie tot' may appear in headlines, telegram-style speech, or casual/frightened exclamations where the verb is omitted.
target_language_example: Warte, ist sie tot?
native_language_example: Wait, is she dead?

meaning: she met her / she met (someone); or 'she hit' in context (past tense of treffen).
additional_notes: Trifft the verb 'treffen' in simple past (Präteritum). 'Sie traf' usually means 'she met' when used with a person (direct object: ihn, Maria, sie). Context can also mean 'she hit' (physical strike) but examples show meeting someone. Word order: subject 'sie' + past verb 'traf'. Use with time expressions (heute Morgen, vor drei Jahren) or places (am Strand).
target_language_example: Sie traf ihn gestern im Park.
native_language_example: She met him in the park yesterday.

meaning: to meet her / to meet them (depending on context)
additional_notes: The pronoun 'sie' can mean 'her' (singular, accusative) or 'them' (plural). Context, verb conjugation, and sentence structure clarify meaning. With reflexive form 'sich treffen' it indicates 'to meet each other' (e.g., 'sie treffen sich' = 'they meet'). Capitalization matters: 'Sie' (formal you) changes meaning (e.g., 'Wieso mussten Sie sie treffen?' = 'Why did you (formal) have to meet her/them?').
target_language_example: Er hat gesagt, dass er sie treffen will.
native_language_example: He said that he wants to meet her/them.

meaning: 'her/them/it' + 'anyway/still' (i.e. 'you still [do something] to/with her/them/it').
additional_notes: Sie is a pronoun: can mean 'she', 'her', or 'them' (formal 'you' as 'Sie' is capitalized — here lowercase so informal third person). Trotzdem means 'anyway', 'still' or 'nevertheless' and usually appears after the verb or object. Together they show that an action involving 'sie' happens despite something else.
target_language_example: Er hat kein Geld, aber er hilft sie trotzdem.
native_language_example: He has no money, but he helps her/them anyway.

meaning: 'kill her/them' (phrasal verb: jemanden umbringen — to kill someone) or in one sentence below, 'put her in a different mood' (umstimmen/um|stimmen).
additional_notes: In most example sentences 'sie um' is part of the separable verb 'umbringen' (Bring sie um! = Kill her/them!). This is violent language — learners should be careful. The last example uses a different verb: 'umstimmen' (to change someone's mind or mood) where 'stimmt sie um' is unusual phrasing; more natural would be 'stimmt sie um' meaning 'puts her in a different mood' (or 'changes her opinion') depending on context. Pay attention to word order and separable prefixes: in present tense the prefix (um-) often moves to the end with the object before it (e.g. 'Er bringt sie um.').
target_language_example: Er bringt sie um, wenn sie es verrät.
native_language_example: He will kill her if she tells.

meaning: 'to kill her/them' (depending on context: 'sie' = her or them; 'umbringen' = to kill)
additional_notes: Common verb phrase: 'umbringen' means to kill, murder or destroy. 'Sie' can be accusative 'her' or 'them' (or formal 'you' in some contexts, but not here). Tense and mood change meaning (wollten = wanted to, würde = would). Strong/serious word—use with caution. Not idiomatic; literal meaning.
target_language_example: Wenn wir sie umbringen, wissen die, dass wir hier waren.
native_language_example: If we kill them, they'll know we were here.

meaning: 'her/them/it' + 'absolutely/definitely/insistently' — expresses a strong desire or need to do something to/with 'sie'.
additional_notes: Unbedingt intensifies the verb: it means 'must/absolutely/definitely' or 'insistently'. 'Sie' can be accusative 'her' or 'them' or formal 'you' (Sie) depending on context; here examples use accusative 'sie' (her/them). Word order: 'sie unbedingt' often appears before the verb or after modal/auxiliary elements (e.g., 'Ich muss sie unbedingt ...'). Use to show strong intent, urgency, or insistence.
target_language_example: Ich möchte sie unbedingt sehen.
native_language_example: I absolutely must see her.

meaning: "she/they unhappy" — indicates that a female person or a group is unhappy or sad; 'sie' can be singular (she) or plural (they) depending on context.
additional_notes: Context and verb forms determine whether 'sie' means 'she' (singular) or 'they' (plural). In reported speech or indirect speech, subjunctive forms (sei/seien) are often used: e.g. 'sie unglücklich sei' / 'sie unglücklich seien'. Common with verbs like sagen, glauben, wissen. 'unglücklich' = unhappy, sad, dissatisfied. The phrase is compositional and can usually be translated literally.
target_language_example: Mary hat gesagt, dass sie unglücklich ist.
native_language_example: Mary said that she is unhappy.

meaning: they/she down; 'down' meaning below, downstairs, or knocked down depending on context.
additional_notes: Context determines whether 'sie' means 'she' (singular, informal) or 'they'/'you formal' (plural) — but in spoken German lowercase 'sie' is ambiguous without capitalization. 'unten' means 'down' or 'downstairs'; in sports or action contexts it can mean 'knocked down' or 'out'. Watch subject-verb agreement in full sentences (e.g., 'Ist sie unten?' for singular 'she', 'Sind sie unten?' for plural 'they').
target_language_example: Ist sie unten oder bleibt sie oben?
native_language_example: Is she down (downstairs) or is she staying upstairs?

meaning: 'she married' or 'they married' — 'verheiratet' is an adjective meaning 'married'; used with the pronoun 'sie' to express that she is married (singular) or they are married (plural) depending on context.
additional_notes: 'Verheiratet' is predicative and requires a form of the verb 'sein' in a full sentence (e.g. 'sie ist verheiratet', 'sie sind verheiratet'). The bare phrase 'sie verheiratet' can appear inside larger constructions (e.g. subordinate clauses or reported speech) without the finite verb shown explicitly in elliptical contexts, but ordinarily you will see the appropriate form of 'sein'. Context and verb inflection determine whether 'sie' is singular (she) or plural (they). Subjunctive and reported forms include 'sie seien verheiratet' or 'als wären sie verheiratet'.
target_language_example: Tom und Maria haben Johannes gesagt, dass sie verheiratet seien.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria told Johannes that they were married.

meaning: infatuated with her / has a crush on her.
additional_notes: Colloquial expression using the separable verb verknallen (sich in jemanden verknallen) meaning to fall for someone or to have a crush. Usually used with a reflexive pronoun and a preposition: sich in sie verknallen (in + accusative). Tense and person change as in the examples (bin/verknallt, war verknallt, hat sich verknallt). Informal and common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich bin total in sie verknallt.
native_language_example: I'm totally in love with her / I have a huge crush on her.

meaning: she demanded / she asked for (insistently)
additional_notes: From the verb verlangen (to demand/require/ask for). In context it usually means a firm request or demand for something (money, help, an item). Can be neutral or forceful depending on context (e.g., legal, transactional, or emotional). With von + dative it means 'demanded from someone'. Often followed by a noun or a clause introduced by 'dass' or an infinitive with 'zu'.
target_language_example: Sie verlangte sofort eine Erklärung.
native_language_example: She demanded an explanation immediately.

meaning: in love with her (or with them - feminine or plural 'sie').
additional_notes: This is part of the verb phrase 'in jemanden verliebt sein' = 'to be in love with someone'. 'Sie' here is the accusative pronoun meaning 'her' (or 'them' when capitalized contextually, but usually 'her'). The full phrase uses a reflexive or dative structure when the subject is first person: 'Ich habe mich in sie verliebt' = 'I fell in love with her.' Commonly used to talk about romantic feelings. Word order: 'in sie verliebt sein' (sein at the end in subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: Ich bin in sie verliebt.
native_language_example: I am in love with her.

meaning: she fell (in love) — past tense of 'sich verlieben' (to fall in love).
additional_notes: This is part of the simple past (Präteritum) form used in narratives: 'sie verliebte (sich) in ...' = 'she fell in love with ...'. In spoken German and informal contexts, the present perfect ('sie hat sich verliebt') is more common. The reflexive pronoun 'sich' is required with 'verlieben' (but in short examples it may be omitted when showing just the verb form).
target_language_example: Sie verliebte sich in ihren Nachbarn.
native_language_example: She fell in love with her neighbor.

meaning: 'they lose' or 'you (formal) lose' depending on context; can also be 'to lose her/them' with different capitalization/pronoun meanings.
additional_notes: In German, 'sie' can mean 'they' (lowercase) or 'she'/'her' (capitalization and context matter). 'Sie verlieren' most commonly means 'they lose' (present tense of verlieren). In other contexts (e.g. 'Er wird sie verlieren') 'sie' is the object pronoun 'her' or 'them' and the phrase means 'he will lose her/them' (future tense shown). Pay attention to context and verb tense to understand whether 'sie' is subject or object. Common uses: lose a game, lose weight (Gewicht verlieren), lose ground (an Boden verlieren), lose consciousness (das Bewusstsein verlieren).
target_language_example: Sie verlieren jedes Spiel in dieser Saison.
native_language_example: They lose every game this season.

meaning: she misses (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common present-tense phrase: 'sie' = she, 'vermisst' = misses (from the verb vermissen). Used to express longing or absence. If context uses 'sie' as object, word order changes (e.g. 'Sie vermisst sie' = She misses them/her). For formal or plural 'you miss' use 'Sie vermissen' or 'ihr vermisst' respectively.
target_language_example: Sie vermisst ihre Familie am meisten.
native_language_example: She misses her family the most.

meaning: she tries / she is trying
additional_notes: Used to describe a female subject attempting or making an effort to do something. Often followed by 'zu' + infinitive (Sie versucht, ... zu ... ) or by a direct object (Sie versucht es). In present tense; 'versucht' is the 3rd-person singular of 'versuchen'.
target_language_example: Sie versucht, jeden Tag ein Kapitel zu lesen.
native_language_example: She tries to read one chapter every day.

meaning: she trusts (someone/something).
additional_notes: Verb: 'vertrauen' takes the dative (to trust someone = jemandem vertrauen). 'sie vertraut' can mean 'she trusts' or, with capitalized Sie, 'you trust' (formal) — here examples use lowercase 'sie' = 'she'. Can be followed by a dative person (ihm, mir, ihren Ärzten) or 'mit' + noun to indicate what is entrusted (sie vertraut ihm mit ihrem Geld = she entrusts him with her money).
target_language_example: Sie vertraut ihrer Freundin komplett.
native_language_example: She completely trusts her friend.

meaning: 'she waits' or 'she is waiting'.
additional_notes: Third-person singular of warten (to wait). Can mean a habitual action ('she waits') or a current action ('she is waiting') depending on context and time expressions. Commonly followed by auf + accusative to indicate what/who is being waited for (e.g. auf dich). Formal spelling: in older texts you may see 'daß' instead of modern 'dass'.
target_language_example: Sie wartet schon seit einer Stunde auf den Bus.
native_language_example: She has been waiting for the bus for an hour.

meaning: 'they wash' or polite/formal 'you wash' (depending on context); also used in constructions with objects/pronouns (e.g. 'wash them' or 'have them washed').
additional_notes: Present tense of the verb waschen (to wash). Capitalization and context determine meaning: 'Sie waschen' (formal you) uses capital 'S' for Sie and polite address; 'sie waschen' (lowercase s) usually means 'they wash'. Followed by a direct object (e.g. 'Salat' or 'sie' = them) or a reflexive pronoun + body part (e.g. 'sich die Hände waschen' = wash one's hands). Can appear in causative/infinitive constructions: 'wollen Sie sie waschen lassen?' = 'Do you want to have them washed?'. Word order and pronouns change meaning—pay attention to capitalization and position of pronouns.
target_language_example: Sie waschen sich die Hände vor dem Essen.
native_language_example: They wash their hands before eating.

meaning: 'they cry' or 'to hear/see them cry' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning: 'they cry' (present tense). In sentences like 'Ich habe sie weinen sehen' or 'Man hörte sie weinen', 'sie' refers to 'them' and 'weinen' is the bare infinitive used after verbs of perception (sehen, hören) to indicate observing the action. Word order and pronoun case: 'sie' can be nominative 'they' (Sie weinen = They/You formal cry) or accusative 'them' after perception verbs (ich habe sie weinen sehen = I saw them crying). Context tells you whether 'sie' = they (subject) or 'them' (object).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie weinen gehört, also bin ich ins Zimmer gekommen.
native_language_example: I heard them crying, so I went into the room.

meaning: she cries / she is crying
additional_notes: Simple present tense of the verb weinen (to cry). In German the present tense can indicate an action occurring now (she is crying) or a habitual action (she cries). 'sie' in lowercase here refers to 'she' (not 'they' or the formal 'Sie').
target_language_example: Sag mir, warum sie weint.
native_language_example: Tell me why she is crying.

meaning: to see her/them again; to meet her/them again.
additional_notes: "sie" can mean 'her' (singular, informal) or 'them' (plural). Note that capitalized "Sie" is formal 'you' and is different. "wiedersehen" is the verb 'to see again' (separable verb: ich sehe sie wieder — in main clause, the verb splits). In the phrase as given, "sie wiedersehen" is the infinitive construction (e.g., after modal verbs or in subordinate clauses). Use context to determine singular vs. plural and formal vs. informal.
target_language_example: Ich möchte sie wiedersehen.
native_language_example: I want to see her/them again.

meaning: 'they lived' (past tense of 'wohnen')
additional_notes: Used to describe where a group of people lived in the past. 'Sie' can mean 'they' here (not formal 'you'). 'Wohnten' is simple past (Präteritum) of 'wohnen'. Common with time/place expressions: 'gegenüber' (opposite), 'in einem Haus', 'in Mexiko'.
target_language_example: Als Kinder sie wohnten nahe dem See.
native_language_example: As children they lived near the lake.

meaning: she would be; she were
additional_notes: 'wäre' is the Konjunktiv II form of 'sein'. It is used for hypothetical, wished-for, or unreal situations. In English, 'sie wäre' can correspond to either 'she would be' or 'she were' depending on context. With a past participle, it often means 'she would have ...', for example: 'sie wäre gekommen' = 'she would have come'.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, sie wäre hier.
native_language_example: I wish she were here.

meaning: she shows / she is showing
additional_notes: Simple present of 'zeigen' with the subject 'sie' (she). Can mean to physically point something out, to display or to show someone something. Context matters: in polite contexts it often means 'she shows me the way' (gives directions); in vulgar contexts it can mean 'she shows her butt' (exposes). The indirect object is often marked with a dative (mir = to me).
target_language_example: Sie zeigt mir das Foto.
native_language_example: She shows me the photo.

meaning: 'she pulls' / 'she puts on' / 'she inhales (a puff)'.
additional_notes: sich ziehen is a separable/ reflexive verb construction: ziehen can mean 'to pull' or 'to draw/inhale' (e.g. a cigarette/joint). When used reflexively (sich anziehen) it means 'to put on (clothes)'. Context and additional words (an, sich, an etwas) determine the meaning. Word order and particle placement change in sentences (e.g. 'sie zieht an' vs. 'sie zieht sich an').
target_language_example: Sie zieht sich den Mantel an.
native_language_example: She puts on her coat.

meaning: them/her/they first; before someone else.
additional_notes: Used to indicate priority in time or order: who/what goes or happens before others. 'sie' can mean 'her' (singular feminine) or 'them'/'they' (plural) depending on context. Word order: 'zuerst' usually comes after the object/pronoun. Common in instructions (let them speak first) and questions (who saw them first?).
target_language_example: Lass sie zuerst gehen.
native_language_example: Let them/her go first.

meaning: 'her' or 'them' by chance; accidentally (met, chosen, or encountered).
additional_notes: 'Sie' can be feminine singular ('her') or plural ('them') depending on context. 'Zufällig' means 'by chance' or 'accidentally'. Common constructions: verb + 'sie zufällig' (e.g. 'traf sie zufällig', 'wählte sie zufällig aus'). Word order can vary (e.g. 'Ich traf sie zufällig' or 'Er wählte sie zufällig aus').
target_language_example: Ich traf sie zufällig in der Bibliothek.
native_language_example: I met her/them by chance in the library.

meaning: 'them' or 'her' everywhere / in all places
additional_notes: Combines the pronoun 'sie' (she/her or they/them, depends on context) with 'überall' (everywhere). Use context to know whether 'sie' means 'she' (singular feminine) or 'them' (plural). Common in sentences to say someone/something is present in many places, expected everywhere, seen everywhere, etc.
target_language_example: Ich sehe sie überall in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I see her/them everywhere in the city.

meaning: she/they are surprised (or 'she/they surprised') — describes someone being surprised.
additional_notes: Context determines whether 'sie' means 'she' (singular) or 'they' (plural) or formal 'you' (rare). In German word order and tense, forms change: 'sie ist überrascht' (she is surprised), 'sie sind überrascht' (they are surprised). In reported speech or subordinate clauses you may see the subjunctive: 'sie sei überrascht' = 'she is said to be surprised'. Here 'sie überrascht' as shown in examples often appears in shortened or reported forms; learners should pay attention to verb forms (ist/sind/sein) and context to know number/person.
target_language_example: Als ich anrief, war sie überrascht.
native_language_example: When I called, she was surprised.

meaning: to arrive at seven / to start at seven (depending on context)
additional_notes: This combination appears because verbs like ankommen (to arrive) and anfangen (to start) are split in German sentences: the verb stem (ankommen → an; anfangen → an) can appear at the end. Context and time words determine meaning: with a subject + time (Kommen Sie um sieben an?) it means 'arrive at seven'; with Es fängt um sieben an it means 'it starts at seven'. Use time expressions (um sechs, um halb sieben) in front of 'an' or before the verb. The phrase can be part of questions and requests (Rufen Sie mich um halb sieben an = 'call me at 6:30').
target_language_example: Der Film fängt um sieben an.
native_language_example: The movie starts at seven.

meaning: 'to get up at seven' (or 'to get up around seven' when used with 'halb sieben' = half past six/6:30).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase 'aufstehen' split into time expression + 'auf' (separable verb). In German, the separable prefix 'auf' goes to the end in main clauses: e.g. 'Ich stehe um sieben auf.' = 'I get up at seven.' 'Um halb sieben' means 6:30 in German. Use with personal subject forms: ich stehe, du stehst, er/sie steht, wir stehen, ihr steht, sie/Sie stehen.
target_language_example: Morgens stehe ich um sieben auf.
native_language_example: In the morning I get up at seven.

meaning: 'seven and' — the number seven followed by 'and' used when listing numbers or giving time ranges/approximate times.
additional_notes: Often appears when listing items or numbers (e.g., "sechs, sieben und zehn") or when giving time ranges/appointments (e.g., "zwischen sieben und acht Uhr"). By itself it is not a fixed idiom; meaning depends on context. For times, use "zwischen ... und ..." for 'between ... and ...' or "um sieben und ..." when giving a departure/arrival close to seven followed by another time. Not idiomatic to use "sieben und" alone without continuation.
target_language_example: Rufen Sie mich bitte zwischen sieben und acht an.
native_language_example: Please call me between seven and eight.

target_language_multi_word_term: sieh sie / sieh sie dir an
meaning: Look at them / take a look at her/him/them (imperative).
additional_notes: Imperative form of sehen with the pronoun 'sie' (them/her). 'Sieh sie an' = 'look at them/her' (direct object). 'Sieh sie dir an' adds the reflexive dative 'dir' = 'have a look for yourself' or 'take a closer look'. Tone depends on context — can be neutral, emphatic, encouraging, or scolding. Negative: 'Sieh sie nicht an' = don't look at them. Informal singular command (du-form).
target_language_example: Sieh sie dir mal genauer an — vielleicht ist es gar nicht so schlimm.
native_language_example: Take a closer look at them — maybe it's not that bad.

meaning: look at me
additional_notes: Imperative form of sehen + the dative pronoun mir; used to tell someone to look at the speaker (often in the face or eyes). Can be followed by präpositional phrases (e.g. in die Augen) or by zu (sieh mir dabei zu = watch me do it). Common in everyday speech and can sound direct or commanding depending on tone.
target_language_example: Sieh mir bitte in die Augen, wenn du sprichst.
native_language_example: Please look me in the eyes when you speak.

meaning: 'see also' — directs the reader to related information.
additional_notes: Commonly used in written texts, indexes, dictionaries, encyclopedias, manuals, or webpages to point to related entries or further reading. Often appears as a cross-reference heading followed by one or more terms or page numbers (e.g. "siehe auch: ..."). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Siehe auch: Kapitel 3 für weitere Informationen.
native_language_example: See also: Chapter 3 for more information.

meaning: look there; behold; used to draw attention to something (like 'look' or 'there you go').
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial interjection used to point something out or express mild surprise. Often used like 'siehe da!' (= 'well, would you look at that!') or before mentioning a fact. Can be placed at beginning or end of a sentence. Not commonly used in very formal writing.
target_language_example: Siehe da, das Haus ist renoviert worden.
native_language_example: Look at that, the house has been renovated.

meaning: look good (you look good)
additional_notes: This is a clipped part of the verb phrase 'du siehst gut aus' (you look good). The full verb is 'aussehen' and the particle 'aus' usually appears at the end in German word order. In casual speech the particle is sometimes heard separated or the subject dropped ('Siehst gut aus'). Use to compliment someone's appearance or clothing. Informal; typically used with 'du' or as a casual remark.
target_language_example: Du siehst gut aus in Weiß.
native_language_example: You look good in white.

meaning: ‘you look today’ — used to comment on someone's appearance or how they seem right now
additional_notes: Common in spoken German as part of the phrase 'Du siehst heute ... aus.' Followed by an adjective (glücklich, müde, hübsch, etc.). 'Du' is often omitted in casual speech if context is clear, but the verb form 'siehst' requires 'du' (singular informal). Use to give a compliment or an observation about someone's current appearance or mood.
target_language_example: Du siehst heute sehr entspannt aus.
native_language_example: You look very relaxed today.

meaning: you look this evening / you look (tonight)
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone's appearance tonight. 'Siehst' is the 2nd person singular of 'sehen' (du siehst). Often followed by adjectives (bezaubernd, schön, gut, etc.) and placed before the adjective phrase: 'Du siehst heute Abend ... aus.' In casual speech you can drop 'heute Abend' or change time (heute, heute Morgen).
target_language_example: Du siehst heute Abend wirklich toll aus.
native_language_example: You really look great tonight.

meaning: you look (and the 'ja' adds emphasis or confirms something obvious).
additional_notes: Used after the verb 'siehst' (from 'sehen') to comment on someone's appearance. The particle 'ja' doesn't change the basic meaning but adds emphasis, surprise, confirmation, or an emotional tone (can be friendly, sarcastic, critical, or reassuring depending on context and intonation). Often followed by adjectives (blass, grauenvoll, fantastisch) and sometimes by 'aus' (du siehst ja ... aus).
target_language_example: Du siehst ja müde aus.
native_language_example: You really look tired.

meaning: 'you look (very) ...' — used to describe someone's appearance or expression; 'siehst' = 'you look' and 'sehr' = 'very'.
additional_notes: Common in the pattern 'Du siehst (sehr) + adjective + aus.' The verb 'aussehen' (du siehst ... aus) means 'to look' or 'to appear.' 'Sehr' intensifies the adjective. You can omit 'sehr' for a weaker statement (Du siehst müde aus). Use with appropriate adjective endings (no extra ending here because adjective follows as predicate).
target_language_example: Du siehst sehr glücklich aus.
native_language_example: You look very happy.

meaning: you look (so)... — used to comment on someone's appearance or impression, often followed by an adjective or clause
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Du siehst so + [adjective] + aus' (e.g. 'Du siehst so müde aus') or 'Du siehst so aus, als ob...' to compare or speculate. 'So' intensifies the adjective ('so gut' = 'so good/really good'). In spoken German, the verb 'aussehen' (to look) requires 'aus' at the end; examples without 'aus' are colloquial shortenings but the full pattern is 'siehst ... aus'.
target_language_example: Du siehst so glücklich aus!
native_language_example: You look so happy!

meaning: you really look / you really seem (appearance or impression).
additional_notes: Common in compliments or comments about someone's appearance. 'Siehst' is the 2nd-person singular form of 'sehen' (du siehst). 'Wirklich' means 'really' or 'actually' and adds emphasis. Usually followed by adjectives (gut, toll, umwerfend) or phrases (wie eine Studentin). Used in spoken and informal contexts; polite/formal address would be 'Sie sehen wirklich...'.
target_language_example: Du siehst wirklich müde aus.
native_language_example: You really look tired.

meaning: 'you look quite' or 'you seem rather' (to describe someone's appearance or state)
additional_notes: Common phrase used with adjectives to describe how someone appears (tired, bored, well, sick, etc.). 'Siehst' = 2nd-person singular of 'sehen' (du siehst). 'Ziemlich' = 'quite', 'rather', or 'pretty' and softens or strengthens the adjective depending on context. Use with 'du' (informal you). For formal address use 'Sie sehen ziemlich ...'.
target_language_example: Du siehst ziemlich müde aus.
native_language_example: You look quite tired.

meaning: 'does that look' / 'does this/that look (like)' (used to ask or comment about appearance or impression).
additional_notes: Common in questions about appearance or how something seems. Often appears in phrases like "Sieht das nicht schön aus?" (Doesn't that look nice?) or "Wie sieht das aus?" (How does that look?). The pronoun (das/so/aus) can change: e.g. "Wie sieht es aus?" or "Wie sieht das für dich aus?" Use with context to refer to an object, situation, or plan.
target_language_example: Sieht das für dich praktikabel aus?
native_language_example: Does that look practical to you?

meaning: adds reassurance or affirmation: 'looks/appear(s) ... (doesn't it?/ I thought so/after all)'.
additional_notes: Used with sehen to comment on appearance and to add a tone of confirmation, mild surprise, or reassurance. 'Doch' here doesn't translate directly; it softens or strengthens the statement (e.g. 'looks good after all', 'surely looks', 'I told you so' tone). Common in everyday speech. Word order follows normal verb patterns: 'Das sieht doch gut aus.'
target_language_example: Das sieht doch sehr professionell aus.
native_language_example: That looks really professional, doesn't it / after all.

meaning: looks happy / appears happy.
additional_notes: From the verb sehen in the 3rd person singular (sieht) + adjective glücklich. Used to describe someone or something that appears happy based on appearance or manner. Common structure: [noun/pronoun] sieht glücklich aus. You can change the subject (ich sehe, du siehst, er/sie/es sieht, wir sehen...).
target_language_example: Das Kind sieht glücklich aus.
native_language_example: The child looks happy.

meaning: looks good / looks nice / appears attractive
additional_notes: Common phrase used with 'aus' (Das sieht gut aus) to say something appears good or attractive. In sentences like 'Er/Sie sieht gut aus' it means 'he/she looks good' (physically attractive). Can describe objects (Das sieht gut aus) or people. Often followed by 'aus' — in casual speech people may omit repeating 'aus' when context makes it clear (e.g., 'Die sieht gut aus.' or simply 'Sie sieht gut aus.').
target_language_example: Das Kleid sieht gut aus.
native_language_example: The dress looks good.

meaning: looks great / looks wonderful
additional_notes: Common phrase using sehen (to look/appear) + adjective toll (great). Used to comment on appearance of things or people. With 'Das sieht toll aus' = That looks great. With a person: 'Er sieht toll aus' = He looks great (handsome). Can be used with or without 'aus' in casual speech (colloquially you might see 'Sieht toll aus!').
target_language_example: Das Kleid sieht toll aus.
native_language_example: The dress looks great.

meaning: 'sees it' (he/she/it sees it) or used in questions/statements: 'you/one can see it' depending on context.
additional_notes: Third-person singular present of sehen (to see) + pronoun es (it). Used to state that someone sees something or to ask if anyone sees it. In spoken German, subject can be omitted (e.g. 'Man sieht es nicht' = 'One cannot see it'). Word order follows German subject–verb–object; in questions the verb comes first ('Sieht es ...?').
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, er sieht es bald.
native_language_example: I hope he sees it soon.

meaning: 'sieht' = (3rd person singular of sehen) 'sees'; 'sie' = she/her (or formal you Sie when capitalized). Together 'sieht sie' can mean 'she sees' (in inverted word order like 'Einer schaut auf und sieht sie.') or 'does she see' in questions (inversion: 'sieht sie...?'), or 'sees her' when 'sie' is accusative. Exact meaning depends on sentence context and word order.
additional_notes: Two separate words: 'sieht' (verb) + 'sie' (pronoun). Lowercase 'sie' can be nominative (she) or accusative (her) — context decides. In questions German often inverts subject and verb: 'sieht sie ...?' = 'does she see ...?'. Capitalized 'Sie' is formal 'you' and is distinct. Word order and surrounding words (e.g., 'aus' in 'Wie sieht sie aus?') change the meaning.
target_language_example: Einer schaut auf und sieht sie.
native_language_example: Someone looks up and sees her.

meaning: 'are also' or 'are too' (plural; present tense of 'sein' + 'also')
additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (wir, ihr, sie, or a compound subject) to add 'also' or 'too'. 'Auch' usually follows the verb in German main clauses. Word order: subject + 'sind' + 'auch' + rest (but 'auch' can move for emphasis). Can translate to 'are also,' 'are too,' or 'also are' depending on English word order.
target_language_example: Wir sind auch eingeladen.
native_language_example: We are also invited.

meaning: 'sind' (3rd person plural of 'sein') + preposition 'auf' used together in various verb + preposition constructions (often perfect tense with 'sein' as auxiliary or present perfect/periphrastic expressions). The overall meaning depends on the verb or phrase that follows 'auf' (e.g. movement to a surface/place, encountering something, being present at an event).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself. 'auf' can govern accusative (movement toward) or dative (location) — e.g. 'auf das Konzert gehen' (go to the concert, accusative) vs. 'auf der Feier da sein' (be at the party, dative). Word order and separable verbs matter: with separable verbs 'auf' may be attached to the verb in infinitive or past participle form. Context determines translation.
target_language_example: Alle sind auf die Party gegangen.
native_language_example: Everyone went to the party.

meaning: are they
additional_notes: A common question pattern: sind + die, where die means "they" here, not "the". It can mean "are they" in the present, or "have they" with verbs that form the perfect tense with sein (for example gegangen, geworden, gestorben, aufgetaucht).
target_language_example: Sind die schon angekommen?
native_language_example: Have they arrived yet?

meaning: are here / are present (at this place).
additional_notes: A simple present-tense phrase combining the verb sein (sind = they/you plural) with hier (here). Used to state that people or things are at the current location. Context determines subject (they, we, you plural, or noun phrase). Can be part of longer sentences (e.g., questions, statements about presence or location).
target_language_example: Die Gäste sind hier schon angekommen.
native_language_example: The guests are already here.

meaning: 'are' / 'were' + 'in' (used to form the present perfect or simple past with 'sein' + location/time phrase)
additional_notes: Combination of the plural/first-person present of 'sein' (sind) or the auxiliary for perfect/passive constructions and the preposition 'in' + dative. Used to describe people or things being/going/located in a place or during a time period. Context determines tense: with a past participle it forms the present perfect (e.g. 'sind im Wald spazieren gegangen' = 'we went for a walk in the forest'). Also used with temporal expressions ('im letzten Sommer' = 'in/during last summer').
target_language_example: Wir sind im Kino gewesen.
native_language_example: We were at the cinema.

meaning: we (are) + last/last (time) — used in perfect tense with a time expression: 'we ... last ...' (e.g. we went last month).
additional_notes: This fragment appears in sentences in the present perfect (Wir sind ... gefahren/geflogen). 'Letzten' is the accusative or dative form of 'letzte' used with a time expression (letzten Monat, letzten Sonntag, letzten Sommer, letzten Montag). In English you usually translate the whole clause as 'we (have) ... last ...' or simply 'we ... last ...' — e.g. 'Wir sind letzten Monat nach Australien geflogen.' = 'We flew to Australia last month.' Pay attention to word order: 'Wir sind letzten + time expression + ... gefahren/geflogen/gezogen.'
target_language_example: Wir sind letzten Freitag ins Kino gegangen.
native_language_example: We went to the cinema last Friday.

meaning: are/ were with the
additional_notes: This phrase combines the auxiliary verb sein (sind) with the prepositional phrase mit dem + mode of transport (Auto, Bus, Zug) to describe traveling by a particular vehicle. In English you usually say "went by/ by (car/train/bus)" or "traveled by (car)". The auxiliary and preposition change with tense/person (e.g., ich bin mit dem Auto gefahren; wir sind mit dem Auto gefahren). Often the verb gefahren or abgefahren follows.
target_language_example: Wir sind mit dem Bus zum Museum gefahren.
native_language_example: We went to the museum by bus.

meaning: 'are from' / 'are by' / 'are caused by' (depends on context)
additional_notes: A present-tense plural form of 'sein' + 'von'. Used to indicate origin (are from), authorship/ownership (are by/from someone), cause or source (are caused by), or passive-like relationships. Exact meaning depends on the noun and context: e.g. origin/place (kommen von), attribution (etwas ist von jemandem), cause (geblendet von = blinded by), or emotion directed at someone (enttäuscht von = disappointed in/by).
target_language_example: Die Bücher sind von verschiedenen Autoren.
native_language_example: The books are by different authors.

meaning: 'sind vor' appears when the auxiliary verb 'sein' (sind) is used with 'vor' + time expression to mean '... ago' in perfect tenses (e.g. 'we/they are ... ago' → '... happened ... ago'). It commonly occurs with verbs that take 'sein' (movement, change of state) in the present perfect.
additional_notes: In German, 'vor' + a time expression = 'ago'. In the present perfect, verbs that use 'sein' as auxiliary combine with 'vor' to state when something happened: e.g. 'Wir sind vor drei Jahren hierher gezogen.' The auxiliary (sind) agrees with the subject (wir/sie). Not all verbs use 'sein' — many use 'haben' — so 'sind vor' specifically appears with verbs that require 'sein'. 'Sind vor' is compositional (literal parts contribute to meaning) but the phrase as a whole functions grammatically to locate an event in the past.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Jahren hierher gezogen.
native_language_example: We moved here three years ago.

meaning: 'are' + 'to' (part of several German constructions: passive, change/become, or 'have come to' conclusions).
additional_notes: This is not a single fixed phrase but the verb sein (sind = we/they are) + zu in different structures. In examples it appears in: 1) 'sind zu ... gegangen' (are/ have gone to...), 2) 'sind zu Blumen geworden' (have become flowers — werden + zu = change/transform), 3–4) 'sind zu dem Schluss gekommen' (have come to the conclusion). Context determines meaning: often part of a perfect or present perfect meaning ('have ...' in English) or a transformation/arrival expression. Pay attention to word order and the noun phrase that follows zu.
target_language_example: Wir sind zu dem Entschluss gekommen, früher zu gehen.
native_language_example: We have come to the decision to leave earlier.

meaning: are too (e.g., are too + adjective)
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'sind' (they/you formal are) and 'zu' used to form 'are too ...' before an adjective (e.g., 'sind zu streng' = 'are too strict'). Common with plural subjects or formal Sie. Context determines subject (sie/ Sie/ ihr). Not to be confused with 'sind zu' meaning 'are to' in constructions with infinitives—here it expresses excess (degree).
target_language_example: Sie sind zu müde, um noch zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: They/You (formal) are too tired to work anymore.

meaning: 'are/has/have ... over' — the auxiliary verb 'sind' (they/we are/have, used as perfect tense auxiliary for motion verbs) + preposition 'über' meaning 'over' or 'across'.
additional_notes: In the example sentences 'sind' is the auxiliary for the perfect tense of verbs of movement (e.g., gehen, fliegen, steigen) and 'über' indicates movement across or above something (over the street, over the Atlantic, over the mountains). English translations often use 'have/has ... over' or simple past like 'crossed/went over/flew over'. Word order in German perfect: subject + sind + past participle (e.g., Sie sind gegangen).
target_language_example: Sie sind über die Brücke gegangen.
native_language_example: They went over the bridge.

meaning: are women
additional_notes: A simple present-tense phrase: 'sind' is the 3rd-person plural of 'sein' (to be) and 'Frauen' is the plural noun 'women'. Used to say that a group (they/we) are women. Context determines the subject (es, sie, wir, etc.). Not idiomatic—literal meaning.
target_language_example: Wir sind Frauen und wir unterstützen uns.
native_language_example: We are women and we support each other.

meaning: are people / are human beings.
additional_notes: Uses the verb sein (to be) + Menschen (people). Commonly used to state that someone or some group are human beings or to emphasize their humanity or membership in the human race. Grammar: 'sind' is the 3rd-person plural present form of 'sein'. Can be used with proper nouns, pronouns, or noun phrases as the subject: 'X sind Menschen.'
target_language_example: Bei Tatoeba sind Menschen jedweder Herkunft willkommen.
native_language_example: At Tatoeba, people of any origin are welcome.

meaning: 'are girls' (third-person plural of 'to be' + 'girls')
additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people/children are girls. 'Sind' is the 3rd person plural form of 'sein' (to be). Replace 'Mädchen' with another noun/adjective to describe a different group (e.g., 'sind Jungen' = 'are boys'). Can be used in statements and in questions about quantity: 'Wie viele ... sind Mädchen?'
target_language_example: In der Klasse sind zehn Schüler, und drei sind Mädchen.
native_language_example: There are ten students in the class, and three are girls.

meaning: are men
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'sind' (are) with 'Männer' (men). Used to describe or identify a group as male. Appears in statements about general attributes, counts, or questions about men. 'Sind' is the 3rd-person plural or 1st-person plural form of 'sein' (to be). Word order follows normal German declarative or interrogative patterns.
target_language_example: Im Park sind Männer und Frauen zusammen.
native_language_example: In the park there are men and women together.

meaning: a polite/formal way to ask whether someone is 'in' or 'part of' something (e.g., in a group, retired, on vacation, in a region or medium).
additional_notes: Used in formal questions (Sie). 'im' is contraction of 'in dem' and needs a noun or noun phrase after it (e.g., Komitee, Ruhestand, Fernsehen, Norden, Urlaub). Depending on the noun, the English translation varies: 'in the committee', 'in retirement', 'on TV', 'in the north', 'on vacation'. For duration questions use 'Wie lange sind Sie im ...?' (How long have you been in/on ...?).
target_language_example: Sind Sie im Vorstand?
native_language_example: Are you on the board?

meaning: Why are you always so... (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: A polite/formal question form (Sie). Used to ask why someone is consistently a certain way (e.g., busy, serious, early, mean). Fill in an adjective after 'so'. Tone can be curious, critical, or teasing depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Warum sind Sie immer so nett?
native_language_example: Why are you always so nice?

meaning: are old
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'are old' (plural). Used with plural subjects (wir, sie, Tom und Maria). Context determines nuance: physical age ('are old') or maturity/eligibility ('are old enough') when followed by a phrase like ‚genug, um...‘ (old enough to...).
target_language_example: Sie sind alt genug, um alleine zu wohnen.
native_language_example: They are old enough to live alone.

meaning: are + out of/except (used in fixed expressions meaning 'are out of' or 'are beside/without' depending on context)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase with a single meaning; 'sind' is the verb 'to be' (plural) and 'außer' is a preposition/particle meaning 'outside of', 'except', or 'beside'. Together they appear in several fixed expressions: 'außer Rand und Band' (wild, uncontrollable), 'außer Schussweite' (out of firing/shot range), 'außer sich (vor Freude/Ärger)' (beside oneself with joy/anger). Context determines the translation. Use the correct case after 'außer' (usually dative or genitive in formal use, but many idiomatic phrases are set).
target_language_example: Wir sind außer uns vor Freude über die Neuigkeiten.
native_language_example: We are beside ourselves with joy about the news.

meaning: 'will be soon' or 'are almost (there/ready/finished)'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'sind' (we/they/you formal are) with 'bald' (soon). In English it often translates as 'will be soon' or 'are almost' depending on context: time/location ('we'll be there soon' / 'we're almost there'), completion ('we'll be finished soon' / 'we're almost finished'), or consequence ('we'll soon be poor'). Subject changes the meaning: e.g. 'ich bin bald' (I will be soon), 'sie sind bald' (they/you formal will be soon).
target_language_example: Wir sind bald mit dem Projekt fertig.
native_language_example: We will be finished with the project soon.

meaning: are grateful / are thankful
additional_notes: Used with 'für' + noun or phrase to say you are grateful for something (Wir sind dankbar für deine Hilfe = We are grateful for your help). Can be used on its own to express gratitude generally (Wir sind dankbar.). Formal and neutral tone.
target_language_example: Wir sind dankbar für deine Unterstützung.
native_language_example: We are grateful for your support.

meaning: are (there) to / are meant to (do something).
additional_notes: Often part of the phrase "(etwas) ist/sind dazu da, ..." meaning "(something) exists/is meant for the purpose of ..." or with expressions like "dazu verpflichtet" (obligated to do so) or "dazu in der Lage" (able to do so). 'dazu' refers to the purpose or requirement mentioned; word order and context determine the exact English rendering.
target_language_example: Die Regeln sind dazu da, uns zu schützen.
native_language_example: The rules are there to protect us.

meaning: are (then)
additional_notes: The word denn here is a particle with no direct translation; it is used in questions to add emphasis, curiosity, surprise, or to make the question sound less abrupt. "Sind denn..." is the inversion used in yes/no or information questions (where sind = are). It does not change the basic meaning but affects tone — often translated simply as "are" in English, sometimes with words like "then" or "actually" depending on context.
target_language_example: Sind denn alle schon gegangen?
native_language_example: Have all of them already left?

meaning: 'are outside' (they/we are outdoors).
additional_notes: Present tense of sein (sind) + draußen (outside). Used to say that people or things are located outdoors. Context determines subject (wir, sie, ihr, etc.); in examples 'sie' or names are the subject. Word order: subject + sein + draußen. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Die Kinder sind draußen und spielen im Garten.
native_language_example: The children are outside and playing in the garden.

meaning: are simply
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or emphasize that something is straightforward, obvious, or characteristic. 'einfach' here means 'simply/just' and modifies the verb 'sind' (are). Common in spoken and written German to express a plain fact or an emphatic opinion (e.g. 'they are just amazing' = 'sie sind einfach unglaublich').
target_language_example: Sie sind einfach sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: They are just very friendly.

meaning: ‘are finally’ or ‘are at last’ (expresses relief that something has happened or changed).
additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (sind = are). Endlich adds emphasis of relief, impatience ended, or a long-awaited change. Can be used with verbs/adjectives (zu Hause, vorbei, weg, trocken, frei). Word order: 'wir sind endlich zu Hause' = 'we are finally home'.
target_language_example: Die Ergebnisse sind endlich da.
native_language_example: The results are finally here.

meaning: are a bit
additional_notes: Used to soften or lessen a descriptive adjective; 'etwas' here means 'a little' or 'somewhat'. Common with plural subjects (sind = are). Placement: subject + sind + etwas + adjective. Useful for polite or mild statements (e.g. "Die Eltern sind etwas nervös" = "The parents are a bit nervous").
target_language_example: Die Fenster sind etwas geschlossen.
native_language_example: The windows are a bit closed.

meaning: 'are exactly' or 'are precisely'.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'sind' (they/you formal/we are) and the adverb 'genau' (exactly/precisely). Used to state exact similarity or precision: e.g. 'sind genau gleich' = 'are exactly the same', or 'sind genau wie...' = 'are exactly like...'. Word order can vary (genau can come before or after an adjective/phrase).
target_language_example: Die beiden Bilder sind genau gleich.
native_language_example: The two pictures are exactly the same.

meaning: are big
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'sind' (are) and the adjective 'große' (big/large). 'Große' is the weak inflected form agreeing with the noun in number and case; the exact English adjective (big/large/great) depends on context (e.g., 'große Werke' = 'great/masterpieces', 'große Fans' = 'big/huge fans' or simply 'big fans'). Used after a noun/pronoun to describe size, importance, or intensity.
target_language_example: Die Hunde sind große Tiere.
native_language_example: The dogs are large animals.

meaning: 'are behind' or 'are after' (physically located behind someone or pursuing/targeting someone).
additional_notes: Used with a personal pronoun or name; 'hinter' takes the dative (dir, Ihnen, mir). Often appears with 'her' to emphasize pursuit (colloquial): 'sind hinter dir her' or without 'her' for literal position: 'sind hinter dir'. Can be used literally (standing behind) or figuratively (chasing, after someone).
target_language_example: Die sind hinter Ihnen her.
native_language_example: They are after you (formal).

meaning: are cold
additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (e.g., Hände, Ohren, Die Winter) to say that something or someone is cold. 'Sind' is the 3rd-person plural form of 'sein' (to be); 'kalt' means cold. For singular subjects use 'ist kalt' (er/sie/es ist kalt).
target_language_example: Meine Hände sind kalt.
native_language_example: My hands are cold.

meaning: are smarter / are more clever
additional_notes: Plural form of 'klug' (smart). 'Sind' is the 3rd person plural of 'sein' (to be). Used to compare or describe intelligence; often appears with a comparison (als) or alone: 'Sie sind klüger' = 'They are smarter'.
target_language_example: Tom und Maria sind klüger, als Sie denken.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria are smarter than you think.

meaning: are sick / are ill.
additional_notes: Plural present form of sein + krank. Used to say that people (we/they/you plural) are ill. Subject determines meaning: Die sind krank = They are sick; Wir sind krank = We are sick. Can refer to temporary illness or being unwell. Used with personal pronouns or noun phrases (Tom und Maria sind krank).
target_language_example: Meine Freunde sind krank, deshalb bleiben sie zu Hause.
native_language_example: My friends are sick, so they are staying home.

meaning: are long
additional_notes: Simple present of sein (to be) + adjective 'lang'. Used to describe length (time, physical length, stories, hair, legs, objects). Word order: subject + sind + lang. Can describe both literal (physical length) and figurative (long stories, long time). For singular subjects use 'ist lang' (he/she/it is long).
target_language_example: Die Straße sind lang.
native_language_example: The roads are long.

meaning: 'are sometimes' — used to say that someone or something has a trait occasionally.
additional_notes: Combine the verb sein (sind = are) with manchmal (sometimes). Used to describe recurring but not constant behaviours or states. Follows the subject (Wir sind manchmal…, Sie sind manchmal…). Can be softened with words like ein wenig/etwas (a little/somewhat).
target_language_example: Manche Menschen sind manchmal nervös, bevor sie sprechen.
native_language_example: Some people are sometimes nervous before they speak.

meaning: there are only three left
additional_notes: Used to say that only three of something remain (items, days, people, etc.). 'Es sind nur noch drei' is a complete sentence in contexts where the noun is understood (e.g., after asking 'How many are left?'). 'noch' emphasizes remaining, 'nur' emphasizes small quantity. Word order may change: 'Es sind nur noch drei Tage.'
target_language_example: Es sind nur noch drei Stück Kuchen übrig.
native_language_example: There are only three pieces of cake left.

meaning: 'are open' (plural; used with plural subjects).
additional_notes: Present-tense form of sein + offen. Use with plural nouns or pronouns (die Fenster, ihre Schnürsenkel, meine/seine Augen). Describes something physically open (windows, shoelaces, eyes) or figuratively open. For singular subjects use 'ist offen'.
target_language_example: Die Türen sind offen.
native_language_example: The doors are open.

meaning: have been (for) three (units of time) — used for 'we/they are' + duration of three time units.
additional_notes: Used with a time unit (Tagen, Monaten, Jahren) to indicate that someone or something has been in a state or at a place for three units of that time. 'sind' is the present tense plural form of 'sein' (to be) for wir/sie; adjust verb and person as needed for other subjects (e.g. 'bin seit drei Tagen', 'ist seit drei Jahren'). The phrase must be completed with a time unit (e.g. 'sind seit drei Jahren', 'sind seit drei Tagen').
target_language_example: Wir sind seit drei Jahren verheiratet.
native_language_example: We have been married for three years.

meaning: 'are even' (adds emphasis: something surprising or unexpected is included/true).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something surprising, unexpected, or noteworthy is included or true. 'Sind' is the plural form of 'sein' (to be); 'sogar' means 'even'. Word order: 'sind sogar' appears when the subject is plural and the verb comes before the emphasized element. For singular use you'd see 'ist sogar'.
target_language_example: In der Schublade sind sogar drei Schlüssel.
native_language_example: There are even three keys in the drawer.

meaning: are late
additional_notes: Used with the subject wir/Sie/er/etc. + sind (to be) to say someone is late or running late. Common phrase: "wir sind spät dran" or "Sie sind spät dran" — adding "dran" is very common in spoken German. Can also be used with an activity (e.g. "wir sind spät für den Strand" = we're late for the beach).
target_language_example: Wir sind spät dran, beeil dich!
native_language_example: We're running late, hurry up!

meaning: 'are in love' (plural or formal 'we/they/you are in love')
additional_notes: Verb phrase using the verb 'verliebt sein' meaning to be in love. 'Sind' is the present plural (or formal 'you') form of 'sein' (to be). Use with a preposition 'in' + person to say who someone is in love with (e.g. 'Wir sind verliebt in sie' = 'We are in love with her'). Common in everyday speech; not informal slang.
target_language_example: Wir sind verliebt ineinander.
native_language_example: We are in love with each other.

meaning: 'are crazy' / 'are mad' (they are crazy)
additional_notes: Present-tense plural form of the adjective verrückt (crazy). Used to describe a group (they) as crazy, mad, or behaving irrationally. Can be strong (insult) or playful depending on tone and context. In German the verb 'sind' is the 3rd-person plural of 'sein' (to be).
target_language_example: Die Nachbarn sind verrückt — sie feiern jede Nacht.
native_language_example: The neighbors are crazy — they party every night.

meaning: to sit on (something); to be seated on top of a surface.
additional_notes: A separable verb construction: sitzen (to sit) plus the preposition auf (on). In German the verb and preposition often appear together in English as 'sit on'. Use sitzen auf with a dative object (auf + dem/der/der/des) when location is meant (where someone/something is sitting). Example contexts: people sitting on chairs, benches, a porch (Veranda), or birds on a branch.
target_language_example: Die Kinder sitzen auf der Veranda und spielen Karten.
native_language_example: The children are sitting on the porch and playing cards.

meaning: to stay seated; (colloquially) to remain where you are or to be held back (e.g., in school)
additional_notes: Common literal meaning: to stay seated (physically). Colloquial uses: telling someone to stay put (imperative), or in school context 'sitzen bleiben' means to repeat a grade. Tone can be neutral or firm; in imperative can sound rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich möchte nur hier sitzen bleiben.
native_language_example: I just want to stay seated here.

meaning: 'to be sitting in / to be located in' or idiomatically 'to be stuck in' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally means to sit in a place (e.g., sitzen in der Kantine = sitting in the canteen). Can also be part of idiomatic expressions: 'in der Falle sitzen' = to be stuck/trapped ('we're in a trap' / 'we're doomed'). Context decides whether it's physical location or idiomatic. Use appropriate article/case after 'in' (usually dative for location: in der Kantine, in einem Büro).
target_language_example: Wir sitzen in der Bibliothek und lernen.
native_language_example: We're sitting in the library and studying.

meaning: to leave someone sitting / to leave someone (in a difficult situation); to abandon
additional_notes: Phrasal verb made of sitzen (to sit) + lassen (to let/leave). Can be literal (leave someone sitting somewhere) or figurative (leave someone in the lurch, abandon them, not help). Context determines whether it's physical or metaphorical. Often used in past/present tense (ließ sitzen / lässt sitzen). Informal but common.
target_language_example: Er hat mich nicht im Stich gelassen und nicht sitzen lassen.
native_language_example: He didn't abandon me or leave me sitting there.

meaning: is sitting at his (place/object) — used to describe someone sitting at or by something belonging to a male person.
additional_notes: Commonly part of a larger sentence like 'Er sitzt an seinem Schreibtisch' (He is sitting at his desk). 'Seinem' is the dative masculine/neuter possessive ('his' or 'its' in formal contexts). The phrase requires a noun after 'seinem' (e.g. Tisch, Schreibtisch, Platz). For feminine nouns the form would be 'sitzt an ihrer'.
target_language_example: Er sitzt an seinem Schreibtisch und arbeitet.
native_language_example: He is sitting at his desk and working.

meaning: a conversational filler or connector: 'so, and...' used to continue, summarize, or change the topic
additional_notes: Used in spoken German to link sentences, draw attention, or move the conversation forward. Often appears at the start of a sentence: 'So, und ...' can signal a summary ('So, und das war's.'), a transition to the next topic ('So, und was nun?'), or to continue a point. Tone and context determine whether it's neutral, casual, or slightly emphatic. Not a fixed idiom with a single translation—translate based on context (e.g., 'so,' 'well,' 'now,' or simply 'and').
target_language_example: So, und was machen wir jetzt?
native_language_example: So, and what do we do now?

meaning: very sorry; I'm so sorry.
additional_notes: Used with the fixed expression 'Es tut mir (so) leid' to apologize or express sympathy. 'so' intensifies the apology ('very' or 'so'). Common in spoken and written German. You can add the person's name after a comma (e.g., 'Es tut mir so leid, Sam'). 'Ja' can be inserted for emphasis: 'Es tut mir ja so leid.'
target_language_example: Es tut mir so Leid, das hätte nicht passieren dürfen.
native_language_example: I'm so sorry, that shouldn't have happened.

meaning: in that way; like that (about manner or appearance).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the manner, style, or feeling of something. Can appear in different structures: with verbs of perception or feeling (sich so anfühlen), with commands about handling or dressing (so anlegen), or as an admonition (so anfassen = touch like that). Context determines exact translation: 'so' = 'like that', 'an' often combines with a verb (anfühlen, anlegen, anfassen).
target_language_example: Bitte leg das Kleid nicht so an.
native_language_example: Please don't put the dress on like that.

meaning: as soon as possible (ASAP).
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to do something quickly; polite requests often add 'bitte' (please). Common in both spoken and written German. Word-for-word it means 'as soon as possible' and corresponds directly to English 'as soon as possible'.
target_language_example: Komm bitte so bald wie möglich vorbei.
native_language_example: Please come by as soon as possible.

meaning: to stay like that / to remain as is.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone or something to remain in the same state, position, or condition. 'So' refers to the current way/situation; context determines whether it's physical position (e.g., stay still) or a general state/behavior (e.g., remain the same). Can be used as a command, suggestion, or observation.
target_language_example: Bitte so bleiben, ich mache ein Foto.
native_language_example: Please stay like that, I'm taking a photo.

meaning: 'so bleibt' = 'stays like this' or 'remains that way'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, state, or condition continues unchanged. Often follows a description or clause (e.g., 'Ich möchte, dass es so bleibt' = 'I want it to remain like this'). Can be used descriptively ('er bleibt so' = he remains that way) or in more general statements about consequences or habits ('Und so bleibt man...').
target_language_example: Wenn wir nichts ändern, so bleibt alles beim Alten.
native_language_example: If we change nothing, everything will stay the same.

meaning: so/free; depending on context: 'so... (adjective/adverb)' = 'as/so ...' or in formula 'ich war so frei' = 'I took the liberty (to...)'.
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) as part of a comparison or degree: 'so frei wie...' = 'as free as.../so free as...'. 2) in the polite phrase 'ich war so frei, ...' meaning 'I took the liberty of...' (i.e. I did something without asking but hoping it's OK). Context decides translation.
target_language_example: Ich war so frei, deine Nummer weiterzugeben.
native_language_example: I took the liberty of giving out your number.

meaning: so early in the (morning/day); 'this early' (emphasizing unusual earliness)
additional_notes: Used before a time noun (often 'Morgen') to express surprise or apology about doing something at an early hour. Common in phrases like 'so früh am Morgen' = 'this early in the morning'. Can be used with informal 'du' or formal 'Sie'.
target_language_example: Entschuldige, dass ich dich so früh am Morgen anrufe.
native_language_example: Sorry to call you this early in the morning.

meaning: 'so feels' / 'feels like this' — used to describe how something feels (emotionally or physically).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'so fühlt es sich (also) an' or 'so fühlt es sich eben an', meaning 'this is how it feels' or 'so that's what it feels like'. Used to report a sensation or emotional impression. 'So' = 'like this/so', 'fühlt' = third-person singular of 'fühlen' (to feel). Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: So fühlt es sich an, wenn man lange unterwegs war.
native_language_example: This is how it feels when you've been away for a long time.

meaning: not completely; not entirely; somewhat
additional_notes: Used to soften a statement: indicates something is only partly true or someone is not fully certain. Often appears in negatives (Nicht so ganz = not quite) or with verbs expressing understanding, usefulness, certainty, etc. Informal to neutral; placement flexible (before adjective, after verb phrases).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das so ganz nicht.
native_language_example: I don't quite understand that.

meaning: meant/intended like that; in that way
additional_notes: Used to say that something was intended or planned in a particular way. Often follows a statement about purpose, intention, or design (e.g. "Ich habe das so gedacht" = "I intended it that way"). Can be used to clarify or defend a choice or to explain how something should work.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Meeting so gedacht, dass alle die neuen Ideen vorstellen.
native_language_example: I intended the meeting to be like that, so that everyone presents the new ideas.

meaning: 'around' or 'at about' (used with times)
additional_notes: Commonly used before times to give an approximate time (e.g. 'so gegen halb fünf' = 'around 4:30'). Can appear at the start or within a sentence. Very useful in spoken and informal written German for estimating times.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns so gegen sieben.
native_language_example: We'll meet at about seven.

meaning: done like that / done that way
additional_notes: Use to describe how something was done (in that way). Often appears with context showing comparison or expectation (wie ...). Can be used in statements, questions, and negations. In casual speech 'so' can mean 'like that' or 'this way'.
target_language_example: Warum hast du das so gemacht?
native_language_example: Why did you do it like that?

meaning: to be as big/tall as (someone or something).
additional_notes: 'so ... wie' is the standard comparative structure meaning 'as ... as'. 'groß' can mean tall (for people) or large (for things).
