When using the infinitive construction with 'sein' it often appears in subordinate clauses or reported speech (e.g., 'Er sagt, so groß wie sein Haus sei das Gebäude nicht.'), but it can also be quoted or used in fixed expressions. The base sentence form is: X ist so groß wie Y.
target_language_example: Er behauptet, sein Hund sei so groß wie sein.
native_language_example: He claims that his dog is as big as his.

meaning: to be that good; to be as good as described or expected
additional_notes: Used to describe the quality or ability of someone or something (often compared to a standard or expectation). Can be used with an adjective, clause, or comparison (e.g. »so gut sein wie…«). Context determines whether it refers to present ability, past performance, or general quality.
target_language_example: Dieser Kuchen kann wirklich so gut sein.
native_language_example: This cake can really be that good.

meaning: almost, nearly; or 'as good as' in comparisons (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common idiom with two main uses: 1) 'so gut wie' = 'almost' / 'practically' (e.g. so gut wie nichts = almost nothing); 2) in comparisons 'so gut wie X' can mean 'as well as X' or 'as good as X' when comparing abilities or knowledge (often followed by a person or clause). Context decides the sense. When combined with 'gar nicht' or negative, it emphasizes 'almost not at all.'
target_language_example: Ich habe das Projekt so gut wie fertig.
native_language_example: I've almost finished the project.

meaning: almost like new; nearly new
additional_notes: Used to say something (item, repair, condition) is practically in new condition but not literally brand new. Common in sales (e.g., used cars) and after repairs. Tone is neutral; can be used emphatically: 'So gut wie neu, was?' = 'Almost like new, huh?'.
target_language_example: Der Wagen ist gebraucht, aber so gut wie neu.
native_language_example: The car is used, but almost like new.

meaning: almost never; very rarely.
additional_notes: Used to say that something hardly ever happens. Literally 'as good as never' — it's equivalent to 'almost never' or 'practically never' in English. Common in everyday speech and can modify verbs or actions.
target_language_example: Ich trinke so gut wie nie Kaffee nach 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: I almost never drink coffee after 6 p.m.

meaning: 'like that' / indicates manner or direction (do/put/stand it that way) or 'to (go) there' in questions about direction
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: 1) with verbs (hinbekommen, hinstellen) to mean 'in that way' or 'to manage/arrange something like that' (Das bekäme ich nie so hin = I could never manage it like that). 2) with sich hinstellen (Stell dich mal so hin) = 'stand like that'. 3) in questions about motion (Und wo gehst du so hin? / Wo eilen Sie denn so hin?) meaning 'where are you going (to) (in such a hurry)?'. 'So' emphasizes manner or degree; 'hin' indicates direction away from the speaker. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Das bekäme ich nie so hin wie du.
native_language_example: I could never manage it like that the way you do.

meaning: as hungry as (someone thinks/claims); used to compare actual hunger with a reported or assumed level
additional_notes: Commonly appears in sentences that compare reality to someone's opinion or expectation: ‚gar nicht so hungrig, wie...‘ means ‚not as hungry as...‘. The comma and following clause typically contains a person and a verb (e.g. ‚wie du meinst/ wie Sie glauben‘). Use ‚so + adjective + wie‘ for equality comparisons; adding ‚gar nicht‘ negates and weakens the comparison.
target_language_example: Er ist gar nicht so hungrig, wie du denkst.
native_language_example: He is not as hungry as you think.

meaning: used to introduce a hypothetical result in conditional (past) sentences; similar to "then would have" or "so would have" in English.
additional_notes: Appears in past unreal conditional (third conditional) sentences. Often follows the protasis (the "if" clause) or the word "wenn" clause and precedes the consequence clause. Emphasizes the result that would have happened but did not. Word order: verb (hätte) often comes at the end of the clause when joined with "wenn", or after "so" for emphasis.
target_language_example: Wenn ich gewusst hätte, dass du kommst, so hätte ich Kuchen gebacken.
native_language_example: If I had known you were coming, then I would have baked a cake.

meaning: that's the way it is; that's how things are.
additional_notes: Used to accept or comment on a situation as unavoidable or normal. Can express resignation, acceptance, or explanation. Often used on its own as a short response. Tone depends on context (neutral, disappointed, resigned).
target_language_example: Man kann den Zug nicht mehr erreichen — so ist das.
native_language_example: You can't catch the train anymore — that's the way it is.

meaning: That's life / That's how life is.
additional_notes: Used to express acceptance or resignation about an unpleasant or unavoidable situation. Can be said alone as a comment (like “that's life”) or followed by context (e.g., describing why something happened). The variants "so ist das Leben nun einmal" / "nun mal" add emphasis ("that’s just how life is").
target_language_example: Du hast den Job nicht bekommen? So ist das Leben.
native_language_example: You didn't get the job? That's life.

meaning: so/thus it happened; that's how (something) came about
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result, explanation, or the way something developed. Often followed by 'es', a clause (z. B. 'so kam es zu...'), or by a pronoun/object (z. B. 'so kam sie zu...'). Can mean 'that's how it happened', 'thus', or 'this is how someone got/received something.' Common in storytelling and explanations.
target_language_example: So kam es, dass wir uns wiedertrafen.
native_language_example: That's how it happened that we met again.

meaning: used to say 'this way' or 'like that' when stating that something is possible or not acceptable (e.g. 'you can't do it like that' / 'that's how you can...').
additional_notes: Combines 'so' (so / like that / this way) with the modal verb 'kann' (can). Used to comment on a situation or method: either to criticize how something is done (negative: 'So kann das nicht weitergehen' — 'It can't go on like this') or to state that something is possible or a way to achieve something (positive: 'So kann man gut sein Englisch verbessern' — 'That's a good way to improve your English'). Word order and context determine exact English translation.
target_language_example: So kann man neue Wörter schnell lernen.
native_language_example: That's how you can learn new words quickly.

meaning: 'only in this way could' / 'that way he/she/it was able to'
additional_notes: Combines 'so' (in that way/thus) with the past tense modal verb 'konnte' (could/was able to). Used to describe that something was possible or happened only by/through that manner or circumstance. Context determines whether it's best translated as 'so he could...', 'that way I could...', or 'only like this could...'. Word order follows German sentence structure.
target_language_example: Nur so konnte ich helfen.
native_language_example: Only in this way could I help.

meaning: 'so könnte' = 'it could be like this' / 'one could (do) it like this'.
additional_notes: A conditional/modal phrase: 'so' = 'like this' or 'in that way'; 'könnte' is the subjunctive/conditional of können (could/might). Used to suggest a possibility, a possible way to say or do something, or to imagine a scenario. Common in tentative or hypothetical statements (e.g. giving an example, a possible formulation, or a polite suggestion).
target_language_example: So könnte man das Problem lösen.
native_language_example: One could solve the problem like that.

meaning: 'to laugh like that' / 'to laugh so (much/that...)' (describes the manner or degree of laughing)
additional_notes: Used to comment on the way or intensity of someone's laughter. 'so' can mean 'like that' (pointing to a specific manner) or indicate degree ('so much' / 'so hard') often followed by consequences (e.g., milk came out of her nose). Common in spoken German. Context determines whether 'so' is demonstrative (like that) or degree (so much).
target_language_example: Warum musst du immer so lachen?
native_language_example: Why do you always laugh like that?

meaning: for so long
additional_notes: Used to indicate duration (how long). Can mean 'for such a long time' or simply 'so long' in comparisons. Often appears with verbs of waiting, seeing, or taking time. In question form it asks why something took that long. Can combine with 'nicht' for 'not seen for so long' (e.g. 'so lange nicht gesehen').
target_language_example: Warum bist du so lange weg gewesen?
native_language_example: Why were you away for so long?

meaning: as long as / while (for the duration that)
additional_notes: Used to indicate duration or a condition that continues for the same length of time. Can be followed by a clause (so lange wie du willst) or a time expression (so lange wie zwei Stunden). When used as a conditional it means 'provided that' or 'as long as' (e.g., 'Ich helfe dir, so lange du ehrlich bist.').
target_language_example: Du kannst bleiben, so lange wie du möchtest.
native_language_example: You can stay as long as you want.

meaning: 'to live like that' / 'to live in that way'
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone's lifestyle or living conditions—can express admiration (positive), envy, disapproval, or disbelief depending on context and intonation. 'So' refers to the manner or situation just described or shown. Often appears in exclamations or questions (e.g., Wie kann man nur so leben?).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht mein ganzes Leben so leben.
native_language_example: I don't want to live like that my whole life.

meaning: to do it that way / to do it like that
additional_notes: 'So' here means 'in this/that way'. Used to instruct or indicate someone should perform an action in the same manner as shown, described or expected. Commonly appears with comparisons (wie ...) or references to instructions. Works with various subjects and politeness levels (du, ihr, Sie).
target_language_example: Du solltest das so machen, wie Tom es dir gezeigt hat.
native_language_example: You should do it the way Tom showed you.

meaning: anyway / in any case / either way
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen regardless of other factors or that a situation is the same under different conditions. Can express resignation, inevitability, or that a choice doesn't matter. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir müssen so oder so zweimal fahren.
native_language_example: We have to drive twice anyway.

meaning: ‘you talk like that’ or ‘you speak that way’ (often used to criticize or forbid a way of speaking).
additional_notes: Used to comment on or respond to the manner/tone someone is using. Often appears in negative commands or reproaches: 'So redest du nicht (mit ...)' = 'You don't talk to (someone) like that.' Can be used in questions to express shock or disbelief ('So redest du mit mir?' = 'You talk to me like that?').
target_language_example: So redest du nicht mit deiner Mutter.
native_language_example: You don't talk to your mother like that.

meaning: 'so schlechter' is a non-standard or marked combination of 'so' + the weak-inflected/comparative form 'schlechter'; intended meaning: 'so bad' or 'in such a bad ...' when modifying a noun (e.g. 'such a bad ...')
additional_notes: In standard German you would normally say 'so schlecht' before adjectives/adverbs or 'so ein(e)(r/s) + adjective' before a noun (e.g. 'so ein schlechter Kämpfer'). 'So schlechter' can appear in colloquial speech but often requires a preceding determiner or different word order to be grammatical: 'ein so schlechter Kämpfer' or better 'so ein schlechter Kämpfer'. Using 'so schlechter Laune' is unidiomatic; prefer 'so schlechte Laune' or 'so schlecht gelaunt'. Learners should be aware adjective endings must agree with gender, number and case, and 'schlechter' by itself is a comparative ('worse') or a weakly inflected form of 'schlecht'.
target_language_example: Aber wie kann denn ein Polizist ein so schlechter Kämpfer sein?
native_language_example: But how can a policeman be such a poor fighter?

meaning: as quickly as possible; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: A common phrase used to ask for or promise urgency. Can be used formally and informally. Variations: "so bald wie möglich" (as soon as possible) is similar. Often abbreviated in writing as "s. s. w. m." only in notes, but not common in speech.
target_language_example: Bitte beantworten Sie die Anfrage so schnell wie möglich.
native_language_example: Please answer the request as quickly as possible.

meaning: so nicely / so beautifully / so well (intensifier showing degree)
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to emphasize degree (how nicely/beautifully/well something is done or was). Can modify verbs, adjectives, or whole clauses. Context determines translation: can mean 'so nicely/beautifully,' 'so well,' or simply 'that nicely' (often with a slightly ironic or wistful tone).
target_language_example: Du hast das so schön erklärt.
native_language_example: You explained that so well / so nicely.

meaning: 'so be it' or 'let it be so' (expression of acceptance or final agreement).
additional_notes: A somewhat formal or literary phrase used to accept a decision, outcome, or wish. Can be used solemnly (e.g. in farewells, prayers) or resignedly to indicate agreement. Often followed by punctuation; 'So sei es denn' is a slightly older/poetic variant.
target_language_example: Wenn ihr das wollt, so sei es.
native_language_example: If that's what you want, so be it.

meaning: to be like that
additional_notes: Used to describe the state or condition of something (being a certain way) or similarity (to be like someone/something). Common in statements and questions: 'Das muss nicht so sein' = 'It doesn't have to be that way.' Often follows 'wie' to compare: 'so sein wie du' = 'to be like you.'
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht, dass alles immer so sein muss.
native_language_example: I don't want everything to always have to be that way.

meaning: 'so did' or part of expressions meaning 'thus did' / 'acted in that way' / 'pretended (to)'. Often appears with 'als' (as if) to mean 'pretended that...'.
additional_notes: 'Tat' is preterite of 'tun'. 'so tat' is not a fixed idiom but a common combination: (1) with 'als' — 'so tat er, als...' = 'he pretended as if...'; (2) narrative/literary — 'so tat ich' = 'thus I did'; (3) can appear in subordinate or elliptical clauses. Registers range from neutral to literary; less common in everyday colloquial speech where 'tat so' or 'hat so getan' might appear. Can generally be translated literally as 'so did'.
target_language_example: Und so tat er das, was sein Herz von ihm verlangte.
native_language_example: And so he did what his heart demanded of him.

meaning: to pretend; to act as if (something were true)
additional_notes: Used to describe pretending or giving the appearance that something is the case. Often followed by a clause introduced with 'als ob' + subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) for hypothetical or unreal situations, but in spoken German the indicative is also common. Can be used with a noun phrase or a verb clause.
target_language_example: Er kann nicht länger so tun, als ob alles in Ordnung wäre.
native_language_example: He can no longer pretend as if everything were fine.

meaning: about; approximately (with numbers) / so much about someone (with verbs like sorgen) — 'around' or 'so much concerning'.
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) with numbers or ages to mean 'around' or 'about' (e.g. so um die dreißig = about thirty). 2) with verbs of concern (sich sorgen um, sorgen um) where 'so um' means 'so much about' or 'that much for' — often followed by a person or thing. The exact sense depends on the verb and context. 'so' adds emphasis ('so much'), 'um' links to the object of approximation or concern.
target_language_example: Sie ist so um die Vierzig.
native_language_example: She is around forty.

meaning: so full / so (filled) / so crowded (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used to describe a high degree of fullness, crowding, or being filled with something (literal or figurative). In sentences 1-2 it means 'that full' or 'so crowded'; in 3-4 it is used in a figurative construction 'so voll von ...' = 'so full of ...'. Sentence 5 likely means 'we were so full' (after eating) or 'we were very full/crowded'. Often translated as 'so' + adjective 'full' in English. Word order: 'so voll' can appear before or after the noun/clause it modifies; with 'von' it takes an object ('voll von Magie' = full of magic).
target_language_example: Der Schrank ist so voll, dass kein Platz mehr ist.
native_language_example: The closet is so full that there's no more space.

meaning: 'to be ready' or 'to be (mentally/physically) at the point of doing something'
additional_notes: Used to say someone is prepared or has reached the stage to do something (often followed by '...zu + Infinitiv' or with a clause). Can also mean 'to be so far' in distance/time contexts. Common in phrases like 'Ich bin so weit' (I'm ready) or 'Bist du so weit, ...?' (Are you ready to ...?).
target_language_example: Ja, ich bin so weit, wir können losgehen.
native_language_example: Yes, I am ready; we can go now.

meaning: so far
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate degree, distance, or progress. Can mean 'so far' (up to now), 'as far as' (to a certain point), or 'to this extent' (to the degree mentioned). Context determines whether it's temporal (progress), spatial (distance), or conditional. Often appears in phrases like 'so weit, so gut' (so far, so good).
target_language_example: Wir sind so weit gekommen, dass wir nicht mehr aufgeben wollen.
native_language_example: We've come so far that we don't want to give up now.

meaning: to go so far (to do something); to go as far as to ...
additional_notes: Used to describe an action or opinion that reaches an extreme or additional step. Often followed by 'zu' + infinitive (e.g. 'so weit gehen, zu sagen...') or by a clause introduced with 'dass' or 'etwas zu tun'. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Er würde für seine Familie so weit gehen, alles zu opfern.
native_language_example: He would go so far as to sacrifice everything for his family.

meaning: 'continue like that' / 'and so on' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) To say something continues in the same way (e.g. 'it kept going on like that') — often paired with verbs like 'gehen' or 'machen'. 2) In lists it can mean 'and so on' or 'etc.' Context determines translation. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Wenn du so weiter lernst, wirst du die Prüfung bestehen.
native_language_example: If you continue studying like that, you'll pass the exam.

meaning: 'thus became' / 'in this way became' (describing how something turned out or became something)
additional_notes: Used to describe the result or outcome reached in a particular way. 'So' = 'thus/in this way', 'wurde' = past tense of 'werden' (to become/become passive). Common in narrative or explanatory sentences: 'So wurde er sauber.' = 'That is how he became clean.' Can also introduce a transformation or result ('So wurde die junge Lady zu meiner Frau.' = 'That's how the young lady became my wife.').
target_language_example: Er half ihr oft, so wurde aus Kollegen ein Paar.
native_language_example: He helped her often; in this way colleagues became a couple.

meaning: such a
additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to describe something as a certain kind of thing: so ein Laden = 'a shop like that' / 'such a shop'. It can also add emotion, especially annoyance or contempt in exclamations like So ein Scheiß! or insults like so ein Trottel. The form changes with gender and case, for example so eine, so einen, so einem.
target_language_example: So ein Auto kann ich mir nicht leisten.
native_language_example: I can't afford a car like that.

meaning: such a (one); that kind of (one).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun or as a pronoun replacing a feminine noun (eine). It points to a specific type or example previously mentioned or implied. Context determines whether it's positive/neutral/critical. Comparable forms: so ein (masculine/neutral), solche (plural).
target_language_example: Hast du so eine? Ich könnte eine gebrauchen.
native_language_example: Do you have one like that? I could use one.

meaning: at/in a place like that; in such a place.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a type of place previously mentioned or implied, often with a negative, surprised or disapproving tone. 'so' + dative demonstrative 'einem Ort' = 'in/at such a place'. Common with verbs like treffen, schlafen, geben, denken, aufziehen. Word order: 'an so einem Ort' (at such a place) or 'in so einem Ort' (less common; usually 'in so einem Ort' means inside).
target_language_example: Ich hätte nie gedacht, dass ich dich an so einem Ort sehe.
native_language_example: I never thought I'd see you in a place like that.

meaning: something like that
additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing, action, or situation of that kind, often when you do not name it exactly. It can sound vague and usually points to something already mentioned or obvious from context.
target_language_example: Ich hätte nie so etwas erwartet.
native_language_example: I would never have expected something like that.

meaning: such beautiful roses / roses that are so beautiful
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the high degree of beauty of the roses. Often appears in questions like "Haben Sie schon einmal so schöne Rosen gesehen?" meaning "Have you ever seen roses this beautiful?" "so" intensifies the adjective; word order: "so + adjective + noun." Can be used with other nouns (so schöne Blumen, so schönes Wetter).
target_language_example: Hast du jemals so schöne Rosen gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen roses this beautiful?

meaning: such a thing
additional_notes: Colloquial for "so etwas." It refers to a thing, action, idea, or remark just mentioned or understood from context. Often used in spoken German, sometimes with surprise, criticism, or disbelief.
target_language_example: Ich habe so was noch nie gehört.
native_language_example: I've never heard anything like that.

meaning: 'as soon as the' (followed by a masculine noun)
additional_notes: Sobald = 'as soon as' (a subordinating conjunction). Der is the masculine definite article in nominative (or dative/genitive depending on context) and agrees with a masculine noun that follows. The clause introduced by 'sobald' describes something that happens immediately after another event. Word order: the verb of the subordinate clause goes to the end (e.g., 'sobald der Zug abfährt').
target_language_example: Sobald der Brief kommt, rufe ich dich an.
native_language_example: As soon as the letter arrives, I'll call you.

meaning: 'there immediately' or 'right there immediately' — indicates someone/something is present or should be present at a place at once.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. 'sofort' = immediately/right away; 'da' = there/here (context-dependent). Used to say someone is already there ('Die Polizei ist sofort da' can mean 'the police are there immediately' or 'will be there immediately' depending on context) or to order someone to come out/ go there now ('sofort da raus' = get out of there immediately). Tone can be urgent or commanding.
target_language_example: Komm jetzt sofort da her!
native_language_example: Come here right now!

meaning: immediately with that / do that right away (with 'damit' referring to a previously mentioned action or thing).
additional_notes: Sofort = immediately. 'Damit' here refers back to something just mentioned (an action, task, or object). Together they instruct someone to start or handle that thing at once. Common in commands or requests: 'Mach sofort damit weiter' = 'Continue with that immediately.'
target_language_example: Fang sofort damit an.
native_language_example: Start that immediately.

meaning: immediately the / right away the (used before a noun or phrase to say do something at once)
additional_notes: sofort = immediately/right away. 'sofort das' itself isn't a fixed phrase — it's the adverb 'sofort' followed by the definite article 'das' starting a noun phrase. Pay attention to context: the noun or clause after 'das' determines the full meaning (e.g. 'das Zimmer' = the room, 'das Thema' = the topic). In commands, 'Verlassen Sie sofort das Haus!' = 'Leave the house immediately!'.
target_language_example: Sag mir sofort das Ergebnis.
native_language_example: Tell me the result immediately.

meaning: immediately (call/get) the ... (used before a masculine accusative noun like 'Arzt' or a role).
additional_notes: Sofort = immediately. 'Sofort den' appears when an imperative or instruction tells someone to immediately contact, hire, stop, or get a specific masculine singular person or role (accusative: den/den + noun). Often used with verbs like 'rufen' (call) or 'stellen' (in some contexts 'employ' or 'place'). The exact action is given by the verb; 'sofort den Arzt rufen' = call the doctor immediately. Word order can vary: 'Ruf sofort den Arzt an.' or 'Rufen Sie sofort den Arzt.'
target_language_example: Ruf sofort den Arzt an!
native_language_example: Call the doctor immediately!

meaning: 'immediately with' or 'right away with' — used when saying you must speak or start something with someone immediately.
additional_notes: Common in phrases like 'Ich muss sofort mit ... sprechen' (I must speak with ... immediately). 'Sofort' means immediately; 'mit' here introduces the person you will speak/start with. Can also appear with actions: 'sofort mit dem Kochen beginnen' = start cooking immediately. Word order: 'sofort mit' is followed by a person (mit dir/Ihnen/ihm) or a noun/verb phrase (mit dem Kochen).
target_language_example: Ich muss sofort mit dir sprechen.
native_language_example: I need to speak with you right away.

meaning: even the/ even (to) the (masculine or accusative definite form)
additional_notes: sogar = 'even' (adds emphasis or surprise). 'den' is the masculine accusative definite article or demonstrative pronoun; together 'sogar den' highlights that something surprising or extreme applies to a specific masculine/accusative person or thing mentioned (e.g. den Jungen, den Cops, den Minister). Word order: 'sogar' usually precedes the noun phrase (with its article). Use with feminine or plural requires different article forms (z. B. 'sogar die', 'sogar das', 'sogar den' for masc./acc.).
target_language_example: Er hat sogar den Nachbarn eingeladen.
native_language_example: He even invited the neighbor.

meaning: even the (masculine or nominative noun) — emphasizes that someone/something surprising or unexpected is included.
additional_notes: Sogar = "even". Paired with der it highlights that a particular masculine noun (subject in nominative) is included unexpectedly. Word order: 'Sogar der Hund ...' (Even the dog ...). In sentence 2 the grammar is nonstandard ('Sogar der Onkel seine Nichte!' is colloquial/elliptical); standard would be e.g. 'Sogar der Onkel hat seine Nichte (gerettet)!'. Use 'sogar die' for feminine/plural as needed.
target_language_example: Sogar der Lehrer war überrascht.
native_language_example: Even the teacher was surprised.

meaning: even in / even at (used to emphasize that something applies in a particular place, time, situation, or context).
additional_notes: sogar adds emphasis ('even'), and in introduces the specific context (place, time, situation). Together they highlight surprise or contrast. Can appear in questions (Sogar in Mathe?) to express disbelief. Word order follows normal German rules: 'sogar' usually directly before the element it emphasizes.
target_language_example: Er arbeitet sogar in der Nacht.
native_language_example: He even works at night.

meaning: even with / even including
additional_notes: Used to add emphasis: points out that something unexpected or noteworthy is included. Often follows a noun or phrase introduced earlier (e.g., 'mit Balkon' = 'with a balcony') or appears before a noun/phrase introduced right after. Can be used in concrete (objects, people) and abstract contexts (price, justification).
target_language_example: Das Auto kostet 5.000 €, sogar mit neuer Batterie.
native_language_example: The car costs €5,000, even with a new battery.

meaning: as long as (the ...); indicates a condition that must hold while something else is true.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time or condition clause. 'Solange' is followed by a clause; 'der' is the definite article agreeing with a masculine noun in the clause (e.g. der Richter, der Körper, der Plan). In English you can translate it as 'as long as the...' or 'while the...'. Word order: the verb in the 'solange' clause goes to the end (subordinate clause).
target_language_example: Solange der Vertrag gültig ist, gelten diese Regeln.
native_language_example: As long as the contract is valid, these rules apply.

meaning: such a mistake; a mistake like that.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific kind of mistake mentioned or implied. Often appears after an article or verb with an accusative object (einen solchen Fehler). Formality: neutral; common in warnings, explanations, or regrets.
target_language_example: Mach keinen solchen Fehler noch einmal.
native_language_example: Don't make such a mistake again.

meaning: should/ought to you (polite indirect instruction: 'I am supposed to... for you').
additional_notes: Used in indirect speech to report instructions or obligations directed at the listener (formal 'Ihnen'). 'soll' is the modal verb 'sollen' in present tense and often appears with an infinitive after it. The speaker is saying that someone (else) told them to do something for the person being addressed. Because 'Ihnen' is the formal dative pronoun, this is polite/formal.
target_language_example: Er hat gesagt, ich soll Ihnen morgen das Paket bringen.
native_language_example: He said I should bring you the package tomorrow.

meaning: 'what is that supposed to mean' / 'what is going on here' (expresses surprise, irritation, or demand for explanation)
additional_notes: Used in questions to show annoyance, disbelief, or to ask for clarification about something unexpected. The particle 'denn' softens or emphasizes the question; leaving it out ('was soll das') is possible but sounds slightly different. Common in everyday spoken German. Can be followed by verbs like 'sein', 'werden' or 'heißen'.
target_language_example: Was soll denn das heißen? Ich habe nichts falsch gemacht!
native_language_example: What is that supposed to mean? I didn't do anything wrong!

meaning: am/are/is supposed to you
additional_notes: ‘soll dich’ pairs the modal verb sollen (in various persons) with the object pronoun dich (you). In many contexts it appears in reported/indirect commands or questions about obligation/intention ('(someone) is supposed to [do something] you' or 'am I/are you/should I be the one to… you?'). Word order can vary: often part of a larger clause (e.g. 'ich soll dich ...' = 'I'm supposed to ... you'). In idiomatic uses, it can express surprise or incredulity: 'Ich soll dich umbringen?' = 'I'm supposed to kill you?' or 'Das soll dich freuen!' = 'That should make you happy!' Pay attention to person and tense of sollen (soll, sollst, sollen…).
target_language_example: Ich soll dich anrufen, wenn ich angekommen bin.
native_language_example: I'm supposed to call you when I arrive.

meaning: used to express surprise/doubt about a claim or to report expected/approved advice (depends on context).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) Expressing disbelief/surprise about something someone said (similar to "That must be a joke" or "You can't be serious"). Common in phrases like "Das soll doch ein Witz sein." 2) Reporting advice, expectation or hearsay with a softening particle (e.g. "Er soll doch im Gefängnis sein" = "He is said to be in prison" or "You are supposed to.../should..." in moral/instruction contexts). The particle 'doch' adds emphasis, contradiction or reassurance and can change tone depending on intonation.
target_language_example: Du hast das schon erledigt? Das soll doch nicht wahr sein!
native_language_example: You already finished that? That can't be true!

meaning: "should/ought to go" or "is to go" (indicating obligation, instruction, or expectation that someone goes).
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' (must/should/be supposed to) in present form with the infinitive 'gehen' (to go). Used to report instructions (Tom said I should go), to express commands or strong suggestions (Er soll gehen! = He should go / He must leave), or to state a rule/general expectation (Wer ... soll gehen). Context and intonation determine force: with exclamation it's stronger (command); with reporting verbs ('hat gesagt') it marks an instruction.
target_language_example: Du sollst nicht bleiben; du soll gehen.
native_language_example: You shouldn't stay; you should go.

meaning: Should I do that? / Shall I (do) that?
additional_notes: Used to ask whether the speaker should perform an action. 'Soll' expresses obligation or suggestion. 'das' refers to a specific thing or action (often can be replaced by another pronoun or a verb phrase: 'soll ich das machen?', 'soll ich das Licht anmachen?'). Common in offers, requests for instructions, or suggestions.
target_language_example: Soll ich das Fenster öffnen?
native_language_example: Should I open the window?

meaning: 'what should I do' or 'what am I supposed to do'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to ask for advice, instructions, or express helplessness about what action to take. Often appears in questions: 'Was soll ich tun?' followed by a specific situation (wenn + clause). 'Soll' is modal verb 'should/ought to'.
target_language_example: Was soll ich tun, wenn ich den Bus verpasse?
native_language_example: What should I do if I miss the bus?

meaning: 'is/should be to' or 'is said to' + destination or person to go to; used to report advice, orders, or hearsay about going to a place or asking about someone.
additional_notes: soll + nach + (place/person) appears in two main uses: 1) giving or reporting an instruction/advice/command: jemand soll nach [Ort] kommen = someone should/has been told to come to [place]. 2) reporting hearsay: jemand soll nach [Ort] gegangen sein = someone is said to have gone to [place]. Use word order and context to tell if it's an order (imperative/reported command) or hearsay (often with past participle or verbs like 'sein'). 'nach' is used before place names (cities, countries without article) and with some fixed expressions (e.g., nach Hause).
target_language_example: Er sagt, ich soll nach Berlin fahren.
native_language_example: He says I should go to Berlin.

meaning: 'should' or 'ought to' + 'his/her/its' (possessive) — indicates expectation, advice, or reported obligation for someone to do/receive something.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the modal verb soll (3rd-person singular) followed by the possessive pronoun seine (his). Usage depends on context: it can express advice, expectation, reported speech (someone is said to do/ought to do), a wish (often emotional), or moral judgment. Note that seine is masculine/neuter singular or a generic neutral possessive; for feminine/ plural possessions forms change (ihre, ihr, seine/ihre depending on the noun). Word order: soll comes before the verb or auxiliary in full sentences (here examples show implied infinitive), and the actual verb may follow (e.g., Er soll seine Hausaufgaben machen).
target_language_example: Er soll seine Hausaufgaben pünktlich abgeben.
native_language_example: He should hand in his homework on time.

meaning: should/ought to (or is supposed to) + us (indirect object).
additional_notes: „soll“ is the present subjunctive/auxiliary of sollen used to report expectations, obligations, or instructions; here it combines with the pronoun „uns“ (us). Depending on context, it can mean: 'is supposed to (do something for us)', 'should (do something) to/for us', or in reported commands: 'X is said/expected to...'. Word order: the verb comes before the object in these examples because they are short clauses (Tom soll uns die Wahrheit sagen).
target_language_example: Die Ärztin sagt, sie soll uns morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: The doctor says she is supposed to call us tomorrow.

meaning: 'is supposed to' or 'am/are/should go to' + destination or purpose (with 'zur' = 'zu der')
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' (in present tense: soll/sollst/sollen) with the contraction 'zur' (zu + der). Use to express obligation, instruction, or reported plan involving going to a place or for a purpose: 'soll zur + noun'. English often uses 'is/are supposed to' or 'should' or 'am/are/is to'. Context determines if it's obligation, plan, or reported instruction.
target_language_example: Ich soll zur Schule gehen.
native_language_example: I am supposed to go to school.

meaning: is that supposed to (be/mean/do)
additional_notes: Used to question the purpose, meaning or appropriateness of something — often in a confrontational or annoyed tone. Common in spoken German. Can be followed by an infinitive, noun, adjective, or nothing: e.g. „Was soll das?“ (What's that supposed to mean?/What are you doing?), „Soll das helfen?“ (Is that supposed to help?). In casual speech it can express disbelief or irritation.
target_language_example: Was soll das heißen?
native_language_example: What is that supposed to mean?

meaning: adds emphasis/annoyed surprise to a question like 'what is this supposed to be?' or 'what's going on here?'.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German. 'Was soll denn ... ?' expresses irritation, disbelief, or demand for an explanation. 'Denn' softens or intensifies the question; it has no direct translation here. Used with words like 'das', 'dies', 'die Scheiße' or 'dieser Blödsinn'. Tone is often annoyed; can be rude depending on context and the noun used.
target_language_example: Was soll denn das heißen?
native_language_example: What is that supposed to mean?

meaning: what's the (meaning of this) / what's that supposed to be
additional_notes: Used in questions to express annoyance, disbelief or demand an explanation about an action or situation. Often appears in phrases like "Was soll der Lärm?" (Why all the noise?) or more strongly: "Was soll der Scheiß?" (What the hell is that / What is that supposed to mean?). Tone is confrontational; informal and often rude depending on the words that follow.
target_language_example: Was soll das Gezeter? Soll der was wollen?
native_language_example: What's all that fuss? Is that supposed to mean something?

meaning: used in colloquial German to express annoyance or ask 'what is this/that supposed to be?' or 'what's this crap?'.
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed question 'Was soll die ...?' followed by a noun (sometimes vulgar) to complain about something unexpected, irritating, or pointless. Tone is informal and can be rude. Use with caution; not appropriate in formal situations.
target_language_example: Was soll die Lärmkacke? Das ist doch kein Ruhestörungstag!
native_language_example: What is this noise crap supposed to be? This isn't a day for disturbing the peace!

meaning: 'what's the idea/meaning/purpose of this' (used to ask why something exists or why someone is doing something)
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase used to express confusion, annoyance or criticism about an object, action or situation. Often appears as a question: "Was soll dieses ...?" followed by a noun (Stück Metall, Kostüm, Verfahren). Tone can be surprised, irritated or skeptical. Translate depending on context: "What's this supposed to be?", "What's the point of this?", or "What is this about?"
target_language_example: Was soll dieses Geschenk? Ich habe doch nichts Besonderes getan.
native_language_example: What's this gift supposed to be for? I haven't done anything special.

meaning: a subjunctive/instructional phrase meaning 'should do it' or 'ought to do it' (reported command: 'told (someone) to do it').
additional_notes: German uses the Konjunktiv I form 'solle' for indirect speech or reported commands to convey what someone said someone else should do. In these examples 'solle es' = '[he/you/I] should/ought to do it' or 'was told to do it.' The literal pronoun (ich/er/sie) is often present earlier in the sentence; here 'solle' follows that subject in subordinate reported-speech structures. For simple advice or obligation in direct speech, modern German often uses 'soll' or modal verbs (e.g., 'du sollst es tun'), but 'solle' appears in formal reporting or written indirect speech.
target_language_example: Sie sagte mir, ich solle es morgen abgeben.
native_language_example: She told me I should hand it in tomorrow.

meaning: should/are supposed to (be) here; indicates obligation, instruction, or expectation about being in this place.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' (should/ought to/be supposed to) with 'hier' (here). Use to say someone is expected, instructed, or required to stay or be in a location. Tone depends on context: can be authoritative (an order), reported speech, or a question about expectation. Word order may change in full sentences (e.g., 'Wir sollen hier bleiben.' or questions: 'Wo sollen hier Menschen herkommen?').
target_language_example: Der Lehrer sagt, wir sollen hier warten.
native_language_example: The teacher says we are supposed to wait here.

meaning: are supposed to (do something) (to us / reflexive)
additional_notes: Combination of modal verb sollen + reflexive/indirect object pronoun uns. Meaning depends on subject and sentence: can mean 'you are supposed to tell us' (Sie sollen uns ...), 'they/you are supposed to connect us' (sollen uns ... verbinden), or reflexive 'we are supposed to (do something to/for ourselves)' as in 'Wir sollen uns melden' = 'We are supposed to get in touch'. Use context to determine whether 'uns' is an indirect object (to us) or the reflexive 'ourselves' (we/us). Tense and subject change the English phrasing (are supposed to / should).
target_language_example: Sie sollen uns morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: You are supposed to call us tomorrow.

meaning: expresses a reported assumption, tentative hearsay, or cautious probability (they/it are said to ... / it will probably ...).
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb sollen (used to report what is said/expected) with wohl (meaning probably/likely). Used to report information heard from others or to make a cautious guess. Tone can be neutral (reporting) or skeptical. Common in contexts like rumors (Er soll wohl zurücktreten — He is said to be resigning) or tentative estimates (Das soll wohl teuer werden — That will probably be expensive). Word order and inflection follow normal rules for sollen in the clause.
target_language_example: Man soll wohl sagen, dass das Konzert abgesagt wird.
native_language_example: People are said to say that the concert will be canceled. / It is said that the concert will probably be canceled.

meaning: 'you should (do) it' or 'you're supposed to (do) it' (informal singular you).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb 'sollen' (modal verb 'should/ought to') in the 2nd person singular (du sollst) plus the pronoun 'es' (it). Used to give commands, instructions, or reproaches to one person you address as 'du'. Tone depends on context — can be firm or scolding. Word order: in main clauses with a verb-first imperative-like emphasis, 'du' may be omitted in spoken commands, but 'du sollst es ...' is a full clause.
target_language_example: Du sollst es nicht kaputtmachen!
native_language_example: You shouldn't/mustn't break it!

meaning: 'you should (do something) to/with me' or 'you are to (do something) to/with me' (informal singular you).
additional_notes: Combines the verb sollen (2nd person singular informal: sollst) with the object pronoun mich (me). It appears in imperative-like or reported commands: someone tells another person what they should do regarding the speaker (e.g., call me, look at me, call me by a name, represent me). Grammar: use 'du sollst ...' for a directive addressed to 'du'. English translations often become 'you should' or 'you are supposed to' or simply 'you should/you must' depending on force. Context determines tone — can be a command, request, or quoted speech.
target_language_example: Du sollst mich morgen anrufen, nicht vergessen!
native_language_example: You should call me tomorrow, don't forget!

meaning: should be abolished / should be done away with
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion that something (a law, practice, custom, punishment, etc.) ought to be eliminated. Grammatically appears as part of a passive construction: 'sollte abgeschafft werden' (should be abolished). Polite or formal; common in debates and opinions.
target_language_example: Die Todesstrafe sollte abgeschafft werden.
native_language_example: The death penalty should be abolished.

meaning: would/should be at; expresses that something ought to be located or directed to a place (conditional or tentative).
additional_notes: This is the modal verb 'sollen' in the subjunctive/conditional form ('sollte') plus the preposition 'an'. It often appears when saying where something should be placed, attached, or to whom something should pass (e.g., 'an sie' = to her). Context determines whether it expresses obligation, expectation, or a hypothetical/conditional idea. Word order may separate 'sollte' and 'an' from the rest of the clause.
target_language_example: Das Bild sollte an der Wand hängen.
native_language_example: The picture should be hanging on the wall.

meaning: 'should be with' / 'was supposed to be at/with'.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollte' (past/subjunctive of 'sollen' used for obligation, expectation, or reported plan) with the preposition 'bei' (meaning 'with' or 'at someone's place'). Used to express that someone was expected or supposed to be with a person or at a location. Context determines translation: can indicate expectation ('He should be with his friends now') or a planned/required event in the past ('I was supposed to be executed at sunrise').
target_language_example: Sie sollte bei ihrer Mutter sein, aber sie ist nicht da.
native_language_example: She should be with her mother, but she isn't there.

meaning: 'should' + 'that/it' (used with a neuter object pronoun); expresses obligation, recommendation, or expectation about something.
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb 'sollen' in the subjunctive/conditional form 'sollte' to soften duty, advice, or hypothetical statements. 'Das' can refer to a neuter noun already mentioned or a general idea ('that/it'). Word order: 'sollte' follows the subject, and the main verb goes to the end if present (e.g., 'Ich sollte das Buch lesen').
target_language_example: Er sagte, ich sollte das Formular ausfüllen.
native_language_example: He said I should fill out the form.

meaning: 'you should' (with modal verb 'sollen' in conditional/obligation or suggestion; direct object 'dich' = you).
additional_notes: Used when giving advice, stating an obligation, making a suggestion, or expressing hypothetical/conditional ideas about 'you'. Tone depends on context: can be helpful (Ich sollte dich begleiten — I should accompany you), neutral (Ich sollte dich doch mal besuchen — I should visit you sometime), or threatening/negative (Ich sollte dich kaltmachen — I should kill you). 'Sollte' is the subjunctive/conditional form of 'sollen' and often translates as 'should' or 'ought to'. Word order: verb (sollte) + object (dich) + main verb later (Ich sollte dich besuchen).
target_language_example: Du bist krank — ich sollte dich zum Arzt bringen.
native_language_example: You're sick — I should take you to the doctor.

meaning: should/ought to (followed by the indefinite article 'eine' introducing a feminine noun phrase). Expresses recommendation, expectation, obligation, or hypothetical concerning a feminine (or occasionally neuter) noun.
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'sollen' in the subjunctive/conditional/soft recommendation form 'sollte' plus the indefinite article 'eine'. Used before a feminine noun (e.g., 'eine Überraschung', 'eine Unterkunft'). Context and sentence structure determine nuance (advice, expectation, hypothetical, obligation). Word order: 'sollte' precedes the noun phrase; complements or infinitives follow as required (e.g., 'Er sollte eine eigene Firma gründen').
target_language_example: Das sollte eine Überraschung bleiben.
native_language_example: That should remain a surprise.

meaning: 'should' + accusative indefinite article (used to recommend or suggest someone/something in the masculine or neuter singular)
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollte' (conditional/polite suggestion from 'sollen') with the masculine/neuter accusative article 'einen'. Followed by a masculine or neuter singular noun (einen Privatdetektiv, einen Arzt, einen Fachmann). For feminine nouns use 'sollte eine' and for plural 'sollten ...' or other plural determiners. Commonly used to give advice, make recommendations, or express what would be appropriate or expected.
target_language_example: Denkst du jetzt vielleicht, ich sollte einen Privatdetektiv darauf ansetzen?
native_language_example: Do you perhaps think now that I should set a private detective on it?

meaning: should/might do something; ought to do something (with 'etwas' = something).
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'sollte' (conditional/polite form of 'sollen') with 'etwas' (something). Used to express advice, expectation, duty, or a hypothetical possibility that someone ought to do something or that something ought to have a certain quality. Context determines nuance (recommendation, mild obligation, or hypothetical).
target_language_example: Ich sollte etwas tun, bevor es zu spät ist.
native_language_example: I should do something before it's too late.

meaning: should go / ought to go (obligation or recommendation; can be tentative).
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' in the subjunctive/polite past form 'sollte' with the verb 'gehen' (to go). Used to give advice, express an opinion that someone ought to leave or go somewhere, or say you yourself ought to leave. Can be stronger or weaker depending on context and tone. For present-time recommendations English speakers often use 'should'.
target_language_example: Ich sollte gehen, sonst verpass' ich den Bus.
native_language_example: I should go, otherwise I'll miss the bus.

meaning: should be here / ought to be here; 'should' + location marker
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollte' (past subjunctive / polite conditional of 'sollen') with 'hier' (here). Used to express expectation, recommendation, or that something ought to happen at this place. Context decides meaning: recommendation/advice (e.g. 'one should not make noise here') or expectation that a person or thing is present ('he should be here' = I expect him to be here). Tone can be neutral, polite, or frustrated depending on context and punctuation.
target_language_example: Die Ärztin sollte hier in zehn Minuten sein.
native_language_example: The doctor should be here in ten minutes.

meaning: 'should him' — modal verb 'sollte' (conditional/subjunctive of sollen) + accusative pronoun 'ihn' meaning 'him' (or 'it' for masculine nouns). Used to express recommendation, obligation, or expectation regarding a male person/masculine object.
additional_notes: 'sollte' is the Konjunktiv II / conditional form of 'sollen' used for polite suggestions, recommendations, or hypothetical obligations. 'Ihn' is the accusative singular masculine pronoun. Word order depends on clause type: in main clauses the finite verb precedes the subject (e.g., 'Ich sollte ihn...'), and in clauses with an infinitive the object may appear before the infinitive (e.g., 'Ich sollte ihn verklagen'). Can appear with impersonal 'man' (e.g., 'Man sollte ihn festnehmen').
target_language_example: Ich sollte ihn verklagen.
native_language_example: I should sue him.

meaning: should always / ought to always
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollte' (conditional of 'sollen' = should/ought to) with 'immer' (always). Used to give general advice, recommendations, or express what is desirable or expected. Tone is polite or general — less forceful than 'soll' or 'muss'. Use with infinitive verb or passive constructions.
target_language_example: Man sollte immer ehrlich sein.
native_language_example: One should always be honest.

meaning: should (do something sometime soon); ought to (maybe) — suggests something is advisable, overdue, or worth considering
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb sollte (polite conditional of sollen) with the colloquial particle mal (meaning 'sometime', 'once', or as a softening filler). Used to give suggestions, express that something ought to be done, or indicate it's about time to do it. Tone is typically mild, tentative, or polite; common in informal to neutral speech. Often followed by an infinitive clause (e.g., 'gebügelt werden', 'etwas lernen', 'zu ihr hingehen und sie ansprechen').
target_language_example: Dieses Hemd sollte mal gebügelt werden.
native_language_example: This shirt should be ironed sometime.

meaning: 'should (do) more' — expresses a recommendation or advice to increase an action or behavior.
additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive/conditional form of 'sollen' (sollte) to give polite advice or state what is advisable. Often followed by a verb (infinitive) or a phrase describing the action to be increased. Can be used with personal pronouns (Ich sollte mehr lernen) or impersonal 'man' (Man sollte mehr zuhören). Tone can be neutral or polite; context determines formality.
target_language_example: Ich sollte mehr lernen.
native_language_example: I should study more.

meaning: should ... me
additional_notes: A compositional phrase: sollte usually means "should," and mir is the dative form of ich. Depending on the verb, mir can be translated as "me" or "to me" (Er sollte mir helfen = "He should help me"; Er sollte mir dankbar sein = "He should be grateful to me"). In reflexive/body-part expressions, mir is part of the German structure and may not appear directly in English: Ich sollte mir die Haare waschen = "I should wash my hair."
target_language_example: Sie sollte mir glauben.
native_language_example: She should believe me.

meaning: should (talk/consult/meet with) — expresses a recommendation or suggestion to do something together with or to consult someone.
additional_notes: Used with a person or role introduced by 'mit' (e.g. mit seinem Anwalt, mit dir, mit Ihnen). 'Sollte' is the conditional/subjunctive of 'sollen' and softens the advice (should/ought to). Often followed by verbs like sprechen, reden, Kontakt aufnehmen, nach ... gehen. For formal suggestions use 'Sie sollten mit...' or 'Sie sollten mit ... sprechen'.
target_language_example: Er sollte mit seinem Rechtsanwalt sprechen.
native_language_example: He should speak with his lawyer.

meaning: 'should (go/come/be transferred) to' — expresses a recommendation, expectation, or conditional obligation toward going/coming/being sent to a place.
additional_notes: Used with a person subject and a destination introduced by nach. 'sollte' is the subjunctive/polite/weak past form of 'sollen' and can soften advice ("you should..."), express what someone is expected or supposed to do, or report a past obligation/expectation. Context and intonation determine whether it functions as a recommendation ("you should go"), a tentative suggestion ("should I go?"), or a past expectation/assignment ("he was supposed to be transferred to").
target_language_example: Ich denke, ich sollte nach Boston gehen.
native_language_example: I think I should go to Boston.

meaning: 'should never' — advice or recommendation that something must not be done.
additional_notes: Used to give general advice or warnings. Often appears with 'man' (one/people) for general rules, or with a personal pronoun (ich, du) to give advice about oneself or someone else. 'Sollte' is the subjunctive form of 'sollen' and makes the recommendation softer than an imperative; 'nie' means 'never'.
target_language_example: Man sollte nie ungeprüfte Links anklicken.
native_language_example: One should never click on unverified links.

meaning: should (ought to) his/its (modal 'sollte' + possessive 'seine').
additional_notes: This is the conditional/polite form of 'sollen' (sollte = should/ought to) followed by the feminine/plural/neuter accusative/dative possessive 'seine' depending on context. It expresses recommendation, moral duty, expectation, or polite suggestion about something belonging to 'him' or 'it' (or 'their' in some contexts). The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows: e.g. 'sollte seine Eltern ehren' = should honor his parents; 'sollte seine Party absagen' = should cancel his party. Use 'sollte' for softer advice or reported expectation.
target_language_example: Er sollte seine Hausaufgaben jetzt machen.
native_language_example: He should do his homework now.

meaning: should / ought to (followed by an infinitive or noun phrase introduced by 'zu' indicating purpose or direction)
additional_notes: "sollte" is the subjunctive II (Konjunktiv II) or preterite form used for polite recommendations or hypothetical suggestions; when combined with "zu" it often introduces an infinitive construction (sollte zu + Infinitiv) meaning 'should [do something]' or can precede a noun indicating something that should be 'for' or 'to' (e.g. 'sollte zu mehr Diskussion führen' = 'should lead to more discussion'). Word order and exact meaning depend on the verb/phrase that follows. For simple advice, you can also use 'sollte' alone with an infinitive clause ('Du solltest mehr üben').
target_language_example: Das neue Gesetz sollte zu besseren Bedingungen führen.
native_language_example: The new law should lead to better conditions.

meaning: you should (formal) + your ... — polite advice addressing 'Sie' (formal you) about something belonging to the listener.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollten' (conditional of 'sollen' = should/ought to) with the formal possessive 'Ihre' (your). Use 'Sie sollten Ihre ...' to give polite recommendations or instructions to someone you address formally. Word order: 'Sie sollten Ihre [Sache] [Verb/Infinitive/Verb phrase]'.
target_language_example: Sie sollten Ihre Versicherungspolice überprüfen.
native_language_example: You should check your insurance policy.

meaning: should + followed by a prepositional phrase with 'auf' — expresses recommendation or obligation regarding an action or relation introduced by 'auf' (e.g., listen to, wait for, stand on, take care of).
additional_notes: This combines the modal verb 'sollen' in its subjunctive/conditional polite form 'sollten' with the preposition 'auf'. The precise meaning depends on the verb or noun phrase that follows 'auf' and the case required (often accusative or dative). 'Sollten auf' appears in constructions like 'auf jemanden hören' (listen to someone), 'auf jemanden warten' (wait for someone), 'auf etwas/jemanden aufpassen' (take care of something/someone), 'auf der Bühne stehen' (stand on the stage). Using 'sollten' makes it a suggestion or mild obligation (should/ought to).
target_language_example: Kinder sollten auf ihre Eltern hören.
native_language_example: Children should listen to their parents.

meaning: should (we/you/they) + a/an — suggests a recommendation to do something involving a singular noun.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' (in the past subjunctive/plural present polite form 'sollten') with the indefinite article 'eine'. Used to give advice or suggest doing something that involves a single, feminine or grammatically feminine noun (e.g. Pause, Diät, Medaille, Pizza). The subject (ich/wir/sie) determines who is advised. For polite suggestions use 'Sie sollten ...' (formal you) or 'wir sollten ...' (let's). Change the article for other genders/cases: 'einen' (masculine accusative), 'ein' (neuter).
target_language_example: Wir sollten eine Reise planen.
native_language_example: We should plan a trip.

meaning: should go / ought to go (suggestion or advice to leave)
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'sollen' in the conditional/plural form 'sollten' plus the infinitive 'gehen'. Used to give polite suggestions, advice, or to say someone ought to leave. Subject (ich, wir, sie, Sie, etc.) determines who should go. Can be softened with 'ich denke' or 'ich finde' as in the examples.
target_language_example: Wir sollten gehen, wenn es schon spät wird.
native_language_example: We should go if it's getting late.

meaning: should go into / should be put into (into + masculine/neuter noun in accusative with definite article contracted: in das → ins)
additional_notes: This is the conditional/plural form of 'sollen' (sollten = should) followed by 'ins' (= in + das). Use to say someone/something should go into or be put into a place (e.g. ins Haus, ins Krankenhaus, ins Gefängnis). Context determines whether it's movement (we should go into the house) or recommendation/judgment (they should be put in prison). For feminine nouns 'in die' and plural 'in die' are used; for masculine 'in den'.
target_language_example: Wir sollten ins Haus gehen, bevor es regnet.
native_language_example: We should go into the house before it rains.

meaning: 'should' (recommendation) + 'with' — used to advise doing something together or using something; literally 'should with'.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' in the conditional/polite form 'sollten' (we/you/they should) with the preposition 'mit' (with). Use to suggest an action that involves someone/something else (e.g. go with someone, travel by some means). Word order: 'sollten mit' is followed by the person/thing in dative (mit + dative) or by the instrument/means. Polite and common for giving advice.
target_language_example: Wir sollten mit dem Auto fahren.
native_language_example: We should go by car.

meaning: 'should not' (polite/modal negative advice or recommendation).
additional_notes: Used with Sie/du/er/etc. plus an infinitive to give advice, a warning, or express that something is not recommended. 'Sollten' is the subjunctive/polite form of 'sollen' (should). For direct advice you can also use 'du solltest nicht' (informal) or 'Sie sollten nicht' (formal).
target_language_example: Sie sollten nicht so spät nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: You should not go home so late.

meaning: should (you formal / she / they) — conditional/indicative modal form of 'sollen' used to give advice, express expectation or obligation
additional_notes: Capitalization matters: 'Sie' (formal you) vs 'sie' (she/they). Word order and meaning depend on context. In questions or subordinate clauses the verb may precede the subject (e.g., 'Sollten Sie...'). Tone can range from polite suggestion to strong judgment depending on sentence. The phrase itself is compositional: 'sollten' (should) + pronoun 'sie'.
target_language_example: Ich denke, Sie sollten sie fragen.
native_language_example: I think you should ask her/them.

meaning: you should (better) / you'd better
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'solltest' (you should) with 'besser' to express a stronger recommendation or warning—equivalent to English 'you'd better' or 'you should (really)'. Often followed by an infinitive or advice clause. Can be used with negation (e.g. 'solltest besser nicht...'). Tone ranges from friendly advice to firm warning depending on context.
target_language_example: Du solltest besser früher losgehen, sonst verpasst du den Zug.
native_language_example: You'd better leave earlier, otherwise you'll miss the train.

meaning: you should (your) — advising someone to do something concerning 'your' + noun.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'solltest' (2nd person singular conditional of 'sollen') with the possessive 'deine' (feminine/plural accusative or nominative depending on the noun). Use to give advice or recommendations about something that belongs to the listener (e.g., deine Zeit, deine Augen, deine Eltern). Change 'deine' to the correct possessive form for other genders/cases (dein, deinen, deinem, etc.). Verb following is usually in the infinitive (e.g., solltest ... nicht verschwenden, solltest ... senken).
target_language_example: Du solltest deine Hausaufgaben nicht vergessen.
native_language_example: You should not forget your homework.

meaning: you should not (do something) — advice telling someone not to do an action
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' in the 2nd person singular conditional ('du solltest') with the reflexive pronoun 'dich' and negation 'nicht'. Used to give gentle advice or a warning not to do something. Followed by a reflexive or other verb phrase: e.g. 'auf andere verlassen', 'aufregen', 'über jemanden lustig machen'.
target_language_example: Du solltest dich nicht über seine Fehler lustig machen.
native_language_example: You should not make fun of his mistakes.

meaning: you should (do something) with / you should talk with / you should use (with)
additional_notes: Combines the conditional/modal verb 'solltest' (should) with 'du' (you) and the preposition 'mit' (with). The exact meaning depends on the verb or noun that follows 'mit': e.g. 'mit ihm reden' = 'talk with him', 'mit einer Waffe umgehen' = 'handle/use a weapon', 'mit der Straßenbahn fahren' = 'go by tram'. Common in suggestions: 'Vielleicht solltest du mit ...' = 'Maybe you should ...'.
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltest du mit deinem Chef darüber reden.
native_language_example: Maybe you should talk about it with your boss.

meaning: you should be proud
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'sollen' in the 2nd-person singular conditional ('solltest') + adjective 'stolz'. Used to tell someone they deserve pride or to praise them. Common in sentences like 'Du solltest stolz sein' (You should be proud). Can be softened with 'wirklich' or strengthened with 'auf dich'.
target_language_example: Du solltest stolz auf dich sein.
native_language_example: You should be proud of yourself.

meaning: you should try (to ...).
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb 'solltest' (second person singular conditional/recommendation of 'sollen') and the verb 'versuchen' (to try). Used to give advice or a suggestion about attempting something. Followed by an infinitive clause with 'zu' (e.g. 'versuchen, ... zu + Infinitiv') or by an object/verb phrase.
target_language_example: Du solltest versuchen, öfter spazieren zu gehen.
native_language_example: You should try to go for walks more often.

meaning: you should (probably); expresses advice or mild recommendation with some uncertainty
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'solltest' (you should) with the particle 'wohl' which softens the advice or suggests the speaker thinks it's likely/appropriate. Use for giving suggestions or implying someone is expected to do something. Tone: polite/mild; not very strong or urgent. Often followed by an infinitive clause (…machen, …sagen, …nachdenken).
target_language_example: Du solltest wohl noch einmal darüber nachdenken.
native_language_example: You should probably think about it once more.

meaning: you (plural, informal) should (do something) — recommendation or advice directed at 'ihr' with a reflexive object.
additional_notes: Combines the modal verb 'sollen' in the conditional/plural form 'solltet' with the reflexive pronoun 'euch' (yourselves). Used to give advice or suggest actions to a group you address as 'ihr'. The verb that follows may be reflexive (sich entschuldigen, sich ausruhen) or take another object/phrase. Equivalent English: 'you should (yourselves) ...' or simply 'you should ...' when addressing several people informally.
target_language_example: Ihr solltet euch mehr Zeit nehmen.
native_language_example: You (plural) should take more time.

meaning: but rather in / instead in (used to correct a previous negative statement by giving the correct location or place)
additional_notes: Used after a negation (often following nicht) with 'sondern' to contrast and provide the correct information; when specifying a place, 'in' introduces the location (e.g. 'in der Mannschaft', 'in Paris'). Word order: negation ... nicht ..., sondern in + noun/place. Useful for correcting where someone or something is.
target_language_example: Er war nicht im Büro, sondern in der Bibliothek.
native_language_example: He wasn't in the office, but rather in the library.

meaning: otherwise (then) can / otherwise (then) be able to
additional_notes: Used to introduce a consequence or alternative: 'sonst' = 'otherwise' or 'if not'; 'kann' is the modal verb 'can'. Often used at the start of a clause to warn that something won't be possible unless a condition is met. Word order: 'Sonst kann ich ...' = 'Otherwise I can't ...'. Also appears in questions like 'Wie sonst kann man...?' = 'How else can one...?'
target_language_example: Gib mir die Unterlagen, sonst kann ich nicht unterschreiben.
native_language_example: Give me the documents, otherwise I can't sign.

meaning: “otherwise you will” or “or else you will” — a warning about a negative consequence.
additional_notes: Common in warnings or advice. 'Sonst' means 'otherwise'/'or else'; 'kommst' is the 2nd-person singular of 'kommen' (to come/get). Together they introduce the consequence that will happen if the previous instruction isn't followed. Often followed by phrases like 'zu spät' (too late) or 'nicht weiter' (won't get further). Can appear at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Fahr langsamer, sonst kommst du nicht sicher an.
native_language_example: Drive more slowly, otherwise you won't arrive safely.

meaning: nothing else; otherwise nothing
additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more beyond what was mentioned. Can appear after a verb phrase (e.g. 'ich habe sonst nichts ...') or as a short question/response meaning 'anything else? / nothing else?'. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Hast du noch Fragen, oder sonst nichts?
native_language_example: Do you have any more questions, or nothing else?

meaning: no one else; otherwise nobody
additional_notes: Used to say that nobody other than the person(s) mentioned does or would do something. Often follows verbs and refers to situations where an action is unique to someone. Can be translated as "no one else," "nobody else," or "otherwise nobody."
target_language_example: Tom übernahm die Aufgaben, die sonst niemand übernehmen wollte.
native_language_example: Tom took on the tasks that nobody else wanted to take on.

meaning: anything else
additional_notes: Used to ask if there is anything more or anyone/something additional. Often follows a question word or subject (e.g., "Ist da sonst noch irgendwas?" = "Is there anything else?"). Can be used with people ("Wer ist sonst noch?" = "Who else is there?") or things/actions. Polite and common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Möchtest du sonst noch etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like anything else to drink?

meaning: to be elsewhere / to be otherwise; used in questions/statements to mean 'else' or 'otherwise' (e.g. 'where else/what else it could be').
additional_notes: Commonly used with question words (wo, wer, was) or in hypotheticals. Often appears as 'wo sollte er sonst sein?' = 'where else should he be?' or 'was es sonst sein könnte' = 'what else it could be'. Not a fixed idiom with a single translation — translate according to context as 'else', 'otherwise', or 'somewhere/somebody else'.
target_language_example: Wo sollte ich sonst sein?
native_language_example: Where else should I be?

meaning: anything else / something else / who knows what (depends on context).
additional_notes: Informal phrase with flexible meaning: 1) In questions like 'Einen Drink oder sonst was?' it means 'or something else' / 'or whatever else'. 2) In expressions like 'Er wäre zu sonst was fähig' it means 'he'd be capable of who knows what' (implying extreme or unspecified actions). 3) As a short question 'Sonst was?' it asks 'Anything else?' or 'Anything more?'. Tone is conversational; choose meaning from context.
target_language_example: Willst du Kaffee, Tee oder sonst was?
native_language_example: Do you want coffee, tea, or something else?

meaning: someone else; anybody else
additional_notes: Used to refer to some other person (not the one just mentioned). Often appears in questions or negative sentences: e.g. 'Ist sonst wer da?' = 'Is anyone else there?'. Can be informal/neutral. Word order: 'sonst wer' or 'wer sonst' (both common).
target_language_example: Ist sonst wer im Büro?
native_language_example: Is anyone else in the office?

meaning: 'otherwise' or 'or else' used to introduce a negative consequence (followed by a verb in future or modal construction).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in warnings or advice: first clause gives instruction or condition, then 'sonst wird' + consequence. 'Wird' is the 3rd-person singular of 'werden' (future/passive). The consequence can be a future event (will...) or a passive result (will be ...). English equivalents: 'otherwise', 'or else', 'if not, (then)'.
target_language_example: Beeil dich, sonst wird das Paket nicht rechtzeitig ankommen.
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise the package won't arrive on time.

meaning: 'I worry' or 'I am worried' (from 'sich sorgen' = to worry/about).
additional_notes: This is the first-person present of the reflexive verb 'sich sorgen' often used with 'um' + person/thing (e.g. 'sorgen um jemanden') to say you worry about someone/something. More common in everyday German is 'sich Sorgen machen' (e.g. 'Ich mache mir Sorgen'). Word order in a full sentence: 'Ich sorge mich (um ...).' Can be followed by adverbs: 'zu sehr', 'nie', 'wahrscheinlich'.
target_language_example: Ich sorge mich um meine Schwester.
native_language_example: I worry about my sister.

meaning: 'to take care of', 'to provide for', or 'to ensure (something happens)'
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun as object. Can mean caring for a person (look after), providing something (ensure supply), or causing/ensuring that something happens. Common constructions: 'für jemanden/etwas sorgen' (take care of someone/something) and 'dafür sorgen, dass ...' (make sure that ...).
target_language_example: Kannst du heute für die Pflanzen sorgen? — Ich werde dafür sorgen, dass alles rechtzeitig vorbereitet ist.
native_language_example: Can you take care of the plants today? — I'll make sure that everything is prepared on time.

meaning: 'when the time comes' / 'when it's time'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future point or situation when something should happen or be revealed. Often appears in the phrase 'wenn es soweit ist' meaning 'when the time comes'. Can also be used in short answers like 'Soweit ist es mit mir.' ('That's as far as I am' / 'That's it for me').
target_language_example: Wenn es soweit ist, ruf mich an.
native_language_example: When the time comes, call me.

meaning: as far as I know; to my knowledge
additional_notes: Used to show that the speaker is giving information based on what they know (not 100% certain). Often placed at the start or mid-sentence. Can soften statements or express uncertainty.
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, hat sie noch nicht die Prüfung bestanden.
native_language_example: As far as I know, she has not passed the exam yet.

meaning: to be ready/finished; to have reached a certain point or stage (in progress).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is ready, completed, or that one has arrived at a particular stage or moment. Common in expressions like "Ich bin soweit" (I'm ready) or "Wenn es soweit ist" (When the time comes). Can refer both to personal readiness and to the progression of events.
target_language_example: Ich bin soweit, alles ist fertig; soweit sein bedeutet, dass man bereit ist.
native_language_example: I'm ready, everything is finished; 'to be soweit' means you're prepared.

meaning: sowieso = anyway / in any case; 'zu' = too / (followed by adjective) too (e.g. too old).
additional_notes: This pair appears in two common uses: 1) 'sowieso' as an adverb meaning 'anyway/in any case' (often used alone before a clause: 'Es ist sowieso zu spät' = 'It's too late anyway'). 2) when 'zu' precedes an adjective, it means 'too (adjective)' (e.g. 'zu alt' = 'too old'). In examples the two can appear together (e.g. 'Du bist sowieso zu alt...') but they are separate words with their usual functions. 'Sowieso' emphasizes that something will/would happen regardless or is already the case.
target_language_example: Das Konzert ist abgesagt, und wir wären sowieso zu spät gekommen.
native_language_example: The concert is canceled, and we would have been too late anyway.

meaning: part of the correlative 'sowohl ... als auch' = 'both ... and' (used to list two items).
additional_notes: This fragment pairs with 'als auch' (usually completed as 'sowohl ... als auch') to connect two things or languages: 'sowohl A als auch B' = 'both A and B'. Word order: both items follow the respective parts. Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Er spricht sowohl Englisch als auch Spanisch.
native_language_example: He speaks both English and Spanish.

meaning: social media platform (literally: social medium)
additional_notes: Used to refer to a social-media service or platform (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). In German, the singular 'Medium' is neuter: 'das soziale Medium'. More commonly you will hear the plural 'soziale Medien' to talk about social media in general.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Profil auf einem sozialen Medium erstellt.
native_language_example: I created a new profile on a social media platform.

meaning: I like to play / I enjoy playing
additional_notes: Combines the verb spielen (to play) with the adverb gerne (gladly/with pleasure) to express that the speaker enjoys doing an activity. Conjugate spielen to match the subject (ich spiele, du spielst, er spielt, wir spielen, etc.). In English you can translate it as 'I like to play' or 'I enjoy playing'.
target_language_example: Ich spiele gerne Gitarre mit meinen Freunden.
native_language_example: I like to play guitar with my friends.

meaning: 'play with' (literal) / 'to entertain the idea of' (idiomatic)
additional_notes: Most commonly means 'play with' in the physical/symbolic sense (e.g., play with someone or something). In some contexts, especially with 'mit dem Gedanken spielen', it is an idiom meaning 'to contemplate' or 'to be thinking about' doing something. Conjugated form here is first person singular present ('ich spiele') + preposition 'mit'.
target_language_example: Ich spiele mit dem Gedanken, ins Ausland zu gehen.
native_language_example: I'm considering the idea of going abroad.
