target_language_example: Sie sammelte die Bücher um sich.
native_language_example: She gathered the books around her.

meaning: 'which' or 'about which' used to ask for specific information about a person, thing, time, cost, etc.
additional_notes: Often appears in questions with 'es handelt sich (um...)' or verbs asking for details. Follows the preposition 'um' and agrees with the gender/number of the noun that follows (welche/welcher/welches). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Um welche Veranstaltung handelt es sich?
native_language_example: Which event is it?

meaning: around what time / at what time (approximate)
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something happens or is expected to happen. Often asks for an approximate time (around when). Common in spoken and written German. Can be followed by a verb or subject (e.g., "bringst du...", "wird... ankommen?").
target_language_example: Um welche Zeit beginnt der Film?
native_language_example: Around what time does the movie start?

meaning: 'by how much' (asks for the amount of change/difference)
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask how much something changes, increases, decreases, or differs (e.g., price, time, temperature, score). Often followed by verbs like steigen (to rise), sinken (to fall), ändern (to change), or a number/unit. Can be used with 'ist' or with a future/auxiliary: 'Wird der Preis um wie viel steigen?'.
target_language_example: Der Preis steigt — um wie viel?
native_language_example: The price is going up — by how much?

meaning: 'at what time' (asks for a specific clock time).
additional_notes: Common question phrase used to ask when something happens or is scheduled. Use it with verbs in different tenses or with modal verbs. Formal and informal forms: same phrase works with du, ihr, Sie. Often followed by a verb or time expression (e.g., um wie viel Uhr beginnt der Film?).
target_language_example: Um wie viel Uhr beginnt der Film?
native_language_example: At what time does the movie start?

meaning: at what time
additional_notes: Common question phrase used to ask for a specific clock time. Polite/formal version uses Sie; du is informal. Can be shortened in speech to "wieviel Uhr" or "um wie viel Uhr" (spacing varies). Often used with verbs of coming, leaving, meeting, eating, etc.
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr treffen wir uns morgen?
native_language_example: At what time are we meeting tomorrow?

meaning: used to ask at what time someone is (doing something) — part of a question like 'um wieviel Uhr bist du da?' (At what time will you be there?).
additional_notes: This fragment isn't a complete sentence on its own; it's normally followed by a place or an activity (e.g. 'bist du hier', 'bist du fertig', 'bist du in Berlin'). 'wieviel' is a variant of 'wie viel' (how much/how many) used in time questions. Common full questions: 'Um wieviel Uhr bist du da?' or more simply 'Um wie viel Uhr bist du da?'.
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr bist du im Büro?
native_language_example: At what time are you in the office?

meaning: A sequence where a verb with 'um' (part of separable verb or preposition) is followed by 'du'—here examples show either separable verbs ('umdrehen', 'umziehen') or the verb phrase 'bringen ... um' (to kill) plus the address 'du' (you).
additional_notes: This input shows two different uses of 'um' in German sentences: 1) as the prefix of separable verbs (umdrehen = turn around; umziehen = change clothes) where 'um' appears separately in sentence position before the object or at the end; and 2) as part of the separable verb construction 'jemanden umbringen' (to kill someone) where 'um' appears after the object or at the end in finite forms. The examples also include strong insults addressed to 'du' (informal 'you'). Warning: sentences 2–3 are violent and offensive language. For learners: pay attention to word order with separable verbs (the prefix goes to the end in main clauses) and the informal pronoun 'du' is familiar/possibly rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Dreh dich um, du Spassvogel!
native_language_example: Turn around, you joker!

meaning: for money / in order to get money (to earn, make, withdraw, etc.)
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or verb phrase to express purpose or goal related to money. Often appears as 'um ... zu ...' (e.g. 'um Geld zu verdienen' = 'in order to earn money') or in shortened contexts like 'um Geld' + verb earlier/later in the sentence. Can refer to earning, making, withdrawing, or showing money depending on context.
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet abends, um Geld zu verdienen.
native_language_example: She works in the evenings to earn money.

meaning: to you
additional_notes: A combination of the preposition 'um' used with an infinitive clause (um ... zu + verb) meaning 'in order to' or indicating purpose, plus the formal dative pronoun 'Ihnen' ('to you'). In many contexts it appears as part of 'um Ihnen zu sagen' = 'to tell you'. 'Ihnen' is the polite (formal) 'you' in German. If speaking informally to friends/family, 'Ihnen' would be replaced with 'dir'.
target_language_example: Ich rufe an, um Ihnen mitzuteilen, dass der Termin bestätigt ist.
native_language_example: I'm calling to inform you that the appointment is confirmed.

meaning: 'in order to (your...)' — used to introduce the purpose of an action that involves something belonging to 'you' (formal 'Sie').
additional_notes: um ... zu + infinitive expresses purpose: 'in order to ...'. Here 'Ihre' is the formal second-person possessive (your) with a feminine/plural or capitalized noun (Sie → Ihre). Commonly followed by a noun (Ihre Frage, Ihre Akten) or by '... zu + verb' construction when the object is the thing being affected. 'Ihre' matches the gender/case of the noun that follows. For informal 'your' use 'deine' instead of 'Ihre'.
target_language_example: Um Ihre Frage zu beantworten, habe ich die Unterlagen gelesen.
native_language_example: In order to answer your question, I read the documents.

meaning: about/for (a period of) time; concerning time (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself and its meaning depends on the verb or context. Common uses: "um Zeit zu sparen" = "to save time" (equivalent to "in order to save time"); "um Zeit gewinnen" (less common) = "to buy/gain time". It can also appear in questions or statements like "Wie viel Zeit haben wir?" with different structures. Beginners will most often see it in the pattern "um + [noun] + zu + verb" meaning "in order to + verb" when referring to time (e.g. "um Zeit zu sparen").
target_language_example: Wir fahren früher los, um Zeit zu sparen.
native_language_example: We leave earlier to save time.

meaning: to be (able) to do something alone; used with an adjective + 'zu' to mean 'too ... to do something alone' or 'old/ready enough to do something alone'.
additional_notes: Appears after an adjective + 'zu' (e.g. 'zu jung', 'groß genug') to indicate doing an action without help or company. Common pattern: '[Adjective] + zu + um + allein + zu + [Infinitive]'. 'allein' here means 'alone' (by oneself).
target_language_example: Sie ist alt genug, um allein nach Berlin zu fahren.
native_language_example: She is old enough to travel to Berlin alone.

meaning: 'in order to be/attend/participate with' (indicates purpose + being/being present at someone/something).
additional_notes: Combines the purpose marker um ... zu (in order to) with bei (at/with). Often appears as part of an infinitive purpose clause: um bei + dative noun + zu + verb or sometimes with a following noun/verb omitted in colloquial speech. Use bei when the action means being present at, staying with, attending, or participating alongside someone/something. Example 5 shows a shortened, emotional use ('and to be with you').
target_language_example: Ich fahre nach Berlin, um bei der Familie zu sein.
native_language_example: I'm going to Berlin in order to be with the family.

meaning: in order to finish/complete (something); to have time to finish it
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase "(Zeit) haben, um damit fertig zu werden" meaning "to have (time) to finish it." "damit" refers to a task or thing mentioned earlier. Common in time-related questions or statements about deadlines. The full infinitive phrase is "um damit fertig zu werden."
target_language_example: Haben wir genug Zeit, um damit fertig zu werden?
native_language_example: Do we have enough time to finish that?

meaning: used with verbs to mean 'in order to (do) about that' or more naturally 'to (do) about it/that' — often part of phrases like 'um darüber nachzudenken' (to think about it) or 'um darüber zu reden' (to talk about it).
additional_notes: um ... zu + verb is a common German infinitive clause meaning 'in order to' or simply 'to' (do something). Darüber refers back to something previously mentioned (about that/it). Together they introduce an action concerning that topic: e.g. um darüber nachzudenken = to think about it; um darüber hinwegzukommen = to get over it. In many contexts English drops 'in order' and just uses 'to'.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um darüber nachzudenken.
native_language_example: I need time to think about it.

meaning: introduces a purpose/result clause: 'in order to' or 'to (do) that' / 'so that'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause (often with 'zu' + infinitive) or to refer back to something previously mentioned (das). Common in constructions expressing purpose, result, or intention: 'um ... zu + infinitive' (e.g. 'um das zu verstehen' = 'in order to understand that'). Word order: 'um' + object/pronoun ('das') + 'zu' + verb (infinitive).
target_language_example: Sie lernt viel, um das Prüfungsergebnis zu verbessern.
native_language_example: She studies a lot in order to improve the exam result.

meaning: part of a purpose or result clause: 'in order to (your/your...)' or 'so that (your...)' / used in constructions meaning 'to ... your (something)'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the preposition 'um' + accusative pronoun 'dein' (your). Commonly appears in infinitive clauses with 'um ... zu' (to/in order to) or in expressions of result/ability like 'zu ... um dein ... zu ...' (too ... to ... your ...). Word order and surrounding verbs determine exact meaning. 'dein' may change (deinen/deine/deines) to match the gender/case of the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ich spare Geld, um dein Geschenk zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I'm saving money in order to buy your present.

meaning: in order to (the) / to (the)
additional_notes: Combines the subordinating preposition 'um' + dative article 'dem'. 'um ... zu' expresses purpose: 'in order to' or 'to' do something. Here 'dem' is the dative masculine/neuter article or demonstrative pronoun ('the' or 'that') referring to a noun mentioned or understood from context (e.g. dem Chor, dem Regen, dem Ende, dem König, dem Sonar). Examples show 'um ... zu' where the verb comes at the end of the clause (e.g. um dem Chor beitreten zu können — in order to be able to join the choir). Also appears in set phrases like 'um dem Regen zu entgehen' (to avoid the rain). Literal translation is possible when you keep 'in order to' + 'the'.
target_language_example: Um dem Zug nicht zu verpassen, laufen wir schneller.
native_language_example: In order not to miss the train, we run faster.

meaning: in order to (pass) the exam / for the exam
additional_notes: Usually part of a purpose clause: 'um ... zu + infinitive' = 'in order to ...'. Here 'um die Prüfung zu bestehen/zu schaffen' means to achieve the goal of passing the exam. 'bestehen' and 'schaffen' both mean 'pass' (slightly different nuance: 'bestehen' = succeed/pass; 'schaffen' = manage/do it).
target_language_example: Ich lerne jeden Tag, um die Prüfung zu bestehen.
native_language_example: I study every day in order to pass the exam.

meaning: to (do) this / in order to (do) this (followed by a noun or verb phrase).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose or intent. Often appears after a time/amount phrase and before a noun or verb phrase (e.g., 'um diese Aufgabe zu lösen' = 'to solve this task'). 'Diese' agrees in gender/number with the noun it refers to. Common structure: [time/amount] + ... + 'um' + 'diese(n/ )' + [noun/infinitive clause with 'zu'].
target_language_example: Wir haben nur fünf Minuten, um diese Aufgabe zu erledigen.
native_language_example: We only have five minutes to finish this task.

meaning: in order to (do something) for this book / to [verb] this book (purpose with 'um ... zu').
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'um dieses Buch' used with the infinitive construction 'um ... zu + verb' to express purpose: 'in order to [verb] this book' or 'to [verb] this book'. Word order can place 'um dieses Buch' at the start or in the middle of the sentence. The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows (e.g., kaufen = to buy, lesen = to read).
target_language_example: Ich lerne viel Deutsch, um dieses Buch zu lesen.
native_language_example: I'm studying a lot of German in order to read this book.

meaning: to be honest / honestly speaking
additional_notes: Used to introduce a frank or candid statement; often placed at the start of a sentence (Um ehrlich zu sein, ...) but can appear later. Tone ranges from neutral honesty to mild criticism or confession. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Um ehrlich zu sein, habe ich den Termin vergessen.
native_language_example: To be honest, I forgot the appointment.

meaning: in order to get some fresh air; to (go) for fresh air.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like gehen, schnappen, treten (e.g., 'gehen, um frische Luft zu schnappen') to explain purpose — you went outside to breathe/refresh yourself. Structure: 'um' + infinitive phrase ('um ... zu' = 'in order to ...').
target_language_example: Ich gehe kurz auf den Balkon, um frische Luft zu schnappen.
native_language_example: I'll step onto the balcony for some fresh air.

meaning: for my / in order to (do something) with my...
additional_notes: Combines the preposition 'um' (used in purpose clauses: 'um ... zu' = 'in order to') with the possessive pronoun 'mein' (my). Often appears in sentences like 'um mein X zu VERB' (to [verb] my X) or in short phrases 'um mein Leben ...' Context decides translation: either 'in order to (use) my...' or simply 'for my...' Note word order: in purpose clause you normally have 'um ... zu' surrounding the verb infinitive (e.g. 'um mein Haar ... zu binden').
target_language_example: Ich spare Geld, um mein Auto reparieren zu lassen.
native_language_example: I'm saving money in order to have my car repaired.

meaning: to (in order) to + with — used to indicate purpose involving speaking or doing something together with someone (often 'in order to [do something] with').
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of an infinitive purpose clause: 'um ... zu' + verb; when someone is the person you interact with, 'mit' introduces that person (e.g. 'um mit ihm zu sprechen' = 'in order to speak with him'). In many sentences the full pattern is 'um + [person] + zu + [Infinitiv]'. In casual speech the order can vary (e.g. 'Tom kommt, um mit uns zu sprechen').
target_language_example: Sie ruft an, um mit dir zu reden.
native_language_example: She is calling in order to talk with you.

meaning: in order to (do something) with you / to (do something) together with you
additional_notes: This phrase combines the purpose marker 'um ... zu' (meaning 'in order to') with 'mit dir' ('with you'). It appears before an infinitive: 'Ich bin gekommen, um mit dir zu sprechen' = 'I came in order to speak with you.' Can be used for positive or negative purposes (e.g. not coming to fight). Word order: 'um' + (optional objects like 'mit dir') + 'zu' + infinitive. Common in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin hier, um mit dir zu lernen.
native_language_example: I'm here to study with you.

meaning: used to emphasize a following comparative phrase (English: 'all the more' / 'even more').
additional_notes: Usually appears before a comparative or consequence clause (e.g. 'umso besser', 'um so wichtiger'); can be written as one word 'umso' or two words 'um so' — both are correct and mean the same. Common in comparative constructions introduced by 'je ... umso/um so ...'. Use to say that because one thing is true, the next thing is even more true.
target_language_example: Je mehr du übst, um so besser wirst du.
native_language_example: The more you practice, the better you'll get.

meaning: in order to / to (used before a masculine or neuter noun with dative) to express purpose or direction toward a place.
additional_notes: Combination of the purpose infinitive marker 'um' + dative article 'zum' (zu + dem). Used before an infinitive clause to show purpose (um ... zu + verb) and when the destination is a masculine or neuter noun requiring dative. English often uses 'to' or 'in order to' / 'to get to'.
target_language_example: Ich nehme den Bus, um zum Bahnhof zu fahren.
native_language_example: I'll take the bus to get to the station.

meaning: 'in order to' / 'to' used with an infinitive to express purpose or result when followed by a destination with the article 'zur' (zu + der).
additional_notes: This is the combination of the purpose phrase 'um ... zu' (used with an infinitive to express purpose or result, e.g. 'um zur Schule zu gehen' = 'to go to school') and the contracted preposition+article 'zur' (zu + der). In examples it appears as 'um zur + noun + zu + Verb' when stating intent, ability, or how long it takes to get to a place. Common in sentences like 'zu ... um ... zu' (too ... to ...): 'zu jung, um zur Schule zu gehen' = 'too young to go to school.'
target_language_example: Er fährt mit dem Bus, um zur Arbeit zu kommen.
native_language_example: He takes the bus to get to work.

meaning: introduces purpose or intention with a following topic ("in order to [talk/think/etc.] about").
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of the construction "um ... zu + infinitive" when expressing purpose (e.g. "um über etwas zu sprechen" = "in order to talk about something"). In some examples it pairs with verbs like reden, sprechen, streiten. It can also appear in other contexts where "über" means "about" (topic) or "over" (spatial), but with "um ... zu" it usually signals purpose. Word order: "um" starts the purpose clause, "über" introduces the topic, and the infinitive verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Ich rufe an, um über das Treffen zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I'm calling in order to talk about the meeting.

meaning: hugged her (masculine/feminine noun depending on context) — past tense of 'umarmen' with a possessive 'ihren'.
additional_notes: Umarmte is the simple past (Präteritum) of umarmen (to hug). 'Ihren' is the accusative singular possessive for 'her' (can modify masculine or feminine nouns depending on gender and case): e.g. 'ihren Bruder' (her brother, masculine), 'ihre Mutter' would use 'ihre'. In the examples the noun following 'ihren' is the direct object being hugged. Use umarmte for narration/written past; conversational past often uses 'hat ... umarmt' (Sie hat ihren Bruder umarmt).
target_language_example: Sie umarmte ihren Freund, als sie ihn nach langer Zeit traf.
native_language_example: She hugged her boyfriend when she met him after a long time.

meaning: 'to be killed' or 'to die (as a result of something violent or accidental)'
additional_notes: Used to say someone dies, often because of an accident, disaster, war, or violent event. More formal or neutral than slang; typically describes fatal outcomes (e.g., 'Bei dem Unfall sind drei Menschen ums Leben gekommen.' = Three people died in the accident). Often used in news reports and formal contexts. You can also use the simpler verb 'sterben' for 'to die.'
target_language_example: Bei dem Feuer sind mehrere Personen ums Leben gekommen.
native_language_example: Several people lost their lives in the fire.

meaning: and (so) what... / and what... (used to ask for more information or add a punchline/contrast).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) in statements as a parenthetical: „und, was noch besser ist,“ introduces an added, often stronger positive point (like 'and what's even better'). 2) as a conversational question starter: „Und, was ...?“ asks for the next information or reaction (like 'And what (now)?' or 'So, what...?'). Common in spoken German; the comma is often written to show the slight pause.
target_language_example: Er hat das Problem gelöst und, was noch besser ist, er hat niemanden enttäuscht.
native_language_example: He solved the problem and, what’s even better, he disappointed no one.

meaning: 'and legs' (the phrase connects 'Arme und Beine' = 'arms and legs')
additional_notes: This is not an idiom by itself; it literally means 'and legs' and appears after another body part (often 'Arme und Beine' = 'arms and legs'). Used both literally (body parts, proportions) and in fixed expressions (e.g. 'Hals und Beine' in some dialects or mistakes). In German you often list body parts with 'und' between them: Arme und Beine, Kopf und Schultern, etc.
target_language_example: Seine Arme und Beine sind müde nach dem Laufen.
native_language_example: His arms and legs are tired after running.

meaning: 'and evil' used in the fixed phrase Gut und Böse meaning 'good and evil' or 'right and wrong'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as the pair 'Gut und Böse' to talk about moral opposites (good vs. evil, right vs. wrong). Can be used literally (moral judgment) or more generally (things that are good and bad). In some contexts it expresses a general notion of morality rather than specific deeds. The phrase is compositional and translates directly to 'good and evil'.
target_language_example: Man muss zwischen Gut und Böse wählen.
native_language_example: One must choose between good and evil.

meaning: 'and Dad' — used to join 'Dad' with another person (here 'Mom')
additional_notes: Common in informal spoken German, especially in families using English loanwords like 'Mom' and 'Dad' instead of German 'Mama'/'Vater'. Appears after another person (e.g., 'Mom und Dad'). Use 'und' to connect two people or items.
target_language_example: Ich komme mit Mom und Dad zum Spiel.
native_language_example: I'm coming to the game with Mom and Dad.

meaning: and German (used to add German to a list of languages or items).
additional_notes: A simple conjunction phrase: 'und' means 'and' and 'Deutsch' means 'German'. Commonly used to list languages someone speaks or understands. Word order and punctuation follow normal list rules (e.g., 'Französisch und Deutsch' or 'Französisch, Englisch und Deutsch'). In negative sentences you may see emphasis like 'und Deutsch schon gar nicht' (and certainly not German) or 'und Deutsch noch weniger' (even less German).
target_language_example: Sie lernt Spanisch und Deutsch.
native_language_example: She is learning Spanish and German.

meaning: and English.
additional_notes: A simple connector phrase: 'und' means 'and' and is used to link items in a list or two languages/skills. Here it specifically pairs another language or item with English. Useful in sentences about languages someone speaks. Word order: 'X und Englisch' = 'X and English.'
target_language_example: Ich spreche Deutsch und Englisch.
native_language_example: I speak German and English.

meaning: literally 'and colour'; used with 'Form und Farbe' to mean 'shape and colour' or more generally 'appearance, look, or outward features'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the fixed phrase 'Form und Farbe' (shape and colour) to describe the visible appearance or characteristics of something. Can be used literally (e.g. comparing two objects) or more poetically (e.g. 'a ballet of form and colour'). The last example ('nur noch Form und Farbe sein') is idiomatic: it suggests being reduced to mere appearance or only outer form remaining. 'und Farbe' alone is not commonly used without 'Form'.
target_language_example: Die beiden Bilder unterscheiden sich nur in Form und Farbe.
native_language_example: The two paintings differ only in shape and colour.

meaning: 'and thoughts' — used to pair 'thoughts' with another noun (often 'feelings').
additional_notes: A simple connector: 'und' means 'and', 'Gedanken' is plural of 'Gedanke' (thought). Commonly appears in phrases like 'Gefühle und Gedanken' (feelings and thoughts). Use when listing mental states or ideas. Word order follows normal German: noun + und + Gedanken.
target_language_example: Sie teilte ihre Gefühle und Gedanken mit mir.
native_language_example: She shared her feelings and thoughts with me.

meaning: 'and violence' — used to list 'violence' together with another noun (e.g. 'chaos and violence').
additional_notes: A simple connector phrase combining another noun with 'Gewalt' (violence). Common in statements about crime, protests, or calls to reject violence (e.g. 'Sag nein zu Hass und Gewalt' = 'Say no to hate and violence'). Tone can be formal or informal depending on context; the phrase itself is neutral. 'Gewalt' can mean physical force, brutality, or coercion.
target_language_example: Wir müssen Frieden fördern und Gewalt verhindern.
native_language_example: We must promote peace and prevent violence.

meaning: 'and God' — the conjunction 'und' (and) followed by 'Gott' (God).
additional_notes: A simple coordination: 'und Gott' joins 'God' with whatever comes before. Used in religious or everyday expressions (e.g. commands with a promise, statements about God, or literary/biblical passages). Grammar: 'und' is the coordinating conjunction 'and' and does not change case; 'Gott' is nominative here in most examples. Can appear in phrases like 'Mensch und Gott' (man and God) or in biblical style ('Und Gott sah...').
target_language_example: Arbeite, und Gott wird dir helfen.
native_language_example: Work, and God will help you.

meaning: and children / and have children (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally 'and children'. In contexts about family or life plans (like 'Kinder bekommen'), 'und Kinder' can appear as part of a larger phrase meaning 'and (have) children'. By itself it simply links 'children' to something previously mentioned (e.g., 'marriage and children').
target_language_example: Sie möchte sich niederlassen und Kinder bekommen.
native_language_example: She wants to settle down and have children.

meaning: and clothing
additional_notes: A simple phrase used after listing another item (e.g., shoes, food, money) to add 'clothing' to the list. Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., charity, retail). 'Kleidung' is an uncountable noun meaning clothes/garments. Word order: the item + 'und Kleidung'.
target_language_example: Er brachte Essen und Kleidung für die Bedürftigen.
native_language_example: He brought food and clothing for the needy.

meaning: literally "and bones"; used in the phrase "Haut und Knochen" meaning very thin, skin-and-bones.
additional_notes: You will mostly see this as part of the fixed expression "(nur) Haut und Knochen" = "(only) skin and bones," describing someone extremely thin or emaciated. Also used contrastively with living/whole bodies (e.g. ghosts: "kein Fleisch und Knochen"). Not used on its own without "Haut" in ordinary speech.
target_language_example: Nach der Krankheit war sie nur noch Haut und Knochen.
native_language_example: After the illness she was only skin and bones.

meaning: 'and tie' — used after a clothing item to mean that a tie is worn/required as well.
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a shirt or suit (e.g., 'Anzug und Krawatte', 'weißes Hemd und Krawatte') to indicate that a tie accompanies that garment or is part of a dress code. Often used in contexts about dress requirements or descriptions of appearance.
target_language_example: Er kam zur Hochzeit mit Hemd und Krawatte.
native_language_example: He came to the wedding in a shirt and tie.

meaning: 'and love' — used to connect 'love' with another noun or idea
additional_notes: A simple connector: 'und' (and) plus the noun 'Liebe' (love). Appears in phrases that pair love with another concept (e.g. 'Güte und Liebe', 'Sex und Liebe'). Useful for listing feelings, qualities, or contrasting ideas. Can be used literally or in more poetic/figurative contexts.
target_language_example: Güte und Liebe machen die Welt besser.
native_language_example: Kindness and love make the world better.

meaning: 'and Mom' or 'and Mum' (used to add 'mom' to a list or to ask about Mom)
additional_notes: Literally 'and Mom.' Commonly appears in lists (e.g., 'Dad and Mom and many guests...') or as a short question/prompt (e.g., 'And Mom?') to ask what about or where Mom is. Capitalization: 'Mama' is a noun and is capitalized in German. Use in spoken language is frequent and natural.
target_language_example: Wir gehen zur Party — und Mama?
native_language_example: We're going to the party — and Mom?

meaning: 'and milk' — used to add milk as another item or ingredient.
additional_notes: A simple conjunction phrase combining 'und' (and) with 'Milch' (milk). Common in shopping lists, recipes, or when someone offers/asks about additions to a drink (e.g., sugar und Milch). Word order follows normal German (item1 und Milch). Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Ich nehme Kaffee und Milch.
native_language_example: I'll take coffee and milk.

meaning: and mouth (used when listing body parts)
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of lists like "Nase und Mund" or "Augen, Nase und Mund". It's not a standalone idiom — it's simply the conjunction + noun used to list body parts (e.g. when describing where to wear a mask or what not to touch). Word order can vary: the noun can appear before or after the article or adjective ("weiße Maske über Nase und Mund" vs. "über Nase und Mund eine weiße Maske").
target_language_example: Trage die Maske so, dass Nase und Mund bedeckt sind.
native_language_example: Wear the mask so that nose and mouth are covered.

meaning: 'and music' — used to connect another activity, subject or thing with music.
additional_notes: A simple conjunction phrase. Commonly follows a noun or verb phrase to indicate that music is included alongside something else (e.g., hobbies, interests, activities). Word order depends on the sentence: after a verb use an infinitive (z. B. 'Musik hören'), after a noun just 'und Musik'.
target_language_example: Sie liest gern Romane und Musik hört sie auch.
native_language_example: She likes reading novels and she also listens to music.

meaning: 'and salt' — used to add salt to a list of ingredients or items.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in recipes and food contexts after other ingredients (e.g., 'Pfeffer und Salz' = 'pepper and salt'). It's just the conjunction 'und' (and) plus 'Salz' (salt). Useful for signing lists or saying you mixed or confused salt with something else.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch Pfeffer und Salz für die Suppe.
native_language_example: I still need pepper and salt for the soup.

meaning: 'and water' — used to list water together with other things (e.g., food, cloth) or in fixed expressions.
additional_notes: Literally means 'and water.' Commonly appears when listing items someone needs (e.g., 'Nahrung und Wasser' = 'food and water'). Also used in idiomatic phrases like 'Luft und Wasser' (air and water) to refer to basic necessities or to say something is taken for granted. Usage is straightforward and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Bring mir bitte Brot und Wasser.
native_language_example: Please bring me bread and water.

meaning: 'and wine' — the conjunction 'und' (and) followed by the noun 'Wein' (wine).
additional_notes: A simple phrase meaning 'and wine'. Used when listing drinks or pairing wine with other items. Grammatically, 'und' joins words or phrases; 'Wein' is masculine (der Wein). Word order and endings stay normal. Not idiomatic — just literal.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern Brot und Wein.
native_language_example: I'd like bread and wine.

meaning: 'and everyone' / 'and all (of them)' — adds the idea of others or the rest of a group
additional_notes: Used to include other people or things not explicitly listed. Can mean 'and all the others' or 'and all memories/things' depending on context. Common in spoken and written German. Word-for-word composition is transparent (und = and, alle = all/everyone).
target_language_example: Mama, Papa und alle anderen sind schon gegangen.
native_language_example: Mom, Dad and everyone else have already left.

meaning: and on the next (day/time/place) / and the next one
additional_notes: A connector phrase combining 'und' (and) with 'am nächsten' (on the next… / the nearest/next one). Often followed by a time expression (am nächsten Tag = and on the next day) or used to compare/schedule events (und am nächsten Tag ging er weg). Context determines whether it means 'on the next (day/time)' or 'the next one' as continuation.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns heute um 18 Uhr und am nächsten Tag um 10 Uhr nochmal.
native_language_example: We meet today at 6 p.m. and the next day at 10 a.m. again.

meaning: occasionally; from time to time.
additional_notes: A common adverbial phrase meaning something happens now and then, not regularly. Can be used with verbs in present or past. Neutral register and suitable for everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Ich treffe ihn ab und an auf dem Markt.
native_language_example: I meet him at the market from time to time.

meaning: and others / and other(s)
additional_notes: Used to contrast or list remaining people or things after mentioning one group. Often follows a plural noun or clause and can be translated as “and others” or “others (do/are)”. Common in comparisons: 'Einige ... und andere ...' = 'Some ... and others ...'.
target_language_example: Einige mögen Tee und andere mögen Kaffee.
native_language_example: Some like tea and others like coffee.

meaning: and work / and (to) work
additional_notes: A simple combination of the conjunction 'und' (and) plus the infinitive or conjugated verb 'arbeiten' (to work). Used to connect actions or list activities (e.g. "essen und arbeiten" = "eat and work") or as part of a sentence where 'arbeiten' is conjugated (e.g. "Wir sind hier und arbeiten"). Very common in everyday and formal contexts. Watch verb position and tense when used in full sentences.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben im Büro und arbeiten bis spät.
native_language_example: We stay in the office and work until late.

meaning: and (he/she/it) works / and works
additional_notes: Combination of the conjunction 'und' (and) with the verb 'arbeiten' (to work). Used to join actions or states (e.g., lives and works). Verb form 'arbeitet' is 3rd person singular present. Useful when describing what someone does in addition to something else.
target_language_example: Sie lebt und arbeitet in Berlin.
native_language_example: She lives and works in Berlin.

meaning: and (he/she) asked/asked for.
additional_notes: Und bat is the conjunction 'and' followed by bat, the past tense (Präteritum) of bitten — 'to ask' or 'to request'. In these examples it means someone asked for something (um + accusative) or asked someone to do something (bat + personal pronoun + infinitive or um + noun). Common in storytelling/narration. For present tense use 'und bittet' or 'und bittet um'.
target_language_example: Er sah den Hund und bat den Nachbarn, ihn hereinzulassen.
native_language_example: He saw the dog and asked the neighbor to let it in.

meaning: and famous
additional_notes: Commonly used after an adjective (often 'reich' = rich) to link two desired or descriptive qualities: 'reich und berühmt' = 'rich and famous'. Very straightforward and literal; used in everyday speech. Can be combined with modifiers (e.g. 'stinkreich und berühmt' = extremely rich and famous).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eines Tages reich und berühmt sein.
native_language_example: I want to be rich and famous one day.

meaning: and blue; literally 'and blue' — used when listing colors or describing something as blue plus something else.
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction 'und' (and) followed by the adjective/noun 'blau' (blue). It appears in color lists (e.g. 'rot und blau' = 'red and blue') or in descriptions ('nass und blau' would be unusual; normally 'und blau' pairs with another color or noun). No idiomatic meaning; use gender/number/inflection if needed (e.g. 'und blaues' rarely used).
target_language_example: Das Shirt ist rot und blau.
native_language_example: The shirt is red and blue.

meaning: and stay; and remain (somewhere).
additional_notes: Used after an imperative or instruction to tell someone to stay in a place or remain with someone/something. Common with location words (dort, drin, da, bei ihr) or objects (im Wagen). Often follows a verb in the imperative: Geh rein und bleib drin = Go in and stay in. Direct, can be used for temporary stays (stay here tonight = bleib über Nacht).
target_language_example: Geh in dein Zimmer und bleib dort.
native_language_example: Go to your room and stay there.

meaning: and (then) broke (something).
additional_notes: Commonly appears after a verb describing an action or accident (e.g., fiel, stürzte) to say that as a result something was broken. Often used with a dative reflexive construction (mir den Arm) to indicate who was hurt and which body part. Can also be used metaphorically (e.g., jemand brach mir das Herz). The simple past form 'brach' is often used in narratives; spoken German may use perfect ('und habe mir ... gebrochen').
target_language_example: Er rutschte auf dem Eis und brach sich das Bein.
native_language_example: He slipped on the ice and broke his leg.

meaning: and (he/she) broke (it) — part of a sentence describing someone breaking something (often a body part).
additional_notes: This is a clause fragment: 'brach' is the simple past of 'brechen' (to break). When reflexive with 'sich' it usually refers to breaking a part of one's own body (e.g. 'er brach sich das Bein' = he broke his leg). The word order here starts with 'und' = and; the full sentence would name the person and the object: e.g. 'Er rutschte aus und brach sich das Bein.'
target_language_example: Sie fiel die Treppe runter und brach sich das Bein.
native_language_example: She fell down the stairs and broke her leg.

meaning: 'and brought' (simple past of bringen)
additional_notes: Used to join two actions: the conjunction 'und' (and) plus the past-tense verb 'brachte' (1st/3rd person singular of bringen in Präteritum). 'Bringen' means to bring, take (someone) somewhere, or cause (something) to happen — context decides exact translation (bring, took, put, caused). Watch for objects: could be people, things, or abstract outcomes. Sentence examples may imply different nuances (e.g., 'brought him to pole position' = caused/put; 'brought him home' = took him home; 'brought him to bed' = put him to bed; 'brought him off' in violent context = killed him).
target_language_example: Sie ging ins Café und brachte ihrer Freundin einen Kaffee.
native_language_example: She went to the café and brought her friend a coffee.

meaning: and (I) bring/bring along/deliver (something) — first-person singular present of bringen used after another action.
additional_notes: Commonly follows another verb connected with 'und' to show a second action the speaker will do (expressed in first person). 'Bringe' can mean to bring something to someone, to take someone somewhere, to put something right (fix), or — in informal/angry speech — to kill (colloquial/violent). Context and object determine the exact meaning.
target_language_example: Ich kaufe Brot und bringe es dir heute Abend vorbei.
native_language_example: I'll buy bread and bring it by your place this evening.

meaning: 'and for that' / 'and because of that' — links a previous statement to a consequence, reason, or purpose.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer back to something just said and introduce a result, punishment, gratitude, purpose, or question about consequence. Tone depends on context: can express consequence ("and therefore"), cause ("and because of that"), or purpose ("and for that [purpose]"). Often appears at the start of a sentence after a previous clause.
target_language_example: Du hast mir geholfen, und dafür danke ich dir.
native_language_example: You helped me, and for that I thank you.

meaning: and that one (over there); and that/that there (pointing to something).
additional_notes: Casual phrase used when pointing to or referring to something a little farther away or previously mentioned. 'das' is neuter demonstrative; form can change to 'der da' (masc.) or 'die da' (fem./pl.) to match the noun. Common in spoken German to add clarity or continue a list: 'und das da …'.
target_language_example: Das hier ist ein Buch, und das da ist ein Foto.
native_language_example: This here is a book, and that one over there is a photo.

meaning: and that has / and that did (depending on tense) — used to continue or emphasize a previous statement.
additional_notes: Commonly used to link back to something just mentioned. English equivalent often depends on context: 'and that did…', 'and that has…', or simply 'and that…'. In questions it can emphasize surprise (e.g. 'And that didn't bother you?'). Word order in German puts the auxiliary (hat) before the subject in yes/no questions and after the subject in statements.
target_language_example: Und das hat sie gestern endlich erledigt.
native_language_example: And that she finally finished yesterday.

meaning: and you know that / and that's something you know
additional_notes: Used to point out that the listener already knows the stated fact. Often followed by pronouns like 'du' or 'auch' (e.g. 'und das weißt du'). Can be emphatic or even confrontational, depending on tone. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Das hast du versprochen, und das weißt du.
native_language_example: You promised that, and you know it.

meaning: 'and in addition' / 'and also'
additional_notes: Used to add another piece of information or emphasize an extra point. Can introduce something positive, negative, or neutral. In conversational German it often shortens to 'dazu' or appears at the start of a sentence as 'Und dazu...'. Tone depends on context (can be emphatic, surprised, or simply additive).
target_language_example: Er hat viel Arbeit, und dazu noch zwei Kinder zu versorgen.
native_language_example: He has a lot of work, and in addition has two children to take care of.

meaning: and fat / and chubby (describing someone or something as additionally fat).
additional_notes: A simple adjective phrase combining 'und' (and) with 'dick' (fat/thick). Used to add 'fat' as another characteristic after describing someone or something (e.g., 'alt und dick' = 'old and fat'). 'Dick' can be neutral ('thick') or negative depending on context and tone—avoid using it about people unless you know it's acceptable in the situation. Word order follows the noun + adjective pattern: 'Er ist alt und dick.'
target_language_example: Die Katze ist klein und dick.
native_language_example: The cat is small and fat.

meaning: 'and ends' (indicates when something finishes or comes to an end)
additional_notes: Commonly used to state the end point or final time of a period, event, or action. It follows a start or duration phrase (e.g., 'beginnt ... und endet ...'). Simple, literal combination of 'und' (and) + 'endet' (ends).
target_language_example: Die Ausstellung beginnt am Montag und endet am Sonntag.
native_language_example: The exhibition begins on Monday and ends on Sunday.

meaning: and tell (or I/you tell) — the verb 'erzählen' in a clause connected by 'und' (and).
additional_notes: Common connector + verb sequence. 'Erzähle' is the first-person or imperative or present-tense subjunctive form depending on context: here it usually appears as 1) present indicative 'ich erzähle' (I tell) with omitted pronoun, 2) imperative 'erzähle!' (tell!), or 3) present tense with pronoun 'du erzählst' in colloquial speech where speakers say 'und erzähle dir alles' meaning 'and I'll tell you everything' (the subject can be omitted). Pay attention to the subject (ich/du/ich werde) from context. Useful in spoken and written German to connect actions: '...und erzähle (dir) alles.'
target_language_example: Ich komme später und erzähle dir alles.
native_language_example: I'll come later and tell you everything.

meaning: and it has / and it rained (used with 'regnen' or in perfect tense constructions).
additional_notes: A combination of the conjunction 'und' (and) + 'es hat' (it has). Often appears before a past participle to form the present perfect (Perfekt) with impersonal 'es' (e.g. 'es hat geregnet' = 'it rained' / literally 'it has rained'). Can also introduce a new clause emphasizing a result or effect ('und es hat mich beinahe zerstört' = 'and it almost destroyed me'). Common in everyday speech; not idiomatic beyond normal grammar.
target_language_example: Es schneite die ganze Nacht, und es hat am Morgen immer noch geschneit.
native_language_example: It snowed all night, and it was still snowing in the morning.

meaning: 'and your' (plural or formal 'your' when addressing a group or using archaic/poetic tone)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'und' (and) with the possessive pronoun 'euer' (your, plural informal). Use 'euer' when speaking to more than one person (or in older/poetic texts). In modern polite singular or formal address, use 'Ihr' (capitalized) instead. Word order and form agree with the noun that follows (euer Vater, euer Kaffee, euer Volk).
target_language_example: Möge euer Tag heute schön und euer Abend ruhig sein.
native_language_example: May your day be lovely and your evening peaceful.

meaning: 'and (I/you/he/etc.) drive/go/ride' or 'and continue (moving)'.
additional_notes: Und = 'and'. Fahre is a conjugated form of fahren (to drive, go by vehicle, ride, or to proceed/continue). Meaning depends on context and subject: ich fahre = I go/drive/ride; er/sie fährt = he/she goes. Can mean 'travel by (train, car, tram)', 'drive', or 'continue' (e.g., fahre fort). Watch for separable verb combinations (fahre fort = continue).
target_language_example: Ich nehme den Bus und fahre zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I take the bus and go to work.

meaning: 'and fast' — part of the fixed adverbial phrase 'tief und fest' meaning 'soundly' (asleep) or expressing being firmly/resolutely (decided).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the idiom 'tief und fest schlafen' = 'to sleep soundly' (deeply). Outside that idiom, 'und fest' can follow an adjective to emphasize firmness or determination (e.g. 'fest entschlossen' — 'firmly/resolutely determined'). Learners should treat 'tief und fest' as a set phrase for sleeping deeply. Word order: 'tief und fest' normally precedes/ follows the verb phrase describing sleep; 'und fest' by itself is not commonly used alone except in fixed combinations.
target_language_example: Er schlief die ganze Nacht tief und fest.
native_language_example: He slept soundly all night.

meaning: 'and finds' (from finden — to find).
additional_notes: A simple connector: und = and; findet = he/she/it finds or you (formal) find. Used to link clauses where someone or something discovers, thinks, or judges something. Context determines whether 'findet' means 'finds' (discover) or 'thinks/considers' (as in 'ich finde, dass...'). Pronounced with final -t sound. Verb agreement changes with subject (ich finde, du findest, er/sie/es findet, wir finden...).
target_language_example: Sie liest den Brief und findet neue Informationen.
native_language_example: She reads the letter and finds new information.

meaning: and ask (ask someone).
additional_notes: A short, conversational instruction combining 'und' (and) with the imperative or infinitive form 'frag' (from fragen). Used to tell someone to go and ask a person or to remind them to ask. Common in spoken German; context decides the subject (e.g. 'Geh und frag sie' = 'Go and ask her').
target_language_example: Geh kurz zur Rezeption und frag, ob das Zimmer fertig ist.
native_language_example: Go quickly to reception and ask if the room is ready.

meaning: and (he/she) asked / and asked (someone).
additional_notes: Commonly used to connect actions: 'und' = and; 'fragte' = asked (past). Often followed by a question clause (ob..., was..., etc.) or 'nach' + noun (nach seinem Namen = about his name). The subject is usually omitted in short phrases because it was mentioned before (e.g. 'Er rief an und fragte...').
target_language_example: Er sah sie an und fragte, ob sie bleiben wolle.
native_language_example: He looked at her and asked if she wanted to stay.

meaning: 'and falls' (literally); used when describing something that falls or drops, often following another clause
additional_notes: This is simply the conjunction 'und' (and) followed by the 3rd-person singular present of 'fallen' (to fall). It often appears in sentences describing movement, temperature, price changes, or metaphorical decline: e.g. 'Die Blätter werden bunt und fallen.' Context decides whether it's physical falling ('falls down') or figurative ('drops', 'decreases'). Word order and tense can change (fallen → fällt).
target_language_example: Die Temperatur sinkt und fällt nächste Woche weiter.
native_language_example: The temperature is dropping and will fall further next week.

meaning: 'and gave' or 'and stated' (depends on the verb following 'gab').
additional_notes: Und is 'and' or starts a question 'And...?' here. 'Gab' is the simple past (Präteritum) of geben (to give) and also used in the separable construction 'angeben' (to state/declare) as 'gab an' = 'stated'. Context decides meaning: e.g. 'gab ihm einen Kuss' = 'gave him a kiss'; 'gab an, ...' = 'stated that...'; sentence-initial 'Und gab es ...?' = 'And were there...?' or 'And did there exist...?'.
target_language_example: Sie nahm das Buch und gab es mir.
native_language_example: She took the book and gave it to me.

meaning: “and loved” — adds 'loved' to something previously stated (e.g., 'seen and loved').
additional_notes: Commonly appears after another adjective or verb in lists (e.g., 'geschätzt und geliebt' = 'appreciated and loved'). Can be used in statements about feelings, relationships, or historical descriptions. Word order may change in full clauses (e.g., 'geliebt zu werden' or 'und geliebt habe ich dich auch nie').
target_language_example: Ich möchte gesehen und geliebt werden.
native_language_example: I want to be seen and loved.

meaning: 'and' + imperative 'hold' / 'keep' (used to give commands or add another instruction)
additional_notes: Und = 'and'. Halt is the informal imperative (du-form) of halten (to hold/keep) or ofhalten in fixed phrases like 'halt die Klappe' (shut up). Together 'und halt' is used to add another command or instruction — often blunt or colloquial. The exact English translation depends on the verb's object: e.g. 'and keep', 'and hold', 'and shut' (in 'halt die Klappe' = 'shut up'). Tone can be rude when used with blunt commands (e.g. 'und halt dein Maul').
target_language_example: Geh in die Küche und halt das Fenster zu.
native_language_example: Go into the kitchen and keep the window closed.

meaning: and (he/she/it) helps / and helps (someone) — conjunction + verb (3rd person singular or imperative stem in some contexts).
additional_notes: Combines 'und' (and) + 'hilft' (from helfen). 'Hilft' is the 3rd person singular present of helfen (er/sie/es hilft). In some sentences this pattern links actions: 'X does A and helps (someone) with B.' Can also appear in imperatives with context (e.g. 'bleibt und hilft' = 'stay and help'). The object of 'hilft' is usually a person or a task expressed with 'bei' + dative or a direct dative (jemandem helfen). Verb requires a dative object: 'jemandem helfen' or 'bei etwas helfen'.
target_language_example: Sie bleibt und hilft den Kindern beim Aufräumen.
native_language_example: She stays and helps the children with tidying up.

meaning: 'and fetch' / 'and get' (used to indicate doing something and then retrieving or obtaining something)
additional_notes: Combines conjunction 'und' (and) with the verb 'holen' (to fetch/get). Often used in commands or plans to say do X and then go get something. In colloquial contexts 'holen' can mean 'bring back', 'pick up' or 'take'. When reflexive ('uns holen') it can mean 'come and get us'. Verb form and subject must agree (e.g. 'hol' → imperative informal 'hol mir' vs 'holen Sie').
target_language_example: Wir gehen zum Auto und holen den Koffer.
native_language_example: We go to the car and get the suitcase.

meaning: 'and listen to me' (spoken phrase used to get someone's attention or emphasize what you're saying)
additional_notes: Common in spoken German as an imperative or urgent request: 'und hör mir (zu)' or simply 'hör mir' = 'listen to me'. Often used to introduce an important point, a warning, or to express frustration. In full forms you may hear 'und hör mir gut zu' or 'hör mir zu'. 'Und' simply connects to the previous sentence, so you'll often see it after another clause.
target_language_example: Das ist wichtig, und hör mir zu!
native_language_example: This is important, and listen to me!

meaning: 'and listens' or 'and is listening'.
additional_notes: Combination of 'und' (and) + verb 'hören' in the 3rd person singular (hört) or imperative plural with 'zu' omitted in some sentences. Can mean 'to hear' (passive perception) or 'to listen' (actively pay attention). Often used with 'zu' (zuhören) to mean 'listen to' someone. Context decides whether it's general listening (Radio, Musik) or paying attention (jemandem zuhören).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet und hört Musik.
native_language_example: She works and listens to music.

meaning: and into the / and in the (feminine or plural noun in accusative or dative depending on context).
additional_notes: A sequence of the conjunction 'und' (and) plus the prepositional phrase 'in die'. 'in die' can mean 'into the' (movement into something) or 'in the' (location) when followed by a feminine plural noun or when case requires the article 'die'. Beginners should note meaning depends on verb (movement verbs use accusative: 'in die Schublade legen' = into the drawer).
target_language_example: Er hat das Buch eingepackt und in die Tasche gelegt.
native_language_example: He wrapped the book and put it into the bag.

meaning: and at some point / and eventually
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something will happen at an unspecified time in the future. Can introduce a consequence, change, realization, or turning point. Common in both spoken and written German; often comes at the start of a sentence for emphasis (capitalized 'Und').
target_language_example: Und irgendwann wirst du sehen, dass es richtig war.
native_language_example: And eventually you will see that it was right.

meaning: and cold.
additional_notes: A simple conjunction + adjective used to add 'cold' to a list or description. Very common in descriptions of weather, rooms, feelings, or atmosphere. Word order: 'und' (and) comes before the adjective. Can appear in short, dramatic fragments (e.g., 'Und kalt.').
target_language_example: Der Flur war leer und kalt.
native_language_example: The hallway was empty and cold.

meaning: 'and came' (often part of phrases like 'and came back' or 'and never came back') or more generally the conjunction 'and' + past of 'kommen' used to link actions/events.
additional_notes: Literally 'and came'. Commonly appears in narrative sequences: 'ging ... und kam (nicht) wieder' = 'went ... and (didn't) come back'. Depending on context, it can mean 'and returned', 'and came back', or in negative contexts 'and never came back'. Also used for other senses like 'and arrived' or 'and became' when combined with adjectives (e.g. 'kam als anderer Mensch zurück' = 'came back as a different person').
target_language_example: Sie verabschiedete sich und kam nie wieder.
native_language_example: She said goodbye and never came back.

meaning: 'and bought' (past tense of 'kaufen')
additional_notes: Used to connect actions in the past: 'und' = 'and', 'kaufte' = simple past (preterite) of 'kaufen' = 'to buy'. Common in narration. Often followed by the object purchased; separable verb forms (e.g., einkaufen) appear as 'kaufte ein' or as in examples 'einkaufen' with context.
target_language_example: Sie sah das Kleid an und kaufte es sofort.
native_language_example: She looked at the dress and bought it immediately.

meaning: and clear / and bright (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective to add 'and clear' or 'and bright'—common in descriptions of weather, visibility, pronunciation, or explanations. In physical contexts (water, sky, air) it means 'clear' = transparent or free of haze; with light (hell und klar) it can mean 'bright and clear'. With explanations (einfach und klar) it means 'clear' as in easy to understand. Word order: 'Adjective und klar' or simply 'hell und klar'.
target_language_example: Der See war ruhig und klar.
native_language_example: The lake was calm and clear.

meaning: 'and smart' or 'and clever' — used to add 'smart' as another quality
additional_notes: A simple conjunction + adjective phrase: 'und' (and) + 'klug' (smart/clever). It is used to list qualities or describe someone/something as also being smart. Common in everyday and written German. Word order follows the noun/pronoun it describes (e.g., 'jung und klug' = 'young and smart').
target_language_example: Sie ist freundlich und klug.
native_language_example: She is friendly and smart.

meaning: 'and come' (imperative phrase used to tell someone to come, come back, or to emphasize a command about coming/returning).
additional_notes: Commonly appears at the start of an imperative clause as a connector: 'und komm ...' adds a command or warning about coming/returning (often with adverbs like 'nicht', 'nie', 'bloß', 'wieder', 'zurück', or time expressions). Tone can be firm, warning, or emotional depending on context. Literal translation is possible, but the phrase functions as part of commands: e.g. 'und komm bloß pünktlich' = 'and make sure you come on time'.
target_language_example: Geh jetzt, und komm morgen früh wieder.
native_language_example: Go now, and come back tomorrow morning.

meaning: and (I) come / and (I) return (to a place).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'und' (and) with the verb 'kommen' (to come). In context it often means 'and then I come back' or 'and I arrive/come' depending on tense and sentence. Common in spoken German to indicate returning soon (e.g., 'komme gleich' = 'I'll be right back') or origin when used with 'aus' ('komme aus' = 'come from'). The subject is usually 'ich' (I) but can be implied from context.
target_language_example: Ich erledige das kurz und komme gleich.
native_language_example: I'll take care of that quickly and I'll be right back.

meaning: and (he/she) laughed.
additional_notes: A simple past-tense phrase combining 'und' (and) with 'lachte' (past of 'lachen' = to laugh). Used to link an action with the reaction of laughing. Subject is understood from context (er, sie, Tom, etc.). Common in narratives and everyday descriptions.
target_language_example: Sie sah die Katze und lachte.
native_language_example: She looked at the cat and laughed.

meaning: and (he) read a (book).
additional_notes: A short sequence: 'und' = 'and', 'las' is the past tense (Präteritum) of 'lesen' (to read) for ich/er/sie/es, and 'ein' is an indefinite article matching a masculine/neuter noun in accusative (e.g. 'ein Buch'). Common in simple past narrative: 'und las ein Buch' = 'and (he) read a book' or 'and was reading a book'.
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich neben ihn und las ein Buch.
native_language_example: She sat down next to him and read a book.

meaning: 'and let' or 'and leave' (imperative/command form with 'lassen').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in spoken and written German when giving instructions or requests (imperative) using 'lass' (du-form of lassen). It can mean 'and let (someone/something do something)', 'and leave (something alone)', or 'and don't omit'. Context determines whether it's permissive ('let') or tells someone to stop/leave something ('leave'). Often used in combinations like 'und lass mich gehen' (and let me go) or 'und lass nichts aus' (and don't leave anything out). The subject is usually 'du' (you) or implied; with 'uns' it becomes 'und lass uns...' (let's...).
target_language_example: Lass das Buch auf dem Tisch und lass mich in Ruhe.
native_language_example: Leave the book on the table and leave me alone.

meaning: "and (I) let/leave" — connects clauses where the speaker causes or allows something, often with first person (ich lasse) or imperative (lasse).
additional_notes: Used after a verb to join actions: the first part is an action, then 'und lasse' introduces a following result or permission. Common with 'ich lasse' (I let/leave/make) and imperatives (Lasse ...!). Can mean "leave (someone) alone", "let (something) happen/enter", or "have someone taken somewhere" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich schließe das Fenster und lasse die Katze herein.
native_language_example: I close the window and let the cat come in.

meaning: and (let) do/leave (someone/something); part of the phrase 'tun und lassen' meaning 'to do as one pleases' or in commands 'and let/leave (it/him) ...'.
additional_notes: Often appears in fixed expressions like 'tun und lassen' (to do as one pleases) or in commands with 'lassen' (to let/leave). In sentence 1 it's part of 'tun und lassen, was er will' = 'do whatever he wants'. In sentence 2 it's used in the imperative: 'werfen Sie ... und lassen Sie ihn los' = 'throw away ... and let him go'. 'Und lassen' by itself usually needs surrounding verbs/objects to make sense.
target_language_example: Lass sie machen, und lassen wir das Thema ruhen.
native_language_example: Let them do it, and let's leave the topic alone.

meaning: and light / and easy (to ...); links two qualities, where 'leicht' can mean physically light or easy/fragile to influence.
additional_notes: Used to connect two adjectives or qualities. 'leicht' commonly means 'not heavy' (physically light) or 'easy'/'easily' depending on context: e.g. 'leicht zu beeindrucken' = 'easy to impress' (i.e. easily impressed), and poetic uses may mean 'nimble' or 'lightly' (as in 'leicht wie ein Vogel'). Pay attention to word order and following infinitives with 'zu' (leicht zu + verb).
target_language_example: Sie ist klug und leicht zu überzeugen.
native_language_example: She is clever and easy to persuade.

meaning: and (he/she/it) reads / and (you) read (present tense).
additional_notes: Common short phrase combining the conjunction 'und' (and) with the verb 'liest' (3rd person singular of 'lesen' or formal 2nd person). Used to link actions or describe someone reading right now. 'liest' is pronounced [liːst]. For other persons: ich lese, du liest, er/sie/es liest, wir lesen, ihr lest, sie lesen.
target_language_example: Sie sitzt im Park und liest.
native_language_example: She sits in the park and reads.

meaning: and (he) left/caused (someone or something) to be in a certain state or place (past).
additional_notes: „ließ“ is the simple past of lassen (to let/leave/allow/cause). In combination with „und“ it links two actions: first action + and then he let/left/caused (something) to happen. Can mean 'left someone somewhere', 'left behind', 'allowed', 'caused to' or 'let in/out' depending on the object and context. Subject is often omitted in short narratives but understood from context.
target_language_example: Er ging zur Tür und ließ die Katze im Zimmer.
native_language_example: He went to the door and left the cat in the room.

meaning: and lively / wide awake; used to describe someone who is cheerful, energetic, or fully awake
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun or verb phrase to add a light, often positive comment (e.g., 'lebt und munter' = 'alive and well'). Can describe physical wakefulness or a cheerful, energetic state. Slightly idiomatic but neutral in register.
target_language_example: Er ist gestern spät ins Bett gegangen und heute trotzdem lebhaft und munter.
native_language_example: He went to bed late yesterday and is still lively and wide awake today.

meaning: 'and had to' or 'and had (to)'.
additional_notes: Combined phrase: und = 'and'; musste = past tense (Präteritum) of müssen = 'must/have to'. Used to link actions in the past and express necessity or obligation that occurred. Common in storytelling: 'and then had to...'.
target_language_example: Sie war alleine und musste das ganze Haus putzen.
native_language_example: She was alone and had to clean the whole house.

meaning: 'and of course' or 'and naturally' — used to add something expected or obvious.
additional_notes: Common linking phrase used to add an expected, obvious, or typical item or comment. Can start a sentence (capitalized 'Und') for emphasis or continuation. Tone is neutral; can be used in spoken and written German. Often cushions statements (softens, implies 'as you would expect').
target_language_example: Er spricht Französisch und natürlich Englisch.
native_language_example: He speaks French and of course English.

meaning: 'and nice' — used to add 'nice' as a second quality or to soften/limit a description.
additional_notes: Literally connects an earlier adjective to 'nett' (nice). Often used to list character traits (e.g., 'intelligent und nett'). Can also imply that 'nice' is the only positive quality (tone depends on context). Common in everyday speech. 'Nett' is milder than 'freundlich' (friendly) and can sound non-committal.
target_language_example: Er ist klug und nett, aber nicht sehr abenteuerlustig.
native_language_example: He is smart and nice, but not very adventurous.

meaning: a strong affirmative like 'you bet' / 'definitely' / 'absolutely'.
additional_notes: 'Und ob' is used as an emphatic reply to agree very strongly with a statement or question. It can be translated as 'you bet', 'definitely', or 'absolutely'. Often appears alone or at the start of a sentence. Informal but common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Hast du das Examen bestanden? — Und ob!
native_language_example: Did you pass the exam? — You bet!

meaning: and without
additional_notes: A simple connector combining 'und' (and) with 'ohne' (without). Used to add another negative or missing element to a list or phrase. Can introduce a phrase that lacks something (e.g., 'without a tomorrow', 'without obligations') or start a clause for emphasis. In speech it may appear together repeatedly (e.g., 'ohne ... und ohne ...') or begin a sentence for dramatic effect. Not idiomatic by itself—meaning is literal.
target_language_example: Er ging weg und ohne einen Abschied zu sagen.
native_language_example: He left — and without saying goodbye.

meaning: and (she/he) ran (away / off / toward).
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'und' (and) with the past tense of 'rennen' (to run). Used to continue an action: e.g. running away (wegging), running toward someone (entgegen), or running around. Subject is usually third person; tense is simple past (Präteritum) common in written narratives. Translate based on context: 'ran', 'ran away', or 'ran toward'.
target_language_example: Sie nahm das Buch und rannte damit zur Tür.
native_language_example: She grabbed the book and ran to the door with it.

meaning: and out / and get out (used with verbs like 'rein und raus' or as a short command '... und raus!').
additional_notes: Common in colloquial German. Often appears in the expression 'rein und raus' (in and out) to describe going in and out or knowing how to enter and exit. As a short imperative (e.g. 'Pack dein Zeug und raus!') it means '...and out!' or '...get out (of here)!' — a blunt way to tell someone to leave. Informal, often used in spoken language.
target_language_example: Pack deinen Kram und raus!
native_language_example: Pack your stuff and get out!

meaning: 'and talk' or 'and speak' (imperative sequence: do X and then talk/speak).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in commands: verb + 'und rede' tells someone to go/do something and then talk to a person. 'Rede' is the imperative (singular) of 'reden' = to talk/speak. Can be used with an object or prepositional phrase (mit + person). Tone can be urgent or instructive (e.g., 'Hör auf ... und rede endlich' = stop ... and finally speak).
target_language_example: Geh und rede mit ihr.
native_language_example: Go and talk to her.

meaning: and tell (someone) / and say (to someone).
additional_notes: Common connective phrase: "und" (and) + verb "sagen" (to say/tell). Used to link actions: do X and then tell/say Y to someone. Usually followed by a direct or indirect object (ihm, ihr, denen) and a clause introduced by dass or a reported imperative. Useful for giving instructions or reporting speech.
target_language_example: Geh rein und sage ihm, dass das Meeting begonnen hat.
native_language_example: Go in and tell him that the meeting has started.

meaning: 'and looked at me' (simple past: someone looked/was looking at me).
additional_notes: A sequence: und (and) + sah (simple past of sehen = to see/look) + mich (me). Used to describe that someone directed their gaze toward the speaker. In many examples 'sah mich an' is used — 'ansehen' = to look at; in past tense 'sah ... an'. Common in narration. Can be separated in German (sah mich an) or combined in infinitive/perfect (ansah/angeschaut).
target_language_example: Sie drehte sich plötzlich um und sah mich an.
native_language_example: She suddenly turned around and looked at me.

meaning: 'and saw' (simple past: he/she/it saw) — used to link actions in the past
additional_notes: Combines the coordinating conjunction 'und' (and) with the past-tense verb 'sah' (from sehen). Common in narratives to connect two past actions (e.g., 'he sat and saw' / 'he switched off and looked'). Often followed by a direction or object (aus dem Fenster, nach draußen, hinaus). Word order and context determine whether it means 'looked' or 'saw'.
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich ans Fenster und sah die Straße entlang.
native_language_example: She sat down at the window and watched the street.

meaning: 'and (he/she/it) looks' — conjunction und (and) + verb schaut (3rd person singular of schauen); can also appear in coordinated clauses or narrative sequences meaning 'and looks' or in imperatives when addressing a group if context supplies different forms.
additional_notes: Compositional: simply und + schaut (schauen = to look). Appears in descriptions (e.g. 'er steht da und schaut') and in narrative sequences. Tone can be neutral; formality depends on surrounding verbs and pronouns. Context determines person and whether it's part of an imperative sequence (e.g. 'Geht und schaut!' uses infinitive imperative + und + imperative verb stem, though 'schaut' there is 2nd person plural imperative).
target_language_example: Da oben schwebt sie jetzt und schaut auf uns hinab.
native_language_example: Up there she now hovers and looks down at us.

meaning: and (he/she) sent / and (he/she) sent off
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of schicken (to send) with coordinating 'und' = 'and'. Used to link actions: '[Someone] did X and sent Y to Z' or 'and then sent everyone home'. Subject is often omitted if clear from context (as in 'schickte es Maria' = 'sent it to Maria'). For spoken German people often use Perfekt (hat geschickt), but Präteritum is common in writing and storytelling.
target_language_example: Er machte ein Foto und schickte es seiner Schwester.
native_language_example: He took a photo and sent it to his sister.

meaning: 'and sleep' — used to add sleeping/resting as another action or state.
additional_notes: A simple connector: 'und' (and) plus verb 'schlafen' (to sleep). Common in lists of activities (e.g., 'kochen, arbeiten und schlafen') or as a goal/desire ('nach Hause und schlafen'). Can be used literally (to sleep) or loosely to mean 'rest' or 'drop off'. Word order follows normal verb placement in sentences (infinitive in lists, conjugated when needed).
target_language_example: Ich will ins Bett, lesen und schlafen.
native_language_example: I want to go to bed, read and sleep.

meaning: and (he/she/it) closed (something).
additional_notes: A simple past narrative connector: 'und' (and) + verb 'schloss' (simple past of schließen). Used to describe a sequence of actions (someone does something and then closed a door/window). In everyday speech present or perfect tenses are common (schließt/hat geschlossen), but in written or narrated past 'schloss' appears. The object being closed is usually mentioned right after (die Tür, das Fenster) or implied.
target_language_example: Er trat ein und schloss die Tür leise.
native_language_example: He entered and closed the door quietly.

meaning: and (he/she) wrote / and (he/she) was writing (past tense).
additional_notes: Und schrieb is simply the conjunction 'und' ('and') followed by the past tense (Präteritum) of the verb schreiben ('to write'). Context determines meaning: it can mean 'and wrote' (finished action), 'and was writing' (narrative past), or 'and texted/was texting' in informal contexts (especially with SMS or messaging). The subject is determined elsewhere in the sentence (und schrieb = and he/she/it wrote).
target_language_example: Er nahm den Stift und schrieb eine Karte.
native_language_example: He took the pen and wrote a card.

meaning: and beautiful / and nice
additional_notes: A simple connective phrase: 'und' = 'and', 'schöne' is the feminine/plural/accusative form of 'schön' (beautiful/nice). Used to link another item with something described as 'beautiful' or 'nice' (e.g., 'und schöne Träume' = 'and beautiful dreams'). Watch adjective ending: gender, number and case affect the form (schöner, schönes, schöne, schönen).
target_language_example: Gute Nacht und schöne Träume!
native_language_example: Good night and sweet dreams!

meaning: and six (used to add the number six to a list or to continue a sentence with 'and six' — often just the conjunction 'and' plus the number six).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom — it's simply the conjunction 'und' ('and') followed by the numeral 'sechs' ('six'). It appears when someone lists items or adds 'and six' as part of a sentence. In one example it begins a new clause ('Und sechs Wochen später...' = 'And six weeks later...'), where 'Und' starts the sentence and 'sechs' is part of the time expression.
target_language_example: Ich habe zwei Bücher, drei Stifte und sechs Hefte.
native_language_example: I have two books, three pens and six notebooks.

meaning: 'and sit' / 'and put' (depends on context); here it's the conjunction 'and' followed by the verb 'setzen' (to sit/put)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase—it's simply the conjunction 'und' (and) + the verb 'setzen'. 'setzen' can mean 'to sit (down)' when reflexive (sich setzen) or 'to set/put' when transitive. In sentences 1–3 it appears as the polite imperative 'setzen Sie sich' (please sit down). In sentence 4 it is part of a different verb phrase 'einsetzen' (to use/deploy) split across words: 'Und setzen die Waffe gegen Menschen ein?' means 'And do they use the weapon against people?'. Pay attention to word order: in imperatives you often see 'und setzen Sie sich' after another command; separable verbs (einsetzen) split in main clauses.
target_language_example: Kommen Sie bitte und setzen Sie sich hierher.
native_language_example: Please come and sit down here.

meaning: 'and she was' (simple past/imperf. or linking phrase used to continue a story)
additional_notes: A common connector: 'und' = 'and', 'sie' = 'she' (or 'they' in formal contexts but here 'she'), 'war' = past tense of 'sein' = 'was'. Used to continue narration or state how someone was (emotion, location, condition) in the past. Word order is subject (sie) then verb (war) because 'und' is a coordinating conjunction and doesn't change normal word order. Context determines whether it's literal past tense or part of a narrative style.
target_language_example: Ich klopfte an die Tür, und sie war bereits eingeschlafen.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, and she was already asleep.

meaning: and they will (do something).
additional_notes: A simple connector + pronoun + future-tense auxiliary. 'Und' = 'and'; 'sie' = 'they' (or formal 'you' in different contexts, but here plural 'they'); 'werden' is the auxiliary for the future tense or to form passive. Used to say what people/things will do in the future (or to form a future passive: 'sie werden ... werden'). Followed by an infinitive or passive participle depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Und sie werden uns helfen.
native_language_example: And they will help us.

meaning: “and seven” — the conjunction 'und' (and) followed by the number seven; used when listing or adding the number seven.
additional_notes: This is not an idiom; it's simply the word 'und' plus the numeral 'sieben'. You will see it in lists, when adding numbers, or when saying a quantity that includes seven. Pronunciation: [ʊnt ˈziːbn̩]. Context determines whether it’s part of a list (Drei und sieben = three and seven) or part of a larger phrase (sieben Tage und sieben Nächte = seven days and seven nights).
target_language_example: Er hat zwei Katzen und sieben Fische.
native_language_example: He has two cats and seven fish.

meaning: 'and see' (imperative form used in instructions or suggestions)
additional_notes: Combines 'und' (and) + 'sieh' (imperative of 'sehen' for du: see/look). Used to add a short instruction or to draw attention to something, often in spoken or informal contexts. Depending on tone, it can mean 'and look' or 'and see for yourself'. In full sentences you may also hear 'und sieh mal' (more colloquial) or 'und siehst du' (question form).
target_language_example: Geh die Treppe hoch und sieh, was oben ist.
native_language_example: Go up the stairs and see what's upstairs.

meaning: 'and see' or 'and look' (imperative: inviting someone to look or check something)
additional_notes: Often follows a verb like komm, geh, or probier and is used in imperatives to invite someone to look, check, or try something themselves (e.g., "Komm und sieh" = "Come and see"). Can be strengthened with words like selbst or mal (Komm und sieh selbst / Komm und sieh mal). 'Sieh' is the imperative form of 'sehen' (to see).
target_language_example: Komm und sieh, was ich gefunden habe!
native_language_example: Come and see what I found!

meaning: 'and so' / 'and stuff' — used to add similar things, sum up, or continue a thought.
additional_notes: Very common filler/connector. Can mean 'and so on' ('etc.'), 'and that's how...' to summarize a situation, or just be a casual filler like 'and stuff' in English. Tone can be informal; context determines exact nuance.
target_language_example: Er hat den ganzen Tag gearbeitet und so.
native_language_example: He worked all day and stuff.

meaning: and so on / etc.
