additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason with added emotion—surprise, disbelief, mild annoyance, or encouragement. Tone and context (and intonation) determine whether it’s friendly, puzzled, or confrontational. Often shorter and more colloquial than a plain 'warum'.
target_language_example: Warum denn so spät gekommen?
native_language_example: Why did you come so late?

meaning: 'why eat' — used to ask why someone eats (something) or why people eat at a certain time/occasion.
additional_notes: Combines the question word 'warum' (why) with the verb 'essen' (to eat). Use word order for questions: 'Warum' + verb + subject (e.g. 'Warum essen Sie...?'). Can refer to specific foods, groups of people, occasions, or habits. Polite/formal: 'Warum essen Sie ...?' Informal/plural: 'Warum esst ihr ...?'.
target_language_example: Warum essen wir heute Abend so spät?
native_language_example: Why are we eating so late tonight?

meaning: 'why (do) [someone] go' — asks for the reason someone goes/does something (with verb gehen = to go).
additional_notes: Combines the question word warum (why) with the verb gehen (to go). Used to ask why someone/some people are going somewhere or why they behave in a way using gehen in various constructions (gehen Sie? gehen wir? gehen Tom und Mary?). Word order: Warum + verb + subject (in formal Sie questions) or Warum + subject + verb in colloquial questions. Can be used with other verbs or reflexive phrases where gehen is part of the expression (e.g., 'mir aus dem Weg gehen' = to get out of my way; 'mir auf die Nerven gehen' = to annoy me).
target_language_example: Warum gehen wir nicht zusammen ins Café?
native_language_example: Why don't we go to the café together?

meaning: 'why don't you...?' or 'why are you going...?' depending on context
additional_notes: This is the start of a question with the verb gehen (to go). Most common use here is as a suggestion or question: 'Warum gehst du nicht...?' = 'Why don't you...?' It can also be literal: asking why someone is going somewhere ('Warum gehst du?'). Add the subject and rest of the sentence to be clear. Common structure: 'Warum gehst du nicht ...?'
target_language_example: Warum gehst du nicht zum Arzt?
native_language_example: Why don't you go to the doctor?

meaning: 'why exactly' or 'for what exact reason'
additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific reason or to challenge a suggestion; adds emphasis compared to just 'warum'. Can be used in polite or confrontational contexts depending on tone. Followed by a clause (subject + verb).
target_language_example: Warum genau willst du das wissen?
native_language_example: Why exactly do you want to know that?

meaning: 'why (do [you/they/one]) believe' — used to ask for reasons behind a belief or opinion.
additional_notes: Combines the question word warum (why) with the verb glauben (to believe, to think). In natural sentences the verb is conjugated to match the subject (e.g. glaubst, glaubt, glauben) but the citation form here shows the infinitive phrase. Can introduce a clause or be followed by a direct question: e.g. "Warum glauben viele Menschen das?" The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Warum glauben viele Menschen an Verschwörungstheorien?
native_language_example: Why do many people believe in conspiracy theories?

meaning: why do (you) believe/think...?
additional_notes: Common phrase used to ask someone for the reason they believe or think something. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'dass' (that) or a question word/pronoun (e.g. 'du', 'er', 'es'). In spoken German you may hear the contraction 'glaubst du' in the middle of the sentence: word order can put the verb before the subject in questions. Use 'warum glaubst du ...?' to ask about the reason for someone's belief or opinion.
target_language_example: Warum glaubst du, dass das stimmt?
native_language_example: Why do you believe that that's true?

meaning: why do you have
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with hast, the du form of haben. With a noun or thing after it, it often means 'why do you have ...?'. If followed by a past participle, it can also form the perfect tense and mean 'why have you ...?' or 'why did you ...?'. The exact English translation depends on what comes next.
target_language_example: Warum hast du so viel Geld dabei?
native_language_example: Why do you have so much money with you?

meaning: 'why does/has' — used to ask for a reason about someone or something (present tense).
additional_notes: Combines the question word warum (why) with the third-person singular of haben (hat). Use to ask why someone/something has or does something now. For other persons/tenses, change the verb: warum habe ich..., warum haben sie..., warum hatte er...
target_language_example: Warum hat das Haus so viele Fenster?
native_language_example: Why does the house have so many windows?

meaning: 'why (do) help' — the start of a question asking why someone helps (used with 'ihr' = you all)
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it appears as the beginning of questions like 'Warum helft ihr ...?' meaning 'Why do you (plural) help ...?'. 'Helft' is the 2nd person plural form of 'helfen' (to help). The following word is usually a person in the dative case (ihm, ihr, uns, ihnen) or a name (Tom). Word order: Warum + verb (helft) + subject (ihr) + object (dative).
target_language_example: Warum helft ihr ihm nicht?
native_language_example: Why don't you (all) help him?

meaning: 'why do you help...' or 'why are you helping...'
additional_notes: A question start using warum (why) + the verb helfen (to help) in the 2nd person singular (hilfst). Commonly completed with a pronoun or noun: warum hilfst du mir?/ihm/ihr/uns? Use hilfst when speaking to one person informally (du). For formal 'you' use helfen Sie: Warum helfen Sie...?
target_language_example: Warum hilfst du mir nicht?
native_language_example: Why don't you help me?

meaning: 'why are you holding' or 'why do you stop/hold (on)'.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of questions using the verb halten (to hold / to stop). The full sentence completes the meaning: e.g. "Warum hältst du an?" = "Why are you stopping?" (halten an = to stop), while "Warum hältst du ihre Hand?" = "Why are you holding her hand?" Use du (informal you) with hältst. Word order: Warum + verb + subject + object.
target_language_example: Warum hältst du meine Hand?
native_language_example: Why are you holding my hand?

meaning: 'why do I hear' / 'why am I listening' (beginning of questions using the verb hören or zuhören).
additional_notes: This is the start of questions with hören (to hear) or zuhören (to listen). Context and reflexive pronouns change meaning: "Warum höre ich Ihnen noch zu?" = Why am I still listening to you? (zuhören + dative). "Warum höre ich nicht auf?" uses aufhören (to stop) with hören as part of the separable verb. Word order: in questions the verb comes second (here inverted as the verb follows 'warum'). Pronouns and particles (mir, dir, ihm, nicht, weiter) modify meaning.
target_language_example: Warum höre ich dir nach all den Jahren immer noch zu?
native_language_example: Why am I still listening to you after all these years?

meaning: 'why can' — used to ask why something is possible or why someone is allowed/able to do something
additional_notes: Combine 'warum' (why) with the modal verb 'kann' (can) to form a question about possibility, ability, permission, or justification. Word order: 'Warum kann' is followed by the subject and the verb infinitive or action. In English it corresponds to 'Why can...' or 'Why can't I/they...'. Often appears as 'Warum kann ich nicht...' for asking why one cannot do something.
target_language_example: Warum kann ich nicht einfach mit dir gehen?
native_language_example: Why can't I just go with you?

meaning: 'why are (you) coming' — the beginning of a question about someone's reason for coming
additional_notes: This is an informal/question fragment using the question word warum (why) plus the verb kommen in the 2nd person singular (kommst). In German questions the verb often comes right after the question word: Warum kommst du? (Why are you coming?). You can replace du with other pronouns or names: Warum kommt er? / Warum kommen Sie? Use du for informal you and Sie for formal.
target_language_example: Warum kommst du heute nicht zur Party?
native_language_example: Why aren't you coming to the party today?

meaning: 'why are (you) learning' — asks for the reason someone is learning something.
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a subject (du, ihr, Sie) and an object (e.g. Deutsch, Spanisch, eine Fremdsprache) or an adverb (so fleißig). Informal when using 'du' (Warum lernst du ...?). For polite form use 'Warum lernen Sie ...?'. Word order: question word 'warum' + verb (lern- conjugated) + subject.
target_language_example: Warum lernst du Deutsch?
native_language_example: Why are you learning German?

meaning: 'why are you (doing) ...' — begins a question asking why someone does something
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question with the verb machen (to do/make). In full questions you will usually add the rest: warum machst du ...? (informal singular 'you'). Depending on context, machen can mean 'do', 'make', 'act', or 'behave'. Word order: warum (why) + verb (machst) + subject (du) + rest. For formal or plural you would say 'warum machen Sie ...?' or 'warum macht ihr ...?'.
target_language_example: Warum machst du dir Sorgen?
native_language_example: Why are you worrying?

meaning: 'why do you like' (second person singular, informal)
additional_notes: Combines warum (why) + the verb mögen (to like). Magst is the du-form (informal you) of mögen used in questions about preferences. Often completed with a pronoun or noun: "Warum magst du das?" or followed by an infinitive/clause. In speech you may also hear "Warum magst du..." (explicit du) — dropping du is informal writing/speech when context is clear but typically you include the subject.
target_language_example: Warum magst du Schokolade?
native_language_example: Why do you like chocolate?

meaning: 'why do you have to' (asks for a reason someone must do something)
additional_notes: Combines the question word warum (why) with the conjugated modal verb musst (2nd person singular of müssen). Used to ask why someone is required or feels compelled to do something. Can be followed by an infinitive or a reflexive/other verb phrase (e.g. gehen, dir angucken, ein Buch lesen). Tone can be neutral, curious, or critical depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Warum musst du das immer machen?
native_language_example: Why do you always have to do that?

meaning: 'why do you have to' / 'why must you' (asks why someone always does something)
additional_notes: Used to question or complain about someone's repeated or habitual behaviour. Often followed by 'du' + verb (infinitive) or by an adjective/phrase. Tone can be annoyed, surprised, or curious depending on context. 'musst' is the 2nd person singular of 'müssen'.
target_language_example: Warum musst du immer so laut Musik hören?
native_language_example: Why do you always have to listen to music so loudly?

meaning: 'why do you want' (polite/familiar form, addressing 'du').
additional_notes: Combines 'warum' (why) + 'möchtest' (second-person singular subjunctive/polite form of 'mögen' used for desires). Used to ask someone's reason or motivation for wanting something or doing something. Can be used in neutral contexts (e.g., job, activities) and in sensitive/personal contexts (e.g., asking about serious intentions) — tone and context determine politeness and seriousness. Replace 'du' with 'Sie' + 'möchten' for formal address.
target_language_example: Warum möchtest du hier bleiben?
native_language_example: Why do you want to stay here?

meaning: 'why do you take' or 'why are you taking' (informal, second person singular)
additional_notes: Combination of Warum (why) + nimmst (2nd person singular present of nehmen = to take). Used to ask someone informally why they take, accept, or are doing something involving 'take'. Often continues with an object or clause: e.g. 'Warum nimmst du das?' or 'Warum nimmst du das Angebot an?' The full pronoun du is often included in standard sentences; in casual speech it might be omitted if context is clear, but grammatically 'nimmst' requires 'du' (or an implied 'du').
target_language_example: Warum nimmst du mein Buch?
native_language_example: Why are you taking my book?

meaning: 'why do you say...' (start of a question or clause asking for reason behind what someone said)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question or subordinate clause using the verb sagen (to say). In full sentences you'll usually see it as 'Warum sagst du ...?' (informal singular you) or 'Warum sagen Sie ...?' (formal). It asks for the reason or motivation for a statement. Word order: question form puts the verb second? Actually 'Warum sagst du ...?' has the question word first, verb second, subject after the verb.
target_language_example: Warum sagst du das?
native_language_example: Why do you say that?

meaning: 'why (does) ... say' — asks for the reason someone says or doesn't say something.
additional_notes: Combines warum (why) + sagt (3rd-person singular or polite/plural form of 'say'). Used to ask why a person or people say something (Warum sagt sie das? = Why does she say that?) or why someone doesn't speak (Warum sagt ihr nichts? = Why don't you [plural/informal] say anything?). Context and capitalization of 'Ihr/ihr' determine whether it's plural 'you' (Ihr) or 'they/she' (ihr). Word order: 'warum' + verb first in main clause, then subject.
target_language_example: Warum sagt er das so oft?
native_language_example: Why does he say that so often?

meaning: 'why are' (plural 'you')
additional_notes: Used to ask why a group of people (ihr) are in a certain state or doing something. 'seid' is the 2nd-person-plural form of 'sein' (to be). In spoken German 'ihr' is often omitted in short questions: 'Warum seid (ihr) so spät?' The structure: Warum + seid + ihr + (rest).
target_language_example: Warum seid ihr heute so müde?
native_language_example: Why are you (plural) so tired today?

meaning: why (do) [they/you/people] speak; asking for a reason someone speaks or says something
additional_notes: Combine warum (why) + sprechen (to speak). Used to ask why someone speaks, why people speak in a certain situation, or why a particular language is being used. Subject and verb order follow German question word order: Warum sprechen + subject? Verb bleiben conjugated as 'sprechen' changes with subject (sprichst, spricht, sprechen). Context determines subject (people, specific person, you).
target_language_example: Warum sprechen die Kinder während des Films?
native_language_example: Why are the children talking during the movie?

meaning: 'why are you speaking' (start of a question: 'why are you speaking...')
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question using the verb sprechen (to speak). It needs an ending to be a complete sentence, for example 'warum sprichst du?' (why are you speaking?), 'warum sprichst du so laut?' (why are you speaking so loudly?). 'Sprichst' is the 2nd-person singular present form used with 'du' (often dropped in spoken German) or in questions with 'Sie' the form is 'sprechen Sie'.
target_language_example: Warum sprichst du so schnell?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking so quickly?

meaning: 'why are you wearing' (beginning of a question)
additional_notes: This is the start of a question using the verb tragen (to wear/carry). You will normally see a complete sentence like "Warum trägst du das?" (Why are you wearing that?) or "Warum trägst du eine Jacke?" The verb will be conjugated to match the subject (trägst for du). Common subjects: ich trage, du trägst, er/sie/es trägt, wir tragen, ihr tragt, sie tragen.
target_language_example: Warum trägst du eine Sonnenbrille drinnen?
native_language_example: Why are you wearing sunglasses indoors?

meaning: 'why were' — a question asking for a reason about a past state or action (plural or formal 'you' / 'we').
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone (Sie plural/formal, wir, or sie) was in a certain state or place in the past. 'waren' is the past (Präteritum) of 'sein' for wir/Sie/sie. Use with different subjects (Warum warst du...? = singular informal). Often followed by a time/place or description.
target_language_example: Warum waren sie gestern so leise?
native_language_example: Why were they so quiet yesterday?

meaning: 'why were' (second person singular past of 'sein' — why were you...)
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone (du) was in a place, in a state, or did something in the past. 'Warst' is the past (Präteritum) form for 'du' of the verb 'sein' (to be). Common in questions: 'Warum warst du ...?' You can change the subject (er/sie war, wir waren) or tense as needed.
target_language_example: Warum warst du gestern nicht in der Schule?
native_language_example: Why were you not at school yesterday?

meaning: 'why does (someone) want' — used to ask for the reason someone wants or intends something
additional_notes: Combine warum (why) with a conjugated verb (here: will = wants/wants to) to ask why a person wants or intends something. Often followed by a clause introduced by dass (that) or by an infinitive phrase. In questions about other people, use the correct conjugation (z. B. warum will ich / warum willst du / warum will er/sie/es).
target_language_example: Warum will Anna das nicht kaufen?
native_language_example: Why does Anna not want to buy that?

meaning: why do you want (to)
additional_notes: A question phrase used to ask someone's reason or motivation for wanting to do something. 'Willst' is the 2nd-person singular of 'wollen' (to want). The infinitive or action follows (e.g. 'werden', 'hin', 'arbeiten', 'wohnen', 'reden'). In polite/formal contexts use 'warum wollen Sie ...' instead.
target_language_example: Warum willst du nach Berlin ziehen?
native_language_example: Why do you want to move to Berlin?

meaning: 'why are you taking (something) off' / 'why are you putting (something) on' — start of a question using the verb ziehen (to pull/put on/off) in 2nd person singular.
additional_notes: Ziehst is the 2nd-person singular (du) present form of ziehen. With a reflexive pronoun (dich) it means 'to undress' ('sich ausziehen' = to take off clothes). With a direct object (die Jacke, die Kinder, es) it can mean 'to put on' (anziehen) or 'to take off' (ausziehen) depending on context and particles: ausziehen = take off, anziehen = put on. 'Warum ziehst ...?' begins a question asking for the reason someone is putting something on or taking it off. Word order: 'Warum ziehst du ...?'
target_language_example: Warum ziehst du die Schuhe aus?
native_language_example: Why are you taking off your shoes?

meaning: 'why that' — used to ask or refer to the reason for something (i.e. 'why this/that happened').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions or statements about causes. 'Warum' = why; 'das' refers to a previously mentioned event or situation. In spoken German you may also hear 'warum das so ist' (why it is like that). Word order can change in questions: 'Warum ist das passiert?'
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, warum das passiert ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why that happened?

meaning: 'why (you) that' — asks for the reason someone does or thinks something
additional_notes: This phrase combines warum (why) + du (you) + das (that/it). It's used in everyday speech to ask or refer to the reason someone did, wants, asks, or thinks something. In full questions the word order normally becomes "warum tust du das?" or "warum fragst du das?" but "warum du das" appears in statements or embedded clauses (e.g. "Ich weiß, warum du das fragst") or in imperative contexts as a direct request ("Erklär mir, warum du das tust"). "Das" can refer to an action, statement, or thing mentioned earlier.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, warum du das gemacht hast?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why you did that?

meaning: 'why you did that' (part of a question or clause asking for a reason).
additional_notes: This phrase is used inside larger sentences to ask or state the reason someone did something. In full sentences it usually appears with the auxiliary verb (e.g. 'hast') at the end: 'warum du das getan hast'. Use it for reported questions or explanations ("I want to know why you did that"). It is neutral and can be used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Er hat mir endlich gesagt, warum du das getan hast.
native_language_example: He finally told me why you did that.

meaning: 'why it' or 'why he/she/they' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Combines the question word warum (why) with the neutral pronoun es. Es can stand for 'it' or be a placeholder subject (expletive) when the true subject is a clause or when gender/number is clear from context (e.g., 'warum es weine' = 'why she/ he is crying' in reported speech). English translation depends on context and speaker: sometimes 'it', sometimes 'he/she/they', or a clause like 'why that is the case.' Often appears in indirect questions (introduced by verbs like fragen, wissen, erklären).
target_language_example: Er fragte mich, warum es gestern so spät wurde.
native_language_example: He asked me why it got so late yesterday.

meaning: something / some of it (colloquial) — used to mean 'something' or 'a share' (often unspecified amount or portion).
additional_notes: Colloquial German. 'was' = 'something'; 'ab' here helps express receiving, getting, taking away, or collecting a portion. Common in spoken language: "was abkriegen" (to get/get some of it), "was abholen" (to pick something up). Exact sense depends on verb: e.g. "was abkriegen" = to receive or suffer (often negative: 'get it'), "was abholen" = to pick up something, "jemandem was abgeben" = give someone a share. Not formal.
target_language_example: Ich hole nur was ab.
native_language_example: I'm just picking up something.

meaning: colloquial: 'something' or 'anything' (used in questions about objects, possessions, changes, or earnings)
additional_notes: Informal spoken German. 'was' = 'something/anything'; 'an' attaches to verbs or nouns to ask if there is something related to that topic (e.g. something in the way of furniture, something on the facade, something to eat). Often appears in dialects/colloquial speech instead of more standard forms like 'etwas' or rephrased questions. Word order and exact meaning depend on the verb: e.g. 'was an Möbeln' = 'anything in the way of furniture', 'was an der Fassade gemacht' = 'done something to the façade', 'was an Süßigkeiten' = 'interested in/has any sweets', 'was an deinen Zeichnungen verdienen' = 'earn anything from your drawings'.
target_language_example: Hast du noch was an Büchern für die Prüfung?
native_language_example: Do you still have any books for the exam?

meaning: 'something' or 'anything' + prepositional phrase (e.g. 'something on...'); used to ask if there is/was something in/on/about X
additional_notes: Colloquial use of 'was' (short for 'etwas') combined with a preposition (here 'auf') and a noun. The exact meaning depends on the noun after 'auf' and the context: e.g. 'was auf dem Kopf?' = 'something on your head?', 'was auf dem Herzen?' = 'something on your heart' (i.e. bothering you). Often used in questions ('Hast du was auf ...?') and informal speech. 'Was' here is informal; the full form is 'etwas auf...'.
target_language_example: Hast du noch was auf dem Computer gespeichert?
native_language_example: Do you still have something saved on the computer?

meaning: 'something' in the context of 'notice something' or 'find/come across something' depending on the verb (often part of verbs like 'auffallen', 'aufheben', 'aufspüren').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but appears after verbs that combine with 'auf' (separable prefix). Common uses in the examples: 'fällt (dir) was auf?' = 'do you notice anything?'; 'heb(t) mir was auf' = 'save/keep something for me' or 'pick something up for me' depending on context; 'spüren wir was auf' = 'do we detect/find something?'. Word order: with separable-prefix verbs in present/simple clauses the prefix 'auf' is separated and placed at the end. 'was' here means 'something' (informal).
target_language_example: Fällt dir was auf an dem Foto?
native_language_example: Do you notice anything about the photo?

meaning: 'something' + preposition 'in/the' — used colloquially to say 'something is going on/there is something in...'
additional_notes: A colloquial/informal combination of 'was' (something) and a following preposition with the definite article (im = in dem). Common in phrases like 'was im Busch' (something's up), 'was im Gange' (something is underway), or literal uses like 'was im Gesicht' (something on your face). Tone is informal; meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, da ist was im Gange.
native_language_example: I think something is going on there.

meaning: 'what does (someone) do' or part of questions like 'what's the matter/what can (I) do?'
additional_notes: Literally 'what does'. Appears in questions or clauses with a verb following (e.g., 'was tut er?' = 'what is he doing?'). Also used in set phrases like 'Was tut man?' ('What do you do?') or in polite offers 'Was tut ich Ihnen?' (less common). In spoken German you more often hear full forms like 'Was macht...?' instead of 'was tut...'.
target_language_example: Was tut er jetzt?
native_language_example: What is he doing now?

meaning: 'something of/from' or 'some (part) of'
additional_notes: Common colloquial contraction of 'etwas von' or 'etwas vom' (etwas + dem). Used in spoken German to mean 'something of/from' or to offer/ask for a share. Often appears before nouns (was vom Essen, was vom Weihnachtsmann) or in questions (Hast du noch nie was vom ... gehört?). Informal register.
target_language_example: Willst du was vom Kuchen?
native_language_example: Do you want some of the cake?

meaning: 'to know something' or in questions/phrases 'anything'/'something' (colloquial)
additional_notes: Colloquial use of 'was' instead of 'etwas'. Often appears in questions (Sollte ich noch was wissen? = Should I know anything else?) or statements implying someone has information. Informal; common in spoken German. Use 'etwas wissen' in more formal contexts.
target_language_example: Sag mir, wenn du noch was wissen willst.
native_language_example: Tell me if you want to know anything else.

meaning: something to
additional_notes: A common colloquial pattern where was often stands for etwas (“something”), especially before zu + infinitive or a noun phrase: was zu sagen = something to say, was zu Weihnachten = something for Christmas. In questions, was can still keep its literal meaning “what,” as in Wer hat was zu wem gesagt? This is common in speech; etwas is more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch was zu erledigen.
native_language_example: I still have something to take care of.

meaning: 'something to say' or 'anything to say' (literally: 'what to say').
additional_notes: Used when referring to having an opinion, comment, or something to tell. Common in questions or statements like 'Hast du was zu sagen?' (Do you have something to say?) or 'Er hat nichts zu sagen.' (He has nothing to say). Informal contraction: 'was' stands for 'etwas'.
target_language_example: Hast du noch was zu sagen?
native_language_example: Do you still have something to say?

meaning: what kind of
additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask about the type or kind of something: "Was für Musik...?" = "What kind of music...?" In exclamations, often with "ein/eine", it means "what a ...!": "Was für eine schöne Burg!" = "What a beautiful castle!" It does not mean English "what for?".
target_language_example: Was für Bücher liest du gern?
native_language_example: What kind of books do you like to read?

meaning: what kind of a
additional_notes: used before a noun to ask about the type of something: Was für ein Buch? = 'What kind of book?' In exclamations, it means 'what a': Was für ein Chaos! The article changes with gender, case, and number, for example was für eine, was für einen, or just was für in the plural.
target_language_example: Was für ein Auto fährt sie?
native_language_example: What kind of car does she drive?

meaning: 'what if' — used to introduce a hypothetical or possible situation.
additional_notes: Common in questions and conditional thoughts. Can start a sentence: 'Was, wenn ...?' or appear in embedded clauses: 'Ich frage mich, was wenn ...'. Often followed by a clause describing the hypothetical outcome. Informal register is acceptable in speech; in formal writing, alternatives like 'angenommen, dass' or 'falls' may be used depending on structure.
target_language_example: Was wenn es morgen regnet?
native_language_example: What if it rains tomorrow?

meaning: 'what you saw' (polite/formal address)
additional_notes: Used to refer to something the listener (formal Sie) observed. Often appears in questions or instructions asking for details about an event (e.g., eyewitness reports, police statements, news). The full clause usually includes a verb at the end (e.g., 'was Sie gesehen haben'). Word order in German places the verb at the end in subordinate clauses.
target_language_example: Bitte erzählen Sie mir genau, was Sie gesehen haben.
native_language_example: Please tell me exactly what you saw.

meaning: 'what you did' (formal singular or plural)
additional_notes: A short clause often used after verbs like wissen, sehen, erklären, fragen, etc. 'Sie' here is the formal 'you' (capitalized). Can appear in questions or statements: e.g. 'Ich weiß nicht, was Sie getan haben.' In spoken German the verb may move to the end of the clause ('haben' in that example). For informal 'you' use 'was du getan'.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was Sie getan haben.
native_language_example: I don't know what you did.

meaning: 'what you can' — referring to the things someone is able to do
additional_notes: Used to tell or describe that someone should do or learn the things they are capable of. Common in imperatives (Bitte tun Sie, was Sie können!) or statements about effort (Ich tue, was ich kann, und Sie tun, was Sie können). Formal/polite because of the polite pronoun Sie. Replace Sie with du/ich/wir as needed (was du kannst, was ich kann).
target_language_example: Tun Sie, was Sie können, und geben Sie Ihr Bestes.
native_language_example: Do what you can and do your best.

meaning: 'whatever' / 'whatever it is' / 'anything you like' (used to indicate indifference or an unknown thing).
additional_notes: Can express indifference (Macht, was auch immer ihr wollt — Do whatever you want) or refer to an unknown/unspecified thing or outcome (Was auch immer das ist — Whatever that is). Often used at the start of a clause: 'Was auch immer ...'. Tone ranges from neutral to dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Mach was auch immer nötig ist, um das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: Do whatever is necessary to solve the problem.

meaning: 'whatever happens' or 'no matter what happens'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that will not change the speaker's instruction, promise or warning. Often placed at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma. Equivalent to 'no matter what' in English.
target_language_example: Was auch passiert, bleib bei mir.
native_language_example: Whatever happens, stay with me.

meaning: 'what may' / 'what may I/you...?' — polite way to ask what someone wants or is allowed to do
additional_notes: Common in polite questions or offers. Often followed by verbs like sein (be), ich (I) + verb, or an infinitive: e.g. "Was darf es sein?" (What can I get you?/What would you like?), "Was darf ich Ihnen anbieten?" (What may I offer you?). Can also ask about permission: "Was darf ich essen?" (What am I allowed to eat?). Tone is polite/formal or neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Was darf ich Ihnen empfehlen?
native_language_example: What may I recommend for you?

meaning: 'what do (you) think' — start of a question asking for someone's opinion
additional_notes: Usually appears in questions like "Was denkst du (darüber)?" or "Na, was denkst du denn?" Use with a subject (du, ihr, Sie) or follow with a prepositional phrase (darüber, davon). Common in casual and neutral speech.
target_language_example: Was denkst du darüber?
native_language_example: What do you think about that?

meaning: adds emphasis to a question — roughly 'what (on earth/then/now)?' or 'what exactly?'.
additional_notes: Used to make a question more emphatic, surprised, irritated, or to ask for clarification. Tone and context change nuance: neutral curiosity ('Was denn für ein Kuchen?' = 'What kind of cake?'), mild surprise ('Was denn, sie hat kein Kind erwartet?' = 'What, she didn't expect a child?'), or irritation ('Was denn, sind Sie taub?' = 'What, are you deaf?'). Often paired with other words (für, zum Beispiel, interjections). Informal when used with slang or rude tone (e.g. 'Was denn, Bro?').
target_language_example: Was denn für ein Film läuft heute?
native_language_example: What kind of film is playing today?

meaning: what you (to yourself) / what you wish for (literally: 'what you to yourself')
additional_notes: Common phrase used when talking about someone's desires, wishes, or things they imagine for themselves. 'Dir' is the dative pronoun (to you/for you) and often appears in reflexive constructions like 'vorstellen' (sich etwas vorstellen) or 'wünschen' (sich etwas wünschen). In English it usually becomes 'what you (wish for)' or 'what you imagine.' The exact translation depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Weißt du schon, was du dir wünschst?
native_language_example: Do you already know what you wish for?

meaning: 'what you said' (a clause referring to something the other person said).
additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger clause: 'was du gesagt hast' (with the auxiliary verb 'hast' for perfect tense) or 'was du gesagt' + verb for completion. Used to report, quote, ask about, or evaluate someone's words. Can begin a sentence ('Was du gesagt hast, ...') to comment on or judge those words. In questions you usually add the auxiliary verb: 'Kannst du wiederholen, was du gesagt hast?'.
target_language_example: Was du gesagt hast, war sehr hilfreich.
native_language_example: What you said was very helpful.

meaning: 'what you saw' (part of a sentence asking or reporting what someone saw).
additional_notes: This is a clause used to ask or report about someone's visual observation. In German sentences it usually appears with a finite verb (e.g. 'hast') — full form: 'was du gesehen hast'. Word order changes in questions and subordinate clauses: 'Erzähl, was du gesehen hast.' or in reported statement fronted: 'Was du gesehen hast, war ...'. Use with past participle 'gesehen' and appropriate auxiliary 'haben' (hast/hatte).
target_language_example: Sag mir, was du gesehen hast.
native_language_example: Tell me what you saw.

meaning: 'what you ... in/at' — the start of a subordinate clause asking or stating what someone did or saw in a place (im = in dem).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but the beginning of many sentences: 'was du im + [Ort] + gemacht/gesehen/gesagt hast' (what you did/saw/said in the ...). 'im' is a contraction of 'in dem' (masculine/neuter dative). Use the correct past participle and auxiliary (haben) to complete the clause.
target_language_example: Er fragt, was du im Kino gesehen hast.
native_language_example: He's asking what you saw in the cinema.

meaning: 'what (you) ... in/at' — introduces a clause asking or talking about what someone did, has, or put somewhere (in a place or time).
additional_notes: Common in questions or statements that report/ask about actions or possessions tied to a location or period. Followed by a noun phrase indicating place or time (e.g., in Hawaii, in der Tasche, in den Sommerferien) and a verb in past or present tense. In English it corresponds to phrases like "what you did in...", "what you have in...", or "what you were doing in...".
target_language_example: Erzähl mir, was du in Berlin gemacht hast.
native_language_example: Tell me what you did in Berlin.

meaning: 'what you (want to) say' or 'what you are going to say'.
additional_notes: Part of a common subordinate clause introduced by 'was' (what) + subject 'du' + verb 'sagen'. In German word order, the full clause often ends with the conjugated verb (e.g. 'was du sagen willst' = 'what you want to say', 'was du sagen wirst' = 'what you will say'). Used to refer to someone's words or intention to speak. Can be followed by modal verbs (wirst, willst) or imperative verbs (Sag ...).
target_language_example: Erzähl mir einfach, was du sagen willst.
native_language_example: Just tell me what you want to say.

meaning: "what he said" (used to refer to something a male person said)
additional_notes: A relative clause phrase introduced by 'was' (what) referring to previously mentioned or implied speech. Commonly completed as 'was er gesagt hat' (what he said has/said). Can be used in questions (Glaubt ihr, was er gesagt hat?) and statements (Alles, was er gesagt hat...). Replace 'er' with another pronoun or noun to change the subject (was sie gesagt, was Maria gesagt).
target_language_example: Hast du gehört, was er gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Did you hear what he said?

meaning: 'what he (has) to' / 'what he should' (do or say).
additional_notes: Usually part of a larger clause: 'was er zu tun hat' (what he has to do), 'was er zu sagen hat' (what he has to say). Expresses obligation, expected action, or content someone should say. Word order and tense of the main clause change the tense of 'zu ... haben' (hat / hatte / haben wird etc.).
target_language_example: Sie weiß jetzt, was er zu tun hat.
native_language_example: She now knows what he has to do.

meaning: 'what do you expect' (start of a question asking someone's expectations)
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone expects from a person, situation, or action. Often followed by a subject (du, ihr, von mir, von uns) or a clause (dass ...). Can sound neutral or slightly annoyed depending on tone and context. Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Was erwartest du eigentlich von mir?
native_language_example: What do you actually expect from me?

meaning: 'what do (you) find' or 'what do (you) think' (in questions asking for an opinion).
additional_notes: Commonly used at the start of questions to ask someone's opinion about something: 'Was findest du ...?' = 'What do you think of ...?' The verb following depends on subject and tense (du findest, ihr findet, Sie finden). In spoken German you may hear shortened forms like 'Was findest du?' or 'Was findest'n ...?'.
target_language_example: Was findest du von dem neuen Film?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new movie?

meaning: 'what pleases' or 'what (someone) likes' (used to ask or state what is pleasing to someone).
additional_notes: Derived from the verb gefallen (to please). Commonly appears in subordinate clauses or questions and requires a dative pronoun or noun to indicate who is pleased (e.g. was gefällt dir? / was gefällt ihm?). Word order and choice of pronoun determine the subject of 'pleases'. Used in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Sag mir, was gefällt dir?
native_language_example: Tell me, what pleases you?

meaning: what's happening / what's up / what matters (depends on context).
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase with two main uses: 1) As a casual greeting or slang question meaning "What's up?" (e.g. "Was geht ab, Leute?"). 2) As a neutral/neutral‑formal question meaning "what's going on?" or "what is happening here?" (e.g. "Was geht hier vor sich?"). In sentence 1 it appears in the sense "that has substance/meaning" ("in dem es um was geht" = "in which something important happens/which has a point"). Tone can be informal; can be rude if used with insults. Not appropriate for very formal settings when used as a greeting.
target_language_example: Was geht ab? Hast du Lust, heute Abend was zu unternehmen?
native_language_example: What's up? Do you want to do something tonight?

meaning: 'what is there' / 'what's up' / 'what is/are (available or happening)'.
additional_notes: A common conversational phrase used to ask what's happening, what's available, what's new, or what there is to do/eat. Context determines exact translation: e.g. asking for news (What's new?), asking about food (What's for dinner?), or asking if there's a problem (What's going on?/What's to be clarified?). Can be followed by a noun or left alone.
target_language_example: Was gibt es heute zum Abendessen?
native_language_example: What's for dinner today?

meaning: what do (you) think of ... / how do (you) feel about ...
additional_notes: Used to ask for opinions. Commonly appears as 'Was haltet ihr von ...?' (informal plural 'you') or 'Was halten Sie von ...?' (formal). The verb is 'halten von' + dative. For singular informal use 'Was hältst du von ...?'.
target_language_example: Was haltet ihr von einem Spaziergang am Nachmittag?
native_language_example: What do you think about a walk this afternoon?

meaning: what do you have
additional_notes: A question beginning with was + hast usually means “what do you have ... ?”, most often with du: Was hast du ...? In patterns like Was hast du vor?, the full verb is vorhaben, so it means “what are you planning?” or “what are you up to?”.
target_language_example: Was hast du in deiner Tasche?
native_language_example: What do you have in your bag?

meaning: "what's going on here" or "what's happening here".
additional_notes: Used to ask about the situation or events in the current place or context. Common in questions and requests for explanation; can be neutral or show surprise/confusion depending on tone. Often appears as part of a full phrase: "was hier los ist" or simply "Was hier los?"
target_language_example: Könnt ihr mir sagen, was hier los ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what's going on here?

meaning: 'all the things I (have/know/did/etc.)' — used to emphasize a list of things related to the speaker (often with surprise or exaggeration).
additional_notes: Often appears in spoken German before a noun phrase, verb phrase, or clause to emphasize the quantity, variety, or unexpectedness of things connected to the speaker. Common in expressions like „was ich alles erlebt habe“ (all the things I've experienced) or „was ich alles vergessen habe“ (all the things I forgot). Tone can be surprised, frustrated, amused, or boastful depending on context.
target_language_example: Du glaubst nicht, was ich alles vergessen habe.
native_language_example: You won't believe all the things I forgot.

meaning: 'what I said' (refers to speech or instructions previously expressed).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the speaker has said. Often appears in clauses like 'alles, was ich gesagt habe' (everything I said) or commands 'tu, was ich gesagt habe' (do what I said). The full phrase in sentences usually includes the auxiliary verb (habe/hatte) or follows a word like 'alles' or 'das'.
target_language_example: Hör auf, was ich gesagt habe, und komm zurück.
native_language_example: Listen to what I said and come back.

meaning: 'what I saw' (part of a clause — incomplete without a verb or ending)
additional_notes: This is a fragment meaning 'what I saw'. In German you normally use it inside a larger sentence, often followed by a verb or the rest of the clause, e.g. 'was ich gesehen habe' = 'what I saw' or 'what I have seen'. Word order and verb placement matter: in subordinate clauses the verb goes to the end. Can appear in questions or statements: 'Weißt du, was ich gesehen habe?' (Do you know what I saw?).
target_language_example: Weißt du, was ich gesehen habe?
native_language_example: Do you know what I saw?

meaning: 'what I (did/said/heard/etc.) yesterday' — introduces something the speaker did, said, heard, or experienced the day before.
additional_notes: Common in questions and statements to refer to a specific action, event, or information from yesterday. Can be used with different verbs (gehört, getan, gesagt, gemacht). In spoken German, 'gestern Abend' (yesterday evening) is often added for time specificity. When used in imperative/request forms (Rate mal..., Raten Sie mal...), it invites the listener to guess.
target_language_example: Weißt du, was ich gestern gemacht habe?
native_language_example: Do you know what I did yesterday?

meaning: 'what I did' or 'what I have done'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to actions the speaker performed. Commonly appears in subordinate clauses (e.g. "das, was ich getan habe") or as a short phrase in speech. Tense can be adjusted with the auxiliary verb (e.g. "was ich getan habe" = present perfect, "was ich tat" = simple past).
target_language_example: Er weiß nicht, was ich getan habe.
native_language_example: He doesn't know what I did.

meaning: what I (am) here (for) / what I have here — depends on context
additional_notes: A short phrase combining a question or relative pronoun + 'ich' + 'hier'. Used either as part of a relative clause ('what I have/started here') or in questions/commands about one's purpose or action in the current place ('what I am doing/should do here'). English translation varies by context: 'what I (am) doing here', 'what I should do here', 'what I have here'.
target_language_example: Ich möchte beenden, was ich hier begonnen habe.
native_language_example: I want to finish what I started here.

meaning: 'what I ... in/at' — a fragment introducing a clause about something the speaker did, found, wanted, etc., with a following noun or time/place (e.g. im Vertrag, im Garten, im Zorn, im letzten Sommer).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but the beginning of a subordinate clause: 'was' (what/that which) + 'ich' (I) + 'im' (in + definite article 'dem' contracted). It is followed by a noun or noun phrase indicating location, time, or context (im Garten = in the garden; im Vertrag = in the contract; im Zorn = in anger). Use to report actions, findings, wishes, or events. Word order: the verb for the subordinate clause goes to the end (e.g. 'was ich im Garten gefunden habe').
target_language_example: Seht mal, was ich im Garten gefunden habe!
native_language_example: Look what I found in the garden!

meaning: "what I (to myself)" — used to introduce something the speaker imagines, hopes for, wishes for, or expects.
additional_notes: Common in phrases like "was ich mir vorstelle/erhofft/gewünscht habe". "Mir" is a dative reflexive pronoun here and often part of verbs like vorstellen, wünschen, erhoffen. English translations vary: "what I imagine," "what I hoped for," "what I want/wish for."
target_language_example: Was ich mir wünsche, ist ein langes Wochenende.
native_language_example: What I want is a long weekend.

meaning: what I (should) do with / what to do with (someone or something).
additional_notes: Common in sentences where the speaker is unsure or explains actions involving a person or thing. Often appears in longer constructions like "ich weiß nicht, was ich mit ... (anfangen/ machen/ tun soll)" (I don't know what to do with ...). Can be followed by a pronoun/noun and a verb phrase. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich mit dem alten Stuhl machen soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what to do with the old chair.

meaning: 'what I still (have/do)' — refers to something remaining that the speaker has, knows, can do, or needs to do.
additional_notes: Common phrase fragment used to talk about what remains (knowledge, possessions, options, actions). Often appears in sentences like "alles, was ich noch..." (everything I still...), "weiß nicht, was ich noch tun soll" (don't know what else to do). The word 'noch' means 'still', 'yet', or 'else' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich noch sagen soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what else I should say.

meaning: 'what I have to say' or 'what I want to say'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the things someone wants or needs to express. Common in commands or statements: "Hör (mir) zu, was ich zu sagen habe" = "Listen to what I have to say." Often followed by a verb (habe/hatte) to indicate tense.
target_language_example: Hör bitte zu, was ich zu sagen habe.
native_language_example: Please listen to what I have to say.

meaning: 'what you (plural) have done' or 'what you did'.
additional_notes: Used to refer to actions that a group of people (ihr = you plural) performed. Commonly appears in reported clauses or questions: e.g. Tom weiß, was ihr getan habt (Tom knows what you did). In spoken German the full phrase often includes the auxiliary: 'was ihr getan habt'. Use with 'ihr' (plural familiar). For formal or singular you would use 'was Sie getan haben' (formal) or 'was du getan hast' (singular familiar).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, was ihr getan habt?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you (all) did?

meaning: 'what ... in the' — introduces a clause about what is happening/was happening inside or within something (feminine noun in dative or prepositional phrases).
additional_notes: Used to ask or describe what is happening, happened, or exists 'in' a specific feminine noun or with certain prepositions that require 'der' (e.g., 'in der ersten Runde', 'in der Welt', 'in der Höhle'). 'Was' = 'what'; 'in der' is the preposition + definite article (dative feminine). Combine with the rest of the phrase: 'was in der ... passiert/geschah/ist'. For masculine/neuter nouns the article changes (in dem → 'im' or 'in dem'), so watch the gender.
target_language_example: Er fragte, was in der Schule los war.
native_language_example: He asked what was going on in the school.

meaning: what happened
additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or change — requests information about something that occurred. Informal/neutral everyday question. Can be used in past context (Perfekt). Common short form: "Was ist denn passiert?" to express surprise or concern.
target_language_example: Was ist passiert? Du siehst so besorgt aus.
native_language_example: What happened? You look so worried.

meaning: what's going on
additional_notes: Casual phrase used to ask about a situation or someone's wellbeing. Can mean 'what's happening?' (neutral) or 'what's the matter?' (concerned), depending on tone/context. Common in spoken German; often used with a name or informal address (e.g., Bruder).
target_language_example: Was ist los mit dir? Du wirkst traurig.
native_language_example: What's wrong with you? You seem sad.

meaning: What's wrong with you? / What's the matter with you? / How are you (doing)?
additional_notes: A common question to ask when someone seems upset, sick, confused, or behaving strangely. Tone and context determine whether it's caring (What's wrong?) or confrontational (What's wrong with you?). Can also be used neutrally as 'And what about you?' when preceded by 'Und'. Informal pronoun 'dir' (du).
target_language_example: Du siehst blass aus — was ist mit dir?
native_language_example: You look pale — what's wrong with you?

meaning: 'what on earth' / 'what in the world' (adds emphasis to a question about something strange or worrying).
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, concern or exasperation about a person, situation or thing. Usually followed by 'los' and a dative object (e.g. 'mit dir', 'mit der Welt'). The word 'nur' here is an intensifier — it doesn't mean 'only'. Tone can be worried, annoyed or incredulous depending on context.
target_language_example: Was ist nur mit dir los?
native_language_example: What on earth is wrong with you?

meaning: 'what are you cooking' (informal, singular/plural depending on context)
additional_notes: Colloquial question formed from 'was' (what) + 'kochst' (you cook / are you cooking). Used to ask someone what they are cooking now or what they usually cook. With tone/context it can be casual curiosity or planning (e.g., asking what to expect for a meal). For formal situations or polite speech, use 'Was kochen Sie?'.
target_language_example: Was kochst du heute Abend?
native_language_example: What are you cooking tonight?

meaning: what am I doing
additional_notes: Usually seen in the pattern Was mache ich ...? It can express confusion about your current actions ('what am I doing...?') or uncertainty about what to do next ('what do I do?' / 'what should I do?'). Words like bloß, eigentlich, and nur add emphasis, surprise, or frustration.
target_language_example: Was mache ich jetzt ohne mein Handy?
native_language_example: What do I do now without my phone?

meaning: 'what one/you/people (in general) ... from' — introduces what is expected, possible, or demanded from someone or something.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to introduce a clause about expectations, possibilities, demands, or what can be seen/obtained from a place or person. 'Man' is the impersonal pronoun meaning 'one' or 'people' (similar to 'you' in general usage). Depending on context, it can refer to general expectations (was man von jemandem erwartet), what you can see (was man von hier sieht/hat), or what is demanded of someone (was man von ihm verlangte). For a specific person, German often uses 'was man von ihm/ihr erwartet' or 'was von ihm/ihr verlangt wird'.
target_language_example: Überleg dir, was man von dir im neuen Job erwartet.
native_language_example: Think about what is expected of you in the new job.

meaning: 'what has ever happened to me' / 'what ever happened to me' used to say something is the best/worst thing that has happened to someone
additional_notes: Often appears in superlative phrases like "das Beste, was mir je passiert ist" (the best thing that has ever happened to me). 'je' means 'ever' and emphasizes the entire life up to now. Commonly used in emotional or evaluative statements. Structure: das/etwas + (Adj/Superlative), + was mir je passiert (ist).
target_language_example: Dein Brief war das Schönste, was mir je passiert ist.
native_language_example: Your letter was the most wonderful thing that ever happened to me.

meaning: what do (you) say
additional_notes: A conversational phrase used to ask for someone's opinion or reaction. Commonly appears as part of questions: 'Was sagst du?' (What do you say?/What do you think?), 'Was sagst du dazu?' (What do you think about that?). The subject (du) can be omitted in casual speech. Context determines whether it's asking for a decision, opinion, or confirmation.
target_language_example: Was sagst du dazu, gehen wir jetzt?
native_language_example: What do you think about it — shall we go now?

meaning: How much do I owe (someone)? / What do I owe (someone)?
additional_notes: Used when asking how much money or debt you owe a person (formal or informal). 'Was schulde ich Ihnen?' is formal (Ihnen). 'Was schulde ich dir?' would be informal. Can also refer to owing something non-monetary in context (a favor), but usually about payment. Word order: 'Was schulde ich ...?'
target_language_example: Was schulde ich Ihnen für das Abendessen?
native_language_example: How much do I owe you for the dinner?

meaning: 'what' or 'everything that' (followed by a verb or noun phrase referring to actions or things that 'she' did or provided).
additional_notes: Combines the relative/interrogative 'was' (what/that which) with 'sie' (she/they/formal you) and the preposition 'für' (for). Context decides meaning: often introduces a relative clause meaning 'what/that which she did for (someone)' or a free relative 'what she considers' when followed by an adjective (e.g. 'was sie für richtig hielt' = 'what she thought was right'). 'Sie' can be third-person singular/plural or formal 'you' (Sie) — use context to tell which. Word order follows German clause rules (verb usually at the end of the clause).
target_language_example: Danke für alles, was sie für mich getan hat.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything she did for me.

meaning: what they/she have/has to (do/say/expect/etc.).
additional_notes: A clause starter: ‚was‘ = 'what' and ‚sie‘ = 'she' or 'they' (context decides). ‚zu + infinitive/verb phrase‘ expresses obligation, possibility, or the infinitive concept (e.g. to do, to say, to expect). In English this often becomes 'what she/they have to...' or 'what she/they are to...' or simply 'what she/they ...'. Choose singular/plural meaning of 'sie' from context.
target_language_example: Erzähl mir, was sie zu sagen haben.
native_language_example: Tell me what they have to say.

meaning: 'what's that supposed to mean?' or 'what's going on?' (expresses surprise, annoyance, or demand for an explanation)
additional_notes: Used to question or challenge an action, situation, or remark. Tone can be annoyed, surprised, or incredulous depending on context and intonation. Can be standalone ('Was soll das?') or followed by more detail ('Was soll das mit ...?'). Common in informal and neutral spoken German.
target_language_example: Was soll das? Er hat mein Buch einfach genommen.
native_language_example: What's that supposed to mean? He just took my book.

meaning: what should
additional_notes: A common question pattern with was + sollten. It asks what someone should do, expect, say, build, etc. Depending on context, sollten can mean advice ('should') or expectation/plan ('were supposed to'). In rhetorical questions, it can also suggest doubt or frustration.
target_language_example: Was sollten wir jetzt machen?
native_language_example: What should we do now?

meaning: 'what are you standing (doing) / why are you just standing there?'
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is standing idle or not doing anything. Common in spoken German; often appears as 'Was stehst du da?' or with colloquial 'rum' instead of 'da herum'. Can sound impatient or annoyed depending on tone. Add 'wie angewurzelt' to emphasize someone is frozen in place.
target_language_example: Was stehst du da und wartest? Geh rein!
native_language_example: What are you standing there waiting for? Go inside!

meaning: 'what (are you/we/they) looking for?'; a question asking what someone is searching for or seeking.
additional_notes: Common question form using 'was' (what) + verb 'suchen' (to look for/search). Verb conjugates with the subject (e.g., Was suchst du? Was suchen Sie? Was sucht er?). Can be used literally (looking for an object/place) or figuratively (seeking information, purpose). Formal vs. informal: 'Sie' is formal; use 'du' with friends.
target_language_example: Was suchen Sie in meinem Apartment?
native_language_example: What are you looking for in my apartment?

meaning: 'what are you looking (for)' (informal, singular 'du' form).
additional_notes: Shortened phrase from the question 'Was suchst du?' Used in casual spoken German to ask someone what they are looking for (literally: 'what search'). The subject 'du' (you) is omitted when addressing someone directly. For formal or plural you would use 'Was suchen Sie?' or 'Was sucht ihr?'.
target_language_example: Was suchst du denn?
native_language_example: What are you looking for, then?

meaning: 'what are you wearing' (informal, second person singular or plural depending on context)
additional_notes: Shortened form of the question using the verb tragen (to wear). Commonly appears in questions like "Was trägst du?" (What are you wearing?) or "Was tragt ihr?" (What are you wearing? — plural). Alone "was trägst" is incomplete; it needs a subject (du, ihr, Sie) or context. Used to ask about clothes, accessories, or items someone has on.
target_language_example: Was trägst du heute zur Arbeit?
native_language_example: What are you wearing to work today?

meaning: what would you do
additional_notes: A conditional question asking what someone would do in a hypothetical situation. Uses the conditional form (würdest/tätest) in German; here tätest is the 2nd person singular subjunctive II of tun. Commonly followed by a clause describing the hypothetical (e.g. wenn..., in dieser Situation). Can be used with names (Was tätest du, Tom?)
target_language_example: Was tätest du, wenn du im Ausland leben müsstest?
native_language_example: What would you do if you had to live abroad?

meaning: 'what are (you) trying (to...)' — used to ask what someone is attempting or implying
additional_notes: This is the start of a question: usually followed by an infinitive or prepositional phrase (e.g. 'was versuchst du zu sagen?'). It can ask about an action (trying to do/achieve) or about an intention/implication (what someone means). Informal or neutral depending on tone; often used in confrontational or puzzled contexts.
target_language_example: Was versuchst du mir damit zu sagen?
native_language_example: What are you trying to tell me with that?

meaning: 'what ... is trying (to ...)' — used to ask what someone is attempting or intending to do/say
additional_notes: Combines the question word 'was' (what) with the verb 'versuchen' (to try). Common in questions like 'Was versucht er/sie zu tun?' The infinitive of the action follows 'zu' (e.g. zu sagen, zu machen, zu verbergen). Subject can change (ich/du/er/sie/wir/ihr). Useful for asking about motive, intention, or attempt.
target_language_example: Was versucht er uns damit zu sagen?
native_language_example: What is he trying to tell us with that?

meaning: a filler phrase meaning 'who knows', 'I don't know', or 'and so on/whatever'.
additional_notes: Used colloquially to indicate uncertainty, to list examples casually (like 'etc.'), or as a shrugging filler at the end of a sentence. Tone can be dismissive or casual. Often spoken; short form sometimes 'weiß ich nicht' or just 'was weiß ich?'.
target_language_example: Komm zum Essen oder ruf an oder was weiß ich.
native_language_example: Come for dinner or call or whatever (who knows).

meaning: what do you want
additional_notes: Usually part of the full question was wollt ihr ...? Wollt is the ihr form of wollen ('to want'), so this is used when speaking to several people. Depending on context, it can ask about what someone wants, plans, or intends to do.
target_language_example: Was wollt ihr heute machen?
native_language_example: What do you want to do today?

meaning: 'what did (you) want' — past-tense question asking about someone's intention
additional_notes: Uses the past tense (Präteritum) of wollen (wolltest for du). Common in questions about intent or purpose: 'What did you want to do/achieve/ say?' Can be followed by infinitive or a clause (e.g. 'damit anstellen', 'da mit ... anfangen', 'mir sagen'). In spoken German, Perfekt (was hast du gewollt) is also possible, but 'was wolltest du...' is very natural.
target_language_example: Was wolltest du damit erreichen?
native_language_example: What did you want to achieve with that?

meaning: 'what did (you) want' — start of a question about someone's past desire or intention
additional_notes: This is the past tense (Imperfekt) question form using 'wolltest' (2nd person singular of 'wollen'). Common in spoken and written German to ask what someone wanted, intended, or planned to do. Often followed by 'du' (you) and can include words like 'da' (there), 'sonst noch' (else/more). Tone can be neutral, surprised, or clarifying depending on context.
target_language_example: Was wolltest du sonst noch fragen?
native_language_example: What else did you want to ask?

meaning: what would (you)
additional_notes: Used to start hypothetical questions (conditional). Usually followed by a subject (du, ihr, er/sie) and an action (tun, machen, etc.). 'Was würdest du tun, wenn ...?' = 'What would you do if ...?'. The verb 'würdest' is the 2nd-person singular conditional (Konjunktiv II) of 'werden' used to form polite or hypothetical 'would' constructions. For other persons the form changes (ich würde, er/sie würde, wir würden).
target_language_example: Was würdest du machen, wenn du im Lotto gewinnen würdest?
native_language_example: What would you do if you won the lottery?

meaning: 'what the hell' / 'what on earth' (strong surprise or annoyance)
additional_notes: Informal and mildly coarse; used to express shock, confusion, disbelief or irritation about something someone said or something you see. Can be used with formal 'Sie', plural 'ihr', or generically. 'Henker' literally means 'executioner', so phrase is stronger than neutral 'was' or 'was zum Teufel' but common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Was zum Henker machst du da?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing there?

meaning: 'what the hell' — an exclamation used to show surprise, anger, confusion, or irritation.
additional_notes: Informal and somewhat strong language (mild profanity). Used to emphasize emotion in questions: asking what is happening, what someone is looking at, or what someone wants. Can be directed politely with formal 'Sie' in examples but remains blunt and rude. Avoid in formal or very polite contexts.
target_language_example: Was zum Teufel machst du da?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing there?

meaning: 'what the hell have (you) ...' — an angry or shocked way to ask what someone did or thought
additional_notes: Informal and strong language: adds emphasis and often expresses surprise, anger, or disbelief. Use with people you know well or in heated situations; avoid in formal contexts. Structure: 'Was zum Teufel hast du ...?' followed by a verb or object.
target_language_example: Was zum Teufel hast du damit gemacht?
native_language_example: What the hell did you do with that?

meaning: Wash that (off) / wash it (imperative, informal).
additional_notes: Informal imperative using 'du' (wash yourself). 'Wasch dir das' often means 'wash that off' or 'wash that (part) of your body' — usually followed by a body part (e.g. 'Gesicht') or understood from context. 'Dir' marks the action is done to oneself. Used in spoken, familiar contexts (parents to children, friends).
target_language_example: Wasch dir das Gesicht mit warmem Wasser und Seife!
native_language_example: Wash your face with warm water and soap!

meaning: I wash (for myself) — reflexive action: 'wash myself' or 'wash [a body part] (for myself)'.
additional_notes: German uses a reflexive dative pronoun (mir, dir, sich) with many body-care verbs: 'Ich wasche mir die Hände' = 'I wash my hands' (literally 'I wash to myself the hands'). The dative reflexive emphasizes that the speaker is doing the action on their own body; English usually drops the dative and uses a possessive ('my'). Use mir for 'ich', dir for 'du', sich for 'er/sie/es/Sie', etc. Common with body parts (Hände, Haare, Gesicht).
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir heute Morgen die Hände.
native_language_example: I wash my hands this morning.

meaning: 'neither French' (part of the correlative pair 'weder ... noch ...' meaning 'neither ... nor ...').
additional_notes: Used with 'weder ... noch ...' to deny two or more possibilities. 'Weder' comes before the first item; the second item follows 'noch'. You can replace 'Französisch' with any language or noun. Word order after 'weder' is normal for the phrase element (typically the language or noun).
target_language_example: Ich spreche weder Französisch noch Deutsch.
native_language_example: I speak neither French nor German.

meaning: neither ... nor ... (used to connect two negatives)
additional_notes: Use to say that two or more options/things do not apply. Often appears in the pattern 'weder X noch Y'. Can negate verbs, nouns, adjectives. Common in both spoken and written German. Word order follows German syntax (e.g., 'weder' before the first element, 'noch' before the second).
target_language_example: Weder Zeit noch Geld habe ich.
native_language_example: I have neither time nor money.

meaning: to be away; to not be present (temporarily or for a period of time)
additional_notes: Common German expression indicating someone or something is not at the location. Used for people, objects, or places and often accompanied by time expressions (eine Weile, den ganzen Tag, wenigstens eine Woche) or location/direction phrases. Can be used in various tenses: Ich bin weg, Ich war weg, Ich werde weg sein.
target_language_example: Ich werde eine Weile weg sein.
native_language_example: I'll be away for a while.

meaning: 'away' or 'gone' combined with 'and' — used when describing someone moving away or being absent, often linking actions or results.
additional_notes: Weg means 'away' or 'gone'. In these examples 'weg und' appears when one clause describes someone leaving or being absent and the next clause connects what happens next (often with implied consequence). It's not a fixed idiom by itself — it's the adverb 'weg' + coordinating conjunction 'und'. Common in spoken and written German. English equivalents: '...away and ...', '...gone and ...', or simply using two sentences ('He ran away, and...').
target_language_example: Sie ging weg und rief später an.
native_language_example: She went away and called later.

meaning: to want to go away; to want to leave
additional_notes: Used to express a desire to leave a place or situation. In German, the modal verb wollen is conjugated and can be placed before an infinitive or, in colloquial usage with separable particles like weg, the particle can appear after the verb or at the end of the clause (e.g., Ich will weg / Ich will jetzt weg). The exact phrase "weg wollen" (infinitive + modal) appears in constructions like "Er scheint weg wollen zu wollen" in more complex sentences, or when listing verbs. Mostly used in spoken and informal registers.
target_language_example: Ich will jetzt weg wollen.
native_language_example: I want to want to leave now.

meaning: for drunk driving; because of being intoxicated while driving.
additional_notes: Legal phrase used to say someone was charged, arrested, or punished for driving under the influence. Often completed as "wegen Trunkenheit am Steuer" (literally: because of intoxication at the wheel). Common verbs with this phrase: verhaften, erwischen, festnehmen, den Führerschein verlieren, angeklagt werden.
target_language_example: Er wurde wegen Trunkenheit am Steuer verhaftet.
native_language_example: He was arrested for drunk driving.

meaning: because of the bad/poor (something); due to the bad/poor ...
additional_notes: Wegen + genitive expresses cause. 'des schlechten' is the start of a genitive phrase ('des' + adjective in nominalized/attributive form) and needs a noun or context to complete it (e.g. 'wegen des schlechten Wetters' = because of the bad weather). In everyday spoken German, 'wegen' is often followed by the dative ('wegen dem schlechten ...'), but in standard written German the genitive is preferred. Make sure to complete the phrase with a noun.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben zu Hause wegen des schlechten Wetters.
native_language_example: We're staying at home because of the bad weather.

meaning: 'to hurt' (physically or emotionally)
additional_notes: Used to say something causes pain or hurts someone. Conjugated with the person receiving the pain as the indirect object: 'jemandem weh tun' = 'to hurt someone'. Can be used in various tenses and moods (e.g. 'wird weh tun', 'würde weh tun'). Common in both physical and emotional contexts. Note spelling: in finite verb forms the parts can be separated ('tut weh'), while in some perfect forms they appear together as 'wehgetan' or 'wehgetan' (colloquial: 'wehgetan' or 'weh getan' historically); the multi-word verb to include here is 'weh tun'.
target_language_example: Das wird jetzt etwas weh tun.
native_language_example: This is going to hurt a little now.

meaning: 'because' + demonstrative 'that' (introduces a clause giving a reason; 'das' refers to something specific mentioned or understood).
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause of reason ('because'). When 'das' follows, it points to a specific thing, situation or fact (that). In English this often appears as 'because that…' or simply 'because…' + a clause: e.g. 'because the weather was nice' = 'weil das Wetter schön war'. In spoken German the 'das' can sometimes be omitted if the thing is clear. Word order: the verb goes to the end of the weil-clause.
target_language_example: Wir bleiben zu Hause, weil das Wetter schlecht ist.
native_language_example: We are staying home because the weather is bad.

meaning: 'because your' — combines the subordinating conjunction 'weil' (because) with the possessive pronoun 'dein' (your).
additional_notes: Weil begins a subordinate clause and sends the conjugated verb to the end of the clause (German word order). 'Dein' matches the gender/case of the noun that follows (e.g. dein Freund, dein Vater, dein Gedächtnis). In speech, word order and intonation may vary, but in writing the verb typically goes to the end: "Weil dein Vater Satan ist."
target_language_example: Weil dein Hund draußen ist, mach die Tür zu.
native_language_example: Because your dog is outside, close the door.

meaning: 'because they / because she / because it (colloquial)' — causal 'because' followed by the feminine/plural definite pronoun 'die' (they/she/those).
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause meaning 'because'. 'die' can refer to feminine singular (she/that woman) or plural (they/those) depending on context and tone. In spoken German, especially colloquial, 'die' is often used to mean 'they' (people or groups) and can sound slightly dismissive. Word order: in a weil-clause the verb goes to the end (e.g. '..., weil die blöd sind'). When the speaker shortens the clause, they may omit the rest and just say 'Weil die!' or 'Weil die abgebrannt ist!' — this is natural in conversation.
target_language_example: Weil die unsere einzige Chance sind, ihn zu besiegen, verstehst du?
native_language_example: Because they are our only chance to beat him, you understand?

meaning: because I (to myself) — 'because I' with a reflexive dative pronoun mir used with certain verbs (e.g., Sorgen machen, etwas ansehen, vorstellen).
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause meaning 'because'. Mir is the dative reflexive pronoun used with verbs that take a dative object (e.g., sich Sorgen machen, sich etwas ansehen, sich vorstellen). In English it's often just translated as 'I' or 'to me' depending on the verb: 'because I am worried' (weil ich mir Sorgen mache), 'because I want to see something' (weil ich mir was ansehen will), 'because I can't imagine' (weil ich mir ... nicht vorstellen will). Word order: verb goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Weil ich mir Sorgen mache, bleibe ich heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: Because I'm worried, I'm staying home today.

meaning: because I know
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause giving a reason; followed by a clause beginning with dass, wer, wie, etc. Word order: verb (weiß) comes at the end of the subordinate clause if additional verbs are present. Common in spoken and written German to explain a reason from the speaker's knowledge.
target_language_example: Weil ich weiß, dass du ehrlich bist, vertraue ich dir.
native_language_example: Because I know that you are honest, I trust you.

meaning: because (to) him
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause meaning "because." ihm is the dative pronoun "him/to him" and often appears with verbs that express feelings, sensations, or states (e.g. schlecht sein, warm werden, das Herz brechen). In natural English you usually translate the whole clause as "because he felt/was/..." or "because it was/.... for him" rather than literally "because to him." Word order: in a weil-clause the verb goes to the end (e.g. „weil ihm schlecht war“ = "because he felt sick").
target_language_example: Er ging nach Hause, weil ihm schlecht war.
native_language_example: He went home because he felt sick.

meaning: "because her" (or "because their" when referring to a female possessor)
additional_notes: Combines the conjunction 'weil' (because) with the possessive pronoun 'ihre' (her/their — feminine or plural depending on context). 'Weil' introduces a subordinate clause and sends the conjugated verb to the end of the clause (e.g., '..., weil ihre Mutter berühmt ist.'). 'Ihre' can mean 'her' (referring to a feminine singular noun) or 'their' (formal 'Ihre' capitalized would be formal 'your'). Pay attention to the gender and number of the noun that follows to know the correct translation.
target_language_example: Ich konnte nicht kommen, weil ihre Schwester krank war.
native_language_example: I couldn't come because her sister was sick.

meaning: 'because my' (introduces a reason that involves something belonging to 'me'—e.g. my car, my brother, my dad).
additional_notes: Weil introduces a subordinate clause giving a reason and sends the verb to the end. 'Mein' is the possessive pronoun 'my' and must match the gender/case of the noun that follows (mein Auto, mein Bruder, mein Dad). In spoken German, clauses starting with 'Weil' can be used alone as short answers (e.g. 'Weil mein Auto kaputt ist.'), but remember the verb placement in full sentences: ... weil mein Auto stehengeblieben ist.
target_language_example: Ich konnte nicht kommen, weil mein Hund krank war.
native_language_example: I couldn't come because my dog was sick.

meaning: 'are you crying?' or an instruction using formal Sie: 'cry' / 'don't cry' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the verb 'weinen' (to cry) used with the formal polite pronoun 'Sie'. In questions it means 'Are you crying?' In commands or requests (imperative) it can appear as 'Weinen Sie ...' meaning 'Please cry ...' or more commonly 'Weinen Sie nicht' = 'Don't cry.' In everyday speech Germans usually use the familiar 'du' with friends/family (»weinst du?« / »weine nicht«).
target_language_example: Warum weinen Sie?
native_language_example: Why are you crying?

meaning: far away; a long way off (in space or time)
additional_notes: Used to describe physical distance (something is physically far from another place) or figurative distance in time/progress (e.g. a solution or goal is still far off). Often followed by a location with von/ vom/ von meinem, or used alone with a comma + clause. Common adjective phrase; can modify places or abstract things.
target_language_example: Die Reparatur ist noch weit entfernt — wir müssen weiter planen.
native_language_example: The repair is still far off — we need to keep planning.

meaning: How far is it from (...)?
additional_notes: Common phrase to ask about distance between two places. Often begins with 'Wie' to form the question 'Wie weit ist es von ... (nach/to) ...?' Use 'von' for the starting point and 'nach' (for cities/countries) or 'zur/zum' (to the coast/station/etc.) for the destination. Can also appear as 'Wie weit ist es von hier?' to ask distance from the speaker's current location.
target_language_example: Wie weit ist es von Berlin nach München?
native_language_example: How far is it from Berlin to Munich?

meaning: far away; a long distance away.
