In spoken German you may also hear 'zwei davon' with the same meaning. Word order: 'zwei von' + object/pronoun.
target_language_example: Ich nehme zwei von den Keksen.
native_language_example: I'll take two of the cookies.

meaning: on the second day / for a second day
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs or time expressions to say that something happens or continues on the second day. Word order may vary: 'am zweiten Tag' = 'on the second day'; without article it can appear in phrases like 'zweiten Tag in Folge' (for the second day in a row). Remember to match case/gender when used in sentences (e.g. 'am zweiten Tag' uses dative).
target_language_example: Wir bleiben am zweiten Tag noch in der Stadt.
native_language_example: We will stay in the city on the second day.

meaning: the Second World War (World War II).
additional_notes: A historical term referring to the global conflict from 1939–1945. In German it is normally capitalized as a proper noun: Zweiter Weltkrieg or der Zweite Weltkrieg; lowercase 'zweiter Weltkrieg' may appear in running text but capitalization follows German orthography rules. Commonly used in phrases like 'im Zweiten Weltkrieg' (during WWII) or 'nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg' (after WWII).
target_language_example: Viele Städte wurden während des zweiten Weltkriegs zerstört.
native_language_example: Many cities were destroyed during the Second World War.

meaning: to read between the lines; to understand the hidden or implied meaning.
additional_notes: Used when someone perceives unstated intentions, emotions, or messages beyond the literal words. Commonly used in conversation and advice (e.g., 'you should read between the lines'). Not literal—it's an idiom.
target_language_example: Du solltest besser zwischen den Zeilen lesen, dann verstehst du, was er wirklich meint.
native_language_example: You should read between the lines, then you'll understand what he really means.

meaning: between (feminine noun in dative case).
additional_notes: Use 'zwischen' with two things/location/time points. The article changes with the gender and case of the following noun; 'der' here is the dative feminine article (e.g. zwischen der Schule, zwischen der Bank). For masculine/neuter dative you'd use 'dem' (zwischen dem Mann), and for plural 'den' (zwischen den Häusern).
target_language_example: Die Katze liegt zwischen der Couch und dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The cat is lying between the couch and the table.

meaning: between you (singular, informal) or among you
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that is located or happening between or among the person you're speaking to (du). Often appears in phrases like "zwischen dir und mir" (between you and me) or "zwischen dir" as part of a larger clause (e.g. "Das bleibt zwischen dir und mir"). Use with familiar/informal address (du).
target_language_example: Das bleibt zwischen dir und mir.
native_language_example: That stays between you and me.

meaning: between a / between one (masculine or neuter singular in dative)
additional_notes: Used to indicate a distinction or position between two items; 'zwischen' requires the dative case. 'einem' is the dative singular of 'ein' for masculine and neuter nouns. If the noun is feminine, use 'zwischen einer'. Common in phrases like 'der Unterschied zwischen einem X und einem Y' (the difference between an X and a Y).
target_language_example: Der Unterschied zwischen einem Auto und einem Fahrrad ist die Motorisierung.
native_language_example: The difference between a car and a bicycle is the motorization.

meaning: between me / among me (used when 'zwischen' governs the dative pronoun 'mir'; often appears as part of a larger phrase like 'zwischen mir und ...')
additional_notes: Literally 'between me'. 'Zwischen' can take dative or accusative; with pronouns when indicating position or relation it commonly uses the dative 'mir'. The standalone fragment 'zwischen mir' is uncommon and usually occurs embedded in a longer expression (e.g. 'zwischen mir und dir'). Use full phrases in practice. Not idiomatic by itself.
target_language_example: Das bleibt ausschließlich zwischen mir und den anderen Kollegen.
native_language_example: That remains exclusively between me and the other colleagues.

meaning: to count on; to rely on (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing in the dative (auf + accusative: auf dich, auf ihn, auf eure Hilfe). Common in contexts of trust, expectation, or dependence: 'Ich zähle auf dich' = 'I am relying on you.' Informal/neutral tone.
target_language_example: Ich zähle auf deine Unterstützung bei dem Projekt.
native_language_example: I am counting on your support for the project.

meaning: I'll count to three (used to warn someone to do something or to signal an imminent action).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a brief warning: the speaker will count to three and then carry out an action if the listener doesn't comply (e.g., punishment, starting something, or prompting children to prepare). Can be literal (actually counting) or formulaic. Tone can be playful, strict, or urgent depending on context.
target_language_example: Mach dich fertig, ich zähle bis drei.
native_language_example: Get ready, I'll count to three.

meaning: to do with the public sphere / relating to public attention (often appears as part of larger phrases indicating moving something into or toward public awareness)
additional_notes: 'Öffentlichkeit zu' on its own is not a complete verbal phrase in German; it typically appears within larger constructions (e.g. 'in die Öffentlichkeit zu bringen', 'an die Öffentlichkeit zu gelangen'). Shown here to illustrate the multi-word sequence; learners should pair it with appropriate verbs and prepositions. Context determines precise translation (make public, reach the public, to the public).
target_language_example: Der Artikel muss jetzt an die Öffentlichkeit zu gelangen versucht werden.
native_language_example: The article must now be attempted to be brought to the public.

meaning: a surprise for (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you have a surprise intended for a person. Followed by a pronoun or name (für dich, für Sie, für ihn, etc.). Formal: 'für Sie' (capitalized Sie). Informal: 'für dich'. Common in gifts, parties, or pleasant announcements.
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Überraschung für dich.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

meaning: older than I (thought/expected).
additional_notes: This phrase is used to compare someone's age to the speaker's expectation. It commonly appears in sentences like "älter, als ich dachte" (older than I thought) or "älter, als ich gedacht hatte" (older than I had thought). In German comparisons with verbs of thinking/expectation use a comma before "als". You can replace "ich" with another subject (z. B. "als du" = than you).
target_language_example: Er ist älter, als ich dachte.
native_language_example: He is older than I thought.

meaning: public opinion
additional_notes: Refers to the general views or attitudes held by the public/community about a topic, policy or person. Used in discussions about politics, society or media. Often appears with verbs like sich wenden (to turn), sein gegen (to be against), berücksichtigen (to take into account).
target_language_example: Die öffentliche Meinung hat sich nach den Ereignissen verändert.
native_language_example: Public opinion changed after the events.

meaning: public means of transport; public transport vehicle (e.g., bus, train, tram).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any transport service available to the public (öffentlicher Verkehr) or a specific vehicle (ein öffentliches Verkehrsmittel). Common in contexts about travel, tickets, schedules, and rules (e.g., masks, tickets, peak hours). Plural: öffentliche Verkehrsmittel. Formal/neutral term.
target_language_example: Ich habe das öffentliche Verkehrsmittel verpasst und musste ein Taxi nehmen.
native_language_example: I missed the public transport vehicle and had to take a taxi.

meaning: 'about women' (talking about the topic of women)
additional_notes: Über + accusative topic = 'about' or 'concerning'. Used when asking or stating opinions, knowledge, or conversation topics. Can be used in questions (Sprecht ihr über Frauen?) or statements (Du musst noch einiges über Frauen lernen.). Neutral phrase; tone depends on context.
target_language_example: Was weißt du über Frauen?
native_language_example: What do you know about women?

meaning: 'about money' or 'on the topic of money'.
additional_notes: Combines the preposition 'über' (about/concerning) with the noun 'Geld' (money). Used to indicate the subject of conversation or thought. Common in questions, statements, and commands (e.g., asking whether people talked about money, telling someone to stop arguing about money). Word order follows normal German rules: 'über Geld' usually appears after verbs like 'reden', 'sprechen', 'streiten' or after prepositions.
target_language_example: Wir sollten nicht ständig über Geld sprechen.
native_language_example: We shouldn't keep talking about money.

meaning: about music; concerning music
additional_notes: Über + noun means 'about' or 'concerning' and is followed by the accusative case (hier: Musik — feminine, unchanged). Commonly used with verbs like reden, sprechen, diskutieren. Can introduce a topic for conversation or inquiry.
target_language_example: Wir sprechen morgen über Musik.
native_language_example: We are talking about music tomorrow.

meaning: 'overnight' — during the night; suddenly/in a very short time (figurative).
additional_notes: Used both literally (happening during the night) and figuratively (happening very quickly or suddenly). Context shows: temporal use (during the night), permission to stay overnight, describing something consumed that night, and figurative use for rapid change (became famous overnight).
target_language_example: Er ist nicht über Nacht reich geworden.
native_language_example: He didn't become rich overnight.

meaning: about everything; about everything/every topic.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is discussed or argued concerning all topics or many different things. Common in phrases like "über alles streiten" (to argue about everything) or "über alles geredet" (talked about everything). Not the same as the historical phrase "Deutschland über alles"; here it simply means 'about everything'.
target_language_example: Wir haben gestern Abend über alles geredet.
native_language_example: We talked about everything last night.

meaning: about your / about your (masculine/neuter singular informal 'du' form).
additional_notes: Über means 'about' or 'concerning'. Dein is the possessive for 'du' (your). Use 'über dein' before a masculine or neuter noun in nominative/accusative (e.g., dein Land, dein Leben, dein Verhalten). For feminine nouns use 'deine' (z. B. über deine Mutter). In spoken German speakers may also use 'über dich' ('about you') when referring to the person rather than something of theirs.
target_language_example: Schreib etwas über dein neues Zimmer.
native_language_example: Write something about your new room.

meaning: past the worst; recovered (idiomatic) / over the hill/by the mountain (literal)
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning someone has passed the worst phase (e.g., of an illness or a difficult situation). Can also be used literally to mean 'over the mountain' or 'across the hill' (e.g., travel, sun rising). Context determines whether it's idiomatic or literal. Informal but widely used in spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Nach der Operation ist sie jetzt über den Berg.
native_language_example: After the operation she is now past the worst.

meaning: toward/over to the river (implies movement in the direction of the river)
additional_notes: A short phrase indicating motion toward or across a river. Grammatically, über + accusative (den Fluss) shows movement over/above or across something. Context decides if it means 'to the other side of the river', 'over the river', or simply 'toward the river'. You will commonly see similar constructions with other places: über die Brücke zu (toward/across the bridge).
target_language_example: Wir gehen über den Fluss zu dem Markt.
native_language_example: We are going over to the river to the market.

meaning: to get by / to make ends meet (manage financially or cope)
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when someone manages to survive financially or cope with a difficult situation, often with limited means. Commonly used in present tense (ich komme über die Runden), past (kam über die Runden) and with modal verbs. Not literal—doesn't mean 'over the rounds'.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wie wir diesen Monat über die Runden kommen sollen.
native_language_example: I don't know how we'll get by this month.

meaning: to get by / to make ends meet (manage financially or survive on limited means).
additional_notes: Used when someone struggles financially or just manages to cover basic needs. Often appears as 'über die Runden kommen' (to get by) and commonly followed by verbs like 'kommen' or 'schaffen'. Not about thriving — about barely managing. Can refer to money, work, or general difficult circumstances.
target_language_example: Ich habe einen zweiten Job angenommen, um über die Runden zu kommen.
native_language_example: I took a second job to make ends meet.

meaning: more than three (used with time periods: hours, months, years).
additional_notes: Used before a time unit (Stunden, Monate, Jahre) to mean 'over/for more than three [units]'. Often appears with verbs like brauchen, warten, kennen (since) and with seit to indicate duration. Word order: 'über drei Stunden', 'seit über drei Jahren'.
target_language_example: Ich habe über drei Stunden auf den Bus gewartet.
native_language_example: I waited for the bus for over three hours.

meaning: more than (a) / over (a).
additional_notes: Used with feminine or dative feminine/masculine/neuter nouns in certain time/quantity expressions to mean 'more than' or 'over' a specified amount (often time durations or quantities). Typical constructions: 'über einer Stunde' (over an hour), 'über einer Million' (over a million). Word order and case depend on the noun and preposition; here 'einer' is the feminine/ dative/ genitive form used in these fixed expressions.
target_language_example: Wir haben sie vor über einer halben Stunde aus den Augen verloren.
native_language_example: We lost sight of them over half an hour ago.

meaning: to make fun of me / to mock me
additional_notes: A common reflexive expression used to say that someone is mocking or ridiculing the speaker. The full verb form is 'sich über jemanden lustig machen'. In sentences the reflexive pronoun changes with person (dich, sich, euch). Often used with an angry or offended tone: 'Hör auf, dich über mich lustig zu machen!'
target_language_example: Hör auf, dich über mich lustig zu machen!
native_language_example: Stop making fun of me!

meaning: about nothing; concerning nothing / not about anything
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not the topic or cause (e.g., 'talking about nothing' or 'have no reason to complain'). Context determines whether it means 'about nothing' (topic) or 'about nothing' as in 'nothing to (verb)'. Often appears in longer phrases (e.g. ‚über nichts anderes‘ = 'about nothing else'). Can be used alone as a short answer: 'Über nichts.' = 'Nothing.'
target_language_example: Wir reden gerade über nichts Wichtiges.
native_language_example: We're talking about nothing important.

meaning: about; concerning (used informally to introduce a topic or comment)
additional_notes: A casual colloquial combination: 'über' (about) + 'so' (so/like). Often used in spoken German to start a remark about something, similar to English 'about' or 'so, about...'. It can soften or introduce a topic (e.g. 'Über so etwas...' = 'About something like that...'). Not a fixed idiomatic phrase on its own; usage depends on context and is more common in conversation.
target_language_example: Über so etwas sollte man vorher nachdenken.
native_language_example: You should think about something like that beforehand.

meaning: 'about our' or 'about our (something)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the preposition 'über' (about, concerning) plus the possessive 'unser' (our). It introduces a topic that belongs to 'us' (our country, our offer, our problem, etc.). The noun that follows will determine case: with 'über' use the accusative (e.g., über unser Angebot → unser Angebot is accusative). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Können wir morgen über unser Projekt sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk about our project tomorrow?

meaning: 'all over' or 'everywhere on' (used to say something is located or happening across the surface/area of something)
additional_notes: Überall means 'everywhere' or 'all over'. When followed by auf + noun, it describes something distributed across the surface or area of that noun (e.g., ‚überall auf dem Tisch‘ = 'all over the table'). Word order: ‚überall auf + [dem/die/das + noun]‘ or in spoken/less formal German you may also see ‚auf... überall‘. Choose the correct article/case after auf (usually dative for location: auf dem/der).
target_language_example: Die Blätter liegen überall auf dem Boden.
native_language_example: The leaves are all over the ground.

meaning: everywhere on the (feminine dative or genitive context)
additional_notes: Überall = everywhere. Auf der is the preposition 'on' with the definite article in the dative (or sometimes genitive) feminine singular. Use when referring to something spread or located across the surface or area of a feminine noun: e.g. überall auf der Straße (everywhere on the street) or überall auf der Verpackung (all over the packaging). Word order: überall auf der + [feminine noun].
target_language_example: Überall auf der Straße lagen Blätter.
native_language_example: Leaves were everywhere on the street.

meaning: everywhere with (someone/something); indicates that someone or something accompanies or is taken along to many/all places
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or thing goes along or is carried to many places. Often appears with a pronoun or noun that is the companion (mit mir, mit dem Fahrrad, mit dir). Word order may vary (e.g., "geht überall mit mir hin" or "nimmt mich überall mit"). "Überall" = everywhere; "mit" = with. Not idiomatic or slang.
target_language_example: Ich nehme meinen Laptop überall mit.
native_language_example: I take my laptop everywhere with me.

meaning: used to express surprise, confusion, or annoyance about someone being here — 'here at all' / 'doing this here'.
additional_notes: Often follows question words (Was/Wieso/Warum) to emphasize that the speaker finds the person's presence inappropriate, unexpected, or unclear. Tone can be neutral curiosity or rude/annoyed depending on context and intonation. Can be used with both du and Sie forms.
target_language_example: Was machst du überhaupt hier?
native_language_example: What are you even doing here?

meaning: 'not ... at all' or 'no ... whatsoever' (used to emphasize a complete absence)
additional_notes: Used before a noun (with appropriate gender/case ending: kein/keine/kein/keine) to stress that something does not exist or is completely absent. Often appears in spoken German for strong negation. Can combine with verbs (e.g., überhaupt kein Interesse haben) or with objects (überhaupt kein Geld). In questions it can express surprise that something hasn't ended or isn't happening at all.
target_language_example: Ich habe überhaupt kein Problem damit.
native_language_example: I have no problem with that at all.

meaning: not at all
additional_notes: Used to strongly negate a verb, adjective, or entire statement. Common in spoken and written German. Can intensify 'nicht' and is often placed before the word or phrase being negated (e.g., before an adjective or after the verb).
target_language_example: Das hat mir überhaupt nicht gefallen.
native_language_example: I didn't like that at all.

meaning: absolutely nothing; not ... at all
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the absence of anything or any action. Often appears with verbs like tun (to do) or haben (to have): "mit jemandem überhaupt nichts zu tun haben" = to have absolutely nothing to do with someone. Stronger than just "nichts".
target_language_example: Ich weiß darüber überhaupt nichts.
native_language_example: I know absolutely nothing about that.

meaning: at all (in combination with a verb: 'to ... at all' or 'to even ...').
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or verb to emphasize whether something happens at all or even happens. Common in questions and negatives: e.g. 'hörst du mir überhaupt zu?' = 'are you even / at all listening to me?'. In sentences like 'ohne sich überhaupt zu verabschieden' it means 'without even (doing) ...'. Place 'überhaupt' before 'zu' + infinitive.
target_language_example: Hörst du mir überhaupt zu?
native_language_example: Are you even listening to me?

meaning: 'I leave (that) to (you/them)'; I let someone else decide or handle something.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that the speaker is handing responsibility, choice, or imagination over to someone else. Commonly followed by a dative object (dir, Ihnen, euch) or a phrase like 'ihrer/deiner Phantasie'. Polite/formal uses use 'Ihnen'; informal uses 'dir' or 'euch'.
target_language_example: Das überlasse ich dir — du weißt besser Bescheid.
native_language_example: I'll leave that to you — you know better.

meaning: surprised like / as (surprised as someone else).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone had the same (oder similar) level of surprise as another person. Common connectors: ebenso (equally), so/fast so (so / almost as). Often appears as 'ebenfalls überrascht wie', 'so überrascht wie' or 'fast so überrascht wie'. Word order: compare two subjects (Ich war ebenso überrascht wie du).
target_language_example: Ich war fast so überrascht wie Anna.
native_language_example: I was almost as surprised as Anna.

meaning: to cheat or swindle someone (to rip someone off).
additional_notes: Colloquial idiom meaning to deceive someone, usually to take their money or advantage of them. Often used in warnings or questions. Literal words 'over the ear hit' don't convey the idiomatic meaning. Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Lass dich nicht übers Ohr hauen — prüf den Vertrag genau.
native_language_example: Don't let them rip you off — check the contract carefully.
